en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Introduction to the Commentary on the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* (The Dispeller of Doubts).

This undertaking is for the purpose of clarifying the obscure passages of that excellent *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā* composed by the Venerable Buddhaghosa, which was proclaimed with the words "The Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha," and so forth.
Commentary on the Introduction to the Book:
"Vippasannena" means with various forms of serene confidence. How [is this shown]? By such passages as: "Thus indeed is he... the Buddha, the Blessed One;
well-expounded... by the wise; practiced well... for the world," and so forth. Because of the word "cetasā" (with the mind), among the three types of homage—
Mental homage is intended here. Homage (*vandana*) is the act of bowing with the body and so forth by means of being inclined toward [the object] and so on;

honor (*māna*) is performing that same act even with the mind by way of its qualities; worship (*pūjā*) is the performance of honoring through the offering of requisites, proper conduct, and so forth;
and respect (*sakkāra*) is the careful preparation of those requisites and so forth. "Vessel" (*bhājana*) means a support or a locus for these.

The elders such as Mahākassapa and others; their lineage is the *theravaṃsa* (lineage of elders). Those who have become like lamps for that lineage through the perfection of both scripture (*āgama*) and realization (*adhigama*) are the "lamps of the lineage of elders" (*theravaṃsappadīpa*);

[the phrase refers to] those lamps of the lineage of elders. Because they cannot be shaken, they are "steadfast" (*thira*). "In the discipline (*vinaya*) and its procedure" means in the *Vinayapiṭaka*;
this expression is used because it is appropriate to begin with that. They were steadfast even in the *Sutta* and *Abhidhamma*.

Thus it is. If one asks why [the teachers] are mentioned separately, rather than saying "to the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha, and the lions who were former teachers," it is for the purpose of showing a specific purpose.

For the purpose of paying homage to the Triple Gem is the removal of obstacles, whereas the purpose of paying homage to one's own teachers, who are one's support, is the demonstration of gratitude for their assistance.

The construction is as follows: having paid homage to the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha; and by the word "and" (ca), one should understand that he also offered salutation to the lions among the ancient teachers.
Alternatively, it should be construed thus: by the phrase "having paid homage" (vanditvā), mental homage is shown; then, by "having made salutation" (namo katvā), verbal homage is shown;
and by "with palms joined" (katañjalī), bodily homage is also shown.
Now, in order to show the purpose of the designation, he said, "The foremost," and so forth. Therein, "the foremost" (*pāmokkha*) means the principal.
For virtue (*sīla*) is the principal among all wholesome states (*kusala-dhamma*) because it is their beginning.

And just as the fourfold food of sentient beings—consisting of what is chewed, swallowed, licked, and drunk—enters through the mouth and pervades every limb, so too does the fourfold [meditative] plane for the practitioner.
Having entered by way of wholesome virtue (*kusala-sīla*), one accomplishes the attainment of the goal. Therefore it is said: "the entrance," and so forth.
Alternatively, "entrance" (*mukha*) means a means (*upāya*); thus the meaning is that it is the entrance, the means, for entering liberation—that is, for the realization of Nibbāna.
The connection is: "that *pātimokkha* which was proclaimed by the Great Seer (*mahesi*). He is called the Great Seer because he seeks (*esi*) the great aggregates of virtue and the rest.

“By means of gentleness (*sūrata*) and by being sheltered (*nivāta*”: [this refers to] gentleness as defined by such passages as, “In this context, what is gentleness? It is bodily non-transgression,” and so forth;

and by being sheltered through humble conduct, in the sense of not elevating oneself due to pride or arrogance. [It is] “endowed with the conduct of the Vinaya” means endowed with right conduct (*cāritta*) and right observance (*vāritta*).

Why was it stated as “by means of gentleness” and so forth, instead of saying “requested by the Elder Soṇa”?)* *Note: The text provided contains a parenthetical commentary explaining the terms and the rationale for the phrasing.*
If it is asked: "Is it not improper to offer praise when requested by one who is immoral, corrupt, or shameless?"—it is not improper.
It is impossible to reject the word of an Elder; rather, this was said to show that even an Elder of such qualities must be treated with respect when approached through a request.
"By name" means by the name of its own qualities. It is beautiful because of the beauty of the characteristics of the words, the beauty of the analysis, and the beauty of what is to be understood.
The commentary on the introduction to the book is finished.
The commentary on the nidāna.

Having said, “For it is comfortable for him when [an offense] is disclosed; therefore, I ask the venerable ones... [as before] ... since you are silent, I shall so hold it,” he spoke according to the method beginning with, “Venerable ones, the Nidāna has been recited.

It is at this very point, at the conclusion of the third proclamation, that at the time of the recitation, having said, “For it is comfortable for him when [an offense] is disclosed,” he says, “Venerable ones, the Nidāna has been recited.”
It has come down in the manner beginning with, "In this matter, I ask the Venerable Ones. It has also come down in exactly the same way in the Uposatha Khandhaka.
In that case, what was stated previously contradicts the sutta that appears later. Therefore, one should accept it after investigating how there is no contradiction.
Some say, "It is not thus contradictory. How so? For it is said: 'When he has revealed [his offense], he is at ease.'"

Having said, “It is so,” [the statement] “Venerable sirs, the introduction has been recited. Regarding this, I ask the venerable ones,” and so forth, constitutes the characteristic of a well-recited [introduction], because it is stated here as well as in the Khandhaka.

Therefore, after saying “It is comfortable,” even that which was not explicitly stated at the point where it says “Regarding this, I ask the venerable ones” should be brought in and included. Why? Because here...
The introduction (nidāna) has not been shown here, because at the time of the recitation (uddesa), the characteristic of what is to be recited was already stated therein.

Furthermore, even one wishing to show the "recitation of the introduction" by extracting the phrase "nidānuddeso," does so after concluding the introduction as it occurs in the text—"Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs...
for when it has been confessed, there is ease"—and then proceeds according to the commentary (aṭṭhakathā) above that.
Having applied the canonical text here, and having completed the introductory narrative (nidānapāḷi) with the words,

“In this matter, I ask the Venerable Ones... [and so on] ...I bear it in mind,” he then says, “Thus I bear it in mind,” and states, “Venerable ones, the introduction has been recited,” and so forth, in order to show briefly, by way of the extracted phrases, the characteristic of the summary of the introduction (nidānuddesalakkhaṇa).

Therefore, in this way, both above and in the Khandhaka, at the time of recitation, after stating, "For it is comfortable for him when [the offense] has been disclosed," only the recitation of the introduction (*nidāna*) is shown, beginning with, "Venerable sirs, the introduction has been recited. Regarding that, I ask the Venerable Ones," and so forth;
it is not the introduction itself.
Regarding the phrase "the statement of the instruction for recitation": if it is argued that it is improper for either the senior or the junior member of the Saṅgha to speak here, we reply:
it is indeed proper. Because the Blessed One stated, "It should be spoken thus by the Pātimokkha-reciter," this is the Blessed One’s own injunction, not that of the reciter.
Here, however, it is stated according to the junior member; yet, in order to show that even a senior elder is permitted to recite, it says, "the Pātimokkha with the elders at its head."
It has been stated. If it is argued that by this Sutta a junior [monk] does not receive [the full ordination], in order to show that, it was said: "Whichever monks there...

and so forth. Just as, having set aside the full ordination, the invitation (pavāraṇā), and the rehabilitation (abbhāna), it is permissible to perform all other Saṅgha-kamma with a quorum of four, so too—without stating "this specific kamma must be performed with a quorum of more than twenty"—because of the use of the word "more than" (atireka).
It indicates another meaning: what is that? It is the phrase beginning with "by a group of four, etc. For that [meaning] is established by those very words. How so?
"Full ordination and the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) are performed by a group of four... nothing whatsoever among the formal acts of the Saṅgha is not permitted to be done by a group of twenty.
Here, by saying "except for the mere act of rehabilitation (abbhāna) by a group of ten," it is implied that even those acts which are to be performed by groups of four or five are included.
[The formal acts] were authorized to be performed by a group of ten. Therefore, it is indicated that they are permissible with more than [ten];
by the word "excepting," it is likewise indicated that they are not permissible with fewer. If you say, "Therefore, one should not say 'a group of more than twenty,'" one must indeed say so.
That which is to be performed by a group of four or five may be performed by a group of six, seven, eight, or nine; and that which is to be performed by a group of ten...
It is shown that [the procedure] must be performed by a group of eleven, twelve... [and so on] up to nineteen.

It is shown explicitly that it is not permissible with fewer than that. However, the Elder Vajirabuddhi has written that it is shown to apply in every way, even when the groups of more than twenty or exactly twenty are mentioned.
From this point onward, whenever "written" is mentioned, it should be understood as being by the Elder Vajirabuddhi.
If it were permissible on days other than the Uposatha, one would not have said, "one should perform the Uposatha";
because it is not permissible to do so on non-Uposatha days, therefore, after saying "today is the Uposatha," it is further stated, "one should perform the Uposatha.
The restriction "only on the full moon of the latter Kattika" is made because there is no day for the Pavāraṇā ceremony or others beyond that. Above this, it is the regular Uposatha.

If it is argued that this [case] should not be stated as "linking sign with sign" along with the aforementioned natural conduct (*pakaticārita*), because it was already stated as "endowed with the threefold perfection" (*tividhasampattiyuttā*)—then it must indeed be so stated. Why?

Because the so-called "threefold perfection" consists of the perfection of the sign (*nimittasampatti*), the perfection of the assembly (*parisāsampatti*), the perfection of the formal act (*kammavācāsampatti*), and so forth.
Having stated, "What is called 'perfection of signs' refers to the sign of a mountain, the sign of a rock," and so forth, it was not said that a sign is connected to a sign.

Furthermore, after showing [the phrase] "endowed with the threefold perfection" among the factors of conjunction (*sampayoga*), it was stated, "having connected sign with sign," in order to show that very same thing again among the factors of abandonment (*pahāna*). [This applies to] rivers, oceans, and lakes.
If one asks: "Why are they called 'boundary-failures' (*vipatti-sīmā*) when formal acts (*kamma*) do not fail within a *sammuti*-boundary or a *udakukkhepa*-boundary?
It is because, after establishing the other characteristics and binding a boundary over a river, the water limit has been made the boundary;
yet, if that same river is subsequently included within it and a pond is constructed, and if one were to perform a formal act within that [new] boundary...

It would be permissible; the formal acts (kamma) within the boundary would not fail. However, since it is not permissible to act in this way, the statement "because of the water-throwing boundary" is irrelevant.
Because the Sangha’s formal act requires a quorum of twenty, twenty-one bhikkhus must sit together with the one who is subject to the act.
"It is not possible," it is said; the intention is that they sit by way of a comfortable posture.
"To sit in a circular form" is what is stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. "Having exceeded three *yojanas*" means, standing in the middle and calculating from there, three *yojanas*.
For from corner to corner it exceeds three *yojanas*, and [the monk] incurs an offense, and the boundary (*sīmā*) [is established].

It is not a boundary. "Having proclaimed" means: having proclaimed even the well-established signs by exchanging their respective names with one another, and also by the names of signless objects; this is the meaning.
Even when sand is heaped up among trees that have grown there, it becomes a mountain of pure sand. It is the size of a lump of sugar because of its thickness.
"Not by weighing or counting" excludes planting [the seed] in things such as baskets or bowls;
however, having removed it from there, even planting it in the ground at that very moment is permissible.

But the emergence of new roots and branches is not a valid reason [for it to be considered planted]. This [rule], however, applies to what has been planted after cutting the trunk. "The size of a needle-shaft" means the measure of the little finger.
By the phrase “eight finger-breadths high,” the height is defined; by the phrase “the size of a cow’s horn,” the circumference is defined.
Even so, they say that although there is no fixed limit to the circumference of a cow’s horn, both small and large [sizes] are permissible.
Having seen only full water in a natural pond as the sign, one should not take [water] that is incomplete and situated in between.
Regarding the statement, “approved as a natural lake (*jātassara*),” it means one does not incur a failure [of the boundary].
In the passage, “approved as a river, approved as the ocean, approved as a natural lake,” salt water is not included here either.

In the passage, “without crossing a fixed boundary or a river, an ocean, or a natural lake,” and also in the passage, “or in a river, monks, or in the ocean, or in a natural lake,” [salt water is likewise excluded].
[They] are not included. Therefore, if it is argued that a salt-pit (*loṇī*) is not a "bound boundary" (*abaddhasīmā*), [the answer is: it is indeed an unbound boundary. Because it is stated:
"Even a pool formed by water that has emerged after breaking through a river or the ocean reaches this definition;

this too is simply a 'naturally occurring lake' (*jātassara*)," it is included under the term "naturally occurring lake," and thus it is not mentioned separately in various places. "As far as [the extent] within that village precinct..."

Because it has been so stated, when another village is included within the boundary for the delimitation of the common-observance zone (*samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā*), it is permissible whether or not monks come to that village at the time of the delimitation.
However, at the time of the delimitation of the non-separation zone (*avippavāsa-sīmā*), they must certainly come.

Regarding the phrase "on paths where one cannot go," they say this refers to a place where it is impossible to go and return in a single day; the meaning is that it excludes the status of a delimited boundary (*baddha-sīmā*).
If it is argued that because it is stated, “on all sides within the range of a water-splash,” it must be taken from every direction—no;
it should be taken from wherever it is available, because it is stated: “The area where natural waves roll in and settle is the *kappiya-bhūmi* (permissible ground) starting from that point;
standing there, it is allowable to perform the Uposatha and other rites. *Anvaḍḍhamāsaṃ* means “every half-month”; it is a compound of *anu* (following) and *aḍḍhamāso*.
Or within half a month. The intention is that it is "not made" even if it has been dug by anyone, down to an animal.
Because it is stated, "Even if it stands not exceeding another boundary of exactly that same size, it destroys the kamma," it is thereby indicated that what stands beyond [that] does not destroy it;
thus says the Elder Upatissa. However, regarding those two water-sprinklings...
This contradicts the statement: "Another single water-splash should be established within [the boundary] for the sake of the precinct.
For in the *Samantapāsādikā*, the phrase "another of exactly that same size" does not exist. Therefore, its intended meaning must be sought.
The meaning should be understood as: "without transgressing the demarcation of the water-splash established for the sake of the precinct of the internal water-splash boundary."—[said by] the Elder.
It was written after further elaboration.

If it is argued that it is permissible to report a *saṅghādisesa* offense that is similar [to the one being concealed] because it is stated that "an offense similar [to the one concealed] is a light offense," we say:
it is not permissible, because what is stated here refers specifically to an offense that leads to confession (*desanāgāminī*). Therefore, in the *Samuccayakkhandhaka*:
"However, it is not permitted to disclose [an offense] in the presence of one who has committed a *saṅghādisesa* of the same class.
If one does disclose it, the offense is indeed disclosed, yet one is not released from the *dukkaṭa* [offense].

It is said that just as the Saṅgha is permitted to perform the *uposatha* after saying, "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me... [he] will make amends," so too may it be done by three or even two [monks].
Having seen another who is pure, it is permissible to perform the Uposatha after saying, "We shall make amends.
It is also permissible for even a single person to perform the Uposatha after forming the intention, "Having obtained one who is pure, I shall make amends.

In the *Aṭṭhakathā* as well, regarding the phrase "the neighboring monk should be addressed thus," only one of the same class (*sabhāga*) should be mentioned; for [addressing] one of a different class (*visabhāga*)—
It is stated in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā: "When [the offense] is being spoken of, quarrels, disputes, schisms in the Saṅgha, and so forth may arise;
therefore, without mentioning that [offense], one should perform the Uposatha after making the resolve: 'Having emerged from this [state], I will make amends.
Since this has not been rejected, it is shown that it is permissible. [This applies when] another pure monk who is free from offenses...
Because it was said, "When he passes away, [he will be reborn] in his presence," and because only a light offense was permitted, and because it was stated in the *Samuccayakkhandhaka*,
it is not permissible to perform the Uposatha after having announced a formal motion (*ñatti*) regarding a *saṅghādisesa* offense of the same class. However,

the term "one for whom ordination is refused" (*yassa upasampadā paṭikkhittā*) was stated in order to show that even those not included by any other term— such as Deva-Brahmas, excluding the category of "animal" (*tiracchānagata*)— are nevertheless included by this one.

However, instead of saying, "In the presence of those who have invited [others] at the end of the four-month period, whether one has not entered [the rains residence], or whose rains residence was interrupted, or who has completed the rains residence," it is stated only as:
"whether one has not entered [the rains residence], or whose rains residence was interrupted.

For one who has completed the rains residence is reckoned as "one who has not entered" at that time because they did not enter [the rains residence] during that period. When all [the invitation] has been concluded, all...

They say that once they have emerged [from retreat] and departed, it is not possible to assemble them; however, it is permissible to assemble some of them and announce their purity (*pārisuddhi*). Why?
Because there is no formal act of the Saṅgha (*saṅghakamma*) to be performed after a motion (*ñatti*) has been established, and thus it does not constitute an incomplete assembly (*vagga*).

This same principle applies to the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) as well. Herein, however, is the distinction: if those who arrived during the earlier period [of the rains] [are present] during the later period...
They have arrived in smaller numbers and are equal [in number], and they fulfill the quorum for a Saṅgha invitation;
thus, a motion (*ñatti*) must be established by way of a Saṅgha invitation. Because it is stated, "There is only one monk... [etc.
...having known the absence of others," they say that it is not possible to perform the Uposatha by means of a formal resolution (*adhiṭṭhāna*) after entering the boundary (*sīmā*).
“‘What is the prior duty of the Saṅgha?’—this should not be stated after having laid down a formal motion (*ñatti*). For that is performed even before the motion.
Therefore, one might think it should be stated thus: ‘Let the venerable Saṅgha listen to me; what is the prior duty of the Saṅgha, if it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha?
Even so, it should not be stated. For that is not included within the scope of the formal motion.”
If it is argued that, this being the case, it follows that this [statement] should not be made because there is no purpose, we say:
No, for it must be stated precisely where it was introduced; what is meant is that it is dependent upon the preceding words.

A Saṅgha or an individual who performs the Uposatha ceremony without having performed this preliminary duty incurs an offense upon exceeding the boundary of the "field of suspension. For when that field has been exceeded—

In the case of performing the sweeping and other duties, there is no release from the offense because that offense is conditioned by the non-performance of a duty that ought to have been performed prior to the Uposatha ceremony.
It does not depend on the conclusion of the formal act (*kamma*), unlike the offense of deliberate lying regarding one’s arrival at the assembly;
therefore, the monk reciting the Pātimokkha, wishing to say, "Venerable sirs, announce your purity," must first...
He causes [the monks] to remember the preliminary duties (pubbakicca) that are the conditions for purity or impurity. For when these are performed, they become a condition for purity;
when not performed, they become a condition for impurity. Precisely because he intends to refer to both possibilities, he says, "What is the preliminary duty of the Saṅgha?

without specifying whether it has been done or not. In this regard, first, with respect to the side of what has not been done, [it is said] for the purpose of showing the sequence for the announcement of purity.
Later, he will say: "He who has an offense should reveal it," and regarding the side that has performed [the rite]: "One should remain silent if there is no offense. And:
"At the very least, having assembled with four bhikkhus," for the purpose of performing the Uposatha.
They say that when the Saṅgha has assembled, one who is outside... [etc. ...must give his consent (*chanda*) even if he does not wish to go.
However, it is also permissible when the Saṅgha has not yet assembled. For this was stated in order to show the proper time for giving consent.

It was also stated to show the procedure to be followed by one who, having performed the Uposatha outside while the Saṅgha had assembled for the purpose of performing the Uposatha, returns after it has been completed. This applies to those residing in the meditation hall (*padhānaghara*).
Desiring to enter the meditation hall, they give their consent (*chanda*) to those monks who are their peers;
if the Saṅgha has assembled, they say, "My consent should be announced," and then enter the meditation hall. This is the practice in the island of Siṃhala.
However, the one announcing [the consent] must announce it once the assembly has gathered. When five monks are living in a single monastery...

Since it has been authorized for one person to bring the *chandapārisuddhi* (consent and purity) and recite the *pātimokkha* for four others, the instruction that "when [the assembly] has gathered, consent must be taken and announced" seems redundant.
Furthermore, because of the statement, "If a person living in communion by theft confesses [their status]," it is permissible even if the consent is brought by a novice (*sāmaṇera*).
And as for the statement, "It does not invalidate the formal act (*kamma*)," if [consent was previously given]...
"If, having given [his consent], he goes outside the boundary and enters again, there is no further need for the formal act of taking his consent;
his procedure is to be understood by way of the authorization of the boundary. And: "The purpose of speaking three times in the giving of consent is this:
the first [indicates] the state of being in harmony; the second, the state of what is to be performed subsequently; the third, for the one who conveys the consent..."
And it is written: "It illustrates the release from a *dukkaṭa* offense. The intention is that she remains as if bound by a chain of cats because she is employed only within the house;
just as [the cat] does not go anywhere else, so too she does not go anywhere else.
Otherwise, the qualification would be meaningless; thus it was accepted by the Teacher (*ācariya*).
If it is asked: "Since it was previously stated that 'it is not permissible to perform the Uposatha without having performed that [sweeping],' why is it said here, 'for this too is both'?
It is because the remaining duties were shown to be those to be performed by one instructed by the Elder;
however, these two may be performed either by the Elder, or by the reciter of the Pātimokkha, or by the proposer of the motion, or by anyone at all—referring to the sweeping and so forth.
In various places, such [other] purposes are accomplished; however, these two do not accomplish any task in those instances.
Therefore, it was said, "This too is both," and so forth, in order to show that one should simply do what must be done without asking, "What is the use of this?
Furthermore, because it was stated in terms of the group by saying, "He pays homage at the feet of the Venerable Ones," it was not stated in terms of the individual.
Because there is no other [recipient] for whom it must be announced.
"It has been recited to the Saṅgha" means it has been recited by the Saṅgha; this is the meaning.

If it is argued that there is no fault here because of the phrase "of the harmonious Saṅgha," since the state of harmony is caused by physical unity (*kāyasāmaggī*)? That is not so, because [the requirement applies] both to the recitation and to the hearing.
Because unity is desirable. For by the words, “Let the Blessed One hear me, venerable sir,” he demonstrates mental concord (*cittasāmaggi*), since in the act of hearing, all have become one.
Regarding the phrase “one commits an offense intentionally”: here, it is only one who commits an offense out of disrespect (*anādariya*) who is shameless (*alajjī*), not the other.

Regarding the phrase "he conceals an offense," it is written here: "One who conceals out of shame is not shameless; rather, one who conceals out of disrespect, thinking 'what is the use of this? is [shameless].
If it is argued that one should not say "of the seven classes of offenses" but should instead say "of six"? [The answer is: Only of seven.

It must be said. For if one who has fallen into an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) confesses his state of being guilty of that offense, the Uposatha of the Saṅgha is successfully performed, and he attains purification through the status of a householder or a novice (sāmaṇera).
"Some teachers" refers, it is said, to the teacher Dhammabhāriya. If one asks why it is stated thus, it is because of the formal proclamation (anusāvana) up to the third time.
The word *nāma* means "three times. Since it does not appear in the text in that way, seeing only the phrase "announced up to the third time," it indicates the meaning:
"Whoever has an offense, let him reveal it. The statement "one who has no offense must remain silent" also indicates that very same meaning.
“By means of silence, indeed, we shall know that the venerable ones are pure”—this too was said, it is said, having taken this very meaning. "Others" refers, it is said, to the Elder Atthadassi.

Regarding the phrase "with reference to this," here, by the expression of the words "even once proclaimed," it appears as if only this much is indicated: that the proclamation must be made three times.
If it is asked, "How is it known that this was said with reference to the essential meaning? it is replied: "This is the exposition handed down through the succession of teachers.
By the phrase "by one who remembers," he shows that intentional lying (*sampajāna-musāvāda*) possesses a conscious mind (*sacittaka*).

The passage beginning with "In the midst of the Saṅgha" is, it is said, a statement defining the characteristics [of the offense]. If one is seated in the midst of the Saṅgha for the purpose of performing the Saṅgha’s *uposatha*, then in that midst of the Saṅgha...
It must be confessed. If one is sitting in the midst of a group for the purpose of performing the Uposatha of the group, it must be confessed in that midst of the group.
If one wishes to perform the Uposatha of purity in the presence of only a single person, it must be confessed in the presence of that single individual.
By this, it is shown that this lying does not occur only in the midst of the Saṅgha; rather, even in the absence of [the Saṅgha], it occurs according to the characteristics stated here.
Logicians say that this is stated as a definition (lakkhaṇa-vacana) because it reveals the following meaning:

even in the case of a communal Uposatha (gaṇa-uposatha), if one who has committed an offense intends to perform the Uposatha but performs it while remaining silent without announcing his state, he incurs an offense of conscious lying (sampajāna-musāvāda). Otherwise, [in the midst of a group...]
"It should not be said [that it is so]," such is their intention. "It was stated by way of the intention of announcing," this is the teacher's conjecture.
For one who announces with the intention, "I announce to the Saṅgha," while making it known, is said to "make it known in the midst of the Saṅgha";
one who announces to those seated on both sides is said to "make it known in the midst of a group"; and thinking, "I shall announce to one person alone,"...
When one reveals [an offense] with a specific intention, it is said that one reveals it to a single person. Even if one is uncertain...
[as before] ...if one has performed the act thinking, "I shall make amends," then for as long as one remains uncertain, one is permitted to receive the confession of a similar offense;
furthermore, one is considered pure regarding other formal acts (*kamma*). However, once one has become free from uncertainty, whether or not one must confess again is not determined.
This is found in the *Pāḷi*, not in the *Aṭṭhakathā*; however, there is no fault in teaching it.

Likewise, regarding the phrase "having emerged from this, I shall make amends for that offense," it is written here that [this applies] when the entire Saṅgha has fallen into a common offense and when one is in doubt.
The commentary on the *Nidāna* is finished.
The Chapter on Defeat (Pārājikakaṇḍa) 1.
Explanation of the First Defeat (Paṭhamapārājikavaṇṇanā).
Standing here, however, the sequence of the training rules (sikkhāpada) must be explained. How so? Of all the training rules...
Fourfold order is obtained: the order of teaching (*desanā-krama*), the order of abandoning (*pahāna-krama*), the order of practice (*paṭipatti-krama*), and the order of arising (*uppatti-krama*).
Therein, Mahākassapa followed the very order of teaching that was authorized by the Blessed One when he permitted the recitation of the Pātimokkha to the bhikkhus at Rājagaha.
First he asked for the recitation of the Pārājika rules; immediately after that, the recitation of the Saṅghādisesa rules;
after that, the recitation of the Aniyata rules; and after that, the detailed recitation. Immediately after that, he asked for the Bhikkhunī-vibhaṅga in that same sequence.
Following that, he asked for the Sekhiya rules, which are comprised within the three aggregates of offenses without a specific numerical limit.
He asked. Asking starting from the section on similar offenses (*āpattikkhandha*), he asked regarding the twenty sections (*vīsatikhandhaka*).
Or, he asked in the *khandhakas* for the purpose of inquiring about those matters included in the enumeration of the origins (*nidānuddesa*) that had not been stated in their specific form.

By this, the grave offenses (*thullaccaya*) prescribed in the *khandhakas* are also included. The Venerable Elder Upāli answered precisely according to the sequence of the questions. This is the point here.
The sequence of the teaching (*desanākkama*). Having extracted [the material] from the *Ubhatovibhaṅga* and the *Khandhaka*, the *Parivāra* was then made into a separate canonical text (*pāḷi*).
It is with reference to this very statement that it is said in the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*): “By this same method, they included the *Khandhaka* in the *Parivāra* as well,” and so forth.
Furthermore, in the Canon (*pāḷi*), it says: “By this same method he questioned the *Ubhatovibhaṅga*. Being questioned, being questioned...”
It was stated only as much as this: “The Venerable Upāli answered. Therefore, the Elder questioned [the Buddha] regarding the two Vibhaṅgas alone.
But when answering, the Venerable Upāli, showing it without omission, taught it by including the Khandhakas and Parivāra within it.
However, at the time of communal recitation (sañjhāya), the Khandhakas and Parivāra were then made into a separate text; such is the sequence of the teaching here.
If it is argued that this introductory recitation (*nidānuddesa*) is the first teaching [of the Pātimokkha], we say no. This is because of the statement in the Uposatha-khandhaka:
“Whatever training rules (*sikkhāpada*) have been laid down by me for the bhikkhus, he should authorize their recitation of the Pātimokkha,” and because of the statement:
“Whosoever has committed an offense. This is due to the fact that unwholesome and indeterminate offenses are conducive to the taints (*āsava*) pertaining to both the present life and the future life.

Because they are to be abandoned through the avoidance of unwholesome conduct by one who possesses restraint in virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*) according to reality, the sequence of abandonment is possible here, as stated in the words:

"At that very time, the four things not to be done should be explained. Likewise, because of the statement, "Having undertaken them, he trains in the rules of training (*sikkhāpada*)," the sequence of practice is also possible through the training in explaining [the precepts] according to reality.

Just as the sequence of practice corresponds to the meaning of the scriptures (*pariyatti*) that are to be mastered according to the order of their teaching, so too, according to these three sequences, the sequence of the origin (*uppatti-krama*) of these training rules (*sikkhāpada*) occurs as far as possible for those rules to be taught.
For instance, regarding whatever matter is common [to both communities], it arises precisely with reference to a monk, such as: "But whichever nun... [and so forth].
It has been laid down for the bhikkhunīs as well, according to the method beginning with "sexual intercourse against her will" and so forth.
Since that [offense] would not have been an unarisen rule for the bhikkhunīs, the statement in the Parivāra—that there is no such thing as an "unarisen rule" in that case—is not contradicted.
Up to this point, regarding the first of the three preceding groups, that which ought to be taught first is the description of the *pārājika* offenses.

Because it was the first to arise, the Venerable Elder Upāli, wishing to set forth the *pārājika* offense regarding sexual intercourse as the very first, placed it immediately after the passage "The Blessed One was staying at Vesālī," thereby bringing it to Vesālī.
Now, the manner in which all the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) were established should be understood. How so? "And furthermore..."
“Monks, you should recite this training rule”—thus it is twofold, according to the distinction between being with a recitation and without a recitation.
Therein, the five classes of offenses that have come down in the Pātimokkha in their own form are called "formulations with a recitation" (*suddesa-paññatti*).

That too is twofold, according to the distinction between explanations with reference to a person and those without reference to a person. Therein, that formulation within which an offense occurs together with...
Or, when a person is shown [in the rule], that is a description with reference to a person (*sapuggalaniddesa*); the other is a description without reference to a person (*apuggalaniddesa*).
Therein, the description with reference to a person is twofold, according to the distinction between offenses where the person is not shown and those where the person is shown.

Therein, the "offenses where the person is not shown" should be understood as the eight rules involving defeat (*aṭṭha pārājikā dhammā*). For in the case of the statement, "He is one who has committed a defeat, he is no longer in communion," it is the person alone who is indicated therein.
If it has been shown, there is no offense. "Offenses that have been shown" refers to the seventeen *saṅghādisesa* rules found in the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha.

For therein, the offense is shown together with the person [who committed it], as in: "This nun too has fallen into an offense that is an immediate transgression, a *saṅghādisesa*, which entails being sent away."

Likewise, the *Apuggalaniddesa* (Exposition of Non-Persons) is twofold, distinguished by whether the offense is shown or not shown. Therein, the *sekhiya-dhammas* (rules of training) are called those whose offense is not shown; it should be understood that the remainder of what has been stated are those whose offense is shown.
That [latter category] is also twofold, distinguished by whether the perpetrator is specified or not specified.

Therein, the rules whose perpetrator is not specified are the training precepts concerning seminal emission, lying, slander, malicious speech, destruction of vegetation, speaking otherwise, censuring, eating in a group, eating in succession, fermented liquor and spirits, poking with the finger, laughing together, disrespect, striking the palm, and the *jatumaṭṭhaka* (use of aphrodisiacs).
By way of this, they become fifteenfold. In that regard, the distinction between mixed and unmixed cases among the case-roles (kāraka) indicated should be understood:
therein, the accusative and locative case-endings are exclusively mixed; the remaining ones are both mixed and unmixed. For example:
first, the nominative (paccatta) is mixed with the accusative in two indeterminate [cases], and with the instrumental (karaṇa) in twelve cases of confession (pāṭidesanīya).

In the training rules concerning robes with fewer than five attachments, it is mixed by means of the agent (*sāmika*); in the case of one under twenty years of age, by means of the location (*bhūma*);
and in the case of the rule on deception, by means of the instrument (*upayoga*), the agent (*sāmika*), and the location (*bhūma*).
Since in the rule on disfiguring, the state (*bhāva*) is intended rather than the agent, the rule on disfiguring does not occur; thus, the direct object (*paccatta*) is fivefold in its mixture.
In the remaining cases, setting aside the first indefinite [offense], there is the personal application found at the beginning in the phrase "Whosoever, however, the monk... and so forth;

or, setting aside the second indefinite [offense], there is the personal application found in the middle among the rules on superior food, the novice, and the third and fourth rules on offenses requiring confession, in the phrases "Whosoever, however, the monk...
and so forth; as well as in the rules concerning corrupt families and those who associate with them.

At the beginning, the word "bhikkhū" (monks) appears only in the nominative case; in the middle, within the training rules concerning those who follow a schism, it appears either in the nominative or in other cases unmixed with others.

It should be understood that in this context, the plural form occurs in the two training rules regarding those who follow a schism and the two training rules on offenses to be confessed involving contact with a second person, whereas elsewhere it is always in the singular.

Likewise, the application (*upayoga*) [of the case endings] is mixed in three ways: in two rules concerning making (*vikappana-sikkhāpada*), in the rule concerning weaving (*tantavāya-sikkhāpada*), it is mixed with the nominative (*paccatta*);

in the rule concerning what is brought (*abhihaṭa-sikkhāpada*), it is mixed with the instrumental (*karaṇa*); and in the rule concerning kings (*rāja-sikkhāpada*), it is mixed with the instrumental and the genitive (*sāmipaccatta*).

Furthermore, the instrumental (*karaṇa*) occurs in the rules concerning building a hut (*kuṭikāra*), large dwellings (*mahallaka*), the second *kaṭhina* robe, the two parts (*dvebhāga*), sitting mats (*nisīdana*), rugs (*santhata*), and making robes discolored (*dubbaṇṇakaraṇa*).

In six cases it is mixed with the personal (accusative) case: in the eight training rules concerning the first and third *kathina* cloths, the eight-fingered foot-cloth, the itch-covering cloth, the rainy-season robe, the water-sprinkling cloth, and the double-layered robe, it is mixed with the agentive (instrumental) case;

thus the construction is twofold mixed. In the remaining seven training rules—the six-year rule, the rainy-season robe, the two-and-a-half-cubit covering, the dwelling-food, the "Great Name," the heavy and light coverings—the case-ending of the construction is unmixed with other case-endings.
In the two training rules concerning the sheep's wool and the single-layered robe, it is mixed with the agentive case.

In the training rules (sikkhāpada) concerning the instrumental case, [the cases] are mixed. However, it should be understood that in the training rules concerning extra bowls and medicines, because of the inclusion of what was not previously included, the genitive case remains unmixed.
Thus, first, regarding the training rules where the factors (kāraka) have been specified:
"In five ways, in three ways, in two ways, and likewise in one way."
The case endings (vibhatti) are fivefold, yet they may all be elevenfold.
Thus, among the training rules (sikkhāpada) designated as "with reference" (suddesa-paññatti), by including those not previously mentioned, there are three hundred and fifty-one;
from these, having excluded ninety-three unindicated factors (aniddiṭṭha-kāraka), there remain two hundred and sixty-six indicated factors (niddiṭṭha-kāraka).
They exist. Among them, there are two hundred and thirty individual rules (*paccattakaraṇa*).
Of these, there are two hundred and twelve unmixed individual rules, and eighteen mixed individual rules.
Among the remaining thirty training rules (*sikkhāpada*), there are five rules involving mixed application, fourteen mixed rules, and seven unmixed rules.

Regarding the two rules on mixing and not mixing, and the two rules on not mixing—among all the specified agents, the phrase "whichever monk" (*yo pana bhikkhu*) does not occur in the following cases:

the following of a schism, the corrupter of families, the first, second, and third *kathina* [rules], the brought-back robe, the small hut, the large dwelling, the two types of assignment, the two divisions, the six-year rule, the sitting mat, the wool, the excess bowl, medicine, the rainy-season robe, the woven robe, the urgent need, the four-night rule, and the two sets of thirty offenses.
It does occur in the middle of the second *aniyata*, the fine food, the novice, and the third and fourth *pāṭidesanīya* rules.
To this extent, nine dyads have been shown: the dyad of "with specification" and "without specification"; the dyad of "with person" and "without person" explanation;

the two dyads of "one who sees individually" and "one who has fallen [into an offense]"; the dyad of "the agent not specified"; therein, among those with the agent specified, the dyad of the "direct case" (*paccatta*) and the "locative case" (*bhummam*);

the dyad of "self-connection" (*sayopanā*) and "other-connection" (*ayopanā*); the dyad of "not connected" (*ayopanama*) and "to-be-connected" (*majjheyopanā*); and the dyad of "singular" and "plural. This is the reason for the distinction.

When each respective training rule (sikkhāpada) is reached, it will become manifest. Thus, having first understood the formal proclamation by enumeration (suddesapaññatti), one should know that whatever proclamation exists in the rest of the Vinaya Piṭaka is a proclamation without enumeration (anuddesapaññatti).

This is sixfold, according to the classification of words (padabhājana), intermediate offenses (antarāpatti), rules for settling disputes (vinītavatthu), prohibitions (paṭikkhepapaññatti), and training rules established by implication (avuttasiddhisikkhāpada).
Among these, [it is said]: "If more than half has been chewed, there is an offense of Thullaccaya; if the mouth is opened in a circular shape without touching [the food], there is an offense..."

The offense appearing in the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājana*) such as, "there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," is called a training rule of the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājanasikkhāpada*).
"And you should not, monks, build a hut entirely of clay; whoever should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing," and so forth, is called an intermediate training rule (*antarāpattisikkhāpada*).
"I allow, monks, for one who is retiring for the day, having secured the door..."

“‘One should dwell in seclusion’”—this and so forth is called a training rule concerning a matter already settled (*vinītavatthu-sikkhāpada*). “‘Monks, one who causes a schism in the Saṅgha, if he is not yet ordained, must not be ordained’”—this and so forth is called a prohibitory training rule (*paṭikkhepa-sikkhāpada*).
For by means of such and such a prohibition, [it is established that] "whichever monk, perceiving a harmonious Saṅgha as being contrary to the Dhamma..."

“Whoever should cause a wound [on the Buddha], he becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion. Furthermore, whatever monk, with a malicious mind, should draw blood from the living body of the Blessed One, he becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense and is no longer in communion”—these training rules (*sikkhāpada*) were thus laid down.
With reference to these, it is said: “For one there is a *chejjaka* offense; for four there is a *thullaccaya*; and for four there is no offense; for all [the remaining cases]...”
It is said, “having a single basis. And it is also said, “There is an offense one incurs while the Blessed One is still present, but not after he has attained Parinibbāna.
Therefore, it is not only this training rule—“Monks, one who knowingly ordains a schismatic of the Saṅgha who is not yet ordained... [etc.
...is guilty of an offense of wrong-doing”—that is established as the proof. “A paṇḍaka...”
In such passages as, "Monks, one who is not ordained should not be ordained;
one who is ordained should be expelled," only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) is prescribed for the preceptor and others, but no offense of defeat (*pārājika*) for eunuchs and the like.
For they possess no status as monks, from which an offense of defeat could arise. Likewise: "One should not depart while the drops have not ceased."
And such rules as these are indeed called "prohibitory training rules" (*paṭikkhepa-sikkhāpada*).

Those offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) and grave offenses (*thullaccaya*) prescribed in the *Khandhakas* are called "prescriptive training rules" (*paññatti-sikkhāpada*). It is said: "In that case, Sāriputta, make him confess a grave offense for following those who cause schism"; thus, even the grave offense is included right there [in the *Khandhakas*].

It proceeds. Some say that although this [offense] does not exist at the moment of the formal act (kamma) because it has not yet been prescribed for them, it nevertheless exists at the moment of purification by virtue of the Blessed One’s word.
From the statement, "Exhort those who side with schism," there follows the training rule for the rest of those who side with schism:
"Whosoever, knowing [the situation], sides with those who are causing a schism in the Saṅgha, there is an offense of thullaccaya."
It should be understood that [the rule] has been laid down. Likewise, all the duties of the Khandhakas and the formal acts of the Vinaya converge in that very same place.
As it is said: “Upāli, that duty for visiting monks has been laid down by me...
Thus, Upāli, the training rule has been well-laid down by me,” and so forth. “But whichever nun [should watch] a dance or a song...”
By this Sutta— “or should she go to see dancing, singing, or instrumental music, it is an offense of expiation” (Pācittiya)—
whatever class of offenses seen in the Commentary, such as “a bhikkhunī might dance, sing, or play music, it is an offense of expiation,” and so forth,
is called a *vinayakamma* or a training rule established by implication (*avuttasiddhisikkhāpada*). This sixfold [category] is [to be understood] through six aspects.
It should be understood that "it is not fit for recitation" refers to the training rule concerning non-recitation (*anuddesa-sikkhāpada*). For example:

because of the incompatibility with the five types of recitations according to their respective occurrence, even when the basis (*vatthu*) is similar, the pair of offenses—*dukkaṭa* and *thullaccaya*—are [excluded];
and because they constitute offenses of a different category from those training rules where intermediate offenses are prescribed, they consist of offenses belonging to different bases.

Because the training rules of prohibition (*paṭikkhepa-sikkhāpada*) and certain training rules established on the basis of disciplinary cases (*vinītavatthu-pannatti-sikkhāpada*) do not show the commission of an offense;

because there is no grave offense (*thullaccaya*) following a schism when the underlying case is not shown; and because the training rules whose fulfillment is implicit (*avutta-siddhi-sikkhāpada*) do not show the basis for an offense.

To this extent, that which was stated—“the formulation of the training rules is twofold, distinguished by those with explicit mention (*suddesa*) and those without explicit mention (*anuddesa*)”—[is explained].
In brief, it has been explained thus:
First, regarding the designation:
"An agent is not specified here, because of the absence of dependence."
"And because there is no need for a formal procedure (*vidhāna*) to be stated beforehand, [the offense occurs] from the very beginning together with the preliminary action (*yogena*).

This is the method to be understood. Its meaning is as follows: regarding those specific training rules (*sikkhāpada*) such as the emission of semen (*sukkavisaṭṭhi*), which were previously mentioned under various classifications and whose agents (*kāraka*) have not been specifically pointed out—in these cases, the agent exists by virtue of the presence of intention (*adhippāya*), the deed (*kamma*), the object (*vatthu*), the person (*puggala*), and the application (*payoga*).
It was not specified [previously] for the purpose of showing their state of expectancy (*sāpekkhabhāva*). All of that will become manifest in each respective training rule (*sikkhāpada*);
however, here, because there is an absence of expectancy regarding the formal definition of a *pārājika*, the agent (*kāraka*) is specified.

As for the agent, as in the case of "when the robe has been finished and the [old one] has been discarded" (*niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunā ubbhatasmiṃ*), etc., there is no prior statement of the rule to be observed.
It is designated not by way of its instrument (karaṇa) and so forth, but by way of its individuality (paccatta), because of the absence of a correlative (apekkhā).

If it were to be designated therein [in the context of the second offense], it would be like the remaining second, indefinite, and superior foods among the third and fourth *pāṭidesanīyas*, where it is not designated in the middle;
for, as in the passage beginning “Not indeed... nor should one hint,” there is no prior rule of formulation to be stated.

Thus it is indicated at the beginning. Even though it is indicated at the beginning, because there was no rule previously to be stated [prior to this], it is not indicated by omitting [the subject]—as in the case of the training rules (sikkhāpada) such as the five types of offenses starting with those that follow the divisions mentioned earlier—but rather it is indicated from the very start with the words "But whichever monk," together with the word *yo pana*. Even though it is indicated in this way, since...

However, one does not incur an offense that originates from another—such as the offense mentioned in the rule, “But if two bhikkhunīs should lie down on the same bed,” and so forth—and therefore it is specified by the singular term, “But whichever bhikkhu.

If it is argued that even the offense of sexual intercourse (*methunadhamma*) originates from another because of the expression “the attainment of the couple with the couple,” that is not so, because the underlying intention (*adhippāya*) must be understood; for [the act] belongs to many.
In that case, there is a restriction that it is an offense for a bhikkhunī and not for a single [laywoman]; however, here there is no such restriction, which is the intended meaning of "unrestricted.

As for those with hunchbacks or flat backs, how could there be an offense of sexual intercourse (*methunadhamma*)? Because of the statement, "the attainment of the two-by-two," they incur the offense of sexual intercourse.

This matter refers to the eight bases [of the *Sahadhammika-vinicchaya*] as "the four conditions for sexual intercourse," and thus it is said, "there may be cutting off on account of sexual intercourse."
And it is to be established by the words spoken regarding the retinue.

In the training rule concerning those who follow a schism (*bhedānuvattaka*), it is stated that more than three [monks] are not to be formally admonished, nor should the Saṅgha be made into one with the Saṅgha.
For the purpose of showing the method, having first made the plural designation "there are monks" (*bhikkhū honti*), [the text] then...
It is stated, “one, two, or three”; otherwise, it would follow that there were more than that who were “followers,” which would contradict the source narrative (*nidāna*).
For indeed, there were about five hundred followers of him. However, in the *Sattasatika-kkhandhaka*, it says:
“The Saṅgha may appoint four Eastern monks and four Pāvā monks... they were appointed,” and so forth.

The *ñattidutiyakamma* (formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation) has been described; that refers to the procedure to be performed by those [members] because it was stated, "Let this legal issue be settled by a committee (*ubbāhikā*).
Alternatively, it is permissible to perform the third [act] as the formal appointment itself (*sammutikaraṇa*).

For they do not become subject to that formal act (*kammāraha*) merely by having had the act performed upon them. The defining characteristic of one who is subject to a formal act is: "he upon whom the Saṅgha performs the formal act."
And at that time, the Saṅgha did not perform any formal act against those eight monks. Even though they were being shunned, they remained subject to the formal act.
For it was considered that they had become subject to the formal act because the Saṅgha had performed the appropriate procedure for the settlement of the legal dispute.
"Those monks are to be formally admonished by the monks up to three times for the relinquishing of that [position]."

If it is argued that the procedure to be performed by them consists merely of a formal declaration (*vacana*), and thus the act (*kamma*) is simply the making of a convention (*sammuti-karaṇa*), that is not so. This is because their intention (*adhippāya*) must be understood;
those monks are to be made subject to the formal act solely for the purpose of their relinquishing [the offense], and not by way of falling into fault.

For the settling of a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa-vūpasama*) does not occur through the formal act of admonition (*samanubhāsana-kamma*) for them, in the same way that it was accomplished through a convention for the Pācīnakas and others.

There is the accomplishment of its relinquishment; for this "consent" (sammuti) is performed only after first obtaining permission and making a formal request, whereas a formal act (kamma) is not done in that way.
However, when a formal act is performed, the purpose is indeed accomplished.
It should be understood that, by the consent of others, those who are more numerous must be appointed.

“Sexual intercourse” (*methunadhamma*)—that which has received its name by way of common usage—is to engage in any one of the acts of insertion, remaining inserted, or extraction, whether by one’s own effort or another’s effort, either in one’s own organ in one’s own path or another’s path, or in another’s organ in that other’s path, by means of consenting to it;
such a person is defeated and no longer in communion. However, some [hold that] “insertion and so forth... [is the definition].
"If he should practice four, or three, or two, or even one [of these acts], he becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense. For it has been said:
'If he consents to the entry, consents to what has entered, consents to the staying, and consents to the extraction, there is an offense of *pārājika*,' and so forth.
According to their opinion, one incurs four *pārājika* offenses for each of the four [acts].
They speak thus: "May he incur the offense of defeat (pārājika) regarding sexual intercourse; may he be one who shares in that offense of defeat for sexual intercourse.
Having incurred offenses of defeat through their own transgressions, and having incurred an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa), they renounce the training;
and while living as householders, having incurred an offense of defeat such as sexual intercourse, they go forth again and receive full ordination.

Because that person becomes free from offense only after having confessed one *saṅghādisesa* offense—whether one or many—he was therefore "one with an offense" during his time as a householder. Even for one who has committed the ultimate offense (*antimavatthu*), there is indeed an offense;
however, because he does not become purified through confession and rehabilitation, it is not stated that "for every attempt, there is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*)."

Although this was not explicitly stated because there was no need for calculation, they state that the reasoning is established by the words "there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika)" in the word-commentary (padabhājana).
If that is so, then in the Mātikā as well, it says: "Whosoever, as a bhikkhu, should engage in sexual intercourse, he is defeated."
It would have to be so stated; furthermore, even the expression "without remainder" (*anavasesa*) regarding a *pārājika* offense would not be tenable.

For the term "without remainder" is used because it remains without leaving out any category of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*) or any number of monks. Thus, the offense occurs at the very moment of entry, and not during the acts of having already entered and so forth.
It is with reference to that single [act] alone that the phrase "for whom there may be an offense" includes even the *pārājika* offense within its scope.

The statement of the introduction to the causes (*nidānuddesa*) should be understood. Therefore, instead of saying "an offense entailing defeat" (*pārājika*) in the summary matrix (*mātikā*), the statement "one becomes one who has committed an offense entailing defeat" (*pārājiko hoti*) is a designation of the person (*puggalaniddesa*);
its purpose is to show that by means of that bodily bond, one is incapable of full ordination (*upasampadā*).
The phrase "an offense of defeat" (*āpatti pārājikassa*) in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) refers to the defeat of one who has committed even the final matter.
This is for the purpose of showing that a person who is not in communion is one whose communion is fraudulent.
For even if he consents to communal life, he is not a fraudulent commensal; therefore, one who is fully ordained is called simply a "bhikkhu. For this very reason it was said:
"A person is impure, having committed some offense involving defeat (pārājika); yet, while maintaining a pure view toward it, he does not grant leave..."
"Having had [the act] performed, if one speaks with the intent to abuse, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for slander.
Since that [offense] does not exist for one who is not fully ordained (anupasampanna), it is established that such a person, being fully ordained, is called simply "a bhikkhu.
Therefore, it should be understood that he gives rise to the offenses of *padasodhamma* and *sahaseyya*, as well as the offenses of malicious speech toward bhikkhus (*bhikkhupesunna*) and so forth.
The introduction consists of the analysis of the matrix (mātikā); the detailed exposition (vibhaṅga) determines that [matrix];
thereafter follows the analysis of offenses, as well as non-offenses and their exceptions—this is the method to be understood.
In this regard, there are the cases of Sudinna, the monkey, and the Vajjiputtakas.

The threefold classification of the offense is the *nidāna* (origin) of this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). From that origin, the analysis of this matrix (*mātikā*)—“Whatever bhikkhu [should commit an offense with a woman]...
[and so forth]... there is no living together”—arose. For therein, by way of the feminine gender, it says: “At the very least, even with an animal;
truly, friends, a training rule has been laid down by the Blessed One, and that indeed concerns a woman.”
“Neither a man, nor a paṇḍaka, nor one with both sexual organs”—just as in the case of the *makkaṭi-pārājika* (the monkey-monk), another person is also capable of casting a pretext (*lesa*).
Therefore, this is stated in order to show an occasion for such a person who is free from a pretext.

The variation in the wording of the summary rule (*mātikā*)—namely, that the source is designated as “even down to an animal” rather than simply “a woman”—is because it demonstrates the accomplishment of sexual intercourse even with those other than women.
Therefore, the *vibhaṅga* (analysis) is its regulator; the *vibhaṅga* is that which regulates the intended meaning of that *mātikā* (matrix).
For in the *vibhaṅga*, by means of such methods as "three types of women, three types of hermaphrodites, three types of eunuchs, three types of men;
for a human woman there are three paths, for a male animal there are two paths," and so forth, all opportunity for error is closed off.

A restriction has been made. Here it is asked: If this is so, then by way of common training rules or by way of the change of gender, it would have to be stated in the Vibhaṅga that even for bhikkhunīs, as for bhikkhus, they are "one who has entered upon the training and the mode of life.

For if that were not said, a bhikkhunī who had become a man through the manifestation of the male gender might say [of herself] while still remaining in the state of a bhikkhu: [that she was one who had entered upon the training and the mode of life].
“I did not, at the time of my full ordination, undertake the training and the way of life of the bhikkhus;

therefore, even though I have not renounced the training, I am not defeated by the act of sexual intercourse. It is said in reply: It should not be stated as you have said, because it leads to an undesirable consequence.
If it were stated thus, it would follow that even bhikkhunīs possess the possibility of renouncing the training; and that is undesirable. This is another undesirable consequence.

"All training rules (sikkhāpada) are indeed common, not uncommon. Furthermore, it was said—"I allow you, monks, to join with the monks for those years, with that very same mentorship (upajjha) and that very same full admission (upasampadā)"—in order to show that this [nun] has entered upon the training and way of life (sājīva) of the monks.
"The breach of the offense from that" means from that analysis (vibhaṅga).
“There is a *pārājika* offense when the body is not destroyed; there is a *thullaccaya* when it is mostly destroyed,” and so forth—this constitutes the classification of offenses (*āpatti-bheda*).

“There is no offense in other cases” means that according to the same *vibhaṅga*, there is a classification of non-offenses (*anāpatti-bheda*) by way of a mode different from that in which the offense was stated. For it is said:
“If one consents, there is a *pārājika* offense; if one does not consent, there is no offense.”
Without the analysis (*vibhaṅga*), it is not made known. To this extent, the meaning of this verse—“The classification of the matrix according to the sources”—has been stated in brief.
However, the specific reasons for each individual training rule will be revealed in their respective places.

First, regarding the initial formulation (*paṭhamapaññatti*): because it was formulated after the first enlightenment had passed, it was during the time when the Venerable Sudinna was eight years old.
The first proclamation was made at the time when he attained the greatness of long-standing seniority; the second proclamation was made at the time when he attained the greatness of great learning.

For that venerable one, having committed the offense of defeat regarding a female monkey, perceived that just as a female animal is not intended in the training rules concerning women, so too it is here; thus he said: "It is true, friend... [and so on]... and that..."
He said, "It must be a human woman, not one belonging to the animal realm.
Regarding the third formulation, because of the statement beginning with "having eaten as much as desired," it arises at the time when one has attained the greatness of gain;
the greatness of abundance is also found in this very context. Thus, based on these three kinds of objects, this first *pārājika* training rule is fourfold according to that time.
It should be understood as "having reached what has been prescribed.

In this context, "but whoever" (*yo pana*) is the phrase that exhaustively includes [all such persons] without exception. "A monk" (*bhikkhu*) is the restrictive phrase that prevents over-extension (*atippasaṅga*) to that [term].

"One who has undertaken the training and livelihood of monks" (*bhikkhūnaṃ sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno*) is its qualifying expression; for not everyone who merely bears the name "monk" [is necessarily meant].

Whatever training has been prescribed by the Blessed One as the minimum to be trained in by bhikkhus ordained by any form of ordination, and whatever "common life" (*sājīva*) has been spoken of—namely, "living together here"—one indeed becomes possessed of both of these immediately upon being ordained by any form of ordination.
But when does one become possessed of them? Immediately after being ordained by any form of ordination.
Whether knowing both of these or not knowing them, one is said to have "entered" (samāpanna) because of having accepted them.
"Living together" means as long as one has not renounced the training or reached the state of a *pārājika*. As for what was stated in the Andhaka-ṭīkā:
"One who fulfills the training has entered the training; one who does not transgress the way of life has entered the way of life. That...

This is stated by way of the highest limit. For one who does not fulfill the training, or who is full of thoughts of sensual desire and the like, or who transgresses some part of the livelihood with a remainder, is certainly not called "one who has entered upon the training and the livelihood.
However, by way of the highest limit, a fourfold classification is obtained: "There is a bhikkhu who has entered upon the training, [but not the livelihood]... [and so forth].
Reflecting thus: there is one who has not entered upon the training and has not entered upon the livelihood, yet transgresses a training rule while being without consciousness;
there is one who has not entered upon the training but has entered upon the livelihood, being full of sensual thoughts and the like, yet remains free from offense;

there is one who has neither entered upon the training nor entered upon the livelihood, yet incurs an offense without remainder; and there is one who has entered upon both, fulfilling the training and not transgressing the livelihood.”
If it is argued that "herein, this fourth type of bhikkhu, the superior one (ukkaṭṭha), must be intended; for it is not fitting for the Blessed One to speak of one who is not superior," we say no.
This is because it would contradict the statement: "In this context, that which is the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) is the training intended.
Furthermore, if the intention were merely to include the superior type, [the text] would have said, "Training means the three trainings."
The intention is that only this much should be said. For one who has attained the three trainings is the most excellent of all.
If it is argued that only the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) is mentioned because of the subsequent statement, "He might engage in sexual intercourse," we say no;
for even that [training] is impossible [for him]. Indeed, while fulfilling the training in higher virtue and not transgressing the livelihood (*ājīva*), he would not [engage in] sexual intercourse.
The intention is that one who is capable of practicing [the training], yet fails to fulfill that training and transgresses the very mode of livelihood (sājīva), would indeed practice [in such a way].

Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as follows: since the mode of livelihood, which consists of the training rules (sikkhāpada), includes only the training in higher virtue (adhisīla-sikkhā) and not the other two trainings, therefore, "therein, that which is the training in higher virtue, this [is what is meant] in this context..."

"Training is intended here in the sense of purpose," it is said. Therefore, the right mode of livelihood (*sājīva*) which includes the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) is called "training-together-with-livelihood" (*sikkhāsājīva*).

Thus, the term "training" (*sikkhā*) was employed for the purpose of specifying the right mode of livelihood. For the very purpose of illustrating that meaning, the *Vibhaṅga* does not mention "training" directly, but says:
"One trains in that; therefore, he is said to be 'one who has entered upon the right mode of livelihood'. By this...

This is shown to be this one single point of meaning. And because one has the duty to train from the moment immediately following the attainment of full ordination (*upasampadā*), one is said to both "train" and to have "entered upon" [the training].

One who has thus come to be designated as "one who has entered upon the training and the livelihood," and who, depending on such conditions, subsequently does not abandon the very training known as the livelihood—
The meaning that "one might engage in sexual intercourse without having disclosed one's weakness" is logical.

However, this contradicts the method of the Aṭṭhakathā (Commentary), and yet that [method] is not something that should be rejected; rather, the underlying intention (*adhippāya*) here must be sought.
This very characteristic of a bhikkhu is common to all training rules (*sikkhāpada*), namely: "Of the bhikkhus..."
“Endowed with training and livelihood. Even a disciple whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) incurs an offense that is unintentional; likewise does one in higher training (sekha);

but an ordinary person (puthujjana) incurs even intentional offenses. Therefore, taking this as a characteristic of a bhikkhu common to those in higher training, those whose taints are destroyed, and ordinary persons, [the term “bhikkhu”] refers—by way of the grammatical rule of singular remainder (*ekasesa*) applied to identical or partially identical forms—as one who is simply endowed with training, one who is simply endowed with livelihood, and one who is endowed with both.

In the commentary, only the "exalted" (ukkaṭṭha) [training] is mentioned because, by taking the exalted as the primary term in the compound *sikkhāsājīvasamāpanno*, the inclusion of the non-exalted is established.

To ensure that this very [non-exalted] is also understood, a resolution is stated here regarding the omission of the word *sikkhā* in the phrase: "He trains in that; therefore he is said to have entered upon the livelihood. For since he also [trains in] the training...
Having stated, "Therefore, it should be understood that in meaning he is one who has entered upon the training (*sikkhāsamāpanna*)," it is further said:
"Without having renounced that training which he has entered upon, and without having revealed his weakness regarding that way of life (*sājīva*) which he has entered upon.

This is the intended meaning of the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) that should be understood. However, according to this intended meaning, [it applies] only to the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*).
It should be understood that "grasping" (gahaṇa) refers to the Vinaya because it is universally beneficial and because it concerns moral virtue (sīla).
Just as one who undertakes a training rule (sikkhāpada) is said to undertake moral virtue, so too it is appropriate to say that one who renounces a training rule renounces moral virtue;
therefore, it is stated therein: "without renouncing that training which has been undertaken."
To this extent, the detailed analysis of what is to be said regarding the phrase “one who has entered upon the training and the mode of livelihood” is concluded in brief.

If it is asked: “What is the purpose of this specific expression? Should it not have been stated simply as: ‘But whichever bhikkhu, without having renounced the training and without having disclosed his weakness...
[etc. ...is one with whom there can be no communal living’? It should not be so stated, because that would lead to an undesirable consequence.

“However, for one who has entered upon the training and the mode of livelihood, yet is a ‘bhikkhu’ by mere designation or mere admission—such as one living in communion through theft (theyyasaṃvāsaka) and so forth—for him too there is the renunciation of the training;
and for one who, without having renounced the training, engages in sexual intercourse, there is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
Or, for one who later, having committed an offense entailing defeat, no longer possesses the training and the mode of livelihood...”

And for him, or for one who—due to being a *paṇḍaka* by birth (*pakkha-paṇḍaka*)—has not entered upon the training and the common mode of livelihood because he has attained the state of a *paṇḍaka*, both of those [factors] exist;
thus [the offense] is incurred. And regarding the category of the state of a *paṇḍaka*, it is stated: "A *paṇḍaka* is not a basis for full ordination.
Therefore, it is established that in the other category [of *paṇḍakas*], there is a basis. One who is fully ordained in that category...
On the side of those with the nature of a *paṇḍaka*, because of being a *paṇḍaka*, one has not entered upon the training and the mode of livelihood;

since there is an absence of the training that must be undertaken, even if one were to engage in sexual intercourse by means of taking another’s genitals into the mouth without having formally renounced the training, from where could there be an offense of defeat (*pārājika*) for him?
This is the intended meaning. This method applies only to one who does not belong to the side of those who are not *paṇḍakas*.

It is logical from this perspective; however, for one who has received [the ordination], even though there is a severance of the life-continuum (*bhavaṅga*) at the moment of attaining wholesome states such as the formless attainments among non-material beings—just as there is no death—the status of being a monk exists even on the side of the condition of a *paṇḍaka*.

Or, for one who consents to living in communion, there is no status of being a "one who lives in communion by theft" (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*), unlike one who has committed the ultimate offense (*antimavatthu*). Nor does it involve sleeping together and so forth.
He generates [the thought]. However, he is not one who completes the quorum, like one who has committed the ultimate offense; he has not entered upon the training and the mode of livelihood.
But he belongs to the other category; this is his distinction from that [other person]. Is he with a cause (sahetuka), or is he without a cause (ahetuka)?
He is not without a cause, because his full ordination was permitted for him in the category of those who are not paṇḍakas, owing to his having a rebirth with a cause.

If it is asked: "Why is it not permitted even for one on the side of being a paṇḍaka?"—it is because of the state of being a paṇḍaka, just as in the case of a paṇḍaka by means of artificial means (*opakkamika*).
Furthermore, by the phrase "one who has entered upon the training and the mode of livelihood," his undertaking of the training is indicated;
it is therefore appropriate to say that he has not renounced that undertaken training and has not manifested weakness therein, and not otherwise.

For this reason, to avoid the aforementioned undesirable consequence, it was stated: "But whatever bhikkhu, having undertaken the training and the way of life of the bhikkhus, without having renounced the training... and so forth. And just as it is here, so too [it applies] to the rule:

"But whatever bhikkhu, having undertaken the training and the way of life of the bhikkhus, without having renounced the training and without having revealed his weakness, [from a village or from a forest]..."
