“Taking what is not given” … [and so on] … “Whatever bhikkhu, having undertaken the training and the way of life of the bhikkhus, without having renounced the training and without having disclosed his weakness, should have a robe made to the measure of the Sugata’s robe”—this should be applied in all instances.
“Even if it is for one belonging to the animal realm” is said with reference to a human woman; for it goes without saying that it does not apply to a paṇḍaka.
It is appropriate to say that it blows toward a person. The rest is exactly according to the method explained in various places.
This, first of all, is the exposition of the summary (mātikā); it should be illustrated by applying it elsewhere as well, according to what is possible.
Sāriputta, Belaṭṭhasīsa, Ānanda, and others [are mentioned] because they were the causes for the laying down of training rules (sikkhāpada) and because they incurred offenses (āpatti).
And why is it that only the *ñatticatuttha* (fourth motion) ordination is mentioned in the Mahāvibhaṅga? The Elder Upatissa says:
"Because there was fear of the consequence of permitting [ordination] after having previously rejected the ordination by going for refuge (*saraṇagamana-upasampadā*).

Alternatively, it is because monks might harbor a wrong grasp or doubt, thinking: "Since that [ordination by going for refuge] is also mentioned there, even though it was previously rejected by the Blessed One, it has been permitted again."
It arises; therefore, it is said that [the term] was not mentioned.
Because of the statement, "An illegal act (adhammakamma) is a factional act (vaggakamma)," even a flawed act (kuppakamma) is sometimes called a "formal act" (kamma);
therefore, it is said, "by an unfluctuating [act]. Since even some unfluctuating acts are not fit to stand (na ṭhānāraha), by which [one] has not attained...
Reinstatement is called "well-reinstated"; therefore, it is said, "by one worthy of the position.
If it is argued that, since this is so, only "by one worthy of the position" should be stated because of the establishment of the unshakable [nature], we say no.

For in this context, one who is ordained by one unworthy of the position—even if unshakable—is not intended, as that would lead to an undesirable consequence. However, when these two are stated together, this is the meaning:
It is understood thus: one who is ordained with that which is entirely unshakable is intended here as a "bhikkhu";
one who is ordained with that which is both worthy of standing and unshakable is also intended here as a "bhikkhu";
whereas one ordained with that which is shakable is not intended.

Because it is stated, “from the moment of taking rebirth until one has not yet completed twenty years,” they say that those who appear by spontaneous birth (*opapātika*) and are sixteen years old are also “not yet twenty years from the moment of rebirth.
Since it is stated, “they appear as sixteen-year-olds,” another four years would have to be expected; however, [the phrase] “from the moment of taking rebirth”...
Some say: "This was stated with reference to those born from a womb. Regarding the phrase "some say," wherever it is written, one should investigate each instance and clearly discern the meaning.
The state of being a *paṇḍaka* (impotent person) through artificial means (*opakkamika*) should be understood according to the method already established. It is recorded:
"A *pakkhapaṇḍaka* (one who is impotent for part of the month) should be ordained during the phase when he is not a *paṇḍaka*, but must be expelled during the phase when he is a *paṇḍaka*."

Regarding the statement, “If one puts on the lower robe without giving the *bindu* (the mark), one does not become a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one who lives by theft),” this must be investigated. “In accordance with the characteristic” means the intention is that he has accepted the status of living in communion as one worthy of being a novice (*sāmaṇera*).

For those who have taken the characteristic [of a monk] out of fear of kings and so forth, even though there is a deceptive thought—“Let householders know me as a ‘monk’”—no fault arises because they lack both the desire to deceive the monks and the desire to live in communion with them. “Whoever... [text continues].

If one does not know that "one who goes forth in this way is called a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*," or "it is not permitted to do it in this way," or "one who has gone forth in this way is not a novice (*sāmaṇera*)," it is permissible. It is written: "If one knows [this], it is not permissible.
Furthermore, one who, for the sake of fleeing from a king, famine, and so forth, puts on the robe and consents to living together [in the Saṅgha] is a *theyyasaṃvāsaka*.
[He] becomes [a thief-living-in-communion]. Why? Because of the impurity of his mind. Again, if he thinks, "I shall practice the pure holy life;

what is the use of this remorse? or "I shall do it because conditions and requisites are easily obtained," and thus becomes pure-minded, then as long as he does not consent to living in communion, he is not a thief-living-in-communion. Thus, starting from the arising of that pure mind...
"If he consents to living together [with her], he is intended to be one who lives in communion through theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*); otherwise, everything would be contradictory," say some.
They further state: "If one kills a father of such a kind who was not born from [sexual] contact and so forth, he is a patricide.
However, one who causes the destruction of virtue (*sīla*) through physical contact is not a "defiler of nuns" (*bhikkhunīdūsaka*), because [the rule applies only to] "the three paths."

Regarding the verbal [aspect]: even if one defiles a nun who has received full ordination through only one of the two ceremonies (*ekato-upasampannā*), he is a "defiler of a nun" (*bhikkhunī-dūsaka*) and is likewise subject to defeat (*pārājika*);

such is the legal determination (*vinicchaya*). Furthermore, if a nun is one who lives in communion by theft (*theyya-saṃvāsikā*), a killer of mother, father, or an Arhat, a shedder of blood [from the Buddha], or one who has gone over to another sect (*titthiya-pakkantika*), the Vinaya-holders accept her as being excluded from the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathāsu anāgata*).

It is said: “In the case of intentional lying, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya). One who does not transgress this established limit is said to train in that training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
A “training rule” is merely a conventional designation for a phenomenon that lacks intrinsic nature; here, it is the formal injunction (*paññatti*) that is intended.
It is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā* that “this is a synonym for restraint from sexual intercourse,” but that was said with reference to the underlying meaning (*attha*).
It is written: *Sikkhā* refers to each respective training rule (*sikkhāpada*), as well as the arising of a state of consciousness that functions by way of training.
*Sājīva* refers to the formal designation (*paññatti*). To demonstrate its meaning, it was previously stated: "This is a synonym for the restraint from sexual intercourse.
Because of the absence of this tradition—which is esteemed for its virtue and esteemed for its merit—there is a manifestation of weakness in the world.

In that context, it is not possible [for weakness to occur]. For that [attainment] is to be yearned for; therefore it is said: "without manifesting weakness regarding that attainment of the way of life he has entered.
Upatissa says that weakness is indeed possible through an order [of the Saṅgha].

Alternatively, the phrase concerning the non-manifestation of weakness should be understood as being either for the sake of the elegance of the phrasing in the section on the renunciation of training, or as serving as a supplementary passage.

Alternatively, because in the case of renouncing the training (*sikkhāpaccakkhāna*), a certain manifestation of weakness (*dubbalyāvikamma*) has not been performed, he said "without manifesting weakness" while explaining the meaning of the phrase "without renouncing the training," with reference to that.
In this regard, it might be argued: since not every manifestation of weakness constitutes a renunciation of the training, therefore [he said] "weakness..."
Having first stated, "because of not having made it known," must one then say, "without having renounced the training," for the purpose of defining its meaning? No;
why? Because there is no sequential order of meaning. For since it was said, "one who has entered upon the training and the mode of livelihood," [the meaning is]:
"without having renounced whichever training one has entered upon, and without having made known one's weakness regarding whichever mode of livelihood one has entered upon."
When it is being explained, the meaning is stated precisely in its proper sequence and not otherwise; therefore, this alone is stated first.
"Of those very same" refers to the fourteen.
"Without having renounced the training" is stated as a general application for all training rules (sikkhāpada), and thus it is said: "This is an additional rule (anupaññatti) here."
“Insertion” (pavesana) means the contact with the sexual organ of one who is inserting it.

“Inserted” (paviṭṭha) refers to the time when it has been inserted up to the base, whether during the preparatory stage or the stage of exertion. At the moment of the emission of semen, the sexual organ is said to be “stayed” (ṭhita).
“Withdrawal” (uddharaṇa) means the time of taking it out. However, in the *Vinayagaṇṭhipada*, it says: “The state [of being stayed] occurs after ceasing from exertion.”
When it is said, "it is called 'standing' (ṭhitaṃ)," that is stated for the purpose of showing it without confusion.
Even at the times of entering, having entered, and withdrawing, there is indeed emission of semen. "Consent" (sādiyanaṃ) means the arising of a mind of indulgence or a mind of acceptance.
It is said, "For this is the source of all training rules (sikkhāpada)," with reference to those formulated specifically in the *Ubhatovibhaṅga*.
Because it is stated, “Ordination [is performed] by a group with a Vinaya-expert as the fifth,” the instrumental case is used here in the sense of association.
Therefore, even if twenty monks are seated, only a Vinaya-expert is required as the fifth.

If it is argued that this invalidates the ordination procedure if the Vinaya-expert is one who has committed a *pārājika* offense, the answer is no; for at the end of the *Parivāra*, in the section on formal acts (*kammavagga*), the characteristic of a failure of the formal act is defined as follows: [text continues].

It was stated [in the Sutta], because that [factor] was absent in that case. If it is asked: "Is this not already included by the phrase 'or from the assembly' (*parisato vā*) in the statement: 'How [does a formal act fail]? Either by way of the subject matter (*vatthu*), or by way of the motion (*ñatti*), or by way of the proclamation (*anussāvana*), or by way of the boundary (*sīmā*), or by way of the assembly (*parisa*)'? No;
for in the commentary (*vibhaṅga*) on that Sutta passage—"Formal acts fail in twelve ways by way of the assembly"—its...

Regarding the phrase "because it has not been examined": since this meaning can be understood from the wording of the Canon (Pāḷi) as it is stated here and there in its own form, it was written here in brief by showing only the method.
Having extracted the word "factor" (*aṅga*), it was stated that "the factors and non-factors of offenses in all training rules (*sikkhāpada*) are to be known";
yet here it is simply said "factor. Why? [Because] of the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth...

It should be understood that this is because the non-factors (*anaṅga*) mentioned there were not defined here either—since they were presented only in brief among the *parivāra* and other sections—and because if the state of being a non-factor were stated both in brief and in detail for every case, it would result in excessive prolixity, requiring everything to be stated without omission in each respective training rule (*sikkhāpada*). The meaning is: "by way of summarizing all offenses."
Those training rules which are called "actions" (kiriyā) should be understood as involving both body and speech together with intimation (viññatti);

those which are "non-actions" (akiriya) should be understood as being without intimation. However, in this context, the mind is immeasurable because an offense originating from the disclosure of the elements (bhūtārocanasamuṭṭhāna) is an action, and because there is no state of being without mind (acittaka).
In that regard, an action-offense should be understood as originating from a mind that is not an intervening factor (anaṅgantara).
Even certain [actions] that do not produce intimation (aviññatti) are, by way of general principle, called "functional" (kiriya), just like the first *pārājika*. For it is said:
"If he consents, there is an offense of *pārājika*; if he does not consent, there is no offense.
Indeed, even an action termed "intimation" does not exist without the mind of pursuit (*sevanacitta*), because it is produced by the aforementioned mind.

Because it is of a modified nature and because it follows the mind. Therefore, this intimation-form (viññatti-rūpa), which is designated as "functional" (kiriya), does not persist without its generating mind, just like other mind-born matter (cittaja-rūpa). However, the other [type], the sound-base (saddāyatana), does persist.
Thus, considering that when there is functional activity, there must necessarily be the "approaching mind" (sevanacitta) that generates it, one does not consent to it.

"It is not appropriate to say 'there is no offense'" means: because even though it is capable of generating an intimation (*viññatti*), the mind of indulgence does not generate an intimation at all times;
therefore, since it arises of its own accord even without an intimation, it is said: "If he consents, there is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*).
If it does not arise, it is called "not consenting," and for him there is no offense. For this very reason, the Blessed One said:
“With what state of mind are you, O bhikkhu?”—it should be understood that by this, one delimits the offense by means of the *citta* (mental state) alone, and not by means of the action (*kiriyā*).

Here, the inclusion of the term "origin" (*samuṭṭhāna*) has the purpose of showing that one incurs an offense only through the bodily and other distinctions of what is to be done or what is not to be done, and not otherwise.

Among those [terms], the inclusion of "action" (*kiriyā*) has the purpose of showing the distinction between the bodily and other [bases] as being with intimation (*saviññatti*) or without intimation (*aviññatti*).

The inclusion of the term "perception" (*saññā*) serves the purpose of demonstrating the distinction between what constitutes a factor (*aṅga*) and what does not constitute a factor of an offense, as well as the specific nature of the mind (*citta*).

Therefore, that state of mind which is present at the moment of either an active (*kiriyā*) or non-active (*akiriyā*) characteristic, or from which an action—whether active or non-active—proceeds, is not indiscriminately a factor or a non-factor of an offense.
Rather, it is that perception by which [the offense] is said to be "released through perception" (*saññāvimokkha*).
It is shown that the consciousness associated with that [state] is a factor (*aṅga*), while the other is not a factor (*anaṅga*).
Now, regarding the consciousness by which a training rule (*sikkhāpada*) becomes "with-mind" (*sacittaka*), its absence makes it "without-mind" (*acittaka*);
because of its faultiness (*sāvajjatā*) without such distinction, it is said to be "only a worldly offense" (*lokavajjameva*). However, being equally faulty, some are worldly offenses, while others—
The inclusion of the term "worldly offenses" (*lokavajja*) has the purpose of indicating that the mind is what is excluded by the term "offense through seeing.

Since it is the mind itself that is called "worldly offense," the inclusion of the term "action" (*kamma*) has the purpose of preventing the undesirable consequence that mental action (*manokamma*) might also constitute an offense.

Furthermore, as for the action here characterized by non-performance, its inclusion has the purpose of preventing the undesirable consequence that it might be excluded from the triad of wholesome states (*kusalattika*).

The inclusion of the "wholesome triad" (*kusalattika*) is for this purpose. As for the inclusion of the "indeterminate" (*abyākata*) here, since one who has attained cessation (*nirodhasamāpanna*) enters into a state that is partially indeterminate yet devoid of feeling, the "feeling triad" (*vedanāttika*) would not otherwise be applicable there;
thus, the inclusion of the feeling triad is intended to prevent such an undesirable consequence (*aniṭṭhapasaṅga*).

For the training rule (*sikkhāpada*), although it may be transgressed by one without consciousness, is designated as "three minds, three feelings" (*ticittaṃ tivedanaṃ*) by way of a person possessing consciousness.

“It is said that ‘the threefold mind is the threefold feeling. Herein, this is the supporting sutta: ‘There is an offense that one commits without a state of mind and emerges from without a state of mind;
there is an offense that one commits with a wholesome state of mind and emerges from with a wholesome state of mind,’ and so forth.
‘With a state of mind indicates an offense; release through perception indicates no offense; without a state of mind indicates not knowing the basis [of the offense].’”
"Non-perception-liberation is the non-knowing of transgression; this alone is their difference," so it is written.
Regarding the phrase "in the category of those involving the mind" (*sacittakapakkhe*), this is first the method of the *gaṇṭhipada*:

"In the category of those involving the mind" is said with reference to drinking liquor and so forth, which are [actions] without consciousness. However, among those involving the mind, that which arises exclusively from the unwholesome—both of these...

This is called a world-transgression (*lokavajja*). For regarding the drinking of intoxicants, if one drinks while knowing it is "intoxicant" (*surā*) or "not permitted to drink," it is indeed unwholesome (*akusala*).

In that context, the statement "knowing it is not permitted" is not tenable, because it would entail the undesirable consequence that even a formal transgression (*paṇṇattivajja*) would be a world-transgression. And wishing to avoid this undesirable consequence, the Venerable Vajirabuddhi [said]:

It is written: “In this context, the investigation as to whether it is ‘with consciousness’ or ‘without consciousness’ pertains only to the knowledge of the object (*vatthu*), not to the knowledge of the formal rule (*paññatti*).
If it pertained to the knowledge of the formal rule, all training rules (*sikkhāpada*) would be offenses by nature (*lokavajja*);
yet not all training rules are offenses by nature. Therefore, it pertains only to the knowledge of the object. This is [the meaning].
It is appropriate. Why? Because in the case of the training rules (*sekhiya*), the mere knowledge of the formal rule (*paññatti*) is the criterion, not the knowledge of the mere object (*vatthu*).

This, however, is the meaning here: taking the offense under the heading of the training rules, that training rule which involves a conscious state where the mind is exclusively unwholesome is a "worldly offense" (*lokavajja*); whereas that which is reckoned as unconscious—whether involving a conscious or unconscious state—is...
And in the case where there is consciousness, the mind is exclusively unwholesome; this too is a worldly offense such as drinking liquor.
It is with reference to this meaning that it was said: "That for which, in the presence of consciousness, the mind is exclusively unwholesome, this is called a worldly offense.
For the expression "in the presence of consciousness" is stated with reference to the state of being without consciousness; for [an offense] is not necessarily [unwholesome] when one is conscious.

Regarding the phrase “in the case of one possessing consciousness,” although there is a purpose for this qualification, even so, the meaning is that what was stated without restriction must be understood according to the restriction.
By the word “but” (*pana*) in the phrase “but as for animals,” he excludes [offenses] such as *thullaccaya*. Regarding the term “action” (*kiriyā*), here [the word] “standing” (*ṭhitaṃ*)...
If it is asked, "How is it that [the text] says 'he consents'?"—it is because "he consents" is stated, it is simply an action (*kiriyā*).
If this is so, should it not be called "bodily action" (*kāyakamma*) or "mental action" (*manokamma*)? No; it is called "bodily action" by way of common usage (*pacuravohāra*).
It is written that this applies to the act performed above the kneecaps (*ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalikā*); it should be understood by correlating it with the method explained previously.
“Monks, when the phrasing and syllables are poorly set down, the meaning too is difficult to discern,” says [the Blessed One].
Even by saying this, he intends that the phrasing and syllables be well-set down solely for the purpose of easily grasping the meaning, not for the sake of mere verbal recitation;
therefore, he said, “For the Protector spoke of the meaning as the refuge,” and so forth.
The commentary on the first *pārājika* is finished.
2. Commentary on the second *pārājika*:
"From a village or from a forest" is stated at the beginning because it was added as a supplementary definition (*lakkhaṇānupaññatti*). For in the entire Vinaya Piṭaka...

The fivefold classification of villages should be understood as follows: the village itself, the vicinity of the village, the fields of the village, the boundary of the village, and the vicinity of the boundary of the village.

Likewise, the fivefold classification of forest areas should be understood as follows: one type of non-village forest within the forest boundary, one type [of forest] for the rules concerning formal arrangements (*saṃvidhāna-sikkhāpada*), one type with a village nearby, one type for the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*), and one type for one who has left the community.

In this regard, there should also be understood the following distinctions: there is a village that does not receive any village-allowance anywhere, and there is a village that does not perform its village-duties;
likewise, there is a forest that does not receive any forest-allowance anywhere, and there is a forest that does not perform its forest-duties.

In that context, regarding the formal act of delimiting a non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*), with the exception of the phrase "the village and its precincts" (*gāmañca gāmūpacārañca*), here "village" (*gāma*) should be understood as follows:
if it is enclosed, it is the interior of the enclosure; if it is unenclosed, it is the interior of the space where an enclosure would stand.
This is what is referred to as "inside the village" (*antogāma*) in the *Udosita-sikkhāpada* and as "between houses" (*antaraghara*) in the *Sāsaṅka-sikkhāpada*.
He has arrived without suspicion. As it was said: “‘Should set it down within the village’ means she should set it down anywhere within the village of her alms-round.
Likewise, this same definition should be understood for the training rules (sekhiya) connected with being within a house. Regarding the rule:
“Whatever bhikkhunī should go alone between villages,” here too this same definition is intended: “of that which is enclosed...”
Because it is stated: "for one who crosses the boundary of a village, or for one who crosses the precincts of an unenclosed village.

As for the reading "for one who enters the precincts" found in certain ancient manuscripts, that was written through negligence by adopting a conventional usage established in the training rules regarding entering a village at an improper time;
it is not authoritative. And as for those manuscripts where [the rule] for entering a village at an improper time...
In the *Vibhaṅga*, it is written: "‘One should enter a village’ means: for one who crosses the enclosure of an enclosed village, or for one who crosses the precincts of an unenclosed village.
This is a scribal error. The reading there should be “for one who enters the precincts” (*upacāraṃ okkamantassa*).
For it is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*: “The precincts of an unenclosed village [are defined] in the context of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*)...”
"It should be understood in the manner already stated. Herein, it is also stated in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*: "Without having asked permission from a monk who is present...
[and so on] ...for one who enters the vicinity," and so forth.
However, as for that which appears in some manuscripts regarding the section on "between villages" (*gāmantara*) concerning a nun: "with one foot [inside] the other village... [etc.]...
The reading found is: “If he crosses the boundary, or enters the precinct, it is a thullaccaya;
as soon as he has crossed with the second [monk], and as soon as he has entered, it is a saṅghādisesa. In this context, the words “entered” and “as soon as he has entered” are redundant;
they were merely added by other scribes who copied the text. In some manuscripts, [it says] “as soon as he has entered...”
The word *ca* (“and”) is not seen [in one version], while the other is seen. These two readings contradict the Pāḷi, for the Pāḷi states:
“For one who crosses the precincts of an unenclosed village. Likewise, they contradict the *Samantapāsādikā*:
“If she crosses with one foot the place suitable for an enclosure, it is a *thullaccaya*; if she crosses with the second, it is a *saṅghādisesa*. Furthermore, in this case...”
For it is said: “...from one’s own village... when she has crossed with one foot over either the enclosure or the precinct of the other village, there is a thullaccaya;
as soon as she has crossed with the second foot, there is a saṅghādisesa.
And in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentary on this, after stating, “for her who is crossing the enclosure,” it says, “the same method applies to the precinct as well.”
And in the *Anugaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: "In some manuscripts, the phrase 'entering the precincts of an unenclosed village' (*okkamantiyā*) is also seen;
that should not be accepted. Furthermore, it is said: "By the expression 'transgressing the precincts of an unenclosed village,' it should be understood in this way:
when entering a village at an improper time, [the offense occurs] after two throws of a clod."

The precinct (*upacāra*) should be delimited in this manner; otherwise, just as here the phrase "one who exceeds" was used by treating the area eligible for enclosure as if it were the enclosure itself, so too there one would have had to say, "of one exceeding the precinct of an unenclosed village.
However, because in that case [the distance] beyond the area eligible for enclosure is only one *leḍḍupāta* (the throw of a clod).
“‘Vicinity’ (upacāra) is what is intended here. Therefore, for the purpose of illustrating that meaning, it was said: ‘for one entering the vicinity of an unenclosed village.

As for that which [is stated] in the Andhakaṭṭhakathā, having perceived the place worthy of an enclosure itself as the ‘vicinity,’ [it says]: ‘of the places worthy of an enclosure and of the places worthy of being beyond the enclosure...’”

It was said [in the commentary] "for the purpose of illuminating the distinction between the interior and the exterior" regarding one who enters the precincts; however, failing to perceive the specific difference in the Pāḷi, [one might think]:

"In the case of an unenclosed village, for one crossing the precincts—here, as if the precinct were an enclosure—for one who steps across that precinct with the first foot, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); for one who steps across with the second foot..."
It is stated, “there is an offense of *pācittiya*,” but that should not be accepted as it is, because there is a distinction in the Canon (*pāḷi*).
In the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, it is stated: “For a nun who crosses the precincts (*upacāra*), there is an offense of *gāmantara*.
Therefore, here in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*, this very reading must be understood: “…with one foot [and] the other… at the mere moment of crossing, there is a *saṅghādisesa*.”
To this extent, it should be understood that a "village" (*gāma*) refers precisely to the aforementioned delimitations within these aforementioned locations.
To illustrate this meaning, it was stated: "A village is said to be even a single hut," and so forth.

By virtue of this [definition], even in the absence of a surrounding boundary (*parikkhepa*), or when there is a transgression of the precincts (*upacāra*), or from the interior of a monastery (*ārāma*), or from a nunnery (*bhikkhunupassaya*), or from the lodgings of heretics (*titthiyaseyya*), or from a place of retreat (*paṭikkamana*).

The offenses related to the village (gāmapaccayā) should be understood as occurring by way of crossing either the boundary of the monastery grounds within that village or its precincts (upacāra) when entering it. Furthermore,

regarding the "precinct of a village" (gāmūpacāra), in the context of the phrase "excluding both the village and the precinct of the village," for a walled village, it refers specifically to the wall itself.
For an unenclosed village, it is simply the space where an enclosure would be. For this is stated in the Commentary:
"The 'vicinity of a village' (gāmūpacāra) is the enclosure of an enclosed village; for an unenclosed village, it is the space where an enclosure would be.
A monk who has resolved upon his robes within these [boundaries] does not receive the privilege. What, then, is the reason here by which this is considered a village or the vicinity of a village?
And how is it that here it is otherwise, while elsewhere it is thus? It is on account of the occasion (aṭṭhuppatti).

For, regarding this occasion—namely, "At that time, monks, thinking 'The Blessed One has permitted the authorization not to be separated from the three robes,' they deposited their robes within inhabited areas"—it was said:
"except for the village and the vicinity of the village. Therefore, wherever there is the perception of an inhabited area, [the rule applies].
In this regard, it should be understood that the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) does not extend there. For that reason, in the *Udositā-sikkhāpada*, it is stated:
"Having deposited one's robe within the village, one must dwell within the village," and "Whether in the assembly hall or at the gate, one must not go beyond arm’s reach.
Indeed, while staying right in the *kappiya-bhūmi* (the place where allowable goods are kept), one [remains in possession of] the robe deposited in the *kappiya-bhūmi*.
He guards [the robe]. Regarding the training rule concerning danger (*sāsaṅka-sikkhāpada*), however, it is said:
"Because one who stays apart from the village where the robe was deposited is said to be staying apart from the robe, therefore he re-enters the village boundary, dwells there, and then departs.
For in that training rule, what is intended by the term "village" is the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*). In that context, at an improper time...

In the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the training rule regarding entering a village, it is stated: "For one who crosses the enclosure of an enclosed village, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
From this statement, it is clear that the enclosure itself is not the village; rather, it is shown by implication to be the village precinct (*gāmūpacāra*).

However, in this particular analysis of the training rule, beginning with the words "What is called the village precinct? and continuing with "of an unenclosed [village]... [the definition is further elaborated].

By the statement, "The range of a clod thrown by a man of medium height standing at the edge of the houses of a village," it is established that for an unenclosed area, the space where the enclosure would have stood constitutes the village precinct (*gāmūpacāra*). Because that meaning is applicable, the *Kurunda-aṭṭhakathā* and the *Mahāpaccarī* also state:
"The range of a clod thrown by one standing at that edge of the house is the village precinct. For the precinct (*upacāra*) is [defined as] "the village..."

In passages such as "a single precinct, not various precincts," it refers to the gateway; in the passage "the open air is a single precinct," it refers to the measurement defined as seven *abbhantara*s on all sides.

Therefore, it should be understood that the *Andhakaṭṭhakathā* states: "'Village precinct' means the enclosure of an enclosed village, and the space of the enclosure of an unenclosed village. The same is stated in the *Kurundi* and the *Mahāpaccarī*.
Likewise, it is seen in the Pāḷi as well in such passages as: “‘Within the monastery’ (ajjhārāmo) means: for an enclosed monastery, the interior of the monastery;
for an unenclosed one, the precincts. ‘Within the dwelling’ (ajjhāvasatho) means: for an enclosed dwelling, the interior of the dwelling; for an unenclosed one, the precincts.
However, in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, it is seen in such passages as “the village precincts” (*gāmūpacāro*). Therefore...
The second stone-throw is intended as the precinct (upacāra).

Because of the occurrence of a specific passage in the Canon stating, "For one entering the precinct of an unenclosed village, there is an offense of pācittiya," it is said that the first stone-throw is the village itself, while the second is the precinct of the village. However, in the case of an enclosed village...
Regarding the statement, "The range of a stone’s throw from the threshold of a middle-sized man is called the village precinct," there is no difference here.
Up to this point, both types of precincts for an enclosed area and the fourfold precincts for an unenclosed area—
wherever they occur and wherever they do not— are all demonstrated.

The characteristics of both the village field (*gāmakhettassa*) and the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*) have been stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* itself. For in meaning, the two are one. Therein, the nature of the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*) as a "village" is to be understood by way of the training rule concerning dangerous places (*sāsaṅkasikkhāpada*).
What is called the "vicinity of the village boundary" (*gāmasīmūpacāra*) is the place frequented by people who are forest-gatherers seeking firewood, grass, flowers, fruits, and so forth.
This vicinity of the village boundary is mentioned in the *Udositasikkhāpada*: "In a forest where there is no village, within seven *abbhantara*s on all sides."
This should be understood from the Khandhaka on the "Place Where [the Buddha] Arrived.
For there, while showing the boundary for monks living in villages, the Blessed One says, "Whatever village or town he dwells near," and thereby demonstrates it.
Immediately after that, by means of the words "in a non-village" and so forth, he shows the seven-league boundary. Therefore, whichever monk [dwells near] a village or a town...

It should be understood that for one who does not dwell in dependence [on a village], but is traveling on a journey by boat or by land, a seven-abhyantara boundary is obtained at each respective location. For it is said:
"There is a caravan belonging to a single family; having deposited one's robe in the caravan, one must not leave the area within seven abhyantaras either ahead or behind," and so forth.
Referring to this very forest, it is said: "In the forest boundary, there is one uninhabited forest area. This refers to what is stated in the Canon:

"In an uninhabited forest, for every half-yojana, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). This is what is called "one uninhabited forest area" in the training rules concerning appointments (*saṃvidhāna-sikkhāpada*).
However, by the former [definition], that which includes dwellings is comprised; by this [latter definition], that is not comprised. This refers to what is stated in the section on leaving the group.

In the *Aṭṭhakathā* it is said: "Regarding the phrase 'in a forest where there is no village,' the definition stated as 'having gone out beyond the threshold post, all this is forest' refers to that which is called 'forest.
However, this is called 'without a village' (*agāmaka*) solely because of the absence of a village, not because of its similarity to the Vindhya wilderness.
With reference to this, it is said: "A dwelling place called 'forest-dwelling' (*āraññaka*) is [located] five hundred bow-lengths..."
"Last" is what was said. This is called a forest dwelling (*āraññaka-senāsana*): for an enclosed area, it is outside the enclosure;
for an unenclosed area, it is outside the space where an enclosure would have been. Whether there are trees or no trees, even if the monastery is crowded with people, it is called a forest.
Likewise, it is said: "One [robe] for one who has left the group. This too is indeed a forest. However, this...

In a place that was previously uninhabited, having departed while possessing the characteristics already described, one incurs only a single offense upon crossing the threshold of the gate (indakhīla) and leaving the range of visibility; beyond that, there is no offense.
However, regarding the rule stated as "one [offense] for the training rules on making arrangements," one incurs one offense for each half-yojana, but not for distances less than that.
The other three [distances] fall short of the aforementioned boundaries; they do not fulfill the rule stated therein, but rather exceed it.
In this way, their mutual distinction should be understood.
Among those, regarding the fivefold village, that which is defined as "the range of a clod thrown from the boundary pillar of an enclosed village" is...
That which was stated has not found application anywhere in the Vinaya Piṭaka;
it was mentioned solely for the purpose of illustrating that "the village precinct" (*gāmūpacāra*) consists of one stone’s throw beyond the area where an unfenced village is enclosed by a fence.
Even for a fenced-in village, one stone’s throw is said to be the precinct equivalent to a *kappiyabhūmi* (an area where food may be prepared), let alone for an unfenced village beyond its enclosure.

It is one [offense]. However, because it is evident and because it occurs in the open air, one incurs this offense when entering [a village], with the exception of the offense regarding the interval between villages for a bhikkhunī.
For bhikkhunīs, while staying within that village vicinity defined as "the range of a second stone's throw," they incur an offense;
and upon entering the village, they incur the offense regarding the interval between villages. Indeed, the place where they stay is reckoned as forest.
For it is said: "While he is walking, his shadow must be measured... [and so on]... you should explain to him the three dependencies and the eight things not to be done.

Furthermore, because the training rules connected with the forest and the training rule regarding entering a village at an improper time are not common to bhikkhunīs, and because it is stated that returning from between the monastery and the bhikkhunīs' quarters constitutes a *kappiya-bhūmi* (a place where food may be accepted).
And because of the formulation of the training rule (sikkhāpada) beginning with, “If one should be left behind from the group,

there is an offense of thullaccaya for one who leaves the range of sight or the range of hearing of her companion nun in a forest that is not a village,” and according to the method of the Bhikkhunikkhandhaka,
starting from the threshold post (indakhīla) of an enclosed village or from the precincts (upacāra) of an unenclosed one.
It is led [there], and because monks dwell there with the four factors combined when robes have been deposited within the village compound, it is therefore called "with a village.
Regarding the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*), one [point] is as follows: "Monks, a bhikkhunī must not dwell in the forest; should she dwell [there]..."

From the statement, "There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," it is established that there is no such thing as forest-dwelling for bhikkhunīs. For if a bhikkhunī-upassaya exists in the forest, there is an offense for one who leaves the vicinity for seeing or hearing even within the boundary of the residence when she is separated from her companion. Therefore, regarding the section on the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*), in the phrase "except for the village and the village precinct," that which [is excluded]— [...is explained as follows: ...the village and its precincts are excluded; however, the forest is not excluded. Consequently, if a bhikkhunī’s upassaya is located in the forest, the entire area of the forest constitutes the non-separation boundary. Thus, even if she leaves the vicinity for seeing or hearing, there is no offense. This is because the forest is not included in the aforementioned exclusion. However, if a bhikkhunī’s upassaya is located within a village, the entire village and its precincts constitute the non-separation boundary. Therefore, if she leaves the vicinity for seeing or hearing even within the village precincts, there is an offense. This is because the village is included in the aforementioned exclusion. Furthermore, if a bhikkhunī’s upassaya is located at the edge of a village, the village and its precincts constitute the non-separation boundary, while the forest does not. Therefore, if she leaves the vicinity for seeing or hearing even within the village precincts, there is an offense. This is because the village is included in the aforementioned exclusion. However, if she leaves the vicinity for seeing or hearing outside the village precincts, there is no offense. This is because the forest is not included in the aforementioned exclusion. In this context, the term "forest" (*arañña*) refers to a place where there are no villages or village precincts, or a place beyond the limit of a village and its precincts. Having clearly observed this method and deliberated upon it, the teachers should apply it there as appropriate.
Otherwise— One who does not understand the great majesty of the Buddha;
He who, being ignorant, praises the profundity of the method of the Dhamma and that Vinaya which is difficult to see— such a person is a cause for the destruction of the Teaching.
He who, failing to understand the Pāḷi and its meaning,
destroys the method of the Aṭṭhakathā,

"Village" means he is placed at the very front by that very same great multitude;

Regarding the phrase "in substance it is one," here the word *saṅkhā* is equated with the word *saṅkhāta*. The term "should take" (*ādiyeyya*) is a common expression applicable to all twenty-five modes of theft.

In the case of a hypothetical arrangement of space, even though the removal from the place is included, it is protected because it was merely a hypothetical arrangement of space. It is simply the transgression of the space [that constitutes the offense].
The measure [of the offense] is due to its having been taken previously with an impure mind. Some say that it remains the same even when taken now with a pure mind;
however, that is not correct. In this matter, the detailed exposition should be understood by consulting the *Samantapāsādikā*.
"There is no removal" means there is no displacement from the position [of the offense].

and not merely by way of accomplishing the purpose. for cutting creepers and so forth, it is indeed an offense of expiation. However, having gone there, for cutting creepers that have grown on the top of a water-jar, it is an offense of wrong-doing because of being a simultaneous preparation.
[As it is said: "In the case of a single load, this is thus heavy; 'you take one side, I too will take one side'..."
"Having made an agreement, saying 'I shall take it,' when the displacement from its place is effected through the application of both [body and speech], it originates from body, speech, and mind.
Otherwise, either the manual act (*sāhatthika*) would not be a factor for the directive act (*āṇattika*), or the directive act would not be a factor for the manual act;
thus it contradicts the stated characteristic," so it is written in the *Vinayagaṇṭhipada*. Furthermore, the word "and" (*pi*) is written in that very same place.
Regarding any offense that may arise from both body and speech,
it is the vocal factor and the mind alone that constitute its formal act (*kamma*). Furthermore, whatever threefold classification of acts there may be—
such as those consisting of action (*kiriyā*) and non-action (*akiriyā*), and so forth— it is likewise defined by these.
"That is not appropriate because of its contradiction; only a single act is appropriate.

3. Commentary on the third *pārājika*.

Just as full understanding through knowledge (*ñātapariññā*) is simply the knowing of the intrinsic nature of phenomena, such as "this is form, this is feeling," whereas full understanding through investigation (*tīraṇapariññā*) occurs by way of impermanence and so forth along with the intrinsic nature of phenomena, such as "form is impermanent" and so on; even so,
here it is said "he would deprive [a being] of life" because there is no taking of life when one has willed [the act] together with [the object] as a single unity.
Because it is stated as "a human being," he says "starting from the kalala" in order to show [the process] beginning from the most subtle state of existence, namely that of those in the womb.
Herein, one who deprives [a being] of life separates them from the present.
In that context, it is impossible to deprive one of the momentary present; rather, [one deprives them of] the serially present or the temporally present.

Or it is possible. How so? When that effort has been made, the life-decad (*jīvitadasaka*)—having received that effort—becomes a condition for [the cessation of] what is ceasing, being weak and its momentum exhausted.

The present-by-continuity (*santatipaccuppanna*) ceases after having impelled two or three thought-moments (*javana*), and the present-by-duration (*addhāpaccuppanna*) likewise ceases by performing its function accordingly; such is the condition.

It exists. Then, whether it is the present of the continuum (*santati-paccuppanna*) or the present of the duration (*addhā-paccuppanna*), it ceases in the interval before reaching the time as delimited.
Thus, both of these can be deprived of life. Therefore, he distinguishes the "present.
With the words, "But for this matter," he explains the meaning stated by way of conventional usage (*vohāra-vasena*) by way of the ultimate sense (*paramattha-vasena*): "A living being..."
"It is to be understood," and so forth, was said. It is called "application" (*payoga*) because it is employed together with volition (*cetanā*) accompanied by bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*).
What is this? It is the striking of the body with a weapon or the like; that is, the application of a weapon to another's body by means of volition accompanied by both bodily and verbal intimations.
"Standing at a distance" means whether one stands far away or nearby. A blow [delivered] by something released from the hand.

It is an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*). "Therein" means in the act of forfeiture. Regarding the phrase "let whoever [be] die," it is not possible here in a large crowd of people [to specify].

"Commanding" (*āṇāpana*) is the accomplishment of the intended object by means of volition accompanied by vocal intimation (*vacī-viññatti*). For this very reason, [the text says] "desiring to make them hear..."
"It does not cause [the offense] to be proclaimed," it is said. "Determiners of the command" means those which accomplish the application of the command;
for it is only when these are not lacking that the application of the command occurs, and not otherwise. Regarding "the presentation of form": here—
If one approaches with a malicious mind, thinking, "May this woman die because of my lack of gain," he is a woman-killer.
But if he approaches for the sake of begging, even though he knows [her state], he is not a killer.
For he is indifferent to her death; he is not concerned with that.
But one who knows, "My wife and my mother are dying through separation from me," and yet separates them while being intent on his own purpose—he is a destroyer.
If, knowing it to be a sign of renunciation and the like, he goes forth, he is not a bringer of death;
for he is indifferent toward that death and has no desire for it.
Having explained the meaning of the word *hāraka* through its various divisions, [the author] says "and the weapon" in order to show that both are one and the same.

The passage beginning with “and that which carries it away” has been stated. By this, he demonstrates the application (*payoga*) of the stable [mind] among the applications such as those performed by one’s own hand (*sāhatthika*).
Although the word *iti* has been extracted in the phrase “thus, mind and thought” (*iti cittamanaso*), its meaning has not yet been explained.

Even though it has not been explicitly stated, one should connect the word *iti* as it occurs by way of topical context; thus, in the phrase “the intention of the mind” (*iti cittasaṅkappo*), one should understand it as “perceiving death. (*maraṇasaññī*)

Because it is stated, “one whose consciousness is directed toward death, one whose intention is death,” it should be understood that he will speak only of death. "By the method already stated" means by way of the six applications (*payoga*).

In the cases of the direct application (*sāhatthika*) and the indirect application (*nissaggiya*), the status of being a direct application is to be understood through the bodily intimation (*kāyaviññatti*) arising together with the seventh volition, which is the volition of final determination (*sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā*). However, in the case of the application by command (*āṇattika*), it is together with all seven types of volition.
Due to the arising of vocal intimation (*vacīviññatti*), seven sounds arise together and, having combined into the state of each individual syllable,

convey one's intended meaning through however many syllables are required; it should be understood that the status of this as an instruction (*āṇattika*) belongs to the vocal intimation co-nascent with the seventh volition (*cetanā*) which originates the final syllable.
The commentary on the third *pārājika* is finished.
4. Commentary on the fourth *pārājika*:
If it is asked how the phrases "thus I know" and "thus I see" are explained here, he says "thus I know," and so forth.
It is indicated by the specific mention of "evil desire" (*pāpicchatā*) alone that there is no offense for one who acts out of dullness or delusion.
When one says, "In the past, I was a stream-enterer," one speaks figuratively, as in such expressions as "The monk who dwells in your monastery is an Arahant.
Likewise, in the training rule (*sikkhāpada*), the phrase "I know thus" refers only to the present.
The commentary on the fourth *pārājika* is finished.

If it is asked, "Since the matricide, patricide, and murderer of an *arahant* have fallen into the third *pārājika*, and the violator of a nun, Lambī, and the other three have fallen into the first *pārājika*, how can there be twenty-four?"—the answer is: No, because their underlying intention (*adhippāya*) was not understood.
For the four beginning with the matricide are intended here as those who have not been ordained at all.
Although the four beginning with Lambī are included under the first *pārājika*, they are mentioned separately because they engage in sexual intercourse by way of a particular method.
Regarding the phrase "he does not obtain [association] with the bhikkhus," here "association" refers to the communal life consisting of the *uposatha* and other such observances.

This much has been said. In the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: “[The Saṅgha] is distinguished by the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, the recitation of the Pātimokkha, and the formal acts of the Saṅgha (*saṅghakamma*).
In the Canon (*Pāḷi*), it is stated: "'Living together' means performing a formal act together, reciting the Pātimokkha together, and being subject to the same training.
It is prohibited that one should perform a formal act of the Saṅgha in any of these three ways. "Monks, [one should not do so] in an assembly where a householder is seated..."
The passage beginning with "the Pātimokkha should be recited" occurs specifically in the context of the Pātimokkha and Pavāraṇā ceremonies;
however, there is no prohibition against performing the remaining formal acts (*kamma*) in other such instances. The teachers also say: "It is permissible to perform the remaining formal act;
there is no offense. [This applies even] when one accuses another who has committed the final offense (*antimavatthu*) of a groundless *pārājika* offense.

It is stated that for one who accuses [another] of a *saṅghādisesa* offense, it is a *pācittiya*, just as it is for a monk; it is not a *dukkaṭa* as it is for one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).
Therefore, the teachers say that sleeping together with such a person and receiving gifts from them is permissible for a monk.
"As before, so after"—this refers to the rule: "A single legal act, a single recitation, and equality in training."
They say that this was stated with reference merely to the incapacity of one who has spoken thus to live in communion; this should be investigated.
Now, as a miscellaneous point common to all four [Pārājikas]: there is one who, by practicing sexual intercourse, becomes defeated (pārājika) and is no longer in communion;
there is one who does not become defeated but is no longer in communion; and there is one who does not become defeated and remains in communion.
Whether in the case of a *dukkaṭa* offense or a *thullaccaya* offense, there is one who commits [an act] and yet is not a *pārājika*:
a *pakkhapāṇḍaka* (one who is a *paṇḍaka* only for half the time) who was ordained during the non-*paṇḍaka* phase, and while in the *paṇḍaka* phase, he engages in sexual intercourse.
He does not incur an offense and is therefore called "not a *pārājika*. For indeed, there is no such thing as an "offense" for one who is not a monk. He...
Since he is one who is not guilty of an offense, he is included among the side of those who are not paṇḍakas; does this constitute non-co-residence (*asaṃvāsa*)? It does. For it is said:
"He is incapable [of the training] by virtue of that bodily bond. And because it is stated: "But whichever bhikkhu, having undertaken the training and the way of life of the bhikkhus...
[is] non-co-resident," it is precisely he who, while possessing the status of a bhikkhu, engages in sexual intercourse who is incapable [of the training].

If it is argued that this does not constitute an *apārājika* offense, we say no. This should be understood as being analogous to the case where it is stated, "The Saṅgha should be informed by a learned and competent monk";
even if the formal act (*kammavācā*) is recited by one who is not a bhikkhunī, the act remains valid because a failure of the formal act (*kammavipatti*) is impossible.
In this regard, however, there is this distinction: if one who has previously been fully ordained [recites] the formal act in this manner...
If he proclaims it and the Saṅgha perceives him as one who has already been ordained, the legal act (*kamma*) succeeds; otherwise it does not—this is the teacher’s view.
Even if a householder, a member of another sect, or a paṇḍaka proclaims the formal act (*kammavācā*), the *kammavācā* has not been uttered by the Saṅgha.
For according to the statement: "The Saṅgha should ordain; the Saṅgha ordains; he is ordained by the Saṅgha."

Because it is to be recited by means of a formal motion (*kammavācā*) by one included within the Saṅgha—or by one who is perceived as being included within the Saṅgha—it should be understood that when spoken by such a person, it is "spoken by the Saṅgha. It is not [spoken] by anyone else among householders, members of other sects, eunuchs, and so forth.
This very principle should be seen as the rule for all formal acts (*kamma*).
Likewise, there is the case of one who commits sexual intercourse;

since it is stated, "He who is a defiler of a bhikkhunī is to be expelled," by that very act he—though not yet fully ordained—incurs the offense of sharing a sleeping place with her or some other similar offense, and for insulting her, there is a *dukkaṭa*. One who commits sexual intercourse with a non-bhikkhunī...
He is not to be expelled; for there is no such passage in the Pāḷi stating, "Bhikkhus, one who has committed an offense involving the ultimate penalty, if not yet ordained, is not to be ordained.
Therefore, he is reckoned as ordained; he does not incur offenses such as sleeping in the same bed, and so forth.

He is merely considered one who is not in communion (asaṃvāsa), and thus he does not count toward fulfilling the quorum. For it is said that "communion" (saṃvāsa) consists in performing formal acts together and reciting the discourses together.
"Because they have trained equally, there is communal living"—on this basis, he does not have [communal living] with him.
However, the phrase "he incurs an offense of *padasodhamma*" indicates that the shadow of the underlying reason is visible.

Just as a nun is not in communal living with the Saṅgha of monks due to the absence of communal living—such as through a single formal act (*ekakamma*)—with her, so too is the monk [not in communal living] with the nun; thus, he incurs an offense of *padasodhamma*.

However, it does not produce [the offense]. Likewise, even one who has committed the ultimate offense (antimavatthu) does not incur [the penalty] because, by the example of the statement "he who is to be destroyed," the shadow of the underlying reason is overlooked.
Furthermore, this is because of the statements, "both are to be expelled" and "the defiler is to be expelled," as well as the statement, "expel the nun Mettiyā."
Furthermore, one who has entered into the midst of the Saṅgha and, while being investigated by an investigator, is defeated—he too is as if unordained;
it should be understood that he does not generate an offense of expiation for abusive speech (*omasavāda-pācittiya*).
Moreover, in this context, the fourfold set regarding those who have renounced the training (*sikkhāpaccakkhātaka*) should be understood. For there exists a person who has renounced the training.

There is a person who has neither renounced the training nor entered upon the mode of livelihood of the training; there is a person who has not renounced the training but has entered upon the mode of livelihood of the training;
there is a person who has both renounced the training and entered upon the mode of livelihood of the training;

and there is a person who has neither renounced the training nor entered upon the mode of livelihood of the training. In this regard, the third [category] refers to a nun who has renounced the training.

This should be understood. For as long as she does not relinquish her gender, even while she is still zealous for the yellow robes and desirous of falling away from the state of a recluse, she remains a bhikkhunī, having entered upon the training and the way of life. Indeed, it was said by the Blessed One:
"There is no renunciation of the training for a bhikkhunī, monks. But when does she cease to be a bhikkhunī?
When she comes to be designated as "one who has gone astray" (*vibbhantā*). For it was said by the Blessed One:
"At the very moment she has gone astray, at that very moment she is no longer a bhikkhunī. But to what extent is she one who has gone astray?

When, desiring to fall away from the state of a recluse, she has no attachment to the saffron robes—either she removes the saffron robe, or she goes about naked, or she goes about having covered herself with grass, leaves, and so forth—even while still wearing the saffron robe...
Or if he dresses in the manner of a householder’s clothing, or puts on white garments,
or enters among the heretics together with their distinctive marks and undertakes vows such as the plucking out of hair, or adopts the sectarian mark of the heretics—
then he is said to have "left the order. In that context, one who, while remaining within the [monastic] marks themselves, undertakes the vows of a heretic, is [one who has left the order].
Like a monk who has gone over to the faction of the non-Buddhist sects (*titthiya*), he does not obtain even the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) later on.

The others obtain only the going-forth, but not the full ordination (*upasampadā*). Although in the Canon it says, "Monks, whatever nun who was formerly in our own community has gone over to the sphere of the non-Buddhists, she should not be ordained upon her return," this refers to one who first disrobed and later [returned].
It appears as if it were permitted that she who has gone over to another religious order (*titthāyatana*) should be ordained upon her return;

however, because the teachers of the Council stated, "There are twenty-four *pārājika* offenses," she may not be ordained again. For this very reason, the Blessed One did not permit the renunciation of the training.
Yet, one who has committed the ultimate offense (*antimavatthu*) remains a bhikkhunī. This also applies to one who is a eunuch by faction (*pakkhapaṇḍakī*).
It is the same for a bhikkhunī. Having applied this method to all four [cases], it should be explained as appropriate.
The commentary on the Pārājika is finished.
The Section on Saṅghādisesa.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Emission of Semen (*sukkavissaṭṭhi-sikkhāpada*).
"Except in a dream" (*aññatra supinantā*): Because the volition (*cetanā*) here has a weak basis, it is incapable of drawing forth rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*).
For the sign (*nimitta*) appearing in a dream is weak. However, in the course of existence (*pavatta*), [that volition] is supported by other wholesome and unwholesome states.

It yields a result. Although it does yield a result, nevertheless, because it arises in regard to what is not its proper domain, it is recorded as being "non-categorical" (abbohārika) volition in a dream.
As for what is stated here—that "the sign appearing in a dream is weak"—that is not an absolute rule;

nor is the occurrence of consciousness weak simply because of the weakness of the object, as in the case of consciousness whose objects are past or future, or whose object is a conceptual construct (paññatti).

Or [it is so] because of its weakness. Therefore, the teacher [Vajirabuddhi] maintains that the phrase "because it has a weak basis" means "because it has a weak heart as its basis," and this is not a mere logical inference.
If it is argued that weakness is appropriate due to the absence of a physical basis (*avatthukatā*), we say no;

for in the case of that which arises from meditation (*bhāvanā*), even though it lacks a physical basis, there is the possibility of an exceeding strength. Indeed, a mind endowed with the power of meditation, even while being formless (*arūpa*), can bear an exceedingly heavy burden.
Having taken up the body born of karma (*karajakāya*), it places it even in the Brahma-world in a single moment of consciousness;
likewise, it makes even an unextended sense-sphere consciousness (*kāmāvacaracitta*) capable of leaping through the air with that very body born of karma.

What, then, is the inferential reason here by which this is known to be the power of consciousness alone? It is because one sees the production of specific actions, such as placing and leaping, brought about through the influence of consciousness.
Because it is unmixed, like matter originated by natural consciousness (*pakaticitta-samuṭṭhāna-rūpa*), and because it issues forth, teachers designate three locations for semen:
the head of the organ, the waist, and the body. It should be viewed as being like snake venom;
yet there is no fixed location for the venom—it occurs according to where one looks with anger. Likewise, for this [semen], there is no fixed location; it occurs according to passion (*rāga*).
"It does not happen for one who merely attempts it," says the Teacher.

If it is objected that the phrase "even without having entered the water" contradicts the phrase "as soon as he has entered," [the author] said "but having fallen from his place," etc., in order to show that.
Its meaning is: having performed an effort toward the sign and having caused the semen to move from its place...
Furthermore, it is not possible to prevent the descent into the stream of water by means of remorse;

nevertheless, having accepted [the matter] with the intention of enduring it, because it is impossible to prevent it from going further up from the stream of water, it is said, "or when it has gone outside.
Therefore, the intention of the Commentary is that once it has fallen from its place, it necessarily descends into the stream of water. Thus:
It should be understood that "both meet.
Here it is asked: Why is the agent not specified in this training rule by means of the formula "whosoever monk," and so forth?
It is said: The agent is not specified because [the action] exists in dependence upon an intention; this is for the purpose of showing its state of being dependent.
How so? For one who intends by way of the volition aimed at scratching an itch and the like, or for one who makes an effort by way of such an effort as scratching an itch;

or for one who makes an effort upon the thighs and other parts that are objects of a *dukkaṭa* offense, or upon wounds and the like that are objects of a *thullaccaya* offense, due to lust for sexual intercourse—even if semen is emitted—there is no *saṅghādisesa*, because [the Sutta states]: "There is no offense for a bhikkhu who does not have the intention to emit."
Because it is [already] stated by way of the words. Therefore, for the purpose of demonstrating that meaning, no agent (*kāraka*) is specified here.
Otherwise, if the agent were specified in the rule, "Whatever bhikkhu should commit an intentional emission of semen, it is a *saṅghādisesa*," there would be a contradiction with the statement:
"If one intends but does not make an effort and emission occurs, there is no offense. Likewise, regarding "intentional emission of semen..."

Even though the locative case is indicated in the phrase "except in a dream, it is a *saṅghādisesa* offense," that same contradiction remains because the restriction of the causal sense (*hetvattha*) is not established.
Therefore, setting aside both of those grammatical sequences, it is stated: "Intentional emission of semen, except in a dream, is a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
In that context, since there is no use of the locative case in the sense of a "sign" (*nimitta*), the restriction of the causal sense does not apply.

It is completed. It should be understood that this meaning is illustrated by the statement: "When that [act] has not been performed, intentional emission of semen, except during sleep, is a *saṅghādisesa*; when there is no undertaking, there is no offense.
In this training rule (*sikkhāpada*), there are two thousand offenses. How so? [In the case of] internal form, such as one's own hand and so forth...
When the sexual organ has become functional through the stiffening of lust (*rāgūpatthambhana*), there is one offense for one who emits semen that is blue for the sake of health;
there are nine for the emission of yellow and so forth when the stiffening of lust occurs within internal forms (*ajjhattarūpa*) alone—thus ten.
In this way, by way of the nine [factors] beginning with "for the sake of pleasure," there are one hundred offenses based on internal forms during the stiffening of lust.

In the same way, for each instance of excrement, urine, wind, high places, small creatures, or being bitten by insects, there are one hundred [offenses], making five hundred in total. Just as there are five hundred offenses regarding internal form, so too for external form or internal-external form,
or when shaking the hips in space, there are two thousand offenses.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the emission of semen is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning physical contact:
By the word "entered" (*otiṇṇo*), his state of intent for sexual intercourse is shown. For that very reason, it refers to one who possesses lust for physical contact.
It is called an "appellation. By the phrase "together with one who has undergone change...," his exertion is shown.
For the word "together" (saddhiṃ) indicates conjunction, and that conjunction is meeting. With what mind?
With a mind that has undergone change, not with the intention of receiving alms-bowls and so forth—this is the intended meaning. By the phrase "he should enter into physical contact," his...
The discernment of contact through exertion is thus shown. For one who, having exerted himself, discerns contact, is said to "enter" [attainment].
In this way, his accomplishment of the three factors is demonstrated. Alternatively, it is like a being such as a *yakkha* who has descended with a transformed mind;
or, this instrumental case is used in the sense of the accusative: "one who has descended into a transformed mind."
A being is like one who has fallen into a well or similar pit.

Alternatively, even a monk who has entered the monastic life with the thought, "I shall emerge from passion," may—due to a mind that has become perverted from its original intention to emerge—fall back into that very same passion, with that [perverted mind] acting as the cause.
This refers to a woman either coming into his presence or having approached him herself. By this, [the nature of] the woman...
Whether there is passion or dispassion, that is what constitutes the "immeasurable" (appamāṇa) here. Regarding the phrase "taking by the hand":
here, the entire body as a grasped entity (upādinnaka) is included, but not external things connected to it such as clothing or ornaments, which belong to a different continuity (bhinnasantāna).
By the mention of "taking by the fist," those things not grasped (anupādinnaka) but belonging to the same continuity—such as the tips of the hair, body hair, nails, and teeth—are included.
It should be understood that what is included here is that which is produced by temperature (utu) conditioned by kamma. Therefore it was said: "even for one who touches hair with hair.

By this, in the phrase "or for anyone else... [omission] ...or touching," one should understand that even the remaining hairs and so forth, though not clung-to (anupādinnaka), serve as constituent parts.
This being so, does it not contradict the rule: "For one who claims contact, there is a Saṅghādisesa offense"?

Why? Because it is by knowing that specific purpose [of contact]. Even one who discerns the state of being touched is said to "acknowledge the contact" (*phassa*), and not merely through the arising of body-consciousness (*kāya-viññāṇa*). Here, body-consciousness is inconclusive; therefore, for this very reason, the discernment of contact is not stated here as a necessary factor.
For if that were stated, there would be the possibility [of the objection]: "And yet, even when my hair is brushed..."
“Body-consciousness has arisen; regarding that, one might have the perception: ‘I do not acknowledge contact. [The commentator] says:

“What is called a *veṇī* is associated with a garland of coins and the like; therein, thinking ‘I will take the *veṇī*,’ one takes only the garland of coins and so forth, not the hair itself, and there is no *saṅghādisesa* offense. This must be investigated.
The commentary on the training rule concerning physical contact is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning indecent speech:
The request, "When will your mother be pleased? is for the purpose of showing the characteristic of an offense under the training rule concerning indecent speech.
This was stated in order to show that not only speech connected with sexual intercourse constitutes "vulgar speech" (*duṭṭhulla-vācā*).

However, the expression "those who possess both genders" (*ubhatobyañjanaka*) is a statement mixed with a basis for an offense involving a non-*saṅghādisesa* [offense] due to the male characteristic. For a male *ubhatobyañjanaka*, the female characteristic is concealed, while the other is manifest.
If one were to produce semen even by means of that [concealed characteristic], how could there be such statements as "you are without a characteristic" (*animitta*) and so forth?
Some say that the words do not produce a *saṅghādisesa* offense; however, that is not correct, because [the term] is also a designation for the male organ.

Furthermore, since the characteristic is stated in the *mātikā* as "in connection with sexual intercourse, there is a *saṅghādisesa*," there is a *saṅghādisesa* when one makes a proposal in connection with sexual intercourse and the other understands it;
if she does not understand it, there is a *thullaccaya*. In the case of proposals by means of other [terms],...
For one who understands [the meaning], it is a thullaccaya; for one who does not understand, it is a dukkaṭa—so say some;
this must be determined after careful consideration. Here it is asked: "When one reviles with words such as 'Sikharaṇī,' a mind of resentment (paṭighacitta) arises;

why, then, is it not said to be 'threefold-feeling' (tivedana), but is instead called 'twofold-feeling' (dvivedana)? This offense is by way of lust (rāga), not by way of resentment. Therefore, it is only by way of lust...
What is intended here is abuse that has actually occurred. Therefore, the statement "two kinds of feeling" is indeed well-said.
The commentary on the training rule concerning offensive speech is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning one who desires his own welfare.
"In one capable of discerning what is grave and what is not grave" means: in one who is able to distinguish between what is a grave offense (*duṭṭhulla*) and what is not.
There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in praising the gratification of one's own desires for another bhikkhu.

There is also an offense of wrong-doing in speaking by way of indirect speech, such as: "Give the finest gift—sexual intercourse—to whoever lives in your monastery. [This applies to] praising the gratification of one's own desires...
Some say it is because it is stated: "One might speak to one like me who is virtuous. Others say it is a *saṅghādisesa* offense because all five factors [of the rule] are present;

this should be determined after careful consideration. Regarding these two training rules, they say that just as in the case of physical contact, there is a *thullaccaya* for indecent speech directed at a female *yakkha* or a female *petī*. However, it is written that this has not appeared in the *Aṭṭhakathās*.
The hermaphrodite (ubhatobyañjanaka), however, belongs to the same category as the eunuch (paṇḍaka).
The commentary on the training rule concerning one's own desire is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule concerning matchmaking (sañcaritta).

“*Alaṃvacanīyā*” means she is not to be spoken to; the word *alaṃ* is used here in the sense of prohibition. Thus, “not to be spoken to” (*nālaṃvacanīyā*) means she is one who should not be addressed.

Because it is stated, “If she accepts, examines, and brings back [the robe], there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*,” they say that for one who definitely incurs a *saṅghādisesa*, these preliminary efforts of accepting, examining, and bringing back do not constitute the offenses of *dukkaṭa* or *thullaccaya*.
It has been written. Although there is no text here stating, "A woman means a human female, not a *yakkhī*, not a *petī*, not a female animal;

a man means a human male, not a *yakkha*, not a *peta*, not a male animal," nevertheless, because in the context of bodily contact and so forth the definition of a woman was established as "a woman means a human female," it is the same here as well.
She is recognized as a human woman. Because of the commonality of the preliminary stage of sexual intercourse, the definition of a man is established precisely by means of the definition of a woman.
For this very reason, it is said: "The fact that those with whom one enters into acting as a go-between are of the human species.
And in the cases of bodily contact and so forth, the *paṇḍaka* (eunuch) and the *yakkhinī* (female spirit) are stated to be grounds for a grave offense (*thullaccaya*); likewise here as well.

Because of their neuter nature, a human hermaphrodite constitutes an offense of *thullaccaya*. It should be understood that all others—human males, non-human males, neuter beings, hermaphrodites, male animals, and so forth—constitute an offense of *dukkaṭa*, as they possess the nature of manifesting sexual misconduct.
The commentary on the training rule concerning matchmaking (*sañcaritta*) is concluded.

6. Commentary on the Training Rule on Building a Hut (Kuṭikārasikkhāpada) Even when only "What, venerable sir? is said, one is permitted to explain the purpose for which one has entered [the village], because it is recorded that the conduct regarding the alms-round is prescribed as something to be asked about.
When requested to perform manual labor, [one may say] "He will provide tools or the materials."
Is it permissible or not permissible to ask for one? Some say it is permissible because one has obtained [the materials] for the purpose of illuminating the dwelling and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "three spans" (*tihatthā*): here, it is by the carpenter’s span (*vaḍḍhakihattha*) that they are three spans. "A bed of standard measure" means a bed measuring nine ordinary *vidatthi*s;
such a bed does not move from its place there, therefore it is four spans in width.

The passage beginning with “it does not exist” has been written. However, there is no requirement for the act of indicating the site by means of a gesture (*akuṭi*), because it is stated that one must perform the plastering (*ullittāvalitta*).
It is appropriate to say: “The state of being *ullitta* and so forth... refers specifically to the roofing. Why?
Because after erecting a wall made of clay, one performs the plastering above, either on the inner side, the outer side, or both.
It is written: "For one who has it constructed so that it is joined to a wall, there is an offense even without the plastering of the wall.
In this way, pillars, beams, rafters, and the like would be useless here. Therefore, it must be understood only after careful consideration.
[One might think: "There will also be a meeting hall (uposathāgāra), and I too shall dwell there," or "I shall dwell together with the bhikkhus or the novices."
It is indeed permissible for one who acts [in this way]. Why? Because it is stated, "for one's own sake," thus it has been written.
However, this training rule (sikkhāpada), like the fourth pārājika, depends upon a specific origin story (nidāna).
