For the monks dwelling on the banks of the Vaggumudā did not themselves bring about for themselves a non-existent superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma) characterized by falsehood and then speak of it.
For they spoke in praise of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) to one another; yet that alone does not constitute an offense involving defeat (pārājika).
However, on account of that slight pretext, the Blessed One took that matter as the occasion (nidāna) and prescribed the rule of defeat;

so it is here as well. For in the introductory narrative (nidāna), it is not stated that "the grounds for the offense were undeclared, contentious, and lacking a way of escape. Rather, it says: "They were immeasurable (appamāṇikāyo)."
However, because it has been stated [elsewhere], for one who exceeds the measure, it is indeed a *saṅghādisesa* offense that depends on the specific context (*nidāna*).

In that regard, although there appears to be an implication of a *saṅghādisesa* offense in the case of a site with living beings (*sārambha*) where there is no space for retreat, the *vibhaṅga* does not prohibit it, since it has been stated that "the *vibhaṅga* is a restrictor of that.
The same applies to a large building (*mahallaka*).
Here it is asked: For what purpose is the matter of an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) stated in the Schedule (mātikā), when it ought to be stated only in the Analysis (vibhaṅga)?
This is indeed so. But why must monks be brought for the designation of the site? That site must be designated by those monks; of what kind?

It must be "without harm" (anārambha) and "with a space around it" (saparikkamana). For otherwise, [it is forbidden] as in the passage: "If a monk, on a site that has harm and lacks a space around it..."

It is stated thus because it has come down by way of incidental mention (*anuppasaṅga*). Since the site (*vatthu*) is of many kinds— there is that which is with injury (*sārambha*) and without space for circumambulation (*aparikkamana*),
there is that which is without injury and with space for circumambulation, there is that which is with injury and with space for circumambulation,

and there is that which is without injury and without space for circumambulation— it is therefore, due to this multiplicity, that the site to be assigned must be one that is without injury and with space for circumambulation.

"Not otherwise" is what is meant. If it is asked, "What is the purpose of the instruction regarding the object (*vatthu*) here?", it is because it serves as the means for avoiding the causes for the formal establishment of a grave offense (*garukāpatti*).

For the instruction regarding the object is indeed the cause for the formal establishment of a grave offense. And these—namely, the formal establishment of a grave offense, the making of a request that has not been made, the causing of distress to householders, and the state of contentiousness which is the cause of one's own suffering and the suffering of others—are [avoided] by means of the instruction regarding the object.

They have avoided [such sites]. For monks do not point out a site for the purpose of building an improper hut, nor for the purpose of causing distress to householders, nor for the purpose of building a hut on a site that is subject to dispute. And regarding this, there are these verses:
“This is the exposition of the matrix (mātikā) of the grounds for an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa);”
Thus have the causes of grave offenses been explained for those very [offenders]:
"Because the causes of grave offenses are avoided by means of teaching the basis [of the offense],
therefore the onset [of the offense] and so forth are abandoned."
The commentary on the training rule concerning the building of a hut is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning the building of a monastery:
This is indeed a non-transgression (*akiriya*) because it arises merely from an act of doing. It is so designated by way of the teaching and the non-performance [of the offense]. Monks...
Regarding the phrase "or not having caused [it] to be brought," the word "or" (*vā*) should be understood here as having the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*).
It should be understood that this too refers back to the introductory narrative (*nidāna*), because it is stated: "The Venerable Channa had a shrine-tree cut down.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the building of a monastery is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Malicious Faults:

Regarding the statement, "Why should I perform salutations and so forth... [it is said] because it is stated that 'the head [of the offense] falls only when there is physical contact,' one should not accept the claim that it is improper to salute one who has committed an ultimate offense (antimavatthu). At the conclusion of the *Parivāra*, in the *Upālipañcaka*: "How many..."
Because it is not stated in the canonical text beginning with, "Are those who have been ordained later, venerable sir, not to be saluted by those who were ordained earlier?

and because it is stated that "one who was ordained earlier is to be saluted by one who was ordained later," for this very reason it is said in this *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*: "One who has received ordination means one who has entered into the number [of the Saṅgha].
However, the intended meaning of the Sutta should be understood as follows: by not saluting, [one incurs] the offense consisting in the rejection of proper courtesy...

It is stated [in the commentary] for the purpose of showing that "one is called a *codanā* (reprover) because one reproves. Therefore, it is said: "And to this extent, there is what is called a *codanā*.
In order to show here the manner in which an offense (*āpatti*) is incurred as intended in this context, it is written:
"'Why do you not perform salutations and so forth toward me? and so on."
"Admission" (*katūpasampadā*) refers to those for whom admission is valid, such as eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*) and others.

Regarding the "field for suspension" (*ṭhapanakkhetta*), there are two types of suspension of the invitation (*pavāraṇā-ṭhapana*): that which pertains to the entire community (*sabbasaṅgāhika*) and that which pertains to an individual (*puggalika*).

Among these, in the case of the communal suspension, it extends from the word "suṇātu" in the formula "Suṇātu me, bhante, saṅgho... pe... tevācikaṃ pavāre" up to the letter "re. In the case of the individual suspension—

However, from the word "saṅghaṃ, bhante, pavāremi" up to this very last letter *ṭi* in the phrase "passanto paṭī," it is established by one who places [the letters] even in a single word. On the Uposatha day, however,
the distinction should be understood according to this sequence, without exceeding the letter *re* in the word "kareyya."
The commentary on the training rule concerning corrupt faults is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning what belongs to another case:

"Aññabhāgiya" means that which has a different portion or part; just as in the word *sovaṇṇa* (golden), where it is derived from *suvaṇṇa* (gold) by the suffix *-a*, meaning "that which possesses gold."
Thus it is said. "The body of that image" and "the body of the stone statue" are illustrative examples.
The name "Dabba" given to the goat is called a "designation. Why? Because [the goat] was used as a pretext even for the Elder, in order to insult the Elder.
Another instance is not [an insult] directed at the Elder alone. *Lissati* means to adhere; it is merely a conventional expression and not [literal] in meaning. Slightly...

The intended meaning is that it is called a *lesa* because it clings (*allīyati*). [The root] *lis* is used in the sense of clinging, as seen in the words *lisa*, *selacha*, *kola*, and *allī*. Therefore it is said:

"A *lesa* is that which clings slightly. Since the country-*lesas* (desalesā) are in substance not different from this, the phrase "taking a certain slight *lesa*" has been extracted, and it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) beginning with: "The ten *lesas* are the *jāti-lesa*," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "it was manifested by way of the origin of the matter (*aṭṭhuppatti*)": what more is there to say here? Because it is not restricted;

for unlike the case of Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, it is not the case that for all others the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) is exclusively a goat-skin (*chagalaka*), as it may also be something else such as a cow or a buffalo.
Furthermore, unlike Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, who took only the stain of name (*nāmalesa*), they do not take merely the stain of name, but also the stain of birth (*jātilesa*) and so forth.
They grasp [the meaning] in that way; therefore, because it is not restricted, it was not analyzed separately.

Furthermore, if it were stated in that manner, the possibility of it being "pertaining to another case" (aññabhāgiyatā) would arise only for a goat and not for anything else, which is why only that [goat] was shown.

Moreover, what is called a "hint" (leso) is indeed a hint and not a genus (jāti) or the like, which is why only that [hint] was shown. Thus, it should be understood that there is the risk of a false apprehension. And here... [etc.]
"Even for one who perceives" means: in this training rule and in the training rule concerning groundlessness.
He who does not train according to the principle of the "pertaining to another" (aññabhāgiya) training rule should go before those learned in the Vinaya;
he indeed [becomes subject to] the "pertaining to another."
The commentary on the training rule concerning those belonging to another faction is finished.
11. Commentary on the training rule concerning those who side with schismatics:

Regarding the phrase "one who performs [an act] for three or more who are subject to formal legal acts," it is recorded here that it is not permissible to perform such an act after stating, "These four," or "This one and that one."
The commentary on the training rule concerning following schism is finished.
12. Commentary on the training rule concerning being difficult to admonish:
One who is to be addressed with difficulty is "difficult to admonish" (*dubbaca*). When being spoken to, he does not endure it.
The commentary on the training rule concerning harsh speech is finished.

Regarding the commentary on the conclusion: the reading is “nāmamattavasena,” though it has been written as “nāmagottavasena. This is what is meant: “This... [is] by way of name alone... [End of sentence fragment].
The meaning is that if one conceals [an offense] knowing that it is not permissible for monks to perform the formal act (kiriya), then it remains concealed.
"Merely sharing a commonality" means merely sharing the commonality of being free from enmity; this is the intended sense.

Regarding the phrase "both the matter and the lineage": here, "matter" (vatthu) refers to transgression or the emission of impurity; "lineage" (gotta) refers to that which protects one from going [to lower realms].

*Gotra* (lineage) means that which protects by not allowing one to go elsewhere from one's own birth; it is the meaning of "protecting" (*gotta*) and "speech" (*vacana*). Furthermore, the *vatthu* (the basis) goes only to its own kind.
Here, "own kind" (*sajāti*) refers to an action that is either distinguished or undistinguished from others, and does not refer to physical contact and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "name and offense": here, "offense" (*āpatti*) is the name for the offense incurred through transgression.

Regarding the phrase "informing the bhikkhus who have arrived again": here, the procedure for informing should be understood as follows—when informing two [bhikkhus], one should say, "Venerable sirs, please bear this in mind";
when informing three or more, one should say, "Venerable sirs, please bear this in mind.

Regarding the phrase "without committing a breach of the formal conduct (vatta) or causing an interruption of the night": here, with the exception of the most junior *pārivāsika* (one on probation), it refers to the rest.

There is a breach of proper conduct (*vatta*) in accepting such acts as salutation even from those deserving of being sent back to the beginning of their training (*mūlāya-paṭikassanāraha*), in sitting in succession [with them], in giving exhortation, and in censuring those performing formal acts (*kamma*). Furthermore, there is a breach in not informing others when within range of sight or hearing,
and in staying in a dwelling under one roof with monks without their knowledge while they come and go.

In cases such as these, there is a breaking of the night. However, because there is no formal disciplinary act (*vinaya-kamma*) performed by those belonging to different communities (*nānā-saṃvāsaka*), there is no breaking of the night if one does not inform them.
According to the statement, "having crossed two throws of a clod," it is not permitted within that distance.
While wandering about having laid down the observances (*nikkhitta-vatta*), even in the presence of the person from whom one previously received [the training] and informed [them], subsequently—
At the time of relinquishing [the training], it must be relinquished only after having announced it.
Therefore, even at the time of undertaking it again, if he goes from there, then even if he does not go that day but announces it during the day, if it is already past that day, one should think:
"When the sun has risen, having announced it in his presence and relinquished the duty, I shall go to the monastery. Having thus announced it in his presence, the duty—
"It should be deposited," it is said. Furthermore, it is said: "Having gone to the monastery, one should inform whichever bhikkhu one sees first and then deposit it.
If there is an interruption of the night, it should be informed to all those included within the monastery boundary (*vihārasīma*).
However, the phrase "having informed him" refers to a case where it has not been informed previously.
This was said for the purpose of protecting the integrity of the formal act (vatta). Therefore, it is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
"another who has either departed from a monastery or is a newcomer.

However, regarding the probation for purification (*suddhantaparivāsa*), if one had previously taken [the offense] thinking, "I have been impure for about a month," then while undergoing that probation, once again—
If one makes a determination that is either deficient or excessive, even for that duration one must simply undergo the probation; there is no need for the formal act of granting probation.
For this is called "probation from the pure end" (*suddhantaparivāsa*); it ascends upwards and descends downwards as well. This is its characteristic.
"Having combined" means having placed it in the position of the original offense, that is, having included it. If the intermediate offense was unconcealed...
Without performing a sending back to the beginning (*mūlāya paṭikassana*), one should undergo the probation (*parivāsa*) by means of the very period of probation previously taken.
However, for one who, having committed an offense and then disrobed, commits it again after being re-ordained; for one who previously concealed it but afterwards does not conceal it;
and for one who conceals it in both instances—for all of these, [the probation is determined] according to the number of days concealed.

Parivāsa (probation) should be granted. Because it is stated in the Pāḷi, “either in the former category of offenses” and “or in the latter category of offenses,” two monks fall into the *suddhika* (pure) [category]; they hold pure views.
One conceals [the offense], the other does not. He who conceals it must be made to confess a *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). “Both...”
Because of the statement, “They should be made to act according to the Dhamma,” it should be understood that one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense by concealing any offense whatsoever.
Regarding the phrase, “Whether they have departed or not, one should proceed in the same manner as before”:

here, this refers to wandering with a deficient group, failing to perform duties, or being separated from the group for even a single night; provided that the Saṅgha remains together at any given moment during the night.
If he had gone for some business before dawn, even in such a case where there is a state of being "separated" (mānatta), it is as follows.

For it is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*: "And because he lived only after having informed the community and having observed the presence of other monks, there is for him neither the fault of wandering with an incomplete group nor the fault of being separated. Therefore, by him—
Once it has been announced, even if he sits for a moment and then departs, there is no separation (vippavāsa).

For one who is undergoing probation (pārivāsika) and for one who has been suspended (ukkhitaka), staying with a regular monk (pakatatta) is forbidden by the falling of water; therefore, it is not permitted even if they are in different enclosures (nānūpacāra) but under the same roof (ekacchanna).
Now, the analysis of the text should be understood: "Nine offenses involving immediate transgression (paṭhamāpattika) and four that require a third admonition (yāvatatiyaka)"—this...
This is a statement regarding the fixed nature of things. By this, he shows that emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*) is not fixed.
For the emergence from certain offenses occurs both through action and through non-action; it is not so with the commission [of the offense], as it were.

The phrase "either one or another" is a statement indicating the absence of a distinction in the sequence of emergence, even though those two [classes of offenses] are divided in two ways. Regarding the expression "as many times as, so many times": here—
The determination of days is by means of the dawn. By the word “knowing,” it is shown that one who has concealed his knowledge must undergo the probation against his will.

The phrase “that bhikkhu must undergo it against his will” is stated for the purpose of showing that while staying there, that bhikkhu must undergo it against his will, and not with changed gender characteristics.
In the expression “by one who has completed the probation,” it refers specifically to one who has already completed the probation at the outset.
Beyond the period of *parivāsa*, according to the rule starting from the beginning, the monk himself must undergo the six-night penance (*chāratta*);

even after changing his gender, he must still proceed toward the *mānatta* for a monk. It is not as in the case of *parivāsa*, where one who has already undergone the penance (*ciṇṇamānatta*) [is exempt].

Only one who has completed the *mānatta* is to be rehabilitated (*abbheta*), not another; nor is it as in the case of *parivāsa*, where one is eligible for *mānatta*. And for a nun who is practicing the fortnightly *mānatta*...

This indicates that when there has been a transgression of the change of gender (*liṅgaparivattanātikkama*), the monk who has completed the *mānatta* penance must again take the *mānatta* from a monk;
only then, having completed the *mānatta*, is he to be rehabilitated (*abbheta*).
"Where there might be" means where there exists a community of monks numbering twenty within the same boundary of common affiliation (*samānasaṃvāsakasīmā*). Even by one... [sentence fragment].

If it is argued that "this group of less than twenty" is not tenable—because if it is deficient, it is not a group of twenty; and if it is a Saṅgha, it cannot be deficient—therefore, should one not simply say, "even if the Saṅgha is deficient by even one"?
No, because this serves the purpose of precluding the application of [the rules for] a fourfold, fivefold, or tenfold assembly.
Therefore, if a Bhikkhu-Saṅgha consisting of a group of twenty is deficient by even one Bhikkhu, it must be regarded as lost. Some...
However, those who do not understand what has been established in the Vinaya say:

"Just as even a Saṅgha consisting of more than four members is called 'a group of four' when performing a formal act that requires a quorum of four, so too, when performing a formal act that requires a quorum of five or ten, even one consisting of more than five or ten members is called 'a group of five or ten.
Therefore, even a deficient group of four, five, ten, or twenty is [valid]."
To prevent them from conceiving such notions, it was said: "Even if he is short by one.

Alternatively, if there is a community of twenty monks, even if it is short by one and thus incomplete (*appakatatta*), then excluding that [one], "even if it is short by one"—this is how the meaning should be understood here.
As for the statement "This is the proper conduct (*sāmīcī*) therein," this refers to what was stated in all cases regarding "that [person]."

It should be understood that this was stated for the purpose of clarifying [the following]: "He grants probation for an offense, sends back to the beginning, grants the period of trial (mānatta), and rehabilitates.

Therefore, among these [procedures], the aforementioned proper conduct (sāmīci) must be regarded as fixed; it is not indefinite, as in the case of the royal training rules (rājasikkhāpada) and others.
For in those cases, it is indicated that there is no offense even if one fails to perform that proper conduct due to some obstacle.
The commentary on the Saṅghādisesa rules is finished.
The Section on the Indeterminate Rules. 1. Commentary on the First Indeterminate Training Rule.

This miscellaneous section (pakiṇṇaka) is undetermined from the very beginning. If it is argued that this section on the undetermined (aniyata-kaṇḍa) is purposeless because there is nothing new therein, we say no;
for it has the purpose of illuminating the characteristics of the imposition and non-imposition of offenses, which are distinguished by the categories of grave (garuka) and light (lahuka).
For here, [it says]: “If she should speak thus: ‘Venerable sir, by me... [and so forth] ... and he admits it, he is to be dealt with according to the offense,” and so on.

By the phrase "the characteristic of the formal act of charging with a grave or light offense," the characteristic of the formal act of *not* charging is also shown by the words "he should not cause it to be done.
If it is argued that it should be recited at the beginning or at the end for the purpose of illustrating these characteristics, we say no, because it is impossible.
How is it impossible at the beginning? Because those training rules (*sikkhāpada*) to which this characteristic applies have not yet been shown.
It is not at the end, because it is mixed with what is grave. Therefore, it deserves to be recited in the midst of both the grave and the light, as it is mixed with both.
Even that light offense designated there as a *pācittiya* is called "grave.
For this very reason, he said: "by means of the secret delight known as the defilement associated with sexual intercourse," and so forth. Therefore...

Some say that [the second indeterminate] is taught immediately after the heavy [courses of action]. If this were so, one might ask: "Is not the first indeterminate alone sufficient, since the definition is established by that much alone;
what is the use of a second? No, for its purpose is to restrict the occasion and to prevent the misconception that it is a condition.
For, because the restriction of the occasion is expressed as "in a concealed seat, not fit for action," this definition applies only in a location contrary to that.
"It was not assigned" is a wrong grasp. The intention is that the second *aniyata* rule is likewise purposeful because it serves as a prohibition against that [wrong grasp].

Why? Because of the distinction of the occasion (*okāsa*), because of its indication of the distinction of seclusion (*raha*), and because of its indication of the distinction of delighting in sitting in seclusion (*rahonisajja*).

Furthermore, when there is no restriction regarding the occasion, the distinction of delighting in sitting in seclusion arises. And there is the discernment of the difference between the two training rules concerning sitting in seclusion.
It may be so, because it illustrates the classification based on physical contact.

For even in an uncovered place, or even in a covered one, physical contact is established by the grasping of hair and so forth that have emerged through windows, door-panels, or cracks while she is sitting;
such methods should be understood in detail.

Herein, this is the illustration of the mere heading: "By way of the distinction of location" means by way of the distinction between those that are suitable for sexual intercourse and those that are not.
For even though it is concealed, some [place] is not suitable for sexual intercourse because it is screened off by windows and the like;

and even though both [doors] are concealed, some [place] is not suitable for sexual intercourse because it is exposed to view to those who know. "By way of indicating the distinction of privacy": although there is a commonality in the state of being private here...
The intention is that "in private" (*raho*) is twofold, distinguished by being concealed or unconcealed.

Regarding the phrase "indicating the distinction between the delight in sitting in private": the meaning is that it indicates such a distinction as sitting for the sake of delighting in sexual intercourse (*methuna*), or sitting for the sake of delighting in what is lewd (*duṭṭhulla*).
"It should be understood that because this method has been introduced here [in the Bhikkhu-pātimokkha], this section is omitted in the Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha."
They say: "Because they had not arisen there [in the case of the nuns] by way of origin (aṭṭhuppatti)," some say; but that is improper because it demonstrates a lack of necessity.
For at all times of the Buddhas, there are five recitations for the monks and four for the nuns.

Some say it is because of the non-commonality of the laying down of the recitation of the Pātimokkha, and thus [the offenses] such as the Saṅghādisesas and Pācittiyas specified therein [do not apply]. For those nuns...
The specific types of physical contact constitute the basis for a *pārājika* offense by way of the "above-the-knees" (*ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalika*) and the "eightfold basis" (*aṭṭhavatthuka*).

This includes consenting, as stated in the words, "or she should consent to the grasping of the hand," or "or he should offer his body for that purpose"; standing together, as stated in the words, "or they should stand together";
going to an appointment, as stated in the words, "or he should go to a rendezvous"; or [entering] a concealed place...
Because of the statement, "one should not enter," entering a concealed place also constitutes an offense; likewise, because of the statement, "in the darkness of night, where there is no lamp,
in a concealed place or in the open air, one should not stand or converse alone with a single person," and considering that indecent speech is also a basis for a *pācittiya* offense,
these [other cases] were not mentioned [in the *aniyata-khaṇḍa*], as it would otherwise result in the fault of making the *aniyata* section inapplicable.
This is their intention. Regarding the miscellaneous points:

because it is stated that "those who are shameless and so forth will accuse those who are conscientious on account of offenses leading to rising from the teaching," [the rule] was established based solely on the admission of the monk himself, rather than on the word of even a suitable female lay follower, for the purpose of supporting those who are conscientious.

Regarding the phrase "it should be done": although it was prescribed for the purpose of showing the characteristics of the offenses, it is appropriate to state it by adopting the detailed method [of the *Vinaya*].
However, because it serves as a demonstration of the summary, it is written as: "Venerable sirs, these two *aniyata* rules are now recited.

In the expression "in secret" (*raho*), the word "secret" is used here by way of common terminology; however, by way of commonality with what is "grave," it refers to the training rules concerning the reporting and concealing of grave matters.
It is like the wording regarding the *pārājika* offense. Therefore, it is said: "But here, by 'seclusion,' what is intended is seclusion for the eye alone.
If one asks, "How is this known?"—it is because it has been stated: "'A woman' means... down to even a girl born on that very day";
thus, it is clearly shown that the speaking of lewd words is not intended here. By the word "even" (*pi*) in the phrase "even within twelve cubits,"...
The meaning is: "even while sitting at the door of a chamber whose door-panel is closed.

In the *Acelakavagga*, under the training rule concerning secluded and concealed seats, it is stated in accordance with the phrase "anyone who has a conscious man as a companion": "But even if there are a hundred women, one certainly does not incur an offense [if such a man is present].
Regarding the term "unfit for use," it means "it is possible to engage in sexual intercourse."

According to the statement in the *Vibhaṅga*, the relish for sitting in private here refers to the defilement based on sexual intercourse, not the defilement of relishing improper speech as in the second [offense].
Therefore, it is evident that "privacy" is not intended to refer to the ear.
"One should speak with one of the three things" means, according to the training rule regarding sitting in private, speaking to one who is seated in accordance with that [rule].
This was stated not merely to indicate a *pācittiya* offense, but also to demonstrate the distinction between offenses such as *pārājika* and *saṅghādisesa*.
Furthermore, why was the acknowledgment of the *vatthu* (the factual basis) stated as "the monk acknowledging the sitting," rather than simply the acknowledgment of the offense?
It is said: when the *vinayadhara* (one who maintains the discipline) has charged someone with an offense and asks, "In what matter [did you commit it]?"...
When the accuser has stated, "In this matter," and the Vinaya-expert has asked, "Did you commit such an act?
the monk must be dealt with while he is still confessing that matter; it is for the purpose of showing this that it is said, "the monk confessing the sitting.
If that is so, is one who confesses the sitting to be dealt with only for the offense? It is exactly appropriate. Thus...

However, it should be understood that here, rather than taking the objects (*vatthu*) of all three offenses, only the act of sitting down is mentioned by way of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*). For when that [act] is taken, the offense is indeed taken as well.

Or else, the word "or" (*vā*) in the phrase "by whomsoever she [is approached]" should be connected with "that monk should be made to act," and that [word] has the sense of an alternative (*vikappa*). Therefore: "Or he should be made to act while confessing..."
The meaning is: "or he should not be made [to confess] if he does not acknowledge it. Therefore, it was said: "if he acknowledges," and so forth.

Since this was stated with reference to an offense caused by sitting together based on the training rule concerning sitting in private (*raho-nisajja*), the offense in the remaining cases should also be understood according to the respective training rules.

Because it was stated that "the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth are exactly like those of the first *pārājika*," it should be understood here that the proclamation of a grave offense (*duṭṭhula-ābhāsana*) is not intended.
The commentary on the first *aniyata* training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the second *aniyata* training rule:
"By means of a *saṅghādisesa*" refers to the accusation of a grave offense regarding physical contact. Therefore, this section on physical contact [is explained] in the Pāḷi as well.
It is written: "It is said that one who is not blind sees the physical contact (*kāyasamsagga*), and one who is not deaf hears the lewd words (*duṭṭhulla*);
therefore, these [offenses] are stated to be exactly like the offense of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*). And here, if it is asked how they arise from body, speech, and mind:
for one who enters into physical contact also utters lewd words, and while uttering lewd words...
And it is possible that he sits down; or rather, this was said with reference specifically to what is indecorous, for that [offense] originates from taking what is not given.
He who taught the teaching—which is like unto the Omniscient One, distinguished by various methods, forms, and diverse divisions—...
The mindful one knows the means for understanding;
he does not perform that merit for the sake of gain.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning what is not fixed is finished.
The commentary on the Indeterminate [offenses] is finished.
The Chapter on Forfeiture, 1.
The Section on Robes.
1. Commentary on the Kathina Training Rules:

The three Kathina training rules in the Section on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa), as well as the training rules concerning the rainy-season robe, the urgent robe, and the expectation of receiving one, should be understood as having their categories of offenses similarly interspersed by way of partial explanation:
The Kathina has four [factors]; the two seasons are simultaneous.
And this is a partial determination of the six training rules.

In that context, "kaṭhina" refers to the inclusion of those very factors such as the act of giving thanks (anumodanā), because of the statement: "Through the giving of thanks by the Saṅgha, the giving of thanks by a group, or the spreading [of the robe] by an individual, the kaṭhina is spread for the Saṅgha."
“Kathina” means: as it is said, “‘Kathina should be known’ refers to the collection, the assembly, the name, and the naming of those very phenomena,” and so forth.
Therefore, this term “kathina” is merely a designation for many phenomena; it is not a single phenomenon in the ultimate sense (*paramattha*).
What, then, is its application (*atthāra*)? It is just one part of it, like a stream of milk. And as it is said: “The application...”
"He is included by one factor through the distinction of speech. There are eight matrices (*mātikā*) known as "concomitant," two obstacles (*palibodha*), and five benefits (*ānisansa*);
these are the fifteen factors. The "two periods" (*samayadvaya*) are the period for the spreading of the Kathina and the robe-season (*cīvara-samaya*).
Among these, the period for the spreading of the Kathina is the last month of the rainy season. The robe-season is that during which the Kathina has not been spread.
In the context of the *kathina*, this is the month of Kattika; together with the four months of the winter season when it is spread out, there are five months.
In that regard, the eight headings (*mātikā*) are those beginning with "the end of the journey" (*pakkamanantika*). All of these arise simultaneously with the spreading of the *kathina*.
Because they are produced by its existence, when the spreading exists, their suspension (*uddhāra*) becomes possible. In that context, they arise together with the spreading of the *kathina*.

The suspension of the *kathina* by one person (*ekanirodha*) is simultaneous with the internal suspension (*antarubbhāra*) and the common suspension (*sahubbhāra*); the remaining types of *kathina* suspensions have a single arising (*ekuppāda*) but different cessations (*nānānirodha*).

In this context, "cessation by one" means cessation together with the act of relinquishing; the meaning is that for both the internal suspension and the common suspension, the state of being suspended occurs at a single moment.
The others are said to cease differently. For even when those [others] reach the state of being suspended, [their processes differ].
The *aṭṭhakathā* explains the meaning as follows: “It remains thus” refers to the exposition of the meaning.

If, when the *kaṭhina* has been spread, a monk who is still attached to that monastery departs from it while the Saṅgha performs an *antarubbhāra*, then for that monk the impediment is severed by the *antarubbhāra*, even though he lacks the completion of his robe-impediment (*cīvara-palibodha*) in his original residence. Even so, [the impediment is severed].
Because it involves expectation and has a purpose. By this method, the suspension of the kaṭhina due to departure is simultaneous in its arising but distinct in its cessation.

Likewise, in the case of suspension during the interval, even for one who hears [the proclamation], as long as it does not reach the completion of the robe, there is the possibility of further postponement;
thus it is "terminating with completion. As long as it does not reach completion—

It is "concluding with determination" because the possibility of relinquishment exists for that long; it is "concluding with loss" because the possibility of relinquishment exists as long as [the robe] has not been lost;
it is "concluding with hearing" because the possibility of relinquishment exists as long as one has not heard [of the robe being lost];

it is "concluding with the cutting off of hope" because the possibility of relinquishment exists as long as the expectation regarding the robe has not been cut off; it is [“concluding with the boundary”] because the possibility of relinquishment exists as long as one does not cross the boundary.
The "one who has crossed the boundary" (*sīmātikkantika*). It should be understood that through the act of lifting [the robe], there is a simultaneous arising and a separate cessation.
In this regard, the two cases of "lifting within" (*antarubbhāra*) and "lifting together" (*sahubbhāra*) occur only within the boundary, not outside the boundary.

The cases of "departing" (*pakkamana*), "hearing" (*savana*), and "crossing the boundary" (*sīmātikkantika*) occur only outside the boundary, not within the boundary. The cases of "completion" (*niṭṭhāna*), "staying" (*saṭṭhāna*), and "cutting off the expectation" (*sāvacchedika*) occur both within the boundary and...

And outside the boundary (*bahisīmāyaṃ*). The internal determination (*antarubbhāra*) depends on the Saṅgha; the departure, the completion, and the determination regarding the crossing of the boundary depend on the individual. The remaining cases are the opposite of both.

In that context, by the phrase "when the robe is finished" (*niṭṭhitacīvaramhi*), it indicates only the absence of the obstacle of the robe (*cīvarapalibodha*), not the absence of the obstacle of the residence (*āvāsapalibodha*).

If it is argued that by the phrase “when the kaṭhina has been removed,” this indicates the absence of both obstacles, and therefore for the purpose of indicating the absence of both obstacles that very [phrase] should be stated—[we reply: No, because there is a distinction. How so?

Granted, this [phrase] is used because of the various ways in which the removal of the kaṭhina occurs for some, and because of whether it is dependent or independent upon the Saṅgha or an individual, and whether it occurs within, outside, or on both sides of the boundary.

When the kaṭhina has been removed by the Saṅgha—not by an individual—due to either the lapse of the time limit or the non-lapse [of the robe-making season], nevertheless, the expression "when the kaṭhina has been removed" is a general term. Therefore, it is specified by the phrase "when the robes have been finished.
What is meant? When the kaṭhina has been removed by the internal removal of the Saṅgha, the impediment of the robe-material is severed.

It should be understood that the phrase "when the robe is finished" is stated because one who has gone outside the boundary, having subsequently returned and being within his own boundary, obtains the benefit [of the robe] even though it is not yet finished.
In this context, the "obstacle of the residence" (*āvāsapalibodha*) means either that he actually dwells in that residence, or that he departs while still having expectations regarding it.
The "obstacle of the robe" (*cīvarapalibodha*) means that the robe is either unmade or half-made.
The expectation regarding robes is not cut off; by the opposite of that, one should understand it as being without obstruction.

In this regard, for those who have not performed the *kaṭhina* ceremony, four benefits are obtained as a rule during the robe season; wandering without having formally undertaken the practice is not a rule.

Therefore, the training rule concerning "grounds for apprehension" was stated. If it is asked, "How are the four [benefits] fixed? [it is said]: "The robe season is called [the time when the *kaṭhina* has not been spread..."

Because of the statement, "The *kathina* [period] is the last month of the rains," for those who have not spread the *kathina*, the acquisition of robes as much as needed during that month is established.
Likewise, according to the third *kathina* training rule, what is called "out-of-season robe-cloth" (*akālacīvara*) refers to that which,
having been received starting from the time of the back [of the rainy season], should— if it is to be obtained from the Sangha— be set aside until the time of the robe-season and then distributed.

It may be accepted. If it is personal property, it is permissible from the fifth day of the sixth fortnight of the rainy season until the time for the robe-season, provided it has not been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) or assigned (*avikappita*), because this is authorized by the training rule on the urgent robe (*accekacīvara-sikkhāpada*); it is not permissible beyond that point.
This is because at that stage, the acquisition of a robe is prohibited by the first *kaṭhina* rule. Regarding this, the method stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*) is as follows:
This should be understood as referring to what belongs to the Saṅgha, and likewise according to the ancient *Gaṇṭhipada*.
Regarding the first *kathina* robe-making ceremony, there is an offense on the eleventh day, either specifically according to the first rule or generally.
For, in order to prevent [the robe] from being worn during the rains, the Commentary states: "When the robe has been finished and the *kathina* has been removed by the bhikkhu..."
It has been stated. This same method applies to the second and third cases as well.

Therefore, [an article] that arises before or during the robe season does not receive any exemption for even a single day beyond the robe season. If it were to receive such an exemption, it would contradict the training rule concerning urgent robes (*accekacīvara*).
[As it says: "It may be kept until the time of the robe season; if one should keep it beyond that, it is an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*)."
For it is said therein: "An *accekacīvara* (urgent robe) obtained from the Saṅgha by virtue of having spent the rains residence becomes one's own property;
an offense occurs only for one who lets the robe-season (*cīvarakālasamaya*) pass, not for one who lets the time for an *accekacīvara* pass.
And because of the statement, "arisen in the eleventh month when the Kathina has not been spread," whatever arising of a robe there may be—
And since it is established that "this shall be for them," the remaining two cases are also established by virtue of the rule regarding eating in a group without being invited,
which states "except at the proper time. Therefore, because of the statement, "Even if given at the right time, if it is given specifically [for oneself],
this is 'out-of-season robe-cloth' (akālacīvara)," a robe-cloth given specifically does not receive the exemption.

If it is argued that one obtains [the robe] precisely when the Kathina has been suspended during the latter Kattika month—on the grounds that it is stated, "when the Kathina has been suspended"—this should not be said.
For six points are stated with reference to specific conditions: the fourth formal act (*adhikaraṇa-catuttha*) regarding the two types of corrupt faults;
the first *niyata* (fixed) offense regarding the ear in private; the robe specifically assigned in the third Kathina; and the training rule concerning the urgent robe (*accekacīvara*).

The phrase “having made a mark, it should be set aside” refers to the two cases of the disclosure and concealment of a grave offense (*duṭṭhulla-ārocana-paṭicchādana*), the formal legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*), and the statement regarding the *pārājika* offense;
and in the three *kathina* training rules, it refers to the expression “one of the eight headings.
Therein, the robe given specifically is said with reference to a robe belonging to the Saṅgha that is to be distributed, not one belonging to an individual.
"It should be deposited after making a mark" is said with reference to the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season) robe.

Because it must be given later by one who has not yet completed the rains-residence, a mark must be made; this does not refer to a personal robe obtained from a relative or an invitation (*ñātippavārita*).
Therefore, it is established that there are two kinds of urgent robes (*accekacīvara*): those assigned to the Sangha and those assigned to an individual. Among these, regarding the Sangha—

An urgent robe-cloth (*accekacīvara*) that has been finished may indeed be kept until the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), starting from the day of the entry into the rains retreat or from the end of the rainy season, because it belongs to the Saṅgha;

even one belonging to an individual may be kept, because it was given with the instruction, "Take it when you have completed the rains retreat. For such a cloth belongs only to its donor until the recipient has completed the rains retreat.
It becomes [the robe] belonging to [the Sangha]. This much is the specific reason (*visesahetu*).

Because of the statement, “If one who does not have an urgent need for a robe perceives it as not being an urgent need and lets the robe-season pass, there is no offense,” that fault belongs only to one who has an urgent need for a robe.
Therefore, the statement “there is a contradiction” is not intended to show a specific reason within the Vinaya.
It must be sought out. If it is argued that [the robe] is beyond measure because it is the domain of the Buddhas, we say no;

for if this were so, then even a robe received as a gift (accekacīvara) belonging to oneself would have to be deposited after making a mark of recognition, and it could not be determined, assigned to another, or relinquished.
Consequently, there would be a contradiction with such statements as: "There is no offense if one determines, assigns, or relinquishes it within the proper time."

This contradiction in meaning should be accepted: that it "may be permitted. Likewise, there is this contradiction in meaning that it "is an offense involving forfeiture (nissaggiya)" based on the statement: "When the kaṭhina has been suspended in the last month of the rains, if one lets the day of the kaṭhina suspension pass while the kaṭhina is still spread in that month, it is an offense involving forfeiture.
And in that regard, [it says]: "There is no offense regarding a robe that is not urgent."
It has been stated that this [allowance] is neither determined nor assigned; this much is the specific reason.
Furthermore, this extra robe constitutes an offense under the first training rule, whereas the other does not constitute an offense at all—this is the Blessed One’s specific reason for this matter.
Likewise, even when less than ten days remain until the full moon of Kattika, for the sake of the Saṅgha’s rainy-season residence...
One must not accept a robe offered as an *accekacīvara* (an urgent robe); it may only be accepted when ten days have yet to elapse—this much is the specific reason [for the distinction].
Furthermore, one might have to tolerate a contradiction with the method of the *Aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary).
For there, having stated that "what arises after the determination (*adhiṭṭhita*) is no longer an *accekacīvara*," a different method is shown. [This is] in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*.
And since this method is stated with reference to what belongs to the Saṅgha, it does not conflict [with other rules]; thus, it is not prohibited.

Just as an extra robe that has arisen after the sixth day may be accepted even if the ten-day limit has not yet passed, and there is no offense even if one accepts it and lets the robe-season pass—this method too should be accepted.

It might be so. Then there would be a contradiction with the first *kathina* rule. If it is argued that "it should be accepted only when ten days have not yet elapsed, and there is no offense for one who, having accepted it, lets the robe-season period pass," then the only distinction made is that "it may be kept for two ten-day periods.
Because it has entered the robe-season within the field where there is no offense, it is as if it were formally determined and then relinquished.
If it is argued that one may obtain [the robe] again after ten days, we say no. If it is argued that entering the time limit is like a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*), we say no;
for this would contradict the statement: "One may determine the *vassikasāṭika* (rainy-season robe) for four months of the rains, and beyond that, one must assign it (*vikappeti*) [to another].
Consequently, there might be no offense even for one who does not assign it for the ten days beyond that period. Furthermore, as for what was stated in the Commentary: "The *vassikasāṭika*..."
"Whatever has been obtained and finished within the rainy season must be determined (adhiṭṭhātabba) within ten days;

if it is finished after the ten days have passed, it must be determined on that very day; if the ten days are insufficient, one must not let the robe-season (cīvarakāla) pass by. By this, one would not be released from the offense.
For the expression "determination" (adhiṭṭhāna) is not applicable to the entry into the [robe-]time. To this extent is the aforementioned alternative meaning.
It is established according to the method of the Pāḷi itself.
Furthermore, regarding what is stated in the Aṭṭhakathā:

"If ten days are not sufficient, the robe-season must not be exceeded"—even in that case, if it arises during the robe-season and there is no making of it when the ten days have not elapsed, that is an *accekacīvara* (urgent robe).
It is established that, just as with an out-of-season robe (*akālacīvara*), one must not let the robe season (*cīvarakāla*) pass by.
Furthermore, according to the Canon (*pāḷi*), if it arises within the [robe] season—even if it arises when ten days are insufficient—it is an urgent robe (*accekacīvara*) that has arisen;
yet such an urgent robe does not cease to be an urgent robe. For it does not acquire the designation "urgent robe" by virtue of a specific time. Indeed, this has been said: "An urgent robe..."
“Or when one wishes to go with an army, or wishes to go on a journey abroad, or is ill, or is pregnant,
or faith has arisen in one who lacked faith… [and so on] … or when it is announced, ‘I shall give a robe for the rainy-season residence’—
this is what is called an ‘urgent robe. Therefore, just as that robe must not be exceeded, so too it is with a non-urgent robe.”
This is established. Therefore it is said in the Commentary: "If ten days are not sufficient, the robe-season must not be exceeded.

Furthermore, if that were so, this specific training rule concerning the urgent robe (*accekacīvara*) would have been prescribed by the Blessed One merely for the purpose of showing the distinction in meaning: "The urgent robe must not exceed the robe-season."

In the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated thus: "Granted that this is already established by the rule, 'An extra robe may be kept for at most ten days,' yet the training precept was laid down by way of a specific occasion (*aṭṭhuppatti*), as if showing a meaning not previously mentioned;
this is for the purpose of illuminating a particular significance. Therefore, it is [stated] for the sake of demonstrating that particular significance."
The word "said" (*vutta*) is already established. Therefore, it must also be understood that no robe whatsoever should exceed the robe-season (*cīvarakālasamaya*).

Furthermore, as it is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*): "But from the sixth day onward, even a non-urgent robe that has arisen, as well as a robe set aside after being relinquished, receives this exemption. By this, [it is meant]: "perceiving a non-urgent robe as a non-urgent robe..."

"Even by the statement, 'There is no offense if one lets the time for robes pass,' it is indicated that even one who does not have an *accekacīvara* (a robe made urgently) receives the benefit of the exemption from the *accekacīvara* rule.

Up to this point, the second alternative meaning as previously stated has been established according to the method of the Pāḷi and the method of the Aṭṭhakathā. Thus, first of all, the incidental discussion has been explained in detail following the subsequent text;

hence it is called "incidental" (*apakiṇṇaka*). There are two impediments: the impediment of robes (*cīvarapalibodha*) and the impediment of residence (*āvāsapalibodha*). Even when one of these impediments exists, there is the benefit [of practicing] such things as moving about without having informed others.
To show that such [a case] does not exist here, it is said: "When the robe has been finished and the kaṭhina has been suspended.
For this very reason, it is said: "For a monk for whom the kaṭhina has been spread," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "one who is worthy of the spreading of the kaṭhina":
"A person endowed with eight factors is capable of spreading the kaṭhina—[namely,] the preliminary preparation..."

"Because of the statement: 'He knows [the cloth], he knows the relinquishing, he knows the determination, he knows the spreading, he knows the matrix, he knows the impediments, he knows the lifting, and he knows the benefit'—a person endowed with these eight factors is said to be worthy of the spreading of the *kaṭhina*.
'Preparation' (*pubbakaraṇa*) refers to the washing, sorting, cutting, sewing, dyeing, and making it fit for use."
Having shown both the type and the measurement by means of the canonical text beginning with “‘Robe-cloth’ means linen,” etc.,
[the author] now states “But as for what was said regarding ‘those that have been determined or assigned,’” etc., in order to show the extra robe (*atirekacīvara*).

Even though it says “having observed the place where it has been set aside,” the determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) remains valid whether or not that specific item which was set aside in that particular place exists there afterwards.
It is as if it were growing. Neither the place where one was previously nor the place where one subsequently stands is a determining factor.
For one who has committed the ultimate offense, "returning to the lower state" means either wearing white robes, adopting the saffron robe, or turning away from the monastic life.
Regarding the eleventh [offense], "at sunrise," the meaning should be understood as occurring at any time prior to that, excluding the very last moment.

In this context, "the last" refers to the first dawn of the subsequent Kattika month. For that, being [still] within the time limit, does not constitute an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).

Here, the instrumental phrase "by a monk whose robe is finished" (*niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ bhikkhunā*) is independent of the introductory narrative (*nidāna*), because the instrumental case is not used in the narrative itself.
Therefore, it is said that "at most ten days" (*dasāhaparamaṃ*) is an additional rule (*anupaññatti*) in this instance. "I allow... [the Blessed One said].

Furthermore, because of such statements as, "Monks, one may determine (adhiṭṭhātuṃ) the three robes, but one must not assign them (vikappetuṃ)," the expression "assigns" used here appears to be contradictory;
yet the Tathāgatas do not speak what is contradictory.
Therefore, its meaning should be understood in this way: the three robes are to be determined only for the purpose of wearing them under the heading of the "three robes."

"I allow [this], but one must not assign it [to another]. However, a rain-cloak (vassikasāṭikā) may indeed be assigned after the four months have passed, but it must not be formally determined (adhiṭṭhātuṃ).

And this being so, for one who wishes to stay apart from one of the three robes (ticīvara), the formal determination of the three robes is rescinded, and an opportunity for assignment is granted for the sake of ease while staying apart."
"And there is no offense after the lapse of ten days. By this method, it should be understood that in all cases, the act of assigning [the robe] is not prohibited; so it is written.
Now, this is the summary of the legal decision regarding this training rule: when the Kathina has not been spread during the winter months...

With reference to robes that arise from the first day of the summer season onwards, once the *kathina* has been spread, the words beginning with "when the robe is finished" (*niṭṭhitacīvaramhi*) and so forth were spoken.

Here it is asked: "Since there is the statement, 'Even for one who has had it washed by dyers and made white, the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is indeed a valid determination,' does the determination take effect even on a robe that has not yet been dyed?"
Having performed the needlework, dyed it, and applied the *kappa-bindu*, must a formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) be made? Is there a rule that it must be made, or that it need not be made?
It must indeed be made. Like a bowl, once determined, it does not lose its determination by returning again to a white state or a copper-colored state;
yet, unlike such a bowl, this [robe] does not undergo such a determination.

It should be understood thus: "He will take up the kaṭhina tomorrow. If one who has obtained robe-cloth does not formally determine it this very day, it becomes subject to forfeiture at the rising of the dawn. Why?
Because the training rule states, "When the robe is finished," and so forth. Within the period of the kaṭhina, one receives an exemption even beyond ten days; [this applies] from the kaṭhina...

But afterwards, one does not obtain it even for a single day. How so? Just as the Saṅgha that has performed the Kathina ceremony obtains the benefit from the day the robes were spread until their removal, but not beyond that;
likewise, one obtains it from the day they were spread until their removal, but once the Kathina has been removed, one does not obtain it even for a single day. Here it is said:
—“Does one receive another ten-day period starting from the day the *kaṭhina* has been removed? No. Why?

Because of the statement: “I allow you, monks, to keep an extra robe for a maximum of ten days. Even within the *kaṭhina* period, if the dawn breaks on the eleventh day, one incurs an offense of forfeiture (*nissaggiya*).
However, in order to prevent an over-extension of that rule, [the text specifies] “when the robe is finished,” and so forth.
It was stated [in that way] for the purpose of showing that the days of the *kathina* ceremony are not "extra days. This meaning will become clear in various places.

Alternatively, it is stated that after taking the name of the *vassikasāṭikā* (the rainy-season robe) as being of non-excess dimensions, it should be formally resolved (*adhiṭṭhātabba*) according to the same method for the four months of the rains;
thereafter, having relinquished it (*paccuddharitvā*), it should be assigned (*vikappetabba*). Here, "having relinquished" (*paccuddharitvā*)—
Regarding the declaration: on the very day of the Uposatha, having relinquished and formally assigned it, it remains so;
thereafter, from the first day of the winter season onwards, there is no further relinquishing. Thus it is written that cloth received within the Kathina period should be understood in the same way.
The commentary on the Kathina training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the Udositaka training rule:
"For one who has performed the Kathina ceremony, having deposited his robe anywhere within the established boundary for the five-month period, and then departing..."
“*There is no offense*,” so it is stated in the Commentary (*Aṭṭhakathā*).

As for the statement, “It is also permissible within an unbound boundary (*abaddhasīmā*),” this is recorded as establishing both the *kathina*-spreading and the forest-dweller’s training rule (*āraññaka-sikkhāpada*) within an unbound boundary. Now:
“The ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) is severed; what is considered dangerous is the inner and outer garment (*santaruttara*);”
“There is no offense regarding the robe, because the relinquishment and so forth are established.
This should be understood as an incidental discussion.

In this regard, the following is the formal decision preceded by an objection: some say that because of the statement “the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) is double-layered,” it is “single-layered” [in other cases].

"A *saṅghāṭi* should not be formally resolved upon (*adhiṭṭhātabba*). If one resolves upon it, it does not take effect," having said this, they grant even those seeking full ordination (*upasampadāpekkha*) only a double-layered *saṅghāṭi* and then ordain them; these [monks] should be informed by means of this scriptural passage.
For the Blessed One first [prescribed]: "A cut-up *saṅghāṭi*, a cut-up *uttarāsaṅga*, and a cut-up *antaravāsaka*."
It was permitted. Then, regarding this case where "for a certain bhikkhu while his three robes were being made, it was not sufficient for all to be cut;
two cut pieces and one uncut piece were not sufficient; two uncut pieces and one cut piece were not sufficient," it was permitted [by the Buddha]:
"Bhikkhus, I allow you to add an extra piece as well. Therefore...
It is established that even a single-layered *saṅghāṭi* is permissible. But as for one that is not large enough even when being cut down—how could it possibly have a double layer?
This is also stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*: "‘To add an extra layer’ means to provide an additional cloth;
however, this [extra layer] should be added only when the robe is insufficient. If it is sufficient, an additional cloth is not permitted; it must simply be cut down."

However, only cut cloth is suitable for the kaṭhina, because it possesses the unique characteristic [of being used for that purpose] and because there is no statement saying, "cut cloth is not sufficient when doubled.
This is the conclusion to be reached here. Regarding the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga):

since the ascetic practice of wearing three robes (tecīvarika-dhutaṅga) does not exist for those who are not fully ordained, one is called a "wearer of three robes" (tecīvarika) by virtue of possessing the three robes alone.
If it is argued that because they lack such a formal resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*), one should say "only by means of what has been resolved," we say no;

for that would entail a contradiction with the division of the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*). For the breach of an ascetic practice occurs through the acceptance of a fourth robe, not through being separated from the three robes, nor through the acceptance of an extra robe, nor through the wearing of an extra robe. However, as for the monks...
Thus, nine robes were authorized by the Blessed One by way of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and described by way of their origin (*jāti*);

however, this was not so for those who are not fully ordained. Therefore, because there is no such restriction on robes for them, that ascetic practice (*dhutaṅga*) was not authorized for householders as it is for others.
Consequently, since there is no mention of its undertaking or procedure, one should reach the conclusion that it does not apply here.
Regarding the phrase "regarded as suspicious": in the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*, the individual factors for this training rule on suspicion are not stated separately;
it is said, "The rest here should be understood according to the method explained under the second training rule of the *Cīvaravagga*," yet that [method] was not actually stated there.
In that case, staying apart overnight was the fourth factor, whereas here it is staying apart for six nights—this is the distinction here.
Therefore, because of the commonality of the factors and the commonality of the designation, they understand this training rule regarding danger to be without limitation;

that [other rule] is with limitation, being restricted to a maximum of one month. In that case, there is no offense for one who, having entered the village boundary even outside the village, dwells there and then departs;
here it is not so. Here, at the rising of the dawn following each successive night, there is an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*); in that case, however, it is not so.
This is the distinction between these two [cases] regarding the seventh [factor].

As for the other factors, they are not stated here because they are established by way of the opposite of the factor of laying down the robe (*cīvaranikkhepanaṅgasampatti*) and by the method explained herein. Although those [factors] are indeed not stated, nevertheless the fourth factor ought to be specified, yet it has not been specified.
What is the reason? Because one has already confessed according to the sequence of relinquishment (*nissajjana*) stated here.

This is for the purpose of confessing the offense and demonstrating the liberation from the offense incurred therein. Even one who has been separated [from his robe] for a year is considered as one who has been separated for a single night, let alone for six nights.
Nevertheless, if the requisite factors mentioned there are present, it must be relinquished according to the method stated therein.
If he relinquishes it during the winter or the summer, it is also [valid] according to the method stated here.
The teacher [Ācariya] says: "The fourth factor was not specified for the purpose of making it known that it is permissible to relinquish [the robe];
therefore, it is not a logical error. Some say: "Even a robe that has exceeded ten days may be called 'exceeded ten days' and then relinquished;
it need not first have been less than a month and then be called 'exceeded ten days,' nor must it be called 'exceeded a month. Nevertheless...

If it is a robe expected [as a gift], it is subject to forfeiture. Having stated that the "ten-day limit" has been exceeded, the original robe, however, should be forfeited by stating that the "one-month limit" has been exceeded.
Regarding the terms "inner and outer robe," "outer cloak," or "robe": does this refer to the three robes, or is it something else as well?

What is the point here? If it were only the three robes (*ticīvara*) that are prohibited, there would be a contradiction with [the rules concerning] robes that have not been cut, robes that are not offered, having them washed, requesting them, and so forth, by way of their being included [in the category].

Or, if other [robes] are also [prohibited], then there is a contradiction with such [phrases] as "when the robe is finished" (*niṭṭhitacīvaramhi*). It is said in reply: this should not be understood as a strict rule (*niyama*), because they must be taken according to what is possible. For instance, [it is said]: "Having laid aside his robe, he went on a journey through the country wearing only the inner and upper robes (*santaruttarena*)."
In such passages as "they depart," it refers specifically to the three robes (*ticīvara*); in such passages as "Monks, one should not enter a village wearing only an inner and upper garment;

at most, one may accept a robe beyond that [the inner and upper garments]," it refers to any robe whatsoever. Likewise, in such passages as "The outer robes (*saṅghāṭi*) should be given with the border-edges folded over;
the undergarment (*nivāsana*) should be given; the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) should be given; come now, friend... it refers to any robe.
In such expressions as "saṅghāṭi, give me the cloth," it is said: "For all robes are called 'saṅghāṭi' in the sense of being sewn together.
Likewise, some say that this also applies here in the phrase "when the robe is finished" (*niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ*). Others say: "The robe was permitted [to be made] within the period as much as needed;
when will all of that be finished? Therefore, it refers only to the triple-robe (*ticīvara*)."
"What is meant by 'there is no offense for one without a robe because of the establishment through relinquishment, etc.'? Some say:

'Because it would follow that the *Udositā* training rule (the rule on leaving clothes behind) would be rendered purposeless, there is an offense for one possessing three robes when separated from his triple-robe (*ticīvara*).
To this it is said: There is no offense because of the establishment through relinquishment, etc., [as stated]: 'There is no offense if he relinquishes or gives it away before dawn.'"

For it has been said: otherwise, for one who relinquishes [the robe] and then gives it away before dawn, one incurs an offense according to the method already stated, as long as another has not yet formally resolved upon it.

Otherwise, regarding "being separated within seven days," this means that when there is separation, it is "from separation" according to the literal expression; and when there is no separation, it is "from non-separation."
The commentary on the Udosita training rule is finished.
3. Commentary on the Akālacīvara training rule:

Because it is difficult to discern the extent of the area eligible for enclosure in the case of an unenclosed space, the text says "Furthermore, for monks... and so forth, in order to demonstrate that.

It has been stated. It should be understood as follows: either from the place where a regular assembly is held at the edge of the monastery, or from the dining hall situated at the boundary, or from the residence where one habitually dwells.

If, being joined in a continuous line with the monks assembled in the monastery, they sit filling even a hundred yojanas, then even that hundred yojanas constitutes the *upacāra-sīmā* (proximate boundary).

The meaning is "it occurs. When it is said, "within the boundary of common affiliation (*samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā*)," this does not extend to those situated within broken boundaries (*khaṇḍasīmā*) and so forth, because those [broken boundaries] constitute separate boundaries of common affiliation.
Furthermore, this is the distinction between the boundary of common affiliation and the boundary of non-separation (*avippavāsa-sīmā*).
However, what is given with the words, "I give within the boundary of non-separation," does not reach those situated in a village. Why? Because, having excluded...

This is because of the statement: "The village and the vicinity of the village. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "within the boundary of common affiliation," it refers even to those standing in a place where there is a non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*). This is also because of the statements:

"It reaches those standing therein," and "When one standing within a fragmented boundary says, 'May the Saṅgha of the eight within the boundary accept [this],' it should be given after delimiting it precisely by the vicinity boundary (*upacāra-sīmā*)."
And: "The meaning is that it reaches even those who are outside the boundary until the suspension of the *kathina*";

and: "But when the *kathina* has not been suspended, if one enters a monastery during the winter and says, 'I give this to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains retreat,' it reaches even those who have completed the later rains retreat there without having broken their residence, even if they are outside the boundary."
The holders of the Vinaya determine this, though it is not mentioned in the Aṭṭhakathā. Therefore, it is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*: "Those who know the characteristics say... and:
"'From the time one begins to expect robes until the last day of winter, we shall give the *vassāvāsika* [robes]'—in such a case, whether the *kathina* has been spread or not."

Regarding the statement from the *Samantapāsādikā*: "In this case as well, if [the robe] has been formally spread (*atthatam*), those who have spent the preceding rains retreat receive it for five months;
if it has not been formally spread, those who have spent the subsequent rains retreat receive it for four months"—this is the explanation.
Furthermore, it is written: "'By whom the rice-gruel was drunk by me' means the intention is 'by whom I was invited, by them the rice-gruel was drunk by me. Therefore, by whom..."
It is stated that when those who have been invited drink the gruel, it belongs to them alone. Otherwise, it is said:
"When one says, 'Those by whom my gruel was drunk,' whether they were invited or uninvited, it must belong to those by whom it was drunk.
Here, by saying, "When the robe has been finished and the kaṭhina has been removed," he makes known that [the period] within this interval [is intended].
"There is no arising of even three out-of-season robes. But why are they explained in detail in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*)?

It is said: This training rule was not stated with reference to the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*), but rather, having permitted [the keeping of a robe] for up to ten days in the first training rule, and that being insufficient, it permits [keeping it] for a month by extending that very period provided there is an expectation [of receiving a new one].
This also illustrates a specific point: an out-of-season robe (akālacīvara) must be distributed in the presence [of the Sangha].
However, that [rule] was stated by adding the training precept (sikkhāpada): "It may be accepted by a monk who so desires.
Therefore, all three [cases] have been explained in detail in the word-commentary (padabhājana).

“‘It must be made up immediately’ means it must be made up quickly, even within ten days”—this, however, was stated in order to indicate that when there is sufficient material, it follows the characteristics of the previous training rule.
Therefore, although it was not stated as “quickly” or “speedily,” etc., it was stated as “within ten days.
Let this be so for one who has performed the *kaṭhina* ceremony; but as for one who has not performed the *kaṭhina*:
When it is asked, "How so?", it shows the rejection of what is disadvantageous; thus it is written: "Not seeing [the truth], he falls into distress.
The commentary on the training rule concerning out-of-season robes (*akālacīvara*) is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning old robes (*purāṇacīvara*).

If it is argued that the statement, “As in the case of the Sākiyānīs, [or] in the pure Saṅgha of bhikkhus,” contradicts the definition, “A bhikkhunī is one who has received full ordination in both Saṅghas,” this is not so,

because the underlying intention is not understood. It should be understood that this was said precisely out of fear that the [case of the Sākiyānīs] might be wrongly associated with it, since full ordination in the presence of bhikkhus alone had been prohibited.
"By one basis" means by whichever first [basis]. "Washes even when not told" means she washes without being told; the meaning is that she dyes and beats it. It has been written:

"Because of the word 'even when not told,' there is no offense in washing and so forth without having her instructed. Here, "robe" (cīvara) refers only to what is suitable for wearing as an undergarment or an upper garment.
If this is so, then it should be stated: "only that which is suitable for wearing as an undergarment or an upper garment."
Why? Because it cannot be said [that this is "old robe-cloth"] since it is already established by that very term. For it has been stated:
"What is called 'old robe-cloth' (purāṇacīvara) is even that which has been worn once or put on once.
The commentary on the training rule concerning old robe-cloth is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Acceptance of Robes (*Cīvarapaṭiggahaṇasikkhāpada*).

The vicinity (*upacāra*) is twelve cubits. If it is asked, "Since this is unintentional, how can a rag-robe (*paṃsukūla*) be permissible? It is because that [rag] was not given to the monk by her, and because the monk did not take it from that nun.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the acceptance of robes is finished.

6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Requesting from One Who Is Not a Relative Regarding the phrase "or when requesting from one who has been invited by a relative": here, in the case of those invited by the Saṅgha, it is permissible to request only the standard measure. Regarding an invitation extended by an individual, it is recorded that one may request only whatever that specific person has invited.
The commentary on the training rule concerning requesting from one who is not a relative is concluded.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding What Is Beyond That (Tatuttari-sikkhāpada):

One normally goes about wearing the inner and outer robes (santaruttara), either due to the removal of the *kathina* privileges or because of the training rule concerning apprehension (*sāsaṅka-sikkhāpada*).
Here it might be thought: "They will not request much robe-cloth out of moderation, nor will they engage in the trade of cloth," and so forth.
Having heard those who were complaining, the Blessed One said to the group of six bhikkhus,
"How can you, foolish men, not knowing moderation, request so much robe-cloth?
Because he had thus laid down the training rule, and because it is stated in this *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* that "it was laid down in the case of requesting many robes," [the offense] is classified as such.
If it is argued that one may request a measurement for the sake of another because the *Samantapāsādikā* states:

"Those whose robes have not been stolen are not permitted to break off branches and foliage for their own use, but they are permitted to do so for the sake of those whose robes have been stolen," we say no.
Why? Because [the prohibition] arises specifically from the introductory narrative (*aṭṭhuppatti*) of the training rule concerning requests made by strangers.

Soliciting from one who is unrelated is prohibited. There is no offense regarding that training rule. In the Canon, with respect to this text on non-offense stating "for the sake of another," it is prohibited because of the statement:
"One who solicits for the sake of another solicits only from those who have prohibited [solicitation] by reason of being related, and not from others.
Therefore, the Blessed One also censured them, saying, "You will solicit many robes."

When laying down the training rule, he permitted taking [food] according to measure by the very method stated as "one may invite [it] to be brought," but not requesting it for another's sake according to measure.

However, because this training rule was laid down specifically regarding the case of requesting for another's sake, the phrase "for another's sake" is not mentioned here; it is not that such a case does not apply.
In the *Aṭṭhakathās*, it is stated: "In a place where one has been invited by those who are not relatives, even a large amount is permissible;

however, because of the reason of [the robe] being cut off, only the prescribed measure is permissible.
