Since that does not accord with the canonical text on non-offenses which states, "There is no offense in the case of relatives or those who have invited one," it is said in the *Samantapāsādikā* that here too, according to the method explained, for one who makes a request regarding an invitation from relatives:
It is recorded that there is no offense for one who takes [the goods] with his own wealth.

Although it was not stated [in the rule] because of its contradiction with the introductory narrative (nidāna) regarding "for the sake of another," nevertheless they say that it is indeed obtainable by the very method stated in the immediately preceding [rule].
The commentary on the training rule concerning excess is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning What Is Set Aside (*Upakkhaṭa-sikkhāpada*).

Regarding the first rule concerning what is set aside: because of the statement "not previously invited," it should be understood that even if one has been invited at that very moment, one is still as if not invited.
The commentary on the training rule concerning what is set aside is finished.
9. Commentary on the Second Training Rule Concerning What Has Been Set Aside If it is asked, "What is the purpose of [the rule] concerning what has been set aside? there is no specific purpose;
rather, it was established solely by way of an occasion (aṭṭhuppatti), just like the training rule for a bhikkhunī regarding sitting in private. This being so, by the compilers of the Council...

The recitation [of the Vinaya] would not need to include it, because that purpose could be accomplished even without it, because he has no authority over it, and because its inclusion was not authorized.
For this has been said: "If the Saṅgha so desires, Ānanda... it may abolish [the rule].
All of this is without reason; for the Buddhas do not utter speech that serves no purpose, much less a training rule.
For this very reason, it is said in the Aṭṭhakathā: "The meaning should be understood by this same method.

For this is like a subsequent rule (anupaññatti) to the preceding one," and so forth. There is no purposeless subsequent rule; thus it is shown that since this is similar to that, it is not purposeless.
This being so, what is the specific distinction in meaning here? To this he says: "In that case, harm was done to only one person..."
“In this case, there are two [offenses]; this is the distinction here. By means of this specific meaning, what other additional meaning is shown?
First, it is stated in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*: “Even regarding a single matter, it is not permitted to cause suffering to both;
this is the additional meaning shown. By this, it is illustrated that “it is not only by counting the robes already obtained...”
“Also by counting the offenses, and by counting the bases of the factors for the person who is oppressed.
And herein there are these verses:
“By way of the basis and by way of counting, an offense may become manifold;”
Thus, for the purpose of illustration, this second alternative is presented here:
"In the Vibhaṅga on the training rule regarding physical contact,
why is it said that even with a single woman there is a multiplicity of offenses due to the repetition of the action?"

Furthermore, this training rule should be understood as having the purpose of demonstrating the method for determining what is to be adopted among all the training rules belonging to that same class. And it has been said:
“Because of the plurality and the mixture of unrelated women;
And because of the plurality and the mixture of offenses.”
"The Teacher spoke this second [statement], 'This has been prepared,' in order to demonstrate that such methods as these are possible.
Herein, this is the investigation preceded by a summary of the intended meaning: A single monk [may use] an old robe..."
If she has two or many nuns wash it, the number of *pācittiya* offenses is according to the number of nuns.
Likewise, if she accepts a single robe shared by two or many [nuns], except in exchange, here too,
if she requests one [robe] shared by two or many, the number of offenses is according to the number of persons requested.
The counting of offenses. In this same manner, the method should be applied to other training rules of a similar kind. This, first of all, is the method regarding multiplicity.
Regarding mixture, however: if one causes a relative and a non-relative to wash one [robe], there is one *pācittiya* offense for the completion of that single act.
Then, if the relative has already washed a small portion and stopped, and subsequently the non-relative washes it thoroughly, there is a *nissaggiya* offense.

It is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). Now, if one who is not a relative washes first and afterwards one who is a relative makes it well-washed, for the monk there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) on account of the effort made by the one who is not a relative.

Whether one causes [a robe] to be washed while perceiving the one who is not a relative as being a relative, or with doubt, or perceiving her as a relative, the enumeration of the various offenses—such as the offense of forfeiture and wrong-doing—should be understood according to the method already stated.
Likewise, if one accepts a robe belonging to both a non-relative and a relative when it is being given by both together as one, it is an offense of expiation (*nissaggiya*).
If one accepts it from the hand of the non-relative alone, it is an offense of expiation. If one accepts it from the hand of the relative, there is no offense.

If one perceives both as non-relatives and so forth, the enumeration of the various offenses—such as the offense of expiation or the offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*)—is to be calculated according to the method already stated.
[The offense] is to be understood [in this way]. Likewise, the method should be applied as appropriate to cases such as requesting from those who are not relatives (*aññātaka-viññatti*).

This is the method regarding the mixed cases. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), however, it is meant that many unrelated persons are requested; there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) according to the number of persons requested.

One gives, one does not give: there is an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*). If, however, one who was not requested gives, there is no offense of relinquishment. Then, regarding those both requested and not requested...
If she gives what was requested for a common purpose, it is an offense of expiation (*nissaggiya*). If both give, it is likewise an offense of expiation.
If she gives what was not requested, there is no offense for the offense of expiation. If she gives what was not requested despite the words of one who had requested, there is no offense at all.
The same principle should be applied, as appropriate, to cases such as "prepared" and so forth.
To this extent, the intended meaning of the verses beginning with "to one who is not a relative" has been stated in brief.

As for the training rule regarding sitting in private with a nun (*raho-nisajja-sikkhāpada*) which was cited here as an example of being purposeless, its specific purpose will become evident in that very context.
In the same way, [the purpose of] other training rules is also established through explicit statement and by way of the arising of specific circumstances.
The specific purpose to be understood has been explained.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning what is prepared is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Kings.
Some say that because it is stated, "He breaks his standing; he destroys the reason for his arrival," he does not receive further admonition.
Some say that his coming is not purposeful, as he will not obtain a robe because hospitality has already been performed.
Some say it was stated on the grounds that it lacks the characteristic of an admonition. [It is said: "Hospitality is not [merely] by way of the intention to teach the Dhamma, etc."
The Elder Upatissa said, "By saying 'he destroys the reason for his arrival,' he breaks grounds for censure; desiring to censure, he has done what should not be done;
on account of that, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the breach of the rule.
But the Elder Dhammasiri said, "If he sits on the seat, by that single act of sitting he breaks two grounds. If he accepts food..."

By a single act of receiving, one destroys two bases. If one speaks the Dhamma, then by a single utterance that falls within the limits prescribed for the training rule on teaching the Dhamma, one destroys two bases. It is with reference to this that it is said: "He destroys the reason for his coming.
By the phrase "this one indeed," one person is designated; "this one is a servant... [and so on]... even though not told."
When it is said, "It is proper to urge [him]," that is the second; but if the messenger, while on his way, says, "I shall give this into his hand," and so forth, that is the third;

and when it is said, "He causes it to be announced by sending another," that is the fourth—just as these four have been specified by the monk, so too are these four specified by the messenger. [Also included are] the one who makes things allowable in the presence [of the recipient] and the one who makes things allowable in the absence [of the recipient].
And it is written that regarding these [persons], one should proceed as with those who are unrelated and have not been invited.
The commentary on the Rājasikkhāpada is finished.
The first section, the Cīvaravagga, is concluded.
2. The Chapter on Wool (Eḷakaloma-vagga) 1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Silk (Kosiya-sikkhāpada) "Should have made" means:
having taken both silk for oneself and for another together as one, it is said; or [it refers to] both.
"It should be understood that this means 'making it by one [party]. In that regard, if it was made by oneself, one should say at the time of relinquishment:
'This is a nissaggiya-pācittiya offense made by myself. If it was made by both, it is exactly as stated in the Pāḷi.
The commentary on the rule concerning silk (kosiya-sikkhāpada) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule on Pure Black [Wool]:

Just as it was stated in the first rule, “even with a single thread of *kosiya* wool,” so here, because there is no statement saying “even with a single [thread] unmixed with another,” they say that even if there is a mixture with another [color], provided its form is not discernible, it is called “pure black.”
The commentary on the training rule concerning purely black [wool] is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning two parts:
Regarding the word "having weighed," it means that just as in the weighing with scales, there are no more black [fibers] than the prescribed amount, so too [in this case], of the black [fibers]...

Two parts may be taken according to the maximum limit. Although the statement that it is an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) when even a single black hair exceeds [the limit] does not accord with the weighing on a scale, nevertheless, because this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is unintentional, the intended meaning is as follows:
if, after having previously weighed and set aside [the wool], even a single hair should fall upon it, it is an offense involving forfeiture. This is our view.
"Reasoning" (takka) is the teacher’s [view]. Non-performance is the failure to grasp according to the stated limits; performance is the making of a mat.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the two parts is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning six years.
Because it is said, “If six years have elapsed,” it is understood that it is permissible to do so once six years are complete;
therefore, the limit of the six years should be known as starting from the day of the formal conclusion [of the rains residence].
Furthermore, whatever [robes] have been made here based on more than six years, or by way of formal agreement (*sammuti*), all of those are permitted to be used together. For one who is ill...
And as for the phrase "one is not sufficient," it is permissible even if there are many.
Some say that from the moment one is able to go out taking a rug because the illness has become mild, neither the formal permission (*sammuti*) nor the illness itself provides protection.
Furthermore, because the training rule regarding the six-year-old [rug] is profound to investigate, they say: "Therefore, the ritual act (*kamma*) was performed for a six-year-old [rug]."
The commentary on the six rules concerning the rainy-season robe (*chabbassa-sikkhāpada*) is finished.
5. Commentary on the rule concerning the sitting mat (*nisīdana-sikkhāpada*).
Why, however, is the training rule "a monk [should not use] a spread" (*santhataṃ pana bhikkhunā*) not prescribed here, but rather the term "sitting-mat spread" (*nisīdanasanthata*) used?
"Has this been prescribed? Surely there must be a reason for it? There is indeed a reason;

it is said that the Blessed One prescribed it in that way for the purpose of showing that those cloths which are spread out and designated as "robes" (cīvara) are not actually robes because they have been discarded.
Therefore, those monks, out of fear of breaking the ascetic practice (dhutaṅga) of the three-robed monk, [refrained from using] those cloths spread out and designated as a fourth robe.
Having abandoned the thirteen ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), they adopted [the use of] sitting-mats, and the Blessed One permitted them to use such mats.
Then, it occurred to those monks: "This sitting-mat has been permitted by the Blessed One as the fourth robe in the form of a sitting-cloth;
how much more so, then, one that has already been made into a mat. Thereupon, regarding their mats...
The intention is that, for this reason, the Blessed One did not prescribe a "rug" (*santhata*) [in general], but rather prescribed a "seated-rug" (*nisīdanasanthata*).

Regarding these five types of rugs, it is recorded that although one may obtain the first three by performing a formal act of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*), they are not permitted for use because they are unallowable (*akappiya*); however, the latter two are permitted.
If it is asked, "How is this known? it should be understood from the statement: "There is no offense if one obtains and uses what has been made by another.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the sitting mat is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule concerning wool.
By the phrase “for one who has set out on a journey,” it is shown that even for one who has set out on a long road by nature,
the items may be carried for a distance of no more than three *yojanas*, let alone for one who has not set out. Furthermore, it shows that for one who has set out,
the term “journey” refers to the act of setting out on the road, just as when a bhikkhunī who has completed the rains residence sets out on a journey against her will.
The connection is with the phrase "for one who has set out on a journey, it is an offense of expiation" (*nissaggiya*).

For this very reason, since the intention to travel has ceased and he is no longer traveling, it is established that there is no offense for one who is reckoned as "not having set out. However, in this alternative interpretation of the meaning, [the text reads]:
"If wool should accrue to a bhikkhu... even when there is no carrier, for one who has set out on a journey, it is an offense of expiation."

The construction should be understood as: "it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Alternatively, since the limit of three *yojanas* is intended starting from the place where the wool originates, and there is no such limit of three *yojanas* for one who has not set out on a journey, it is therefore stated: "they should arise for one who has set out on a journey.
By this, it is established that there is no offense for one who, having received what was stolen, carries it away.
For their "acquisition" (paṭilābha) is indeed their "arising" (uppatti).
By the phrase, "They should be accepted by a bhikkhu who so desires," it is shown that an offense occurs only when one has accepted them oneself and then carries them beyond three yojanas.
By this, it is established that there is no offense for one who, not desiring [to keep them], carries away items belonging to others that have been accepted [on his behalf].
Regarding the limbs [of the robe], it should be understood that the sense of "belonging to oneself" is absent;
this meaning is indicated by the phrases "should arise for a bhikkhu" and "having recovered what was taken away. Furthermore, in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, it is stated:
"If he goes while having another bhikkhu carry it, there is no offense for either of them. Therefore, two bhikkhus may go up to three yojanas at most.
It is established that if they take [the goods] after having exchanged one another's belongings, there is no offense.
Regarding the rule "they may be carried by hand for a maximum of three yojanas": they may be carried by oneself for a maximum of exactly three yojanas. For what purpose is this?
Because this is the limit within the boundary (*sīmā*). For it has been said: "I allow you, monks, [to carry them] for a maximum of three yojanas."
"...to establish a boundary. This is the maximum extent for one who goes with the intention of staying overnight or the intention of returning.
For it has been said: "The group of six bhikkhus established excessively large boundaries... [and so on]...
the bhikkhus arrived while the Pātimokkha was being recited, or they arrived when it had just been recited, or they stayed overnight along the way."
"In the absence of one who carries it by command" means when there is no one to carry it by order.

It is written that if even a single hair becomes entangled in the robe of one walking while sitting upon a woolen blanket, an offense occurs once three *yojanas* have been exceeded, because it has become disentangled from the blanket.
That is appropriate, since because the blanket was accepted [for the monk], it was indeed accepted for his own sake.
The commentary on the training rule regarding wool (eḷakaloma-sikkhāpada) is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule regarding gold and silver (jātarūpa-sikkhāpada):
It is written that "even the shadow of a tree that has grown [there] does not exceed the boundary of the tree."
The commentary on the training rule concerning gold is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning trading in money:
"Exchanging gold and silver" is stated as the upper limit.
The commentary on the training rule concerning bartering with silver is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning buying and selling:
Regarding the statement "when it is absent, a *pācittiya* must indeed be confessed," is this a pure *pācittiya* or a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*? It is exclusively a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*.
The commentary on the training rule regarding buying and selling is finished.
Herein, this supplementary matter:

the eighth training rule prohibits the taking, causing to be taken, or consenting to the taking of a rag-robe or money that is being given by another for one’s own benefit, or being given as an exchange.
The ninth [offense] prohibits the exchange of money, whether belonging to another or to oneself.

The tenth is the exchange of non-money. The statement, “There is no offense for one who perceives non-money as non-money when exchanging with any of the five [kinds of currency],” indicates that there is an offense when exchanging with the others.
Furthermore, non-money is a matter of *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). Therefore, in the case of its exchange—

"It is an offense entailing relinquishment (*nissaggiya*) when it exists" is stated categorically. If it is argued that there is no offense at all when exchanging [an article] with any of the five things involving an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), because that would lead to the consequence of non-offense—this is not so; for only suitable articles (*kappiya-vatthu*) are mentioned therein.

If it is argued that if a suitable article is subject to relinquishment, how much more so an article involving wrong-doing—this is not so; for there is no fixed rule regarding the gravity or lightness of the article based on the gravity or lightness of the offense.
For even if pearls, gems, lapis lazuli, and so forth— though they are of great value and sufficient for an *nissaggiya* offense—
are considered objects for a *dukkaṭa* offense when they are excluded from the category of *nissaggiya* objects, the pearls and such become light [in gravity]. Regarding this light object,

the teachers of the *Aṭṭhakathā* maintain that just as there is a *dukkaṭa* for accepting an object of *dukkaṭa*, likewise there is a *dukkaṭa* for either exchanging it oneself or having it exchanged by another.

Alternatively, regarding what was stated, “Because only allowable things (kappiyavatthu) are mentioned therein,” although faulty things (dukkatavatthu) are also intended there, it is said that they were not explicitly mentioned in the Pāḷi for fear of involving the section on non-offenses (anāpattivāra).
Even when pearls and so forth are mentioned, one points out to the one who makes them allowable that there is no offense, saying: “This pearl and so forth belongs to us; and for us...”
If one says, "I have need of this or that [item], such as a beryl," the intention may be that one incurs an offense by means of the tenth [offense].
However, since this involves the transaction of informing the kappiyakāraka (the one who makes things allowable) and so forth, it should be understood that this is stated under the ninth [offense].
Even though it constitutes buying and selling, it is permitted because it concerns allowable articles; it is for this very reason [that it is included here].

Even though one incurs what is intended as a *dukkaṭa* offense in the tenth [case], it must nevertheless be understood that it is not intended here because it contradicts the *Aṭṭhakathā*. What, then, is the shadow of the reason here?
If it is argued that it is "no offense" because there is no possibility of non-offense for the five together in that case, we say no, because it has not been mentioned therein.
If it is argued that it was stated because of a future [rule], we say no, because the basis for the offense applies to all five together.

Because there is no specific reason for it to be an exception to the rule regarding non-offenses, and because it is unallowable (*akappiya*), there must be an offense even when [the exchange] is with the five [types of persons];
thus the position of the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*) is established.

Another method: if, on account of an article that is an object of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭavatthu*), there is a forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) due to buying and selling, then the same principle applies to an allowable article (*kappiyavatthu*).
In that regard, [if one were to say] "it could be obtained there, but it is not actually obtained," those [points] should be stated precisely in the ninth [case].

Therefore, regarding what is called "commerce" (*saṃvohāra*)—which includes buying and selling as well as other forms of exchange conducted through barter—it is not said, "It is permissible to barter by releasing the act of buying and selling, saying 'give this for that'";
rather, it is according to the method stated in the tenth section on non-offenses (*anāpatti*).

In the case of their exchange, because it contradicts the forfeiture [rule] regarding consent, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for causing them to be acquired, according to the method stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* by way of the subject matter of wrong-doing.
If it is argued that these constitute a forfeiture through buying and selling, we say no; for all such buying and selling is prohibited.
Therefore it was said: "But in the Andhaka-ṭīkā, however, it is stated: 'If one should engage in buying and selling, it is a forfeiture...'"
"It was stated that [this is] a *pācittiya*, but that is ill-stated. Why? Because there is no such thing as buying and selling other than the taking and giving [of goods].
This is because, according to his own reasoning, in the tenth section on non-offenses—which he considers to define the characteristics of buying and selling—the same method of explanation applies;
furthermore, it contradicts the rule regarding forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) for consenting to the exchange of those items. Or, let this be prohibited by him personally.

The reason is that in the tenth [offense], those things must necessarily be known; since they consist precisely of buying and selling, their state of being *nissaggiya* (to be forfeited) is established.
Thus, the commentary’s position is proven.
Regarding this, the ancients said: "If one makes one's own silver come into the hands of another, one commits an *ajjhācara* offense; it is a *dukkaṭa*."
If one makes another’s silver come into one’s own hand, it is an offense of expiation (nissaggiya) by the eighth [rule]. How does it become an offense in the case of exchanging an acquired object?

It becomes an indeterminate offense (abbohārika). Then, if one first makes another’s silver come into one’s own hand, because the acceptance of silver has been performed, it is an offense of expiation by the eighth [rule]. Regarding silver belonging to oneself...
“He makes it his own after it has come into another’s hand; through the act of bartering, there is an offense entailing relinquishment.

For it is stated therein: “By the mere taking of money, there is an eighth offense; subsequently, upon the exchange, there is a ninth”; that [interpretation] is indeed appropriate. However, the statement “if he deals with it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)” is poorly stated.
This is because, due to the possibility of an indefinite application of the term *dukkaṭa*, it would follow that [the rule] applies even to the procedures for relinquishing [the object].
It has indeed been shown. What is meant? If there were to be two offenses of forfeiture (nissaggiya), then in the procedure for forfeiture, one would have to say:
"Venerable sir, I accepted money and engaged in various kinds of transactions involving money," because in all instances throughout the Canon, the acceptance of money is what is stated.

To this extent, that which was stated in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*: "By one who avoids buying and selling by means of an article involving an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), when each of the four articles involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) has been taken, there is an offense of forfeiture on the eighth.

By means of an article involving an offense of wrong-doing, if one takes [an article] with the thought, 'Give this for that,' there is an offense of forfeiture by that very act. Buying and selling..."
"Having removed [the object] and taken it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); in the case of taking money for the purpose of exchanging, there is an offense on the eighth day;

in the case of bartering, on the ninth day," and so forth—[this means that] without having personally benefited oneself, but having removed it in accordance with what is allowable (kappiya), it is permissible to exchange it together with five fellow practitioners (sahadhammika).
Thus, that [objection] is cleared away. Furthermore, it is stated therein: "In the absence of anyone to whom the forfeiture (nissaggiya) should be made, how..."
Regarding the *pācittiya* [offense] for one who says, "He does not discard it," even though the money has been relinquished:
if the lay follower who has relinquished it takes that [money] and gives something else to the monk, it is allowable"—this too is poorly stated.

For by the fact of its being taken, it does not become a different object. Furthermore, it is stated there again: "For one who says, 'Take this,' there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the misappropriation of what was given in faith."

"To one who says, 'Give this,' there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the act of requesting"—this is poorly stated. For in that case, an offense of wrong-doing pertaining to the preliminary effort (payoga-dukkaṭa) appears more appropriate.
The miscellaneous section is finished.
The Second Chapter: The Section on Goat’s Hair. 3.
The Section on Alms Bowls.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Alms Bowls.

The two [types of bowls] have not yet been formally received; therefore, these may be used by way of physical enjoyment (*bhājanaparibhoga*), but they do not come under the categories of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) or assignment (*vikappaṇa*).
This is the meaning. Because it has departed from what is befitting for a recluse, the iron bowl must be cooked five times, while the clay bowl must be cooked twice.
"Because the accumulation of bowls is prohibited for a nun, that [iron bowl] is also considered 'unsuitable' for a monk."
And it has been written that [the phrase] "having made [it] an old bowl and having relinquished it" was spoken;
however, that is not correct, because in the Pāḷi it is said: "He may make a hoard" means "not determined and not assigned.
For even a single [bowl], like the "hoarding and storing" mentioned in the Kathina-khandhaka, is called a "hoard" on the following day. In the immediately preceding training rule...
However, because of the determination, "The second is prohibited," it is fixed; therefore, one is not permitted to determine two bowls [as one's own].
If one determines them as one, both remain undetermined. If one determines them separately, the second remains undetermined.

But one is permitted to assign (vikappeti) even many [bowls]. Regarding the phrase "even so much as a kākāṇika coin," here the particle *pi* [is used] in the sense of "it produces even a single cooking."
It consolidates the cooking. Alternatively, it should be understood that the quantity of the cooking is not specified because it is permissible even if cooked as a single batch.

Because it has not yet been received [as a bowl], it does not come under the category of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*). Regarding the statement "it must be assigned by one who does not discard the old," the meaning written is:
"By one who does not discard the old bowl, that bowl must be assigned."
The commentary on the training rule concerning cloths (*patta-sikkhāpada*) is concluded.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning less than five mends (*ūnapañca-bandhana-sikkhāpada*):

Regarding the term "having been invited," it is written that in a place where one has been invited by the Saṅgha, only a cloth with five mends is permitted; however, in a place where one has been invited by an individual, even a cloth with fewer than five mends is permitted.
He who, even though it was said, acts for the sake of less than five ties,
having approached one who has attained [the state of] less than five ties—
[thus ends] the commentary on the training rule concerning less than five ties.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Medicines:
By stating, "having accepted things to be used as ointments," it is indicated that it is permissible to accept and keep them for the purpose of rubbing the feet and so forth;
this is what has been written. By the statement, "the meat of those [animals] which is allowable," regarding whose meat...
Those who say that ghee and so forth are not allowable for them are speaking without understanding.
For it is said that ghee and the rest are for those for whom meat is allowable, in order to demonstrate the limits of the seven-day temporary and forfeitable articles.
Likewise, in the training rule concerning fine foods, milk and the like are considered fine foods only for those for whom meat is allowable.
It is stated [thus] in order to show that it does not mean anything else. "Honey" (madhu) refers to the great honey found in the hives of honey-bees and flies, which resembles resin;
it is recorded as being permissible for life. The commentary on the training rule concerning medicine is finished.
The Third Chapter on Robes.
The commentary on the offenses entailing relinquishment and confession (Nissaggiya-pācittiya) is finished. The Section on Confession (Pācittiya-khaṇḍa).
4. The Chapter on Eating (Bhojanavagga) 2. Explanation of the Training Rule on Group Eating (Gaṇabhojana-sikkhāpada):
Devadatta ate after having requested [food] at the proper time; because of that, the Blessed One declared: "In eating in a group, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)."
The training rule (sikkhāpada) has been laid down. However, in the word-commentary (padabhājana), it is analyzed by taking only "invitation" (nimantana), stating "she eats having been invited.
In the Andhaka-ṭīkā, however, it is written that even "requesting" (yācana) by means of solicitation (viññatti) is mentioned according to the specific case (vatthu).
Why? Because in the Parivāra itself it says: "Eating in a group (gaṇabhojana) arises in two ways: either from solicitation (viññatti) or from invitation (nimantana)."

Because it is stated [as such]. Therefore, it should be understood that it is not mentioned in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) precisely because it is already evident in the introductory narrative (*aṭṭhuppatti*).
And regarding the phrase "taking together," even if others have already taken their food, if they remain standing until others finish taking theirs, they are indeed said to be "taking together.
Furthermore, the expression "anyone who has gone forth" means among fellow practitioners of the Dhamma, or among those of other sects (*titthiya*).
And it is written: “The absence of an agreement means the absence of the seven agreements for non-offenses”;

“There are four [monks] including one who has obtained the agreement”; “One who has obtained the agreement is himself released, but because he serves as the completer of the quorum for the others, he becomes an offender.”
Here it is asked: "It was stated that 'in this case, the act of receiving alone is the measure'; why then is it said in the Pāḷi:
'A group meal (gaṇabhojana) is where four... [etc. ...eat'? It is replied: In that context, the word "eat" is a statement defining the act of receiving.
For monks do not eat what has not been received.
The commentary on the training rule concerning eating in a group is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning eating in succession:

Regarding the phrase "except at the proper time," some say that it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for one who, apart from an invitation or a distribution, looks toward food while eating in succession. One.

A bhikkhu, while wandering for alms, receives food; however, another lay follower invites him and has him sit down at home, and the meal he received from the alms-round has not yet been finished. If that bhikkhu eats the food obtained from wandering for alms, there is an offense. Why is that?
Because "successive eating" (paramparabhojana) refers to [eating] with any one of the five kinds of cooked food...

Because it is said: "Having been invited, if one eats any one of the five kinds of cooked food other than that [invited meal], this is called 'successive eating' (paramparabhojana)," it is similar to the first *kathina* rule;
however, the reading here is "this is a *kriyā-akriyā*" (action-non-action).
The commentary on the training rule concerning successive eating is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Kāṇamātā:
"Two or three bowlfuls may be accepted" means that one who has need of the cakes brought in that manner may accept them according to the maximum measure of a bowl.
[The offense occurs] by accepting an excess under the impression that it is prepared for the purpose of provisions for a journey and so forth, with the thought, "Do not accept anything more here."

In the cases of announcing [the food] and not sharing it, one is not released because the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is without mental intention (*acittaka*). Furthermore, if one takes what has been stored up, one is likewise not released.

However, there is no offense regarding not sharing because it is improper (*akappiya*). Some say that the state of being without mental intention arises solely from the absence of knowledge of the formal designation (*paṇṇatti*), and not from the absence of knowledge of the object (*vatthu*).
Regarding the factors [of the offense], it is "not knowing the state of having been prepared for the sake of provisions for a journey and so forth."
The ancient teachers say that if one does not speak intentionally because one has not been told, it is a *pācittiya*.

Regarding "accepting what is in excess," the fifth factor alone is stated therein; therefore, because it was not accepted, it is not a *pācittiya*, but rather a *dukkaṭa* due to the failure to do what ought to be done.
Otherwise, this would result in the fallacy of both action and non-action. Alternatively, "not restraining" or "not informing" should be stated as the sixth factor.
The commentary on the training rule concerning Kāṇamātā is finished.
5. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Invitation (Pavāraṇā).
"Having eaten" (*bhuttāvī*) refers to the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) consisting of five factors. Among these, by the phrase "food is discerned," it is indicated that one has "eaten."
Since this has already been established, no separate establishment of meaning is seen. If it were seen, it would have been written as "the demonstration of the sixfold nature of the factors.
The phrase "food is perceived" is said with reference to what has been brought [to the table].
By the word "pi" (also) in the expression "even flour made by grinding," *kuṇḍaka* (bran/scum) is included. However, for those that are split while being evenly cooked, they are dried in the sun.

Or *kuṇḍaka* (fried rice), or whatever grains there may be—since it is stated as "just this much"—one offers for invitation the powder of rice from paddy that has been equally fried, or the husks of the paddy;
likewise, one also offers *kuṇḍaka* made of paddy that has been coarsely fried.
It is recorded that even uncooked *sattu*-modakas, made by kneading together fried *sattu*, are offered. If there is a remainder...
There is no [need for] formal invitation (*pavāraṇā*). Why? Because there is an absence of "unfinished food," which is defined as food that has not been fully consumed.
However, although unallowable meat (*akappiyamaṃsa*) stands in a position where it ought to be rejected, when it is being eaten, it does not lose its nature as meat;
therefore, one invites [the guest]. If, while eating in the dining hall, someone brings a portion that has not reached oneself...
He refuses it and does not accept it by invitation. Although he may refuse it, if the monastery attendants pour it into his bowl, it is not permitted for him to eat it;
for this is considered to have arisen from a wrong search (an-esanā) that is censured by the Buddha.
For just as when an immoral person gives alms-food obtained from the Saṅgha, and one refuses it and does not accept it by invitation—it is exactly the same in this case.
And if one who is modest gives a portion, he rejects it not out of a desire to swallow it, yet he invites [the donor to eat].
Because of falling into the error of thinking "meat-flavor" (*maṃsarasa*) is the same as "equal-flavor" (*samaccharasa*), when it is said "meat-flavor," there is rejection;
however, it is stated that this analysis (*viggaha*)—"the flavor of meat is 'meat-flavor'"—is not intended. [This refers to food] mixed with rice.
Having brought rice gruel, he says, "Take rice gruel," but does not invite [them to take more]. When it is said, "Take food," he invites them.

Why? Because of the presence of that for which he was asked. In this case, however, if he says, "Take rice gruel mixed with food," and therein the rice gruel is either more abundant or equal in amount, while the food is meager, he does not invite them.
If the rice gruel is little and the solid food is more abundant, he offers it [to the recipient].
This cannot be rejected because it is stated in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). However, the reason for this is difficult to see. He says, "Take it mixed with the solid food.
In that case, whether the solid food is more abundant, equal, or less than the gruel, he still offers it. Or, regarding the solid food...
If, without having tasted the gruel, he says, "Take it mixed," and therein the solid food is more abundant or equal [in amount], he invites [the guest] to partake.
If it is less, he does not invite him. All of this must be investigated.
Regarding fruit or tubers and roots that have not been made permissible (*kappiya*) by the five allowable practices for monks (*samaṇakappa*): here, by those who have not had them made permissible...
Even if one has had banana fruits and so forth made into *atiritta* (leftover food), it is permissible to eat the remainder after setting aside those banana fruits and so forth.
Furthermore, because they have been mixed together, it is permissible to eat them again after having them made *kappiya* (rendered allowable) and placed in another vessel.
Why? They say it is because, previously, no formal act of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*) had been performed regarding them.
Dust that has fallen into the bowl is not yet formally accepted. Therefore, alms must be received before they are taken.
Because it is stated, "For one who takes them without having accepted them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (vinaya-dukkata)," they say that this is not permitted for others either.
Regarding the statement, "But for one who eats after accepting it again, there is no offense," it is exactly the same in this case as well. However, in this [matter]...
“In what has been made ‘leftover’ (atiritta), it is as if it were not made leftover”—here too it is exactly like this.
However, in this case, it is shown that the determination should be understood after investigating by means of such statements as, “What has been made leftover is as if it were not made leftover.
“This is enough for you all”—the meaning is: “This much is sufficient for you; you shall receive nothing other than this.”
“For the purpose of food”: some say this means only at the improper time. The reading is: “These are like the first *kaṭhina* [offense], but this one is both an act and a non-act.
It should be understood that it is a bodily action because of swallowing, and a verbal action because of not causing [the recipient] to speak with the words, “Venerable sir, make it leftover.”
The commentary on the first *pavāraṇā* training rule is finished.
6. Commentary on the second *pavāraṇā* training rule:

Because it is stated in the *mātikā* as "an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) when [the meal] has been eaten," it is said that there is an offense of expiation at the conclusion of the meal, not for every single mouthful swallowed.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning the invitation ceremony is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning eating at improper times:
"The limit of time for Jambudīpa is as follows," so it is said.
The commentary on the training rule concerning eating at improper times is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule concerning storing food:
Because it is stated here in the manner beginning with “it is difficult to wash,” [the text says] “having washed the bowl that was difficult to wash, again...”

Regarding this, because it is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*: "In that case, the state of being free from moisture is to be known by either pouring clear water over it or rubbing it with a finger," it is established—and thus written—that the moisture remaining in the rim of a clay bowl constitutes storage (*sannidhi*).

As for the phrase "having personally received it and not yet relinquished it," here "not yet relinquished" means not relinquished without regard for those who are not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).
“Not having abandoned”: regarding this, the Elder Dhammasiri says, “‘Receiving’ here means that the state of having been received itself produces storage.
This contradicts the canonical text which states, “If he receives it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
However, since for him there is no further function of receiving, this must be investigated.
The commentary on the training rule concerning storing up food is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning exquisite foods:
“Meat, milk, and curd are what is intended here”—this defines the scope of the offense entailing expiation (pācittiya).
However, there is no restriction regarding allowable milk and so forth; therefore, it is said that milk and other such items are permissible for anyone.

Furthermore, if one requests the fivefold set of medicines—such as ghee and the rest—for the purpose of medicine when the Saṅgha has been invited according to the Mahānāma-sikkhāpada, this falls under the category of "not requesting medicine for the sake of making medicine."
Therefore, it is written: "Thereby, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
The commentary on the training rule concerning superior food is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning tooth-sticks.
Because it is stated, “by means of a part of the body,” receiving [food] with the mouth is permitted.

Furthermore, regarding the statement, “it is not allowed in leaves such as those of the *ciñcā* tree when spread upon the ground, but it is allowed there on fertile soil,” and because of the phrase, “having taken it oneself,” this specifies that it is not only one bitten by a snake who is meant, but anyone else who has been bitten. It is also written: “It is allowed to take it oneself and consume it.”
The commentary on the training rule concerning tooth-sticks is finished.
The fourth chapter, the Section on Food, is concluded.
5. The Section on Naked Ascetics.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Naked Ascetics (Acelaka-sikkhāpada) Since those such as the naked ascetics (acelaka) are considered here to be merely sectarians (titthiya),
the triad was therefore cut off by means of the term "sectarian."

The determination is that it is permissible for one who is not a member of another sect, even if he is naked, as well as for one who bears the sectarian marks of another sect; and likewise for a householder and for a monk.
[It is permissible] for one who is not a member of another sect by way of intention, and for one who is a member of another sect by way of sectarian marks.
It is our opinion that it is permissible here to give [food] to those who are stream-enterers and so forth.
The commentary on the rule regarding naked ascetics (Acelaka-sikkhāpada) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Rule Regarding Eating with Others (Sabhojana-sikkhāpada).
It should be understood that there is a state of being with intention by means of the thought of sitting down after having entered [the dwelling].
The commentary on the training rule concerning eating together is finished.
4–5. Commentary on the training rules concerning sitting in private and secluded places.
The fourth [offense] is in the first *aniyata* rule; the fifth is in the second *aniyata* rule, according to the same method already stated. Here, the fifth becomes the fourth for Upananda.
The commentary on the training rules concerning secret concealment and sitting in private is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Traveling Together.

"Having eaten together" means "an invited meal," according to the ancients. Regarding the rule: "If a monk is present, without having asked for permission, before the meal or after the meal, except at the proper time"—this constitutes the fourfold supplementary regulation (*anupaññatti*) here. In that context, there are two "proper times.
"The house of one who provides food" refers either to the house of the person who has invited him, or the house of those who provide meals by ticket (*salākābhatta*) and so forth.

“The origin and so forth are the same as in the first *kathina* rule; however, the reading here is ‘this is both an action and a non-action. Some say that ‘here, an invitation is an invitation to what is not allowable.
And if, having gone for alms before the meal, one eats [thereafter];”
There may be a transmission through succession, but that would not occur after the meal.
And if one who is about to depart goes to his former home after the meal,
some say there is indeed an offense, while others say there is no offense.
For they consider it an offense when moving between families;
others here say that expectation of a meal in common [is an offense].
They consider it an offense regarding the meal of a courtesan; they meet at an invitation.
"Regarding 'while discharging [semen],' some say it refers to being face-to-face, while others say otherwise.

This training rule (sikkhāpada) is understood by the wise as consisting of: the purpose of reaching a conclusion, the various distinctions of what is to be investigated, and the conduct of one who is discerning."
The commentary on the training rule on conduct is finished.
7. Commentary on the Mahānāma Training Rule:
Regarding what was stated in the training rule on exquisite food—that "one should act in accordance with the Mahānāma training rule"—this is its meaning.

If one requests the five kinds of medicine, such as ghee and so forth, for the purpose of medicine when the invitation has been performed by way of the Saṅgha, it is recorded as a *pācittiya* offense by virtue of the statement: "One does not request medicine when there is no need for medicine.
Only one who is actually ill is permitted to request [medicine] after having explained the situation as it truly is, saying: "We have already been invited by you; we have need of this and that."
Nor does the phrase “for another’s sake” mean that [the food] was invited for his relatives, or that it was invited for himself by one who is related;
nor does the phrase “invited with an unlimited invitation” refer to those who, having performed an invitation for the Saṅgha and for individuals, are the givers.
Therefore, although the term “invitation for the Saṅgha” is mentioned, the term “invitation for individuals” is not explicitly stated.
By the expression “transcending the limit,” the sick person is included; therefore, it was not stated as “the state of being sick or not sick.
Even so, the reading “the state of having performed the invitation (pavāraṇā) by means of the Saṅgha’s invitation” has also been written down, and this should be investigated.
The commentary on the Mahānāma training rule is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning an Arrayed Army (*Uyyuttasenāsikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā*) "Regarding 'each one among the elephants, etc.':

this includes even a single elephant mounted by a single man, or even a single man with an arrow in his hand. The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*), etc., are similar to those of the wool-clipping rule (*eḷakaloma*); however, this is a worldly offense (*lokavajja*), consisting of unwholesome consciousness (*akusalacitta*) and three types of feeling (*tivedana*).
This is the reading. The commentary on the training rule concerning an arrayed army is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Military Encampments (*Senāvāsasikkhāpada*).

"Obstructed by anyone" means obstructed by someone who is hostile or by someone who is a ruler. It should be delimited by the military encampment itself, or by a place suitable for an enclosure, or by the boundary of the area for walking about.
The commentary on the training rule concerning military encampments is finished.
The Fifth Chapter: On the Naked Ascetics.
6. The Chapter on Drinking Liquor.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding the Drinking of Liquor.
It is recorded that drinking [liquor] while knowing it as "surā" or "it is not permitted" is indeed unwholesome (*akusala*).

Regarding the term "unwholesome mind," it is said that this was stated with reference to the majority of cases. If one asks: why is it stated in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā* (Commentary on the Vinaya) that "it must be drunk only with an unwholesome state"?
It is because, in the case of intentional action (*sacittaka-pakkha*), it must be drunk only with an unwholesome state.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the drinking of fermented liquor is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule regarding poking with the finger:
Although the offense is the same—a *saṅghādisesa* for physical contact—the penalty is a *dukkaṭa* for both a nun and one who is not fully ordained.
"In the case of one who is fully ordained, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)"—this was stated thus to show that it depends on the individual.
Regarding the phrase "when there is a purpose," the intended meaning here is that he touches a man when there is a purpose, not a woman.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the poking with a finger is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Joking (Hasadhamma-sikkhāpada):
Because of the phrase “or in mud,” throwing even a pebble while playing at tossing games constitutes a *dukkaṭa* offense.

Regarding the fact that there is a *pācittiya* for [throwing] above the ankle and a *dukkaṭa* elsewhere, it is stated that “there is a *pācittiya* for joking in water” with reference to the purpose of the subject matter of the *pācittiya*.
If this is a liberation through perception (*saññāvimokkha*), how can there be a triad of *pācittiya* offenses?
That it is "not play" like "play" would be due to a false grasp.
To this extent, how could it be play? Thus, this is indeed [an instance of] play.
"One should perceive this as playlessness and undertake it for the sake of discipline.
Since one who is entirely unskilled delights in play,
therefore here only an unwholesome mind is found."
The commentary on the training rule concerning envy is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning disrespect:
"His word" means: "This person has been suspended, or reviled, or censured; his word has not been heeded."

He shows disrespect [thinking], "It will happen. Regarding the "Dhamma": he shows disrespect because he does not wish to train in that which might be lost, destroyed, or disappear during this discourse. It is written:
"It is not permissible for one who, having transgressed what is forbidden by the world, says, 'This is our teacher's tradition.'"
The commentary on the training rule concerning disrespect is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule concerning fire:
Because it is stated, "one who desires to kindle [a fire]," it is permissible for another person and for others as well.
Whether they are many or numerous, sages kindle [fires] together;
yet one alone causes it to go out, not many, due to the distinction in their intention.
The commentary on the training rule on fire is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Making [the Robe] Discolored (*Dubbaṇṇakaraṇasikkhāpada*).

Regarding the phrase "on a peacock’s eye, a mandala, or the back of a finger," they say that it is not necessarily restricted to these; rather, anything additional or even something smaller is permissible. It is also allowable on a single corner; thus, it is allowable as even a single drop anywhere.
The commentary on the training rule concerning making [the robe] discolored is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule on Reassignment (*Vikappaṇasikkhāpada*).

"The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth are similar to those of the first *kaṭhina* rule; however, this is both an act and a non-act," is the reading. Herein, bodily action (*kāyakamma*) occurs through the act of using [the robe], while verbal action (*vacīkamma*) occurs through the failure to relinquish it.
The commentary on the training rule on reassignment is concluded.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule on Hiding.
According to the ancients, there are offenses according to the number of needles when [the needle case] contains needles and has a needle-case.
The commentary on the training rule on hiding is finished.
The sixth chapter: The Chapter on Drinking Alcohol (Surāpānavagga).
7. The Chapter on Living Beings (Sappāṇakavagga).
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Intentional Killing (Sañciccasikkhāpada).

By way of counting the bases, there is a counting of the acts of binding by karma, the volition, and the killing; it is not by way of counting the acts of binding by karma that the volition and the killing are counted. Herein, this distinction should be understood: that many living beings may die through a single volition.
The commentary on the training rule concerning intentional action is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Water with Living Beings.

Regarding "containing living beings": it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) by virtue of the death of the living beings, not an offense of expiation by virtue of the consumption of water containing living beings;
therefore, it is called a "formal offense" (*paṇṇattivajja*). It is an offense of expiation due to an impure state of mind; there is no offense when the mind is pure.
It is recorded that its status as a formal offense is stated because it is like lighting a lamp.
"Throwing into water is the former [offense], while this is entering into water;
thus the difference between the two should always be known by the wise.
The commentary on the training rule concerning living beings is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Those Under Twenty Years of Age:
"He ordains another"—if the preceptor himself both recites the formal act (*kammavācā*) and [performs the other duties].
"Some say that the formal act succeeds," says the one skilled in discipline.
"Since an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) has been prescribed for both the teacher and the group,
therefore here the teachers and preceptors are indeed separate and distinct."
The commentary on the training rule concerning those under twenty years of age is concluded.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Arrangements:

Here, these three—those fully ordained for less than twenty years, female trainees (*sikkhamānā*), and female novices (*sāmaṇerī*)—are included together; however, it should be understood that this [training rule] applies to these three, and furthermore, it represents a distinction from the case of women in general.
The commentary on the training rule concerning formal arrangements is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning communal living with one who has been suspended:
“‘With one who has not relinquished that view’ refers to one who is of a different communion due to a difference in tenets,” so it is written. *Ticitta* means...
In this context, the meaning should be understood as "one might lie down together with a mind that is indeterminate as a result of kamma (vipākābyākata-citta).
Otherwise, because the training rule (sikkhāpada) pertains to a state possessing consciousness, it would not be applicable with reference to an indeterminate state of action (kiriyābyākata).
The commentary on the training rule concerning social intercourse with one who has been suspended (ukkhitto) is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule on Thorns:

“This novice monk is one who has committed a defeat (pārājika). If he relinquishes that view, having informed the Saṅgha, he may be ordained with the Saṅgha’s consent”—this is stated in the *Porāṇagaṇṭhipada*, but it is not appropriate. [For there is] expulsion by means of disciplinary action.
For here, these [offenses] are intended. If he is one who has committed a *pārājika* offense, there may be what is called the "removal of the emblem" (*liṅganāsanā*).
Furthermore, the view that "practicing those [acts] is not sufficient for an obstacle" is not the same as the view that the Teacher is not a teacher and so forth.

If he who in whom that [view] arises becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense, then in his case too one should proceed in exactly the same way; for one who does not abide in restraint, there is the removal of the emblem.
"He should be expelled"—this was the teacher's thought.
The commentary on the Kaṇṭaka-sikkhāpada is finished.
The seventh chapter, the Sappāṇaka-vagga, is concluded.
8. Sahadhammika-vagga 4.

Commentary on the Training Rule on Striking (Pahāra-sikkhāpada) If it is argued that, just as in the case of the [previous] factors, one must state "the absence of the intention to kill" rather than "the absence of the intention for liberation," we reply: it need not be so stated. Why?

A bhikkhu who himself desires to give a blow, having determined that there is no application [of effort] toward his death by way of intention, possesses only the intention for non-death because his concern is with non-death;
thus, like those [other cases], this is not mentioned [as an offense]. However, for one whose intention is liberation, there is no anger;
therefore, it is stated that there is no offense.
The commentary on the training rule regarding striking is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule regarding the hand-sling (*tala-sattika*).
"Hand" (*tala*) itself is the "hand-sling. Some say it is called a "sling" (*sattika*) in the sense of being capable of throwing. Because of the desire to strike...
If one strikes with the first [intention], it is a *pācittiya*; if one merely utters [the words] out of a mere desire to speak them aloud, there is a *pācittiya* by this [rule].
However, because a blow was given after having missed [the mark] with this [second intention], there is a *dukkaṭa*, since it was not given with the desire to strike.
Is this *dukkaṭa* due to the cause of the striking, or rather due to the cause of the uttering? It is a *dukkaṭa* precisely due to the cause of the striking.
Regarding the rule "the first [instance] is a *pācittiya* offense due to vomiting," it is appropriate that this be a *pācittiya* accompanied by a *dukkaṭa*.

For the first instance was the vomiting, and the subsequent instance was the striking. The teacher maintains that the first instance of vomiting cannot be rendered free from the basis for an offense merely on account of the subsequent striking;
therefore, he does not accept that as a valid argument.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the palm of the hand is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning intentional action:

Whether or not another person actually gives rise to remorse is irrelevant. It should be understood that the third factor, "the inducing of remorse," is stated according to the intention of the agent.
The commentary on the training rule concerning intentional speech is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule concerning eavesdropping:
Just as *upakujjha* is called "near the mound" (*samīpakujjha*), so too *upassuti* is "eavesdropping nearby" (*samīpassuti*).
It should be understood as follows: the meaning is "the place where one stands while listening. Furthermore, in this context, *suti* refers to the sound of the speech of others;
for that which is heard is called *suti*. Alternatively, it is *upassuti* because one listens closely (*upasuyyati*) there; thus, *suti* refers to the location.
In the phrase "having heard these," the word "speech" (*vacana*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the text.
The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other factors should not be understood as being identical to those of the two preceding offenses. Its origin is from a caravan of thieves.

It may be an act (*kiriya*) when one goes and hears it; it may be a non-act (*akiriya*) by way of its origin when one does not cause another to know while they are speaking at the place where one is standing.

It is with liberation through perception (*saññāvimokkha*), accompanied by consciousness (*sacittaka*), a worldly offense (*lokavajja*), bodily action (*kāyakamma*), verbal action (*vacīkamma*), and an unwholesome mind (*akusalacitta*).
"painful feeling" is written [in the text].
The commentary on the training rule concerning eavesdropping is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning obstructing formal acts (*kamma*).

However, for one making a robe from even a small amount of cloth, the needles and other items mentioned in the commentary on the *Senāsanakkhandhaka* should be given even without seeking formal permission (*apalokana*).
If one gives more than that, a formal act of seeking permission must be performed.
The intention is that such a formal act of seeking permission possesses the very characteristic of a formal act (*kammalakkhaṇa*). Thus, in all cases, it possesses the characteristic of a formal act.

It should be understood that in monasteries within the village boundary (*gāmasīmā*), formal acts of the Saṅgha such as reinstatement (*osāraṇā*) are not permitted; however, transactions involving the distribution or dismantling of property are permitted.
Furthermore, one should seek permission by saying, "This belongs to the Saṅgha of this monastery," rather than stating it generically as "This belongs to the Saṅgha.
The origin and other factors are similar to those of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), but this [offense] is characterized by painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
And it is written as "pāṭho. The commentary on the training rule concerning the warding off of legal acts is finished. 10.
Commentary on the training rule concerning departing without having given one's consent.

Some say that if one does not give consent without having come to the assembly, there is no offense. Others say it is an *dukkaṭa* because of the intention to obstruct a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*).
The commentary on the training rule regarding going without giving consent is finished.
11. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Weak.
"By means of what is unallowable" (*akappiyena*) means by means of a bedstead made of gold, silver, and so forth.

"An allowable bedstead should be accepted" is said with reference to that which has been given saying, "We give it to the Saṅgha"; however, if they say, "We give it to the monastery," then even unallowable bedsteads made of gold, silver, and so forth should be accepted.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "a water-chest that holds much water," and "by means of the enjoyment belonging to the Saṅgha":
If monastery attendants and others have put it away and return it, it is permissible to use it;

and because it is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā* that "even if a vessel made of bronze, copper, or other metals has been given to the Saṅgha, it is not permissible as a personal possession," one does not receive permission to take it up with one's own hand and put it away oneself; and [it is said] "they say the fastener belongs to the waist-belt"; and "asafoetida..."
Furthermore, there are readings such as "cinnabar, yellow orpiment, realgar, and eye-ointments," and "either made of wood...
even a box without legs," and "a wooden vessel means a wooden water-vessel," and it is written as "in the case of pillars, scales, steps, planks, and so forth.
The commentary on the weak training rule is finished.
12. Commentary on the Training Rule on Diversion (*Pariṇāmana-sikkhāpada*).
If a certain bhikkhu wishes to give to one who has been suspended (*ukkhitaka*), but having prevented that person from receiving the gift, he causes it to be given to another, there is no offense.

Likewise, if he causes [the gift] to be given to someone else while diverting what was intended for a faithful donor, or if he says, "The bowl of such-and-such a person belongs to those dependent upon me," there is no offense.
If those wishing to give ask for permission, and [the owner] says, "This is unsuitable; give it to someone suitable," there is no offense because it has become one's own burden.

However, if one causes another to give it to someone else when that person wishes to give it, there is indeed an offense. In all cases, after having asked for permission, one may let the person wishing to give dispose of it as they please.
The commentary on the training rule concerning diverting [gifts] is finished.
The eighth chapter, the Chapter on Fellow-Practitioners (Sahadhammika-vagga).
9. The Chapter on Jewels (Ratana-vagga). 1. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Royal Palace (Antepura-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā).
“In the vicinity of a dwelling” means in places such as the roots of trees located outside the enclosure.

Regarding the statement, “If he is a khattiya but not anointed, or if he is anointed but not a khattiya, he guards [the robe],” the Teacher says this is because both “being a khattiya” and “being anointed” are stated as constituent factors for the offense.
The origin and other details are similar to those of the first *kaṭhina* rule; however, the reading is that this is a “non-action” (*akiriya*) offense.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the inner apartments is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning gems:
The entire course of the narrative proceeds by way of rejecting both the depositing and the concealing [of items] under the pretext of the treasurer.
The commentary on the Jewel Training Rule (Ratanasikkhāpada) is finished. 3.
Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Entering a Village at an Improper Time (Vikālagāmappavesanasikkhāpada):

Regarding this, the text reads: "A monk who is present," "without having asked permission," and "such urgent business"—these are the three [factors] here. "The origin and so forth are the same as for the Kathina [rule]; however, this is both an act and a non-act," so the text says.
The commentary on the training rule regarding entering a village at an improper time is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding the Needle Case:

"Taṃ assa" means that for that offense involving breaking, there is a first instance of breaking, because one must subsequently confess after having first committed the breaking. This same method applies to the others as well. "Vāsijaṭe" means on the handle of a chisel.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the needle-case is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule concerning beds and chairs:
“With legs eight finger-breadths [high]” is a masculine form used in the neuter. The act of placing [the bed] upon the frame-assembly is itself the construction of the support.
The commentary on the training rule concerning beds and chairs is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule concerning [beds] covered with cotton:

Although it appears that the offense is a *pācittiya* at the very moment of acquisition, the offense should be understood as occurring only upon use. The statement, "If one acquires something made by another and uses it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," is the proof for this point.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the stuffed mattress is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning the sitting mat:
Although the origin story of the sitting mat is not seen here, nevertheless, because it was permitted in the Cīvara-kkhandhaka, [it is included].
Regarding the statement, “The nine robes must be determined,” it should be understood that because it is included within that category, the class of robe itself is its "class.

Some say, “If one obtains it with a border, it is permissible; if not obtained with a border, even one without a border is permissible”; however, that is not correct, because its shape is fixed by the rule: “A sitting mat is said to have a border.”
The commentary on the training rule concerning sitting mats is finished.
The ninth chapter, the Chapter on Jewels, is finished.
The commentary on the pure *pācittiya* rules is finished.
Pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍa 1.
Commentary on the First Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule:

Regarding "what is kept for a watch of the night" (yāmakālika) and so forth, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) only when it is for the purpose of food. Even in that case, if the flavor is not mixed with other foodstuffs (āmisa), it is an offense of wrong-doing; however, if it is mixed and becomes a single flavor, it is a Pāṭidesanīya offense.
The commentary on the first *pāṭidesanīya* training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the second *pāṭidesanīya* training rule:
"The origin and other factors are the same as those for the *kathina* [rules], but this is both an act and a non-act," so the text reads.
The commentary on the second *pāṭidesanīya* training rule is concluded.
4. Commentary on the fourth *pāṭidesanīya* training rule:

"Having received it in a monastery or in the vicinity of a monastery, while consuming it" means: having received it in a monastery or in the vicinity of a monastery, while consuming it in a monastery or in the vicinity of a monastery; such is the meaning.

There is no offense for one who receives [food] outside the monastery grounds and eats it inside the monastery grounds. Regarding the factors, it should be understood as: "receiving either inside the monastery grounds or in the vicinity of the monastery grounds.

For when the interior of the monastery grounds is shown, the vicinity of the monastery grounds is necessarily shown as well. The reading is: "The origin and so forth are the same as those of the Kathina;
however, this is a 'kriyā-akriyā' (an act that may or may not be performed)."
The commentary on the fourth training rule regarding offenses entailing confession is finished.
The commentary on the offenses entailing confession is finished.
The Section on the Training Rules.
In the *Sekhiyas*, the term "one who acts" (*kāraka*) is not mentioned in order to show that even when there is a transgression, the offense belongs only to one who has disregard (*anādariya*).

For this is the nature of the Vinaya: namely, that the designation of "one who acts" applies only when there is such disregard; it is a rule within the stated restriction, and it functions as an ablative.

It is permissible to wear the lower robe after letting it down even more than eight finger-breadths. However, for one who lets it down beyond that point, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).

This is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. "In a monastery" (*ārāme*) means at times such as when attending upon the Buddha. "Should be worn" (*pārupitabbaṃ*) is said with reference to the duty of wearing the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).
Regarding "standing," it is written here that even one who is walking is permitted to do so in order to observe whether there is any danger.
Just as it is permissible for one who has entered an inhabited area to sit with the body uncovered, so too [is it permissible] in his presence.
Even for one wishing to go, it is permissible to go as one pleases without fastening the waistband, without putting on the outer robe (saṅghāṭī), and without announcing the entry into the village.
Therefore, when traveling on a long journey, one monk should fulfill the duty of entering the village;
having entered the village and reached a lodging situated ahead, he should set down his requisites.
If he has entered upon the rains residence, it is permissible for others to go to him at their convenience.
How much more so, then, is it permissible to go to those monks who have resolved to stay for four or five days, as well as to those who have entered upon the rains residence?
It is also permissible to go at one’s convenience to perform worship of the Buddha. And this has been stated in the Commentary:
“There is no offense if one looks here and there for a reason. In this context, it is recorded that “reason” should be understood as material offerings and honor.
The commentary on the twenty-six appropriate [rules] is finished.
Since the statement, "Almsfood should be received so as to be level-full," indicates that almsfood should be received until it is full to the brim,
it is thereby indicated that even if the almsfood being given into the bowl held in one's own hand becomes heaped up,
it is permissible. This applies even in the case of requesting soup and rice, where, after having placed it in the mouth, regret arises and one wishes to vomit it out again.
If one enters [the dwelling] suddenly, this is called "eating unintentionally" (*asañcicca*).

If one takes and eats food—whether it has been formally requested or not—that is situated in one place, having done so suddenly and without reflection, this is called "eating through lack of mindfulness" (*assatiyā*).
If one is oneself traveling in a vehicle, it is just as it is for one who is traveling in a vehicle.
“[The rule] ‘A vessel that is suitable’ and likewise ‘not suitable,’ ‘with an umbrella,’ and ‘to one holding an umbrella.

The reading is: “The training rule regarding the request for soup and rice originates from theft and a caravan; it is an action (kiriya), liberated by awareness (saññāvimokkha), involving volition (sacittaka), a worldly offense (lokavajja), bodily action, verbal action, an unwholesome mind, and painful feeling.
The commentary on the Sekhiyas is finished.
The Commentary on the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
The Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha.

Regarding the phrase "Pārājika-kanda is merely a matter of expression": here, there are two types of expression—“Venerable Sir” (*bhante*) used for juniors and “Friend” (*āvuso*) used for seniors; however, in this case, both seniors and juniors are addressed with the single term “Noble One” (*ayya*).

Regarding the phrase “in the manner stated for bodily contact”: here, by way of its predominance, it is stated that [the offense] originates from action (*kiriya-samutthāna*). [The text continues: “Bodily contact...”
Since it was stated not as "he should enter [the state]" but rather "he should consent," it should be understood that this offense also originates from non-action (*akiriya*).

And just as here, so too in the preceding section—where, by way of the method beginning with "for one who practices the sexual act with a human woman in the three ways, there is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*)"—the origination from action (*kiriyasamutthāna*) was stated, immediately following that: "enemies of the bhikkhus..."
Since it has been stated in such a manner—as in "having brought a human woman into the presence of a bhikkhu, they cause him to sit down with her organ against his anus;

if he consents to the insertion"—that even for an offense originating from non-action (akiriyasamuṭṭhāna), the first *pārājika* should likewise be understood as originating from action (kiriyasamuṭṭhāna) according to the predominant principle.
For the quality of originating from action is not seen in cases such as the mere consenting to the insertion.
And here, the movement of the genitals (*aṅgajāta*) is not to be regarded as essential.

For in the passage: "If he does not consent to the insertion, does not consent to what has been inserted, does not consent to its remaining, but consents to its withdrawal, there is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*)," the state of "not consenting to its remaining" is already fulfilled by the natural movement itself. Furthermore, the movement of enjoyment resulting from consent is what is intended here.
"It is not seen" means that, according to the principle of majority rule (*tabbahulanaya*), it should be understood as originating from action (*kiriyasamuṭṭhāna*).
