Furthermore, since in the first *pārājika* for a nun, that consent was stated in its specific form, [the text] says "originating from action" alone, having considered the method of the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) in accordance with that. And just as in these cases, by way of the principle of majority...
The state of being originated by action (kiriyasamuṭṭhānatā) has been stated, as well as the fact that [offenses] such as drinking liquor must be incurred through unwholesome [volition] alone.

Otherwise, if it were stated, "That which one incurs only through unwholesome [volition] is a world-transgression (lokavajja); the rest are transgressions by rule (paṇṇattivajja)," then the defining characteristic of the restriction between world-transgressions and transgressions by rule would be established.
Likewise, instead of stating that, if it were said, "That for which, in the category of those involving consciousness, the mind is exclusively unwholesome, is a world-transgression..."
When it is stated, "The rest are excluded from the category of formal rules (paṇṇatti-vajja)," the expression "worldly offenses" (loka-vajja) would be redundant;

for even in the case of not knowing the substance [of the offense], one must incur the penalty by means of an unwholesome state of mind alone. Since there is no arising of an unwholesome consciousness (akusala-cittuppāda) in that instance regarding the transgression of drinking liquor, therefore, in the Khandhaka-aṭṭhakathā, it says:
"But in the case of drinking intoxicants, even if a bhikkhu does not know [it is forbidden], starting from the seed..."

It is stated: "For one drinking intoxicants, there is an offense entailing expiation (pācittiya). A novice monk incurs a breach of virtue only if he drinks knowing [it to be intoxicating], not if he does so unknowingly.

It is not stated: "In the case of not knowing the substance, even if there is an unwholesome state of mind similar to that which brings about the accomplishment of killing and so forth, the novice monk does not incur a breach of virtue. This is a statement based on dogmatic insistence regarding killing and so forth.

Because novices (*sāmaṇera*) share the same status regarding the drinking of fermented liquor (*surā*), there is no possibility of unwholesome (*akusala*) action for one who, knowing the substance to be "fermented liquor" (*surāmeraya*), transgresses by way of drinking it and so forth.
Therefore it was said: "In whose case, on the side of being with consciousness," and so on. What is the point here?

By this statement of reasoning, since [unwholesomeness] does not enter into Arahants, there is a restriction of the unwholesome to both the sides of being with consciousness and without consciousness.
Why? Because, by way of natural law (*dhammatā*), even for those in training (*sekkha*), [unwholesome states] do not enter.

To show the absence of the "unwholesome certainty" (*akusala-niyama*) in the case of one without consciousness, examples such as drops of liquor and the like should be cited, similar to a drop of water placed in the mouth of one who is sleeping.

For when the meaning is grasped according to the principle of predominance (*tabbahulanaya*), it accords with both the Commentary and the Canon (*pāḷi*) from beginning to end. Even the Teachers [hold this view] regarding the drinking of liquor...

They state that there is simply an absence of unwholesome necessity (*akusala-niyama*). However, some say that its arising from functional [karma] (*kiriya-samuṭṭhāna*) is merely according to the majority rule, and not in the case of the first *pārājika*.
How so? The training rule on bodily contact (*kāyasaṃsagga-sikkhāpada*) arises from the first *pārājika*.
Here, when there is bodily contact between a monk and a nun, even if the nun does not touch his body part, [the offense is incurred].
One consents, commits the offense, and so forth by means of the mind alone; it is not so for the bhikkhu. Rather, the bhikkhu commits the offense only when there is physical contact (*copana*);

likewise, even in the case of the first *pārājika*, one commits the offense only when contact exists, not when it does not. Regarding the phrase "consents to the insertion," here "consenting to the insertion" means the arising of a mind intent on sexual intercourse, or they maintain that it is the desire for the way [of entry] or for what has entered the way.
Even for her, there is certainly bodily movement. Nevertheless, it is written that "one should accept [the offense] after having investigated.
The Commentary on the Pārājika is finished.
The Section on Saṅghādisesa.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Litigation for Gain:
Having reached the Saṅghādisesa offense for bhikkhunīs, and in order to demonstrate the procedure for rehabilitation, the specific individual is identified by the rule stating, "This bhikkhunī...
has fallen into [an offense]," and it is defined as a Saṅghādisesa that is "to be brought out" (nissāraṇīya) from the perspective of the Pārājika offenses.
The enumeration of the offenses has been completed. The reading is: "The origins and so forth are the same as in the first *kathina* [rule], but this is only an act (*kiriyā*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning one who acts as a legal advocate for gain is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning One Who Causes a Thief to Be Discharged.

In some cases, for one who sits down and acts while remaining in the very place where she sat down without having gone elsewhere, it is [an offense] through speech, mind, and body; for one who has gone to a broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*), etc., it is through body, speech, and mind.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the expulsion of thieves is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Going Between One Village and Another.

Because it is stated, “without intention (*ābhoga*),” there is no offense when such intention is present; however, in this training rule, the *Samantapāsādikā* states that an offense occurs upon crossing the boundary (*upacāra*), whereas here it is stated to occur upon entering [the village].
Although stated in both places, the meaning is identical: the *saṅghādisesa* offense for going between villages is spoken of with reference to the boundary.
This contradicts the case of withdrawing from a group. As for the term “in the forest” (*araññe*), this is according to its actual sense.
It has been stated that this [offense] occurs even within a village boundary.

Regarding the verse, "The training rules were praised by the Best of Buddhas," it is also stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā* that "crossing a river" is included within the category of "going between villages.
The commentary on the training rule concerning going between one village and another is finished.
“But by concealing it, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)” means:
“One incurs a grave offense with remainder;
one conceals it out of disrespect.”
"A bhikkhunī would not incur blame"; this question was pondered by those skilled in the Dhamma.
This [verse] contradicts that [previous statement]. Therefore, one should investigate the meaning here, for it appears like a scribal error. [Regarding] the bhikkhus...

In the discussion on the *mānatta* penance, it is stated: "having passed two *leḍḍupāta*s beyond the enclosure of an enclosed monastery, or beyond the place suitable for an enclosure in the case of an unenclosed one";

however, here it is stated: "two *leḍḍupāta*s from the vicinity of the village (*gāmūpacāra*) and from the vicinity of the monks' dwellings (*bhikkhūnaṃ vihārūpacāra*)," and so forth. In that context, having passed the area described as being for the monks...
Some say that it is permissible for him to perform that action even within a village, but for bhikkhunīs, it is not permissible in a village; therefore, it was stated in this way.
Others, however, maintain that it is not permissible for bhikkhus either in a village. A "bhikkhu-vihāra" is one that stands already beyond the vicinity of a village (*gāmūpacāra*);
therefore, instead of mentioning the village, the vicinity of the vihāra itself was mentioned below. As for bhikkhunīs...
A monastery (vihāra) is permissible only within the village, not outside it; therefore, both the village precinct (gāmūpacāra) and the monastery precinct (vihārūpacāra) are indicated here.
Consequently, they say that there is no difference in meaning between the two. One should accept whatever is logical.
The commentary on the Saṅghādisesa rules is finished.

In the second [offense] of the *Nissaggiya-kanda*, a robe obtained through having it distributed here becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*); even after the formal disciplinary act (*vinaya-kamma*) has been performed, one does not receive it oneself.
In the third, the reading is: "The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth are similar to those of taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), but this [offense] is of painful feeling (*dukkha-vedanā*)."

In the fourth [offense], if one does not obtain the first requested item but obtains another that is even smaller than it, it is still a *nissaggiya* offense because the essential factors are fulfilled.
The commentary on the *nissaggiya* rules is finished.
The Section on *pācittiya* offenses.
1. Commentary on the First Chapter In the first [section], *haritaka* is green in color. *Cāpala-suṇa* is *amiñjaka*. For it has only the mere sprout.
Onions (*palaṇḍuka*) and so forth are permissible by their very nature, even when used as a sauce for soup or the like, and even in rice gruel or a meal.

It is written that it is permissible to put [garlic] [into food]; however, the tradition of the Abhayagiri monks holds that garlic is allowable for a sick nun only before the meal, and not for one who is not sick.

Regarding the second point, it is permissible to have garlic collected on account of illness after having requested permission from the Saṅgha of nuns; in this case, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for both the monk and regarding the garlic itself.
In the seventh [offense], the reading is: “The origins and so forth are similar to those of the training rule on the highway.
In the ninth, a “wall” (kuṭṭa) means a house wall; a “rampart” (pākāra) means a surrounding rampart.
Regarding “abandoned field”: this refers to an old field. It is permissible for a monk to abandon [something] belonging to the Saṅgha, because it is included within the property of the Saṅgha.
For nuns as well, it is permissible in the same manner as described for property belonging to the Saṅgha or the Bhikkhu-saṅgha.
Nevertheless, it is recorded that it should be done according to what is appropriate.

In the tenth [offense], the phrase "for one who herself makes those things," and so forth, does not exist in this training rule (sikkhāpada). Why? Because its origin (samuṭṭhāna) is from wool (eḷakaloma).
If one asks, "Why was it stated thus? it is because of the Great Authorities (mahāpadesa) in accordance with the Suttas.
For if one is not permitted to see or hear dancing and so forth, let alone to perform them oneself, this is stated because such a principle (naya) is obtainable by way of inference.
Otherwise, the Great Authorities would be rendered meaningless. "In this same manner, the principle should be applied elsewhere as well. The origin (samuṭṭhāna) has also been explained here."
"The teachers say that it should be understood by taking [the offenses] according to their six origins (*samuṭṭhāna*).
Here, 'origin' refers to the offense stated in the interval of the fundamental rule; therefore, others maintain that it is indeed originated from the *eḷakaloma* rule.

Regarding "standing in the monastery," one incurs [the offense] not only by standing there, but also by going from there, even through all postures (*iriyāpatha*). However, as for "standing in the monastery":
The meaning is "included within the monastery grounds. Otherwise, even if she were sitting [there], she would not be permitted [to do so].
The commentary on the first chapter is finished.
2. Commentary on the second chapter.

In the fifth [offense], the preliminary stage (*upacāra*) extends twelve cubits. The reading is: "The origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth are the same as for the *kaṭhina* [robe]; however, this is both an act (*kiriya*) and a non-act (*akiriya*).
In the seventh, regarding "a permanent installation," it is for the sake of the nuns.
"Families" means households. The commentary on the second chapter is finished.
3. Commentary on the Third Chapter:
In the fourth [chapter], there is the distribution of the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) and so forth for those who have formally determined them as such.
In the fifth, the reading is: "But this is indeed 'action' and 'non-action'."
In the sixth [offense], "a dukkaṭa for another requisite" refers to any one among such things as a bowl-stand (*thālaka*) and so forth, or ghee, oil, and so forth.
The commentary on the Third Chapter is finished.
4. Commentary on the Fourth Chapter.
Regarding the sixth training rule on living in association: “The rest here is exactly like the explanation stated for the first training rule concerning Ariṭṭha.
The commentary on the fourth chapter is finished.
5. Commentary on the fifth chapter.

Because it is stated in the Pāḷi, “A ‘pavilion’ (cittāgāra) is that which has been built anywhere for people to play and enjoy themselves,” pavilions and such were made for the benefit of all, not for the king alone.

In the seventh [offense], it is stated that it is permissible to relinquish it by means of this. There is also a Pāḷi passage stating, “Having relinquished it, he uses it. “The origin and so forth are similar to those of the Kathina; however, this is a *kriyā-akriyā* offense,” is the reading. The same reading applies to the eighth as well. The commentary on the fifth chapter is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Sixth Chapter.
In the tenth [section], the reading is: “The origins and so forth are similar to those of the *kathina*; however, this is both an action and a non-action.
The commentary on the Sixth Chapter is finished.

8. Commentary on the Eighth Chapter In the first, second, and third [rules], one should not say "married" (*gihigatā*) or "unmarried maiden" (*kumāribhūtā*). If one does so, the formal act (*kamma*) is invalid.
In the eleventh [rule], "without having relinquished her consent" means not saying "as she pleases. Here, however, this is the detailed analysis (*vinicchaya*):
Having extracted the phrase “by the giving of consent by one who is undergoing probation,” the word-commentary states, “when the assembly has risen.
Regarding this, however, it is said in the *Samantapāsādikā*: “When the assembly has risen means:
when it has risen after having relinquished its consent, either by body, or by speech, or merely by the act of relinquishing consent. Here, regarding the consent...
However, it is stated that because [the formal act] has not been relinquished, it is permissible to perform the ritual action.
Therefore, it is recorded that as long as one has not relinquished one's consent, it is permissible to remain within a twelve-fathom radius and subsequently convene another assembly.
The commentary on the eighth chapter is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Ninth Chapter.
In the third [section], the reading is: “The remainder is to be understood according to the method already stated; however, this is an unwholesome consciousness.
Regarding the phrase “according to the method stated,” it refers to the method stated in the third [section].
In the eleventh [offense], the text reads: "The origin and so forth are the same as for the *kathina* robe;
however, this is both an act (*kiriyā*) and a non-act (*akiriyā*). In the twelfth, the text reads: "The origin and so forth are the same as for the *padasodhamma* offense;
however, this is both an act and a non-act. In the thirteenth, the Pāḷi states: "'Saṃkaccika' means that which is below the collarbone and above the navel; it is for the purpose of covering that."
Because it has been stated [in that context], here too the reading is: "for the purpose of covering the body, which is defined as being below the neck and above the navel.

Regarding the delimitation of the offense when there is no enclosure, it is written that one should not adopt the version from the *Samantapāsādikā*, but rather take it according to the method explained here.
The commentary on the ninth chapter is concluded.
The commentary on the pure *pācittiya* rules is finished.

Regarding the commentary on the determination of origins (*samuṭṭhāna-vinicchaya*), as for the origins, since it is stated that "the mountain-top festivals and so forth are unintentional and offenses by worldly convention" (*acittakāni lokavajjāni*), [they are determined accordingly].

Because one incurs [the offense] merely by seeing or by anointing, even without knowing it is "dancing" or "perfume," these are *acittaka* (without mental fault) due to the mind’s lack of knowledge regarding the object.
However, for one who sees or anoints while knowing it is "dancing" or "perfume," they are *lokavajja* (worldly offenses) precisely because of their unwholesome nature.
As for acts such as raising up a female thief, since the offense is incurred only when one performs them after knowing the object—such as that she is a "thief"—[they are classified accordingly].

[These actions] are performed with a conscious mind (*sacittaka*). Because ordination (*upasampadā*) and so forth cannot be performed with an exclusively unwholesome mind, they are offenses by way of formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*).

It has been written: "In this context, the state of being 'with mind' or 'without mind' should not be understood in terms of knowing or not knowing the formal rule (*paṇṇatti*), but rather in terms of knowing or not knowing the objective basis (*vatthu*).
This is because [the latter] is what is intended, and because there is no presentation [of the former] in brief.
The state of being without consciousness (acittakatā) is considered twofold: by way of the physical basis (vatthu) and by way of non-knowledge (aññāṇa).
Knowledge (ñāṇa) spoken of here is also twofold: that which is known by its own name and that which is known by another’s name.
Regarding the physical basis, there is a single [instance] in the case of forceful application (balakkāra).
"In the case of the 'equal' (samacārika) [perception], there is a dependence upon that [object] in one way.
Knowledge by means of another's name occurs in two ways regarding pearls and the like;
they consider it to occur in one way regarding body hair and the like—this distinction should be understood."
The rest here is clear; it is not extracted because the analysis has already been stated regarding the points that were not clear.
The commentary on the determination of origins is finished.
The commentary on the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha is finished.
The Ancient Commentary on the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* is finished.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The New Commentary on the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*.
The Introduction to the Work:
I pay homage to the Buddha, the ornament of the three worlds, the mine of pure virtues,
whose heart has been cooled by compassion, and whose arising is honored.
I pay homage to that sublime and profound True Dhamma, which was honored by that very King of Dhamma, the Teacher of the World.
It is purified by the stainless rays of the True Dhamma from the moon of the Lord of Sages.
I always pay homage to that Saṅgha, which is like a bed of white water-lilies, awakened by the Buddha.
It is the Saṅgha that, through its mastery of the Discipline profound in its methods, has reached the further shore in every respect;
it is the Saṅgha of speakers who have crossed the impassable and bottomless great ocean of all the world’s teachings.
This well-composed commentary on the Schedule, titled *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*, was composed by the Elder Buddhaghosa, whose mind is steadfast,
and by the Elder who knows the Vinaya, who is firm with a flood of manifold virtues.
At the request of Sumedha— the wise son of the Sage,
endowed with noble conduct and desiring the preservation of the Vinaya—
I shall describe it, perfectly pure and unconfused.
"O virtuous ones, listen to me as I speak with due care.

This concludes the commentary on the introductory discourse for the commencement of the book. Regarding the Pātimokkha, which is the foremost of all wholesome states, which brings about vast and noble distinctions of excellence, and which is supremely profound:

Desiring to compose this commentary on the meaning (*atthasaṃvaṇṇana*), this teacher first purifies his own mental continuum by means of paying homage to the Triple Gem with the words "Buddha, Dhamma," and so forth.

For wisdom, when supported by a purified mental continuum, becomes capable of reaching the conclusion of the intended commentary through its attainment of sharpness and clarity. Furthermore, by means of this homage to the Triple Gem...

In his mental continuum, all defilements have been shaken off; thus, even those obstructive karmas accumulated over other existences are incapable of creating an obstacle to the intended exposition of the meaning due to the deficiency of necessary conditions. This, too, is the Teacher’s homage to the Triple Gem.
Regarding that, first, concerning the word *buddha*: “He is a *buddha* because he has awakened to the truths; he is a *buddha* because he awakens people,” and so forth.

The meaning should be understood according to the method of exposition (*niddesa*). Alternatively, he is "Awakened" (*buddha*) because of the absolute departure of the sleep of ignorance together with its latent tendencies (*savāsanā-ajñāna-nidrā*), or because of the state of blossoming of his intelligence; thus, he is "Awakened" in the sense of waking and blossoming.

Alternatively, it is because there is no knowable phenomenon whatsoever that has not been awakened to by him, and because of the fact that he has made all specific objects of knowledge his own through action.
Because there is no desire for a formal ritual statement (*kammavācā*) due to his non-grasping, the designation of "agent" is obtained solely in the sense of understanding;
thus, he is "Buddha" because he has awakened (*buddhavā*), just as one says, "the ordained one does not give.

In terms of meaning, however, he is precisely the one who, by means of self-born knowledge (*sayambhuñāṇa*) refined by the perfections (*pāramitā*), has—along with its latent tendencies—removed and destroyed all defilements without exception, and is the locus of an immeasurable multitude of qualities such as great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) and omniscient knowledge (*sabbaññutaññāṇa*).
The Buddha is the continuum of aggregates (khandhasantāna). As it is said:

"The Buddha is that Blessed One who is self-become (sayambhū), teacherless, who by himself fully awakened to the truths among doctrines unheard before, and therein attained omniscience and mastery over the powers.
To that Buddha.

It is called *dhamma* because it "supports" (*dhāreti*). For this [Dhamma] supports one who practices according to the instructions from falling into the suffering of the states of misery (*apāya*) and the suffering of *saṃsāra*;
here, "supporting" refers to the destruction of the defilements that produce those [states].
And having established it thus, both the Noble Path and Nibbāna—by virtue of being the cause for the accomplishment of that purpose—support [the practitioner] in the primary sense.

Furthermore, it should be understood that both the noble fruit (*ariyaphala*)—by virtue of its being conducive through the subsiding of the defilements completely severed—and the Dhamma of the scriptures (*pariyattidhamma*)—by virtue of being the cause for its realization—are metaphorically designated as "Dhamma. The word *ca* has the sense of conjunction; by it, one should understand:
"having paid homage to the Buddha as previously described, and to this Dhamma," [thus] with the Jewel of the Buddha.
Along with the act of homage, one gathers the jewel of the Dhamma.

To show that it is not merely these two [the Buddha and the Dhamma], he says, "and the Saṅgha. The Saṅgha is so called because it is bound together and joined by the noble commonality of view and virtue;
it is the assembly of the eight noble persons (ariyapuggala). By means of those respective paths and fruits, [one gathers] the distress of the defilements...
It is called the *saṅgha* because it has been properly destroyed through eradication and subsiding;

furthermore, since even the worldly (*pothujjanika*) *saṅgha* stands upon the preliminary practice, it should be understood as being included here in the act of giving, just like the preceding volition.
For although that [worldly *saṅgha*] is not comprised by the noble commonality of view and virtue, it nevertheless belongs to the side of what leads to liberation.
Because it is a unified body, the Saṅgha alone is worthy of prostration as one deserving of offerings; thus, [the text says] "that Saṅgha.

The meaning of the word *ca* (and) here should also be understood according to the method already stated. To specify what kind of Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha, he says: "the recipients of salutation, honor, worship, and respect."
And this qualification should be applied to each [term]: "the recipient of homage, honor, worship, and respect: the Buddha...

[and so on] ...and the Saṅgha, the recipient of homage, honor, worship, and respect. In that context, *vandanā* (homage) is the prostration performed by the world together with its devas because of his preeminence through qualities such as arahantship;
*māna* (honor) is respectful treatment; and *upahāra* (offering) consists of perfumes, flowers, and so forth.
Worship (*pūjā*), the giving of prepared requisites, honor (*sakkāra*), and homage (*vandanā*)—as well as pride (*māna*)—are "worship, honor, homage, and respect" (*vandanāmānapūjāsakkārā*).
Because it is a vessel (*bhājana*) and a receptacle (*ādhāra*) that renders these [acts] of great fruit, it is called "the vessel for worship, honor, homage, and respect.
By this, he shows the incomparable nature of the Triple Gem in terms of qualities such as its worthiness (*arahatta*). Even the mere sight of it... [is for one who has performed the preparation].

It should be understood that the purpose [of the word *nipacca*] is to indicate the capacity for producing the intended exposition of the meaning by means of the respectful service (*nipaccakāra*) performed through the body,

speech, and mind. "Having paid homage with a serene mind" (*vippasannena cetasā vanditvā*) means having worshipped together with the body and speech acting as instruments, by means of a mind that is variously or specifically serene through the recollection of the many distinct qualities such as those of an Arahant.
"Having paid homage by way of the three doors"—this is what is meant. And this homage is threefold, by way of bodily, verbal, and mental homage.

Therein, a volition belonging to either wholesome or functional consciousness of the sense-sphere, having the qualities of the Buddha and so forth as its object, arises by way of the doors of body and speech after giving rise to bodily and verbal intimation;
this is called bodily and verbal homage. [Both types of] intimation...
However, the "mental homage" (manovandanā) arises by way of the mind-door without having been formally undertaken;
this connects with the phrase "I shall explain the commentary on this word.
Having thus shown the salutation to the Triple Gem, [the author now proceeds] to [those who are] his own supports, the teachers of the Aṭṭhakathā.
Showing his salutation, he said: “Of those who are lamps for the lineage of the Elders,” and so forth. Therein, the connection is:
“having paid homage with palms joined to the lions among the ancient teachers. One who has made the *añjali*—that is, the hollowed hands—is called *katañjalī*.

Here, the vowel is lengthened for the sake of meter (*chandānurakkhaṇattha*); thus it means “having become one with palms joined. The “ancient teachers” (*pubbācariyā*) are the authors of the ancient commentaries of Tambapaṇṇi.

Those great elders (mahātherā) are called "Lions" (sīha) because they resemble lions in their endurance of dangers, their destruction of the defilements which are their adversaries, and their being unassailable by the wild beasts that are rival disputants; thus they are the "Lions who were former teachers.
As to what kind of former teacher-lions they were to whom you pay homage, he says: "Lamps of the lineage of the Elders," and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "of the lamps of the lineage of the Elders" (*theravaṃsappadīpānaṃ*): they are called "Elders" (*therā*) because they are endowed with the stable aggregates of virtue and so forth;

Mahākassapa and others are such individuals. Their lineage, or succession, is the "lineage of the Elders" (*theravaṃso*). By this, he rejects the lineages of the seventeen schismatic sects, such as the Mahāsaṅghikas and others.
However, being included within the lineage of the Elders and being perfected in both scripture and realization, by means of the light of their wisdom...
Because they illuminate that lineage of the Elders (Theravamsa), they are "Lamps of the Lineage of the Elders"; [they are] the lions among the ancient teachers (pubbācariya).

Of those lamps of the lineage of the Elders. Because they are unshakable, they are "steadfast" (thira). The phrase "in the Vinaya procedure" (vinayakkame) is a statement corresponding to the commencement [of the work]; however, they are indeed steadfast even in the Sutta and Abhidhamma.
Having thus shown homage to the teachers of the commentaries (aṭṭhakathācariya), [the author now states] the benefit of mentioning the specific Dhamma to be commented upon:
And showing the perfections of the Teacher, he spoke the words beginning with “the Pātimokkha. Therein, the connection is: “the Pātimokkha which was proclaimed by the Great Sage (Mahesi).
Regarding that term “Great Sage”: he is a Great Sage because he seeks and searches for the five aggregates of Dhamma, such as virtue and the rest;
or alternatively, he is great because he is sought after by the great, owing to his distinction from those who seek—namely, worldlings, those in training, and those beyond training.
"Isi" means a great seer (*mahesi*), that is, the Perfectly Enlightened One; [the text refers to] "by that great seer.

"Pātimokkha" refers either to the virtue of the training rules (*sikkhāpada-sīla*) which constitutes the restraint of the seven classes of offenses, or specifically to the textual *pātimokkha* known as the two Vibhaṅga Suttas, because it illuminates that [restraint].

To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says "The foremost" (*pāmokkha*), and so forth. It is "foremost" (*pamokkha*) because it is excellent (*sādhu*) at the head (*pamukhe*); being foremost, it is "the foremost" (*pāmokkha*).

The meaning is that it is the beginning and the foundation for blameless wholesome states—namely, concentration and wisdom—which are classified as limited, exalted, and supramundane, because these are the opposites of what is blameworthy.
For it is said: "A wise person, established in virtue, should develop the mind and wisdom.
"Like a mouth" means a door; for just as there are [ways of access] for beings by way of what is to be chewed, eaten, licked, and drunk...

Just as even the fourfold nutriment, having entered through the mouth, pervades the limbs and members of the body, so too does the wholesome [kamma] belonging to the four planes, having entered through the door of virtue (*sīla*), accomplish the attainment of the goal. Therefore it is said: "It is like a mouth, thus it is a 'mouth' (*mukha*).
Alternatively, "mouth" means a door for entering liberation (*mokkha*), that is, for the realization of Nibbāna. For it has been said:
“Ānanda, wholesome virtues have non-remorse as their purpose.
Likewise:
“Non-remorse is for the purpose of gladness; gladness is for the purpose of rapture; rapture is for the purpose of tranquility; tranquility...”

"For the sake of happiness; for the sake of concentration through happiness; for the sake of knowledge and vision of things as they really are through concentration; for the sake of disenchantment with regard to knowledge and vision of things as they really are;
for the sake of dispassion through disenchantment; for the sake of liberation through dispassion; for the sake of the knowledge and vision of liberation through liberation;
and for the sake of final Nibbāna without clinging through the knowledge and vision of liberation. Thus it was said.
Having thus shown the name and other attributes of the Dhamma to be commented upon, he now recited the fourth verse beginning with “Sūratenā” in order to show the cause for the commentary.
Therein, “sūratenā” means one who delights (rata) in what is beautiful (sobhana); by lengthening the vowel *u* [to *ū*], it becomes *sūrato*.
Thus, “by that sūrato,” the meaning is: by one who delights in beautiful bodily and verbal actions. “Vinītenā” [means...]
It has been said. "Living in a windless place" means living with humble conduct. "One whose conduct is pure and austere" (*sucisallekhavutti*):
one whose way of life (*vutti*) or practice (*paṭipatti*) is pure and capable of eradicating the defilements (*kilesa*) is "one whose conduct is pure and austere";

by that term, it means being endowed with a completely purified conduct of fewness of desires (*appiccha*). "Endowed with the conduct of the Vinaya" means being perfected in the virtue of both prohibited and prescribed behavior (*vāritta-cāritta-sīla*).
Alternatively, "discipline" (*vinaya*) here refers to the discipline of restraint (*saṃvaravinaya*), which is divided into the restraint of the Pātimokkha and so forth.

"Conduct" (*ācāra*) refers to the conduct befitting a recluse (*samaṇasāruppācāra*) as it appears in the description of conduct and resort (*ācāragocara-niddesa*). "By the Elder Soṇa": here, "Soṇa" is his name;

he is called an "elder" (*thera*) because he is endowed with the firm aggregates of virtue (*sīlakkhandha*) and so forth. "Requested" means entreated. For the elder [perceived] the difficulty of fathoming the profundity of the Pātimokkha.
Having recognized the teacher’s capability for its commentary, he made a request out of reverence for the benefit [of the teaching], saying:
"The exposition of the meaning of the Pātimokkha should be performed by you; for in this way, the long endurance of the Dispensation is secured.
Demonstrating that this request of his served as the introduction to his own commentary, he said: "Being requested."
And here, by the phrase "with gentleness" (*sūratena*), his gentleness (*soracca*) is expressed. By the phrase "with humility" (*nivātena*), lowliness of mind and humble conduct are meant;

being endowed with such humble conduct, a person becomes one whose pride is subdued, whose arrogance is subdued, like a foot-wiping cloth, like a bull with broken horns, and like a snake with its fangs extracted—gentle, amiable, and pleasant to converse with.
"By one whose livelihood is pure and austere"—by this, the virtue of purity of livelihood dependent on the restraint of the sense faculties is indicated.
"By one endowed with Vinaya conduct"—by this, it should be understood that the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha is stated.
Thus, there is praise of him by way of these manifold qualities; for it is not possible to make a request of a fellow celibate who is endowed with the aforementioned qualities.
"To ward off" is stated for the purpose of showing that the commentary on the meaning of the Pātimokkha, though supremely profound, is being undertaken. Furthermore,
it should be understood that this commentary was composed because, by virtue of such a request, the exposition of the meaning—
made possible through the influence of that request and my own attainment of enthusiasm— will reach its conclusion before long.

Having thus shown the sign for the commentary, he now speaks the two verses beginning with “Therein” (tattha) to demonstrate the purpose, the manner of its composition, the basis, and the title of that commentary, in order to inspire respect among those who hear it.
Therein, “therein” (tattha) refers to that Pātimokkha which was said to have been “proclaimed by the Great Sage.
“Of those whose doubts have arisen” means of those whose doubts have arisen through the investigation of the words and their meanings.
The meaning is "of those whose doubts have arisen. "For the purpose of overcoming doubt" means for the purpose of transcending the aforementioned uncertainty.
"Of that" refers to the Pātimokkha. It is called a *vaṇṇanā* because by it the meaning (*attha*) is praised (*vaṇṇīyati*) or explained;
that is, the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*). This term is connected with the phrase "I shall explain. To the question "Of what nature is it?", he says: "Complete in its analysis," and so forth.
"Complete exposition" means that it is a complete exposition because it elucidates both the unique exposition— by way of the Khandhaka, Parivāra,
word-commentary (*padabhājana*), and so forth— and the exposition common to all training rules (*sikkhāpada*), which is seventeenfold by way of the introduction (*nidāna*) and other such categories.
"Of the Mahāvihāravāsins": A monastery established on the grounds of the Mahāmeghavana garden is the "Great Monastery" (Mahāvihāra);
those who dwell there by virtue of their moral conduct are the "Mahāvihāravāsins," and it is of them that this is said.
"Dependent upon the path of recitation" means dependent upon the path of discourse; the meaning is that it is dependent upon the commentaries (aṭṭhakathā) of the Mahāvihāravāsins.
"Relying here upon the method of the Sinhalese commentary" is what is meant. "I shall explain" means I shall set it forth.

"By name" means by my own name as a quality. "The Dispeller of Doubt" (*kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*): that by which doubts are dispelled is the Dispeller of Doubt; that [is] the Dispeller of Doubt. "Beautiful" (*subha*):
because it is endowed with both meaning and phrasing, it is beautiful in its phonetic characteristics, beautiful in its analytical determination, and beautiful in its intelligibility.
And it is beautiful and perfectly pure. Here, by the phrase "for the purpose of overcoming doubt," he shows the motive;

by "a complete exposition," he shows the manner of the commentary; and by "based on the oral tradition of the Mahāvihāravāsins," he shows the purity of the source of the commentary through its avoidance of the fault of confusing the tenets of other schools. [He says] "I shall explain."
It should be understood that by this he shows his own intention. There is also a reading: “I shall cause [it] to proceed.
The commentary on the introductory discourse for the commencement of the book is finished. Now begins the commentary on the Nidāna.
Having thus shown the preliminary section beginning with the homage to the Triple Gem, and because it was stated,

"Now I shall explain the commentary on the Pātimokkha," we shall first define the Pātimokkha by way of its etymology, its essential nature and divisions, its textual divisions, its classification by recitation,
and its delimitation by recitation; and this commentary will follow the sequence of that recitation.
In order to show that it will come to pass, the passage beginning with "therein the Pātimokkha" is commenced.
Therein, "therein" (tattha) refers to that verse-line. "Pātimokkha": from the letter *pa*, it is that which is exceedingly foremost (*ati-mukha*) among the virtues (*sīla*).
"Atipamokkha" is another way of stating that same term by means of a different prefix. Alternatively, the word-division is *pa-ati-mokkha*.

He states the meaning by means of the prefix (*upasagga*) as “the supreme. Having thus provided the word-commentary according to its divisions, he explains it according to the meaning of the term (*saddatthato*) as:

“The meaning is ‘the most excellent’ (*atiseṭṭhaṃ*), ‘the most sublime’ (*atiuttamaṃ*). And here, the *pātimokkha* of virtue (*sīla-pātimokkha*) is to be understood as “excellent” because it is the root of all qualities;
the *pātimokkha* of the text (*gantha-pātimokkha*), however, is “excellent” because it is accompanied by those excellent qualities.
The same method applies here for the word *uttama*. *Iti* means "thus. By this, he indicates the meaning of the words as they have been stated above.
For this word *iti* has the sense of indication, as in such passages as: "‘Everything exists,’ Kaccāna, is one extreme;
‘nothing exists,’ Kaccāna, is the second extreme," and so forth. *Iminā* (by this) is a term referring to what is proximate and directly perceived.

By the word *iti*, there is the expression of the meaning of the speech that was just indicated and which has entered the cognitive process (*vīthi*) of the recipients' auditory consciousness and so forth.
Alternatively, *iminā* (by this) is a term denoting immediate presence, because it brings the aforementioned meaning of the speech directly before one's eyes.
*Vacanatthena* means by the verbal sense of the word "most excellent" (*atiseṭṭha*). *Ekavidham pi* (even though it is of a single kind).

"Even a single section. It is twofold due to the division of the *sīlagantha* (the bond of virtue). This means that it is again twofold by way of the further classification known as the *sīlagantha*, being twofold as the *Sīla-pātimokkha* and the *Gantha-pātimokkha*.
Now, in order to show how both of these have come down in the Suttas, the words beginning with "For thus" (*tathā hi*) were spoken. Therein, *pāti*...
It protects, thus it is a "guard" (*pāti*); it liberates one from the sufferings of the states of woe and so forth, thus it is "liberation" (*mokkha*).
Therefore, it is the *pātimokkha*. Restraint is *saṃvara*; it is the non-transgression by body and speech. The *pātimokkha* itself as restraint is *pātimokkhasaṃvara*.
One who is restrained and endowed with that *pātimokkhasaṃvara* is "restrained by the restraint of the *pātimokkha*" (*pātimokkhasaṃvarasaṃvuta*). "Dwells" (*viharatī*) means he conducts himself.
"Ādimetaṃ" means that this virtue of the training rules is the "beginning" (ādi) in the sense of being the first to arise. For it has been said:
"Therefore, Uttiya, you should first purify the beginning among wholesome states. And what is the beginning of wholesome states? It is virtue that is perfectly pure and a view that is straight.
Just as a city-builder, desiring to construct a city, first clears the site for the city, and only afterwards...
He builds a city by dividing it according to the layout of four-way streets, crossroads, and so forth;
or just as a dyer first washes a cloth with three alkaline substances and then applies whatever dye he desires to that perfectly clean cloth;
or just as a skilled painter, wishing to paint a figure, first performs the preparatory work on the wall.
Just as form arises later on, so too the practitioner, having first purified his virtue (*sīla*), realizes later on such states as serenity (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
Therefore, virtue is called the "beginning. The phrases "this is the entrance" and so forth have already had their meaning explained.
By the word "beginning," the canonical passage beginning with "restraint according to the Pātimokkha" is included.
"Virtue" (*sīla*) is twofold, according to the distinction between engagement and avoidance; it refers to the virtue of the training rules (*sikkhāpada-sīla*) included within the Vinaya Piṭaka.

However, from the perspective of the Dhamma, virtue should be understood as the states of consciousness such as volition (*cetanā*) belonging to one who abstains from killing and so forth, or who fulfills the performance of duties.
For this has been said in the *Paṭisambhidā*: "What is virtue? Volition is virtue; it is a mental factor..."
"Virtue is restraint; virtue is non-transgression; virtue is morality"—thus it is said. "Both Pātimokkhas for him" refers to the two Pātimokkhas by way of the Bhikkhu and Bhikkhunī Pātimokkhas;
the meaning is that there are two matrices (mātikā). "For him" (assa) means for the one who exhorts the bhikkhunīs. "In detail" means together with both Vibhaṅgas.
"Well-arrived" (svāgatāni) means well-attained. By the word "etc. (ādi), the canonical text beginning with "one should recite the Pātimokkha" is included.
He embraces. "Therein" means among those *sīlagantha-pātimokkhas*. "Whoever" (*yo*) is an indefinite designation for any person whatsoever.
"It" (*taṃ*) refers to the virtue included within the Vinaya. "He guards" (*rakkhati*) means that having formally undertaken it, he protects it without violating it.

That which is established in the *pātimokkha* virtue is given the name "the bowl" (*pāti*). "He liberates" (*moceti*) means that by acting as a cooperative cause, he brings about liberation from the states of woe (*apāya*).

That which is born is "born-in-an-evil-state" (*āpāyika*); suffering is the first of those things, hence they are called "the evil-state and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), all other suffering of *saṃsāra* is included.
Regarding "by self-reproach and so forth": self-reproach is "self-reproach" (*attānuvāda*); that is the first of those things, hence they are called "self-reproach and so forth.
By the word "and so forth," reproach by others, punishment, and the fear of an evil rebirth are included.
It encompasses [them]. "Because it illuminates that Pātimokkha" means because it reveals that Pātimokkha of virtue (sīlapātimokkha).

However, the meaning of the word stated at the beginning refers to the meaning of the words stated at the beginning by the phrase "most excellent" (atiseṭṭha), and so forth. This [meaning] is common to both:

the Pātimokkha of virtue is "most excellent" because it is the root of all qualities; the Pātimokkha of the text (ganthapātimokkha) is "most excellent" because it is accompanied by those most excellent qualities.
"In that regard" means among those two: the *sīlapātimokkha* (the Pātimokkha as moral virtue) and the *ganthapātimokkha* (the Pātimokkha as a text).
By "this commentary," he refers to the commentary that is about to be explained. First, let it suffice for the *ganthapātimokkha*; but how does it apply to the *sīlapātimokkha*?

To this he says, "For in the text," and so forth. "For" (*hi*) is a particle used in the sense of a reason. "Of that" means of the text. "Meaning" (*attha*) means moral virtue (*sīla*). It is "only described" (*vaṇṇito va hoti*).
Because the meaning itself is explained by way of explaining the text. This is what is meant:
since when the text is explained, its meaning is also explained because it is inseparable from it, therefore this [method] is also appropriate for the Pātimokkha of the precepts.
Having thus defined it according to its specific nature and divisions, he now says, "But that very... and so forth, in order to define it according to the divisions of the texts.
“In those two” means in those two, namely the Bhikkhu-pātimokkha and the Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha.
“By which sections are delimited” refers to those successions of words that will be explained; these are the “delimiters of the sections. “Established” means situated without confusion.
Having thus established [the Pātimokkha] by way of its division as a text, he now says “in those two,” etc., in order to establish it by way of the analysis of its sections.

It is called *uddesa* because it is pointed out (*uddisīyati*)—that is, explained by its own form—or because it is the means by which [something] is pointed out; thus, the pointing out of the introduction (*nidāna*) is the "introduction-pointing-out" (*nidānuddesa*).
The same applies to the remaining cases. A detailed exposition itself is the "detailed-pointing-out" (*vitthāruddesa*).

Now, in order to demonstrate the specific scope of the introduction-pointing-out and the others, the passage beginning with "Therein, the introduction-pointing-out" (*tattha nidānuddeso*) is commenced.
"In each of those" refers to those five summaries (*uddesa*). The connection is: "the summary of the introduction (*nidāna-uddesa*) has been recited.

Now, having shown the textual passage of the introduction that has come down here—by way of demonstrating the section on the summary of the introduction with the words, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs...
[omission] ...for it is comfortable for him when he has revealed [his fault]"—[the author proceeds] to show what must also be stated at the time of the subsequent summary.

It should be understood that the connection for the passage, “Venerable sirs, the introduction has been recited,” was not made, and instead it was shown by connecting only the formal proclamation and so forth with the words, “In this matter, I ask the venerable ones,” etc.;

this was done either for the purpose of showing the section on the recitation of the introduction preceding the display of the incomplete Pāḷi of the introduction, or because its lack of connection was made due to its being well-known through the Khuddaka-peyyāla. This was at the time of the recitation.
However, it should be stated only after having applied [the rule]. For he will say: "But this is seen at the end of the *pārājika* rules and so forth, not at the end of the *nidāna*.

Even though it is not seen there, nevertheless, at the time of the recitation, after saying, 'For one who has confessed it, there is comfort,' it must indeed be stated by way of the formula beginning with:
'Venerable sirs, the *nidāna* has been recited; therein I ask the venerable ones... and so on.

"By what has been heard regarding the remainder" means that the remaining four sections, beginning with the recitation of the *pārājika* rules, have been made known by way of what was heard, as follows:
"Venerable sirs, the four *pārājika* rules have been heard by you... [and so on] ...you should train yourselves without disputing.
To show that the remaining three sections of the *Pātimokkha* recitation should be understood in this same manner, he said, "of the recitation of the *pārājikas*, etc."
The connection is that the sections beginning with the recitation of the *pārājikas* are to be joined. Having recited the *nidāna* from the beginning through to the conclusion of the *pārājikas*,
and so on— the *nidāna*, the *pārājikas*, both of those together with the *saṅghādisesas*, and the *tadubhayas* along with the *aniyatās*—
having thus recited them in due order and brought the *pārājikas* and the rest to their conclusion, they are to be joined "with the remainder by way of hearing."
It should be connected with such passages as: "The Pārājika section has been recited in the presence of the Saṅgha," and so forth.
Regarding the statement, "The remainder should be announced by way of hearing," it is said in the Uposatha Khandhaka:
"Monks, there are these five ways of reciting the Pātimokkha: having recited the Nidāna, the remainder should be announced by way of hearing..."

“This is the first recitation of the Pātimokkha. Having recited the Nidāna and having recited the four Pārājikas, the remainder should be announced by way of hearing; this is the second recitation of the Pātimokkha.
Because it is stated thus in such passages—as in “in which [recitation] it is interrupted,” meaning in which recitation it has not been completed—and “an obstacle arises,” meaning...

Among the ten obstacles, whichever obstacle may arise. The ten obstacles are as follows: the obstacle of kings, the obstacle of thieves, the obstacle of fire, the obstacle of water, the obstacle of humans, the obstacle of non-humans, the obstacle of wild beasts, the obstacle of reptiles, the obstacle to life, and the obstacle to the holy life (*brahmacariya*).
In this regard, if among the monks [the thought arises], "We shall perform the Uposatha,"...
While they are seated, the king arrives—this is an obstruction by the king. Robbers arrive—this is an obstruction by robbers.
A forest fire approaches, or a fire breaks out in the dwelling—this is an obstruction by fire.
A cloud arises, or a flood comes—this is an obstruction by water. Many people arrive—this is an obstruction by people. [A] monk...
A *yakkha* seizes him: this is an obstacle caused by non-human beings (*amanussantarāya*). Fierce wild animals such as tigers and the like approach:
this is an obstacle caused by beasts of prey (*vāḷantarāya*). Snakes and the like bite the bhikkhu: this is an obstacle caused by reptiles (*sarīsapantarāya*).
The bhikkhu becomes ill, or passes away, or enemies wishing to kill him seize him: this is an obstacle to life (*jīvitantarāya*). People [seize] one...
Or many monks, desiring to cause one to fall away from the holy life (*brahmacariya*), seize hold [of them]; this is an obstacle to the holy life.
Thus, the meaning of what was stated—“an obstacle arises”—is clarified as being any one of the ten obstacles that may arise.

“Together with that” means together with the unfinished recitation (*vippakata-uddesa*). The remainder must be announced by means of the *suta* (what has been heard), because it depends upon the recitation already delivered.
Regarding the remaining words: as it was said, "Having recited the Nidāna," and so forth. Therefore he said, "But in the case of the recitation of the Nidāna," and so forth.
The intention is that there is nothing to be announced by means of what has been heard; rather, it would merely be an obstacle to the Uposatha.
The recitation of the Aniyata rules is omitted because there is no promulgation of the Aniyata training rules for bhikkhunīs. And the reason for their absence is this very [text]: "This alone..."

It should be understood that this is stated by taking the characteristic [of the previous section] as having followed into this one as well. "The rest" (sesa) indicates the remaining sections of the enumeration.
The connection is with the phrase "of these two Pātimokkhas. "Tāva" means first.
"Idaṃ" (this) points out in general terms what is now to be said—that which is revolving in the mind—as speech fixed in a composition determined by syllables and words.
"It is called" means "it is spoken. What is it? He says: "‘Let the Sangha hear me,’ and so forth.
Therein, “‘Let the Sangha hear me,’ and so forth” refers to the scriptural passages found in the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha, beginning with: “Venerable Sir, let the Sangha hear me;
today is the Uposatha day. “The determination of the meaning” refers to both the literal meaning (*abhidheyyattha*) and the intended meaning (*adhippāyattha*).

The meaning is "ascertainment" (*nicchayana*) and "determination" (*vavatthāpana*). For by means of this commentary, both their literal meaning (*abhidheyyattha*) and their intended meaning (*adhippāyattha*) are determined in manifold ways.
Alternatively, that which is "decided" (*nicchinna*) is a "decision" (*nicchaya*).
A discourse that cuts off doubt, proceeding like the removal of a splinter from knotted places [in a tree], is a "decision"; thus, "the decision regarding the meaning" is *atthanicchayo*.
"That determination of meaning" means what is being stated by me, namely both the meaning (*attha*) and the detailed exposition (*vinicchaya*).

"Endowed with virtue" (*sīlasampannā*): "endowed" (*sampanna*) means completely spread out, attained, or fulfilled; those for whom virtue is thus fulfilled are "endowed with virtue," which means they possess complete virtue.
Alternatively, "endowed" (*sampannā*) means having properly reached or arrived; those endowed with virtue are "endowed with virtue."
"Endowed with virtue" means being possessed of the restraint of the Pātimokkha.
"Desirous of training" means those who desire that training which consists of the three trainings—higher virtue, higher mind, and higher wisdom—in the sense of being things to be practiced.
"Let them hear me" means let all those bhikkhus listen attentively from my presence; by this, he enjoins them to listen respectfully to his own praise.

For all success in the Dispensation is dependent upon careful listening. And here, only those monks who are endowed with virtue and desirous of training are intended, because others are not suitable vessels for this commentary;
for they would not consider the Vinaya as something to be heard or put into practice.

"In this" means in this verse-line, or within these words beginning with "Let my hearing be attended to," which are included in the verse. "The statement of the command for hearing" means the statement that is the command regarding hearing.

Although it is a statement of the command for hearing, because it was spoken by the Blessed One as something that must be said by the reciter of the Pātimokkha, it is the Blessed One’s command, not the reciter’s; therefore, even one who is junior may [speak].
It is appropriate to say this because it is spoken with reverence and deference, being accompanied by respect for and high esteem toward the Saṅgha.
For the Saṅgha, due to its possession of specific qualities such as right practice, is the supreme object of reverence and deference.
To address the question of who said all this, where, and when, he says: "And all this... and so forth. [This was said] by one who authorized the recitation of the Pātimokkha.

“I allow you, monks, to recite the Pātimokkha. And thus, monks, it should be recited: a competent and capable monk should inform the Saṅgha, saying, ‘Let the venerable Saṅgha listen to me. By permitting [the recitation] with these words, [he speaks].
“At Rājagaha” means in the city of that name. For because it was occupied by Mandhātā, Mahāgovinda, and others, it is called “Rājagaha.
Furthermore, this city existed during the time of a Buddha and during the time of a Wheel-turning Monarch (Cakkavatti).
At other times it is empty, possessed by *yakkhas*, and remains as a dwelling place for them.
Therefore—meaning because this is the statement that must be spoken by the reciter of the Pātimokkha—[the question is asked]: "Do both of them recite the Pātimokkha, such that it must be said thus?
To which he replies, "Either the senior of the Saṅgha," and so forth. "Dependent on the elders" (*therādhika*) means dependent upon the elders.
The meaning is that it should be dependent upon the elders (*therāyatta*). Alternatively, there is the reading *therādheyya*, which has the same meaning.
"Therein" means in that assembly. "Expert" (*byatta*) means endowed with proficiency of wisdom; the meaning is one who is well-versed in the *mātikā*.
"Capable" (*paṭibala*) means able to speak; what is meant is that he is fearless. And here, although the *Pātimokkha* [may be recited] even by a junior who is expert...

It is permitted; however, this is the intended meaning here: if five, four, or three recitations of the Pātimokkha do not come to the Elder, but two are unbroken and well-mastered by heart, then the Pātimokkha depends entirely on the Elder.
But if he is unable to make even that much clear, then it depends on a learned monk.
Now, because the term "Saṅgha" was stated without qualification, he said, "By this word 'Saṅgha,' however," and so forth, in order to show the specific Saṅgha intended here.
*Kiñcāpi* is a particle used in the sense of concession; its meaning should be understood as "even though.
It is called *dakkhiṇā* (an offering) because by means of it beings prosper with the desired attainments.
Having faith in the next world, one should give a gift; that [recipient] is worthy of the offering (*dakkiṇā*), or is beneficial to the offering.

He is called "worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyya*) because he purifies it by making it yield great fruit. He is a "community" (*saṅgha*) because he is bound together by the combination of right view and virtue.

Thus, he is both worthy of offerings and a community, hence "the community worthy of offerings" (*dakkhiṇeyyasaṅgha*). By "convention" (*sammuti*) is meant the Vinaya formulation consisting of the fourfold assembly and so forth.

The established Saṅgha is the conventional Saṅgha (*sammuti-saṅgha*). "Without distinction" means without distinguishing them as either "noble ones" (*ariya*) or "worldlings" (*puthujjana*), but by way of their commonality.
"It" refers to the conventional Saṅgha. "Here" refers to this formal motion for the Uposatha. It is intended here because the formal motion for the Uposatha does not make such distinctions.
Now, one might ask: "Is it not the case that this [conventional Saṅgha] is also fivefold? Among those, which one is intended here? Addressing this inquiry, he says:

“*So panesā*,” etc. “By way of formal act” (*kammavasena*) means by way of a disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*). It is “fivefold” (*pañcavidho*) because it has five kinds or modes (*pakāra*) within this conventional Saṅgha. For they explain that the words *vidha*, *yutta*, *gata*, and *pakāra* have the same meaning.

A group (*vagga*) consisting of four is a “fourfold group” (*catuvaggo*); or, a group associated with the number four is a “fourfold group. The same applies to the “fivefold group” (*pañcavaggo*), and so on.
Now, in order to specify those actions by virtue of which this [Saṅgha] is fivefold, he says “therein,” and so forth.
Therein, “therein” means in the fivefold Saṅgha. Because the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*) must be performed by a group of ten in the Middle Countries, it is said:
“excepting... and full ordination. By the word “likewise,” [it is shown that] no formal act of the Saṅgha can be performed...
He refers by extension to this meaning: "it is not allowable. If that is so, for what purpose was the "group of more than twenty" mentioned?
To this he says: "But that," and so forth. "By more than [the required number]" means: an act requiring a group of four or more performed by a group of five or more;
and an act requiring a group of ten performed by a group of eleven or more. "For the sake of showing" means for the sake of making it known.
And since this alone is the action to be performed by him, it is said: "It is fivefold by way of action.

One should understand that there is no room for such an objection as, "How could this be appropriate if there were no restriction regarding the action? However, in this context, the term refers to the *uposatha*.
This word *uposatha* applies to the recitation of the *Pātimokkha*, the virtue of the fast-day observance (*upavāsa*), and the day on which the observance is prescribed. For it is thus:

In such passages as, “Come, friend Kappina, let us go to the Uposatha,” it appears in reference to the recitation of the Threefold Code (*Ti-mokkha-uddesa*); in such passages as, “Thus, Visākhā, when the Uposatha is observed complete with these eight factors,” it refers to virtue (*sīla*);
in such passages as, “For the pure one there is always the month of Phagguna; for the pure one there is always the Uposatha,” it refers to the observance (*upavāsa*);
in such passages as, “The Uposatha is the name of a king of serpents,” it refers to a designation (*paññatti*); and [in the passage], “Monks, do not... [it refers to a prohibition].
In such passages as "on that Uposatha day, from the monasteries with bhikkhus," it refers to the day;
here too, it is intended in the sense of the day itself, hence he says, "Today is the Uposatha day," and so forth. It is called *uposatha* because they fast (*upavasanti*) therein.
They fast either by means of virtue, or by total fasting—known as abstaining from food—or by merely drinking milk, honey, and so on.
The meaning is: "having approached [the assembly], they dwell [there].
Since all sentences include the sense of the particle *eva*, the word "Uposatha" acquires the meaning "only Uposatha";
thus he said, "By this, he rejects any day that is not Uposatha. What was refuted by this restriction is as follows:

It shows [this]; or else, since a word expresses its meaning by way of excluding the meanings of other words, it is said that for the term "Uposatha," the meaning is "there is no non-Uposatha," which is why it says, "By this, he rejects a day that is not Uposatha.
By the phrase "This method applies to the fifteenth [day]," he likewise rejects any other Uposatha day. "By this" means...
“By the word ‘Uposatha’: it is the fifteenth by way of completing the fifteen lunar days (*tithi*). By the term ‘pannaraso,’ he excludes any other day as the Uposatha day.
To show in detail the meaning stated in brief, he said, “By way of the day,” and so forth.
That which is connected with the fourteenth day is *cātuddasika*. Likewise for the *pannarasika*. The *sāmaggi-uposatha* (the Uposatha of concord).
The *nāma-saṅgha-sāmaggika* (the Uposatha for the sake of unity) is to be performed on that day. Regarding the phrase "of the three seasons—winter, summer, and the rains":
here, the winter season (*hemanta-utu*) consists of four months beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight of the month of Kattika and ending with the full moon of Phagguṇa;
the summer season (*gimha-utu*) consists of [four months] beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight of Phagguṇa and ending with the full moon of Āsāḷha.
The four months of the rainy season (*vassānuṭu*) are those beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight of Āsāḷha and ending with the full moon of the latter Kattika;
these constitute the four months. Regarding the "two [days] in each of the third and seventh fortnights," making two for each, there are six fourteenth days:
two fourteenth days in the third and seventh fortnights of the winter season (*hemanta*), and likewise for the other seasons—thus there are six fourteenth days.
"The remaining fifteen" means that the remaining eighteen [days] consist of fifteen-day periods. And herein it is said:
"From the dark fortnight of Kattika until the full moon of Phagguna, this should be known as the 'winter season'; there are eight Uposatha days."
“From the dark fortnight of Phagguṇa until the full moon of Āsāḷha, it should be known as the ‘hot season’; there are eight Uposatha days.
From the dark fortnight of Āsāḷha until the full moon of Kattika...”
"It should be understood that 'the rainy season' (vassakāla) consists of eight Uposatha days.
Regarding the three seasons, on the third and seventh fortnights—
the fourteenth day— those who know the method recite the Pātimokkha."
*Pakaticārittaṃ* (normal conduct) is that which should be performed by virtue of the condition of there being no more than a few residents (*nabahutarāvāsika*) and so forth.

However, when the condition of there being more than a few residents exists, it is permissible to perform it on another fourteenth day as well. Therefore he said, "once" (*sakiṃ*), and so forth. *Sakiṃ* means in one instance.
Regarding "it should be followed by the residents": by the residents, in the preliminary duty [of saying], "Today is the Uposatha, the fourteenth,"...
While it is being performed, one must comply and not object. By the word "etcetera," there is the statement:
"The resident monks must comply with the visiting monks," and the statement: "Monks, I allow those monks to perform two or three Uposathas on the fourteenth day;
how can we perform the Pavāraṇā before them?"

He includes [them]. And here, it should be understood that the suttas beginning with "by those who have arrived" are presented because the meaning is possible even according to the normal practice (*pakaticāritta*), namely that for each season, the Pātimokkha should be recited once on the fourteenth day of the third or seventh fortnight, or on the fifteenth day for the remainder. Such being the case, when there is a corresponding condition...
"Satīti" means when there exists a suitable condition for performing the Uposatha on another fourteenth day, such as "the resident monks are more numerous," and so forth.
"Aññasmimpi cātuddase" means on a fourteenth day other than the fourteenth days of the third and seventh fortnights of the three seasons.
To show that these are not merely Uposatha days, he says: "But for those who have completed the previous rains-retreat," and so forth. "Mā" means...
The moon (*canda*) is so called because it measures the day by its movement; when it is full here through the completion of all its phases, it is called *puṇṇamā*.

The full moon of the month of Kattika (October–November) is the *pubbakattikapuṇṇamā*; [it is also] the *assayujapuṇṇamā*. That [latter term] is stated thus in order to exclude the later Kattika month.
"Of those very same" means of those who have already spent the rains-retreat of the previous year. "By those who cause quarrels" means...

“By those who cause quarrels”: they draw back. The meaning is that, by way of accusation against those who cause strife, they cast aside the full moon of the Assayuja month and so forth, and thus draw the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) upward into the dark fortnight or the bright fortnight.
“May the venerable residents listen to me; if it is opportune for the venerable ones, let us now perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha.”
"Let us recite the Pātimokkha now; we shall perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony at the coming dark fortnight," or "Venerable sirs, let the residents listen to me:
if it is convenient for the venerable ones, let us now perform the Uposatha and recite the Pātimokkha; we shall perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony at the coming bright fortnight.
This is what is meant by postponing the Pavāraṇā by means of a formal motion (ñatti).
Now, *atha* is a particle used in the sense of immediate sequence. *Cātuddasa* means the fourteenth day, which completes the fourteen.

With reference to this, they passed a motion saying, "We shall perform the *pavāraṇā* on the approaching full moon. However, on that approaching full moon of the *Komudī Cātumāsī*, one must certainly perform the *pavāraṇā*.
For it is not permitted to perform the *pavāraṇā* after having passed that date. Indeed, this has been stated:
“Monks, even if those monks who are makers of strife, makers of quarrels, makers of disputes, makers of contention,
and makers of legal issues in the Saṅgha should spend that bright fortnight [there], all those monks, monks,
must nevertheless perform the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) at the coming bright fortnight of the Komudī Cātumāsinī, even against their will.”

For this very reason, it is said: “The last *vassa* (rainy-season) residence and the full moon of the last *Kattika* month. For if one were to perform the *pavāraṇā* after that [date] has passed, one would incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Indeed, this has been stated: “Monks, the *pavāraṇā* should not be performed when there is no invitation [to do so], except for the sake of the harmony of the Saṅgha.
It is called the “day of *pavāraṇā*” because it is suitable for the *pavāraṇā* of purification. By the word “also” (*pi*), it is indicated that it is not only...

This shows that it is not only on the day of the *pavāraṇā*, but also on the day of the *uposatha*. Now, referring to that day of the *sāmaggī-uposatha* which was mentioned, and in connection with that also showing the day of the *sāmaggī-pavāraṇā*, he says "But when... and so forth.
"When that monk has been reinstated" means when the suspended (*ukkhitaka*) monk has been reinstated; having taken him [with the others], they go to the boundary (*sīmā*).
"Having caused the offense to be confessed, it is said that [the transaction] is introduced by means of the cessation of the formal act (*kamma*) through the *kammavācā*.
‘Of that matter’ (*vatthu*) means of that legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*). ‘Having set aside at that time...’—the connection is ‘it becomes what is called the Uposatha day.
As for the reason why, he says ‘at that very moment,’ etc. Therein, ‘at that very moment’ (*tāvadeva*) means on that very day. From the statement..."

Because it is stated in the Kosambaka Khandhaka. However, where they suspend the Uposatha or Pavāraṇā because of a minor matter while disputing over bowls, robes, and so forth, once that legal issue has been settled, they are not permitted to perform an intermediate Uposatha of concord, thinking, "We have become united.
If they were to do so when it is not the Uposatha day, [it would be invalid].
The Uposatha is said to have been performed. Regarding the phrase "within the month of Kattika":
here, the "month of Kattika" refers to the twenty-nine days and nights starting from the first day of the dark fortnight of the former Kattika month until the full moon of the latter Kattika month;
it must be performed within that period, as it is not permitted after or before it. This may be on any day whatsoever.
Here too, in the Kosambaka Khandhaka, the kind of concord (*sāmaggī*) should be understood as being identical to that [of the previous case].
However, those who become reconciled after having suspended the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) for some slight reason should perform the invitation ceremony at the very time of the invitation;

it should not be performed immediately [after the suspension]. For those who do so, the invitation ceremony is considered performed even though it was not [formally] invited. It simply should not be performed [at all].

This shows that if one performs it as a rule [without the proper conditions], it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). For in that regard, there is an offense of wrong-doing in performing the Uposatha; for this has been said:
"Monks, the Uposatha should not be performed on a non-Uposatha day, except for the sake of the concord of the Saṅgha.

By the phrase "only when the time is appropriate" (*pattakālaṃ eva pattakallaṃ*), he shows that the suffix is used in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāvappaccaya*) within its own meaning. The words "not when it is absent" reinforce from the perspective of exclusion (*vyatireka*) what was already stated from the perspective of inclusion (*anvaya*).
"Suitable" means worthy and appropriate; "to the master," it is said. "At least four" means at the very minimum four;
without them, that Uposatha ceremony is not performed, nor do their consent (*chanda*) or purity (*pārisuddhi*) proceed.
But as for the remainder, even if they number as many as a thousand, provided they belong to the same community (*samānasaṃvāsaka*), all are indeed entitled to give their consent.
It happens that whether they come after having given their purity of intention (*chandapārisuddhi*) or not, the legal act (*kamma*) is not invalidated.

"Regular members" (*pakatatta*) means those who have not been suspended and have not committed a defeat (*pārājika*). "Within arm's reach" (*hatthapāsa*) means a distance measuring one and a half cubits.
And what is this "boundary" (*sīmā*)? It is that place where those standing without relinquishing the range of an arm's reach are said to be "attained for the legal act."

Intending to show the boundary with reference to Anuyoga, [the author] says, "And this boundary," and so forth, because for those possessing discernment, the manifestation of the intrinsic nature occurs precisely through the demonstration of distinctions.
"Sambhindantena" means by one who mixes. "Ajjhottharantena" means by one who overwhelms;
it is said to mean by one who brings [it] inside. The connection is: "These are called the boundaries of failure. Why?
Regarding the phrase "the boundaries of failure," it says "by eleven," and so forth. "By modes" means by causes.
"From the statement" refers to its being spoken in the *Kammavagga*. This *saṅghakamma* (formal act of the community) has a maximum limit of what is to be performed by a group of twenty;
thus it says, "where twenty-one monks cannot sit. In whichever boundary, according to the lower limit, there are those eligible for the formal act...
Twenty-one monks together are unable to sit in a circular formation; this means that such a [boundary] is called "too small.

Even if such a boundary has been formally authorized, it is as if unauthorized; it is just like the field of a village, and any formal act (kamma) performed therein is invalid. This same principle applies to the other types of boundaries as well.
“Sammatā” means bound; the meaning is that the formal act (kammavācā) has been recited. For the very recitation of the formal act is what is called “binding.
“Animittupago” means one who does not approach the signs (nimitta); thus, it refers to one who is “animittupaga,” meaning one who is fit for the signless (animitta).
“Tacasārarukkho” refers to trees such as the palmyra palm and the coconut. “Paṃsupuñjavālukāpuñjānaṃ” means of heaps of dust and heaps of sand.
“In the middle. This is a genitive case used in the sense of selection (*niddhāraṇa*). However, in some manuscripts the reading “a heap of dust or a heap of sand or one or another” is seen;
that, however, is not the correct reading, for it does not construe with the word “one or another” (*aññatara*).

“Between” (*antara*) means between the sign-possessing object (*nimittupaga*) and the sign (*nimitta*). And here, that which is being bound by the three signs among those that do not possess a sign...
Having established a single sign between any one of these—such as a bark-tree (*tacasāra-rukkha*) or others—the boundary is defined;

this is called a "broken sign" (*khaṇḍanimitta*). However, it is understood by those who have approached the signs that when a boundary is being fixed by four or five signs and so forth, having established a single sign between any one of these bark-trees and others, it is not called a "broken sign."
Because of the existence of three signs (*nimitta*). However, it is stated without distinction in the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*); therefore, it should be understood after careful investigation.
"In every way" means in all its aspects. "Consent given by one standing outside the signs" means the formal act of motion (*kammavācā*) is recited by one who stands outside of them.
But it is permissible for the signs to be proclaimed by one standing both inside and outside.
"Even though thus agreed upon" means even though agreed upon by means of the formal ritual (*kammavācā*) after proclaiming the boundary markers.

This is connected with the phrase "it remains as if not agreed upon. "Bhikkhus, every river is a non-boundary" means that any stream possessing the characteristics of a river—even if one has proclaimed the boundary markers and performed the act, thinking, "We shall establish this as a fixed boundary"—is a non-boundary; the meaning is that it does not become a fixed boundary. Of oneself...
By its very nature, however, it is like a boundary that has been fixed; it is permissible to perform any *saṅghakamma* (formal act of the Saṅgha) everywhere within it.
The same principle applies even to oceans and mountain lakes. By the phrase "with interlocking branches," he indicates their mutual proximity.
"It is fixed" is said with reference to the boundary in the western direction. "A portion of it" means a part of it. Standing where—
It is meant that such a place is one where monks are able to perform formal acts (*kamma*).

However, it should be understood that when those standing in a place where it is impossible to perform a formal act define a boundary by including such a location within it, they are said to "interfere with" (*sambhindanti*) one boundary with another, but not to "encompass" (*ajjhottharanti*) it.
