In the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries, however, it says: "Interference means [the boundary] of others..."
"Having designated one or two boundary marks for a boundary and taken a mere line, there is the binding.

'Overlapping' means: having designated the boundary marks within another person's boundary, one who makes that [other boundary] either entirely or partially inside [one's own], designates marks outside of it in one or two directions and performs the binding. Thus it is said.
The perfection of signs refers to the excellence of signs such as mountains and so forth. A mountain itself as a sign is a "mountain-sign";
the same applies to the others. "When these have been declared" means when they were declared in the *Uposathakkhandhaka* during the formal act of establishing a boundary (*sīmāsammuti*).
Furthermore, it is permissible to establish a boundary using these eight signs, whether they are unmixed or mixed with one another.
Therefore he said: "In each respective direction, the signs that have been obtained and which partake of the sign.
However, it is not permissible to appoint [a boundary] by means of one or two signs;
but starting from three, it is permissible even with a hundred of the types of signs mentioned above. The Vinaya-master should ask: "What is the sign in the eastern direction?"
When it has been said, "Venerable sir, it is a mountain," the one who holds the Vinaya must again designate the sign (nimitta) by saying, "This mountain is the sign.

However, it is not permissible to designate it by saying, "We are making this mountain the sign," "we shall make it the sign," "the sign has been made," "let it be the sign," "it is [the sign]," or "it will be [the sign].
This same method applies to rocks and so forth as well.

Therefore he said, "What is the sign in the eastern direction? and so forth. Whether one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*) or one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) explains it thus, "A mountain, venerable sir; water, venerable sir," it is indeed permissible. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [it includes]:
"What is the sign in the intermediate eastern direction? A rock, venerable sir; this rock is the sign. In the southern direction..."

"In the intermediate direction of the south, in the western direction, in the intermediate direction of the west, in the northern direction, and in the intermediate direction of the north, what is the sign?
Water, venerable sir; this water is the sign"—this summarizes it.
But here, instead of stopping there, [the text continues]: "In the eastern direction, what is the sign? A mountain, venerable sir; this mountain is the sign."
Thus, having first designated the characteristic mark (*nimitta*), it should be established. For in this way, the mark is joined with the mark.
"Having correctly designated" means: not by exchanging their respective names, nor by designating those who have no marks by name, but by designating them according to the very method already stated.
"Consent" (*sammatā*) refers to the procedure beginning with "Let the venerable ones hear me," as set forth in the Uposatha Khandhaka.
It is bound by a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) that has been uttered and purified.

In this regard, the boundary markers (*nimitta*), even if recited only once, are indeed considered recited. However, in the *Andhakaṭṭhakathā*, it is stated: "The boundary marker should be recited three times while connecting the circle of the boundary."
“Therein” means among those eight signs. “Appropriate for the sign” (nimittūpagata) means fit for the sign.
Because of the statement, “starting from the size of an elephant,” even one the size of an elephant is indeed appropriate for the sign.
An elephant, however, is either seven cubits or seven and a half cubits [in height]. “Smaller than that” means smaller than that size of an elephant. If, in the four...
In the various directions there are either four mountains or three;
it is permissible to designate the boundary by means of four or three mountain markers, but it is not permissible to designate it by means of two or one.
This same principle applies to the subsequent markers, such as stone markers and so forth. Therefore, when establishing a mountain marker, one must ask:
“Is it connected as one, or is it not connected as one? If it is connected as one, it should not be made [into a boundary].
For even if one were to recite it in four or eight directions, it would still be recited as a single sign.
Therefore, when a mountain stands surrounding a monastery in the shape of a wheel, having recited that in one direction, one should recite it as being outside in the other directions.

Having established the boundary, other signs must be designated within it. If they wish to include a third part or a half of a mountain within the boundary, they should not designate the mountain itself;
rather, for as much of the area as they wish to include within, they must designate some other sign—such as a tree, an anthill, or the like—found on that very mountain beyond that point.

If they wish to enclose within [the boundary] an entire mountain measuring one or two *yojanas*, the landmarks such as trees, anthills, and so forth, located on the ground beyond the mountain, must be designated.
"It comes to be reckoned" (*saṅkhaṃ gacchati*) means it comes to be included in calculation or conventional usage. "The measure of a ball of molasses weighing thirty-two *palas*"—
It is by thickness, not by weight or measurement. Regarding this, they say that "one *pala* is equal to ten *kalañjas*.
Even large bricks are not permitted. Likewise, a heap of stones that have reached the state of being unshaped is forbidden, let alone a heap of dust or sand.
Whether it be a back-slab (*piṭṭhipāsāṇa*) level with the ground like a threshing floor, or a stone rising from the earth like a stump, that too [is not permitted].
If it is of a standard size, it is permissible. However, even if a back-slab (*piṭṭhipāsāṇa*) is very large, it is still considered merely a stone;

thus he said, "But as for the back-slab," and so forth. Therefore, if one wishes to designate a single portion of a large back-slab within the boundary (*sīmā*), that [portion] must not be designated;
rather, another stone should be designated on top of it. If, however, around the back-slab...
They build a dwelling, and a backstone passes right through the middle of that dwelling; such a backstone is not permissible.

For if they mark it out, the dwelling would be on top of the *nimitta* (boundary marker), and since the *nimitta* is outside the boundary, the dwelling would also fall outside the boundary. However, a backstone that stands surrounding the dwelling...
Having praised [the forest] in one place, it should not be praised elsewhere.
Regarding the phrase "in a forest-indication," a grass forest or a forest of trees with heartwood is not permitted; thus he said, "with those having heartwood within" (*antosārehi*), and so forth.

"Those having heartwood within" (*antosārā*) refers to mangoes, rose-apples, jackfruits, and the like. "With those mixed with heartwood within" means: those in which there is heartwood inside are "those having heartwood within."
"Intermingled with those, mixed with inner heartwood" means by those [trees]. "Even the measure of four or five trees" states the minimum limit;
however, at the maximum, even a forest of a hundred yojanas is permissible.

In this context, if it is the measure of four trees, three must be of heartwood and one of non-heartwood; if it is the measure of five trees, three must be of heartwood and two of non-heartwood—this is how it should be understood.
If, however, they construct a monastery in the middle of a forest, that forest must not be marked out.
Even for those wishing to establish a portion [of the monastery] within the boundary, the trees, rocks, and so forth therein must be marked out without marking out the forest itself.
Having marked out the forest standing around the perimeter of the monastery, it must not be marked out elsewhere.
Regarding the sign of a tree, even a *tacasāra* (bark-essence) tree is not permitted; thus he says "with inner pith.
By the phrase "established on the ground," he excludes [trees] situated in things such as baskets or bowls.

However, having removed it from there and planted it in the ground at that very moment, one may then construct a fence, pour water, and perform the consecration (*kittana*), provided that new roots and branches have not yet emerged.
This is not the reason. However, this [definition] is appropriate when [the tree] has been planted after being cut from its stump.
Regarding the phrase "the size of a needle-shaft," they say it is "the size of a writing-stick in the island of Sri Lanka," and that should be understood as the measure of the little finger.
Furthermore, when one is designating a tree as a physical sign (nimitta), it is permissible to call it simply "tree," or to specify it as "sāka-tree" or "sāla-tree."
However, it is not permissible to mark a tree that is firmly rooted and shaped like a banyan tree in one place and then mark it in another.
Regarding the signs for the path, he said "or a footpath" and so forth, because forest tracks, fields, rivers, ponds, and [other] paths are not permitted as signs.
As for a footpath that diverges from a cart-track and then re-enters that very same cart-track, or those [paths where] a footpath and a cart-track [meet]...
Those who have been consecrated [with the upasampadā] are not permitted [to travel]. Therefore he said:

"By means of infantry-roads and cart-roads," and so forth. In this context, it should be understood that if they take the track of the final wheel of a cart as the boundary-mark (*nimitta*), the road is outside the boundary (*bahisīmā*).
If they take the track of the outer wheel as the boundary-mark, then the outer wheel-track itself is outside the boundary, while the remainder belongs to the interior of the boundary (*antossīmā*).

Even if two paths emerge and later merge like the yoke of a cart, they need not be marked again after having been marked once at the point where they diverged or at the point where they join; for this constitutes a single continuous boundary-mark.
If four roads lead to the four directions surrounding a monastery, one should mark one in the center.
It is not permissible to mark out another [boundary]. For this is a single, continuous boundary.
However, it is permissible to mark out that which has passed beyond after piercing through a corner. But a path that has passed through the middle of the monastery must not be marked out;
for if it were marked out, the monastery would be situated on top of the boundary marker. And by one marking out this path, [it should be declared]: "The path, the road..."
It is permissible to designate [the boundary] by any one of the ten names mentioned beginning with "patho.
However, a road that has gone around a monastery, having encircled it in the shape of a moat, may be designated in one place, but it is not permissible to designate it in another.
As for the river, which I shall explain under the characteristics of the unconfined boundary (*abaddhasīma*) in the passage beginning with "In the time of righteous kings... and so forth.
This was stated because it will be explained later regarding the water-splashing boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*) in the context of a river.
However, if a river—like a road—surrounds a monastery in the shape of a cart-track or a moat, one may designate [the boundary] at one point, but it is not permissible to designate it elsewhere.
This also applies to a set of four rivers that intersect one another at the four directions of the monastery.
The same method applies here. However, it is permissible to describe all four [kinds of streams] as "unmixed" (*asammissa*) and so forth.

If, like one building a dam, they block the course of the river by digging at its base and obstructing it with creepers, straw, and the like, such that even though the water overflows, the obstruction remains in place, it is permissible to take that as the sign. But it must be done in such a way that the water does not flow through.

When a dam has been built, it is not permissible to establish a river-mark (*nadī-nimitta*) for a river that no longer flows. It is permissible to establish a river-mark at the place where it used to flow, and a water-mark (*udaka-nimitta*) at the place where it does not flow.
However, if a river does not flow due to a lack of water during a period of drought or in the summer heat, it is permissible [to treat it as such]. From a large river...
They divert water from a main channel, and it becomes like a small stream that flows constantly, providing for three crops.

Although it flows thus, it is not permissible to make a formal boundary-mark (nimitta). However, that which, though originally issuing from a great river at its source, later breaks through the riverbank by the same path it emerged and flows on its own, and as it flows further, becomes infested with crocodiles and other such creatures—[that is what is meant].
If there is a river that must be crossed by means of boats and such, it is permissible to make that a sign.
"Not flowing" (*asandamāna*) means not moving. "Flowing" (*sandamāna*) refers to water in floods, rivers, torrents, or channels.
"Not remaining beyond the stated limit" refers to the stated limit as expressed in the phrase: "remaining steady until the conclusion of the formal act" (*kammavācā*).
"Not standing. "Contained in a vessel" means water that has gone into vessels such as boats, buckets, and so forth.
As for what is stated in the *Andhaka-ṭīkā*—"One should not take as a sign water that is being splashed up in deep pits and the like"—that is poorly said;
it is merely his own personal opinion. However, even if it is standing [water], even in a pigsty or in a village children's play-pool...
If he remains until the conclusion of the formal ritual proclamation (*kammavācā*), it is perfectly permissible whether that duration be short or long.
At that spot, however, for the purpose of forming a mental sign (*nimittasaññā*), a heap of stones, sand, or soil, or a stone pillar,
or a wooden pillar, should be made.

Having thus shown the possession of the perfection of the site (*nimitta*), he now says, "endowed with the perfection of the assembly," and so forth, in order to show by which characteristics the assembly is said to be endowed with perfection.

Since this formal act (*kamma*) is to be performed by a quorum of four, it is stated, "by four bhikkhus. Furthermore, those desiring to bind this boundary should [consult] the neighboring monasteries...
The monks, having asked about the boundary limits of each respective monastery,
and having set aside the interval between boundaries for those monasteries with established boundaries, as well as the precincts of the boundary for those monasteries without established boundaries,

if they wish to establish a boundary within a single village field at a time when wandering monks are not moving about, [they should consider] those monasteries therein that have established boundaries.
Among them, [the monks] should be sent to the other monasteries with the instruction: "Today we shall bind a boundary; you must not go outside the limits of your respective boundaries.
In those monasteries where no boundary has been bound, the monks should be assembled together, and the consent (*chanda*) of those entitled to give it should be brought forth.
Therefore it was said: "As many as there are in that village precinct," and so forth.
"In that village district" means: in whichever village district they recite the formal act (kammavācā) while standing, in that village district.
"If they wish to include other village districts as well within [the boundary], then those monks who reside in those villages must also come;
for those who do not come, their consent (chanda) must be brought," said the Elder Mahāsumma. The Elder Mahāpaduma...

Furthermore, he said: "Those called 'fields for non-returning' (*nānāgāmakhettāni*) are like separately established boundaries (*pāṭiyekka-baddhasīmā*); from them, neither consent (*chandā*) nor purity (*pārisuddhi*) comes.

However, monks who have gone within the boundary marks (*antanimitta*) must come. Having said this, he further stated: "At the time of delimiting a boundary for common affiliation (*samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā*), both coming and not coming are permissible;
but at the time of delimiting a boundary for non-separation (*avippavāsa-sīmā*), by those who have gone within the boundary marks..."
“They must come; for those who do not come, their consent must be brought.
Now, in order to show by which characteristics the formal act (*kammavācā*) is said to be “endowed with perfection,” he says: “endowed with the perfection of the formal act,” and so forth.
By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), [he includes]: “If it is timely for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha [act] by these signs...”
The Saṅgha should authorize a boundary for common residence and a single Uposatha; this is the motion. Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me:
as far as the marks have been proclaimed all around, the Saṅgha authorizes a boundary by these marks for common residence and a single Uposatha.
Whichever venerable one approves of the authorization of the boundary for common residence by these marks, [let him remain silent].

“...for the sake of a single Uposatha; he who does not approve should speak. The boundary has been authorized by the Saṅgha through these marks as a common residence for a single Uposatha. It is approved by the Saṅgha; therefore it is silent. Thus do I understand this.
This includes the remainder of the Pāḷi. “Vuttāya” means stated in the Uposathakkhandhaka. [This refers to] the faults of the motion (ñatti) and the faults of the proclamation (anussāvana).
Because it is devoid [of defects], it is pure.
A "fragmentary boundary" (*khaṇḍasīmā*) is a small boundary. A boundary authorized for the purpose of common affiliation is a "boundary of common affiliation" (*samānasaṃvāsakasīmā*).

A boundary authorized for the purpose of not being separated [from one's robes] is a "boundary of non-separation" (*avippavāsasīmā*). Now, regarding these three boundaries, by those who authorize the boundary:
For the sake of making the Saṅgha-kammas, such as the going-forth (pabbajjā) and full ordination (upasampadā), easy to perform, the "broken boundary" (khaṇḍasīmā) must first be established.
Those establishing it, however, must know the proper procedure (vatta).

For if they establish it after having already constructed all the sites—such as the Bodhi-tree shrine, the dining hall, and so forth—in a monastery that has already been built, they must not fail to establish it in the center of the monastery, at a place where many people gather.

It should be tied up in a secluded spot on the outskirts of the monastery. When tying it up in a monastery that has not yet been built, those doing so should observe the locations for all sites, such as the Bodhi tree and the cetiya, and tie it up in such a way that the secluded spot on the outskirts of the monastery falls upon a site where [buildings] will eventually be established.
At its minimum extent, it is permissible if it accommodates twenty-one bhikkhus.
Beyond that, it is not permitted. Even if one takes more than a thousand bhikkhus, it is permitted.
Those binding it must place boundary-marking stones around the perimeter of the boundary enclosure;

those standing within a minor boundary (khaṇḍasīmā) must not bind a great boundary (mahāsīmā), nor should those standing within a great boundary bind a minor boundary. However, standing only within a minor boundary, a minor boundary may be bound.
Standing right within the great boundary (mahāsīmā) itself is the great boundary.
Herein, this is the method for its binding: having designated the boundary marks all around by saying, "This stone is a mark," the boundary should be formally authorized by means of the *kammavācā*.
Then, for the purpose of strengthening that very same [boundary], the *kammavācā* for non-separation (*avippavāsa*) [should be performed].
It must be done in this way; for otherwise, those who have come with the intention, "We shall abolish the boundary," will not be able to abolish it.
Having demarcated the boundary, boundary-stones should be placed outside the boundary. Even a space of four finger-breadths at the rear limit serves as the boundary-interval (*sīmantarikā*).
However, if the monastery is large, two, three, or even more than that many fragmentary boundaries (*khaṇḍasīmā*) should be established.
Having thus authorized the minor boundary (khaṇḍasīma), at the time of authorizing the great boundary (mahāsīmā), they should emerge from the minor boundary,
stand within the great boundary, and while walking around it on all sides, designate the boundary-stone markers (sīmantarikapāsāṇa). Then, having designated the remaining boundary marks,
they should authorize the common-residence boundary (samānasaṃvāsakasīma) by means of the formal act (kammavācā) without departing from hand’s reach (hatthapāsa), and of that...
A formal act of non-separation (*avippavāsakamma*) should also be performed for the purpose of strengthening [the boundary].
For otherwise, those who have come with the intention, "We shall abolish the boundary," will not be able to abolish it.

However, if they first designate the marks for the broken boundary (*khaṇḍasīmā*), then designate the marks for the intermediate boundary (*sīmantarikā*), and finally designate the marks for the great boundary (*mahāsīmā*), having thus designated the marks in these three places—
Whatever boundary they desire, it is permissible to bind that first. Even so, it should be bound starting from the fragmentary boundary (khaṇḍasīmā) according to the method already described.

Once the boundaries have been bound in this way, monks standing within a fragmentary boundary do not invalidate the formal acts (kamma) being performed within a great boundary (mahāsīmā), nor do those standing within a great boundary [invalidate acts] within a fragmentary boundary.
...of those performing [the work]. However, those standing within the boundary-mark (*sīmantarikā*) do not cause disturbance for either group.

But for those performing work while standing within the village precinct (*gāmakhette*), those standing at the boundary-mark do cause disturbance; for the boundary-mark belongs to the village precinct.
When the demarcation of a non-separation boundary (*avippavāsasīmā*) has been performed, that becomes what is called a non-separation boundary. Therefore he said: "Of that very..."
"...the classification. "Of that very same" means of the boundary established by formal demarcation (*baddhasīmā*).

However, this is the distinction: because of the statement, "excluding the village and the vicinity of the village," the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsasīmā*) does not extend into the village or the vicinity of the village;
but the common-ordination boundary (*samānasaṃvāsakasīmā*) does extend even there. [This is] the common-ordination boundary.

In this regard, it extends according to its own natural character; however, the non-separation boundary (*avippavāsa-sīmā*) extends only where there is a common-residence boundary (*samāna-saṃvāsa-sīmā*), for there is no separate proclamation of signs for it.

In that case, if there is a village at the time of the formal resolution (*sammuti*) for the non-separation [boundary], it does not enter into it. But if the village exists after the boundary has been resolved, [it is included].
If one settles there later, that too comes to be included within the boundary.
And just as with one who settled later, even an area expanded after the initial settlement also comes to be included within the boundary.

Even if houses were built at the time the boundary was authorized, or if there was an intention to enter saying, "We shall go in," but people had not yet entered, or if it was an ancient village or their own homes; [in all such cases, they are included].

Having abandoned [the village] and gone elsewhere, this is indeed a non-village (*agāma*), and the boundary (*sīmā*) enters it. But if even a single family has entered or not left, it is indeed a village, and the boundary does not enter it.
Having thus shown the established boundary, he now says "But the unestablished boundary... and so forth, in order to show the unestablished boundary.
The village itself is the boundary; thus, it is a "village-boundary" (*gāmasīmā*). Here, by the mention of "village," one should understand that towns and cities are also included.

To whatever extent the village-chiefs of that village receive tribute from a certain area—whether that area be small or large—that is called a single "village-field" (*gāmakhetta*). Furthermore, even within a single village-field, a certain portion [is designated as]: "This..."
Having demarcated [the area] by saying, "Let this be a separate village," if the king gives it to someone, that too indeed becomes a separate village boundary.

Therefore, both that [newly defined area] and the other [original] natural village boundary are exactly like a formally established boundary (*baddhasīmā*). However, it simply does not receive the exemption from the offense of being separated from the three robes (*ticīvara-vippavāsa*).
"In a forest devoid of a village" means in a forest such as the Viñjhāṭavi wilderness. Thus he said: "What is called 'devoid of a village'... and so forth. But this—
One also gains the exemption from the offense of being separated from one’s three robes within the boundary. "Fishermen" means those who are fishermen by trade.
"On paths where there is no way to go" means on paths where it is impossible to travel; what is meant is: on such paths where it is not possible to go and return on the very same day.
However, within the limit of their range of movement, it is reckoned as the village boundary.
In that regard, it is not permissible to perform a formal act (*kamma*) without first purifying the village boundary (*gāmasīma*).

"Seven *abbhantara*s in all directions for those standing in the middle" means that from the position of the monks standing in the center, there are seven *abbhantara*s in every direction. "Therein" means within those *abbhantara*s.
"Therefore" means because it increases by way of the assembly (*parisa*); therefore. "For the purpose of the precinct" means for the purpose of the precinct of the boundary (*sīmopacāra*).

"Having rejected the non-existence of a boundary" means having rejected the non-existence of a formally established boundary (*baddhasīmā*). "Sharing a common residence" (*samānasaṃvāsā*) means that there is a common dwelling therein.
"Sharing a single Uposatha" (*ekūposathā*) means that there is a single Uposatha ceremony therein.

And here, since the Uposatha has been mentioned separately, the state of sharing a common residence should be understood by way of the remaining formal acts (*kamma*). It is said [in the text] in order to show the delimitation of an unestablished boundary (*abaddhasīmā*).
[These rules] are stated in the Uposathakkhandhaka. *Anvaḍḍhamāsaṃ* means "every half-month"; that is, in each half-month.

The same applies to expressions such as *anudasāhaṃ* ("every ten days"). *Devo* means "cloud. In the phrase *vigatamattesū valāhakesu*, the locative case is used to indicate the state by which another state is characterized (*bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇe*).

*Sotaṃ* refers to the flow of water. The words *otaritvā* ("having descended") are to be supplied [to the text], whether by way of a proper ford (*titthena*) or not by way of a proper ford (*atitthena*).
“Having covered the three circles” means having dressed in such a way that the covering of the three circles is achieved.

“Crossing over” means crossing at any place whatsoever. It is stated as “of a bhikkhunī” because the definition of a river is presented in the Pāḷi according to the case of a bhikkhunī in the *Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga*, and not because there is some specific distinction [between them].

"Not dug by anyone" means not even dug by an animal. "Having broken through a river or the ocean" means having broken through a riverbank or the tide-line of the ocean. "This characteristic" refers to the characteristic described as:
"where, during the rainy season, water remains in a river of the aforementioned kind. Even salt water is indeed reckoned as *jātassara* (naturally occurring water).

It flows away. However, when during the rainy season in the manner described, as soon as the rain has ceased, there is no water available for drinking or for washing one’s hands and feet, and it dries up, this natural pond goes only so far as the village fields.
Regarding the term *udakukkhepā*, he says "by the throwing of water" (*udakukkhepena*), because the ablative case is used here in the sense of the instrumental. But how is water thrown?
Regarding the phrase "it should be thrown," he said "therein," and so forth. "By a man of middle strength" means by a man of middling physical power.
"This is called a water-throw" means that this is called a boundary delimited by a water-throw;
the meaning is that as long as the assembly increases, this boundary also increases, for the measure is simply the water-throw extending to the limits of the assembly. If...

However, the river is not very long; from its source up to its mouth, the Saṅgha can sit everywhere along it, so there is no need for the formal act of establishing a water-throw boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*). The entire river belongs to these very same monks.
"In the normal rainy season" refers to the aforementioned period of the normal rains. "During the four months" refers to the [rainy] season.
During the four months [of the rains], when there is excessive rain, a place flooded by a torrent must not be taken as a boundary;
for that is considered to belong to the village boundary itself. This same rule should be understood to apply to lakes, ponds, natural pools, and even islands formed by boulders within them.
However, if a river is full and its banks overflow, one may remain within the river even while wearing one's bathing robe (*udakasāṭikā*).

The formal act (kamma) must be performed. If they are unable [to do so on land], it may be performed even while standing in a boat; however, it is not permitted to perform it while the boat is moving. Why?
Because the boundary consists merely of the splash of water, and a boat quickly passes beyond that.
This being the case, the motion (ñatti) would be in one boundary and the proclamation (anussāvanā) in another; therefore, [the boat] should be held by means of a rudder...
Setting it aside, one should perform the ritual by hanging it on a stone or tying it to a tree growing within the river.
It is permissible to perform the ritual even when standing on a raft tied within the river or on a tree situated within the river.
However, if the branch of the tree or a shoot emerging from it extends onto the outer bank or into the monastery boundary (*vihārasīma*), [it is not permissible].
The formal act (kamma) should be performed either standing within the village boundary, or having cleared the boundary, or having cut a branch.
It is not permissible to perform the act by mooring a boat to a branch or a shoot of a tree growing on the bank outside a river that has entered into the interior of the river.
Those performing it must either clear the boundary or cut the branch. Of that...
The portion established on the outside must be destroyed. However, on a riverbank, it is not permissible at all to build a binding structure after having hewn stakes into the ground.
If they construct a bridge over a river, if the bridge or the bridge-piers are situated entirely within the river, it is permissible for those standing on the bridge to perform work.
But if the bridge or the bridge-piers are established on the outer bank, [it is not permissible] to perform work.

It is not permissible; the boundary must be cleared and then the formal act (*kamma*) performed. However, if the bridge-piers are inside [the boundary], but the bridge itself stands in the air above both banks, it is permissible.
The same principle applies to a natural lake (*jātassara*).
By the phrase, "in whatever place the natural waves roll in and settle," it refers to that area where the water rises during a flood.
Or if natural waves come with great force and inundate it, he shows that it is not permissible to perform the ritual there.
If the force of the waves is oppressive, one should perform it while standing on a boat or a platform.

The detailed explanation regarding these cases is to be understood in the same manner as that stated for rivers. However, if the ocean should inundate the boundary of a village or the boundary of a town...
It remains; it becomes like the ocean. It is permissible to perform work there. From that point on, it is called a "kappiya-bhūmi" (a consecrated area);
the meaning is that starting from the edge of the water that has settled after being covered over, the interior is known as a river, a pond, a lake, or the ocean.
This was said with reference to the times of drought and the winter season. "And even in dry places" means even where there is no water. And just as in the case of digging a pond...
In this way, it should be understood that even when digging ponds, lotus pools, and so forth, it remains village territory (*gāmakhetta*).
"Or they sow crops" means they sow crops such as gourds (*lābu*) and beans (*tipusa*). "That place" refers to the location where a reservoir (*vāpi*) or similar structure has been made;
however, any other area is a *kappiyabhūmi* (a permitted ground). But if, having filled a natural lake, they create dry land [there], [it is considered village territory].
Having built a dam in one direction, they construct it as a single great lake; thus, even the Ajātasara becomes entirely one.
It comes to be reckoned as a village boundary.
If they destroy even a river and construct a lake, with a dam built at the bottom, the water flows in and fills the lake.
If it remains full, it is not permissible to perform work there.
Water that has been discarded in an upper area flows down and overflows a river; from the point where it begins to flow, it is permissible to perform work.

If a certain river, after rising at intervals, overflows and flows across the boundary of a village or town, it remains a river, and it is permissible to perform work there. If [it overflows] the monastery boundary...
It covers [the area] and thus comes to be designated as a "monastery boundary" (*vihārasīmā*). Therefore, because it goes within, for that reason.
"The delimitation by the splash of water must be made all around" is said with reference to a sufficient space;

however, where it is not possible, as in the case of small streams and the like, the delimitation by the splash of water should be made from a sufficient point. "For the sake of the precincts" means for the sake of the precincts of the boundary.
But why must one distinct *sattabbhantara* (seven-fathom space) and one distinct *udakukkhepa* (water-splash) be established for the purpose of the precinct (*upacāra*)?

To this he says, "For this," and so forth. This is what is meant: because both this *sattabbhantara* boundary and the *udakukkhepa* boundary are obtained starting from the standing place of the monks, and those monks are not always identical.
Sometimes they increase, and sometimes they decrease. When they increase, there is a confusion of boundaries (*sīmāsaṅkara*).
Therefore, another one *sattabbhantara* and another one *udakukkhepa* should be set aside for the purpose of the precinct (*upacāra*).
As for what is stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*: "More than that is indeed permissible, but less is not permissible."
That [distance] also is for this very purpose; however, it should not be understood as referring to the non-arising of karma performed there. Regarding the delimitation:

even though it stands without exceeding that same extent of delimitation outside, it means outside of whatever constitutes the delimitation of their seven-fathom space or the water-splash—by way of one's own seven-fathom space or by way of the water-splash.
The meaning is: "even though it stands without exceeding that very same limit. How is this understood? He says:
"This is the conclusion in all the Aṭṭhakathās," which means that this is the determination in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā* and other such works, namely, "it destroys the kamma.
"Thus, this... and so forth is the conclusion of what has been stated. And there is this [verse]:
“In this regard, by way of being bound and unbound, the boundary (sīmā) there is twofold:
that which is endowed with the three attainments and that which possesses eleven defects.
The bound boundary is threefold: first, the fragmentary [boundary], and so forth, starting from the village boundary.”
This "similar offense" is of two kinds: similar in respect of the objective basis (*vatthusabhāgā*) and similar in respect of the offense itself (*āpattisabhāgā*).
Here, it is the similarity of the objective basis that is intended, not the other; thus he said, "That which the entire Saṅgha [commits] by way of eating at the improper time, etc.

A "light offense" (*lahukāpatti*) is so called because it is purified by a light disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*); it refers to those classified as *thullaccaya*, *pācittiya*, *pāṭidesanīya*, *dukkaṭa*, and *dubbhāsita*.

There are five kinds of offenses. Even when there is an offense involving a formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa) that is similar in substance to the matter at hand, the Uposatha ceremony is not valid.
As it is said: "It is not permitted to disclose [an offense] in the presence of one who has committed a similar saṅghādisesa offense.
If one does disclose it, the offense is indeed disclosed, but one is not released from the dukkaṭa [offense]. However, regarding that which does not require confession...
Thus it was said. "Similar in respect of the basis" (*vatthusabhāgā*) means similar by way of the basis; what is meant is that they belong to the same category.
It is not permissible to confess this very [offense] as being similar in respect of the basis, because it has been stated: "Monks, an offense similar in respect of the basis must not be confessed;

whoever should confess it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). However, this does not refer to similarity in respect of the offense itself. Therefore he said: "On account of eating at an improper time..."
"But having fallen into [an offense]," and so forth. *Āpattisabhāgaṃ* means sharing the same nature as an offense.

*Sāmanta-āvāsaṃ* means a neighboring residence; the meaning is a nearby monastery (*samīpa-vihāra*). *Sajjukaṃ* means for the purpose of arriving on that very day. *Pāhetabbo* means he should be sent.
*Iccetaṃ kusalaṃ* means "thus this is skillful," that is to say, it is excellent, auspicious, and considered appropriate.
This has been said. "If he does not obtain [one]" means: if, due to the distance of the monasteries or because of obstacles on the road and so forth, he does not obtain one.
By this statement, "He will confess it in his presence," it is indicated that even a similar offense (sabhāgāpatti) may not be permitted to be confessed.
If he were to obtain one, he should perform the Uposatha after having confessed it. But if, however—
If the entire Saṅgha has fallen into a common *saṅghādisesa* offense, it is not permissible to perform the Uposatha after having put forward a formal motion (*ñatti*);
it would indeed be an obstacle to the Uposatha. Both [the proposer and the Saṅgha] incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
"Monks, a common offense is not to be confessed; whoever should confess one, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Monks, a common offense..."
Because it has been stated: "It should be accepted; whoever should accept it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). "Doubt" means uncertainty; one who is engaged in that is "doubtful.
The statement, "Having become free from doubt once again, one must indeed confess," exists neither in the Canon (pāḷi) nor in the Commentary (aṭṭhakathā);
however, once confessed, there is no fault. "In the manner already stated" refers to: "Venerable sirs, [declare] your purity... and so forth.
By the method beginning with "you must announce," it is stated that one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense for performing the *uposatha* while guilty of an offense;
this is according to the very manner already explained. Why is only a similar offense mentioned? To this he says, "For among these," and so forth.
Even when dissimilar offenses exist, the proper time [for the *uposatha*] still remains; however, when dissimilar offenses exist, [the procedure applies] only to those specific individuals.
It is an offense, but not for the Saṅgha; thus it is indeed a matter fit for the Saṅgha to deal with.
One who has committed an ultimate offense (*antimavatthu*) is one who has fallen into any one of the four *pārājika* offenses.
The detailed analysis of eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*) and others will be made clear later in the section on the *pārājikas*. "An animal" (*tiracchānagata*) refers to any [being], even down to a *sakka*.

Anyone belonging to a non-human species—beginning with the king of the gods (devarāja) and including such as the young nāgas (nāgamāṇavaka)—is to be understood here, not animals such as horses or oxen.
Therefore he said, "And herein," and so forth. In that context, "herein" refers to this discussion of persons who are to be excluded. Regarding the phrase "for whom ordination is forbidden":
[it refers to those for whom it is stated], "Monks, an animal is unordained; he is not to be ordained."
The ordination of non-human beings such as *nāgas* and *supaṇṇas* has been forbidden;

the meaning here is that even such a being is called a "non-human" (*tiracchānagata*). For in that context, anyone belonging to a non-human species—starting from the gods down to a *nāga-māṇavaka*—is intended by the term "non-human. Indeed, it is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*: "O monks, a 'non-human'..."

"In this context, whether it be a *nāga*, or any other among the *supaṇṇas*, *māṇavakas*, and so forth—even including Sakka, the king of the gods—anyone whatsoever belonging to the class of non-humans is to be understood as 'an animal' (*tiracchānagata*) in this sense. A "tenet" (*tittha*) refers to a philosophical view;
those who possess such a tenet are "tenet-holders" (*titthika*). Tenet-holders themselves are "sectarians" (*titthiya*); the meaning is: those who hold views other than this [Buddhist teaching].
The recitation of the Sutta is the *suttuddesa*. The Uposatha that is itself purity is the *pārisuddhi-uposatha*. The same method applies here to the *adhiṭṭhāna-uposatha* as well.
"It" refers to the recitation of the Pātimokkha. The Pātimokkha is indeed the exhortation (*ovāda*);

its recitation, that is, its exposition according to its own form, is the *ovāda-pātimokkhuddesa*. [This includes the instruction: "In the case of such a transgression, this is the specific offense. Thus...
Commanding and enjoining by way of an offense is "command" (āṇā); the rest is exactly as in the preceding [section].
Regarding the three verses beginning with: “Patience is the supreme austerity, forbearance…”—they are called the three verses thus stated.
The Buddhas declare Nibbāna to be supreme;
for one who harms others has not gone forth,
nor is one a recluse who oppresses another.
“Refraining from all evil, the cultivation of the wholesome,
and the purification of one’s own mind— this is the teaching of the Buddhas.
Non-reproach, non-violence, and restraint according to the Pātimokkha...”
"Knowing moderation in food, a remote dwelling place,
and application to the higher mind— this is the teaching of the Buddhas.
These are the three verses.
In this context, "patience is the supreme austerity" means that patience by way of endurance is the supreme austerity.
"Forbearance" (*titikkhā*) is a synonym for patience; the meaning is that patience by way of endurance, known as forbearance, is the highest austerity. "They say Nibbāna is supreme":
the Buddhas declare Nibbāna to be "supreme" in every respect. For one who has gone forth does not harm others.
One who, due to being devoid of the patience of forbearance, harms, oppresses, or injures another, is not called a renunciant (*pabbajita*).

The fourth line, moreover, is a synonym for that same point. For "not a renunciant" has "not a recluse (*samaṇa*)" as its synonym; and "one who harms others" has "one who vexes another" as its synonym. Now...

"Or one who harms others" means one who harms virtue (*sīla*). For virtue is called "the other" (*para*) in its supreme sense. And the meaning is that whatever ascetic, by harassing any being whatsoever, becomes a harmer of others and a destroyer of his own virtue, he is not truly called a renunciant.
Alternatively, it refers to one who, due to the absence of patience characterized by forbearance, is a harmer of others—[namely] another...
If one intentionally deprives even a gadfly or a mosquito of life, he is not a renunciant. Why?
Because he has not renounced defilement (*mala*). “Having renounced the defilement within himself, for that reason he is called a ‘renunciant’”—this indeed is the characteristic of a renunciant.
Furthermore, even if one does not strike or kill, but rather harasses [beings] with sticks and the like, [he is likewise not a renunciant].
One who harms others is not a *śramaṇa*. Why? Because of the lack of restraint regarding harm. For it is said:
“Because of the restraint of evils, one is called a *śramaṇa*”; this indeed is the defining characteristic of a *śramaṇa*.
In the second verse, “of all evil” means of all that is unwholesome (*akuśala*). “Non-doing” means non-arising. “Of the wholesome” means...
Of the wholesome [states] belonging to the four planes. *Upasampadā* means attainment, acquisition.
*Sacittapariyodapanaṃ* means the cleansing of one’s own mind, making it luminous, purifying it in every respect; that, moreover, occurs through Arahantship.
Thus, having abandoned all evil by means of the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*), one [cultivates] the wholesome through mundane and supramundane calm (*samatha*) and insight (*vipassanā*).
"Having accomplished this, the mind must be purified by the fruit of arahantship"—this is the teaching, the exhortation, and the instruction of the Buddhas.
In the third verse, "non-reproach" means not reproaching anyone with speech. "Non-injury" means not causing injury to anyone with the body.
Regarding the *pātimokkha*: that which is the *pātimokkha*, the *paatimokkha*, the *atipamokkha*.
It is the supreme virtue (*sīla*). It protects (*pāti*) one from various miserable states (*agati*), or it liberates (*mokkheti*) one from the fears of bad rebirths;

or, because it protects that which it liberates, it is called the "Pātimokkha," and [the text refers to] that Pātimokkha. "Restraint" (*saṃvara*) is the restraint characterized by the non-transgression of the seven classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*).
"Knowing the proper measure" (*mattaññutā*) is the knowledge of the right amount with respect to receiving and using [alms].
"Remote lodgings" (*pantañ ca sayanāsanaṃ*) refers to a dwelling that is secluded, free from the bustle of crowds, and devoid of people.
Here, it should be understood that contentment with all four requisites is illustrated by means of two alone;

for, by virtue of the commonality of "contentment with requisites," the other two are also indicated through the method of characteristic transfer (*lakkhaṇahāranaya*). And "application to higher consciousness" (*adhicitte ca āyogo*) refers to that which establishes insight (*vipassanā*).
The mind of the eight attainments; even more than that, the mind of the path and fruition is itself "higher consciousness" (*adhicitta*).
The meaning is: application and devoted practice toward that aforementioned higher consciousness. "This is the teaching of the Buddhas" refers to this:
not censuring others, not harming others, restraint according to the *Pātimokkha*, moderation in receiving and using [robes and alms], and mastery over the eight attainments.

"Resorting to secluded lodgings is the teaching, the advice, and the instruction of the Buddhas. Furthermore, it should be understood that these three verses are the *pātimokkhuddesa-gāthā* (recitation verses of the *pātimokkha*) for all Buddhas; they are recited by the Buddhas alone, not by their disciples.

That which is spoken in the manner beginning with "Let the Saṅgha listen to me, venerable sirs," is called the *āṇā-pātimokkha* (the *pātimokkha* of formal command); that is [recited] by the disciples.
Only the disciples recite it; the Buddhas do not perform formal acts of the Saṅgha (saṅghakamma), nor are they included therein. Therefore he said: "Only the disciples recite it, not the Buddhas.
Regarding the phrase "in this matter": it refers to the meaning of "one should recite the Pātimokkha.

One who has "not arrived" (anupagata) means one who has received full ordination right there, or one who has not arrived during the first three-month period due to forgetfulness. Regarding the term "cātumāsiniyā": [it refers to] the four-month period.

"Cātumāsiyaṃ" means: it is called "cātumāsī" because it marks the completion of four months; that very thing is termed "cātumāsinī," and [the word] "cātumāsiniyaṃ" refers to that period. The meaning is: on the full moon day of the latter Kattika month.
"Kāyasāmaggiṃ" means the state of being together in body; what is meant is coming within arm's reach.

This, however, is the analysis here: if five monks have entered the rains residence during the earlier period and five also during the later period, then after the former have performed the formal motion (*ñatti*) and completed the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), the latter should perform the purification and Uposatha ceremony in their presence;
one should not perform two formal motions at a single Uposatha assembly. This applies even if they have entered during the later period.
There may be four, three, two, or one; the same method applies. Or, if there are four in the earlier period, there may likewise be four, three, two, or one in the later period;
the same method applies. Or, if there are three in the earlier period, there may likewise be three or two in the later period;
the same method applies. This is the defining characteristic here: if [the number] in the later period... by those who arrived during the earlier period.

If those who have arrived are fewer but equal in number [to the quorum], and they complete the requisite number for a formal invitation of the Saṅgha, then having laid down a motion (*ñatti*) by way of a formal invitation of the Saṅgha,
they should perform the invitation together with the previous monks. However, if there are three in the earlier period and one arrives in the later period, making four with him,
it is not permissible to perform the invitation after laying down a motion of the Saṅgha for four.
It is permissible. However, by means of a formal motion (*ñatti*), he becomes a member who completes the quorum;

therefore, having established the motion on the basis of the group, the *pavāraṇā* should be performed with the former monks, while the latter should perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* in their presence.
This same method applies even if there are two in the first period, two or one in the second period, or if there is one in the first period and also [one] in the second.
One person should perform the *pavāraṇā* ceremony in the presence of another; one person should perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha*.

If those who have entered the rains retreat later are even one person more numerous than those who entered the earlier retreat, then after first reciting the *Pātimokkha*, the *pavāraṇā* should subsequently be performed in the presence of the smaller group.
However, regarding the *pavāraṇā* on the fourth month of the Kattika season, if [the later arrivals] are first...

If those who have entered the rains residence have performed the Great Invitation (*mahāpavāraṇā*), and those who have arrived later are either more numerous or equal in number, they should perform the invitation after setting aside the formal motion for the invitation (*pavāraṇāñatti*). Once they have invited, the others may subsequently perform the Uposatha of purification (*pārisuddhi-uposatha*).
Alternatively, if many have performed the Great Invitation and those who have entered the rains residence later are few, or even just one, [the same procedure applies].
Or, after the Pātimokkha has been recited, he should perform the Pavāraṇā ceremony in their presence.
"Having arranged the upper robe over one shoulder" means having properly placed the upper robe over one shoulder.
"Having raised the hands in añjali" means having lifted up the añjali, which is radiant with the joining of the ten fingernails. But if, in that case...

There is also the case of one who is undergoing probation (pārivāsika). Sitting in the place of the most junior member of the Saṅgha, he should perform the Uposatha of purity according to the text while remaining seated right there.
However, when the Pātimokkha is being recited, he should not remain seated according to the text;
rather, having left the text behind, he must sit without releasing his handspan’s distance from it. This same method applies to the Pavāraṇā as well.
"Everything that must be done beforehand" refers to the ninefold preliminary duty beginning with sweeping.
And just as the entire Saṅgha, having fallen into a similar offense, is permitted to perform the Uposatha after proposing a motion thus: "Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me... [etc.
...I shall make amends," so too here, by means of three [monks] saying: "Let the venerable ones hear me; these monks have fallen into a similar offense..."

Having established a formal motion for the community (*gaṇañatti*) with the words, "We have fallen into an offense; when we see another bhikkhu who is pure and free from offense, we shall then confess that offense in his presence," it is permissible for two [bhikkhus] to perform the Uposatha after saying, "Having seen another who is pure, we shall confess [the offense]. It is also permissible for one [bhikkhu] to do so, thinking, "Having obtained one who is pure, I shall confess [the offense]."

It is permissible to do so after making an effort. "On that day" (*tadahū*) means on that very day; this is the meaning. "By those of different affiliations" (*nānāsaṃvāsakehi*) means by those who differ in their tenets.
"A non-residence" (*anāvāso*) refers to any place whatsoever, such as a construction site or the like.
"Except with the Saṅgha" means except in the presence of monks sufficient to constitute a Saṅgha. "Except for obstacles" refers to the ten kinds of obstacles mentioned previously.
Except for these [specific reasons]. However, at the very least, it is permissible to go if there is an obstacle involving oneself as the fourth person.

Just as one should not go to a residence (*āvāsa*) and so forth, likewise, if they perform the Uposatha in that monastery, one should not go even to the boundary (*sīmā*) or the river for the purpose of determining the Uposatha. But if there is some monk there, one may go into his presence.

It is permissible. It is also permissible for one who has neglected the Uposatha to go to another residence. Having gone there in this manner, he may also perform the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna).
Even a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, having wandered for alms in the village on the Uposatha day, should return to his own monastery.
If he enters another monastery, he must return only after performing the Uposatha there; it is not permissible to return without having performed it.
It is not permitted. However, one may go to such a residence if one knows: "I will be able to go there this very day.
For by performing the Uposatha there together with the monks, he will not have created an obstacle to the Uposatha.
"Water together with a seat" means drinking water and water for washing along with a seat. From the assembly of the Saṅgha...

The preliminary duty (*pubbakaraṇa*) is that which must be done first. Although it may also be performed after the preliminary duty, it is called the "prior task" (*pubbakicca*) because it must be done prior to the Uposatha ceremony. Since both of these must be performed prior to the Uposatha ceremony, they are referred to here simply as the "prior task";
thus he said: "In this way, the ninefold prior task is designated by two names."

Regarding the phrase "it has been shown," he asks, "What is that which was done? and thus says, "Not indeed," and so forth. It is not permissible to perform the Uposatha without having done that [sweeping], because of such statements as:
"Monks, when commanded by the Elder, one who is not ill must sweep; whoever does not sweep incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
For this very reason, he says, "Therefore, when commanded by the Elder," and so forth.
But if, even when commanded, he does not obtain a broom even for a short time, he should sweep by having a branch-bending made allowable;
for one who does not obtain that either, it becomes allowable as soon as it is obtained.
"Water for drinking and water for washing should be set out" means that water for drinking and water for washing should be set out for the sake of the newcomers. "A seat should be prepared" means...

Seats such as stools, benches, and so forth, should be prepared. If there are no seats in the Uposatha hall, they should be brought from the Sangha’s residence, prepared, and then returned. In the absence of seats, it is permissible to prepare even straw mats or wooden planks.

If even these are unavailable, one should have branches broken off, have them rendered *kappiya* (made allowable), and then prepare them. [One should instruct] the *kappiyakāraka* (the one who makes things allowable).
For one who does not obtain [the materials], it becomes permissible once obtained. "A lamp should be made" means it should be lit; what is meant is that the lighting of the lamp should be performed.
However, the one giving the order should say: "In such-and-such a place there is oil, or a wick, or a bowl; take that and do it.
If the oil and other items are not present, they must be sought. Having sought them...
For one who does not obtain [the requisites], what is permissible becomes obtained. Furthermore, a fire may also be lit in a potsherd.

And when assigning duties, one who performs some work, or one who is always alone as a burden-bearer, or anyone such as a reciter of the Suttas or a preacher of the Dhamma, must not be assigned [a task];
however, the rest may be assigned by turns. Therefore he said: "Even by an elder, what is appropriate..."
"Having understood this, he should be instructed.

Regarding "having come after performing the Uposatha outside": the formal consent (*chandah*) must be given by one who has come after performing the Uposatha anywhere—whether at a river or within a boundary (*sīmā*).
The intended meaning is that one is not permitted to remain [thinking], "The Uposatha has been performed by me. One who is occupied with business...

Or [the Uposatha may be performed] by one who is occupied with duties such as attending to the sick. If the sick person is unable to give his consent and purification, the Uposatha should be performed after bringing him into the midst of the Saṅgha on a bed or a chair.
If it occurs to the monks who are attending the sick person: "If we move this sick person from his place, his illness will increase," [then...]
“...or death will occur,” he must not be moved from that place;
the Saṅgha should go there and perform the Uposatha, but the Uposatha must not be performed by a faction of the Saṅgha.
If one should do so, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). If there are many such sick persons, the Saṅgha should stand in a row and [perform it] for all of them.
They must be within arm’s reach. If they are far apart and the Saṅgha is not complete, the Uposatha should not be performed on that day;
however, the Uposatha must never be performed by an incomplete Saṅgha.

This is because the Blessed One has said: "Monks, I allow that on the Uposatha day, one who gives formal purity (pārisuddhi) may also give consent (chanda), for there is business to be done for the Saṅgha."

When issuing the formal act (*āṇā*), it was said, "I give my consent" (*chandaṃ dammi*). Because of such statements as, "Monks, if the one who carries the consent departs from that very place after the consent has been given, the consent must be given to another," he said again, "Carry my consent," in order to dispel the fatigue of having to give his own consent repeatedly.
[And because of the statement: "Monks, if the one who carries the consent, having been given the consent, arrives at the Saṅgha..."
Because it is stated, "If one does not report it intentionally, the formal consent (*chanda*) has been brought [but not communicated];
there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the one who brings the consent," one says, "Report my consent," in order to be released from that *dukkaṭa*.
It must be made known either by body, by speech, or by both; thus, having reflected with the mind, one performs a bodily exertion.

By any limb or member whatsoever, or by means of speech if one is able to utter it, or by both body and speech if one is able to do so in either way—it must be made known; that is, it must be communicated.

However, because of the statement "this is the matter," it is permissible to communicate by whatever language of the body or speech is appropriate, whether in the giving of full purity (*pārisuddhi*) or in the giving of consent (*chanda*).
The analysis is exactly as previously stated. However, when giving that [pārisuddhi], one must first confess any existing offense (*āpatti*).
For one who is still possessed of an offense is not permitted to say: "I give purity; take my purity; announce my purity.
When it should be said, "There are duties for the Saṅgha," by way of a verbal inversion, it is said: "There are..."
It is said, "it is a duty for the Saṅgha. Regarding the phrase "he gives the consent and the purity of himself and theirs":

here, *chanda* (consent) and *chandapārisuddhi* (purity of consent) together are termed *chandapārisuddhi*; the meaning should be understood according to the method of *sarūpekasesa* (retaining only one member of a similar pair).
"The other" refers to the consent and purity of others. Regarding the term *biḷālasaṅkhalikā chandapārisuddhi*: here, *biḷālasaṅkhalikā*...
This is called the "cat's chain" (biḷālabandhana). For in that case, the first ring of a chain reaches only the second ring, but not the third;
likewise, this purity of intention (chandapārisuddhi), once given by the donor to a specific person, does not go elsewhere.
Therefore, because it resembles a cat's chain, it is called a "cat's chain. And the mention of the "cat's chain" here [serves as an illustration].
It should be understood that this is merely an illustration of any such fetters whatsoever. Regarding "the announcement of the season" (*utukkhāna*):
it is called *utu* because it causes a lack of interest (*arati*) in various activities; the announcement of that is *utukkhāna*, meaning the proclamation of the season.
To show the nature of that proclamation as it actually occurs, the words "of the winter season, etc. (*hemantādīnaṃ*) and so forth were stated.
“Enumeration” means reckoning. “Exhortation of the nuns” (*bhikkhunovāda*) refers to the exhorting of the nuns by means of the eight weighty rules (*aṭṭhagarudhamma*).

Regarding the phrase “having come [thinking] ‘The Uposatha is tomorrow’”: when it is said, “The Uposatha is tomorrow,” this means that having come on that very day—on the fourteenth of the fortnight during a fifteen-day Uposatha, or on the thirteenth during a fourteen-day Uposatha—it is stated, “having come. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, [it says]: “Of the fortnight...”
It is said: "Having arrived on the thirteenth day itself, one should ask: 'Is this Uposatha the fourteenth or the fifteenth?
And when asked in this way, the monk, if they perform the Uposatha on the fourteenth day, should say: "Sisters, it is the fourteenth-day [Uposatha].
If they perform it on the fifteenth day, he should say: "Sisters, it is the fifteenth-day [Uposatha]."

Because it was said, “Monks, I allow you to receive the exhortation from those remaining, excluding the fool, excluding the sick, and excluding one who is about to travel,” he said, “excluding him,” and so forth.
In that context, a “fool” (bāla) is one who does not know the procedure for the announcement.

A “traveler” (gamiya) is one who wishes to go on the Uposatha days of the fourteenth or fifteenth, or on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pāṭipada); [this refers to] from the second day of the fortnight...
However, from that point onward, as he travels further, there is no one here for him to go to. One who dwells in the forest is an *āraññika*.
He too cannot refuse, thinking, "I am a forest-dweller; tomorrow is the Uposatha; I will not stay in the monastery.
If he were to refuse, he would incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). For this has been said: "Monks, the exhortation..."
"It should not be accepted; whoever should accept it incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). However, an appointment must be made for the purpose of returning it.
For this has been said: "I allow you, monks, for a forest-dwelling monk to accept the exhortation and to make an appointment, saying:
'I will return here. Therefore, if a forest-dwelling monk [meets] the nuns...
If alms are obtained in the village where one is staying, one should wander right there; having seen the bhikkhunīs, one should inform them and then depart.
If alms are not easily obtained there, one should wander in a neighboring village, and upon returning to the village of the bhikkhunīs, act in the same manner.
If it is necessary to go a long distance, an appointment should be made: "I shall [meet you] at such-and-such a place."
“I shall go to the village gate, or to an assembly hall, or to a pavilion, or to the foot of a tree;
you should come there. The bhikkhunīs must go there; it is not permitted for them not to go. For this has been said: “Bhikkhus, it is not for a bhikkhunī not to go to an appointment;
whoever does not go incurs an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). “At the place of the Uposatha” means at the location where the Uposatha is performed. “By eight factors” means—

“He is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training. He is learned, one who has retained what he has heard and accumulated what he has heard;
those teachings that are good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, which are entirely complete and pure—”

They declare the holy life to be perfectly pure; such teachings as these have been heard much by him, retained in mind, mastered verbally, examined with the intellect, and well penetrated through right view.
Furthermore, both Pātimokkhas have been properly received by him in detail, well analyzed, well mastered, and well investigated.

[He is proficient] by way of the discourses and by way of the phrasing. He is one of lovely speech, possessing lovely enunciation. For the most part, he is dear and pleasing to the bhikkhunīs. He is capable of exhorting the bhikkhunīs.
Furthermore, he has never previously committed a grave offense (garudhamma) against a woman who has gone forth under the Blessed One and wears the saffron robes. [He must be] twenty years of age.
"Or he is more than twenty years of age"—this refers to these eight factors. "With inspiring [conduct]" means with faultless bodily, verbal, and mental action that brings about confidence.
"Let him accomplish" means let him accomplish the threefold training (*śikṣā*). But when those bhikkhunīs see only the one who recites the *Pātimokkha*...
When the exhortation was requested, and the community of monks had assembled at the Uposatha hall, they asked as a preliminary duty, "Are there any bhikkhunīs requesting the exhortation?

When [the messenger] was told, "Speak thus," he had another person speak the words he was to say; then, having himself stated, "Is there any monk appointed as the exhorter of bhikkhunīs? and so forth—
Furthermore, having gone there oneself, one should inform the nuns; or else, another monk should cause the Pātimokkha to be recited on that day.
Here, the plural form “by them” (*tāhi*) refers to [the group]. “Together” means at the same time.
“By one who establishes a motion” (*ñattiṭṭhapakena*) refers to a place where the recitation of the Pātimokkha does not take place for three [monks], and there a motion is established.

Or, by the other: where two bhikkhus reside, or even just one, there, if he has been appointed by himself, the other bhikkhu should say, “I [am appointed]. “In the same way” means exactly as stated regarding the Uposatha hall.
By the phrase “or having announced,” he rejects the failure to announce. “Bhikkhus, the exhortation must not be left unannounced.”

"Whoever does not report it incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Because of this statement, it is not permissible to receive the exhortation (*ovāda*) and then fail to report it at the Uposatha hall.
"Purified state" means being pure regarding any offense. "Report it" means make it known. Here, there might be [the following] inquiry:
"In this phrase, 'I shall recite the Pāṭimokkha,' what could that inquiry be? He said: "The Saṅgha..."
"One should perform the Uposatha," and so forth. "The preceding connects with the subsequent" means that the later statement proceeds in connection with the earlier statement.
"By way of concord" means by way of the harmony of body and mind. "Of the group" refers to the remaining bhikkhus in a quorum of four, excluding the reciter.
"It has been recited for the Saṅgha" means it has been recited by the Saṅgha. And here, this [word] is used in the sense of the agent.
The word "sāmī" is a term denoting ownership. "Therein" refers to the recitation of the Pātimokkha. "Characteristic" means intrinsic nature.
Regarding the phrase "elders, novices, and those of middle standing": herein, those with ten years or more than ten years of seniority are elders;
those with less than five years are novices; and those with five years or more than five years are of middle standing. "Making it one's bone" means [making oneself] firm by means of that Pātimokkha.
"Making it a matter of concern" means making that *pātimokkha* one's own concern, thinking, "This is my *pātimokkha*.
"Attending to it" means fixing it in the mind. "By way of the ear-door" means by way of the impulsion-consciousness (*javana-viññāṇa*) belonging to the ear-door.
"Applying our whole mind" means we advert to it and discern it with the entire mind, not allowing the mind to go even slightly outward.

The meaning is: "We shall attend to it" means we shall advert to it; the meaning is, "we shall direct our attention to it. Furthermore, this attention here does not have the characteristic of directing the mind toward an object;
rather, it has the characteristic of placing the mind in a state preceded by the attention that directs the process through the cognitive sequence (vīthi) and the impulsion (javana).
Thus he said, "Having become one-pointed in mind, we shall place [the mind] in the mind. "It does not coincide" means it does not come together.

To the question, "Why does it not come together? he says, "For one who is united," and so forth. Furthermore, to the question, "And what more? he says, "And the reciter of the Pātimokkha," and so forth.
"Included in the Saṅgha" means included within or belonging to the Saṅgha.
The connection [of the text] is: "Now, in order to show that. "Venerable sirs" is an address using a term of endearment to those assembled.
“Without shame” (*alajjitā*) means by way of shamelessness, that is, by way of the state of being shameless; for this is the nominative case in the sense of the instrumental.

The same principle applies to the terms “ignorance” (*aññāṇatā*) and so forth. “Overcome by remorse” (*kukkuccappakatatā*) means by way of being overwhelmed by remorse. “Forgetfulness of mindfulness” (*satisammosa*) means due to the absence of mindfulness.
“Transgression” (*vītikkama*) refers to the transgression of the training rules (*sikkhāpada*).
“Intentionally” (*sañcicca*) means having intended; the meaning is that one sends forth a mind of transgression while knowing full well the state of being unallowable (*akappiya*).

“He conceals” (*parigūhati*) means he hides it, does not confess it, and does not emerge from it. He shows that one who conceals out of shame is not shameless, whereas one who conceals out of disrespect, thinking “what is the use of this?”, is indeed shameless. And he goes upon a wrong course (*agatigamana*).
He goes on wrong courses, such as the various forms of partiality (chandāgati) and so forth, in matters concerning articles of property and the like.
An "unconscientious person" (alajjipuggala) is one who is devoid of internal moral shame (lajjā).

And here, by the word "intentionally" (sañcicca), it refers to one who incurs an offense through sheer disrespect, or who conceals an offense already incurred, or who engages in wrong courses regarding articles of property and the like.
This shows that one who goes [on such a journey] is shameless, whereas the other is not.
"Dull" means dull in wisdom; this is a designation for one who lacks wisdom. "Deluded" means utterly bewildered. "Fails" means he does not succeed or accomplish.
"Remorse" refers to doubt regarding the Vinaya. "If something allowable should need to be done," [means] having asked a master of the Vinaya.

Having examined the basis [of the rule], and having examined the summary outline (mātikā), the word-by-word commentary (padabhājana), the intermediate offenses, and the non-offenses, one should do what is required when it is said:
"It is allowable, friend; do not be doubtful in this matter.

Regarding the terms "sleeping together," "being separated from one's robe," and so forth: here, "sleeping together" means [staying] for more than two or three nights with one who is not fully ordained.
The offense of sleeping together; "separation" refers to separation for one night or for three nights.

By the word "etcetera," it includes offenses such as exceeding seven days and so forth. "Of the seven classes of offenses" means of the seven classes of offenses known as *pārājika*, *saṅghādisesa*, *thullaccaya*, *pācittiya*, *pāṭidesanīya*, *dukkaṭa*, and *dubbhāsita*.
"Either confess or reveal": this means either to confess or to reveal it in the midst of the Saṅgha, in the midst of a group, or before a single individual.
And here, what is called "confession of a *pārājika* offense" is the relinquishing of the status of a monk.
However, because it is a specific kind of confession, "revelation" (*vuṭṭhāna*) should be understood as "confession. "Or reveal" means or announce it.
"Thus not having committed [an offense]" means not having committed it by any one of the six modes [of concealment].
"Or having emerged" means having emerged by means of probation (*parivāsa*) and so forth. "Or having announced" means having made it known.
And when announcing, he may say: "I announce one offense in your presence," or "I declare it," or "I report it," or "Know that I have fallen into one offense."
If one says, “I confess one grave offense,” or follows a similar pattern, it is considered confessed in every respect.
However, if while confessing a grave offense one says, “I confess a light offense,” or follows a similar pattern, the offense remains unconfessed.
Whether one reports the matter (*vatthu*), reports the offense (*āpatti*), or reports both, it is likewise [unconfessed] in all three ways.

"It has been announced" (ārocitāva hoti). In the phrase "in the case of a non-existent offense" (asantiyā āpattiyā), the locative case is used to indicate a characteristic by means of its state (bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇe).

Regarding the expression "even by silence" (tuṇhībhāvenāpi hi): here, the meaning of the particle *api* should be understood as "not only when it is said, 'Yes, we are pure,' but also even by silence."

In order to demonstrate that matter by way of the differing opinions of the teachers (ācariya) regarding the investigation of what is called "announced up to the third time" and how it becomes "announced up to the third time," it was said: "Regarding the phrase 'it has been announced up to the third time,' here... and so forth.
Therein, the connection is with the words "that which has been announced three times. [The phrase continues: "by way of the distinction in meaning and phrasing (atthabyañjana-bhedato)."

The meaning is "it is known" (*ariyati*), which is the *abhidheyya* (the denotable object). That by which the meaning is manifested (*byañjīyati*) is the *byañjana* (the expression), namely the syllable (*akkhara*).
Both the meaning and the expression are "meaning-and-expression" (*atthabyañjanāni*). Their differentiation is the "differentiation of meaning and expression" (*atthabyañjanabheda*);
thus, the meaning is "due to the dissimilarity between the meaning and the expression."
Now, in order to clarify that very point, he said: "For what is called 'proclamation'... and so forth. The particle *hi* is a nipāta used in the sense of a reason (*kāraṇatthe*).
Its connection, however, should be understood with the word "unbroken" (*abhinnaṃ*). "By that" means by way of being broken.
"Of this" refers to the triad of statements beginning with "for whom it may be. And this must necessarily be accepted in this way; otherwise, there would be an over-extension (*atippasaṅgo*).
In order to show that it "might be," he said, "If, moreover," and so forth. "This" refers to the triad of statements beginning with "for whom it might be.
Others maintain that the word *anusāvitaṃ* does not indicate a past sense, but rather a future sense;
for they argue that even a suffix prescribed for another time is appropriate when connected to the root meaning in a different time. Therefore, he said: "Others [say] ‘anusāvitaṃ’..."
“...of the word,” and so forth. “At the end of the subsequent recitation” means at the conclusion of the recitation of the *pārājika* rules.
“Because of the absence of future meaning and reason” means because of the non-existence of both a future purpose and a causal basis.

Now, in order to clarify that very point, he said, “For this,” and so forth. How is this to be understood? He said, “If it were for her,” and so forth. “This” refers to the future time. “It will have been announced.”
"Should speak" means that the Buddha would say, "It shall have been announced," making it a future time without a subsequent application [of another suffix]. This is the underlying intention here:
