if the suffix *ta* were connected to the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), then such a connection to the root-meaning would constitute a relationship of qualifier and qualified (*visesanavisesyabhāva*).
And that [relationship] arises when there is a state of identical meaning with the subsequent application, not when there is none.
“He laughs” would refer to a non-application [of the rule], yet it is not so stated. Therefore, it does not indicate the future;
rather, it indicates only the past time. Because of the word “while being recited,” which is a term for the present tense—since “while being recited” denotes the present time—if this is so, one asks:
what is the meaning of “it has been recited up to the third time”? To this he says: “up to the third time,” etc. What is characterized by that?
Thinking that this might be a mere statement of definition, he said, "By that," and so forth. "By that" means by the reason of being a mere statement of definition.
"This very" refers to the Pātimokkha. "But this" refers to the threefold proclamation beginning with, "In this matter, I ask the Venerable Ones.
"Is not seen" means it is not obtained. "And this very meaning" refers to this very meaning stated by us. For if...

The intention [of the author] is this: the triad of statements beginning with “for whom there may be an offense,” which occurs up to the third proclamation, is what should be stated in the Uposatha Khandhaka, and not the passage beginning with “it has been proclaimed even once.

One might ask: “Is this analysis not found in the Aṭṭhakathās? Then from where was it obtained? To this he says: “This is here,” and so forth. [It is for those] who have gained proficiency in the points of the Vinaya...

The lineage (*paveṇi*) is the succession of teachers (*ācariyaparamparā*) that makes known various matters to the teachers; what is brought down or transmitted by that is "brought down through the succession of teachers" (*ācariyaparamparābhata*).
[One might ask: "Should there not be an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for a deliberate lie? Then how is it that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)? To this he said:

"And yet, that is not by way of the characteristic of a deliberate lie," and so forth. Regarding the question "What occurs in the case of a deliberate lie?", [he refers to] this which is called "a deliberate lie":
When it is asked, "What does he become regarding the offense? the meaning is: what kind of offense does he incur? "He incurs a *dukkaṭa*" means he incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense.

"An offense originating from non-action through the door of speech" means that for this monk, who sat in silence after giving an illegal admission (*adhammikā paṭiññā*), there is no such thing as an offense at the door of the mind. However, because [the matter] must be disclosed...
It was not a boatman; therefore, it should be understood that this offense arises from non-action through the door of speech.

Now, in order to establish the very meaning just stated by means of the Canon (Pāḷi), he says, "And this has also been said," and so forth. The meaning is: "And this has also been said" in the *Sedamocanagāthā* of the Parivāra by the Elder Upāli.
"Not conversing with any person" means not addressing anyone with speech.
"Nor should one utter a word to others" means that, thinking "these people will hear it," one should not even emit a sound with reference to other individuals.
"One would incur a verbal offense" means one would incur an offense arising from speech. "This question was considered by those who are skilled."
Here, it is stated with a change of gender as "this question" (*pañhāmesa*); the meaning is that this question has been considered by the wise.
This question was spoken with reference specifically to this false speech (*musāvāda*).
It is called such because, by way of being an obstacle to various attainments, it comes (*eti*) and enters into the midst (*antare*) of the continuum of beings (*sattasantāna*).

An obstacle (*antarāya*) is an evil consequence pertaining to the present life and so forth. It is called "obstructive" (*antarāyika*) because it is connected to that obstacle in the sense of transcending [the path], or because it deserves the fruit of an obstacle, or because its nature is to create an obstacle. Therefore he said:
"By being a basis for remorse," and so forth. In that context, "by being a basis for remorse": remorse (*vippaṭisāra*) is a mental state of regret characterized by subsequent repentance.

The meaning is "by way of being its cause. What is meant is: by way of being the condition for remorse (*vippaṭisāra*), which is the opposite of non-remorse (*appaṭisāra*) that serves as the requisite condition for the first jhāna and so forth.
Regarding "the arising of joy (*pāmojja*) and the rest": *pāmojja* is a very mild form of rapture (*pīti*); those things of which it is the first are "joy and the rest" (*pāmojjādayo*).
Their arising—that is, their acquisition—is "the arising of joy and the rest" (*pāmojjādisambhavo*); that [is what is referred to]. By the word "and the rest" (*ādi*),...
This is the inclusion of zest, tranquility, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "of the first jhāna and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) here includes:
"an obstacle to the attainment of the second jhāna, an obstacle to the attainment of the third jhāna, an obstacle to the attainment of the fourth jhāna;
[an obstacle] to the jhānas, to the liberations, to the concentrations, and to the attainments."
The inclusion of the second jhāna and so forth—spoken of as "an obstacle to the attainment of renunciations, of deliverances, of seclusions, and of wholesome states"—is to be understood here.
Regarding the phrase "Therefore" (*tasmā*), because the relationship between the words *yaṃ* and *taṃ* is invariably connected, the sense of "since" (*yasmā*) is already present;
thus he says, "Therefore means since," and so on. "By one who knows" (*jānantena*) means by one who is cognizant.
By this, he shows that the deliberate lie is intentional (*sacittaka*). "One who looks for purification" means one who has a desire for purification (*visuddhāpekkha*);

thus, it is by such a person "desiring purification. And that purification here refers to emergence (*vuṭṭhāna*) and so forth; therefore, he says, "by one who desires to emerge and desires to be purified. This means:
by one who desires to emerge from a *saṅghādisesa* offense leading to emergence, and by one who desires to be purified from one leading to confession (*desanā*).

The meaning is as follows: "In the midst of the Saṅgha, or in the midst of a group, or to a single individual" means that it should be announced either in the midst of the Saṅgha by way of reporting to the Saṅgha at the Uposatha hall;
or in the midst of a group by way of reporting to those seated together right there;
or to a single individual by way of reporting to the person immediately next to one. "Having emerged from here" means having emerged from this Uposatha hall.

In this case, however, only one who belongs to the same class (sabhāga) should be mentioned. For if one who is not of the same class (visabhāga) were mentioned, there would be quarrels, disputes, schisms in the Saṅgha, and so forth.

Therefore, the Andhaka Aṭṭhakathā states that, instead of mentioning such a person, the Uposatha should be performed after making the formal resolve: "Having emerged from this [transgression], I shall make amends."
"In the sense of the instrumental" means in the sense of the third case ending (*tatiyāvibhatti*). This is a nominative form used for the agent with reference to the word *phāsu*.
"Nominative form" means the first case ending (*paṭhamāvacana*). "It is comfortable for the attainment of the first jhāna, etc. means that it is comfortable for the purpose of attaining those states;
for that bhikkhu, there is comfort and ease because restraint is a cause for non-remorse. Hence he said: "rooted in non-remorse," and so forth.

Non-remorse (*avippaṭisāra*) is the absence of mental regret regarding what has been done or not done in terms of evil or merit. Those things for which this is the root or cause are "rooted in non-remorse" (*avippaṭisāramūlaka*). Being rooted in non-remorse is precisely what is meant by "rooted in non-remorse"; [the phrase] "of those rooted in non-remorse" refers to these.
"The pleasant way of practice succeeds" means that the pleasant way of practice is accomplished; it is through ease that the first jhāna and the others are attained.
The intended meaning is that there is attainment. And in this regard, there is the following:
“The motion for the formal act in the introduction, the inquiry regarding the preliminary duties, the recitation and hearing of the introduction, and the procedure for the announcement of purity.”
"And there is an offense in not reporting it; this should be known as the pentad for the sake of alms-food.
Thus ends the *Līnatthappakāsanī*, the commentary on the *Vinayatthamañjūsā*, which is the commentary on the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Pātimokkha*.
The commentary on the Introduction (Nidānavaṇṇanā) is finished.

Now, in order to explain the meaning of the exposition of the offenses entailing expulsion (pārājika-uddesa) which was spoken immediately after the exposition of the Introduction, [the text] begins with the words "Now" (idāni), and so forth. This constitutes the section on the offenses entailing expulsion (Pārājikakaṇḍa).

“Commenced. “Immediately after the introduction” (*nidānānantaraṃ*) is a neuter locative compound; it means having made the introduction immediate. “Therein” (*tattha*) refers to the section on the defeats (*pārājika-kaṇḍa*).
“In the Pātimokkha” (*pātimokkhe*) refers to the Bhikkhu-pātimokkha. “Four” (*cattāro*) is a numerical delimitation, intended to exclude any lesser or greater number.
“Defeats” (*pārājikā*) is the specific name for that class of offenses. “Offenses” (*āpattiyo*) is the general name common to all.
“Uddeso” means that which is pointed out (uddisīyati). This is an explanation where the abstract state (bhāva) is emphasized; therefore, he said, “the state of being something to be pointed out.
Regarding the phrase “but whoever” (*yo pana*): here, *pana* is merely a particle, while *yo* is the substantive word, and it refers to a person without specific restriction.

He illuminates [this]. Therefore, in order to show its meaning, he said, "Whoever. However, since anyone who is called "somebody" must necessarily be known by way of one or another aspect—such as gender, class, name, clan, virtue, dwelling, range, or age—he said, "By means of short, long, etc.," in order to make that known in such a way.
By the word "etc.," the inclusion of new construction work and so forth is intended. [The phrase] "by way of the distinction of gender, etc."...

That by which something is characterized or indicated is a *liṅga* (mark); those things of which this is the first are "the marks and so forth" (*liṅgādayo*). Their differentiation is "the differentiation of marks and so forth" (*liṅgādibhedo*), and [it is] by that differentiation of marks and so forth.
Here, however, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), things such as "conjoined" (*yutto*) and the like are included. This is what is meant:
regardless of its gender—whether it be such or such—whether it be long or short, black or white, soft-skinned or emaciated.
Or whether he be stout; let him be engaged by way of his duties—whether occupied with new construction, occupied with recitation, or occupied with the responsibility of residence;
let him be of whatever birth—whether a khattiya, a brahmin, a vessa, or a sudda;
let him be of whatever name—whether named thus or named so, such as Buddharakkhita.
Or whether he is Dhammarakkhita or Saṅgharakkhita; by way of clan, let him be of whatever clan, such as Kaccāyana, Vāsiṭṭha, or Kosika;
by way of virtue, let him be of whatever virtue, such as one whose virtue consists in new construction, one whose virtue consists in recitation, or one whose virtue consists in the duty of residence;
and even regarding monasteries, let him be a dweller of whatever monastery, such as this or that monastery.
Whether he is one who dwells in building-work, or one who dwells in study, or one who dwells in the responsibility of residence;
whether his range of activity is such as it may be, or that which conforms to the tradition, or the range of building-work, or the range of study, or the range of residence;
and whether his age is whatever it may be—whether elder, junior, or middle-aged—all such a person is referred to by the word "who" in this context.

Now, in order to comment upon the word "bhikkhus," he says "ordination by 'Come, bhikkhu,'" and so forth. Therein, "ordination by 'Come, bhikkhu'" (ehibhikkhūpasampadā) is the state of being a bhikkhu through the mere utterance of the Blessed One's words, "Come, bhikkhu.

"Ordination by going for refuge" (saraṇagamanūpasampadā) is the ordination obtained through the threefold repetition of the formula for going for refuge, beginning with "I go to the Buddha for refuge," spoken three times.
Regarding the formal acceptance of instruction and ordination:

"Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: 'A keen sense of shame and dread of wrongdoing shall be established in me toward elders, juniors, and those of middle standing. Thus, Kassapa, should you train yourself. Therefore, Kassapa..."

"You should train yourself thus: 'Whatever teaching I hear that is connected with the wholesome, I will listen to it all, having made it my purpose, having applied my mind to it, having focused my whole heart, and with attentive ears.
In this way, Kassapa, you should train yourself. Therefore, Kassapa, you should train yourself thus: 'Accompanied by joy...'"
"And may mindfulness directed to the body not abandon me"—in this way, Kassapa, you should train yourself.
By this acceptance of instruction, the Elder Mahākassapa’s admission to the higher ordination (*upasampadā*) was authorized.
The admission to the higher ordination by way of answering questions refers to the authorization of Sopāka’s higher ordination. It is said that the Blessed One was at the Pubbārāma monastery...
As the novice Sopāka was walking back and forth, the Blessed One asked him ten questions concerning the ten foulness-meditations:
"Sopāka, is the perception of a bloated corpse and the perception of form these things different in meaning and different in phrasing, or are they one in meaning and only the phrasing is different?
He answered them. The Blessed One, having expressed his approval, said: "How many years of seniority do you have, Sopāka?"

He asked: "I am seven years old, Blessed One. "Sopāka, you have answered the questions in accordance with my omniscient knowledge," he said, and being pleased in heart, he granted him full ordination; this is ordination by answering questions.
Ordination by accepting the eight weighty rules (*aṭṭhagarudhamma*) refers to the ordination permitted through Mahāpajāpatī’s acceptance of the eight weighty rules.
Ordination by messenger (*dūtenūpasampadā*) refers to the ordination permitted for the courtesan Aḍḍhakāsī.

Ordination by eight proclamations (*aṭṭhavācikūpasampadā*) refers to ordination by means of these two formal acts (*kamma*): from the community of bhikkhunīs by a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*), and from the community of bhikkhus by a motion followed by three proclamations.

Ordination by a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakammūpasampadā*) refers to the ordination of bhikkhus at present. "By a motion followed by three proclamations" means...
By three proclamations (*anussāvana*) and one motion (*ñatti*); thus it is "by a motion as the fourth" (*ñatticatutthena*).

Although the motion is indeed spoken first, because there is no difference in meaning or phrasing among the three proclamations, the motion—which differs in meaning and phrasing from them—is considered their "fourth," and is therefore called "the motion as the fourth. "Irreversible" (*akuppena*) means the state of being unshakable.
And by one who has approached [the state of] being beyond reproach. "Worthy of the occasion" (*ṭhānāraha*) means worthy of the cause, worthy of the Teacher’s dispensation.
"Ordained" (*upasampanna*) means having attained a higher status; the meaning is "one who has reached it.
For the state of a bhikkhu is indeed a higher status, and because he has attained that through the aforementioned procedure, he is called "ordained. But why is this so?
Is it meant that only one ordained by this [method] is included here, and not by others? It is said: the *ehibhikkhu* (come, monk) ordination is for those in their final existence;
the ordination by going for refuge is for those who are pure; the ordination by the acceptance of instruction and the answering of questions is for Mahākassapa and Sopāka;
and they are incapable of committing a *pārājika* or other world-transgressing offenses. This also applies to the acceptance of the eight *garudhammas* and so forth.

[Full admission] was permitted for bhikkhunīs alone. This bhikkhu, therefore, is understood here as one who has received full admission through the formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*), and not by other means.

However, regarding the training rules concerning transgressions of the formal injunctions (*paṇṇattivajja*), others such as those admitted by the "Come, bhikkhu" (*ehibhikkhu*) formula are also included. For he will say: "But regarding the training rules concerning transgressions of the formal injunctions..."

“Others also come under inclusion. Now, in order to explain in detail the meaning stated in brief as “one who is ordained by means of one who is unshakable and worthy of the position,” he said, beginning with “But for him...”.

Therein, “among those five” refers to those five [factors]. It is called a *vatthu* (basis) because one dwells (*vasati*) therein; it is the support, the foundation. Therefore he said, “one seeking ordination...”
"A person. One who has fewer than twenty years, not having completed twenty years, is "under twenty" (*ūnavīsativassa*).

Whatever needs to be said regarding this, we shall explain it later in the section on the training rule concerning those under twenty (*ūnavīsati-sikkhāpada*) within the Chapter on Living Beings (*sappāṇaka-vagga*).

"Among them" refers to the eleven types of persons incapable [of full ordination], beginning with the *paṇḍaka*. Here, the *paṇḍaka* is of five kinds: the *āsitta-paṇḍaka*, the *usūya-paṇḍaka*, the *opakkamika-paṇḍaka*,...

There are the neuter (*napuṃsaka-*) eunuch and the periodic (*pakkha-*) eunuch. Among them, admission into the order is not forbidden for the drenched (*āsitta-*) eunuch and the envious (*ussūya-*) eunuch, but it is forbidden for the other three.
Even among those, for the periodic eunuch, admission into the order is forbidden during the very period in which he is a eunuch.
And here, these three are [excluded] because they are incapable of receiving the going-forth and full ordination.

These are non-grounds. Therefore he said, "and the *āsittapaṇḍaka*," and so forth. Therein, one for whom the feverish distress (*pariḷāha*) is pacified by taking another’s sexual organ into his mouth and being drenched with impurity is an *āsittapaṇḍaka*.
One for whom the feverish distress is pacified when envy arises upon seeing another’s transgression is an *usūyapaṇḍaka*. One for whom [it is pacified] by means of an effort...
The seeds have been removed; this is the *opakkamika-paṇḍaka*. However, he who is born as one lacking [sex organs] even at the moment of rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) is the *napuṃsaka-paṇḍaka*.

Furthermore, some become a *paṇḍaka* during the dark fortnight through the power of unwholesome karmic fruition, while his feverish distress subsides during the bright fortnight; this should be understood as the *pakkha-paṇḍaka*.
"One who dwells together through theft" (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*) means one whose dwelling is by way of theft. And here, it is not intended merely as one who steals the dwelling itself;
rather, it refers to one who steals either the outward sign (*liṅga*), both of those, or [the status]. Thus he said: "But the 'one who dwells together through theft' is of three kinds," and so forth.
"He does not count his years as a monk" means that, having spoken falsely, saying "I am ten years [ordained] or twenty years [ordained]," he [does not count] his years as a monk.
"He does not count [seniority]. He does not consent to the salutation of monks or novices according to seniority;
having himself committed a falsehood, he does not accept salutation according to seniority as if it were in accordance with the rains-residence (vassa) he has displayed.
"He does not block [another] from a seat" means he does not block them from a seat by saying, "Move aside, this one belongs to me. "He does not appear at the Uposatha and other ceremonies" means...

He does not appear at the observance day (uposatha), the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā), and so forth. By the word "only" in the phrase "of the mere outward sign alone," he excludes formal association (saṃvāsa).
"Common" means being the same. "Of an association corresponding to the outward sign" means of an association as a novice (sāmaṇera) that corresponds to the outward sign of a novice.
However, if, having cast aside the yellow robe, he is naked or clothed in white garments, and [engages] in sexual intercourse and so forth—
Having become one who is no longer a *śramaṇa*, he wears the saffron robes; he is a mere wearer of the outward mark.

If, desiring the state of a householder, he makes the saffron robe into a loincloth or wears it in some other manner as a householder’s garment for the purpose of testing, thinking, "Does this householder's mark look good on me, or does it not?", then he still maintains [the offense] for that long; but having accepted it, thinking, "It looks good," [he falls].
If he consents to the sexual organ again, he becomes one who acts for the sake of the sexual organ.

The same principle applies to putting on white garments for the purpose of testing or receiving [sexual pleasure]. Even if he tests or receives [pleasure] after putting on white garments over his already donned saffron robes, he is still protected.
This same principle applies even to one who has committed the ultimate offense; that is, it applies in the case of a monk who has fallen into a *pārājika* offense.

The meaning is as follows: Suppose some bhikkhu, while still intent upon the saffron robe, puts on a white garment, engages in sexual intercourse, and then puts on the saffron robes again and undertakes all the formal procedures, such as the counting of the rains-retreat;
because he has not relinquished the outward sign (liṅga) granted by the bhikkhus, he is not one who has abandoned the sign, and thus his communal residence remains in accordance with that sign.
"Because he has been overcome, he is not one who has abandoned co-residence. "Another country" means a foreign land.
This is stated to show a place where it would be possible to deceive [the authorities]. However, whoever acts in this way even within his own country is likewise one who has abandoned co-residence.
By the phrase "merely by the act of co-residence," he rejects the [specific] gender. If someone who has gone forth at an old age counts his years as a monk in large baskets and so forth...
One who accepts almsfood being given [by falsely claiming seniority] is also a dweller in communion through theft.
However, one who is still a novice (sāmaṇera) and accepts [alms] by counting false years according to the sequence of novices does not become a dweller in communion through theft.
But a monk who accepts [alms] by counting false years according to the sequence of monks must be dealt with according to the value of the stolen goods.
"Is it not the case that 'communion' (saṃvāsa) means performing the same formal acts, reciting the same scriptures, and training under the same rules? To this he replied:

"It is the counting of a bhikkhu’s years of seniority, and so forth. By this, he shows that what is intended here by "communion" is not only the distinction of ritual acts such as those mentioned, but rather something else, namely the counting of a bhikkhu’s years of seniority and the like.
"In this matter" refers to the section concerning those who live in communion through theft. *Sikkhaṃ*...
"Having renounced" means having abandoned the training. This is what is meant:

if any bhikkhu, having renounced the training and not discarded his [monastic] marks, whether or not he has committed an act of immorality, thinks "no one knows me" and again adopts the entire procedure previously described—such as the counting of the rains-residence and so forth—he is a thief-living-in-the-community (theyyasaṃvāsaka).
But if a king is angry with someone, that person, thinking, "In this way my safety will be secured," takes up the religious marks himself and flees.
Seeing him, they report it to the king. The king, thinking, "If he has gone forth, nothing can be done to him," subdues his anger toward him.
Thinking, "The danger from the king has subsided for me," he [returns] to the midst of the Saṅgha.

Having returned after wearing lay clothing for some years, he should be granted the going-forth. Furthermore, if one who has developed a sense of spiritual urgency—thinking, "I have obtained this life by depending on the Dispensation;

come now, let me go forth"—comes with that very same attire and does not consent to the duties of a guest, he should, whether questioned or unasked by the monks, reveal his true identity as it actually is.
If he requests the going-forth (*pabbajjā*), he should be ordained after removing his [lay] marks.

However, if he consents to the duties, points out a dwelling for those who have gone forth, and adopts everything previously mentioned—such as the calculation of the rains-retreat (*vassa*) and so forth—he should not be ordained.

In this case, however, there may be someone who, being unable to survive during a famine, takes up the marks himself and partakes of the alms-food intended for all religious sects (*sabba-pāsaṇḍiya-bhattāni*).
While eating, once the famine had passed, he returned without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha and instead assumed the appearance of a householder;
all of this is exactly as before.
Another person desired to cross a great wilderness, and a caravan leader was traveling while taking along renunciants.
Thus, thinking, "The caravan leader will take me and go," she herself took up the religious garb and,
having crossed the wilderness together with the caravan leader and reached a place of safety, she returned without re-entering the midst of the Saṅgha,
having instead taken up the garb of a householder; all of this was exactly as before.
Another, when the danger of illness arose and being unable to survive, took the robes himself and ate the food provided for all ascetics;
then, when the danger of illness had subsided, he returned without having re-entered the midst of the Saṅgha and assumed the layman’s dress—
all of which is exactly the same as the previous case.
Another person has an enemy who is angry with him and wanders about seeking to kill him.
Thinking, "In this way I shall be safe," he himself takes up the religious marks and flees.

The enemy, searching for him and hearing that he has fled after going forth, thinks, "If he has gone forth, it will not be possible to do anything to him," and thus he subdues his anger toward him. He...
“‘The fear of my enemies has been stilled’—having said this, he returned without having entered the midst of the Saṅgha and took up the marks of a householder;
all of this is exactly as before.
Another, having gone to his kinsmen’s home, renounced the training and became a householder, thinking: ‘These robes will be ruined here.’”
"If I go to the monastery taking these [valuables], they will seize me on the way, thinking, 'He is a thief.
What if I were to go after making them into articles for the body? Having thus dressed and put on the robes for the purpose of carrying the robes, he goes to the monastery.
Seeing him coming from afar, the novices and the young monks go out to meet him.
They point out the duties to him. He does not consent, but reveals his true state as it is.
If the monks, thinking, "We will not let him go now," desire to ordain him by force, they must remove his saffron robes and he must be ordained again.
But if, thinking, "These [monks] do not know my state of having returned to the lower life," he acknowledges that very status of being a monk—
If one undergoes the entire procedure previously described, such as the calculation of the rains-retreat and so forth, this person is not to be ordained. Therefore he said:
"Or due to fear of kings, famine, wilderness, disease, or enemies," and so on.

Here, the word *bhaya* (fear) should be construed with each term individually, as in "fear of kings," "fear of famine," and so forth. "He takes the mark" means he assumes the disguise. "Here" means in this [text].

In the Dispensation, he does not consent to living together. As long as he is one of pure mind—meaning that because there is an absence of the desire to deceive the monks, even though he has a deceptive thought such as "Let householders know me as a 'monk'"—as long as he does not consent to living together, there is no fault due to the absence of the desire to deceive the monks;
thus, he is a *theyyasaṃvāsaka* (one who lives in communion by theft).
The meaning is that it is not called by name.
One who has gone over to the sectarians is a *titthiyapakkantaka*. And he does not become a *titthiyapakkantaka* merely by having entered among them;
rather, it is by adopting their tenets (*laddhi*). Therefore, he said, "But whoever," and so forth. "One who is fully ordained" (*upasampanna*).
By this, it is shown that one who has not been fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) is not one who has gone over to another sect (*titthiyapakkantaka*).
For this is stated in the *Kurundi-aṭṭhakathā*: "And this so-called 'one who has gone over to another sect' is spoken of in reference to a fully ordained monk;

therefore, even if a novice (*sāmaṇera*) goes to the sphere of another sect while still wearing his own [monastic] robes, he may again receive the going-forth and full ordination. Regarding the phrase "grass-cloth, etc.," here the word "etc. (*ādi*)— [...]*

This refers to the taking up of wooden planks, fragments, matted hair, and so forth. Even if one considers this renunciation to be "the best" and thus adopts its excellence, one is not released from the offense;
one remains precisely a "one who has gone over to a sect of outsiders. "Vows" (vatāni) refers to practices such as the exertion of squatting on the heels (ukkuṭikappadhāna) and so on.
However, if it is for the purpose of investigation, thinking, "Does my renunciation of a sect of outsiders look good, or does it not look good? [there is no offense].
He puts on garments of kusa grass and so forth, or binds his hair in matted locks, or takes up the khārikāja staff;
as long as he does not accept that doctrine, he remains protected [as a monk]. But at the very moment he accepts it, he becomes one who has gone over to the faction of the heretics.

However, one whose robes have been stolen, while putting on garments of kusa grass and so forth, or while assuming the marks of a heretic out of fear of kings and the like, is not [a heretic] due to the absence of that doctrine.
He is not one who has gone over to the faction of the non-Buddhist sects (titthiya).
"The rest of all" refers to those such as nāgas, supaṇṇas, yakkhas, gandhabbas, and so forth. Whatever needs to be said regarding this has already been stated below.
He says "of human birth" because the kamma is more serious when there is the violation of one of the same species, and not so when it is of a different species.

The designation "mother" and "father" is based on the relationship of children; furthermore, the conventional usage of the term "son" is seen in the world even by way of those given away, adopted, or born of other wives.
However, because that [usage] is merely figurative, the word "janettī" (the progenitress) is used to show that the meaning is established in its primary sense.

"Janettī" means "she who gives birth," which is to say, "mother. Just as for one remaining in a human existence, there occurs the attainment of a state of sharpness, clarity, and courage regarding wholesome qualities...

Just as it was for those three Bodhisattvas in the accomplishment of their seats of enlightenment, so too, while remaining in a human existence, one may attain a state of sharpness, clarity, and courage regarding unwholesome states;
thus he said, "by one who has become a human being. "Intentionally" means having willed with a murderous intention accompanied by the perception that "this is a living being.
"This one is called a matricide" refers to one who, through an act of immediate retribution (*ānantariya*), [is so designated].

One is called a "matricide" by virtue of the act of killing one's mother. However, for one who kills a female human being who is not his biological mother—whether she be a foster mother, a stepmother, a paternal aunt, or even a biological mother—or a non-human female who is his mother, his admission into the order is not prohibited, nor does he incur an immediate offense (*ānantarika*).
[Likewise] for one who, while himself being an animal, [kills] a mother who is a human female...
Even though he was killed, it does not constitute an immediate offense (*ānantariya*). However, because he was an animal, his admission into the Order was prohibited;
nevertheless, his karma was grave, remaining as an immediate offense even though it did not reach the level of an *ānantariya*.
This refers to one who, while being human, intentionally deprived his own biological father—who was also human—of life.
Pointing out by way of analogy that one who commits the patricide of an immediate-offense (*ānantariya*) is called a "patricide," he said:

"The same principle applies even in the case of a patricide. For even if he is the son of a courtesan and does not know, "This is my father," yet he is born from a certain man and that man is killed by him, he is nonetheless reckoned as a "patricide" and incurs the immediate-offense.
The "Tetrad on the Sheep," the "Tetrad on Battle," and the "Tetrad on Thieves" should be explained here.

For even with the intention "I am killing a sheep," one who kills a human being—such as one's mother or father—standing in the place of that sheep, incurs an immediate retribution (*ānantariya*), because by the very intent to kill, the basis for that immediate retribution has been violated. This is so even when there is the intention regarding a sheep.
However, one who kills a sheep with the intention directed toward his mother or father does not incur an ānantariya (immediate) offense, because the objective basis for such an offense is absent.
But one who kills his own mother or father with that same intention directed toward them certainly incurs the offense. This same principle applies to the other two tetrads as well.

For in all cases, the preceding intentional thought is not the decisive factor; rather, it is the murderous intent at the moment of killing and the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) that serves as its object.
The criterion for what constitutes an immediate offense (*ānantariya*) and what does not is as follows:
even a killer of an *arhat* should be understood only in terms of a human *arhat*. Therefore, it is said:
"by whomsoever, even one staying in the garb of a householder," and so forth. However, this refers to an *arhat* of human birth, or any other noble person (*ariyapuggala*) of human birth.
Having killed [an arahant], one does not incur an immediate retribution (ānantarika-kamma), nor is his going forth (pabbajjā) forbidden; however, the kamma is indeed powerful.
Even a beast, having killed a human arahant, does not incur an immediate retribution, yet the kamma is grave—this is the distinction here.
Just as it is with mother and father, so too regarding an arahant, the "fourfold ewe" (eḷakacatukka) and other such cases are to be understood.
"A regular bhikkhunī" refers to a bhikkhunī who is pure in virtue and fully ordained in both Saṅghas.
However, for one who brings about the destruction of virtue through physical contact, neither his going-forth nor his full ordination is barred.
Even one who, by force, makes her put on white garments and defiles her while she is unwilling, is indeed a defiler of a bhikkhunī.
However, one who violates by force a woman who has put on white garments and desires [the act] does not become a "defiler of a bhikkhunī.
Why? Because as soon as she accepts the state of a householder, she ceases to be a bhikkhunī.
But one who later violates a woman who has once fallen from virtue, or who misconducts himself with a sikkhamānā or a sāmaṇerī, is indeed a defiler of a bhikkhunī.
One becomes [a monk], one receives the going-forth (pabbajjā), and one receives full ordination (upasampadā).
"Contrary to the Dhamma" (uddhamma) means that which has emerged from or departed from the Dhamma. The same method applies here for "contrary to the Vinaya" (ubbhinaya).

"Of the four legal procedures" (catunnaṃ kammānaṃ) refers to the four types of legal procedures known as: the motion (apalokana-kamma), the motion followed by one proclamation (ñatti-dutiya-kamma), and the motion followed by three proclamations (ñatti-catuttha-kamma). Of these, one or another...
When one performs separate *saṅghakamma* (formal acts of the Saṅgha) within a single boundary (*ekasīmā*), the Saṅgha is said to be "split. Therefore it is said:
"He splits the Saṅgha by means of one of the four formal acts.
To clarify the meaning of the phrase "with a corrupt mind," the term "with a murderous mind" (*vadhakacitta*) is used. [This refers to] the volition of murder (*vadhakacetanā*).
For a defiled mind is what is meant here by "a malicious mind. "He causes blood to flow" means he causes blood to arise within the body itself;
the intention is that he brings it together. Indeed, because the Tathāgata’s body is indestructible, blood does not flow from a wound inflicted by another's assault;
rather, the blood [is produced] at a single spot within the body itself.
It flows out; when it is agitated by resentment, it becomes accumulated—it is with reference to this that it was said.

However, one who, like Jīvaka for the sake of healing a disease, cuts open [the body] with a knife, removes putrid flesh and blood, and restores it to health, is not a shedder of blood; rather, he generates great merit.
"Both kinds of genitals" means both kinds of genitals arising from the two aforementioned types of kamma: the female sign and the male sign.

By this analysis, it is shown that "one with both genitals" (*ubhatobyañjanako*) is a *bahirattha-samāsa* (compound with an external referent) involving non-co-referential terms (*asamānādhikaraṇa*), and that there is no elision of the case-ending in the first member of the compound. That [person] is of two kinds: one with both genitals who is female, and...
"And the hermaphrodite male. In this context, for the hermaphrodite female, the female characteristic is manifest and the male characteristic is concealed;
for the hermaphrodite male, the male characteristic is manifest and the female characteristic is concealed. When the hermaphrodite female exerts masculinity toward women...

The female characteristic is concealed and the male characteristic is manifest. In the case of a man with both sets of characteristics who assumes a female state, the male characteristic is concealed and the female characteristic is manifest.
A woman with both sets of characteristics conceives a fetus herself and causes another to conceive. A man with both sets of characteristics...
But while one does not take [the robe] oneself, one causes another to take it—this is the distinction between these two.

"Non-appropriations" means non-acceptances and non-statements. "Not announcing that 'this person is so-and-so'" means not announcing the identity of the one for whom the full ordination (*upasampadā*) is being performed; [for example: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: this is Dhammarakkhita..."
When it should have been said, "The one seeking full ordination for the Venerable Buddharakkhita," it was not stated, "This is Dhammarakkhita.
Regarding the failure to name the preceptor when saying, "He seeks full ordination for such-and-such a person," [the formula should be]:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: this Dhammarakkhita seeks full ordination for the Venerable Buddharakkhita."
When it should be said, "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me; this Dhammarakkhita desires full ordination," one fails to say, "of the venerable Buddharakkhita.
This constitutes a complete failure to recite the motion (*ñatti*);

having omitted the motion, one performs the formal act of proclamation (*anussāvana-kamma*) four times by means of the ritual formula (*kammavācā*) alone. "Accomplished" (*sampanna*) means endowed with [the proper procedure].
"Omission" means relinquishing. Even if one has set forth a motion (*ñatti*) but performs the proclamation (*anussāvana*) only once or twice, this too is indeed an omission of the proclamation.
"Mispronunciation" means speaking something other than what should be said regarding a particular syllable.
Therefore, by a monk performing the ritual formula (*kammavācā*), this—
“Lax and emphatic, long and short;
heavy and light, as well as suppressed;
connected and distinct, and liberated.”
"The division of phonetic cognition is tenfold"—this has been stated;
it should be well observed. For herein, "soft" (*sithila*) refers to the first and third letters among the five consonant groups (*vaggas*).
"Hard" (*dhanita*) refers to the second and fourth letters of those same groups. "Long" (*dīgha*) refers to vowels such as *ā* and so forth, which require a long duration to be uttered.
The short [vowels] are to be pronounced with half the duration of what is to be said [for the long ones], beginning with the letter *a*.
"Heavy" (*garuka*) means only the long [vowel], or that which is spoken followed by a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*), such as:

"Of the venerable elder Buddharakkhita, to whom it does not please. "Light" (*lahuka*) means only the short [vowel], or that which is spoken not followed by a consonant cluster, such as: "Of the venerable elder Buddharakkhita, to whom it does not please."
"Having made" (katvā) is so called because it is uttered by restraining the vocal organs, not releasing them, and pronouncing with the mouth unopened, using the nasal resonance (*sānunāsika*).
"Connected" (*sambandha*) is that which is uttered as "tuṇhissā" or "tuṇhassā" by connecting it with a subsequent word.
"Separated" (*vavatthita*) is that which is uttered by not connecting it with a subsequent word, but rather by making a pause.
“Tuṇhī assā” or “tuṇha assā” is what is said. “Vimuttaṃ” is that which is spoken with the vocal organs unrestrained, released, with the mouth open, and without nasalization.
In that regard, where one should say “suṇātu me,” by changing the letter *ta* to the letter *tha*, the expression “suṇāthu me” occurs; this is [an example of] the lax [articulation].
The hardening of a sound (*dhanitakaraṇaṃ*) is, for example, saying “*pattakallaṃ esā ñatti*” when one should say “*pattakallaṃ esā ñatti*,” or saying “*patthakallaṃ esā ñatti*” and so forth.

The softening of a hard sound (*dhanitassa sithilakaraṇaṃ*) is, for example, saying “*bante saṃgo*” when one should say “*bhante, saṅgho*,” by changing the *bha*-sound and *gha*-sound into the *ba*-sound and *ga*-sound.
When one should say “*suṇātu me*” with an open mouth, [saying] “*suṇantu*... [is another example].
When one should say "me" or "this is the motion" (esaṃ ñatti), saying "esaṃ ñatti" with the mouth unopened and producing a nasal sound is called the pronunciation of a *niggahita*.
When one should say "it is appropriate" (*pattakallaṃ*) with the mouth unopened and producing a nasal sound,
saying "pattakallā" with the mouth opened and not producing a nasal sound is [the pronunciation] of the *niggahita*.
This refers to the term *vimutta*. Thus, when a soft consonant (*sithila*) should be used, a hard one (*dhanita*) is used; when a hard one should be used, a soft one is used;

when a release (*vimutta*) should be used, a nasal stop (*niggahita*) is used; and when a nasal stop should be used, a release is used. These four types of syllables corrupt the formal act (*kamma*) within the *kammavācā*.
For one who speaks in this manner is said to be speaking something other than the syllable that ought to be spoken, and thus commits a "mispronunciation" (*durutta*).
Regarding the other six consonants, such as *dīgha* (long), *rassa* (short), and so forth: where there is a long vowel, one must use a long vowel;

where there is a short vowel, one must use a short vowel. Thus, the *kammavācā* should be performed by pronouncing each syllable exactly according to its proper place, without breaking the traditional lineage that has come down in succession.
However, if one does not do this, and instead uses a short vowel when a long one should be used, or a long vowel when a short one...
Or, when it should be said "long," he says "short"; likewise, when it should be said "heavy," he says "light," or when it should be said "light," he says "heavy";

or when it should be said "connected," he says "distinct," or when it should be said "distinct," he says "connected"—even when spoken thus, the *kammavācā* is not invalidated. For these six types of phonetic variation do not invalidate the ritual act.
However, as for what the Suttantika Theras say—that "the letter *da* becomes *ta*, the letter *ta* becomes *da*;
the letter *ca* becomes *ja*, the letter *ja* becomes *ca*; the letter *ya* becomes *ka*, the letter *ka* becomes *ya*;
therefore, when the letters *da* and so forth are to be used, the use of the letters *ta* and so forth is not contradictory"—that [is the case] regarding the formal ritual utterance (*kammavācā*).
It is not permissible to do so. Therefore, the holder of the Vinaya must not change the letter *da* into *ta*, nor [change other letters]...

up to ... nor change the letter *ka* into *ya*. Having purified the etymology according to the Pāḷi, and avoiding the faults mentioned in the tenfold phonetic etymology (*byañjananirutti*), the formal act (*kammavācā*) must be performed.
Otherwise, it is said that one "omits the proclamation. The connection is: "Having set aside the motion (*ñatti*), performing the first proclamation."
"As many bhikkhus as are competent for the formal act" means as many bhikkhus as are fit, suitable, and appropriate for that act of full ordination.
At the very least, these must be five regular bhikkhus standing within a single boundary (*sīmā*) without having left hand's reach of one another.
For without them, that act cannot be performed, nor does their consent need to be brought forth. As for the remainder...

But even if they number as many as a thousand, if they are within the same boundary (*sīmā*), in the same place, and belong to the same community (*samāna-saṃvāsaka*), all of them are indeed entitled to give their consent (*chandārahā*);
whether they come after having given their consent or not, the formal act (*kamma*) is not invalidated. "Objection" (*paṭikkosa*) means a prohibition.
It is called a "ground" (*ṭhāna*) because the fruit stands upon it, due to its being dependent on that; it is thus a cause. But here—

Because it is the cause for performing the formal act of full ordination (*upasampadā-kamma*), the word of the Blessed One—consisting of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*) for full ordination—is so called.
Therefore, he said: "On account of its being worthy of being the cause, and on account of its being worthy of the Teacher’s instruction.

And just as it was instructed by the Blessed One that "this must be done," performing it accordingly is the cause of the formal act of full ordination; thus, it is called "worthy of the occasion" (*ṭhānāraha*).

However, some say that regarding the phrase "in the case of a ground for censure" (*ṭhānārahena*), "the Teacher’s instruction—beginning with ‘Monks, one whose hand has been cut off is not to be ordained’—is the ‘ground’.

Regarding the word "here" (*idha*), it means in this *pārājika* rule. And just as it is here, so too in all training rules concerning worldly offenses (*lokavajja*), this very [definition] should be understood as intended.

Therefore he said, "But in the case of those involving formal rules" (*paṇṇattivajjesu panā*), and so forth. "Others too" (*aññepi*) refers to those ordained by the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhu*) and others.
How is this understood—that even other [offenses] are included among the training rules (sikkhāpada) except for those that are merely conventional (paṇṇatti)?
Because they are included by way of their meaning (attha). For it is stated in general terms: “Two persons are incapable of committing an offense: Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas;
two persons are capable of committing an offense: monks and nuns. Thus, because it is stated generally, [the inclusion of others is established].

Those who have received full ordination by the "Come, monk" formula (*ehibhikkhu-upasampadā*) and others also incur offenses that are formal rules (*paṇṇattivajja*), such as the offense of sharing a sleeping place with one who has not been formally ordained, when done unintentionally, through lack of mindfulness, or without conscious thought;

thus they are effectively included [in the category of those subject to training]. Now, without separately commenting on the word "of monks" (*bhikkhūnam*) because it lacks a specific meaning [here], [the text proceeds to] whatever training...

Because he has entered into the life and discipline of the bhikkhus, he is one who has entered into the training and the communal life of the bhikkhus; showing this, the text says, "one who has entered into the training and the communal life of the bhikkhus," and so forth.
That which is to be trained in is the *sikkhā* (training), namely the virtue of restraint according to the *pātimokkha*.

That in which they live together is the *sājīva* (communal life), which refers to the formal rules (*paṇṇatti*) classified as the *mātikā* and so on. Thus, the *sikkhā* and the *sājīva* together constitute the *sikkhāsājīva*.
"Having entered upon and approached both of those" means having entered upon the training and the mode of livelihood. Therefore he said, "that which belongs to the bhikkhus," and so forth.

And here, because it is associated with the mode of livelihood, by the term "training" (*sikkhā*) only the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*) is intended; thus he said, "designated as higher virtue.
Higher virtue is virtue that is superior or excellent; that which is designated as "higher virtue" is "designated as higher virtue" (*adhisīla-saṅkhātā*).
But what here is virtue (*sīla*), and what is the higher virtue (*adhisīla*)? It is said: first, the virtue of five or ten factors is merely virtue;
it is not the higher virtue. However, the virtue of restraint according to the Pātimokkha is called the "higher virtue.
For that is superior to all mundane virtues, just as the sun is to other lights, or Sineru is to other mountains.
And it is supreme; it occurs only when a Buddha has arisen, not without the arising of a Buddha.
For no other being is able to establish that designation after having extracted it [from the world];
rather, only Buddhas—having completely cut off the stream of misconduct at the doors of body and speech—establish the various restraints of virtue appropriate for each specific transgression.

Furthermore, while virtue associated with the path and its fruits is indeed "higher virtue" (*adhisisa*) even when compared to the virtue of restraint according to the *Pātimokkha*, that is not what is intended here.
For one who has entered into that [higher state] does not engage in sexual intercourse.

"These" refers to the monks who are distinguished by various differences of country, birth, clan, and so forth. "Live together" means together by way of common recitation of the precepts and other such factors.
They proceed together. Therefore he said: "Sharing one livelihood, following a common way of life. "Designated as training rules" means designated as formal designations (*paññatti*).
For that too is called a "training rule" (*sikkhāpada*) because it illuminates the abstentions and so forth. And this has been stated:
"A training rule is the body of names, the body of phrases, the body of terminology, and the body of phonemes therein. "Therein" means among those [rules]. "Fulfilling the training" means...
The meaning is that he fulfills the twofold virtue (sīla) known as "abstention" and "performance," by way of avoiding what should not be done and doing what should be done;

that is to say, he causes within himself a volition associated with abstention through the virtue of abstention, and a volition dissociated from abstention through the virtue of performance. Furthermore, "not transgressing his livelihood" means not violating the training rules (sikkhāpada).
The intention here is that these two alone—restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvaraṇa*) and not transgressing the way of livelihood (*sājīvānatikkamana*)—are what is meant by "attaining" in this context.

Among these, not transgressing the way of livelihood is the condition for the fulfillment of the training (*sikkhā*). For it is through not transgressing that the training is fulfilled up to the level of the Path (*magga*).
Furthermore, in this context, by the phrase "fulfilling the training," [the author] refers to that which consists of the volition of abstinence (*viraticetanā*).
Specifically, the time when the restraint of virtue (*sīlasaṃvara*) actually occurs within the mental continuum is what is grasped [by the term "endowed"];

however, by the phrase "not transgressing," even the time when it does not occur is included. For one who causes the training to proceed within oneself by way of fulfilling it, as well as one who does not cause it to proceed due to sleep and so forth, is said to be "possessed of the training" because of the absence of transgression.

Since the partial disclosure of weakness constitutes a form of renouncing the training, he said "without disclosing weakness" in order to explain the meaning of the phrase "without renouncing the training," referring specifically to that case. To show this, he stated:
"Without renouncing the training, without disclosing weakness," and so forth. In this regard, it might be asked: since...

Is it not the case that not every manifestation of weakness constitutes a renunciation of the training; therefore, having first stated "without manifesting weakness," one should then say "without renouncing the training" in order to define its meaning? That is not so. Why?

Because there is no sequential order of meaning. For since it has been said, "one who has entered upon the training and the mode of livelihood," [it follows that] whichever training one has entered upon—

When it is said, "without having renounced that [training], and without having manifested weakness regarding that livelihood which he has undertaken," the meaning is stated precisely in this sequence and not otherwise. Therefore, this alone was stated first.
Now, in order to make both of these clear, he says "tattha" and so forth. "By the absence of those... refers to their...
By the absence of the mind and so forth. "With a mind desiring to depart" means with a mind wishing to go away. "Suddenly" (*davā*) means impulsively.
For if one who wishes to say something else impulsively says, "I renounce the Buddha," this is called speaking suddenly.
"In error" (*ravā*) means by missing the mark. For if one who wishes to say something else misses the mark and says, "I renounce the Buddha"—

“He speaks”—this is what is meant by “he speaks. If it is asked, “What is the distinction from the previous case? The previous case refers to a wise person speaking something else due to acting impulsively;
this case, however, refers to one who, being dull-witted and deluded, stumbles and speaks something else with the thought, “I will say one thing.

Or, it is when one is unable to speak what ought to be said, either because of a lack of proficiency in the phonetic structure (*akkharasamaya*) or due to an absence of skill in articulation (*karaṇasampatti*).
Some say that one who, having offered an oblation, speaks while making a noise is called a *ravā-bhaṇa*.

One who contemplates what is blameworthy and what is blameless is an *upajjhāya*; [one refers to] that *upajjhāya*. An *ācariya* is one who trains another in conduct by saying, "It should be recited thus," "One should approach thus," and so forth.
One who habitually dwells near or at the end [of the teacher's presence] is an *antevāsī*.
By the elision of a case ending, as in “*vanekaserukā*. One who has the same preceptor is a *samānupajjhāyaka*.
Likewise for a *samānācariyaka*. A *sabrahmacārī* is a bhikkhu;

for he practices this holy life (*brahmacariya*) in common—namely, “the same formal acts, the same recitation, and the same training”—therefore he is called a “fellow practitioner of the holy life” (*sabrahmacārī*). Of those spoken of in this way...

[These are] those spoken of in the *padabhājaniya*. Just as in the world the place where crops grow is called a "field" (*khetta*), so too these bases beginning with the Buddha are called "fields" in the sense of being the places where the renunciation of training grows;
thus he said, "of these twenty-two field-bases. Furthermore, because of their synonyms...
There is the renunciation of training; therefore, it is said, "of synonyms" (*savevacanassa*). A variety of words for a single meaning is *vivacana*;
*vivacana* itself is *vevacana*, which is a synonym or alternative name. Together with these synonyms is *savevacana*; [it refers to] that *savevacana*.
And herein, there are one thousand names found in the *Vaṇṇappakaraṇa*, and one hundred names in the verses of Upāli.
Furthermore, other names obtained according to their qualities should be understood as synonyms for "Buddha.
All names for the Dhamma should be understood as synonyms for "Dhamma. This method applies everywhere.
Among those [names], if one wishes to speak of anything at all while speaking of something else, there is a renunciation of the training; thus, among those twenty-two...

The meaning is this: if one who intends to say any one of the "field-terms" (*khettapada*) utters some other word as a vocal expression, there is a renunciation of the training (*sikkhāpaccakkhāna*), because that [other word] is included within the field-terms. This is what is meant:
if, for instance, one intending to say "I renounce the Buddha" (*buddhaṃ paccakkhāmīti*) deviates from the word and says "I renounce" (*paccakkhāmi*);
Or he might say "Buddha," or he might express that same meaning in one of the languages of the non-Aryans (milakkhas) and so forth;
or, wishing to say "I renounce the Buddha," he might say out of sequence, "I renounce the Dhamma" or "I renounce my fellow-celibates";
just as, for example, in the analysis of superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma), one says, "I attain the first jhāna."

Desiring to speak, he says, "the second jhāna. If one knows even this much—that the person to whom he speaks is saying this because he wishes to renounce his status as a monk—then there is no failure;
the field itself has been entered, and the training is indeed renounced.
For such a person, it is as if they have already passed away from the dispensation, like a being who has fallen from the state of Sakka or Brahmā.
"Let it be so" (*alanti hotu*) means "let it be mastered" (*pariyatti*). "What indeed for me? (*kiṃ nu me*) means "what is my duty, what is to be done, what is to be accomplished?
"It is not for my benefit" (*na mamattho*) means "there is no purpose for me. "I am well-freed" (*sumuttāham*) means "I am thoroughly liberated.
"By the preceding fourteen phrases" refers to the fourteen preceding phrases beginning with the Buddha and ending with the fellow-celibates.
Regarding the words *padehi*: here, in the phrase *yannūnāhaṃ paccakkheyyaṃ*, the expression *yannūna* is a particle used to indicate reflection.
This is what is meant: “If I were to renounce the Buddha, it would indeed be well for me.
By the word *ādi* (and so forth), one includes such forms as *paccakkhiṃ*, *paccakkhissaṃ*, *bhavissaṃ*, *homī*, *jātomhi*, or *amhi*.
This refers to the grasping of such persons. However, if one says, "From today onwards,
consider me a 'householder'," or "Know me as such," or "Recognize me as such," or "Keep me in mind," whether speaking in an Aryan tongue or a non-Aryan tongue—
when this meaning has been stated, if the person to whom it is said understands it, the training is renounced.
This same method applies to the remaining seven terms, beginning with “upāsaka. Here, “Ariyaka” refers to the Magadhan usage.
“Milakkhaka” refers to non-Ariyans, such as the Andhas, Damilas, and so forth.
“Writing of syllables” refers to the writing of syllables for the purpose of showing others, such as “I renounce the Buddha,” and so on.
A hand-gesture (*hatthamuddā*) is a movement of the hand, such as the contraction of the fingers, which communicates one’s intention.
In this context, the word "hand" (*hattha*) should be understood as referring to its parts, namely the fingers—as in expressions such as, "While eating, I shall not put my whole hand into my mouth.

Therefore, the seeing of a hand-gesture or the like, which consists of a movement of the hand such as the contraction of the fingers that communicates one's intention, is what is meant by "the seeing of a hand-gesture," and so forth.
In this context, the meaning should be understood in this way. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the shaking of the head, the act of looking, and so forth are included.
Regarding the phrase "one who is insane, deranged in mind, or afflicted by pain": here, "insane" (*ummattaka*) refers to one insane from bile (*pitta-ummattaka*).

"Deranged in mind" (*khittacitta*) refers to one whose mind is distracted by *yakkhas*; what is meant is "one insane by a *yakkha*" (*yakkhummattaka*). However, the distinction between these two is explained in the section on non-offenses (*anāpattivāra*).

It will become manifest. "One afflicted by pain" means one who, struck by intense painful feeling, has fallen into a state of fainting; while thus delirious, even if [the precept] has been renounced, it is as if it were not renounced.
"Is of human birth" means he is any human being—whether of the same class or a different class, whether a householder or one gone forth, or anyone who is intelligent.
Regarding the phrase "of those who are insane, etc.," here the word "etc. includes those with deranged minds, those afflicted by pain, deities, and those who have gone into the animal realm.

Regarding the taking up [of the precepts]: in that regard, even if one has renounced them in the presence of those who are insane, deranged, afflicted by pain, or belonging to the animal realm, it is as if they have not been renounced because of their lack of understanding.
However, in the presence of a deity, it is as if they have not been renounced because of the deity’s extremely swift understanding.
Deities—being of great wisdom, possessing a rebirth-linking with three roots—understand very quickly; moreover, this mind...

Because it changes rapidly, he rejected the renunciation of the training in the presence of the deity, thinking, "Let there not be too swift a destruction for this person whose mind is so light, acting merely according to the whims of his mind. Therefore it is said:
"Nor one who is among those such as the insane," and so forth. "By means of a messenger" refers to the verbal instruction: "Tell [him] that I have renounced the training."
"Or by a messenger. "Or by a letter" means by way of sending what has been written on a leaf.
"If they know the state of his having renounced the training"—this is the connection. "At the time of mental advertence" means at the time of attending to the meaning.
By this, he shows that at that very moment it is difficult to discern whether [the act] was first or last. "Immediately after the speech."
“Immediately after the speech” means at the very moment of adverting [the mind]. By the word *eva* (only/just), he rejects the notion that knowledge occurs after a long delay.
“Distressed” (*ukkaṇṭhita*) means having reached a life of hardship in this teaching due to a lack of delight.
Alternatively, it refers to one who dwells with his throat upturned, thinking, “I will leave today; I will leave tomorrow; I will go from here; I will go there.”
"Distraught" means "one-pointedness-less. And this is an indicative mark for such statements as, "not delighting in it, desiring to fall away from the state of recluseship," and so forth.

"By whatever means... they know": if they know by whatever mode—whether as "he is dissatisfied," or "he aspires to the state of a householder," or "he does not delight in it," or "he desires to fall away from the state of recluseship"—that there is an act of renouncing the training.

They know this. For this rule on renouncing the training (*sikkhā-paccakkhāna*) and the subsequent rules on false accusation (*abhūta-ārocanā*), grave speech (*duṭṭhulla-vācā*), self-aggrandizement (*attakāma*), corrupt intent (*duṭṭha-dosa*), and false accusation (*bhūta-ārocanā*) share a single delimitation;
they reach their conclusion only when [the offense] is known at the moment of mental advertence (*āvajjana*).

If it is known only after a long time by one who is doubting, "What is he saying?", they do not reach their conclusion. Therefore he said, "Then at a later time," and so forth. Now, regarding the place where the two stand...
Having specified both of them, she says, "I inform these two.
Even if only one among them knows, or even if both know, the training is indeed renounced. This should be understood in the same way regarding many people as well.

"By the method stated" means by the method stated beginning with "immediately after his words," and so forth. "Any person whatsoever" means any human being at all, including even a construction worker.
For this has been stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
"But if one who is oppressed by dissatisfaction and fearing [the discovery of] his fellow monks makes a loud noise, saying 'Let anyone know it!
and declares, 'I renounce the Buddha,' and if a builder or someone else standing nearby..."
A person who understands the proper occasion, upon hearing this, knows: "This ascetic is dissatisfied; he aspires to the state of a householder;
he has fallen away from the Teaching," and thus his training is considered as good as renounced.
Even if, despite understanding the meaning of the words, one does not know whether "he is dissatisfied" or "he aspires to the state of a householder," [the same applies].

The training remains unrenounced. However, even if one does not understand the literal meaning [of the words], if it is known that [the person] is "disenchanted" or "desires the state of a householder," the training is indeed renounced. "Even for sport" means even with the intention of play.
"Or by way of the mind and so forth" means by way of the six factors beginning with the mind. And on this point there is [this verse]:
“Mind, field, time, application, person, and likewise understanding—
these are the six factors for the renunciation of training.
Or else, by way of not renouncing at all, as in the expressions “I renounce the Buddha,” and so forth, by whichever method...
There is no renunciation of the training, because there is not even a single instance of such renunciation.
By this, however, he shows the absence of the arising of a thought-process such as, "I shall make this word heard; I renounce the training.
For one who lacks such an arising of thought does not, in any sense at all, "renounce" it. Regarding "of the renunciation of the training":

Regarding the renunciation of the training (sikkhā-paccakkhāna) such as “I renounce the Buddha”: when one says or declares, “I renounce the Buddha,” thinking it to be a certain form of weakness (dubbalya),

then— according to what is stated in passages such as, “In this way too, monks, there is both a disclosure of weakness and a renunciation of the training”— by those words, there is both a renunciation of the training and a disclosure of weakness.
Without having manifested that weakness consisting in the meaning of the words "I renounce the Buddha," and so forth;

however, when "I renounce the Buddha," and so forth, have been spoken, since the state of weakness regarding the fulfillment of the training is also implied, it should be understood that this manifestation of weakness is the purpose of the renunciation of the training.
And here, by the phrase "consisting in the meaning," [it refers to] "What if I were to... [renounce] the Buddha.
The phrase "he would renounce" and so forth rejects the disclosure of weakness (*dubbalyāvikamma*).
For that which constitutes both the renunciation of the training and the disclosure of weakness is precisely what constitutes the actual meaning of the renunciation of the training;
however, that which constitutes only the disclosure of weakness and not the renunciation of the training does not constitute its actual meaning.
Because it leads to a state of union through the obsession of lust, it is called "sexual intercourse" (*methuna*);
thus he says, "by the obsession of lust," and so forth. In this context, "obsession of lust" means by the arising of lust;
the meaning is that the mind is enveloped by the manifestation of sexual lust. "Dhamma" here refers to misconduct (*ajjhācāra*). "Palambate... [The text continues:]... hangs down.

In such passages as "he delays" (*vilambate*), there is no specific meaning for the prefix; thus he says, "one should practice" (*seveyya*). "One should transgress" (*ajjhāpajjeyya*) means one should go beyond by overcoming [the restraint].

"By the very last" (*sabbantimena*) means by the very last among all [beings], from the Paranimmitavasavatti gods down to the Cātumahārājika gods, humans, women, nāgas, garuḷas, māṇavikas, and so forth.
"To a female animal" (*tiracchānagatāya*) means to one born among animals. Therefore he said, "by way of rebirth-linking" (*paṭisandhivasena*).
And here, only those female animals who constitute the basis for a *pārājika* offense are to be understood as "animals" (*tiracchānagata*), not all of them.
In this regard, the following is the delimitation:
"For footless beings, the snake and the fish; for two-footed beings, the hen."
"The cat among quadrupeds; this is the basis for a *pārājika* offense.
In this context, by the mention of "snakes," all species of long-bodied creatures—such as pythons, cobras, and so forth—are included.
Therefore, among the long-bodied species, that place where it is possible to insert even a single sesame seed into any one of the three [orifices] constitutes the basis for a *pārājika* offense.
The remainder should be understood as matters of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*). By the term "catching fish," all aquatic species—such as fish, turtles, frogs, and so forth—are included.
Within that category as well, the basis for a defeat (*pārājika*) and the basis for wrongdoing should be understood according to the same method explained for the long-necked species.
However, this is the distinction: there are those called "cricket-mouthed frogs" (*pataṅgamukha-maṇḍūka*); their mouth-shape is as follows: [text continues].
If it is large and the opening small, such that entry is not possible, yet the shape of the mouth constitutes a wound, then this should be understood as a basis for a *thullaccaya* offense.
By the mention of "cock," all species of birds—such as crows, pigeons, and so forth—are included.
In those cases as well, the basis for a *pārājika* offense and the basis for a *dukkaṭa* offense should be understood according to the method already stated.
By the inclusion of "bone-marrow," all species of four-footed animals—such as trees, dogs, mongooses, iguanas, and so forth—are encompassed.
In this regard also, the basis for a *pārājika* offense and the basis for a *dukkaṭa* offense are to be understood according to the method already stated.
"He becomes one who has committed a *pārājika*" means he is defeated; he has fallen into defeat. For this term *pārājika* applies to the training rule, the offense, and the person.

It applies. In this regard, it should be understood as applying to the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) thus: "It is impossible, Ānanda, it is out of the question that the Tathāgata would, for the sake of the Vajjis or the Vajjiputtakas, rescind a training rule for disciples that has been laid down as a *pārājika* offense.
It applies to the offense (*āpatti*) thus: "Bhikkhu, you have fallen into an offense of *pārājika*. It does not...
"This one is defeated; that which was taken away is defeated"—thus it should be understood as referring to the person (*puggala*).
However, in passages such as "one should accuse another of an offense involving defeat" (*pārājikena dhammena anuddhaṃseyya*), they say it refers to the offense (*dhamma*).

But since in those instances the term "offense" (*dhamma*) is intended in some cases to mean the transgression itself and in others the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) alone, it should not be treated as a separate category.
In this context, the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is called "defeat" (*pārājika*) because it defeats whoever transgresses it;

the offense (*āpatti*), however, is called "defeat" because it defeats whoever commits it; and the person is called "one who has met defeat" (*pārājika*) because he has been defeated and has fallen into defeat. But here, it is the person who should be understood [as the subject].

He said: "He becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense," and so forth. By this, he also demonstrates: "In the word *parājita*, by applying a vowel-increment (*vuddhi*) to the prefix and changing the letter *t* to *k*, it is defined as *pārājiko*.

Furthermore, the fourfold formal act (*saṅghakamma*)—beginning with the motion for consultation (*apalokanā*)—must be performed together by the regular monks (*pakatatta*) within the boundaries of the *sīmā*.

Because it is to be performed as one, it is called "a single act" (*ekakamma*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of "single recitation" (*ekuddesa*) and "common training" (*samasikkhatā*).
In that regard, even though the Pātimokkha recitation is fivefold, it is called "single recitation" because it must be recited together as one.

With the exception of those specifically permitted for certain individuals—such as the barber-priests and others—the remainder of all training rules (*sikkhāpada*) must be trained in equally by all modest persons (*lajjipuggala*).

"Training together" means this: because all those who possess a sense of shame dwell together in these [communal] acts and so forth, and not even one of them is seen outside of them, therefore, taking all of them together, it is called the threefold "dwelling together," beginning with communal acts.
Thus he said: "And that aforementioned dwelling together does not exist with that person; for that reason..."
“Such a person who has committed a *pārājika* offense is said to be ‘one with whom there is no communal living.
Now, since the basis for a *pārājika* offense is not merely the sign of a human female, but rather includes non-human females,

females among the animal realm, and furthermore, not only females, but also hermaphrodites (*ubhatobyañjanaka*), eunuchs (*paṇḍaka*), and males, therefore [the text speaks of] those beings and their...

"Whatever sign constitutes the basis, that very sign—and how one who indulges therein becomes guilty of a *pārājika* offense—all this is shown in detail by saying, 'But here is the analysis (*vinicchaya*) of this,'" and so forth.
"In this" means in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). "Among those" refers to the thirty paths mentioned. "Or of oneself" refers to one with a pendulous back or a flat back.
This was said with intentional meaning (*sandhāya*). "Of that which is covered" (*santhatassa*) means:

having wrapped it with any kind of cloth, leaf, woven grass, hide, or a bandage made of tin, lead, and so forth; or having inserted it inside and concealed it. "Of that which is not gnawed" (*akkhāyitassa*) means:
of that which has not been chewed by dogs, jackals, and the like. "Of that which is mostly gnawed" (*yebhuyyena akkhāyitassa*) means: until it is half-gnawed.
There is no such thing as [touching] what is thus described. "In an open space" means in an uncovered space.

"Covered" means that very same cloth or other material being concealed by anything whatsoever. This is the summary of the meaning here: it is not the case here that what is not clung-to (anupādinnaka) touches what is not clung-to;
there is liberation. Rather, let what is clung-to (upādinnaka) strike what is not clung-to, or let what is not clung-to [strike it].
Or, the appropriated with the non-appropriated, or the non-appropriated with the appropriated, or the appropriated with the appropriated.
If it is stated that a *pārājika* offense occurs when a certain amount has been inserted, and one inserts that same amount with the intention of sexual intercourse,
then in all such cases, he is said to have incurred a *pārājika* offense.

Having thus shown the offense for one who enters with a mind of enjoyment (*sevanacitta*), he now says "or by another" and so forth, in order to show that this entry is not only through one's own effort (*attūpakkama*), but also through the effort of another (*parūpakkama*).
Even in that case, the offense belongs only to one who consents and possesses the mind of enjoyment, and not to the other.
In this context, "by another" refers to a hostile monk (*bhikkhu-paccatthika*) or the like.
"By any other means whatsoever. Regarding "the insertion, having inserted, remaining, and withdrawing": here, "insertion" (*pavesana*) refers to the act of inserting from the tip down to the base.
"Having inserted" (*paviṭṭha*) means that the penis has been inserted in its entirety to whatever extent of space is capable of receiving it.
"Remaining" (*ṭhita*) refers to the period during which it remains in between, starting from the moment one begins to withdraw what has been thus inserted.

In the *Samantapāsādikā*, however, the phrase "at the time of the emission of semen" is said with reference to the moment when, having reached the emission of semen, one has completely ceased from effort and remains still.
"Extraction" (*uddharaṇa*) means the time of drawing it out as far as the tip.

"Consents" means he arouses the intention for sexual intercourse. "The unique determination" refers to [the offense] distinct from all others such as taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*), and so forth.
