The *vinicchaya* (explanation) regarding the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) is non-common.
The phrase "the meaning of the common explanation" refers to the meaning of the common explanation by way of the *parivāra*. *Mātikā* means "mother";
the sense is "progenitor. It is called *nidāna* because it places [the teaching]—that is, it demonstrates by way of the location of the teaching, making known what was previously unknown.
It is called *paññatti* because it is made known (*paññāpīyati*). Its method is the *paññattividhi*. It is called *aṅga* because it leads to, brings about, or makes known; thus, it is a cause.
It is called *samuṭṭhāna* because offenses arise (*samuṭṭhahanti*) by means of it; it is the cause of their arising, and its method is the *samuṭṭhānavidhi*.

Regarding the phrase "and the classification of faults" (*vajjakammappabhedañca*), the word *pabheda* (classification) should be applied to each [term]: "the classification of faults" (*vajjappabhedaṃ*).
"And the classification of actions. Therein, "in each case" means in each respective training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
"The basis for the formulation" means the ground for establishing the formulation; the meaning is that it is the location where the training rules are formulated.
Regarding the term "person" (*puggala*), only the original perpetrator is intended here; thus he said: "A person is whoever [the rule] was directed toward."
"That training rule was laid down"—this refers to each respective individual; and herein there are these verses:
"Sudinna, Dhaniya, the many [monks] at Vaggumudā, Seyyasaka, Udāyī, Cāḷavaka, Channa, and Mettiyā."
“Devadatta, Sājīputta, Nabbasī, and any one of the group of six;
Hatthaka, Anuruddha, and Cūḷapanthaka—these seventeen.
Belaṭṭhasīsa, Ānanda, and the one named Sāgata and Ariṭṭha.”
With the Elder Nanda as the twenty-third, there were the original performers among the bhikkhus.
[The nuns were] Sundarīnandā, Thullanandā, any one of the group-of-six,
Caṇḍakāḷī, several others, and two other bhikkhunīs.
"But for bhikkhunīs there are only seven; they are the original offenders.
"Of this or that person" means: with reference to whichever person, such as Sudinna and others, a training rule was laid down, it refers to that specific person.
"Laid down" means the first laying down. It was established subsequent to the first laying down.
A formal rule (paññatti) and a supplementary rule (anupaññatti). A formal rule established when no fault has yet arisen is an "unoriginated formal rule" (anuppannapaññatti).
A formal rule established in all places—namely, both in the Middle Country and in the bordering regions—is a "universal formal rule" (sabbatthapaññatti).
A formal rule established only in the Middle Country is a "local formal rule" (padesapaññatti). [And] for the bhikkhus...

A rule that is common to both bhikkhus and bhikkhunīs is a "common rule" (sādhāraṇapaññatti). A training precept prescribed for bhikkhus alone, or for bhikkhunīs alone, is an "uncommon rule" (asādhāraṇapaññatti). A rule prescribed for both is an "ubhato-paññatti.
"With the holder of the Vinaya as the fifth" means with the teacher who performs the proclamation as the fifth. "Layered sandals" refers to those with four layers.
Sandals made from the time [the hide] has been tanned, and not those with one, two, or three layers. "Leather spreader" means leather that is to be spread out.
By way of these, there are four kinds of what is called "local prescription" (*padesapaññatti*);
because these four kinds of prescriptions were prescribed only in the Middle Country, they are called "local prescriptions. For this very reason, he said: "Only in the Middle Country," and so forth.

Because an offense occurs only when one transgresses the aforementioned grounds within the Middle Country (*majjhima-desa*) and not in the bordering provinces (*paccantima-janapada*), the meaning is that it is a "local promulgation" (*padesa-paññatti*). "The mere prohibition of constant bathing" means simply the forbidding of regular bathing.
And here, by the word "mere" (*matta*), three other training rules (*sikkhāpada*) are excluded; for those [rules] are: "I allow..."

[These matters] have been recorded in the Cammakkhandhaka (the Leather Chapter) beginning with: "Monks, in all outlying districts, ordination may be performed by a group consisting of a fifth member who is an expert in the Vinaya.
For this very reason it was said: "Apart from that, there is no other so-called 'local enactment' (padesapaññatti).

The word "all" refers to all the training rules (sikkhāpada) remaining after those [eight]. The word "therefore" (tasmā) is used because the "unpromulgated enactment" (anuppannapaññatti) pertains to the eight weighty rules (garudhamma).

[The training rules] have come down for the bhikkhunīs alone; and because, with the sole exception of the prohibition against regular bathing, all the training rules in the Pātimokkha are prescribed as being applicable everywhere (sabbattha-pannatti);

and because the pair of categories concerning common prescriptions and the pair concerning prescriptions made for one side differ only in phrasing while being identical in meaning—therefore, "everywhere" means in all [instances].
Regarding the training rules (*sikkhāpada*): here, the classification of offenses (*āpatti*) is referred to as "offense" (*āpatti*) by means of eliding the latter member of the compound;
thus he says, "‘Offense’ refers to the classification of offenses according to the preliminary action and so forth. Regarding "failures in virtue, conduct, view, and livelihood":

here, the first two aggregates of offenses are called failure in virtue (*sīlavipatti*), while the remaining five are called failure in conduct (*ācāravipatti*); [the last is] wrong view (*micchādiṭṭhi*).

Furthermore, the "falling away from view" (*diṭṭhivipatti*) consists of views such as those that grasp at extremes; the "falling away from livelihood" (*ājīvavipatti*) consists of the six training rules prescribed on account of livelihood.
Thus, the meaning is: "any one of these falling aways from virtue, conduct, view, or livelihood.
He says, "they are also called 'those originating from the training rules' (*sikkhāpada-samutthānāni*)," to show that they are not spoken of solely in the manner already described.
For although these are the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) of offenses, they are not the origins of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*);

rather, they are spoken of in this way for the sake of linguistic convenience. "Therein" means among those six origins. "Among them" refers to those [offenses] that are with-mind (*sacittaka*) and without-mind (*acittaka*).
It is called "having a single origin" because it has one origin as its cause of arising; or, it is called "having a single origin" because its origination is by means of one [cause].
The same method applies to [the terms] such as “arising from two origins” (*dvisamuṭṭhānā*).

“By way of origin” (*samuṭṭhānavasena*) means by way of the head of the origin. “That which has the first *pārājika* as its origin” is *paṭhamapārājikasamuṭṭhānā*. The same applies to [the terms] such as “having the taking of what is not given as its origin” (*adinnādānasamuṭṭhānā*).

Because an offense arises both through one’s own bodily act of digging the earth and through commanding another to dig it verbally, [it is said to arise] “in the case of digging the earth, etc. (*pathavikhaṇanādīsu*).
Thus it is said. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the inclusion of taking what is not given and so forth is intended. Regarding the first *kathina* offense:
it occurs for one who does not perform the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) or the assignment (*vikappana*) that ought to be done by body or speech, but not for one who does perform them;
hence it is said, "like the first *kathina* offense. The offense of receiving a robe from the hand of an unrelated nun refers to [receiving] a robe from her hand.
It arises from both action and non-action (*kriyā-akriyā*) because it occurs for one who accepts [the object] and for one who does not give a change.

Regarding the phrase “it may be for one who acts” (*siyā karontassa*) and so forth, the word *siyā* is a particle synonymous with “perhaps” (*kadāci*), as in such passages as “it might perhaps occur to you, O Brahmin” (*siyā kho pana te brāhmaṇa evam assa*).
The offense of accepting gold and silver (*rūpiya-paṭiggahaṇa-āpatti*) is an action (*kriyā*) because it is incurred through the act of taking.
It might be argued that there is no offense for the non-doing of what is prohibited; therefore, he said, "like the offense of accepting money.
Regarding the offense of building a hut (*kuṭikāra-āpatti*): it may occur for one who builds after having had the site designated, but exceeds the prescribed dimensions.

However, it may also occur for one who builds without having had the site designated, whether they build within the proper dimensions or do not build at all; thus he said, "like the offense of building a hut."

"Because there is liberation through the absence of perception, it is called 'liberation by perception' (*saññā-vimokkha*); this should be understood as a *majjhepadalopa* compound," he said, beginning with "since, by means of the perception of transgression... The term "the other" refers to that which is not liberated through the absence of the perception of transgression;
this is because the word "other" (*itara*) has as its referent the counterpart to what was previously mentioned. That [liberation] which is either without consciousness or mixed with consciousness...
"Arises" means that an offense arises sometimes through a mentalless origin (*acittaka-samuṭṭhāna*) and sometimes through a mixed mental-origin (*sacittaka-missaka-samuṭṭhāna*).

Here, it should be understood that the pair concerning perception (*saññā-duka*) is stated by way of non-offense (*anāpatti*), while the pair concerning the mental (*sacittaka-duka*) is stated by way of offense (*āpatti*).
Regarding the phrase "for which, on the side of the mental, the mind is exclusively unwholesome": this refers to that mental offense for which the mind is indeed unwholesome.

It is unwholesome itself; and in the case of an offense such as drinking fermented liquor—which is classified as both with and without consciousness—the mind that knows the object of the offense belongs to the category "with consciousness" and is indeed unwholesome: this is a world-transgression (*lokavajja*). For the expression "in the category of being with consciousness" is stated with reference to both offenses that are with consciousness and those that are without consciousness;
for it is not exclusively in the case of an offense that is definitively with consciousness that the phrase "in the category of being with consciousness" is used.

There is a purpose for the qualification. As for what is stated here in the *Gaṇṭhipada*: “For in the case of drinking liquor, if one drinks knowing it as ‘liquor’ or knowing ‘it is not permitted,’ it is indeed unwholesome (*akusala*).

In that regard, the statement “knowing ‘it is not permitted’” is not tenable, because it would entail the consequence that even a transgression by rule (*paṇṇattivajja*) would be a transgression by nature (*lokavajja*). However, in the case where [the text says] “on the side of being with consciousness”...

There is no fixed rule that "the mind is exclusively unwholesome"; rather, this [offense] is a formal prohibition (*paṇṇattivajja*). To demonstrate this point, he said, "The remaining ones are formal prohibitions.
For indeed, in the case where one possesses a mind that knows the object, the mind may be wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate;
thus, there is no fixed rule that it is "exclusively unwholesome. This applies to both cases.

"Should be committed" means that an offense is to be committed in both places— namely, at the door of the body and at the door of speech— and these are offenses such as taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*) and so forth.

The statement "there is no such thing as an offense at the door of the mind" should be understood as being said by way of general rule, since an offense can still arise in cases such as consenting to something placed near one.

"One commits with an unwholesome mind" means that one commits an offense—such as those categorized as *pārājika*, emission of semen, bodily contact, grave misconduct, sexual service, corrupt intent, schism in the Saṅgha, striking, or using the hand or a clod of earth—with an unwholesome mind.

One commits such an offense with a wholesome mind when teaching the Dhamma word-by-word to one who is not fully ordained, or when teaching the Dhamma to a woman. One commits [an offense] with an indeterminate mind in cases such as unintentional co-sleeping.
One incurs it. Whatever an Arahant incurs, he incurs it entirely with an indeterminate (abyākata) state of mind. Therefore, it is said: "or with a wholesome or indeterminate mind.
Or, one who possesses painful feeling incurs it: when one incurs an offense such as the corruption of a fault (duṭṭhadosa), one incurs it while possessing painful feeling;
however, when one incurs an offense such as sexual intercourse (methunadhamma), one incurs it while possessing pleasant feeling. When one possesses pleasant feeling...
One who commits [an offense] while being neutral commits it while possessing neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling (*adukkhamasukhavedanā*).
Therefore, he said: "Or one possessing either of the other two feelings. Furthermore, these two triads are stated by way of general prevalence.
For one who has lain down and attained cessation (*nirodhasamāpanna*) is without mind and without feeling, yet incurs the offense of lying down together. Even though...
Thus it was stated without specific restriction; however, in order to show that there is a distinction here, the words "Even though this is so" (*evaṃ santepi*) and so forth were spoken.
For the phrase "even though this is so" is appropriate only as an admission for the purpose of stating a specific qualification.

"Three types of consciousness by way of all [three]" refers to the three types of consciousness—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—by way of the *padasodhamma* (words of similar meaning) and so on.

Now, in order to apply that seventeen-fold classification—beginning with the aforementioned causes and ending with the four types of feeling—to this training rule, he says, "In this case, moreover," and so forth. "In this" (idha) means in this first *pārājika* training rule.
"Vesālī" refers to the city known by that name, where common usage proceeds according to the feminine gender. For that city was thrice increased in its enclosure by the addition of ramparts.

Because it had become vast (*visālībhūta*), it is called "Vesālī. Furthermore, it should be understood that this city reached its full perfection in every respect only when the Perfectly Enlightened One had attained omniscience (*sabbaññutā*).

The two supplementary rules (*anupaññatti*)—"without having renounced the training" and "even down to an animal"—are stated with reference to the cases of the monkey and the son of Vajjī. [The phrase] "even down to an animal" refers to...

And the two supplementary rules (anupaññatti) are: “without having renounced the training” and “[the offense] becomes an offense. “It becomes an offense” means it becomes an offense separately from the first rule of enactment (paññatti).
“As in the case of the training rule on speaking otherwise, etc. means as in the case of the training rule on speaking otherwise and so forth, beginning with the words “one who harasses,” etc.
By the word “etc.,” the rule on complaining is included. For here, [the offense arises] from speaking otherwise and so forth.
In each case, including for one who causes vexation and so forth, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). As it is said:

"When vexation has been brought forward in the midst of the Saṅgha, if one who is not being appointed to the matter or the offense remains silent—neither wishing to speak about it nor wishing to clear it up—and thus vexes the Saṅgha, there is an offense of expiation," and so forth.
Even the volition of taking pleasure in emission, though present in a dream, is not subject to formal designation because it lacks the necessary conditions for an offense.
He said, "It is non-offensive," as in the passage beginning, "except in a dream.

For, because the mind is overcome by sloth and torpor, the mind in a dream is not reckoned [as a formal act]; and because the mind is not reckoned, the volition that initiates the preparatory action is also not reckoned.
Indeed, this has been stated: "There is such a volition, monks, but it is not reckoned"; therefore...

“Except in a dream”: this is a subsequent rule (*anupaññatti*) that has become one that causes non-offense. By the word “etc. (*ādi*), it includes [the rules] such as “except out of overweening pride” (*aññatra adhimānā*).
“As in the case of taking what is not given, etc. means: as in the case of taking what is not given, etc., there is [a rule] beginning with “from a forest,” and so forth.
Here, however, by the word “etc.,” the first *pārājika* and the others are included; for here [it says], “And that moreover, in a village, not...”

The supplementary rule (anupaññatti) beginning with "or from the forest" was stated for the purpose of burning away the pretext of those who cast out a pretext in the manner beginning with "in the forest.
Therefore, it serves as a support. For this very reason, the monks said: "Friend, is it not just so?
"In the type of path mentioned" means in the thirty types of paths described in the manner beginning with "by way of humans, non-humans, and animals."

This, moreover, is connected with the word "cut" (*chinne*). "Without leaving any remainder of the skin and so forth" means without leaving behind any of the outer layers of skin remaining on the site of the sign.
It is said that "only the shape of the sign is discerned" because the skin and flesh still exist within the flesh of the sign. "A piece of hide" (*cammakhila*) means a fragment of skin.

Some also call it "the fleshy protuberance" (*uṇṇigaṇḍa*). For that [organ] is indeed a "sign" (*nimitta*) because it is produced from a sign. Therefore he said: "When there is a mind of sexual intercourse, it is a *pārājika* offense.
"A mind of sexual intercourse" means a mind for engaging in sexual union. However, when there is a mind for physical contact, it is only a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
"That wherein the bodily tissue has perished" (*naṭṭhakāyappasāda*) refers to a scrotal swelling (*sukkhapīḷaka*) or a dead skin [membrane].

The meaning is "it blows. Because it is stated that there is an offense of *pārājika* when [the organ] is destroyed, or mostly destroyed, even for one who inserts it into a female sexual organ whose bodily tissues have perished, there is indeed an offense of *pārājika*.

"Without leaving even the mere shape of the sign" means without leaving behind even the flesh and so forth of the aforementioned sign as it exists in the form of the sign. "By way of a summary of the wound" means...

By way of the inclusion of wounds. Regarding the grave offense (thullaccaya) in a wound, it should be understood by way of this sutta: "If one inserts [the organ] into what is not the path by means of what is not the path, there is an offense of thullaccaya.

For in that sutta, it is stated that there is a thullaccaya for one who, having inserted [the organ] through one of two mixed wounds, withdraws it through the second. Indeed, it is said in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
"In this case, for a living being, a grave offense (thullaccaya) is to be understood everywhere according to the classification of wounds (vaṇa-saṅkhepa) by way of conformity.
However, since even the eyes and so forth of human beings fall under the category of wounds, he said "likewise" and so on, showing them as being of one definition with a wound.
Their inclusion in the category of wounds is according to such suttas as: "The nine doors are a great wound."
It should be understood. In that context, "of humans" refers to the four kinds of humans: women, men, eunuchs, and those with both sexual organs.
"In the receptacles of the bladder" means in the bladder-pouches of men, and in the sheaths of the male organs.

"And of animals such as elephants and horses" refers to animals belonging to the animal realm, such as elephants, horses, oxen, camels, donkeys, buffaloes, and so forth. [This concludes the section on] animals.
"Panā" means all animals. "Sabbesaṃ" means of all those previously mentioned, such as humans and so forth.
Having thus shown the specific offense incurred regarding a living body, he now says "in a dead body," etc., in order to show the specific offense incurred regarding a dead body.
[The phrase refers to] the anus, the urinary passage, and the mouth.
When two of the four parts have been set aside and the other two parts have been eaten, it is then called "half-eaten.
It is not putrid means that it is not putrid by way of being bloated and so forth; the meaning is that it is fresh.
However, when the body becomes bloated, putrid, covered with blue flies, and swarming with hosts of worms—
Because it has been ejected through the nine openings of the body by way of its former state as a corpse, it is impossible even to approach;

at that time, it abandons both the basis for a *pārājika* offense and the basis for a *thullaccaya* offense, and becomes only a basis for a *dukkaṭa*. Thus he said, "In the case of a putrefied [corpse], there is a *dukkaṭa*.
"Putrefied" means having reached the state of being bloated. For regarding such a body, there is a *dukkaṭa* for any intentional effort made against it anywhere.

Likewise, for one inserting the sexual organ into a mouth that has been turned like a bowl without touching it, the meaning is that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one inserting the sexual organ into an open mouth without touching the four sides or the palate.
However, if one inserts it while it touches [the sides] below, above, or on both sides, it is a defeat (*pārājika*). [This applies when] by means of the four sides...
Having inserted it without touching [the organ], he touches the palate inside; this is indeed a *pārājika* offense.
For one who inserts the sexual organ into a tongue that has protruded outside or into the teeth, there is a *thullaccaya* offense; such is the connection [of the rule].
Even in the case of a living body, if the tongue has protruded outside, there is likewise a *thullaccaya*. However, if [he inserts it] into the mouth after the tongue has been wrapped around outside—

If he inserts it, it is an offense of defeat (pārājika). However, if the teeth are very smooth, there is no space inside the mouth, and the teeth are covered on the outside by the lip-flesh, then for one who inserts even as much as a sesame seed—provided it is not touched by the wind and is in a non-public space—it is indeed an offense of defeat.
But if the lip-flesh has been torn away and he makes an effort against the teeth themselves, it is a serious offense (thullaccaya).
Even when a tooth that has fallen out comes out and remains outside, it cannot be closed by the lips;
the same principle applies there as well. "Afflicted by feeling" (*vedanāṭṭa*) means oppressed by feeling. Regarding the term "insane," it refers here to one who is insane through bile (*pitta*);
thus he said, "one who, by way of bile," and so forth. "By way of bile" means by way of the bound bile (*baddhapitta*). For within that bound bile, from the gall-bladder (*pittakosa*)...
When beings go out after having become agitated, they become insane; with distorted perceptions, they cast aside shame and moral dread and engage in improper conduct.
Even while trampling upon the light and heavy training rules, they do not realize it; even through the administration of medicine, they remain incurable.
For such an insane person, there is no offense. However, unbound bile is like blood.
When it pervades all the limbs, if it becomes deranged, beings suffer from boils, scabs, bodily tremors, and so forth; these are pacified through the application of medicine.
Therefore it is said: "by way of bound bile (*baddhapitta*). One whose mind is "deranged" (*khittacitta*) is called one whose mind is distracted or possessed by a *yakkha*;
thus he says: "one whose mind is deranged by *yakkhas*. It is said that *yakkhas* [present] terrifying objects...
Having shown [the corpse] and thrusting a hand into the mouth, or crushing the heart-flesh, they cause beings to become deranged in mind and distorted in perception;
there is no offense for one who thus deranges the mind. However, this is the distinction between these two types:
one intoxicated by bile is perpetually insane and does not regain his natural state of consciousness, whereas one intoxicated by a *yakkha*...

From time to time, he regains his natural awareness. However, in this case, whether one is intoxicated by bile or possessed by a spirit, if someone is so utterly forgetful that they know nothing at all and wanders about crushing fire, gold, excrement, and sandalwood as if they were all the same, there is no offense for such a person.
This is provided that, from time to time, he regains his natural awareness.
But for one who acts with knowledge, there is indeed an offense. Therefore he said, "And of these two," and so forth.
"With intense feeling" means with excessive measure of painful feeling. One who is engaged in a first action is a "first-action-doer" (*ādikammika*);
and since one who is engaged in a first action is the very beginning of that action, he said, "Whoever," and so forth. But here—
The Elder Sudinna was the first offender; for him there was no offense. For the rest—the monkey, the ascetic, the Vajjiputtaka, and so forth—there was indeed an offense.
"Causing to be performed" means bringing about its accomplishment. It is called an "action" (*kiriya*) because one incurs the offense while actually performing it.

However, this is stated by way of the majority of cases, since in the case of sexual intercourse, if the other party initiates the act and one consents, it arises from non-action (*akiriyasamuṭṭhāna*).
It is a "liberation by perception" (*saññāvimokkha*) because one is liberated through the absence of the perception of sensual desire connected with sexual intercourse.

For it is said: "There is no offense for one who does not know, or for one who does not consent. It is "with consciousness" (*sacittaka*) because one commits this act only with a mind of sexual intent, and not without such a mind.

It is "worldly transgression" (*lokavajja*) because it must be committed solely through the influence of lust. It is "bodily action" (*kāyakamma*) because its origination occurs only through the door of the body.
In this context, however, the mind (citta) is merely a factor; the status of being "kamma" is not obtained by virtue of it.

It is an unwholesome state of mind because it must be committed with a mind characterized by greed (lobha). It possesses two types of feeling, because one commits it while experiencing either pleasure or equanimity.

But surely the origin (samuṭṭhāna) and other such factors pertain to the offense (āpatti), not to the training rule (sikkhāpada); so why are the origin and other factors discussed in relation to the training rule?

Regarding the phrase "they have been stated," he says: "And these names, such as 'origination' (samuṭṭhāna) and so forth," and so on. "They pertain to an offense" means they pertain to transgression (ajjhācāra).
"Muti" is from the sense of measuring (muna) and assenting (anumana); it is knowledge (ñāṇa). One who possesses this is "mutimā," meaning one who has knowledge.
The commentary on the first Pārājika is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Second Pārājika.
"Therein" means among these two. The connection is that all [settlements], including those consisting of a single hut and so forth, should be understood as a "village.
In this context, "consisting of a single hut and so forth" refers to a village where there is only one hut or one house, such as in the Malaya country.
This is what is called a "single-hut village. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it includes the various types mentioned, such as "a two-hut village," "a three-hut village," and "a four-hut village.

However, a newly settled single-hut village or similar settlement does not attain the designation of a "village" until people have entered and established their residence there. To the question "Of what nature is it? he says: "enclosed."
“Or,” and so forth. In this context, “enclosed” means surrounded by anything starting from a brick wall down to even thorny branches.

The opposite of that is “unenclosed. A “non-human being” (amanussa) refers to one who has become possessed by a *yakkha* due to the total absence of humans, or one from whom humans have departed even though they intended to return for some purpose.
But since they depart having become indifferent [to the village], that [place] does not count as a village.

To show that it is not only [the case of] a single hut and so forth, he said "even as little as" and so on. "Any caravan whatsoever" means any caravan at all among those such as pedestrian caravans, wagon caravans, and so forth.
In this training rule, just as with villages and towns, the village precincts are also included by the mention of "village"; thus he said:

“Excluding both the village and the vicinity of the village. Otherwise, the definition of the locations for theft would not have been made exhaustively in the matrix (mātikā), and the Buddhas do not prescribe a Pārājika offense with any omissions.
“Therein” means within those villages and vicinities of villages. “At the door” means inside the point where water falls from the eaves.
“In the interior of the house” means inside the front entrance. “Enclosed” means enclosed by walls, fences, and so forth.
However, the definition regarding the falling of a clod of earth and so on is stated here with reference to an unenclosed house.

It should be understood that the “vicinity of the house” (gharūpacāra) is not merely the area in front of the house, but rather the extent of space surrounding it on all sides. The phrase beginning with “in front” [is used]...
However, it is stated [in that way] because worldly people act accordingly. "Of one of medium strength" means of medium power; it is said that he is neither of little strength nor of great strength.

By the passage beginning with "Just as young men," it is shown how a woman, when scaring away crows, throws a clod of earth by simply raising her hand straight up, and just as they throw water during a water-sport.
In this way, he rejects the place where a thrown clod of earth falls. "Having rolled" means having turned over;
it is said to mean having revolved. "If there are two gateposts for that [enclosed village]" means if that enclosed village has two thresholds (ummāra), just like Anurādhapura.
But for one that has only one, [the distance] is within the range of a clod's throw from the center of the two door-posts of the village gate.
This is called the vicinity of a village (*gāmūpacāra*). However, where there is no boundary pillar (*indakhīla*), it is the midpoint between the two doorposts of the village gate.

Where even doorposts do not exist, there the midpoint between the ends of either a fence or a wall on both sides must be understood as the "boundary pillar," since it occupies the position of the boundary pillar.
Furthermore, regarding a village that was formerly large but later...
When villages have disappeared, it is small; its extent from the dwelling-place can be delimited by the distance of a clod-throw.
However, its previous limit—whether the area is enclosed or unenclosed—is indeed immeasurable.

Now, does this demonstration of the precinct for an unenclosed area not appear as if it contradicts the word-commentary? For therein it says: "The precinct of a village (*gāmūpacāra*) refers to that which is enclosed..."

Having stated, "the range of a clod thrown by a medium-sized man standing at the village gatepost," it was only said, "the range of a clod thrown by a medium-sized man standing in the vicinity of the houses of an unenclosed village";

however, that range of the clod was not defined as the "village compound" (*gāmasaṅkhepa*), and what follows that was not called the "vicinity of the village" (*gāmūpacāra*). Therefore, he said: "Even in the word-analysis (*padabhājana*)..."
"For the meaning should be understood by this very method.
This is the intended sense here: in this context, a village is of two kinds—enclosed and unenclosed.
Of these, for that which is enclosed, the enclosure itself constitutes the boundary. Therefore, without stating a separate boundary for it, [the text says...]

“The village precinct (*gāmūpacāra*) is defined as the distance of a stone’s throw by a man of medium height standing at the threshold (*indakhīla*) of an enclosed village,” so it is stated in the Canon.
However, for an unenclosed village, the boundary of the village must be specified. Therefore, in order to show the village boundary of such a village, [it is said]:
“In the case of an unenclosed village, within the vicinity of the houses (*gharūpacāre*)...”

It is said: "the range of a clod thrown by a man of middle stature standing there. Since the boundaries of the village have already been shown, the definition of the village precinct (*gāmūpacāra*) can be understood through the same method explained previously;
therefore, it was not stated again as "the range of a clod thrown by a man of middle stature standing there," for the meaning there is also exactly as previously described.
However, as for one standing in the precinct of a house...
If one says that "the vicinity of a village" (gāmūpacāra) is merely the range of a thrown clod, then it follows that the vicinity of a house would be the "village.

Consequently, the distinction between a house being the vicinity of a house and a village being the vicinity of a village would become confused. Here, the determination must be understood without such confusion.
Therefore, having reconciled the canonical text (pāḷi) with the commentary (aṭṭhakathā), the village and its vicinity should be understood here exactly according to the method already stated.
"In those two" refers to those two types of precincts (*upacāra*). The connection is: "that precinct which has been shown.
Regarding the phrase "in entering a village at the wrong time, etc.," the word "etc. includes entering a village without wearing an inner robe (*asaṃkaccika*).
However, that precinct described for an enclosed village has not found application anywhere in the Vinaya Piṭaka; it applies only to an unenclosed [village].
This is stated for the purpose of making it known that "another single stone's throw from the boundary is called the village precinct. For when this is said, it is understood:

"If even one stone's throw from an enclosed village is called the precinct when it constitutes a *kappiya-bhūmi* (an area where food may be prepared), how much more so one [stone's throw] from an unenclosed village from the location of its boundary. This is for the purpose of showing these limits.
These were stated in the Commentary for the purpose of showing the boundaries of villages and forests.
"The basis for a *pārājika* offense" means [stolen goods] worth one *pāda*. "Of one who takes away" means of one who seizes.

"What is not given" refers, in the case of the training rule on tooth-sticks (*dantapona*), even to what belongs to oneself, provided it has not been formally accepted and is suitable for consumption.

It is said that here, whatever property belonging to another, having an owner, has not been given by those owners either by body or by speech—that is "what is not given" (*adinnam*). However, in order to show only that which is sufficient for theft, it is stated as "the possession of another human being.
This is because the word *saṅkhā* has been spoken with the addition of the letter *t*.
“It is said that ‘the conditioned (saṅkhā)’ and ‘the conditioned thing (saṅkhata)’ are one in meaning. In this context, “one in meaning” means one in the sense of the word-meaning (*padattha*);
it is stated that they do not have different meanings. This is the name for a portion, given because it is reckoned (*saṅkhāyati*) and appears as a part.
Regarding “proliferations of the conditioned” (*papañcasaṅkhā*): they are called *papañcā* because they cause beings to proliferate and linger in *saṃsāra*; they are craving, conceit, and views.

Alternatively, those [states] that have arisen in someone are called *papañca* because they cause one to proliferate (*papañcenti*) and manifest [them] as "lustful," "intoxicated," or "established in wrong view.
*Saṅkhā* refers to a portion; thus, *papañca-saṅkhā* means the portions of proliferation, which is to say, craving, conceit, and views.
"Designated as a thieving mind" means it is described as "a thieving mind."
"One portion of the mind" refers to a portion of the mind distinct from those portions of the mind that proceed by way of taking [an object] through trust, for a moment, and so forth.
"By what is reckoned as theft" means by a portion of the mind that has become theft.

If this is so, then why is it said in its analysis (vibhaṅga), "one whose mind is intent on theft, one whose mind is intent on taking away"? To this he says, "And whoever," etc. This is the phrasing (byañjana).
"Without taking up" means not paying attention to the literal expression; it is said to mean "without regard for the etymological meaning.
"The meaning itself" refers to the essential meaning.
"Those thefts" refers to those twenty-five types of theft. "Various kinds of goods" refers to property that is either animate or inanimate.
“Of this group of five” means various articles; a collection of five thefts is a “group of five” (*pañcaka*); or, that which has five as its measure is a “group of five.
A “group of five” consisting of various articles is a “group-of-five-various-articles” (*nānābhaṇḍa-pañcaka*). That which has one article by way of being animate is a “single-article” (*ekabhaṇḍa*).
The rest is exactly as explained above. A “group of five” involving [the act] with one’s own hand is a “hand-group-of-five” (*sāhatthika-pañcaka*).
And this name is given by way of its first member, just as the term "wholesome triad" (*kusalattika*) is used for the triad beginning with the wholesome.
Therefore, it should be understood in meaning as "the pentad beginning with 'by one's own hand'. This same method applies to the other two pentads.
"Of this very [term]" refers to the very heading-word "he should take up. "By way of these words" means by way of these five words. And here—
It should be understood that the first phrase is stated by way of active effort; the second, by way of one who goes taking another's goods;
the third, by way of goods deposited as a pledge; the fourth, by way of animate beings;
and the fifth, by way of goods placed on dry land and so forth.
Now, in order to show the application of their meaning, he said, "Therein," and so forth. Therein, "therein" means in those two pentads.
"The other" refers to the pentad of a single article. "Garden" means a flower garden or a fruit garden.

"Brings a charge against" means that, having falsely stated regarding another's property, "This is indeed my own," one brings a charge, urges [the matter], or initiates a lawsuit; this is the meaning. Even in the case of intentional lying (*sampajāna-musāvāda*),...
Because it is the preliminary stage (*pubbapayoga*) for taking what is not given, he said, "there is an offense of wrong-doing" (*dukkaṭa*);
the meaning is that there would be an offense designated as *dukkaṭa*. Alternatively, the meaning is "the committing of a transgression known as *dukkaṭa*.

This same method applies to [the phrases] "an offense of serious transgression" (*thullaccaya*) and so forth. "He arouses doubt in the owner" means by virtue of his skill in legal determination (*vinicchaya*).
Or, by means of such things as relying on powerful persons, one creates doubt in the owner of the monastery. How so?
Seeing that [monk] thus intent on making a decision, the owner thinks: "Will I be able to make this monastery my own, or will I not?
In this way, the perplexity arising in him has been produced by that [monk]. "He lays down the burden" means:
But when the owner, thinking, "This man is stubborn and harsh;

he might even create an obstacle to my holy life," gives up his responsibility and abandons his effort—meaning he becomes indifferent toward making it his own property—there is an offense of *pārājika* if he himself has also given up his responsibility; this is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, even when the owner has laid down the burden, if the claimant, without laying down his own burden,
remains intent on giving— thinking, "I shall press him hard, demonstrate my authority, and establish him in the state of one who obeys commands before I give"—
then he still protects [the property]. Moreover, if the claimant, having seized it, thinks, "I will not give this to him now," [he still protects it].
The wife lays down her burden, but the husband does not;

she seeks an ally, waits for the right time, thinking, "I will first obtain a circle of modest people, and afterwards I shall see," and thus she remains hopeful regarding the acquisition itself and continues to guard it.
But when both lay down their burden, thinking, "He too will not give it," and "The husband too will not receive it," [then it is lost].
At that time, the one who makes the charge incurs a *pārājika* offense.
"Carrying away another's goods" means carrying away another's property either for a wage or out of friendship.
"A burden on the head" means a load situated on the head. First, regarding the head: there is the throat-opening at the front of the neck, and for some, [the hairline] at the back of the neck.

There is a whorl at the edge of the hair; on both sides of the neck, in some individuals, hair grows descending [from there], which is called the "ear-tufts" (*kaṇṇacūḷikā*), including their lower portion—this is the lower limit. Above that is the head;
what is meant is the burden situated within this interval. "He lowers the shoulder" means starting from the ear-tufts on both sides.
Below, starting from the hair-knots; above, starting from the hollow of the nape and the hollow of the throat;
below, starting from the hollow at the center of the back and the middle of the chest; and above, starting from the hollow of the heart—the shoulder.
He removes that. Now, this is the detailed analysis here: a monk who has not been instructed by the owners, saying, "Take this and go there," [commits an offense].
If one says oneself, "Give me this," and then, while carrying their goods on one's head, touches that merchandise with a thieving mind, it is *dukkaṭa*.
If, without exceeding the aforementioned limit of the head, one rubs it here and there, shifting it back and forth, it is a *thullaccaya*. [If it reaches] the shoulder...
As soon as it has been laid down, even though the owners have the intention, "Let it carry [the load]," it is a *pārājika* offense because they have not given the command.
However, even without laying it on the shoulder, for one who causes it to move even by the amount of a hair from the head, it is a *pārājika*.
But in the case of a double load where one part rests on the head and the other on the back, the legal determination is made according to those two locations.

This should be understood. However, this has been stated specifically with reference to the burden of the head alone. Furthermore, whatever determination has been stated regarding the burden of the head should be understood to apply equally to the burden of the aggregates and so forth.
"Goods deposited" refers to goods placed in one's own hands by others for the purpose of protection. I...
The connection is with the words "I do not take. This is a present-tense verb used in the sense of the past; the meaning is, "I have not taken.

There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) even for a conscious lie, because it constitutes a preliminary act to the taking of what is not given. Even for one who says things such as, "What are you saying?
This is neither suitable for me, nor for you," there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing. [This applies when causing] doubt in the owner...
"Causes doubt to arise" means that she causes doubt in the husband’s mind by thinking, "I placed this in his hand in private; no one else knows of it.
Will he give it to me, or not? "Lays down the burden" means that, having seen his harshness and so forth, she abandons her effort.
In that case, if the monk is still intent on giving, thinking, "I will give it to him even after making him weary," he is protected.
To that extent: if he is disinterested in giving it away, but the owner of the goods is intent on taking it back, [the monk] still guards it.

However, if he is disinterested in giving it away and the owner of the goods also gives up the effort, thinking, "He will not give it to me," then through the relinquishment of effort by both, the monk incurs a *pārājika* offense. Even if he says with his mouth, "I will give it."
However, if one is unwilling to give because of the mind [of theft], even by thus relinquishing the responsibility to the owner, it is a *pārājika* for the bhikkhu.
Having thought, "I will take the goods along with the carrier," meaning "I will take the goods together with the carrier of the goods.
He steps across the first foot: having threatened the carrier and blocked his path, he takes the path of his own choosing.
He steps over with one foot. "Placed on dry land" means set upon dry ground;
the meaning is that it has been placed anywhere—on the surface of the earth, on a rock, a mountain top, or the like—whether in a concealed or unconcealed spot. "He makes it quiver;
a grave offense (thullaccaya)" means that for whoever makes it quiver, there is a grave offense for each individual act of effort; for the mere touching, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The *thullaccaya* for moving [the object] and the *thullaccaya* for touching occur separately for one who performs the respective acts of touching and moving with the intention to steal.
However, they say that "for one who takes it in a single act, there is only a *pārājika* upon its removal, and not the *dukkaṭa* or *thullaccaya* offenses.
From the place where it stands means from the spot where it is situated. If that which is on dry land is heaped up, [it is considered to be] inside the vessel.
It should be determined by the decision regarding the cutting of a hand or a fist contained within a vessel.
If it is a single mass, such as resin or exudate, it should be determined by the decision regarding cooked honey or molasses.

If it is heavy and bound together, such as a lump of iron, a jar of ghee, or a jar of honey, it should be determined by the decision regarding its displacement from its place in a pot. And for that which is bound by chains, there is a distinction regarding its location.

It must be observed. However, if one takes hold of a woolen rug, a mat, or similar object that has been spread out and pulled straight toward oneself, there is an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*) when the point of contact at the far edge passes beyond the near edge.

Likewise, if one takes hold of it in that same way and pushes it away, there is an offense entailing defeat when the point of contact at the far edge passes beyond the near edge. Or [if one pulls or pushes] from the left or the right...
Or, for one who is removing [the object], when the space touched by the left side or the right side has been passed by the right side or the left side, it is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika).
If one removes it after wrapping it up, it is an offense entailing defeat for one who makes even a hair’s breadth of it enter into the air.

"With one's own hand" (sahattho) means: that which is produced by one's own hand, or that which belongs to one's own hand; this is "taking by one's own hand" (sāhatthiko), namely, the act of theft. "Commanding" (āṇāpanaṃ) [is the next category].
An *āṇatti* is an order; the theft produced by that order is *āṇattika*. *Nissajjana* is relinquishing;
it is the act of casting goods outside while standing in a customs station or a designated place; thus, relinquishing itself is *nissaggiya*.

It is called "accomplishing the purpose" (*atthasādhaka*) because it effects the objective—namely, the offense of defeat (*pārājika*)—even prior to the completion of the physical action. Of the "burden" (*dhura*), which is to say, the accumulation...
The laying down of the burden (*bhāra*), the relinquishing, the reaching a state of effortlessness, is the casting off of the yoke (*dhuranikkhepa*).

Now, without paying attention to the literal phrasing (*byañjana*) and showing only their essential meaning (*atthamatta*), he said: "In that regard, what is called 'by one's own hand' (*sāhatthika*)," and so forth.
*Sahatthā* means "with one's own hand. This is an ablative form used in the sense of the instrumental. [He says: "Steal such-and-such a person's goods," [addressing] another...
Regarding the phrase "he commands," here too the offense should be understood as occurring at the very moment of the command.

If this is so, what is the distinction between this [type of command] and one that accomplishes the purpose? The application of a command consists in enjoining someone to take possession at that very moment, whereas a command that accomplishes the purpose consists in enjoining them for the sake of taking possession at a later time;
this is the distinction between the two. For this very reason it was said: "When you are able to take the goods of such-and-such a person..."
"Then he carries it off or causes it to be carried off.
Regarding the phrase "customs houses and designated places": *suṅkaghātaparikappitokāsā* means customs houses (*suṅkaghāta*) and designated places (*parikappitokāsa*); [the compound refers] to those.
Therein, "customs house" (*suṅkaghāta*) refers to a place for collecting tolls that has been demarcated by signs such as trees, mountains, and so forth.

This is a synonym. For it is because those who carry goods out from there without paying the king’s share or the toll (*suṅka*) "strike" (destroy) the king’s toll—that is, they ruin it—therefore it is called a "toll-house" (*suṅkaghāta*).
Someone who has entered another’s monastery enclosure or similar place, having seen some object capable of arousing greed, [might act] by way of the gate-front and so forth...
The "imagined place" is that situation where one imagines: "If they see me in the meantime, I will show it to them as if I were carrying it about out of a desire to be seen;
but if they do not see me, I will take it away. At the very moment of the command, there is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*);
that is, at the very moment of the volition that accomplishes the purpose, there is an offense of defeat. Even if the thief [delays] for more than sixty years...
He steals that merchandise; however, the sender dies along the way, or returns to a lower state, or having ceased to be a monastic, will either die or return to a lower state.

But for the thief, it is an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika) at the very moment of stealing. Regarding the phrase "oil worth a quarter-coin" (pādagghanakatela), here "quarter" (pāda) means one-fourth part of a kahāpaṇa; it is so called because it is worth that amount.
"Pādagghanaka-tela" means a quarter-kaḥāpa coin and that oil; thus, "oil worth a quarter-kaḥāpa. "Sandals and so forth" refers to those items beginning with sandals.
By the word "and so forth," there is the inclusion of fine cotton cloths, leather pieces, and the like.
"He puts it inside" means he puts it inside with a thieving mind. Therefore he said: "It is an offense involving defeat (pārājika) at the very moment it leaves the hand," provided that—

If someone else pours ghee or oil into one's own pot, and one then, with a mind of theft, places a vessel for drinking oil therein, it is an offense of defeat (*pārājika*) by the method already stated.
Application (*payoga*) consists of the employment of body or speech, that is, giving an order; this is so because it precedes the taking of the goods by the one who has been ordered.

"Pubba" means "prior"; thus, that which is both prior and an application (*payoga*) is a "prior application" (*pubbapayoga*). An act of theft (*avahāra*) occurring together with such an application is "with application" (*sahapayoga*).
"Concerted theft" (*saṃvidhāvahāra*) is the taking away after having made an agreement, being united as one, and having deliberated;

what is meant is that it is a theft committed through the arising of mutual consent. "Convention" (*saṅketa*) is the recognition [of time] by way of delimiting periods such as "forenoon" (*pubbaṇha*); its function is...
*Saṅketakammaṃ* (the act of agreement). *Nimittakammaṃ* means the act of a sign; the meaning is the making of some sign for the purpose of producing recognition.

*Tattha* refers to the five [factors], beginning with the preliminary effort (*pubbapayoga*), as previously stated. "By transferring the barren soil (*khila*) and so forth, and by taking possession of the field (*khettādi*)" means:
having transferred the barren soil, the rope, the fence, the boundary, or the wall.
It is by means of taking possession of a field—whether by transferring a boundary marker, a rope, a fence, a limit, or a wall—and by means of taking possession of a site.
However, if it is to be taken by means of two boundary markers, there is a *thullaccaya* (grave offense) at the first marker and a *pārājika* (defeat) at the second.
If it is to be taken by means of three, there is a *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing) at the first, a *thullaccaya* at the second, and a *pārājika* at the third.

In this way, even when there are many [plaintiffs], having set aside two at the end, for those preceding there is a *dukkaṭa*; for one of the two at the end there is a *thullaccaya*, and by the other, a *pārājika*.
This same method applies to the transfer of ownership of fields and so forth. As for what is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
"And that is by the relinquishing of responsibility by the owners," that refers to such passages as: "If he sues for a field, there is an offense of *dukkaṭa*."
Because it is stated in the context of [the specific] authority, it should be understood as referring to grasping by way of application (*abhiyoga*).
"Having made an agreement" (*saṃvidahitvā*) is a synonym for this very term. "Having consulted together" (*saṃmantayitvā*) means having spoken with a single desire and a single intention.

In order to avoid confusion regarding this act of taking, he said: "When they have gone after having thus made an agreement," and so forth. "The act of identification" (*sañjānanakamma*) refers to the delimitation of time, such as the morning and so on.
It is for the purpose of making a sign. Therefore he said, "If indeed," and so forth.
And here, when it is stated, "Steal before the meal," whether one steals today before the meal, or tomorrow, or in a future year, there is no discrepancy in the agreement;
for both, it is a *pārājika* offense. But if [it is said], "Today, before the meal..."
When told, "Steal it," he steals it on the following day. If he steals it later, having transgressed the appointment fixed for "today," it is considered stolen after [the appointed time].

If, when told, "Steal it tomorrow before the meal," he steals it today before the meal, it is considered stolen prematurely, having failed to reach that appointment fixed for "tomorrow. For one who steals in this manner, it is the thief himself who is guilty.

It is a *pārājika* offense; there is no offense for one who has established the root-condition (*mūlaṭṭha*). When it is said, "Tomorrow, before the meal," even if one steals on that very day, or tomorrow after the meal, one is stealing both before and after that appointment.

However, he who does not act thus, but steals only at the time specifically delimited, should be understood as stealing that which is neither before nor after the appointment. This same method applies to the periods after the meal and during the night.

In this context, the nature of the convention and non-convention should be understood by way of the first watch, the middle watch, the last watch, the dark fortnight, the bright fortnight, the month, the season, and the year.

Because it is the cause for the arising of the perception of taking another's property, the winking of the eyes and so forth are the "signs"; thus, they are called "the making of signs such as winking the eyes.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there are many other types [of signs], such as raising the eyebrows, shaking the head, jumping with the hands, striking with the palms, snapping the fingers, craning the neck, and rising from one's seat.
He gathers [them]. The rest here is exactly according to the method explained under the heading of "conventional acts" (*saṅketakamma*).

*Thena* means a thief; its state is *theyya* (theft). Taking away by means of that is *theyyāvahāra* (taking by theft). Taking away by force, having overcome [the victim], is *pasayhāvahāra* (taking by force).
Determining and fashioning [an object] such as a cloth or a thread is *parikappa*; taking away by means of that is [the offense of] *parikappāvahāra*.
*Parikappāvahāra* (fraudulent taking by artifice). *Paṭicchannāvahāra* (concealed taking) is the taking of what is hidden by grass, leaves, and so forth.
*Kusāvahāra* (taking with a blade of grass) is taking [something] by means of a blade of grass. Regarding "by means of false measures, false coins, and so forth":

here, a false measure (*mānakūṭa*) is threefold, according to the deception of the heart (*hadaya*), the deception of the top (*sikhā*), and the deception of the cord (*rajju*). Among these, the "heart" refers to the interior of measuring vessels such as the *nāḷi*; its deception is...
Making a hole means piercing the heart; this occurs at the time of taking up ghee, oil, and the like.
For one who takes these, having said "pour slowly" while using a measuring vessel with a hole at the bottom, causes much of the liquid to flow out into the container before taking it;
and when giving, one covers the hole and gives quickly after filling [the recipient's vessel].

The "fraud with the crest" (*sikhābheda*) occurs at the time of measuring sesame, rice, and so forth. For one who takes these, he does so by slowly raising the crest; one who gives them, however, fills [the measure] quickly and gives while cutting off the crest.

The "fraud with the cord" (*rajjubheda*) occurs at the time of measuring fields and lands. For those measuring fields and such, they measure even what is not large as large, and what is large as not large.

A counterfeit coin made of copper, bronze, or other materials is a "counterfeit kahāpaṇa" (*kūṭakahāpaṇa*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [one includes] fraud with scales, fraud with bronze-measures, deception, and so on.
He includes [this]. In that regard, cheating with the balance is fourfold: cheating by the form, cheating by the limb, cheating by the grasping, and cheating by concealment.
Therein, "cheating by the form" means making two balances identical in appearance;
when taking, one takes with the larger one, and when giving, one gives with the smaller one. "Cheating by the limb" means that when taking, one holds the balance with the hand at the back...
Regarding "stepping on": when taking, one steps on it at the front; when giving, one steps on it at the front.

"The deception of grasping" means that when taking, one grasps the rope at the base, but when giving, one grasps it at the tip. "The deception of concealment" means that having made a hollow in the scale and filled the inside with iron filings, one places it at the rear when taking, but at the front when giving.
*Kaṃsa* refers to a golden bowl; deception by means of that is *kaṃsakūṭa*. How so? Having fashioned one golden bowl, they make two or three other bowls of iron with a golden color.
Then, having gone to a district and entered some wealthy family, they say, "Buy golden vessels," and when asked the price, they wish to give them at a lower price.

[They] were there. Then, when they asked, "How is it to be known whether these are gold?", he said, "Examine them and take them," and having rubbed a golden bowl against stones and given away all the bowls, he departed.
Deceit (vañcanā) means deceiving others by various means. In this regard, there is this one story: it is said that once...
The hunter returned carrying both a deer and a fawn. A certain rogue asked him, "Sir, what is the price of the deer?

What is the price of the fawn? When he was told, "The deer is worth two kahāpaṇas, and the fawn is worth one," the rogue gave him one kahāpaṇa, took the fawn, and after walking a short distance, turned back and said, "Sir, I have no need for the fawn."
“Give me a deer,” he said. “In that case, give me two kahāpaṇas,” he replied. He said, “But sir, did you not already give me one kahāpaṇa?
“Yes, it was given; take this young fawn. Thus, there will be two kahāpaṇas:
that one kahāpaṇa and this young fawn, which is worth a kahāpaṇa. Perceiving that he was speaking with reason, he agreed.
"Having taken a fawn, she gave it to the deer.
*Pasayha* means having overcome others. *Gāmaghātakā* means village-destroyers; these are thieves who strike at the village.
Those of whom they are the first are "the village-destroyers and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), highwaymen and others are included here. Only [in the case of] plundering...
*Pārājika*: This is because the intention "If there will be a cloth, I shall take it" has arisen as a mental construction (*parikappa*), and because a cloth was actually present there.
"He must be made to pay by the foot-step" is said because he examined [the object] without having set it down on the ground.
*Bhaṇḍadeyya*: The meaning is that the price of what was lost by another, or that very same article, must be given.
“Of him” means of one who imagines in this way; it is connected with the phrase “there is the taking away.
“Of others” means of other people who are playing or entering [the place]. “He conceals it with dust or with leaves, thinking, ‘I will take it later’” means:
“If I were to bend down and take it right now, [people would ask], ‘Why is the ascetic taking it?’”
Thinking, “If they know me, they might harass me; I will take it later,” one conceals it with dust or leaves.
“There is no removal” means there is no displacement from its place. “The owners” refers to the people who are the owners of the goods and who wish to enter the village boundary.
“Removal” (uddhāra) means in the sense of taking away; the meaning is displacement from its place. And here, displacement from its place is to be understood according to the method explained below.

It should be understood thus. "Inserts" means he inserts by way of displacing it from its place; the meaning is that he inserts it so as to pass beyond even a hair’s breadth of the space touched by the lower edge with the upper edge.
"Of less value" means of lesser worth. "Theft is committed merely upon its being extracted" because the application of its own nature has been brought to completion.
Not by way of accomplishing the purpose. In the case of "he protects during the removal," it is because he has removed [the portion] with the desire to cast it into his own share.
This same method applies to the phrase "he also protects during the casting down.

Although the meaning "he does not protect during the casting down" is already established by the statement "he protects only during the removal," the passage beginning with "having removed that" is given to demonstrate the meaning by way of accomplishing the purpose.

It has been said. However, if he causes the stick that fell within both portions to disappear, then when the remaining monks have departed, the other says, "Venerable sir, my stick is not to be seen. [The first] replies, "Friend, mine is not to be seen either.
[The other asks], "But which portion, venerable sir, is mine? [The first] shows his own portion, saying, "This is your portion."
Whether they have quarreled over it or not, once he has taken it and departed, the other sets aside his share;
at the moment of setting it aside, there is a *pārājika* offense. Even if the first person says, "I will not give my share to you;

you take your own share after identifying it," and the other, although knowing "this is not mine," nevertheless takes that very share, at the moment of setting it aside... [there is a *pārājika* offense].
It is a *pārājika* offense. However, if the other person, thinking, "This is your share, this is my share—what is the use of this dispute?

says, "Let the bowl belong to me or to you; whichever is the superior portion, you take that," then it is considered "given" (*dinnaka*) and taken; there is no theft (*avahāra*) here. If that monk is afraid of a dispute...
When told, "Take whatever you like," one sets aside the best portion of one's own bowl and takes only the inferior part;
in that case, there is no theft even for the other person who takes what remains after the selection.
Thus, by combining these five groups of five, these twenty-five types of theft are to be understood. The section on "should take" is finished.
This is the analysis of this term. Therefore he said: "Thus, that which was stated... [etc. ...the meaning of which has been clarified.
Although the word "kings" (*rājāno*) is stated without distinction, it is intended here specifically for those who possess authority as judges in matters of punishment corresponding to the offense;
thus he said: "The phrase 'kings' is spoken with reference to Bimbisāra alone," for he, being a righteous king (*dhammika-rāja*), [possessed such authority].
He acts according to the very sequence [of the offense]. However, others might cut off the head for even a mere *kākaṇika* coin, or they might do nothing at all even for a great amount.
Therefore he said, "But others," and so forth. "Killing" means both striking and cutting; thus he said, "with hands, etc.," and so forth.
By the word "etc.," there is the inclusion of foot-stools, whips, half-staffs, and the like. "By means of binding with ropes, etc. means...
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of binding with ropes, binding with shackles, house arrest, city confinement, and guard-oversight.
"They would expel them" means they would drive them out from the kingdom. Regarding the phrases "You are a thief...

you are a robber," the word "they would revile" (*paribhāseyyun*) must be supplied here because of the deficiency in the syntactical construction. Therefore he said: "They would revile them with these words."
However, since it depends on the specific form [of the offense] starting from the foot, he says: "Of a *pāda* or of what is worth a *pāda*.
A *pāda* is one-fourth of an ancient *kahāpaṇa*. That which is worthy of a *pāda* is "worth a *pāda*" (*pādāraho*); [the phrase refers to] "of that *pāda* or of what is worth a *pāda*.
And here, by the term *pāda*, only an unallowable commodity (*akappiyabhaṇḍa*) worth one-fourth of a *kahāpaṇa* is meant.

It shows a suitable article for the feet worth one foot-measure. At this point, it should be understood that by showing the lower limit, the basis for constituting the second *pārājika* offense has been demonstrated in every respect.

"Of an ancient coin" means of a coin produced in accordance with ancient teachers, endowed with the proper characteristics, and resembling a blue *kahāpaṇa*. By this, [coins such as] *rudradāmaka* and others are excluded.
Having thus shown the specific determination (*asādhāraṇa-vinicchaya*), he now says "In Rājagaha," etc., in order to show the general determination (*sādhāraṇa-vinicchaya*).
"Of the king" means of King Bimbisāra. A *māsaka* is the twentieth part of an ancient *kahāpaṇa*; it is also called "mañjeṭṭhī" in the world.
Now, in order to show the determination regarding this taking of what is not given (*adinnādāna*), he says "In all cases," etc.
It has been stated. "In all cases" refers to [theft] involving less than a māsaka, more than a māsaka, or five māsakas.

"By way of whether the value has been diminished or not" means by way of whether the value has been reduced or not. This is the summary here; however, the detailed explanation should be understood as follows:
for one who is deciding upon this offense of taking what is not given, when the matter has been brought forward, one should not decide hastily, but rather [consider] the five...
The following points must be considered. With reference to these, the ancients said:
"The wise person, having weighed five factors— The object, the time, the place, The value, and fifthly, the use— Should accept it for his own benefit."
In this context, "the object" (*vatthu*) means the goods. For even when the thief says, "I have stolen such-and-such," one must not yet charge him with an offense;
rather, that property must be investigated to see whether it has an owner or is ownerless.

Even if it has an owner, one must investigate whether the owners still have an attachment (*sālayabhāva*) for it or are without attachment (*nirālayabhāva*). If, at the time they still have an attachment...
Having had the stolen goods appraised, the offense should be determined. If it was taken at a time when there were no owners present, one should not be charged with a *pārājika* offense.
However, when the owners of the goods come to have them recovered, the goods must be returned; this is the proper procedure in such a case. Thus should the matter be examined.
As for "time," it refers to the time of the theft. For that very same article may sometimes be of low value and sometimes of great value. Therefore—
At whatever time that article was stolen, at that very time its value must be determined; by that value, the offense is to be adjudicated.
In this way, the time is to be considered.
As for "place," it refers to the place of theft. For at whatever place that article was stolen, at that very place its [value is to be determined].

Value: by that value the offense must be adjudicated. For the goods are of lesser value at the place where they were located, but of greater value elsewhere. Thus the location must be considered. "Value" means the value of the goods;
for whatever is the value of new goods, that subsequently diminishes, just as [the luster of] freshly washed [cloth fades].
A bowl worth eight or ten [units] later becomes of little value if it is broken, cracked, or damaged by the knot-fastening;
therefore, the value of an article should not always be determined solely by its original price. Thus should the value be examined.
"Use" refers to the use of the article. For even through use, the value of articles such as axes and the like diminishes.

Therefore, it should be investigated in this way: if someone steals an axe worth one quarter of a coin from another person, the owner of the axe should be asked, "For how much did you buy this axe? He replies, "For a quarter, venerable sir.
[The owner asks], "But did you keep it after buying it, or did you use it? If he says, "One day I used it as a tooth-stick..."
“Whether it be a piece of dyed bark or a piece of wood for boiling cloth, if it has been cut, or rubbed, or sharpened,” then its former value is lost;

this should be understood. And just as with an adze, so too with a collyrium box, or a collyrium stick, or a key, or straw, or husks, or brick-dust—if they have been used even once by being rubbed, then [the value is lost] merely by washing them.
It is destroyed by the mere rubbing of a three-tiered bowl with a shark-tooth scraper; by the single act of wearing a bathing robe as an undergarment or an upper garment;
by the mere placing of it on the shoulder or the head for the purpose of use; by the shaking off of rice and so forth;
even by removing one or two grains from it; and at the very least, by picking out a single pebble or stone.
The value is forfeited even by merely discarding it; even by transferring the contents of vessels containing ghee, oil, and so forth;
even by merely removing a fly or an ant from them before discarding them;

or even by scratching with a fingernail and taking a mere atom-sized portion for the purpose of testing the sweetness of a lump of sugar. Therefore, anything worth even a penny (pāda) [is subject to forfeiture].
In the manner already described, it is the owner who has made the item deficient through his own use; therefore, the monk who took it should not be dealt with according to a *pārājika* offense.
In this way, the use [of the object] should be examined.
Having thus weighed these five points, a discerning person should maintain the meaning—whether it be an offense or no offense, whether heavy or light—and should place the offense in its proper place.
Having thus shown the determination of the offense in that case, he now says "of one who perceives it as her own" (*sakasaññissa*) and so forth, in order to show the non-offense (*anāpatti*).

Therein, "of one who perceives it as her own" means: for one who takes even another's property while perceiving it as her own, thinking, "This article belongs to me," there is no offense at the time of taking;
however, what has been taken must be returned. If she is told by the owners, "Give it back," [she must do so].
If he does not give it back, there is a *pārājika* offense when he has abandoned his responsibility for it. Taking on trust means that even in the case of taking on trust, there is no offense.
However, the definition of taking on trust should be understood from this Sutta:

"I allow you, monks, to take on trust from one who possesses five qualities: he is a kinsman, he is a friend, he is someone with whom one converses, he is living, and he knows: 'He will be pleased when I have taken [the goods].'"
In this context: "A friend seen" (*sandiṭṭha*) means a mere acquaintance. "An associate" (*sambhatta*) means a firm friend.
"One addressed" (*ālapita*) means one who has been told: "Whatever you wish from my belongings, you may take; there is no need to ask for permission when taking.

"While he lives" (*jīvati*) means as long as he has not reached the cessation of the life-faculty, even though he lies on his back due to inactivity. And "delighted when it is taken" (*gahite ca attamano*).
When it has been taken, he is pleased in mind. It is permissible for one who knows that "he will be satisfied when it is taken" to take what belongs to such a person.
These five factors have been stated by way of taking everything without remainder. However, borrowing on trust succeeds through three factors. How so?
He is a personal acquaintance, he is living, and he is pleased when it is taken; he is a trusted friend, he is living, and... [he is pleased when it is taken].
"Contented when it was taken, addressed, and living"—thus it is said.
However, in the case of one who lives but is not contented when [the property] was taken, even if his belongings were taken on the basis of trust, they must be returned again.
And when returning them, first regarding the wealth of the deceased, those who are masters over that wealth—whether householders or renunciants—[should be informed].
Or, it should be given to them. If he is displeased, the property must be returned to him alone.

However, one who has already expressed approval—either by verbal expression or merely by a thought—saying at the very outset, "You have done well in taking what belongs to me," does not deserve to have it taken back from him even if he later becomes angry for some reason. And as for one who is unwilling to give it back, [he must be dealt with accordingly].
However, he accepts it with his mind and says nothing; even he is not permitted to ask for it back again.
But if someone says, "I have taken what belongs to you," or "I have used it"—whether it has been taken or used—he may say:
"I have set that aside for some particular purpose; it is proper to restore it to its original state."
If he says this, he is permitted to have it returned.
Regarding "borrowed for a short time": there is no offense even in taking something borrowed for a short time by one who says, "I will return it" or "I will restore it.
However, if the owner of the goods—whether an individual or a group—gives permission, saying, "Let this remain yours," [then there is no offense].
This is wholesome. If he does not grant permission, it must be given when they bring it back. However, as for what belongs to the Saṅgha, it is permissible only to return it.

Regarding "the possession of the *petas*": here, all those who have been reborn in the realm of *petas*, those who have died and been reborn in that very same personal existence (*attabhāva*), and even the gods of the Four Great Kings and above—all these are reckoned simply as "*petas*"; [it refers to] their possession.
There is no offense. However, for those performing an offering of food (balikamma) dedicated to a deity, there is nothing at all to be said regarding garments hung on trees and the like.
But this applies only when they have not been claimed as property by guardians; it is not permitted to take what has been so claimed.
"Claimed by non-human beings" (tiracchānagatapariggaha) refers to the possession of non-human beings such as nāgas, supaṇṇas, and others. For even if...

If a deva, nāga, or supaṇṇa sets up a shop in human form, and a monk possessing the divine eye recognizes it as such and takes what belongs to them and departs, it is permissible. Regarding "one who perceives it as a rag-robe":
there is no offense even if one takes it while perceiving, "This is a rag-robe without an owner. If...
However, if that [stolen property] has an owner, it must be given back when those who seek it come forward. The cases of the insane and so forth are exactly as previously described.

In this context, Dhaniya is the first offender (*ādikammika*). For the rest—namely, the thieves of the dyers’ baskets and so forth, including the group of six monks (*chabbaggiya*)—there is indeed an offense.
It is called "originating from taking what is not given" because it originates through the three origins involving volition (*sacittaka*). Likewise...
For that which is "by means of the hand" (sāhatthika) arises from both body and mind. That which is "by command" (āṇattika) arises from speech and mind.
That which is "both by means of the hand and by command" (sāhatthikāṇattika) arises from body, speech, and mind; however, this is obtained when, having made an agreement such as, "This is heavy;
you take one side, I will take the other," there is the displacement of a single object through the combined effort of both. This is called "bodily and vocal action."
However, silence [is not an offense] because, in such a case, it is merely a factor of body and speech.
