Rather, one must determine the offense by way of that volition which, having originated the application (payoga)—whether manual or through command—accomplishes the displacement from the place as its primary function.
Otherwise, manual action would not be a factor for a command, nor would a command [be a factor for manual action].
This contradicts [the definition of] "with one's own hand. It is "liberation through perception" because one is exempted due to the absence of the perception, "I am taking what is not given.
Bodily action is *kāyakamma*; the meaning is that it is performed by way of the body-door. The same principle applies here to "vocal action" (*vacīkamma*).
It is "threefold feeling" because one engages in it while being either pleased, afraid, or neutral. The rest is as in the first training rule.
It should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.
The commentary on the second *pārājika* is finished.
3. Commentary on the third *pārājika*.
There are prepositions (*upasagga*) used with the verbal root itself. Along with that, this is a term expressing exertion (*ussukka*); thus he said "having intentionally" (*sañciccā*), and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "a term expressing exertion," here "a term expressing exertion" refers to a word denoting an action occurring at a prior time.

For this is the grammatical designation for a word denoting a prior-time action among words denoting actions occurring at prior and subsequent times when they share the same agent (*samānakattuka*). Now, "together with... [the text continues].
Having stated the very same point briefly with the words "having intended," he says "a living being" (*pāṇo*) and so forth in order to make that meaning clear.
Therein, "with the perception itself" means without abandoning the perception "a living being"; what is meant is: immediately after the arising of the perception "a living being.
And having done so [by explaining the sequence], one might ask: how can there be two objects for a single consciousness at one and the same moment?
Such an objection should be regarded as having no basis. However, some maintain:

"Just as through the full understanding by knowledge (*ñātapariññā*) one applies the three characteristics (*tilakkhaṇa*) to phenomena whose intrinsic nature has been seen, and simultaneously with that knowledge of their intrinsic nature—such as 'form is impermanent'—one knows the characteristic of impermanence and so forth;
likewise, simultaneously with the perception (*saññā*) 'this is a living being,' one knows 'I do not kill.'"
Others, however, do not speak thus even in that regard.

And here, instead of saying "a human form," the word "living being" (*pāṇo*) is used in order to show that it constitutes a *pārājika* offense even for one who kills with the mere perception of a sentient being, without knowing "this is a human.
"Having intended" (*cetetvā*) means having thought; "having planned" (*pakappetvā*) means having deliberated thoroughly.
The meaning is: "having made a definitive determination.
Now, in order to show the human existence starting from the beginning, he said, "the human form," and so forth.
Therein, "starting from the *kalala*" means starting from the *kalala*-matter that arises together with the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhiviññāṇa*). The *kalala*-matter...
For women and men, there are thirty material phenomena by way of the body-base decad; for those who are neuter, there are twenty by way of the body-base decad.
Therein, the embryonic matter (*kalala-rūpa*) of women and men is as clear and translucent as a drop of oil drawn up by a single fiber from a lotus stalk.
For this has been said in the Commentary:
“As a drop of clarified butter, unmixed, in a test tube,
so too is that which resembles [that] color called ‘kalala.
Thus, beginning with this minute substance, it gradually reaches full growth in the interval until the time of death.
It is said that "individual existence" (*attabhāva*) means a human form. And this is stated by way of the majority [of cases].

For even humans who are of spontaneous birth (*opapātika*) or moisture-born (*saṃsedaja*) are subject to the grounds for a *pārājika* offense. "Even at the stage of the *kalala*" means even during the first seven days.

For it is possible to deprive of life the individual existence reckoned as a *kalala* that proceeds there by way of the continuity of existence (*santati*), but not [the embryo] at the very first moment.
The form of the *kalala*. For together with the rebirth-linking consciousness (*paṭisandhicitta*), thirty types of kamma-born material phenomena (*rūpa*) arise.

While those [material phenomena] persist, sixteen life-continuum consciousnesses (*bhavaṅgacitta*) arise and cease. During this interval, there is no danger for the child who has taken rebirth-linking, nor for his mother.
This is indeed called "the non-period of death. By means of providing medicine...

“By giving medicine for causing abortion. “And even beyond that” means even in the case of the *abbuda*, *pesi*, and other such stages. “Should deprive of life” means one should cause it to be removed from the life-faculty (*jīvitindriya*) by way of disrupting the continuity (*santati*).
“But of this matter” refers to the meaning of the phrase: “If one should intentionally deprive a human being of life.”
"Āvibhāvatthaṃ" means for the purpose of making manifest. "Pāṇassa atipāto" is "pāṇātipāto"; what is meant is the taking of life, the killing of a living being.

"Satta" refers to the continuum of the aggregates (khandhasantāna), for it is there that the designation "being" (satta) applies. "Jīvitindriyaṃ" refers to both the material and immaterial life-faculty (rūpārūpajīvitindriya).
For when the material life-faculty is disrupted, the other [the immaterial] also perishes due to its connection with it. "Yāya cetanāya" means by which volition...

When there is a living being and one perceives it as such, by means of that volition which proceeds through either the door of body or the door of speech—however, there is no state of killing for the murderous volition that proceeds through the mind-door.

"That volition" refers to the murderous volition proceeding through either the door of body or the door of speech, which originates the effort that cuts off the life-faculty. This is what is meant: by whichever volition...

When the great primary elements (mahābhūta) that serve as the support for the life-faculty (jīvitindriya) are subjected to an external assault, the great primary elements arising conditioned by those [assaulted] elements will not come into existence;
the volition (cetanā) that initiates such an application is the taking of life (pāṇātipāta).
For when the great primary elements have received an assault, they are no longer clear like the other [unassaulted] elements, and thus they do not act as causes for those of their own kind.
One who has the taking of life is a "taker of life" (*pāṇātipātī*). This *i* vowel is used here for the sake of euphonic conjunction (*saṃsagge*).

Therefore he said: "the person endowed with the aforementioned volition. One's own hand is "with one's own hand" (*sahattho*); the means of action produced by that is "by one's own hand" (*sāhatthiko*). Relinquishing is "relinquishment" (*nissaggo*);

that which consists of relinquishment is "by relinquishment" (*nissaggiyo*). Likewise is "by command" (*āṇattiko*). That which consists of knowledge is the application of the recitation of mantras. That which consists of psychic power is that which consists of the psychic power born of the maturation of karma.
Now, in order to explain those same six modes of action by analyzing them, the passage beginning with “Therein” was stated.
Therein, “therein” means among those six modes of action. Regarding “by one’s own hand,” since the hand is taken here as a representative illustration, he says “or by the body,” and so forth.
Therein, “by the body” means by the hand, or by the foot, or by the fist, or by the knee.

"By any limb or member whatsoever. Here, "a part of the body" refers to the hand and so forth; it is a metaphorical designation of the whole by means of its parts, as in the expression, "the village has been burned. "By something connected to the body" means by a weapon such as a sword that has not been released from the body.

"A weapon" is intended here as that which accomplishes the desired object through the volition to kill, accompanied by bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti). Or, [it may be accomplished] by the body itself.
The relinquishing of spears and the like, or of whistling-stones and the like connected with the body, should be applied as appropriate.
"Therein" means among those offenses involving relinquishment by hand (*sāhatthika-nissaggiya*).

"By way of the distinction between designated and non-designated" means by way of the distinction in their occurrence as having been designated (*uddissa*) or not designated (*anuddissa*). "Designation" (*uddisa*) is the act of designating; that which has this [designation] is "one who designates" (*uddisaka*), namely, the application [of the action].

In that [context]. It is "bound" (*baddha*) because one is bound by this; thus, "bound by karma" (*kammabaddha*) means karma itself is the bond. Alternatively, "bond" (*baddha*) means binding; "bound by karma" (*kammabaddha*) means bound by action. This [bond] belongs to him;

what is meant is that the karma of killing living beings has been accomplished for him. "In both cases" refers to both the *uddisaka* (the one who designates) and the *anuddisaka* (the one who does not designate). Or, afterwards...

The construction is: "May he die from that very same disease. "At the very moment of being struck" means that at the very instant the blow sufficient for death is received, one becomes bound by karma.
This is the intended meaning: that if one must inevitably die because of it.

However, if, after giving a blow with the intention of causing death, another blow is given with a different state of mind while the person has not yet died, then even subsequently, [the result] is due to the first blow alone.
If he dies from that first blow, then he is bound by the kamma. If he dies from the second blow, there is no offense of taking life.
Even if he dies from both blows, he is bound by the kamma of the first blow alone; if he does not die from either, there is no offense of taking life.
This same principle applies when many people give a single blow. For even in that case, he is bound by the kamma of whichever blow causes his death.
“Commanding” (*āṇāpana*) means the accomplishment of the intended purpose by means of a murderous volition accompanied by verbal intimation (*vacī-viññatti*).
Now, in order to show the sixfold rule for the purpose of knowing the state of being signaled or unsignaled within this practice of commanding, he says “*tattha*,” etc.
Therein, “*tattha*” means in that practice of commanding. “The determinants of the command” (*āṇatti-niyāmaka*)...
It is that which accomplishes the application of an order. For it is only when these [factors] have not failed that there is the application of an order, and not otherwise.
"The person" refers to the person to be killed. Therefore he said, "Whichever," and so forth.

"The offense of the commander" means the offense of the commander at the moment of giving the order, and [the offense] of the one ordered at the moment of killing. "The commander is released" means that the karmic bond attaches only to the one who was ordered.
In this context, however, there is a distinction in the action and a distinction in the offense depending on the specific basis.

One who is commanded, "Kill before the meal," and kills only before the meal [commits an offense according to the specific time]. But one who is commanded, "Kill before the meal"—without specifying whether it be "today" or "tomorrow"—kills at some point before the meal.
Furthermore, one who is told, "Today, in the morning," but kills at midday or in the evening...
Or if he kills him at his own mealtime or during the morning, there is a failure of the appointment (*visaṅketa*); the giver of the order incurs no karmic liability.

The same principle applies even if the victim dies at midday while the killer was striving to kill him during the morning. By this method, the distinction between a successful appointment and a failed appointment should be understood for all divisions of time.
Having thus shown the conventional and non-conventional nature regarding objects and times, he now says, "By this method," etc., while extending [the principle] to places and so forth.
Therein, "place" refers to a village, a forest, a house-door, and so on.
"Weapon" refers to a sword, an arrow, a spear, and so on. "Posture" refers to the posture of one who is to be killed...
“Going or sitting,” and so forth. “A specific action” refers to piercing, cutting, breaking, shaving the head with a conch-shell razor, and so forth.
In these cases, whatever manner the executioner is commanded to act, if it is done accordingly, there is an offense for the commander;
if it is done otherwise, there is a discrepancy. Therefore he said, “By this method,” and so forth. In that regard:
"In all cases" refers to the four [factors] beginning with the location. And herein it is said:
"When that which was commanded has been performed by means of the command itself, there is an offense for the commander; if it is performed otherwise than directed, there is a transgression."

Regarding the instruction (*āṇatti*), however, this is the distinction: "having resolved" (*adhiṭṭhāya*) means having made a resolution, one instructs; it should be understood that [the offense] is incurred according to the canonical text which says, "Pierce thus, strike thus, kill thus.

A pit (*opāta*) is so called because things fall into it; it is a hole. The digging of that is "pit-digging" (*opātakkhaṇana*). The provision of a support (*apassenasaṃvidhāna*) means the furnishing of a support.
A bed, a chair, or a support-board that is used constantly in the daytime place [is what is meant].
For one sitting, it is a backrest post or a tree growing there; for one standing on a walking path, it is a supporting tree or a supporting plank.
All of this is called a "support" (*apassena*) in the sense of something to lean against.
Having acted toward that support in such a way that it would pierce or cut one who leans upon it—such as with axes, hatchets, spears, arrows, thorns, and so forth—[one should train].
The meaning is: "the placing of a certain weapon.
"Setting down" (*upanikkhipana*) means placing near. "Presentation of form" (*rūpūpahāra*) is the bringing forward or placing near of a form, whether pleasing or unpleasing;
or it is standing while having assumed for oneself the guise of a *yakkha*, a *peta*, or the like. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*),...

The apprehension of sounds, tactile objects, and so forth. "In this case too" means even in the case of permanent undertakings (*thāvara-payoga*). The distinction between those undertaken for a specific purpose and those not so undertaken (*uddissa-anuddissa-bheda*) should be understood;
for even there, one becomes bound by the deed (*kamma-baddha*) in the same manner as previously explained. However, this is the distinction:
in the sense of being the "root" (*mūla*), even if others are given money for pits and such, or even for free, if anyone dies because of that, it falls upon the one who was the root-cause alone.
He is bound by the karma. Even if he himself or someone else fills that pit up until it is level with the ground,
and while the earth is being carried away or while those digging for roots are digging roots and creating a pit, or while mud forms when it rains,
if anyone there falls in or clings on and dies, the one who originally caused the pit is bound by the karma.
But if the one who obtained it, or another, makes it more extensive or more profound, and someone dies because of that, both are bound by the karma.
However, just as roots meet with roots, so too, when the dry land has been made there, one is released.
Likewise, in the case of providing a support or similar acts, as long as those actions continue, [the responsibility remains].
It should be understood that one is bound by karma according to the circumstances.
"Reciting spells" refers to the chanting of mantras by those who practice the Atharva-veda and by holders of magical knowledge (*vijjādhara*).

"By means of psychic power born of the ripening of karma" means by means of a psychic power produced by an especially potent karma, which arises simultaneously with the ripening of that karma, or by way of being the result of such karma.
Regarding "by means of the supernormal power (iddhi) that has arisen": "purpose" (payojana) means "causing to proceed," which is the sense of "instrument";

what is meant is the performance of a transformation of supernormal power born of kamma-vipāka for the sake of killing, like the fang-slicing and so forth of those whose weapons are their fangs (dāṭhāvudha).
Alternatively, this word *hāraka* is instrumental in meaning (kamasādhana), since the suffix *ṇvu* is established there by the rule of frequent usage (*bahulavidhāna*).

He says, “Or else,” and so forth. Since it is stated by way of two alternatives—that either the weapon which takes life, or the very weapon that must be placed [on the victim], is the “taker”—he says:

“It is both the weapon and the taker, thus ‘weapon-taker’ (satthahāraka). It should be understood that although one ought to say “taker-weapon” (hārakasattha), it is stated in this way by placing the qualifier at the end. “Should seek” means should search for.
By the phrase “he should act according as he obtains it,” the intended meaning (*adhippāyattha*) is expressed;
by the phrase “he should set it aside,” the literal sense (*sikhāpattattha*) is expressed. For otherwise, the meaning “he should set it aside” would not be intended for this [verb] “he should seek.
“At the very moment of having sought” means at the very moment of having searched. If that is so, then why [is it said...]?

In the Pāḷi it is said: “‘He might seek out a weapon-bearer for him’—that is, a sword, or a spear, or a javelin, or a club, or a stone, or a knife, or poison, or a rope. Thus he says, “But in the word-commentary,” and so forth.
“For him” (assa) refers to this phrase: “He might seek out a weapon-bearer for him. It is complete according to the literal expression.

Because the meaning has not been explicitly stated, it is said: "without regard for the literal expression. It is called *sattha* because it pierces (*sasati*) or harms (*hiṃsati*), or else it is called *sattha* because one pierces or harms by means of it.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the remainder of the canonical text beginning with "or a spear" (*sattiṃ vā*) is included.
Therein, *laguḷa* means a club. Whatever remains after what was mentioned as *sattha* should be understood as any sharp-edged instrument.

"One who dies thus" means one who dies by taking up a weapon, or by consuming poison, or by hanging with a rope, or by falling into chasms and the like, or by other means such as entering fire or entering water.
"He obtains wealth," and so forth, according to this method: he obtains wealth, or he obtains fame, or heaven...
Or he goes [to the other world], or the Dhamma becomes his—this is according to this method. To the question, "What is to be understood by this?", he says, "By this," and so forth.
Therein, "by this" means by the statement, "or he should praise death. "Not so here" means that here, in the case of a Pārājika offense involving a human being, it is not so;
the meaning is that one is not released by way of figurative speech (*pariyāyakathā*). Therefore he says, "he should praise," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase “‘Bring a weapon,’ etc.,” the word “etc. (ādi) includes all means of death, such as:
“Eat poison, or kill yourself by hanging with a rope, or throw yourself into a waterhole, a pit, or a precipice.
And here, what is called a “pit” (naraka) is a great chasm that has formed naturally in ground that is crumbling away in various places.
Where even elephants fall, and where thieves remain hidden. "A precipice" means a place severed on one side, either between mountains or within a coastal plain.
"By the wicked" means by that which is base. "By a miserable life" means by a life full of suffering, because it is a life of pain.
"Death is better for you than life" means that death is more excellent for you than living. "Citta" is so called because he possesses consciousness (*citta*).

The same applies to the mind (*mano*). The word "iti" should be understood here as indicating an illustration, as in such passages as: "‘Everything exists,’ Kaccāna, is one extreme; ‘nothing exists,’ Kaccāna, is the second extreme.
This is because it illustrates the death that was previously described as revolving within the intellect. For this very reason, he said: "Death is better for you than life," and so forth.
Now, one might ask: "If here too the term 'mind' (mano) is in meaning nothing other than consciousness (citta), then why was it stated? To this he says, "And here," and so forth.

It was stated for the purpose of illustrating the meaning of consciousness; this word "consciousness" does not have the sense of "variegated" and so on, as in the case of "resolve of consciousness" (cittasaṅkappa) and similar phrases, but rather it is a synonym for "consciousness" (viññāṇa).
Therefore, it was stated for the purpose of illustrating its meaning. By this, the fault of redundancy is avoided.
[The text] shows this. How is this to be understood? He says, "By that very [reason] of hers," and so forth.

One who has a *citta-saṅkappa*—that is, a thought (*saṅkappa*) of various kinds (*citto nānāppakārako*)—is one whose thought is manifold. Here, the word *citta* has the sense of "variegated" (*vicitta*), as in such passages as:
"Bhikkhus, I do not see even a single class of beings that is so variegated in mind as these animals, bhikkhus. Therefore he said:
Regarding the phrase "with a pure intention" (*vicittasaṅkappo*): here too, the word *iti* should be supplied.

Thus, even in this term *cittasaṅkappo*, the word *iti* must be supplied by virtue of the context. For although this is not explicitly stated as "thus with a mental intention" (*iti cittasaṅkappo*), it is effectively stated through the force of the context.
Furthermore, in this instance, *saṅkappa* does not refer exclusively to *vitakka* (applied thought), as in such passages as "reasoning, applied thought, intention" (*takko vitakko saṅkappo*).
The phrase "and so forth" (*saṅkappoti cā*) and so on is undertaken in order to show that it is not merely a name, but rather [the intention] of both him and others.
"Of mere coordination" (*saṃvidahanamattassa*) means of all coordination consisting of perception, volition, and thought.
Here, the word *matta* has the sense of generality (*sāmañña*), as in expressions such as "he feeds a mere Brahmin. Therefore he said, "And that coordination," and so forth. By this, coordination...
This shows that there is no fixed rule here. "Intention" (adhippāya) means thought (vitakka).
"By high and low reasons" means by great and small means.
In this regard, concerning the praise of death, the lowly nature should be understood as seeing the disadvantage in life, while the lofty nature should be understood as speaking in praise of death.
Regarding incitement [to suicide], the "high degree" should be understood as the incitement to death by means such as striking with fists or knees;
the "low degree" should be understood as the incitement to death or similar outcomes by means such as putting poison into the fingernails of one who is eating alone.
Having thus explained the non-common determination (*asādhāraṇavinicchaya*), he now spoke the words beginning with "In Vesālī" in order to show the common determination (*sādhāraṇavinicchaya*).

Regarding "an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) in digging up a pit, etc.": here, even if one digs into earth that has already been formed, because it is a preliminary act to the taking of life, there is an offense of wrong-doing for every such act.
A "human-like being" refers to an animal such as a nāga or supaṇṇa; a "human-like animal" refers to a being belonging to the animal realm who resembles a human.
"Yakkhas, petas, and human-like animals" refers to those who are yakkhas, petas, and human-like animals.

For them. By the word "thus" (*tathā*), he extends the reference to the *thullaccaya* offense. Now, by the phrase "by this method" (*iminā nayanā*) and so forth, he extends the aforementioned classification of offenses to cases such as providing support (*apassena-saṃvidhāna*) and the like.
"In all instances" (*sabbattha*) means in all applications, such as providing support and so forth.

Now, in order to show the non-offense (*anāpatti*), he says "unintentionally" (*asañcicca*) and so forth. And here, "unintentionally" refers to [the absence of] the preparatory effort (*upakkama*) that leads to death.
This was said with reference to non-deliberation; "of one who does not know," however, refers to not knowing the instrument that leads to death;
"of one who has no intention to die" refers to the absence of an intention to die even though one knows the means.
Therefore he said, "without intending," and so forth. "Without reflecting" means without deliberate consideration; it is the same as saying "having overlooked."
"As in the case of the story concerning the pestle: At that time, a certain bhikkhu, while preparing a seat in the dining hall within a house, took hold of one pestle when the pestles were raised.
The second pestle fell down and struck a young boy on the head; he died. He [the bhikkhu] was filled with remorse."
“...was it so? ... What was your state of mind, monk? “I did not intend it, Blessed One. “There is no offense, monk, for one who does not intend it,” as in this case.
And as in the case of the alms-food containing poison: “Now at that time, a certain monk who was wandering for alms...”
Having received almsfood containing poison and carried it back, he gave it to the senior monks among the bhikkhus.
Those bhikkhus died. He became anxious... [pe] ... "With what state of mind, bhikkhu, did you act?
"I did not know, Blessed One. "There is no offense, bhikkhu, for one who does not know," as in this case.
Regarding the case of medicine: At that time, a certain barren woman said to a monk who was associating with her family, "Come, venerable sir, know of some medicine by which I might give birth.
He replied, "Very well, sister," and gave her medicine. She died. He felt remorse... [as before] ...there is no offense for the monk.
As in this case [of the rule]: "For one who commits a *pārājika* offense, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Here, for those monks who were the first offenders and who killed one another, there is no offense. For the rest, such as those who praised death and so forth, there is indeed an offense.
Now, how is it a painful feeling? Is it not the case that when kings see a thief, even while laughing, they say, "Go, kill him"?
When they say [this], are they speaking the truth? They speak while laughing, yet that laughter pertains to something else;
their decisive volition (*sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā*) is indeed associated with suffering (*dukkha*). For this has been stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
"Even if a king, reclining on his royal couch and enjoying the bliss of sovereign power, were told, 'O King, a thief has been brought,' and he were to say, 'Go, kill him!'"

"One should understand that he speaks while laughing, yet speaks with a mind of displeasure (*domanassa*). However, because it is interspersed with pleasure and lacks continuous connection, this is difficult for ordinary persons (*puthujjana*) to discern.
The commentary on the third *pārājika* is concluded.
4. Commentary on the Fourth Pārājika:

"Not knowing" (*anabhijānaṃ*) means not being aware of it. For whatever state (*dhamma*) has been realized by someone, that becomes manifest to him; thus he says, "in one's own continuity" (*sakasantāne*), and so forth.
"Of superhuman beings" (*uttarimanussānaṃ*) means of those human beings who are superior to ordinary humans.
"Of superior human beings" is the meaning. "Dhamma" refers to the attained dhamma consisting of the sublime (mahaggata) and supramundane (lokuttara).

Alternatively, "superhuman states" (uttarimanussadhamma) means that which transcends the human state. The so-called "human state" (manussadhamma) is the dhamma of the ten courses of wholesome action (dasakusalakammapatha), which can be produced by humans naturally without the mental application of meditation (bhāvanā-manasikāra). For that [human state] exists merely through the mental resolve of humans.
Because it succeeds, that developed state remains as if it were established; thus it is so called.
And the mention of "human" here is because [such states] mostly occur among them. However, since jhāna and so forth are contrary to that [ordinary human state], they are "beyond that";

thus, "superhuman states" (*uttarimanussadhamma*) means those which are superior to human states. The meaning here should be understood in this way: "that superhuman state. "Practicing" means announcing.
Although all wisdom—both mundane and supramundane—is called "knowledge" (*ñāṇa*), here it should be understood as only that which is sublime and supramundane;
thus he said, "Sublime and supramundane wisdom is knowledge in the sense of knowing. Because it is far removed from defilements, it is noble in the sense of being utterly pure;
thus he said, "Noble, purified, supreme. And here, the word "noble" (*ariya*) is a synonym for "purified."

It is not expressed in the supramundane manner. By the word "etc. in the phrase "the distinction of jhānas, etc.," it includes: liberation, concentration, attainment, knowledge and vision, development of the path, realization of the fruit, the abandoning of defilements, the mind’s freedom from hindrances, and delighting in empty dwellings.
The phrase "to one who is wise and of human birth" is an indication of the person to whom it should be announced.
For when this has been announced, it is truly announced; it is not [announced] to the devas and brahmās, nor even to the pretas, yakkhas, or those who have gone to the animal realm.

"Should announce" means he should speak; "should inform" is what is meant. "Without using a pretext" means without a pretext such as, "The monk who lives in your monastery is an attainer of the first jhāna," and so forth. "Right here" means...
“‘Thus I know, thus I see’—this refers to this very phrase. ‘Therefore it was said,’ etc., is the conclusion.
‘Being pressed for an account’ means being questioned; regarding that matter which has been reported, [he is asked]:
‘What have you attained? How have you attained it? When did you attain it? Where did you attain it? Which...’”
It is said: "When one is addressed by someone saying, 'Those defilements have been abandoned; of which states are you a possessor?
*Asamanuggāhiyamāno* means not being addressed by anyone.
[The phrase] "Being incapable of attaining the jhānas and so forth while remaining in the state of a bhikkhu" is because the transgression of the training rules acts as an obstacle.
It has been said: for the state of being a bhikkhu is both an obstacle to heaven and an obstacle to the Path.
Indeed, this has been stated: "The ascetic life, when wrongly grasped, drags one toward hell. Furthermore, it has been said: "For a lax wandering life scatters even more dust [of defilement].
"State of being a bhikkhu" refers to one who, having committed a *pārājika* offense, still claims, "I am an ascetic."

The state of being a bhikkhu is established merely as a conventional designation (*vohāramatta*). "By means of giving and so forth" means by means of giving, taking refuge, the restraint of virtue (*sīla-saṃvara*), and so on.
Regarding the phrase "only not knowing," here *eva* is a particle used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇatthe*).

They also read it as "ajānameva. In that case, however, it should be construed with the words: "Thus I know, thus I see. Because of the absence of the meaning of the statement: "First... [text fragment].

Because it is devoid of the meditative absorption (jhāna) and so forth that constitute the meaning of such statements as "he attained absorption," it is empty, like a vessel empty of water and the like.
"False" (musā) refers to either a verbal or bodily application intended to deceive another by one whose primary aim is deception.
Thus he said: "Falsehood [arises] from the intention to deceive. Both the falsehood and the intention to deceive exist at the moment preceding the actual act.
And at that very moment. For it is said: "Either previously he thinks, 'I shall speak falsely,' or while speaking he thinks, 'I am speaking falsely.
These two factors constitute the essential conditions; as for the other [the actual utterance], whether it occurs or not is irrelevant.
By saying "he did not speak," I mean that he made no communication.

"Apart from overweening conceit" (*aññatra adhimānā*): "Conceit attained" (*adhigato māno*) or "excessive conceit" (*adhiko māno*) is "overweening conceit" (*adhimāno*); the meaning is "stiffened conceit. The meaning is "he removes that.
Now, in whom does this overweening conceit arise, and in whom does it not arise? First of all, it does not arise in a noble disciple (*ariyasāvaka*).
For he, by means of the reviewing of the paths, fruits, Nibbāna, the defilements abandoned, and the remaining defilements, [is free from it].

Having become joyful and free from doubt regarding the penetration of the noble qualities, the conceit "I am a once-returner," and so forth, does not arise in those who have attained the stage of stream-entry and beyond.
It does not arise in one who is immoral, for such a person has no hope at all of attaining the noble qualities.

Nor does it arise in one who, though possessed of virtue and observance of precepts, has abandoned his meditation subject and is devoted to the pleasure of sleep and the like; rather, it arises in one whose virtue is perfectly pure.

However, it arises for one who has applied himself diligently to the meditation subject, who has defined name-and-form, who has crossed over doubt by discerning the conditions, and who, having applied the three characteristics, is comprehending formations as one whose insight has been commenced. Therefore he said, "That which...

and so forth. In that context, "having applied the three characteristics" means having applied the triad of characteristics beginning with impermanence by way of the comprehension of groups (*kalāpasammasana*).
"Having applied. "To one who is comprehending" means to one who is practicing insight (vipassanā).

"One who has begun insight" means one who has begun insight through the contemplation of arising and passing away (udayabbayānupassanā). "Not yet attained" means not having arisen within one's own continuity; it is said to mean "not yet realized.
"The state of being considered as attained" refers to the state of being considered thus: "I have attained the superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma)."
Excessive conceit arises. Once arisen, it places one who has attained pure serenity or pure insight in between [the stages].

For even though he sees no manifestation of defilements for ten, twenty, or thirty years, he imagines, "I am a stream-enterer," or "a once-returner," or "a non-returner. [He thus obstructs] one who has attained serenity and insight.
but he establishes him in Arahantship alone. For by the power of his concentration, the defilements have been suppressed;
by the power of his insight, conditioned phenomena have been thoroughly mastered. Therefore, for sixty years, eighty years, or even a hundred years, the defilements do not manifest;
his mental conduct is that of one whose taints are exhausted. Thus, for a long time, the manifestation of defilements...
Not seeing [the truth], he does not stop midway but conceives the thought, "I am an arahant.

By the phrase "setting aside that overestimation" (*taṃ adhimānaṃ ṭhapetvā*), it is shown—by referring to the word "except" (*aññatra*)—that "from overestimation" (*adhimānā*) is an ablative used in the sense of the accusative.
Regarding "evil desire" (*pāpicchatā*): one who has evil desires is *pāpiccho*; the state of being such is *pāpicchatā*; by that, namely, by evil desire.

The meaning is "through desire. By this, it is meant: through that desire to be esteemed for qualities one does not possess, which was described in the manner beginning with, "In this case, someone who is actually immoral thinks, 'May people know me to be virtuous.

However, by this [statement], he shows that there is no offense for one who acts out of dullness or delusion. Furthermore, by the word "also" (api), he shows that this is not only the case for the three previously mentioned [offenses].

"Non-existent" means unreal. "Dhammas such as jhāna," etc., refers to the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) mentioned thus: "jhāna, liberation, concentration, attainment, knowledge and vision, development of the path, realization of the fruit, the abandoning of defilements, freedom of the mind from hindrances, and delighting in empty dwellings.
"To whom he reports" means by means of speech or by gestures of the hand and so forth.
Or, it is when one informs a person standing within the range of communication by means of the movement of limbs and members.
However, if someone standing beyond the range of communication knows—having seen with the divine eye or heard with the divine ear—that this has occurred, there is no *pārājika*.
Furthermore, if one falls into doubt, thinking, "What is this person saying? for a long time...
Or, having investigated, he later comes to know; yet, because he does not truly understand, he is reckoned as one who "does not know.

Furthermore, one who does not know the jhānas and so forth—either by way of personal attainment or through study and interrogation—but has merely heard the mere words "jhāna" or "liberation," when that person says it, [others think]: "He has surely entered jhāna!"
If he knows even this much—that "this person speaks"—he is reckoned as one who "knows," and when he has spoken thus, it is indeed a *pārājika* offense.

As for the rest—the distinction regarding whether [the speaker] is one, two, or many, and whether they are specified or unspecified—all should be understood according to the method already stated in the discussion on the renunciation of the training (*sikkhā-paccakkhāna*). However, in the case of speaking by way of synonyms, such as "I... [the rule applies].

Because it was not said, there is a *thullaccaya* offense even for one who understands [the meaning] once it has been spoken. Because the application of false speech (*musāvāda*) was made with the intention of deceiving, there is a *dukkaṭa* offense even for one who does not understand;
thus he said: "Whoever dwells in your monastery... [etc. ... *dukkaṭa*.
"Of one who lacks the intention to misrepresent" means of one who is devoid of the intention to misrepresent, that is, devoid of the intention to state what is untrue.

The meaning [is as follows]. Those who are insane and so forth are exactly as described by the method previously stated. However, in this case, the monks from the banks of the Vaggumudā River were first offenders; for them, there is no offense.
The commentary on the fourth *pārājika* is finished.
Commentary on the conclusion of the *pārājikas*.
*Idha* means in this *Bhikkhu-pātimokkha*. "Merely a clarification of the recited *pārājikas*" means it is simply a statement clarifying the four *pārājikas* that have been recited.
The restriction (*avadhāraṇa*), however, is for the purpose of showing that it does not apply to others as well. Therefore he said, "But having brought them together," and so forth.
In that context, *samodhānetvā* means having gathered together right here those [rules] which have appeared in various places.
"Having thrown them together and made a heap"—this is the meaning. "Included in the text" means included in the recitation text (*uddesapāḷi*).

"Four not shared with nuns" means these four—*ubbhajāṇumaṇḍalika*, *vajjappaṭicchādikā*, *ukkhitānuvattikā*, and *aṭṭhavatthuka*—are those not shared by nuns with monks. For [the offenses] such as those of a paṇḍaka...
Because the state of being incapable [of spiritual progress] for these eleven types is similar to the offense of a *pārājika*, it is called a "pārājika" in the passage beginning with "for the eleven.

By those characterized as "incapable states"—meaning by those characterized as being unworthy of the going-forth (*pabbajjā*) and full ordination (*upasampadā*) due to defects in the basis (*vatthu*), and so forth—the three types, namely the eunuch (*paṇḍaka*), the animal (*tiracchānagata*), and the hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*), are those whose basis is defective;
they possess rebirth-linking (*paṭisandhi*) that is devoid of roots (*ahetuka*).

For them, heaven is not barred, but the Path is barred; for they are incapable of attaining the Path because they have failed in the essential basis. Even their going forth [into homelessness] is rejected;

therefore, they too are indeed *pārājika*. [They are: one who dwells in communion through theft, one who has gone over to another sect, a matricide, a patricide, a murderer of an *arahant*, a defiler of a nun, one who sheds the blood [of a Buddha], and a schismatic of the Saṅgha.
These eight have reached a state of incapacity because their own actions have failed; thus, they are indeed *pārājika*.

Among them, for these three—the one living in communion through theft (*theyyasaṃvāsaka*), the one who has gone over to another sect (*titthiyapakkantaka*), and the defiler of nuns (*bhikkhunidūsaka*)—heaven is not barred, but the path [to liberation] is indeed barred.
For the other five, both are barred; for they are beings destined to be reborn in hell immediately thereafter.
When a bhikkhunī, desiring to disrobe, puts on either the saffron robe or a householder’s garment in the manner of a householder’s lower robe, she is then said to have committed a *pārājika* offense;
thus it is said: "for one aspiring to the state of a householder," and so forth.
For even without having committed a transgression through misconduct, she at this point becomes what is called a non-recluse (*assamaṇī*).
"Lambi" means one whose organ hangs down due to its length. He does not become defeated (pārājika) by that much alone;
rather, when, being oppressed by lack of self-control, he inserts his own organ into his own mouth or anus, at that time he becomes defeated.
"Mudupiṭṭhika" means one who has a soft back; that is, one endowed with a back that has been made soft through preparatory treatment.
When he, being oppressed by lack of lust, inserts his own organ into either his own mouth or anus, he becomes one who has committed a *pārājika* offense.

"He takes another's organ with his mouth" means that one, being oppressed by lack of lust, takes the organ of another person—whether they are asleep or heedless—with his mouth. [Regarding] another's organ...

"He sits down upon" means that one who, oppressed by lack of lust, seeing another's genitals to be functional, sits upon them with his own anus and inserts his own anus [into it]; this is the meaning.
For these four, because they constitute a state of equality between both parties through the influence of passion, are called "the act of sexual intercourse. Therefore...

Because, by one method, they are to be incurred merely through the act of entering the path [of sexual intercourse] without actually engaging in the act of sexual intercourse itself, they are called "conformable Pārājikas" (*anuloma-pārājikāni*) as they conform to the Pārājika offense of sexual misconduct. Here it is said:
the matricide, the patricide, the murderer of an Arhat, and the defiler of a bhikkhunī have fallen into the third Pārājika.
Since Lambī and the other three have all committed the first *pārājika* offense, how can there be twenty-four? It is said:
the four beginning with the matricide are intended here as those who are not yet ordained (*anupasampanna*).
Although Lambī and the others are included under the first *pārājika*, they are excluded from this count because, by one way of reckoning, they have not engaged in sexual intercourse.
Therefore, they are stated separately. In the second alternative, the word division for *kaccittha* should be made as *kacci attha*.
Thus ends the commentary on the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Pātimokkhavaṇṇanā* within the *Vinayatthamañjūsā*, specifically in the section titled *Līnatthappakāsanī*.
The commentary on the *pārājika* rules is finished.
Regarding the section on the *saṅghādisesa* offenses:
"Addressing with endearing words" means addressing with words that are to be cherished; it is stated that this refers to addressing virtuous people with affection.
...it exists. For virtuous people address others as "sirs," or "beloved of the gods," or "noble sir," or "venerable sirs.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Emission of Semen: The word *saṃ* has the sense of existence;
thus he said, "it exists" (*saṃvijjati*). "Intention" (*cetanā*) refers to the preliminary intention that proceeds toward the transgression.
The meaning is "volition consisting in the pleasure of emission. Regarding the word *assa* (of it), it refers to the emission of semen.

Since the emission of semen is already expressed by the compound itself as a term denoting a different referent (*aññapadatthasamāsa*), there is no separate meaning for the suffix *-ika*; thus he says, "volition itself is volitional" (*sañcetanāva sañcetanikā*).
Now, showing that the suffix *-ika* itself expresses the sense of "having the purpose of," he says, "or [volition] which has that as its object," and so forth. It exists.
Volition is intentional action. "Of the pure" means of the possible. "Emission" (*visaṭṭhi*) means discharge.

Now, having briefly explained at what time one emits it, with what intention one emits it, by what means one emits it, and what the object of that intention is—all of this—the emission itself will be described according to its own nature.

To demonstrate this, he said, "In cases of lustful rigidity (*rāgūpatthambha*) and so forth. Therein, "lustful rigidity" refers either to the state of lust being powerful, or to the rigidity—that is, the stiffening—of the sexual organ due to lust.
Those for which that is the first are "lustful rigidity and the rest. Regarding these, "lustful rigidity and the rest":

by the word "and the rest," there is included rigidity of the anus, rigidity of the urinary tract, rigidity caused by wind, rigidity from embracing a tall woman, and rigidity from being bitten by insects.
"Seizing" (*gahaṇaṃ*). "Having attained serviceability" (*kammaññataṃ patto*) means having attained a state fit for action due to its capacity for the act of releasing;

the meaning is that it has attained a state capable of being acted upon with respect to internal forms and so forth. "Healthiness" (*ārogyaṃ*) is the state of being healthy (*arogassa bhāvo*); those things of which health is the first are "health and the rest" (*ārogyādayo*), and [the phrase refers to] "among those health and the rest.
By the word "and the rest" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of happiness, the giving of medicine, merit, sacrifice, heaven, seed, testing, and giving away.

"Internal form" (*ajjhattarūpa*) is internal appropriated form (*upādinnarūpa*). Those things for which that is the beginning are "internal form and so forth" (*ajjhattarūpādayo*); [the phrase refers to] among those.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of external form, internal-external form, space, and the shaking of the hips. The gratification in releasing is pleasant feeling; thus it is "gratification in releasing" (*mocanassāda*).
It is the lust (*rāga*) occurring in the prior stage for the sake of releasing. And here, by way of the heading "gratification associated [with the object]," it is lust.
It has been said; by that, one rejects the volitions associated with it—the volition of relishing liberation, and by that [volition]. By this, he rejects the volitions associated with these:

relishing release, relishing what has been released, relishing sexual intercourse, relishing contact, relishing scratching, relishing seeing, relishing sitting, relishing speech, domestic affection, and the breaking of the forest [of restraint];
for one who exerts effort toward the sign by means of those [volitions].
There is no offense even when emission occurs. By the phrase “one who makes an effort upon the organ,” however, he rejects [acts such as] massaging the thighs and so forth.
For by that, even though there is the pleasure of emission, since there is no effort directed toward the organ, there is no offense even when emission occurs.

Indeed, this has been stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*: “And that [offense] occurs only for one who makes an effort upon the organ, by performing manual work on the hands, manual work on the feet, or manual work on the limbs.”
"Even if impurity is emitted, there is no offense.

Regarding "due to the diversity of the receptacles and elements": this refers to the diversity of the receptacles of bile, phlegm, pus, and blood, as well as the four primary elements such as earth, or the seven elements such as chyle and blood. Regarding "falling from its place": this refers to semen.
From whatever place there is a falling away—that is the "place. For regarding semen (*sukka*), they designate three places: the head of the organ, the waist, and the whole body.
It is said that one teacher stated, "The head of the organ is the place of semen," another said, "The waist," and another said, "The entire body.
Among these, the statement of the third is well-spoken. For the place of hair of the head, body hair, nails, and teeth is a location distinct from flesh.
Excluding feces, urine, spittle, snot, and stiff, dry hides, the entire remaining body— encompassing skin, flesh, and blood—
is merely the locus of the physical sensitivity, the life-faculty, the bound bile, and the origin of existence. For instance,
in elephants overcome by the obsession of passion, the seminal flow issues forth from both ear-tips.

And here, by the phrase beginning with “in the cases of the stiffening due to lust, etc.,” the time is indicated. For it is at times such as when there is stiffening due to lust that the sexual organ becomes functional;
when it is functional, one discharges, and beyond this there is no other time.

Indeed, without the stiffening due to lust and so forth, the divisions of time such as forenoon and the rest do not serve as a cause for discharge. By the phrase beginning with “in the cases of health, etc.,”...
However, the underlying intention (*adhippāya*) has been shown. For one liberates by means of such a distinction of intention, and not otherwise.

By the words "In internal form, etc.," the method (*upāya*) is shown; for whether one should liberate in internal form, or in external form, or in both, or shaking the hips in space—beyond this there is no other method.
Furthermore, by the ten [phrases] beginning with "By way of blue, etc.,"...
The basis for the ninth intention has been shown. For when one investigates, one investigates by way of one or another of the blue and so forth, and not as something separate from them.
By the phrase "falling from its place," however, emission is shown in meaning. As it is said:
"Emission is called falling from its place. And this falling of that semen from its place occurs by way of lust.
For this has been stated in the *Kathāvatthu-aṭṭhakathā*: “Emission of semen is originated by lust. “Except in a dream”:
a dream itself is a “dream-state” (*supinanta*); the meaning is “excluding that. Therefore he said, “that which [occurs] in a dream,” and so forth.
“Saṅghādisesa”: this is the name of this class of offenses. Therefore he said, “that which [occurs] except in a dream,” and so forth.

“Classes of offenses” (*āpattinikāya*) means a collection of offenses. Although this is indeed a single offense, it is called a “class” (*nikāya*) by way of conventional usage (*ruḷhisadda*), either as a designation for the whole applied to its parts, or like [the expressions] “one aggregate of feeling” (*vedanākkhandha*) or “one aggregate of consciousness” (*viññāṇakkhandha*).
“Of it” (*assa*) means of the class of offenses. But is this formulation not improper? For it has been stated: “The Saṅgha should be mentioned both at the beginning and at the end.”

“No, indeed. [The opponent asks: “Is it not the case that the Saṅgha is intended at both the beginning and the end of a class of offenses (āpatti-nikāya), rather than for the rehabilitation (vuṭṭhāna)?
Keeping this objection in mind, [the author] says, “What is meant? and so forth, in order to clarify the intended meaning so that there is no contradiction. [The answer is:
The Saṅgha is intended at both the beginning and the end of the rehabilitation from an offense; [it is intended] by means of the offense itself.
"Is intended" (icchito) is the meaning here. "Emergence from an offense" (āpattivuṭṭhānaṃ) means emergence from the offense; the sense is the attainment of the state of being free from offense.
"The stream of water" (dakasotaṃ) refers to the urinary passage; it is said to be the region of the generative organ.

If this is so, then why is it stated in the Commentary, "merely upon entering the stream of water"? To this he says: "But having fallen from its place," and so forth. It is certainly [the case that] the stream of water...
It descends because, having been accepted, it cannot be stopped in the interim.

However, from the point of descending into the stream of water onwards, because it is released from what is clung-to (*upādinnaka*), the materiality of production remains as being produced solely by temperature (*utusamuṭṭhāna*);

it should be understood that there is no other materiality produced by the remaining three [causes]. Therefore—meaning: because that which has fallen from its place descends into the stream of water—therefore.
"Of one intending to relieve oneself" means: of one who smears a sign with medicine, or who voids excrement and so forth.

"Of one seeing a dream" means: of one seeing a dream due to these four causes—disturbance of the elements, past experience, the influence of a deity, or a prognostic omen. But does one who sees [a dream] see it while asleep?
Is he awake, or neither asleep nor awake? What follows from this? First, if one sees while asleep, it would entail a contradiction with the Abhidhamma.
For one sleeps by means of the life-continuum consciousness (*bhavaṅga-citta*), and that does not have visible forms or signs as its object, nor is it associated with lust and so forth;
yet such states of consciousness arise for one who is seeing a dream.
If he sees while awake, he incurs an offense contrary to the Vinaya; for whatever one sees while awake, one sees with a mind characterized by deliberate intent (*sabbohārika-citta*).
And when a transgression is committed with a mind characterized by deliberate intent, there is no such thing as "no offense.
However, even if a transgression is committed by one seeing in a dream, it is invariably "no offense" indeed. But if he sees neither while asleep nor while awake, [there is no offense].
Who indeed sees [this], and if this were so, would it not follow that there is an absence of dreams altogether? It is not an absence. Why?
Because one who is overcome by "monkey-sleep" sees it. For this has been said: "Great King, one who is overcome by monkey-sleep sees a dream.
"Overcome by monkey-sleep" means possessed of the sleep of a monkey; for just as the sleep of a monkey is characterized by rapid shifting.
Thus, when sleep— which turns over rapidly because it is interspersed with wholesome and other types of consciousness—
occurs such that there is a repeated emergence from the life-continuum (bhavaṅga) during its course, one endowed with that sleep sees a dream. And for one who sees thus in a dream,
as if engaging in sexual intercourse or as if entering into physical contact and so forth, [the dream occurs].
If impurity is discharged due to a dream, there is no offense for that [monk].
However, if a dream arises and he experiences a sense of gratification, he must remain motionless; he must not manipulate the organ with his hand.
But it is permissible to take hold of it with the hollow of his hands and go to a place with water to clean it, for the purpose of protecting the saffron-colored robe-spread.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the emission of semen is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning physical contact:

Regarding the word "otiṇṇo" (immersed/involved), it is either an accusative construction (*kamma-sādhana*) or an agentive construction (*kattusādhana*); thus, he demonstrates the meaning according to both possibilities.
He said, “Beings [are like] those [afflicted] by yakkhas and so forth. Regarding the phrase “without having observed”: this means without having investigated according to their true nature;
that is to say, without seeing how those sense objects such as forms—which produce delight—are established in the manner of being impermanent, suffering, foul, and non-self.
“By transformation” means by change. Therefore he said, “Just as when changing,” and so forth.
"By way of lust for what has been uttered" means by way of lust for physical contact. "Even for one born on that very day":

she whose birth occurred on that day is "born on that day" (*tadahujātā*); alternatively, she who was born on that day is "born on that day. The meaning is: even for her who was born on that same day;
it is said, "even for one who is just born, having the color of a piece of raw flesh."
“Assa” refers to the phrase “should engage in physical contact. Now, in order to show the classification of the hand and so forth, he said:
“In this context, ‘hand’ means from the elbow onwards,” and so on. “From the elbow onwards” means starting from the second major joint (*mahāsandhi*).
Elsewhere, however, the hand extends from the wrist (*maṇibandha*) up to the fingertips. Or, having entwined...
The connection is that this is a designation for a braid of hair that has been braided.
In that context, "having braided" means having tied it with three strands of hair. "A golden fillet" means a golden band.
Having set aside the hand and the braid, he says "of the remainder of the body" and so forth, referring to the rest of the body as the "limb."

For one who, even with the intention of sexual intercourse, merely experiences, consents to, and undergoes physical contact with an immovable body, there is no offense because there is no offense in a mere arising of consciousness; thus he said, "without exerting oneself with the body," and so forth.
"With the intention of release" means with the intention of desiring to be released from the woman. "Unintentionally" means [not thinking], "By this means, this..."
"Without intending, 'I shall touch,'" means that if one does not have such an intention, there is no offense even when touching a part of a woman's body while receiving her bowl and so forth.
"By way of non-attention" means one is distracted; there is no mindfulness with the thought, "I shall touch a woman.

Thus, for one who touches while stretching out a hand or foot and so on at such a time due to lack of attention, there is no offense. "Of one who does not know" refers to [one who touches] someone standing in the guise of a child.
If one touches a girl for some purpose while not knowing she is a woman, there is no offense for one who touches her without knowing she is a woman.
"Without consenting" means there is no offense for one who does not consent to physical contact, such as a monk who has been led away by a succession of arms.
In this case, however, the Elder Udāyī was a first-offender. For a first-offender, there is no offense.
The commentary on the training rule concerning physical contact is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning indecent speech:

"By way of the gratification of indecent speech and lust" means that indecent speech is *duṭṭhulla-vācā*; the volition of enjoyment derived from that is the gratification of indecent speech (*duṭṭhulla-vācassāda*).
By way of the lust associated with that [mind]. To indicate the woman intended here, he says "a woman" (*mātugāma*), and so forth.
"Capable of discerning what is indecent and what is not indecent" means capable of knowing speech connected with what is contrary to the true Dhamma and what is in accordance with the true Dhamma.
However, one who is old, foolish, or mute is not intended here. "Complexion" (*vaṇṇo*)...
Praise (*thomanā*) is the lauding of the two paths by addressing them as, "You were endowed with the marks of a woman, with auspicious marks," and so forth.

Censure (*avaṇṇa*) is the reviling of the two paths by stating the opposite of what was said, namely, the disparaging of them as, "You were not endowed with the marks of a woman, with auspicious marks," and so forth.
Begging (*yācanā*) is [expressed as], "Give to me; you ought to give to me."
“Speech. “Entreaty” means speech such as: “When will your mother be pleased? When will your father be pleased? When will the deities be pleased?
When will there be for you an auspicious time, an auspicious hour, and an auspicious moment?
When shall I obtain sexual intercourse with you? “Inquiry” means: “How do you give to your husband? How...”

“...you give to the paramour,” such is the statement. “Questioning” means the statement: “Is it indeed so that you give to the husband in this way, and give to the paramour in that way? “Explaining” means, when asked, saying: “Give in this way;
by giving in this way, you will be dear and pleasing to your husband. “Instructing” means, even without being asked, saying: “Give in this way; in this way...”
“With teeth like these, you will be dear to your husband and pleasing to him”—this is the dwelling place [of the thought]. “Abuse” means the speech:

“You are without marks, you are merely a mark, you are bloodless, you are constantly bleeding, you are always stained with menstrual blood, you are a dripper, you are a ‘top-knot’ woman, you are a eunuch-woman, you are a man-like woman, you are a promiscuous woman, you are a hermaphrodite. Because it is connected with sexual intercourse...

There is no speech more gross than that which pertains to sexual intercourse; therefore, it is said that the phrase "connected with sexual intercourse" demonstrates the defining characteristic of the most extreme offense among gross forms of speech, but not because speech connected with sexual intercourse alone constitutes gross speech.
"Sikharaṇī" means those from whom the seminal flesh has been expelled. "Sambhinnā" means those whose anus and urinary passages have become intermingled.
"Those with both sexual characteristics" (*ubhatobyañjanakā*) means those endowed with both male and female characteristics.
In this context, when describing her appearance, he says, "She was endowed with the female marks and auspicious marks," but the matter does not yet end there.
He further says, "Both your anus and your urinary passage were beautiful, well-formed, and pleasing to behold."
If one says, "You were indeed endowed with such a female characteristic, a beautiful characteristic," the head is reached;
the meaning is that it constitutes a *saṅghādisesa* offense.
However, in the case of speaking dispraise, if the dispraise is not joined with the eleven phrases beginning with "You were without marks," the head is not reached.

Even when combined with these, if it is combined with these three—namely, "you are a *sikharaṇī*," "you are a *sambhinnā*," or "you are a hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*)"—then it is indeed a *saṅghādisesa*.

Even in the case of a request, the offense does not culminate by merely saying "give it to me"; rather, it is only when combined with sexual intercourse, such as "give me the act of sexual intercourse," that it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
Even in words of entreaty such as "When will your mother be pleased? and so forth, the offense does not culminate by merely that much; [only when one asks] "When... [does it culminate].
If one is instigated by sexual intercourse through such means as saying, “Your mother will be pleased;
when shall I obtain sexual intercourse with her? or “When your mother has become favorable, I shall obtain sexual intercourse with her,” it is a *saṅghādisesa*.

Even in the case of interrogative statements such as, “How do you instruct your husband? it is a *saṅghādisesa* only when the words “sexual intercourse” (*methunaṃ dhamma*) are used. The same principle applies to responsive statements such as, “It seems you instruct your husband in this way.”
Regarding the act of explaining, even if one says, "Give it in this way," or "Giving in this way," it does not constitute an offense;

however, when it is connected with sexual intercourse (*methuna-dhamma*) by such means as, "Give the sexual act in this way," "Approach her in this way," or "By giving and approaching her in this way through sexual intercourse, she becomes dear to her husband," etc., it is a *saṅghādisesa* offense. The same principle applies to words of instruction as well.

Furthermore, among the eleven types of verbal abuse, only these three phrases—“You are a woman with a protruding vulva,” “You are a woman of loose character,” and “You are a hermaphrodite”—are pure and constitute the head-offense.

Thus, these three, together with the previous three phrases concerning the anus, the urinary tract, and sexual intercourse, make six pure phrases that constitute offenses. The remaining phrases, such as “You are without marks,” etc., [apply] to one who is without marks; [the phrase] “sexual intercourse”...

It should be understood that offenses are incurred only when one engages in sexual intercourse according to such methods as saying, "Give me the Dhamma," or "You are signless; give me the Dhamma of sexual intercourse.
"Below the collarbones" means from the collarbones downwards. "Above the kneecaps" means from the kneecaps upwards.
"Above" means from the collarbone upwards. "Below the kneecaps" means from the kneecaps downwards.
However, the collarbone and the kneecaps themselves are included within this field of *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing), just as in the case of physical contact with a nun;
for the Buddhas do not prescribe a grave offense that leaves a remainder.
“Connected with the body” means a cloth, a flower, or an ornament.

Regarding the phrase “having the meaning, the Dhamma, and the instruction as their primary concern”: one who explains the meaning of words such as “signless” (animitta) and so forth, or who recites the commentary (aṭṭhakathā), is said to have the meaning as their primary concern;
likewise, one who causes [others] to recite the Pāḷi or who performs the recitation [of it].

Speaking with the Dhamma as the primary consideration means saying: "Even now you are without signs; you are a hermaphrodite; you should now practice heedfulness, so that in the future you may not become like this again.
Speaking with instruction as the primary consideration means saying: "Now you should practice heedfulness, so that in the future you may not become like this again.
Thus, there is no offense for those who speak while placing the meaning, the Dhamma, and the instruction foremost. However, whoever...

If one teaching the Pāḷi to bhikkhunīs abandons the normal method of recitation and, laughing repeatedly, says, "You are a *sikharaṇī*, you are a *sambhinnā*, you are a hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*)," there is an offense for him. In this case, the Elder Udāyī was a first-offender;
for a first-offender, there is no offense. [Objection: Is it not the case that for one who reviles with words such as "*sikharaṇī*," there is a mind of resentment (*paṭighacitta*)?
If it is argued that because [the word] "arises" is used, there ought to be painful feeling as well, then why is it said to be "two feelings"? This is not a fault.

For this offense occurs by way of lust (*rāga*), not by way of aversion (*paṭigha*); therefore, it is verbal abuse proceeding solely by way of lust that is intended here, and not that proceeding by way of aversion as well.
The commentary on the training rule concerning indecent speech is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning one who desires [sexual] pleasure:
"By way of service for one’s own desire" means by way of passion (*rāga*) for service for one’s own desire. Here too, it refers only to those capable of discerning what is indecent and what is not.
"A woman is intended" means: "by a woman of the type described under the heading of 'corrupt conduct'. "In the vicinity" means within earshot.
"Standing" is a word to be supplied from the context. "Attending to one's own desires": that which is desired is *kāma*, namely sexual intercourse;
*paricaraṇa* is service or attendance, and that itself is *pāricariyā*. Service for the sake of desire is *kāmapāricariyā*; [service] to oneself...
*Attakāmapāricariyā* means service for one’s own pleasure; that is to say, attendance by way of sexual intercourse for one’s own benefit.

Alternatively, *kāmitā* (that which is desired) are the *kāmā*; *attakāmā* is one’s own desires. It is *attakāmapāricariyā* because it is both one’s own desire (*attakāmā*) and service (*pāricariyā*).
The meaning is: attendance performed out of one’s own longing due to lust for sexual intercourse. Thus he said:

“By what is termed the act of sexual intercourse,” and so forth. Herein, by the first interpretation of the meaning, he shows three meanings termed service for the sake of sensual desire; by the second, two meanings termed service according to one’s intention.
However, without attaching importance to the literal phrasing (*byañjana*), in order to show merely the meaning, [he says]: “one’s own sensual desire, one’s own motive, one’s own intention.”
The word-commentary (*padabhājana*) states: “for one’s own service. For when it is said, “for one’s own desire, for one’s own sake, for one’s own service,” the wise will understand:
“To this extent, service for the sake of one’s own sensual pleasure has been described.
And when it is said, “for one’s own intention, for one’s own service,” they will also understand: “To this extent, it is in the sense of what is desired and wished for by oneself...”
“Service to one’s own desires is what was spoken of.
Because he is endowed with beautiful and auspicious qualities, he is called “one of beautiful nature” (kalyāṇadhamma). Therefore, he said, “By both of these,” and so forth.
“May she delight” means may she satisfy. “The foremost of these” means this is the best. “Of services” means in the midst of services.

This genitive case ending is used here for the purpose of specification (*niddhāraṇa*). One might ask: "Is it not the case that the request for sexual intercourse was already mentioned in the training rule regarding indecent speech (*duṭṭhullavācā*)?

Why, then, is this stated here? This is not a fault. For in that instance, it was stated by way of the passion for the indecent speech itself, whereas here it is stated by way of the passion for one's own sexual intercourse.
"At that very moment" means at the moment of speaking. However, the hermaphrodite (*ubhatobyañjanaka*) is not mentioned separately because he belongs to the category of the *paṇḍaka*.

Regarding these two training rules, they say that just as in the case of physical contact, there is a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) for indecent speech even when addressed to a *yakkhinī* or a *petī*.
"At that very moment" [refers to] when one perceives a *paṇḍaka* as a woman, for the sake of one's own sensual pleasure.

There is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) even for praising [sexual intercourse]. There is also an offense of wrong-doing for speaking by way of indirect suggestion, such as: “Give the best gift—namely, the practice of sexual intercourse—to whoever stays in your monastery. Some say:
“There is an offense of wrong-doing because one praises the service of one’s own desires, since it was said that [this applies] to one who says of someone like me, ‘He is virtuous.
Others say: “Because all five factors are present, it is an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa). [The phrase is: “By means of what is connected with sexual intercourse.”
Because it has been stated thus, it is said: "There is no offense for one who speaks [of the matter] by means of robes and so forth...
The commentary on the training rule concerning one's own desire (*attakāma-sikkhāpada*) is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule concerning matchmaking (*sañcaritta-sikkhāpada*).
*Saṃcaraṇaṃ* means wandering; one who has this is a *saṃcarī*. Alternatively, a *saṃcarī* is one whose nature is to wander.

The state of being such is *saṃcaritta*; the meaning is "wandering. And since that [wandering] is described later by the words "the mind of a woman toward a man," and so forth, it occurs in the interval between women and men;
thus he says, "the state of wandering between women and men. These are: accepting, testing, and returning.
In this context, "acceptance" means that when a man, a woman, or both their parents and so forth say, "Venerable sir,

please speak thus to such-and-such a woman or man," one accepts by making a vocal utterance in any manner whatsoever— such as saying "Very well," "So be it," or "I shall speak"— or by nodding the head and so forth.
"Deliberation" (*vīmaṃsana*) means that, having received the message in the manner described, one goes into the presence of that woman or man,
or their parents, brothers, sisters, and so forth— who must necessarily be informed— and communicates that message to them.
"Bringing back a reply" (*paccāharaṇa*) means that when he has gone and reported it, that woman or man accepts it, saying, "Very well."
Whether out of anger, or out of fear, or out of shame, let him remain silent; then, having returned, he reports that occurrence to that woman or to that man.
"Āpajjeyya" means he would act [in such a way].

Regarding the phrase "to that woman the thought of a man, or to that man the thought of a woman," one should understand that the words "he would report" (*āroceyya*) are to be supplied as the remainder of the text.
For this very reason, he said “therein,” and so forth. “In the state of being a wife” means in the state of being a spouse (*bhariyā*).

“In the state of being a lover” means in the state of being a husband; here, the locative case is used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*). Therefore, the meaning is: “She reports because of the state of being a wife, because of the state of being a husband;

on account of the state of being a wife, on account of the state of being a husband; by reason of the state of being a wife, by reason of the state of being a husband. This same method applies to the term “in the state of being a husband” (*jāyattane*).
In passages such as “she announces,” etc., the phrase “whether in the husband’s bed or in the lover’s bed” is stated for the purpose of showing that she announces her intention to them.
Now, however, in order to show the meaning according to the method explained in the word-commentary (*padabhājaniya*), he says “Moreover,” and so forth.
Although the word-commentary was stated using the feminine gender, [it applies to] “in the husband’s bed.”
Since the definition "or a paramour's wife" is common to both genders, it should also be applied by way of the masculine gender;
thus he said, "By this very method," and so forth. "A momentary woman" refers to a courtesan.
He said, "By this very method," and so forth, because the phrase "even for a mere instant" is merely an illustration.
"Except for one who is not fit to be spoken to" means, excluding one who has not relinquished [the relationship] through the giving of leaves and so forth according to local custom.
Some say that "one not fit to be spoken to" (*nālaṃvacanīyā*) refers to a woman who cannot be addressed by a monk on account of acting as a go-between;
excepting such a person. "Bought with wealth" (*dhanakkītā*) means bought with little or much money. However, she is not a wife merely by being bought.
However, she is called a "wife" because she has been purchased for the purpose of living together; therefore, in its definition it is said: "having bought her with wealth, he causes her to dwell.
As for "one who dwells by choice," she is a *chandavāsinī* because she dwells according to her own desire (*chanda*).
But since she does not become a wife merely by her own desire, but rather because she has been accepted by the man, therefore in its definition it is said: "beloved..."

It is said, “she dwells with what is dear. By the word “etcetera” (ādi), there is the inclusion of these eight modes: one who dwells for wealth, one who dwells for clothing, one who dwells by the water-pot, one whose head-ornament has been removed, a wife who is a slave, a wife who is a laborer, one carried away as a prize, and a momentary wife.
And just as in the case of “one who dwells by consent” and so forth, there is a lack of common understanding for one who speaks according to any one of these [modes].
There is no such thing; likewise, even when speaking by way of any one of those expressions indicative of cohabitation—

though not explicitly stated in the Canon— such as, “Be the wife of so-and-so,” “consort,” “mistress,” “mother of children,” “housewife,” “mistress of the house,” “cook for the husband,” “obedient one,” or “attendant,” there is no lack of consensus [regarding the offense], for it is indeed an offense when the three factors are fulfilled.
Regarding the phrase "speak of one protected by her mother": here, "protected by her mother" (*māturakkhitā*) means she is guarded by her mother;
the sense is that she does not permit cohabitation with a man, being thus protected by her mother. For this very reason, it is said in its word-commentary (*padabhājana*):

"The mother protects and guards her; she exercises authority and maintains control over her. Regarding "those protected by their father," etc., [it refers to] "one protected by her father" (*piturakkhitā*), and so forth.

Regarding those described as "protected by mother and father," "protected by brother," "protected by sister," "protected by relatives," "protected by clan," "protected by Dhamma," "with protection," and "with legal penalty":
just as it is here, so too should the method be understood in such cases as "speak of one protected by father," and so forth.
"Going on account of the Saṅgha, a cetiya, or a sick person":
here, there may be something unfinished belonging to the Bhikkhu Saṅgha, such as the Uposatha hall or some other work.

In that case, a lay follower (upāsaka) might send a bhikkhu to a female lay follower (upāsikā), or a female lay follower might send a bhikkhu to a male lay follower, for the sake of providing food or wages for craftsmen; such is "an affair of the Saṅgha."
There is no offense for one who goes. The same rule applies even when work at a cetiya is being performed.
