There is no offense for one who goes when sent by a layman to a laywoman, or by a laywoman to a layman, for the sake of medicine for the sick.
Although it is said here: "A woman means a human female, not a *yakkhī*, not a *petī*, not a female animal. A man..."
There is no such thing as a "human male" or a "yakṣa," and so forth; nevertheless, it is women and men of human birth who are intended here, hence he said, "their being of human birth.
"Inexpressible as distinct" (nālaṃvacanīyatā) means that, according to the method already stated, they have abandoned being "inexpressible as distinct.
For in this context, the word *alaṃ* has the sense of "prevention" or "prohibition. "Not inexpressible as distinct" (*nālaṃvacanīyā*) means not [to be] inexpressible as distinct. Not...
"Unfit to be spoken to" (*nālaṃ-vacanīya*); the state of being that is "unfitness to be spoken to" (*nanālaṃ-vacanīyatā*). It is expressed as "fitness to be spoken to" (*alaṃ-vacanīyatā*).
"A designation" (*paṇṇatti*) refers to this training rule (*sikkhāpada*). "By means of a bodily gesture" (*kāyavikārena*) means by means of a bodily gesture such as raising the head and so forth.
"Having tested in that very way and responding in that very way" means having tested by means of a bodily gesture such as a hand-sign (*hatthamuddā*) and then responding again.
[The offense applies] to one who, having arrived, reports it exactly as it was. "He will come" means he will come into your presence for the purpose of hearing the Dhamma and so forth.
"If told by someone" means if someone tells [the parents] while they are seated in the assembly hall or elsewhere.
For if the mother and father of one whose taints are destroyed become angry and are no longer to be spoken to, and the father says this to the bhikkhu who has entered the house:
“Father, my mother has abandoned me, an old man, and gone to her own family; go and send her back to attend upon me.
If he goes and says this, and then reports back to his father whether she has returned or not, for one who reports it thus, it originates from both body and speech.
Therefore he said: “But for one who does not know the formal rule,” and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "even for one whose taints are destroyed" (*khīṇāsavassa pi*): here, by the word "even" (*pi*), it is indicated that there is nothing at all to be said concerning those in training (*sekkha*) or worldlings (*puthujjana*).
"By the words of her father" means by the words of her own father. "Having gone" means having gone into her presence.

Even for one who does not know both—the designation (*paṇṇatti*) and the state of being one who may be spoken to as fit (*alaṃvacanīyabhāva*)—it arises from body and speech. "Both of those" refers to the designation and the state of being one who may be spoken to as fit.

However, regarding the statement that when one who knows the designation (*paṇṇatti*) engages in sexual misconduct through these same three methods—arising from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind—these three [offenses] are called "with-mind-arisen" (*sacittaka-samuṭṭhāna*) because of the mind that knows the designation: that is incorrect.
For even after knowing the designation, for one who thinks, "She is not fit to be spoken to," [the offense does not arise] through those [actions] accompanied by a conscious mind.
It is appropriate to say that an offense arises through the origins (samuṭṭhāna), because volitional intent for transgression (vītikkamacetanā) is impossible [in this case].
The commentary on the training rule concerning matchmaking (sañcaritta-sikkhāpada) is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule concerning building a hut (kuṭikāra-sikkhāpada).
Regarding the phrase *saññācikāya pana*: here, *pana* is a particle expressing the sense of the third case (*tatiyatthe*) as a synonym for *attā* (self);
*yācikā* is a noun derived from the action (*bhāvasādhana*); and these two form a compound with the elision of the middle term (*majjhepadalopa*).

*Pana* is merely a particle. Therefore he said, “It is called a request initiated by oneself. For that which is initiated by oneself belongs to oneself; thus he said, “Therefore,” and so forth. Is it not [the case that...]?
In order to show the intended meaning—that it is not possible to build a hut by means of begging alone—he said, "with things personally requested," and so forth.
Therein, "personally requested" means by means of things requested by oneself, such as "Give me an axe, give me a hatchet. "With implements" refers to axes and the like.
"By another"—meaning by the owner of the goods—refers to the act of guarding and protecting [the items] with the thought, "This is mine," rather than relinquishing them.
"Appropriated by another" means belonging to another; it is said that one has freed it from the state of being another's property and made it one's own by way of cutting its root.
For thus, for one who asks from a place not authorized by a stranger, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to the solicitation of a stranger. However, [if it is] temporary...

"It is allowable" means it is allowable to request [the service] on a temporary basis. "One should not request one's own work" is stated for the purpose of guarding against the training rule concerning the taking of life.
One should not request even by saying "Give manual labor," without specifying [the task].

For if they were requested in such a way, they might say, "Very well, Venerable Sir," dismiss the bhikkhu, and then kill even a deer and bring it back. However, having specified [the task], such as "In the monastery..."
One should request: “There is work to be done; please provide manual labor.

Since it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) that “a hut (*kuṭi*) means either plastered on the outside, or plastered on the inside, or plastered both on the outside and inside,” it is said: “‘A hut’ means any one of those beginning with ‘plastered on the outside.
In this context, *ullittā* means plastered facing upwards; for when they plaster the interior, they plaster in this manner. Below...
“Licked” means smeared; they smear in this way while actually smearing on the outside. Therefore he said, “In that context, ‘licked’ (ullitta) means,” and so forth.

“A door-joint of plaster” refers to the door-posts. By the phrase “with lime or with clay,” he shows that, setting aside these two types of plaster, everything else—such as the varieties of ash, cow dung, and so on—is not considered plaster (alepa).
However, since one who builds a hut by means of begging must proceed according to the method stated here [for the previous case], it is said:
"either by doing it oneself or by having it done through an order.

And here, by the phrase "by doing it oneself," he states the meaning obtained by implication (*sāmatthiya*), but not the literal meaning of the words (*padattha*). As for "or by having it done through an order":
But [this is] according to the meaning of the words. And having established it thus, if one were to say, "by one doing it or by one causing it to be done," the phrasing would become contradictory.
For one who causes another to do it is not called "one doing it" oneself; therefore, such an objection should be seen as having no place.

She has no master (sāmī) or husband (pati); thus she is "without a master" (asāmikā). "Without a master" means "without a lord" (anissara), which is the sense. This is the state of being without a lord (anissaratā).
And here, regarding the phrase "by having it made," he said, "made by one who is devoid of a donor.
"Uddesa" means that which is to be pointed out. Regarding the word "tatra," since it is a locative case used in the sense of "belonging to" (sāmī), he said, "of that hut.
Regarding "dīghaso," since it is an ablative case (nissakkavacana), he said, "in length. "Bahikuṭṭe" means outside the wall; a lump mixed with chaff is a "thusapiṇḍa," of that...
"Having the size of a lump of husks" means having the size of a lump of clay mixed with husks; what is meant is "by way of the size of a lump of clay mixed with husks.
However, white plastering on top of a lump of husks is not subject to the formal rule. "Internal" (*abbhantarimo*) means that which exists within;
by that [term]. "In which" (*yattha*) means in which hut. "Proportionate in measure" (*pamāṇayutto*) means measuring nine spans of the ordinary *vidatthi*.
“Seven spans across” is stated as the maximum measurement; therefore, it is said that “at the minimum limit, it is not less than four cubits in width.
“Having cleared it” means having made it level, like the circle of the earth’s horizon. “Having requested the Saṅgha three times in the manner stated in the word-commentary” means:
“Having approached the Saṅgha, having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, [having paid homage] to the elder bhikkhus...”
Having prostrated at his feet, sat down in the *ukkuṭika* posture, and raised his joined palms, he should speak thus:
“Venerable sir, I desire to have a hut built by means of solicitation for myself, without an owner; therefore, Venerable sir, I request the Saṅgha to inspect the site for the hut.

Having made this request three times according to the method stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), [the site is approved] by the Saṅgha or by those authorized [by it]. This is what is stated in the word-commentary.

“Appointed by the Saṅgha” means authorized by the Saṅgha through a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*), or by a formal act consisting of a mere announcement (*apalokanakamma*). “Site” (*vatthu*) refers to the site for a hut.
“Without encroachment” (*anārambha*) means free from danger or harm. “With a walkway” (*saparikkamana*): it is called a walkway (*parikkamana*) because one moves or walks around it;
that which exists together with such a walkway is “with a walkway,” meaning it is provided with a space for circumambulation. This is why he said, “by those monks,” and so forth.

"Of ants and so forth": here, "ants" (*kipillikā*) refers to any kind [of ant] distinguished as red, black, brown, and so on; those of which these are the first are "ants and so forth" (*kipillikādīni*), [meaning] of them.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the inclusion of termites and others is intended. "Abode" (*āsaya*) means a place of fixed residence;

those of which this is the first are "abodes and so forth" (*āsayādayo*), [meaning] by them. And by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) here, that which is dependent [on the abode] is also included. "By the sixteen calamities" (*soḷasahi upaddavehi*).
Or it may be the dwelling place of ants, or of termites, or of rats, or of snakes, or of scorpions, or of centipedes;

or it may be the dwelling place of elephants, or of horses, or of lions, or of tigers, or of leopards, or of bears, or of hyenas, or of any other kind of animal; or it may be dependent on stored grain.

...or it is dependent on a market, a slaughterhouse, a cemetery, a park, a royal site, an elephant stable, a horse stable, a tethering shed, a tavern, a brothel, a street, a crossroads, an assembly hall, or a marketplace.
Thus it is said, referring to these sixteen calamities. In this context, "market" (*abbhāghāta*) means a place of execution.

"Slaughterhouse" (*āghātana*) means a place where animals are killed for meat. "Cemetery" (*susāna*) means a great cemetery. "Marketplace" (*saṃsaraṇa*) means a public thoroughfare that cannot be closed off, a path of constant coming and going.
"Because it is possible to traverse" means because it is possible to walk around due to the absence of broken banks and the like.

"By that bhikkhu" refers to the bhikkhu who built the hut. "Having requested" means: having arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, having paid homage at the feet of the elder bhikkhus, having sat down on his haunches, and having extended his joined palms, he should [request] thus:
He should be addressed thus: “Venerable sirs, I wish to have a hut built by means of solicitation, for myself, with no owner.

Venerable sirs, I request the Saṅgha for the designation of a site for the hut. When this has been requested three times, [the formal act] is performed by a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*):
“Let the Saṅgha, venerable sirs, hear me. This monk named so-and-so wishes to have a hut built by means of solicitation, for himself, with no owner...”

[He] has requested the site for a hut from the Saṅgha on his own behalf. If it seems appropriate to the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha grant the site for a hut to the monk named so-and-so. This is the motion. Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me:
this monk named so-and-so desires to have a hut built by means of solicitation for himself, on a site where he is the owner and for his own use; he [thereby] requests the Saṅgha.
He requests the assignment of a site for a hut. The Saṅgha assigns a site for a hut to the monk named so-and-so.
Whoever among the venerable ones approves of the assignment of a site for a hut to the monk named so-and-so, let him be silent.
Whoever does not approve, let him speak. The Saṅgha has assigned a site for a hut to the monk named so-and-so; this is pleasing to the Saṅgha.

"Therefore, be silent; thus do I hold this"—this refers to the formal act (*kamma*) consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiya-kamma*), as stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*). As for the "monks of Āḷavī": they were children born in the province of Āḷavī;
even at the time of their going forth, they were known simply as "Āḷavikas. It was with reference to them that it was said, "the monks of Āḷavī."
"Plastered" means either plastered on the inside—having joined the wall and the ceiling together with the inner plaster—or plastered on the outside—having joined them with the outer plaster.
"And two *dukkaṭas*" refers to the offenses incurred by way of causing damage and by way of the lack of a circumambulatory path (*aparikamma*).
"Failed in both" means failed or devoid of both measures regarding the confession; it is one whose material has not been confessed.
The meaning is "exceeding the measure. *Tasmiṃ* means in that door-panel or in the window.
*Lepo na ghaṭiyati* means the plaster previously applied does not join with the door-panel or the window; it is said that it does not remain as a single continuous whole.
*Taṃ* refers to touching that door-panel or window. *Paṭhamameva* means "right from the very beginning."

The intention is that because the task of plastering has been completed, it refers to the very moment the plastering is finished, since the doors and windows have already been set in place beforehand.

"If a monk builds a hut on a site that has been designated, which is of the prescribed measure, where harm is caused, and which lacks space for access, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If a monk builds a hut on a site that has been designated, which is of the prescribed measure, where no harm is caused, but which lacks space for access..."
Because it is stated in the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājaniya*) that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*), the phrase "merely for the sake of provocation" and so forth was said.
"Incomplete" means unfinished. "And giving to another" means giving to another person or to the Saṅgha.
A "cave" (*guhā*) is either a cave made of brick, a cave made of stone, a cave made of wood, or a cave dug in the earth. A "grass hut" (*tiṇakuṭi*) may even be seven stories high.
A palace with a thatched roof is called a "grass hut" (*tiṇakuṭikā*). "Of another" means of a teacher (*ācariya*), a preceptor (*upajjhāya*), or the Saṅgha.
"Excluding one's own dwelling place" means excluding a dwelling place used for one's own residence.

"In the Uposatha hall, etc."—here, by the word "etc.," the inclusion of the sauna (*jantāghara*), the dining hall (*bhojanasālā*), and the fire-hall (*aggisālā*) is intended. "The possibility of [meeting] the lower measurement" means...
"Four cubits in width. "He builds without having it measured out" means: he builds either exceeding the measurement or even one that is within the measurement, without having the site measured out.
And herein, not having the site measured out is the non-action; the building of the hut is the action.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the building of a hut is finished.

7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Building of a Monastery (*Vihārakārasikkhāpada*) It is "large" (*mahallaka*) because it takes (*lāti*) or grasps (*gaṇhāti*) much; thus, it is that which is large. And since he who grasps something possesses that thing, it is said: "It is 'large' (*mahallaka*) because it has the quality of largeness.
Now, by what is that quality of largeness [constituted], and from where does it come?
He says, "By way of having an owner," and so forth. To show that it is not only by way of having an owner, he says, "Or because," and so forth.
If this is so, then why is only this much stated in the word-commentary: "A 'large' monastery is called one with an owner"?
He says, "But because," and so forth. A *vihāra* is a dwelling (*āvāsa*) where they dwell; [in the *Mātikā*,] monks...
In the phrase *vā anabhiññeyya*, the word *vā* has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇattha*), as in such expressions as “This, indeed, is that great nāga.
*Kosambiyam* means in the city of that name. It is said that in various places within that city, such as its parks and lotus ponds, *kosamba* trees were particularly abundant;
therefore, it came to be known by the designation “Kosambī. [The word] “*kusumbassa*... [is used].
"Because it was built not far from the hermitage of the seer Nāma," say some. "With reference to the Elder Channa" means:

with reference to that Elder Channa who went forth together [with the Buddha] at the time of his renunciation, and upon whom the Teacher imposed the *brahmadaṇḍa* at the time of his final passing away (*parinibbāna*).
"Cetiyarukkha" (the Shrine-tree): in the sense of being honored (*cittīkata*), it is a designation for those shrines worthy of worship among the deities.
A “tree regarded as a shrine” (cetiyarukkha) is a tree that is considered a shrine (cetiya).

Because it is committed through the non-specification of a site, it is said to have an “originating nature from mere non-action. By the word *matta* (“mere”), the originating nature from action is excluded.
However, some say: “Because it originates both from the non-specification of a site and from the act of building a hut, it originates from both action and non-action.”
They say: the distinction lies precisely in the absence of a fixed limit for the measurement.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the construction of a dwelling is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule concerning corrupt faults.
It is called *duṭṭha* because it corrupts; it is called *dosa* because it corrupts another, that is, destroys them. Therefore he said, "Corrupted indeed," and so forth.
Now, in order to demonstrate in detail the very meaning stated in brief by the phrase "both corrupted and a corrupter," he said, "For when a fault has arisen," and so on.
"Causing the natural state to be abandoned" means causing the gentle state to be abandoned; it means having brought about a transformation.
This is what is meant. "By way of the diversity of modes" means by way of the difference between these two modes:
the mode of the defiled and the mode of the defiler. "Not arrived at" means not approached or not reached by means of rapture, pleasure, and so forth;
the meaning is "not having come near. And since one who is not approached by rapture, pleasure, and so forth is said to be devoid of them, he says: "by rapture, pleasure, and so forth..."
"Free from faults. And one who is free from those faults is not said to be "assailed" by them;
thus he says, "not assailed," meaning it is not pervaded by rapture, pleasure, and so forth. "It has no root" means it is rootless (*amūlaka*).
Since that state of being rootless is intended with respect to the accuser and not the accused, he says "by the accuser" and so forth to demonstrate that meaning.

It has been stated. In that context, "that" refers to the *pārājika* offense. "This" refers to whether the one who has been accused has actually committed the offense or not. "Here" means in this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
Now, in order to explain what was just mentioned by himself—namely, "seen" and so forth—it is said, "And here," and so on.

"In the same way" refers by extension to this meaning: "either by the ear of faith or by the divine ear. Furthermore, suspicion is threefold: suspicion regarding what has been seen, [suspicion regarding what has been heard, and suspicion regarding what has been suspected].
"Suspected on account of what was heard" (*suta-parisaṅkita*) and "suspected on account of what was inferred" (*muta-parisaṅkita*).

In this context, having seen a monk and a woman in such a place, to suspect—"Surely this has been done by these two," or "They will do it"—this is called "suspicion on account of what was seen" (*diṭṭha-parisaṅkita*).
Or, having heard the conversation of a monk and a woman in the dark or in a concealed place...
For one who does not know the presence of a second person, there is suspicion according to the method previously explained;

this is called "suspicion based on what has been heard. Having seen a place where scoundrels and women had gone after enjoying flowers, perfumes, meat, liquor, and so forth in a border monastery, a pavilion, or a hall, and while investigating, "By whom was this done?", someone there—

When a bhikkhu has performed worship with perfumes and the like, or has drunk an elixir (*ariṭṭha*) for medicinal purposes, and having smelled its scent, he suspects, "This must be that [alcohol]," this is called "suspected by what is smelt" (*mutaparisaṅkita*).
The absence of these three kinds of suspicion is "not suspected" (*aparisaṅkita*). Therefore he said: "not suspected by the mind on account of what is seen, heard, or smelt."
Furthermore, this [offense] does not apply only when one accuses oneself; therefore, it says, "of oneself or of another.

Since an offense indeed occurs even for one who accuses [another] with words such as, "You are a paṇḍaka," it is stated [in the Suttavibhaṅga]: "by any one of the nineteen [grounds] appropriate for a bhikkhu.
If that is so, then why is it said in the word-commentary (padabhājana), "by a pārājika dhamma" [referring specifically] to the four?
Since it was stated [in the Sutta] as "by another," he said, "But in the word-commentary (padabhājana)," and so forth.

Because prepositions (upasagga) and particles (nipāta) function by way of indicating their meaning once they have been determined as expressive words, it is said, "he would destroy" (dhaṃseyya). And here, "destruction" (dhaṃsana) means overcoming (abhibhavana).
Therefore, he said, "he would overcome" (abhibhaveyya). It proceeds according to the method beginning with, "You have practiced the sexual act," and so on.
It occurs thus: "You have engaged in sexual intercourse, you have taken what was not given, you have caused a human being to be killed, you have spoken what is false.

In this context, some say: "Because it is not stated that 'you are no longer an ascetic' is a reason for not paying homage, one who has committed an ultimate offense (antimavatthu) should not be paid homage";
however, that should not be accepted, because among those who are not to be paid homage, there is one who has committed an ultimate offense.

Because it has not been stated [otherwise], and because it has been stated that "one who was ordained earlier is to be saluted by one who was ordained later," this [statement] was made in order to show what should be said by oneself.
"In the vicinity" means within a space measuring twelve cubits. For the renunciation of the training itself is indicated by the gesture of the hand over the head.
It does not come; however, this is indeed a form of disparagement and the proclamation of what is unreal. Therefore he said, "or even by means of hand gestures.
Regarding *brahmacariya*: it is called *brahmacariya* because it is the conduct (*cariya*) that is *brahma*, meaning supreme and praised;
or alternatively, it is *brahmacariya* because it is the conduct of the *brahmas*, namely the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, and noble disciples, who are the most excellent.
Therefore, it is the holy life (*brahmacariya*). For this reason, he said, "the best conduct. May it indeed be entirely auspicious for him.

The intention of one who accuses another of an offense with the thought, "We shall perform the seven kinds of formal acts, beginning with the act of censure (*tajjanīyakamma*)," is the "intention regarding the formal act" (*kammādhippāya*).

The intention of one who thinks, "We shall restore [him] from his offense," is the "intention regarding restoration" (*vuṭṭhānādhippāya*). The "intention regarding investigation" (*anuvijjanādhippāya*) is...

[It is] with the intention of investigating; with the intention of examining. "By the investigator" means by the master of discipline (vinayadhara) seated in the midst of the Saṅgha to adjudicate the legal issue (adhikaraṇa) that has arisen. "What have you seen? means: "What was seen by you?
Was he seen committing the first *pārājika*, or was he seen committing the second, third, or fourth *pārājika* offense?"
This has been stated. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), it includes this method: "What have you seen? When did you see it? Where did you see it?

It is called *adhikaraṇa* because it is to be attended to (*adhikātabba*) by means of reconciliations (*samatha*) that proceed for the purpose of reconciliation (*samanatthāya*). For, by way of reconciliation...
The state of being predominant among the *samatha* methods applies to disputes (*vivāda*) and so forth; likewise, disputes and the rest must be dealt with by those [methods].
Therefore he said, "by way of being settled through the *samatha* methods," and so on. For by this, the accusative derivation (*kamma-sādhana*) of the word *adhikaraṇa* is stated.

*Adhikaraṇa* refers to the dispute-settlement (*vivādādhikaraṇa*), the accusation-settlement (*anuvādādhikaraṇa*), the offense-settlement (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), and the business-settlement (*kiccādhikaraṇa*).

There are four kinds of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*). The methods of settling, such as face-to-face resolution (*sammukhāvinaya*) and so forth, are called "settlers" (*samatha*) because they settle and resolve legal issues such as disputes (*vivāda*).
Alternatively, it is called a "legal issue" (*adhikaraṇa*) because legal issues are brought forward (*adhikarīyanti*) therein. What is brought forward? The methods of settling.
How are they brought forward? By way of settlement. Thus, the meaning here should be understood as: "those which settle and resolve legal issues are the methods of settling."
"Excepting the legal issue of offenses (*āpattādhikaraṇa*), because there is no formal accusation regarding the remaining legal issues, it is said:

'But this is intended as the legal issue of offenses alone, namely that which is designated as a *pārājika*. A legal issue that is itself an offense is a 'legal issue of offenses' (*āpattādhikaraṇa*). The meaning is:
at the very moment of the accusation, it is a *saṅghādisesa*; if he recognizes it at that very moment, that is the intention."
*Mettiya-bhūmajaka* refers to Mettiya and Bhūmajaka; these were the foremost among the group of six (Chabbaggiyā).
*Suddhaṃ vā* means not having incurred a *pārājika* offense. By the phrase "if he knows it at that very moment," [the text] indicates the time of mental advertence (*āvajjana*).
Knowing it at that very moment is difficult; however, once one has adverted to it through the process of attention and then known it, it is indeed known. Afterwards...

If one knows this, it does not reach the head. Regarding the training rules on renouncing the training, making false accusations, speaking of a grave offense, acting according to one's own will, and making false accusations out of malice—all of these indeed have the same determination (*ekapariccheda*).
However, because there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who speaks in the absence of the person regarding all seven classes of offenses, it is said:
"But for one who reproaches in the absence of the person, it does not reach the head. These are the offenses according to the stated method.
The offenses of *saṅghādisesa* and *dukkaṭa* are according to the method stated by the phrase “with each word,” and so forth. “In the same way” means with each word indeed.

“Of one who speaks” means of one who speaks face-to-face to one who is fully ordained (*upasampanna*) regarding any of the seven classes of offenses. “Precisely according to the stated method” means with each word indeed.
For one who, having requested permission, speaks face-to-face to one who is fully ordained, there is an offense of *pācittiya* for every word.
He said: "For one who speaks after having obtained leave, it is indeed a *pācittiya* offense. By the word "indeed" (*eva*), a *dukkaṭa* offense is excluded.
For one who speaks in the absence [of the person concerned] regarding even all seven classes of offenses, there is a *dukkaṭa*.

"The sevenfold legal act" (*kamma*) refers to the sevenfold legal act consisting of: censure (*tajjanīya*), demotion (*niyasa*), banishment (*pabbājanīya*), reconciliation (*paṭisāraṇīya*), and the three types of suspension (*ukkhepanīya*).

Regarding the statement, "There is no formal act of granting leave for one who suspends the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā," here, even if it is suspended before or after the Uposatha, it is considered not suspended.
However, if it is suspended within the boundary (khetta), it is indeed suspended. Therefore:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: today is the Uposatha of the fifteenth day. If it is timely for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha..."
Regarding the phrase "one should perform [it]," as long as one is reciting up to the letter *re*, it must be suspended; this is the field [of application].

However, when the letter *yya* is uttered, for one who suspends [the act], it is said to be "suspended afterwards. For one who suspends it before the words "May it be heard by me" have been commenced, it is "suspended beforehand.
Furthermore, the suspension of the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) is of two kinds: collective and individual. Among these—
In the *sabbasaṅgāhika* [formula], from the word "suṇātu" up to the letter "re" in "pavāreyya," the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) remains incomplete;
during this interval, even by one who pauses for a single word, the invitation is considered suspended.
But when the letter "yya" is reached, it is indeed completed; therefore, from that point onward, by one who pauses—

It is "suspended. However, in the case of suspending for an individual, from the words "Venerable Sir, I invite the Saṅgha... [and so on]... For the third time, Venerable Sir, I invite the Saṅgha regarding what has been seen...
[and so on]... seeing it, I shall confess it," as long as one stops short of this very last syllable *ṭi*, the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) remains incomplete;
yet, by stopping at even a single word within that interval, it is considered "suspended."
The invitation (pavāraṇā) takes place [only when the formal act is completed]. However, when one says, "I shall perform it," the invitation is already concluded;

therefore, upon reaching this phrase "I shall perform it," even if the procedure is suspended, it is as if it were not suspended. This same principle applies to the two-vocal and one-vocal invitations, as well as those for those of the same year (samānavassikā).
For in these cases too, the limit for suspension is precisely the ending of the syllable *ti*. Hence he said: "But the field for suspension must be known."

"Regarding the matter having been brought forward": when that which should be stated by the accuser has been declared in the midst of the Saṅgha, such as "He does this and that"—namely, he commits the taking of life, he commits the taking of what is not given, and he accepts gold and silver.

For one who speaks in the presence of another with the intention of reviling, saying "So-and-so and so-and-so are not true recluses, they are not lay followers," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); [but if it is] in their absence...

But for one who speaks [in such a way], it is indeed a *pācittiya*. Therefore he said: "If, however, having specified [the person] by name," and so forth. "Entering into a reckoning" means entering into common usage.
The commentary on the training rule concerning corrupt faults is finished. 9.
Commentary on the training rule concerning matters belonging to another case.
"Aññabhāgassa" means "of another portion"; that is to say, of another category such as the animal realm, distinct from the category of birth and so forth of the one whom he wishes to accuse.
"Idaṃ" (this) refers to the goat and so forth by way of a neuter designation;
the meaning is "this goat and so forth," or rather, it is expressed in the neuter in view of the word denoting the locus (adhikaraṇa), meaning "this locus consisting of the goat and so forth."

It has been stated. "Another part" (*aññabhāgo*) means either another division distinguished by species such as the animal kingdom and so forth, or [another part] of the goat and so forth. "Belonging to another part" (*aññabhāgiyaṃ*) refers to the goat and so forth.

Herein, the meaning of the first compound is "that which is connected with another part is 'belonging to another part,'" while the meaning of the second compound is "that which possesses another part is 'belonging to another part. However, setting aside the animal kingdom and so forth...

It should be understood that even though, in the ultimate sense (*paramatthato*), there is no separate goat or similar animal, the expression "this belongs to another part" or "another part exists for it" is used by way of worldly convention (*lokavohāra*) based on the conceptualization of difference where there is actually non-difference, as in the case of expressions such as "the body of the image.
That wherein something is located is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Therefore he said: "The support (*ādhāra*) should be understood."
That in which something is supported is a "basis" (ādhāra), meaning a foundation. Therefore he said: "The 'subject matter' (vatthu) is what is meant by 'the basis' (adhiṭṭhāna).

Now, taking up exactly that meaning which was stated briefly in the phrase "this belongs to another part," etc., and analyzing it solely for the sake of demonstrating the method as it appeared in the *Aṭṭhuppatti*, he says "For whoever... and so forth. By this, [it is asked]: "Is it not [the case] in the future?"...
This training rule was laid down for the purpose of extinguishing even a slight opening for those wicked bhikkhus who thus incite others;
it was not, however, for the sake of Mettiya and Bhūmajaka. Since they were beginners, there was no offense for them;
therefore, the meaning should be analyzed in its general sense, and not according to the specific detail such as, "He who, in the origin story, was Dabba Mallaputta," and so forth.
Such an objection should be understood as having no basis. The particle *hi* is used in the sense of a reason; "because" is what is meant. Regarding the phrase *aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ*:
the arising of a matter (*attha*) is *atthuppatti*; *atthuppatti* itself is *aṭṭhuppatti*.
In that *aṭṭhuppatti*, it means "in the origin of the training rule. *Chagalaka* refers to a white goat. *So*... [text continues]
“Chagalaka. This, moreover, is connected with the word “hoti” (there is).

Regarding “of another... and of the state of being a goat”: the meaning is “of another portion, part, or side,” namely that which is designated as “both the animal species and the state of being a goat.
From where does this “other” come, since it was stated as “of another portion”? To this he says: “That which is... from that. In this context, the human species—
The connection is: "the portion, the part, which is both human birth and the state of being a bhikkhu.

The meaning is: "the portion, the part, known as 'both human birth and the state of being a bhikkhu'. "From that" means from the portion consisting of "both human birth and the state of being a bhikkhu.
Or, "that is another portion" refers to what is designated as the state of being a beast and a goat, as previously mentioned.
"Another part" (*aññabhāga*) means another portion. "Of him" (*assa*) means of the goat. "Exists" (*atthi*) means it is found.

"Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because there is another part belonging to the goat, and because that [other part] exists as his; therefore. Regarding the phrase "it receives the designation 'pertaining to another'":
here, having brought over the word "that" (*so*) from the expression "that which is this" (*so yvāyaṃ*), one should connect it thus: "That [goat] receives the designation 'pertaining to another'."
The word “so” (thus) should be understood as a remainder of the text. The particle “ca” has the sense of conjunction.
Furthermore, it should be seen as following the word *adhikaraṇa*, and it should be understood that [the term] “*adhikaraṇa*” [is used here]. “Of them” means of Mettiya and Bhūmajaka.
“We shall make this one ‘Dabba Mallaputta’”—this was said after they saw a goat mating with a she-goat.
“Friends, we shall give this goat the name Dabba Mallaputta,” they said. Regarding the phrase “by means of the perception of naming”:

it refers to the perception designated as naming. Here too, having supplied the words “he who,” and so forth, that goat which was mentioned in the *aṭṭhuppatti* (the introductory narrative) as “named Dabba Mallaputta” is the support (*ādhāra*) and the basis (*vatthu*) for that perception of naming.
The term *adhiṭṭhāna* (resolution) should be supplied.

Now, how is it understood that this [term] means "legal issue" (*adhikaraṇa*)? Here, it should be understood as the locus (*ādhāra*), not as one of the specific types of legal issues such as disputes (*vivādādhikaraṇa*).
With reference to this, he says, "With reference to that," and so forth. In that context, "that" refers to the designation by which the name is applied.

He refers back to the goat that served as the formal basis (*adhiṭṭhānabhūta*). The connection is that it was not stated with reference to any one of the legal issues such as the *vivādādhikaraṇa* (legal issue arising from dispute).
Therein, he asks for the reason: "Why? He states the reason: "Because of impossibility.
Now, in order to make that very impossibility clear and show it, the passage beginning with "For they did not take [it]" was spoken. "For they did not take [it]" means:
"Connection. "They took up" means they grasped. To the question, "Is there even a trace of the four kinds of legal issues (adhikaraṇa) present here, such that it was stated thus?
he says, "And not even a trace of the four kinds of legal issues," and so forth. Now, in order to support that very point, he says, "For there are stains of birth (jātileśa) and so on," and so forth.
In this context, "birth-stain" (jātileśa) means birth itself as a stain. By the word "and so on" (ādi), the stains of name (nāmaleśa) and the rest are included. And there is a verse here:
“The *lesas* are by way of birth, name, clan, gender, and offense;
and by way of bowl, robe, preceptor, conduct, and residence—these are the ten.
Regarding the *lesa* of offense: it is when one is seen committing a light offense, yet another accuses them of a *pārājika*: “You are no longer a recluse!”...
"Are you not a follower of the Son of the Sakyan?"—for every word [spoken], there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
Thus, because the classification of offenses was stated by attributing them specifically to the individual, it is said that "the inclinations (*lesā*) were stated only with respect to individuals.
And that name, "Dabba Mallaputta," was given to him by the Mettiya-Bhūmajakas; and that name "Dabba Mallaputta" [was thus applied]. In this way...
Having demonstrated the impossibility [of the former], he now says “And here,” etc., in order to explain the meaning of the terms *desa* (place) and *lesa* (part) within this very context.
“Here” means in these two [cases of] place and part. A “place” (*desa*) refers to conventional usage divided into categories such as genus (*jāti*), and so forth. Therefore he says, “In genus, etc.
He also says “another basis” (*aññampi vatthu*); that is, setting aside the specific basis upon which [the term] is established, there is yet another.
[He asks: "How does it adhere? To this he says: "By way of mere conventional expression (*vohāramattena*) alone," the intention being that it is not [so] in terms of actual meaning.
By the phrase "it adheres slightly" (*īsakaṃ allīyati*), he shows that "blemish" (*leso*) is a derivative form of the root *lisa*, in the sense of "adhering.
Although there is a difference between the regions and the blemishes in terms of their verbal expression according to the method already stated, there is none in terms of their meaning.
He said: “This is a designation for one or another category among birth and so forth.

But if it was stated as “of a legal issue belonging to another class” with reference to the goat that served as the basis for the naming convention, then why was it not analyzed in the word-commentary?
[It was stated: “Of a legal issue belonging to another class” means “one belonging to a different class of offense.”
Because it was said, "Is it a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) or one pertaining to something else (*aññabhāgiya*)? and so forth, he says, "But in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*)," and so on.

"That" refers to the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) reckoned as the locus (*ādhāra*). "Manifested" means made clear. "By way of extracting the meaning" means by way of extracting the meanings that ought to be stated by it.
But is it not the case that "words settle upon the mere meaning," and thus [the meaning] is not [conveyed] by a single word?

"Are many meanings expressed? This is true when specific words are considered; however, this investigation, being stated by taking into account the commonality of those various meanings as being expressible by the word *adhikaraṇa*, is called "the extraction of the meaning of the word *adhikaraṇa*.
For this very reason he said: "By way of the commonality of expression, [the following] proceed by way of the extraction of the meaning: *adhikaraṇa*..."
“There are four legal issues. *Aññabhāgiyatā* means belonging to another side. *Tabbhāgiyatā* means belonging to that same side.

[The meaning] is not evident from the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), because there is no other place where it is shown except here. At the end, regarding the charge of being one who belongs to another side in relation to an offense:
“A bhikkhu is seen committing a *saṅghādisesa* offense; he perceives it as a *saṅghādisesa* offense...”
This was said with reference to such an accusation as, "It exists, and he accuses him of a *pārājika* offense.

For each individual legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) is distinct from the other three—belonging to a different category, a different side, and a different division—because its subject matter (*vatthu*) is dissimilar.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the text refers to] such passages as, "How is a legal issue distinct from another legal issue? and so forth.
The division of the words has been included.

Regarding the phrase "taking a certain portion, merely by way of a hint," since what ought to be said on this point was already stated below in connection with demonstrating the impossibility [of other interpretations], it was said:
"The remaining exposition is exactly like that which was stated in the eighth [chapter]. In that context, the "remaining" [portion]...

"Explanatory discussion" (*vinicchayakathā*) refers to the discussion of legal analysis beginning with, "Regarding 'an offense entailing defeat' (*pārājika*), it is by one of the nineteen [offenses] appropriate for a monk," and so forth.

"Is exactly like what was already stated": here, that which is to be said regarding this training rule (*sikkhāpada*) is intended as being "exactly like what was stated" because it is common to that previous training rule;
it does not refer to that which is uncommon and thus requires a new commentary.

Because it is intended [there]. For that very reason, he said, "But this," and so forth. Since there is no offense for one who perceives it in that way even regarding the previous training rule, it is stated, "And here.
"Even for one who perceives it in that way" means even for one who perceives, "This person has indeed fallen into a *pārājika* offense.
The word *iti* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*) or the sense of "manner" (*pakāra*). By that, [it refers to] some other person of kṣatriya birth by some monk...
He was seen committing an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*).
Then, seeing another monk of kṣatriya birth who was his own enemy, he took that mark of kṣatriya birth as a pretext and accused him thus:
"A kṣatriya was seen by me committing an offense entailing defeat; you, being a kṣatriya, have committed an offense entailing defeat. Then...
"Whether you are a khattiya or no other, you have committed an offense involving defeat (pārājika); you are no longer an ascetic, you are no longer a son of the Sakyans;
there is no Uposatha, nor Pavāraṇā, nor any formal act of the Saṅgha with you. For every such statement, there is an offense of Saṅghādisesa for each individual utterance.
And in this context, among those khattiyas, [the offense applies] to each respective person who is different from the others, whether tall or otherwise.

Alternatively, "belonging to another category" (aññabhāgiyatā) should be understood by way of what has been seen and so forth, and "the basis for a legal question" (adhikaraṇatā) by way of being the foundation for the designation of the Khattiya caste.
This same method applies to the "traces of names" (nāmalese) and so on as well.
Regarding the "traces of offenses" (āpattilese), however, it may happen that some monk is seen by another monk committing a light offense.
If he accuses that bhikkhu of a *pārājika* offense, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa* for every word spoken.

If this is so, how is it that the legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) is "belonging to another category" (*aññabhāgiya*)? For that legal issue regarding the light offense he has committed is "belonging to another category" in relation to the *pārājika*;
it is merely a trace (*leso*) of that legal issue belonging to another category. As for that...
Just as the status of being a khattiya is common to all khattiyas, so too is the status of being an offense (āpatti) common to all offenses.
By this very method, it includes specific instances such as: "A certain bhikkhu was seen by another bhikkhu committing a saṅghādisesa offense," and so forth.
He who does not train in the training pertaining to another with proper application should be led by those knowledgeable in the Vinaya to the status of one pertaining to another.
The commentary on the training rule concerning "pertaining to another" is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule on Schism in the Saṅgha (Saṅghabhedasikkhāpada).
“Of one who is united” (*sahitassa*) means of one who has become one in both body and mind. Therefore, he said: “The meaning is ‘not separated from mind and body.
“*Assa*” refers to the word “of one who is in harmony” (*samaggassa*). “Of common affiliation” (*samānasaṃvāsako*) means having the same [formal] acts, such as the Uposatha, and so forth.

"One who has common residence" (*samānasaṃvāsaka*) means one who possesses common residence; that is, one who is free from both difference of tenet (*laddhi-nānāsaṃvāsaka*) and difference of formal act (*kamma-nānāsaṃvāsaka*).
"By granting physical concord" (*kāyasāmaggidānato*) means by granting with the body, or by granting the state of being together through physical concord;
what is meant is: by coming within arm's reach for those various formal acts of the Saṅgha. [The thought is: "How indeed might this person be split?"
"By what means indeed might this Saṅgha become divided? "He would strive" means he would exert effort, seek out a faction, and form a group—this is what is meant.
It is called *karaṇa* because it produces its own fruit; any cause whatsoever is a *karaṇa*.
An "additional cause" (*adhika-karaṇa*) is an *adhikaraṇa*, meaning a specific cause. And that specific cause is for the schism of the Saṅgha.
It is said: “Of schism,” and so forth. It is of eighteen kinds by way of the grounds for causing schism:
“Here, Upāli, monks proclaim what is non-Dhamma as ‘Dhamma,’ and they proclaim what is Dhamma as ‘non-Dhamma.
They proclaim what is non-Vinaya as ‘Vinaya,’ and they proclaim what is Vinaya as ‘non-Vinaya. They proclaim what was not spoken, not uttered by the Tathāgata as ‘spoken... [and so on].
They proclaim that which was spoken by the Tathāgata as "not spoken, not uttered by the Tathāgata"; they proclaim that which was uttered by the Tathāgata as "not spoken, not uttered by the Tathāgata.
They proclaim what was not practiced by the Tathāgata as "practiced by the Tathāgata," and they proclaim what was practiced by the Tathāgata as "not practiced by the Tathāgata.
They proclaim what was not prescribed by the Tathāgata as "prescribed..."
They proclaim what was taught by the Tathāgata as "not taught by the Tathāgata," and they proclaim what was not taught by the Tathāgata as "taught by the Tathāgata.
They proclaim a non-offense as "an offense," and they proclaim an offense as "a non-offense.
They proclaim a light offense as "a heavy offense," and they proclaim a heavy offense as "a light offense. They proclaim an offense with remainder as "without remainder" [and vice versa].
They explain an offense that is without remainder as "an offense with remainder"; they explain an offense that is with remainder as "an offense without remainder.
They explain a grave offense as "not a grave offense"; they explain an offense that is not grave as "a grave offense.

Thus, it is eighteenfold by way of the eighteen causes for schism mentioned in the *Kammakkhandhaka*. For the cause is called the "basis" (*vatthu*) because the fruit dwells therein due to its dependence upon that cause. And there are these verses on the subject:
The pairs concerning what is spoken in the Dhamma and Vinaya and what has been practiced and laid down;
the pairs concerning offenses that are light or grave, and those with remainder.
These eighteen are called the "bases for causing a schism."
“Seized by perversion, they are the basis and support for dispute.
*Paggayha* means having grasped, uplifted, and made manifest.

*Tiṭṭheyya* means that one should remain exactly as one has undertaken [the position] and exactly as one has grasped it. For when one grasps and remains thus, that [position] is both displayed and not relinquished.

Because it exists, it is therefore said: "he would illuminate [it] and yet not relinquish it. Regarding the question of how far one must hear and then go before there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for those who do not speak, he says:
"at least as far as the limit," and so forth. Here, the word *pi* is used in the sense of "even" or "at least";
its connection should be understood with the phrase "only half a *yojana*. In that context, "only half a *yojana*" means...
By this, it is shown that there is no need to speak [of the offense] when staying in the same monastery.

By the word "having gone," it is shown that there is no release from the offense even for one who speaks after sending a messenger or a letter; rather, one must go in person and restrain him, saying: "Friend, schism in the Saṅgha is grave; do not strive for schism in the Saṅgha."
"Let him come together" means let him become one. Since becoming one occurs by way of having the same conviction (*laddhi*), he said, "let him be of one conviction.
One who has a single conviction or grasp is "one of one conviction" (*ekaladdhika*); the meaning is "one of a single view" (*ekadiṭṭhika*).
"By mutual attainment" means by the attainment consisting of mutual conformity of view and mind. [It refers to] "the mutual acquisition of virtues and so forth."
Some say, "In the case of prosperity. For when a community is not in concord, it recites the Pātimokkha separately, either outside the boundary or within the monastery grounds;
thus, it is not a single recitation. Therefore he said: "The meaning is 'the recitation of the Pātimokkha proceeding from one [source]'".

Regarding "an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who does not relinquish," this refers to an offense of wrong-doing according to the number of those speaking separately. "A formal act of censure (samanubhāsanakamma) should be performed" means...
The formal act of admonition (samanubhāsanakamma) must be performed up to three times;

that is to say, the act is to be carried out by means of the three formal proclamations of admonition consisting of a motion followed by three statements (ñatticatuttha), as set forth in the word-commentary beginning with: “Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: this monk named so-and-so is striving for a schism in the harmonious Saṅgha. Regarding the phrase “he strives for a schism”:
Because it is stated separately, it should be understood that a formal act of admonition (samanubhāsanakamma) must be performed against one who,
having undertaken and maintained a legal issue conducive to schism, was previously striving for a schism in the Saṅgha by means of seeking partisans and so forth.
It is said, "There is safety for that bhikkhu," because there is no offense for one who relinquishes [the position].
Although a bhikkhunī does not actually cause a schism in the Saṅgha, she nevertheless strives for its division; therefore, it is said that this is a "common prescription" (sādhāraṇapaññatti).
For one who commits a *saṅghādisesa* offense, the *dukkaṭa* incurred by the formal motion (*ñatti*) and the *thullaccaya*s incurred by the two subsequent proclamations (*kammavācā*) are suspended;
thus he says, "in the formal act of admonition," and so forth. Both that *dukkaṭa* and those *thullaccaya*s [are suspended].
"They are pacified" means that the *dukkaṭa* offense incurred at the conclusion of the motion (*ñatti*), and the two *thullaccaya* offenses incurred during the two proclamations (*kammavācā*),
these three offenses are pacified like uncommon offenses (*asādhāraṇāpatti*) through the change of gender.
However, if at the conclusion of the motion he falls into a sense of shame, restraint arises, and he relinquishes [the offense], [then it is pacified].
Having confessed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the motion (*ñatti*), he is released.

But if he does not relinquish it, and both strives for a schism and persists in taking up and adhering to a legal issue conducive to a schism, the wrong-doing for the motion is quelled, and he stands established in a grave offense (*thullaccaya*) at the first formal proclamation (*kammavācā*). This same method applies to the subsequent formal proclamations as well.
There is no offense of *saṅghādisesa* even for one who does not confess when being exhorted, nor for one who does not relinquish [the offense].
However, for one who does relinquish it— whether before the motion (*ñatti*), at the moment of the motion, at the conclusion of the motion,
or during the first, second, or third proclamation (*anussāvana*)— as long as he relinquishes it before the syllable "yya" is reached, there is no offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
There is no offense. Therefore he said, “And for one who is not being formally admonished,” and so forth.
Here, however, because it is stated in the Parivāra that “Devadatta strove for the schism of a united Saṅgha;
in that matter,” Devadatta is the first offender, but only with respect to his striving for the schism of the Saṅgha.
It does not apply to one who does not relinquish [the view], for that action has not been performed by him. If it is asked, "How is this to be known?"—it is from the Sutta.

For it is stated in the Parivāra regarding the case of the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-catcher: "The monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-catcher, did not relinquish a wicked view despite being exhorted up to three times concerning that matter. Thus it is established for Ariṭṭha.
It is recognized that Devadatta’s action was committed, whereas Devadatta’s [action] was not so [recognized].

Even if someone were to say, based on their own mere preference, "He must have committed it," nevertheless, for one who does not relinquish [the offense], there is no such thing as "no offense" for a first-time offender.
For there is no exemption from offense for one who transgresses a prescribed training rule, except where it has been specifically permitted.

[The name] is seen [in the texts]. Furthermore, as for the phrase "for a first-offender" (*ādikammikassa*) that is written in manuscripts within the section on non-offenses in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) to the Ariṭṭha training rule (*sikkhāpada*), that is a scribal error; and the fact that it is a scribal error is evident from the passage in the Kammakkhandhaka which states:
"First, the monk Ariṭṭha should be accused; having been accused, he should be reminded; having been reminded, the offense should be formally charged. Thus it is said.
It is to be understood from the imposition of the offense.
In this case, because the formal act was not performed against Devadatta while he was striving for schism, no offense was actually incurred by him;
however, since the training rule was promulgated with reference to him, he is called "the first offender."

Thus it was stated. Therefore, because there is an absence of an offense, it is stated that there is no offense for him. Now, although this [exemption] is already established by the phrase "of one who is not being formally admonished," it is nevertheless said:
for one who is "not being formally admonished" refers to one for whom they do not perform a formal admonition at all;

such a person is called an "original offender" (*ādikammika*), and not one who has committed the act repeatedly. And since Devadatta is indeed an original offender, therefore [the text says]: "of an original offender."
This has been stated. By this very method, the exposition for all formal admonitions (*samanubhāsanā*) should be understood, with the exception of the Arittha training rule (*ariṭṭha-sikkhāpada*).
In terms of origination, it originates from body, speech, and mind; it originates from the act of formal admonition.

However, because one incurs the offense even without making a physical gesture or uttering a verbal expression while saying "I relinquish [the view]," it is a non-action (*akiriya*). As for "I do not relinquish":
It is called "liberation through perception" because one is liberated by means of the absence of perception. It is "with consciousness" simply by the conscious thought, "I do not relinquish [it].
The commentary on the training rule concerning schism in the Saṅgha is finished.
11. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Those Who Follow the Schism.
“Of that very person” means of one who is striving for schism. *Kho* is a mere particle. *Panā* is a particle used for emphasis.

He says, “They call a divisive speech ‘factional’ (*vagga*) here,” meaning that speech which creates factions—that is, divides even a group that is otherwise united—such speech is called “factional” in this context; thus he says, “they speak a factional word, a word belonging to the side of discord. Regarding the side of discord:

Those who belong to the faction of dissension are quarrelsome; their speech is "speech belonging to the faction of dissension" (*asāmaggipakkhiyavacana*). Alternatively, speech that arises within the faction of dissension is "speech belonging to the faction of dissension.

The statement, "Indeed, the Saṅgha does not perform a legal act against the Saṅgha," is said with reference to a legal act that must be performed by way of formal censure (*niggaha*); however, for a legal act such as a committee (*ubbāhikā*), even many [monks] may perform it.

It is indeed proper to do so. "One who speaks according to the Dhamma" means one who speaks what is factual. "One who speaks according to the Vinaya" means one who speaks for the sake of pacification.
Regarding the phrase "he knows," here too the words "desire and approval" (*chandañca ruciñca*) should be supplied and connected [to the verb]. Therefore he said: "He knows our desires and so forth.
Regarding the word "speaks," here the word "not" (*no*) is to be construed by changing its case ending. Therefore he said: "Thus..."

"He says 'I do' because he speaks with us. By the word "this," they refer back to his action; thus he said, "that which he does," and so forth. "He" refers to one who is striving for a schism in the Saṅgha. Regarding the phrase "May the venerable ones agree," he said, "the mind of the venerable ones," because the word "mind" (*citta*) must be supplied here. "Just as was stated before" means: ... [text continues] ... In this context, the meaning is that it is not possible for the minds of those who are not in agreement to be united. Why? Because there is no commonality of view among them. For it is said: "The mind of one who is angry cannot be united with the mind of one who is pleased; the mind of one who is pleased cannot be united with the mind of one who is angry; the mind of one who is deluded cannot be united with the mind of one who is wise; the mind of one who is wise cannot be united with the mind of one who is deluded; the mind of one who is lustful cannot be united with the mind of one who is free from lust; the mind of one who is free from lust cannot be united with the mind of one who is lustful; the mind of one who is hateful cannot be united with the mind of one who is free from hatred; the mind of one who is free from hatred cannot be united with the mind of one who is hateful; the mind of one who is deluded cannot be united with the mind of one who is free from delusion; the mind of one who is free from delusion cannot be united with the mind of one who is deluded. Thus, because their views are different, the minds of those who are not in agreement cannot be united. Therefore, it is impossible for the minds of those who are not in agreement to be united. This is the meaning. "But the minds of those who are in agreement can be united" means: because there is a commonality of view among them, the minds of those who are in agreement can be united. Why? Because it is said: "The mind of one who is angry can be united with the mind of one who is pleased; the mind of one who is pleased can be united with the mind of one who is angry; the mind of one who is deluded can be united with the mind of one who is wise; the mind of one who is wise can be united with the mind of one who is deluded; the mind of one who is lustful can be united with the mind of one who is free from lust; the mind of one who is free from lust can be united with the mind of one who is lustful; the mind of one who is hateful can be united with the mind of one who is free from hatred; the mind of one who is free from hatred can be united with the mind of one who is hateful; the mind of one who is deluded can be united with the mind of one who is free from delusion; the mind of one who is free from delusion can be united with the mind of one who is deluded. Thus, because their views are the same, the minds of those who are in agreement can be united. Therefore, it is possible for the minds of those who are in agreement to be united. This is the meaning. What ought to be said has already been stated below in the commentary on the *aññabhāgiya-sikkhāpada*.
The commentary on the *bhedānuvattaka-sikkhāpada* is finished.
12. Commentary on the *dubbaca-sikkhāpada*.
One who cannot be spoken to because of suffering, whose very nature is such that he cannot be instructed, is "difficult to speak to" (*dubbacajātiko*);

he acts in opposition. Therefore, it says "one whose nature is difficult to speak to," and so forth. One who cannot be spoken to means one who cannot be advised because of intolerance when anything is said to him.
That which is recited is the "recitation" (*uddeso*), namely the *Pātimokkha*; those included within it, contained therein, are "included in the recitation" (*uddesapariyāpannā*).

Regarding those [rules] included in the recitation (uddesa): that is why he said, “In the recitation,” and so forth. Now, in what way are all the training rules (sikkhāpada) included in the recitation of the Pātimokkha?
He says: “Because they are thus comprised by the statement, ‘He who has an offense should reveal it.
By the phrase “he who has an offense,” all offenses whatsoever are indeed included in the recitation of the Introduction (nidāna-uddesa). Regarding the training rules...
The meaning is: "in the Vinaya formulations which serve as the means for attaining the training in higher virtue (*adhisīla-sikkhā*).

However, because that [meaning] is already evident, it was not stated in the *Aṭṭhakathā*. "By five fellow practitioners of the Dhamma" refers to the monks, nuns, male novices, female novices, and probationary nuns.
"Because they must train" means because they must train according to what is applicable to them; for by them, their respective training...
One is trained, but not in everything. “By what is prescribed by the Buddha” means established by the Buddha; the sense is that it has been ordained.
Alternatively, the meaning here should be understood as: “being spoken to by one who is in accordance with the Dhamma and for a valid reason.
Regarding the word *vacanāya*, he says “from my speaking” because the dative case is used in the sense of the ablative (*nissakka*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning abusive speech is finished.
13. Commentary on the training rule concerning the corrupter of families:
Since a city is also a particular type of village, the term "village" here includes the city as well; thus he said, "the city also..."
"Or it is included within the village"—by the word *vā* (or), in the sense of an alternative option (*anuttavikappa*), the inclusion is stated thus.

Furthermore, in this context, the distinction between these three should be understood: a *nigama* (market town) is one surrounded by a rampart but possessing market stalls; a *nagara* (city) is one with both ramparts and market stalls; and a *gāma* (village) is the opposite of each of those.
"He defiles families" refers to [families] according to the classes of Khattiyas, Brāhmaṇas, Vessas, and Suddas.
It brings about a transformation in the four castes. And when "defiling," he does not defile them with impure mud and the like;
rather, through his own misconduct, he destroys their confidence. Therefore he said, "By the giving of flowers and so forth," and so on.
Therein, whether by bringing [them] himself, or having them brought, or by summoning himself, or having them summoned, or to whomever among those who have approached him of their own accord...
A gift of flowers (*pupphadāna*) is the giving of one’s own flowers for the purpose of supporting families; those things beginning with that are "gifts of flowers and so forth" (*pupphadānādayo*).
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of gifts of fruit, powdered clay, tooth-sticks, bamboo, medical treatment, and messages delivered on foot.
"Destroying faith" means producing a lack of confidence in other virtuous monks who do not act in such a manner.

"By not being seen": it should be understood that when those people—through such acts as giving flowers and the like by which they had gathered a following—do not act in the same way toward other well-behaved persons, those others become envious and do not associate with them; thus, he destroys their confidence.

"Evil practices" means base practices because they are censured by the Buddha. Furthermore, these [practices], such as planting flowering trees and so forth, are for the purpose of gathering a following.
This is what is intended here; therefore, it is said: "planting flowering shrubs and so forth.

However, for the sake of monasteries (*ārāma*) and the like, planting and so forth is permissible through appropriate terminology (*kappiya-vohāra*). In this context, "flowering shrub" (*mālāvaccha*) refers to a young flowering tree.

For young flowering trees as well as flowering creepers are indeed called "flowering shrubs" (*mālāvaccha*); the planting of such is "planting flowering shrubs," and that is the beginning [of the list].
"Of those [people] by whom those plantings of garlands and so forth were performed.

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there is here the inclusion of planting, causing to be planted, sprinkling, causing to be sprinkled, plucking, causing to be plucked, stringing, and causing to be strung. "Are seen" means they are seen by those who see them directly;
they are perceived through the door of the ear by those who hear them from others. "Corrupted" means defiled. "Enough for you here..."
"By dwelling": the meaning is, "Enough with your dwelling here; let there be no dwelling for you here. For the word *alaṃ* is used here in the sense of prohibition.

"One who has undergone the act of banishment" refers to one who, after being accused, reminded, and charged with an offense, is [formally] addressed by the motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatutthakammavācā*) as stated in the word-commentary beginning: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: these Assaji and Punabbasuka... and so forth.
One who has undergone the act of banishment (*pabbājanīyakamma*). "In whatever monastery he dwells" refers to a monastery outside the village.

"He does not even obtain [the right] to wander for alms in that village... etc. Even if the village or town extends at most twelve *yojanas* and the monastery extends at most three *yojanas*, he does not obtain the right to wander for alms in that village or town, nor in the monastery.

To dwell. While dwelling in that monastery, one should not go for alms even in the neighboring village; likewise, while dwelling in a neighboring monastery, one should not go for alms in that [original] village.
However, it is permissible for one dwelling in a neighboring monastery to go for alms in the neighboring village.
Regarding the offenses to be incurred: there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for giving from what belongs to oneself for the purpose of winning over families.
These are the offenses: a *thullaccaya* for giving what belongs to the Saṅgha out of a sense of lordship, and a *pārājika* for giving by force.
In the *Mātikā*, the phrase "because he has departed" is stated as a rule of conduct for one against whom a *pabbājanīyakamma* (act of banishment) has been carried out;
however, at the beginning [of the section], it should be understood as referring to the *pabbājanīyakamma* itself. "Assaji and Punabbasu" refers to both Assaji and Punabbasu.
The commentary on the training rule concerning those who corrupt families is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the conclusion of the *saṅghādisesa* rules:

as for the phrase "first offense" (*paṭhamāpatti*), it is a compound analysis based on its parts; the meaning of the whole compound is expressed thus: "those for whom the first [offense] occurs. Therefore, he said: "those for whom this is the first offense."
"An offense involving immediate transgression. "At the very moment of the transgression" means at the very moment of transgressing the object [of the rule].
By the word "eva" (only/precisely), he excludes the moment of the formal act of admonition (*samanubhāsanakamma*). "Ahassa yattako paricchedo yāvatīhaṃ":
by this he says, "as many days as there are. And "ahāni" means days.
“By way of the basis (*vatthu*)” means by way of the mere transgression, such as the emission of impurity and so forth. “This” refers to this very transgression.
“By way of the name alone” means by way of the name without the basis, such as “this is a certain offense,” or “this is an offense called a *saṅghādisesa*.
Here, the word “mere” (*matta*) excludes the basis. However, in some manuscripts, it says “by way of name and clan (*nāmagotta*).”
Some write "or," but that is not correct because it has been stated, "this is such-and-such an offense. The connection is: "Now, I will not tell anyone about this.
Having laid down the burden means having abandoned the effort regarding the disclosure.
It is not only for one who conceals while perceiving the offense solely by way of the substance and the name; rather, it also applies to one who, not knowing it thus, [conceals] merely...
If one conceals [the offense] with the perception that it is an offense, thinking, "I shall conceal the offense," it should be understood that for him also,
it is concealed. However, if in this case he perceives it as not an offense, or perceives it as belonging to another class of offense,
or is doubtful, yet— desiring to conceal it by thinking, "Now I will not tell anyone"— he abandons his responsibility and lets the dawn rise, [then it is concealed].

The phrase "it remains uncovered" should be brought forward and applied here. However, there is no offense whether one perceives it as an offense or does not perceive it as an offense when covering it;

it simply remains covered. Or, if one conceals a light offense thinking it is "heavy," or a heavy offense thinking it is "light," and stands on the side of the shameless, the offense nonetheless remains uncovered. If, however, while considering a heavy offense to be "light," one confesses it...
It is neither revealed nor concealed.
One whose self (attā) is manifest and natural is a *pakatatta*; the meaning is that he is not one whose nature has been altered by kamma. Therefore it is said:

"one who is not suspended and belongs to the same community. "In the manner already stated" refers to what was said in the passage beginning with, "Now I shall not tell anyone about this," and so forth.
According to the method. Now, if one conceals [an offense] while perceiving that "a formal act has been performed against me by the Saṅgha" when it has not been performed, it remains unconcealed.

However, whether one who has not been subjected to a formal act perceives it as such, or one who has been subjected to a formal act perceives it as such, even if it is concealed, it remains unconcealed. And this has also been said:
“One incurs an offense that is heavy with remainder;
one conceals it out of disrespect;
there is no nun, yet she would not be touched by the fault.”
“This question was thought out by those who are skillful.
This question was indeed spoken by Ukkhittaka.
Whatever needs to be said regarding the ten obstacles has already been stated below. However, if one—due to being of a timid nature—...
If, perceiving it as an obstacle due to fear of non-human beings or fierce wild animals in the darkness, one conceals [the fact that one has reached the boundary],
it is as if unconcealed. Even for one dwelling in a mountain hermitage, if he must report [his arrival] after crossing a ravine or a river,
and if there is danger from fierce beasts, non-humans, and the like on the way, or if pythons lie across the path, or if the river is full—
If, while there is indeed an obstacle, one perceives it as an obstacle and conceals it, it remains unconcealed.
Furthermore, for one who conceals what is an obstacle—whether perceiving it as an obstacle or not perceiving it as an obstacle—it remains unconcealed.
"A bhikkhunī" refers to a bhikkhu of similar status. Even if there is a slight pimple on his mouth or a jaw ache...
Whether he is pierced by a thorn, or his tooth aches, or he receives scanty alms—by that much alone he is neither able to speak nor to go.
Furthermore, he perceives, "I am unable"; this is called one who, being capable, has the perception of being incapable.
By this [perception], even what is covered is not uncovered. However, for one who is truly incapable and unable to speak or go—
Whether one perceives it as much or little, even if it is covered, it is as if uncovered.
"This is obvious" means that these two factors are indeed of obvious meaning.

However, if, having set aside the responsibility with the thought, "I will cover it," one falls into a state of shamelessness either before the meal, after the meal, or during the first watch of the night and so forth, [the offense occurs] even before dawn.
If he informs [another], this is called "one who wishes to conceal but does not conceal. However,
for one who has committed an offense while staying in a place where no other monks reside,
and who either waits for the arrival of a fellow monk or goes into the presence of a fellow monk, yet allows half a month or even a full month to pass, [this constitutes a concealment].
This refers to one who does not wish to conceal but yet conceals; he too remains unconcealed.

However, if one, as soon as the offense has occurred, like a man who has stepped upon fire, immediately withdraws and goes to a place where there are companions to disclose it, this is one who does not wish to conceal and thus does not conceal. The measure is simply that of being in the company of others.
The measure [of the offense] is simply that it must be of a similar nature. Indeed, it should be reported in the presence of one who is of a similar nature.
However, it should not be reported even in the presence of a preceptor who is of a dissimilar nature and who, upon hearing it, would wish to proclaim it.
In this regard, whether the offense was committed before the meal, after the meal, by day, or by night, it remains so until dawn.
It should be confessed before dawn has risen. Once the sun has risen, it is concealed;
and on account of that concealment, one incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "In brief" means in summary. However, the intention is that the details are stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*.
"One must wear [the robe] even against one's will" means that because an unremediated offense acts as an obstruction to heaven and liberation, one must wear it even if one is unwilling.
The meaning is "one must undergo the probation. Therefore he said, "not by one's own will," and so forth.

"Having undertaken the probation" means having formally accepted the duties of probation in the midst of the Saṅgha. Although there are four kinds of probation—probation for unconcealed offenses, probation for concealed offenses, probation to the end of purity, and probation by combination—nevertheless, here it is the probation for unconcealed offenses that is intended.
He said: "In that regard, there is concealed... [etc. ...the threefold parivāsa. "In that regard" means in that statement.
Parivāsa that is to be given when there is a concealed offense is called *paṭicchannaparivāsa* because its object is concealed.

Parivāsa that is to be given starting from the end of the period of purification (*suddhanta*) is called *suddhantaparivāsa*. Parivāsa that is to be given by combining [the periods] is called *samodhānaparivāsa*.
Now, in order to show those three types of *parivāsa* according to their specific forms, he says "Therein," and so forth. "Hi" means because.
