"Concealed for one day" (*ekāhappaṭicchannā*) means [an offense] concealed for one day. "By the method stated" refers to the method stated by the passage beginning with "And there is an offense.

Regarding the term "concealed for one day" (*ekāhappaṭicchanna*), here the particle "iti" is used as in such passages as "or thus, or refraining from such frivolous spectacles" (*iti vā, iti evarūpā visūkadassanā paṭivirato*).

The word *viya* has the sense of "beginning" (*ādi*). By this, it includes the remainder of the canonical text: “Venerable sir, I, being guilty of a single offense of intentional emission of semen, concealed for one day, request a one-day probation from the Saṅgha.
“Having thus caused him to request probation” means having caused him to request it up to three times. “In the manner handed down in the Khandhaka” refers to the Samuccaya-khandhaka.
"By the method already explained. "From that fortnight onwards" means starting from that point. "Concealed for more than a fortnight": *atireka-pakkha* means exceeding a fortnight;
the meaning is "concealed for that [period]. "From that" means starting from the thirtieth day. "Concealed for a month":
a *māsa* is so called because it measures the life-span of beings as if bringing them to their end; it consists of thirty nights and days. "Concealed for that" means concealed for such a period.

The meaning is as follows: "When the year is complete" (*saṃvacchare puṇṇe*): it is called a *saṃvacchara* because, as if gathering together various beings and the occurrence of phenomena, it remembers—that is, it proceeds—[through them];
[it consists of] twelve months; when that is fulfilled.
"By way of describing the basis" (*vatthukittanavasena vā*): the meaning is "by way of describing the basis together with the name. For by that very [reason], later on...
The inclusion of the word "mere" (*matta*) in the phrase "or by way of mere name" (*nāmamattavasena*) should be understood as having been made for this purpose.

"By way of mere name" means by way of the name alone, without the mention of the underlying objective fact (*vatthu*). "Therefore" (*tasmā*) means because, among the two kinds of names, "offense" (*āpatti*) is a name common to all;
therefore [it is said]. "Emission of semen" (*sukkavissaṭṭhi*) means this is called "emission of semen. Here, the word "thus" (*iti*) indicates the sense of what is to be stated.
This is shown. And this is merely an illustration, because even bodily contact and so forth must be accepted as being the basis (*vatthu*) and other factors.
It is both the "basis" (*vatthu*) because it is a transgression, and the "clan" (*gotta*) because it is not shared by others.
It is called "clan" (*gotta*) because it protects (*tāyati*) the lineage; that is, by not permitting the intellect to go elsewhere—such as to bodily contact—it protects the family line.
The meaning is that he guards his word. *Saṅghādisesa*: this is what is called a *saṅghādisesa*.
Here, however, the word *iti* indicates the collection of the term and its referent. Therefore he said: “both the name and the offense. Because it is a name common to its own class, it is “the name”;
and because one falls into it through various transgressions, it is “the offense”—this is the meaning. This too is merely an illustration.

Regarding the phrase “offenses” (*āpattiyo*): it is because these [terms] must also be understood by way of their names and so forth. Alternatively, the word *iti* has the sense of “and so forth. By taking it in this way, the statement beginning with “also by the words ‘bodily contact,’ etc. is likewise justified.
With reference to the inquiry as to which specific words within the formal ritual procedure (*kammavācā*) include this, he says “therein,” and so forth.
"Offense" (*āpatti*) is a name common to all [categories] because it is what must be committed through transgression;
thus he says, "also by the word 'offenses' (*āpattiyo*)," meaning it is both a name and an offense. "Therefore" (*tasmā*) means:

because this disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*), such as probation (*parivāsa*) and so forth, is indeed permitted to be performed according to the subject matter (*vatthu*), the clan (*gotta*), the name (*nāma*), and the offense (*āpatti*).

“In these” means in the matters such as the subject matter (vatthu) and so forth, or in the cases such as the emission of semen (sukkavissaṭṭhi) and so forth. “The duty (vatta) is to be undertaken” means that it should be undertaken by even one of the two parties mentioned above;
however, it is best when undertaken by both. For this very reason, he will say: “The same principle applies to the undertaking [of the agreement].
“Having announced” means—
“Venerable sir, I committed one offense of intentional emission of semen, concealed for one day.
I requested of the Saṅgha a one-day probation for that one offense of intentional emission of semen, concealed for one day;
the Saṅgha granted me a one-day probation for that one offense of intentional emission of semen.”
"Having confessed a one-day concealment, he granted me a one-day *parivāsa*; I am now undergoing that probation.
Venerable Sir, may the Saṅgha remember me as one who 'confesses' (*vedayati*).
Having announced this and other such matters according to the appropriate application, and having grasped this meaning, [he should speak] in whatever language [is suitable].
It is indeed proper to announce it. The phrase, "by one announcing it to the monks who have arrived again and again," is said with reference to an incoming monk.
And here, when announcing it to one person, at the end one should say, "May the Venerable One bear me in mind";
to two, "May the Venerable Ones bear [me] in mind"; and to three, "May the Venerable Ones bear [me] in mind."

"Without breaking the observances (*vatta*) or interrupting the night": this refers to the ninety-four observances prescribed in the *Pārivāsikakkhandhaka* by such passages as, "Monks, a monk under probation must not consent to the salutation or the service of regular monks (*pakatatta*)," and so forth;
as well as that which was said: "Upāli, there are three [cases] for one under probation..."
"Breaking the night [of co-residence], living together, living apart, and failure to inform"—thus the "breaking of the night" was mentioned; and having not done that, here is the analysis:
if incoming monks pass through the middle of the monastery, whether they rest for a moment or do not rest at all, one must inform them as well.
If they depart while he is unaware of it, [the offense is incurred].
And he knows when they have departed; having gone, it should be announced.
For one who is unable to reach them, there is only the breach of the night [of the observance], not the dukkaṭa offense for breaking the duty.

Even those who do not enter the interior of the monastery but go after entering the precinct boundary—if he hears their sound of umbrellas, or their coughing, or their sneezing—then [he must announce].
One should know that he is a visitor; having gone there, one must inform him. Even if one knows [of his arrival] only after he has departed, one must still follow after him and inform him.
For one who is unable to reach him, there is only a breach of the night-period (*ratticcheda*), but no offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for breaking the rule of conduct (*vatta*).

However, even one who arrives at night and departs at night causes a breach of the night-period for him; yet, because it was not known [in time], there is an offense of wrong-doing for breaking the rule of conduct.
There is none. The *Kurundi* states: "If one performs the rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) without even knowing [the offense], it is as if it were not done at all.
Therefore, it should be performed by including the additional nights. This is the practice of the "unerring method" (*apaṇṇakappaṭipadā*).
Even for one traveling by boat on rivers and so forth, or standing on the opposite bank, or traveling through the air, or on mountain slopes, in forests, and so on—

If, upon seeing a bhikkhu even from a distance, there is the recognition that he is a "bhikkhu," one must inform him—either by going by boat or other means, or by making a loud noise, or by pursuing him swiftly.
For one who fails to inform him, there is both a breach of the night (ratticcheda) and an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the violation of the rule.
If, despite making an effort, one is unable to reach him or make oneself heard, [there is no offense].
There is only a breach of the night-period; there is no offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for breaking the formal procedure (*vatta*).
Even if one has gone to another monastery, it must still be reported to the monks.
If he sees them all staying in one place, he should report it while remaining in that very place. But if they are staying separately at the foot of trees and so forth, [he should go to each of them].

One must go to each respective place and report it. For one who intentionally fails to report it, there is both a violation of the night-period (*ratticcheda*) and an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for breaking the proper conduct (*vatta*).
However, if while searching he does not see some [of the monks], there is only a violation of the night-period, but no offense of wrong-doing for breaking the proper conduct.
But for one who intentionally fails to report it, there is both a violation of the night-period and an offense of wrong-doing for breaking the proper conduct.

“In that very place” means in the precinct of the hall (*māḷaka*) itself. However, once the monks have departed from the hall, it is permissible to deposit [the bowl] in the presence of even a single person.
Having emerged from the hall, one who has regained mindfulness should deposit it in the presence of someone going along with him.
Therefore he said, “in the presence of a single individual. If that person also departs, [one should deposit it elsewhere].
If it has not been reported to another person in that courtyard, one should report it to him and then set it down.

"In the place of those who are regular" means in a place fit for performing formal acts (*saṅghakamma*) of the Saṅgha. "Having passed two stone-throw distances" is said for the purpose of leaving the vicinity where the sound of monks reciting can be heard.
"Having descended from the main road" is said for the purpose of leaving the vicinity of monks traveling along the road.
"In a place concealed by a thicket or a fence" is stated for the purpose of relinquishing the range of visibility.
"Having undertaken the duty, it should be announced": having undertaken the duty in the manner already described, the probation (*parivāsa*) must be announced.
Furthermore, although it is stated generally as "it should be announced," if the one announcing is junior, he should address the other as "friend" (*āvuso*). If...
One who is senior should say, "Venerable sir. If another bhikkhu comes to that place for some business, if he sees him or hears his voice, he must inform him.

For one who fails to inform him, there is both a breach of the night-period and a transgression of the rule of conduct. Therefore it was said: "Even if he sees another bhikkhu, he must certainly inform him as well."

Now, if one enters within twelve cubits of the precinct and departs without even knowing [of the departure], there is indeed a breach of the night-period, but there is no breach of the formal observance (*vatta*). "When it has risen" means when it has gone up.
"Whichever nun first"—meaning whichever nun sees another nun first, whether she is departing from the monastery or arriving as a guest—to her he should announce it and then set down [the bowl].
It would be an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who does not announce it; this was said with reference to that, but not with reference to the interruption of the night.
For otherwise, he would have said, "having announced it to all those included within the monastery boundary. "As long as the nights are fulfilled" means:
for however many nights the offense has been concealed, for that many nights, until they are fulfilled, one must undergo the probationary period (*parivāsa*).

In the *Samantapāsādikā*, however, it is stated: "Having thus lived on probation for as many days as the offense was concealed, or even for more than that, for the purpose of dispelling remorse. "Vitthāra" means elaboration.
"In the other two," namely, in the midst of the two—*suddhantaparivāsa* (probation until the end of the purity) and *samodhānaparivāsa* (combined probation)—refers to the *Khandhaka*.

In the Samuccayakkhandhaka: regarding the terms *cūḷasuddhanta* (the short purification) and *mahāsuddhanta* (the long purification), here one who—starting from the date of full ordination (*upasampadā*) in direct order, or starting from the day of the announcement in reverse order—is asked, "Do you know that on such and such a day, fortnight, month, or year, your state was pure? is [addressed].
If he says, “Yes, venerable sir, I know; for such a length of time I was pure,” the *suddhanta-parivāsa* granted to him is called the “minor *suddhanta*.
Having taken that [period], whatever amount of time he knows his own state of purity for, that much should be subtracted.
The remainder of one month or two months must be spent in probation.
If, having recognized, "I am impure for only a month," he undertook the probation, and while on probation he remembers another month, that month must also be spent in probation;
there is no need to grant the probation again. But if, having recognized, "I am impure for two months," he undertook it...
While undergoing probation, if one makes the determination, "I have been impure for only a month," then only a month must be spent on probation;
there is no need to grant probation again. For this probation to the limit of purity (suddhantaparivāsa) ascends above and descends below;
this is its characteristic.
But if one who is questioned according to the aforementioned method, both in direct and reverse order, neither knows nor remembers the limit of the night,
or is uncertain as to that limit of the night, the *suddhantaparivāsa* granted to him is called a "great *suddhanta*" (*mahāsuddhanta*).
Taking that [period] and counting the nights from the day it was accepted until the day of full ordination (*upasampadā*), he must undergo the probation.
This [period] does not ascend further, but rather descends downwards.

Therefore, if while undergoing probation one makes a determination regarding the limit of the nights, thinking, "Whether it be a month or a year for me who has committed [an offense]," then one must undergo probation for that month or that year.
And in this regard, although the *cūḷasuddhanta* (short purification) applies to one who says, "For such a length of time I have been pure,"...
Even though it is given, because there is necessarily an absence of knowledge [of the offense], it is said: "Both of these kinds... must be granted.
The procedure for granting that is found in the Khandhaka; thus, the procedure for granting both kinds of *suddhanta* is stated in the Samuccaya-khandhaka as:
"Then, monks, that monk, having approached the Saṅgha... he should speak thus," and so forth.
He has arrived. Therefore, the intention is that it should be understood there according to the method already stated.
This same principle applies here as well, since the detailed discussion of the analysis (*vinicchaya-kathā*) has been set forth in the *Samantapāsādikā*.
"Combining by weighing" (*odhāna-samodhāna*) means combining after shaking, tossing aside, and abandoning. [This refers to] the value of things long concealed.

“Combination” (*samodhāna*) means a combination of weights (*aggha*). “Mixed combination” (*missaka-samodhāna*) means a combination of mixed [offenses]. Now, in order to show briefly those three kinds of probation by combination (*samodhāna-parivāsa*), he said “therein,” and so forth.
Regarding “one who, having committed an intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*), conceals it”:
this refers to one who, having taken up probation and remaining on probation without having relinquished his observances, while the [original offense] is still not yet concluded...
If, during the period of probation (*parivāsa*), one commits a *saṅghādisesa* offense in the midst of it and conceals it, [the rule applies] to him.
The phrase "on the day the probation has been completed" is a technical term (*lakkhaṇavacana*); by this, it is also implied that it refers to "the day of the *mānatta* practice.

"Having rubbed out" means having rubbed out by means of a formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*) through the process of sending back to the beginning (*mūlāya paṭikassanā*). "Having reconciled" means [having reconciled] at the place where the original offense occurred.

"Setting aside" means "having inserted. "Parivāsa to be given" refers to the probation that must be granted through a formal act consisting of one motion and three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*), beginning with the words: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me. This is what is meant:

one who, having taken probation for a concealed offense, is either undergoing probation, or is eligible for the *mānatta* penance, or is currently performing the *mānatta*, or is eligible for rehabilitation (*abbhāna*).
If one who has not relinquished their observance commits another offense and conceals it for as many nights as were concealed for the previous offense—
or for fewer nights— one must, by means of sending him back to the beginning (*mūlāya paṭikassanā*),

shake off all those days already spent in probation and all the days spent in the trial period (*mānatta*), treating them as days not yet elapsed; then, having combined the subsequent offense with the original offense, the probation must be granted.
If, however, the intermediate offense was concealed for a longer period than the root offense, then after treating that as a root offense,
the probation must be granted by combining the other [period] with it. But if the intermediate offense was unconcealed,
one should continue the probation using the previously taken probation without having undergone a sending back to the beginning (mūlāya paṭikassana).

"Whether it be one... pe ...or all long-concealed": the meaning is that whether it be one offense long-concealed, or two, three, or many offenses long-concealed. "Of those" refers to those offenses that have been long-concealed.
Furthermore, the procedure for granting [the penance] for this should be understood according to the method stated in the Khandhaka.

But for one who has one hundred offenses concealed for ten days, another hundred offenses concealed for ten days, and yet another hundred offenses concealed for ten days—in this way, having done so ten times, there is a thousand offenses concealed for one hundred days. What should be done with that?
Having combined them all together, [one should perform the parivāsa] for ten days.
It must be undergone. In this way, by means of a single ten-day period, even a hundred days of probation are fulfilled. And it has been said:
“Having concealed a hundred offenses—a thousand nights— by dwelling for ten nights, one who is on probation shall be released.”
This is called the "combination by value.
Now, in order to explain the "mixed combination," he said, "The mixed combination is as follows," and so forth. Herein, this is the method:
"Venerable sir, I have committed several *saṅghādisesa* offenses: one of emission of semen, one..."
One offense of physical contact, one grave verbal offense, one offense of acting on one’s own desires, one offense of matchmaking, one offense of building a hut,
one offense of building a monastery, one offense of malicious intent, one offense related to another matter, one offense of schism in the Saṅgha,
one offense of siding with a schismatic, one offense of being difficult to speak to, and one offense of corrupting families— Venerable Sir, I [confess] these offenses to the Saṅgha.
“I request a probation consisting of simultaneous expiation.”—
Having had him request this three times, the probation should be granted by means of a formal act (*kammavācā*) corresponding thereto.

And here, whether one says, “I have committed offenses involving formal meeting (*saṅghādisesa*) of various bases,” or simply, “I have committed offenses involving formal meeting,” it is thus [the case] previously.
It is indeed permissible to perform the formal act (kammavācā) by applying it according to the method already stated—whether by way of the basis, the clan, the name, or the offense.

This is the combined treatment (missakasamodhāna). However, at the conclusion of all the formal acts for probation, the discussion regarding whether the duties have been fulfilled or not, and so forth, should be understood in the same manner as before.
Since only the mere meaning has been stated in all three types of combined probation, [the details of] the analysis and so forth...
Or, because it has not been specifically mentioned, it is said: "This is a summary statement regarding the three types of *samodhānaparivāsa*.
Since the investigation of *samodhāna* covers a vast scope, from where could it be obtained in its entirety? Thus he says, "The detailed exposition," and so forth. Regarding the term *chāratta*:
the word *ratti* means that which is crossed over (*tīyati*) or cut through (*chijjati*); it is the time for the pacification of the distress of living beings.
The meaning is as follows: "six nights" (*cha-rattiyo*) is a compound; or, the collection of six nights is "six-nights" (*cha-rattaṃ*);
"six-nights" itself is "six-night-period" (*chārattaṃ*), because a whole does not exist apart from its parts, the meaning is stated as "six nights.

Regarding the statement "without granting probation, only the *mānatta* penance should be granted": this is because the offense was unconcealed, and because [the offender] is recognized solely by virtue of having committed it.
He is one who deserves the *mānatta* (probationary) penance; therefore, without granting him *parivāsa* (the period of probation), only the *mānatta* itself should be granted.
That which is given to one who has completed the *parivāsa* for a concealed offense is called "concealed *mānatta*";
thus he said, "for whom it is concealed," and so forth. "This" refers to the concealed *mānatta*. "Here" refers to this sentence. How?
However, because the procedure for granting those two types of *mānatta* and the discussion of their legal analysis must be understood, he said, "But for both of them," and so forth.

He used the word "this" (*ayaṃ*) with reference to what is about to be stated. Regarding the phrase "the area described in the section on *parivāsa*": for an enclosed monastery, it is beyond the enclosure;
for an unenclosed one, it is beyond two *leḍḍupāta*s (the distance of a stone's throw) from the place where an enclosure would be appropriate, excluding the main road.
Having gone to a place concealed by a thicket or a fence. "Having undertaken" means having undertaken it before sunrise. "Having announced" means:
"Venerable sirs, I have committed one offense of intentional emission of semen, unconfessed;
therefore, venerable sirs, I [approach] the Saṅgha regarding this one offense of intentional emission of semen, unconfessed..."
“I requested a six-night *mānatta* penance; the Saṅgha granted me a six-night *mānatta* for that one offense of intentional emission of semen, unconfessed.
I am now practicing the *mānatta*; Venerable Sirs, may the Saṅgha remember me as one who acknowledges: ‘I acknowledge it. And so forth.
Having announced [the offense] in accordance with the day it was committed, it is indeed permissible to announce this matter in whatever language one chooses.
From the time it has been announced, it is permissible for the rest of the monks—excepting one—to go about their business if there is something to be done.
When the dawn has risen, the formal duty (vatta) must be relinquished in the presence of that monk. If...
He too, having gone out before dawn for some business, should deposit [the bowl] after announcing it to whoever he first sees— whether another who has departed from the monastery or a visitor.
And because he lived only after announcing it to the community and observing the presence of monks, there is no fault of wandering with an incomplete group.
Or there is no separation [from the robes]. But if he does not see anyone, he should go to the monastery and, having informed the first person he sees, deposit them there.
Therefore he said: "Then, whether they have gone or not gone, one should proceed according to the previous method. "Where there may be" means:
in whichever boundary of common affiliation (*samānasaṃvāsaka-sīmā*) there exists a community of monks consisting of a group of twenty. "Should be summoned" means...
He should be summoned by means of the act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna-kamma*). But how is the act of rehabilitation performed? To this he says, "But as for the act of rehabilitation," and so forth.
"By way of the canonical text" (*pāḷivasena*) means by way of the text beginning with, "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. "By way of the legal exposition" (*vinicchayavasena*) means:
"First, those who have been rehabilitated should be made worthy of rehabilitation. For this person, because he has laid down his duties, stands in the position of a regular monk (*pakatatta*)."
"It is not permissible to perform the rehabilitation (*abbhāna*) of one who has not yet fulfilled his duties; therefore, he must be exhorted to undertake the duties.
Once the duties have been undertaken, he becomes eligible for rehabilitation. He too, having undertaken the duties and announced them, must request rehabilitation.
However, for one who has not set aside his duties, there is no requirement to undertake further duties; for he becomes eligible for rehabilitation simply by the lapse of six days," and so forth.

By way of formal determination (*vinicchaya*). However, because all these procedures beginning with *parivāsa* are easily understood through both the Canon (*pāḷi*) and the Commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*), we have not elaborated on them here for fear of excessive prolixity; those who desire them should take them from those very sources.
Since this particular procedure must be performed by a quorum of twenty, it is invalid if performed by fewer than that. Therefore, he said:
“Even with one person... [as before] ... not being negligent. This refers to what has been stated above. *Sāmīcī* means proper conduct (*vatta*).
Thus ends the commentary on the *Pātimokkha* within the *Vinayatthamañjūsā*, specifically in the section explaining the hidden meaning (*līnatthappakāsani*) of the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*.
The commentary on the Saṅghādisesa rules is finished.
The Section on the Indeterminate Rules. 1. Commentary on the First Indeterminate Training Rule.
Having said "by a woman," because it is further stated "by one [woman]," it is explained as "by a single woman who is reckoned as a woman.

"In secret" (*raho*) means a place lacking visibility. And regarding this lack of visibility, he says "in secret from the eye," because for one who commits an offense there, it is not within the range of sight.
Is it not the case that: "Secret means secret from the eye, secret from the ear"? "Secret from the eye..."

Regarding the phrase "the seclusion of the ear" (*sotassa raho*) found in the word-commentary (*padabhājanapāḷi*), it is stated that one is unable to see [an object] while the eye is being rubbed, or while the eyebrow is being raised, or while the head is being lifted;
yet, one is not able to hear ordinary conversation when there is the "seclusion of the ear.
Why, then, is this not mentioned, and why is it said only "the seclusion of the eye" (*cakkhussa raho*)?
He says, “Even though,” and so forth. By this, he shows that in the Pāḷi, the phrase “the seclusion of the ear” is stated by way of a general extraction of the meaning.
Now, how is it known that “only the seclusion of the eye is intended here”?
Because of the statement “in a concealed seat” and because it is said, “it is possible to engage in sexual intercourse. For this very reason, he says:
“Even if,” and so forth. By the phrase “of one whose door-panel is closed,” he shows the absence of privacy for the eye due to its being concealed.
However, one sitting at the door of a room whose door-panel is not closed incurs no offense;
it should be understood that one does not incur an offense only by sitting at the door of a room whose door-panel is not closed, but also by sitting within a space of twelve cubits.
Therefore he said, "But where it is possible to see," and so forth.

Because one who is lying down and sleeping, overcome by drowsiness like that of a monkey, may open his eyes for a short time and close them for a short time, yet does not fall into a deep sleep, it is therefore stated:
"Even while sleeping, one incurs no offense. However, one who is sleeping after having lain down is not like that.
He said, "Even one who is lying down and sleeping does not perform [the act]"; the meaning is that he does not commit an offense.
A woman does not serve as a companion for sexual intercourse. For women conceal each other's faults.
Therefore, when a monk was lying down with the door open in the Great Forest at Vesālī, many women provided him with as much as he required.
They departed. Therefore he said, "But he does not do it even with a hundred women. "That action" refers to the action of transgression.
Since one lies down only after having sat down, in order to show that lying down is included within the phrase "he should arrange for sitting," he said, "And here," and so forth.
"He should be dealt with according to one of three rules" refers to one who admits to the sitting.
It is said that there must indeed be the application of one of three rules.
However, in the case of a *pārājika*, a *saṅghādisesa*, or a *pācittiya*, he should be dealt with only if he confesses the sitting down in that manner; not if he does not confess it.

"One who does not confess the sitting down" means that one who does not confess the sitting down should not be dealt with by any one of the three rules. For even one who is shameless [is dealt with] only if he confesses.

He is to be dealt with according to his offense. As long as he does not admit it, he should be described as neither "pure" nor "impure," but rather he is to be dealt with through the sequence of formal proceedings. For this has been said:
"Confession is effective among those who are modest; among the shameless, it does not exist in this way."
“Even if one who is shameless should speak much, one should have him act according to what is connected to the matter.
This shows that it is not only when there is an accusation based on one of the three grounds that he must be made to act upon such an admission;
rather, it applies even when there is an accusation accompanied by a manner of sitting or other such behavior. Thus: “Or by whomsoever whose word is trustworthy...”
It is said: "If a female lay follower (*upāsikā*) should speak [thus], that bhikkhu is to be dealt with accordingly. For this very reason, it says:

"In the modes such as sitting," and so forth. And here, although the word "confessing" (*paṭijānamāno*) is not explicitly stated, because of the context, it is understood that "only if he confesses is that bhikkhu to be dealt with accordingly.
Furthermore, since there is no possibility of falsehood in the speech of such a female lay follower, what she has seen is indeed as it appears.
"Otherwise it may also happen" shows the possibility of change in the act of seeing. "Indeterminate" means not fixed because of its non-unequivocal nature.
Therefore he said: "Of the three offenses," and so forth.
If, desiring to go into the presence of a woman out of a craving for sitting in private, one applies collyrium to the eye, it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing). [The same applies to] the undergarment...
He puts on his lower garment, fastens his waistband, and robes himself; for every such action, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

As he walks, for every step, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Having gone, when he sits down, it is likewise an offense of wrong-doing. Therefore he said: "by that which is reckoned as the defilement based upon sexual intercourse," and so forth.

And here, although there may be an absence of actual lust for sexual intercourse in one who delights in sitting in private, it is stated [as an offense] because of the presence of the defilements connected therewith.
“By that which is designated as the defilement dependent upon sexual intercourse. For this very reason, the term “dependent” (*sannissita*) was included. “Because of the pleasure of secrecy” means:
because of the pleasure arisen from the thought, “I shall sit in secret with such-and-such a person and engage in laughing, talking, and so forth.

There is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for sitting; if [the man] is not present, it is [an offense] for lying down when he has gone within the vicinity, provided he is not asleep and is not blind, and there is a conscious male person present.
This is the intended meaning. If that woman, having risen repeatedly for some business, sits down again and again, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for each sitting.
If she who was intended has not been seen, and another comes and sits down, there is an offense of expiation when enjoyment arises.
If several women come, there is an offense of expiation according to the number of women. If...
Rising again and again, they sit down repeatedly; there are *pācittiya* offenses even for each act of sitting.

Even for one who goes with the intention, "I will engage in secret dalliance with whomever I see," and sits down, the offenses should be understood according to the same method already stated—by way of the successive arrivals [of women] and by way of the repeated acts of sitting. "In a man of the aforementioned type" means one who is not blind.
"Regarding a person of understanding": when one has come within twelve cubits (*dvādasahattha*).
If a woman, having approached and sat down near a man who has gone there with a pure mind, should give rise to a secret conversation, even in this case there is no offense.
The commentary on the first undetermined training rule (*aniyata-sikkhāpada*) is concluded.
2. Commentary on the Second Training Rule Concerning the Fixed (Aniyata) Offense:

Regarding the phrase "nor even one that is concealed," it should be understood here that even an area such as a courtyard or a compound which is enclosed on the outside but open on the inside is included within this category.
For in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "Such a place is indeed taken as being unconcealed."
It has been stated. "Or by a *saṅghādisesa*" means by that *saṅghādisesa* offense known as bodily contact or the announcement of a grave matter (*duṭṭhulla*).
For it is for this very reason that the word-commentary states: "If she should say:
'Venerable sir, I saw you sitting together with a woman, engaging in bodily contact,'" and so forth. This training rule [is formulated] on account of grave speech.
[The offense] has occurred. Furthermore, having heard such lewd speech, even a woman does not conceal it.
For instance, regarding the training rule on lewd speech (*duṭṭhullavācā*), those women who were modest went out and complained to the monks;
therefore, it is said here that "even a woman" incurs no offense because she did not conceal it. Alternatively, because she did not conceal it here, even a woman [incurs no offense].
He commits [an offense]; however, because it was concealed during the first instance, he does not commit an offense even with a hundred women—thus should the meaning here be understood.
Regarding "not blind and not deaf": here, he is called "not blind" by virtue of physical contact, and "not deaf" by virtue of indecent speech.
As for the origin and other factors, this training rule has three origins: from body and mind, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.

It originates from [four causes], is a functional act (*kiriya*), has perception as its liberation, possesses consciousness, is a worldly offense, is bodily action and verbal action, is an unwholesome state of mind, and consists of two feelings—namely, pleasant and neutral feeling. Therefore it was said:
"But here, the origins and so forth are exactly the same as for taking what is not given. And herein, one who engages in physical contact also utters lewd speech.
Regarding the statement that "one sits while speaking lewdly," it should be understood as meaning that [the offense] "arises from body, speech,
and mind," or else that it was stated specifically with reference to lewd speech alone.
The commentary on the second *aniyata* training rule is finished.

They say: "This [offense] is of indefinite description; one is to be dealt with for an offense only when, upon being accused on the basis of seeing or other such grounds, he admits the matter, and not otherwise.

This was stated for the purpose of showing the characteristics of attributing or not attributing an offense. Thus ends the *Līnatthappakāsanī*, the commentary on the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Pātimokkhavaṇṇanā*, within the *Vinayatthamañjūsā*.
The commentary on the Indeterminate [offenses] is finished.
The Section on Forfeiture, Chapter 1:
The Subchapter on Robes.
1. Commentary on the Kathina Training Rule (Sikkhāpada): "In the case of finished robes" (*niṭṭhitacīvarasmiṃ*): that which is both finished and a robe is "finished robes";

the meaning is "when the robes [obtained through] the basis of merit have been finished, or when the expected robes [have been finished]. However, since those robes are also finished by way of being made (*karaṇena*), [the term is used].
Nor by means of non-existence and so forth; therefore, it is said: "or with the completion of needlework," and so on.

In this context, whatever is to be done with a needle—the work concluding with the fastening loops, the cloth-straps, and the knots—that is called "the completion of needlework," and [the robe is finished] by that.
"Lost" means taken away by thieves and the like. This too is called "finished" because the obstacle of the act of making has been brought to an end.
It is said: "Spoiled" means eaten by ants and the like. "Burnt" means burnt by fire.
"The expectation for a robe has been cut off" means that whatever expectation for a robe had arisen, such as "I shall obtain a robe from such-and-such a family," that expectation has been severed.
Since these also fall under the category of the "obstruction of making," their state of being finished should be understood as the completion of that very obstruction.
Therefore he said, “Or in these,” and so forth. By this, the absence of the impediment of robes (*cīvara-palibodha*) is stated. Therefore he said, “The meaning is:
when the impediment regarding the making of robes has been severed. How is this to be understood? He said, “For one for whom the *kaṭhina* has been spread,” and so forth.

In the sense of holding [the monks] together by not allowing them to go elsewhere, despite there being five benefits, it is called *kaṭhina*; the meaning is that it is firm. The *kaṭhina* has been spread.
“By whom” means by that person for whom the *kathina* has been spread; “of him” means of that one for whom the *kathina* has been spread. The particle *hi* is used in the sense of a reason.
Regarding the phrase “he obtains the benefits of the *kathina* for that long,” one must supply the words “the monk for whom the *kathina* has been spread”;

thus it should be understood as: “for that long, that monk for whom the *kathina* has been spread obtains the benefits of the *kathina*, such as wandering without having asked permission. [The commentary continues: “Of him for whom the *kathina* has been spread...”
The phrase "for a bhikkhu" should be construed by changing the case ending to "bhikkhus who have spread the kaṭhina," as follows:

there are two impediments, namely the impediment of robes and the impediment of residence. Since, even when one of these impediments exists, one obtains benefits such as wandering without prior announcement, whereas one does not obtain them when it does not exist—why is that? Because [the rule states], "when the robe has been finished."
"The obstacle regarding the making of this robe has been severed"—this is the meaning understood here.

"Of the Saṅgha" means by the Saṅgha; this is the genitive case used in the sense of the agent. "Ubbhate" means when it has been removed by one of the eight methods for removal, or by the intermediate removal (*antarubbhāra*).
"Therein" means in that *kathina* ceremony. "Removal" (*ubbhāra*) means taking away. [This refers to] the thirty Pāveyyaka monks who had completed the previous rains-residence.
Because the Blessed One authorized the kaṭhina in the Kaṭhina-khandhaka by saying, "I allow you, monks, to spread the kaṭhina for those monks who have completed the rains residence," it is said:
"For this so-called spreading of the kaṭhina... is authorized.
In that context, "those who have completed the prior rains residence" means those who have completed the prior rains residence without having interrupted it.

The meaning [is as follows]. By this, it is shown that, first of all, by way of having completed the rains residence (*vuṭṭhavassa*), only those who have entered the rains residence during the earlier period (*purimikā*) obtain the spreading of the Kathina cloth, not those who have entered during the later period (*pacchimikā*). Let it be so for now by way of having completed the rains residence;
however, regarding the number, he asks "How many obtain it? and says "He," etc. "He" refers to the spreading of the Kathina cloth. "By the lowest limit" means...

By way of counting, it is the minimum limit. "It is allowable for five persons" means that four donors of the *kathina* cloth and one recipient—thus for five persons—it is allowable. Some, however, say:
"Because it is to be performed by a group of five, it is said 'it is allowable for five persons'"; that is merely their own opinion, for [the text says]: "In that case, monks..."
Because it is stated in the Campeyyakkhandhaka: "This fourfold Saṅgha of bhikkhus, excluding three formal acts—namely, ordination, the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), and rehabilitation. Therefore:

because it is not known [otherwise] that those who have completed the previous rains-retreat are [necessarily] those who have completed the current rains-retreat; and because it is permissible for as few as five persons; therefore. "Where" means: *Note: The provided text fragment ends with "yatthāti". The full sentence from the source text continues with the definition of "where": "yattha nāmaṃ vā gottaṃ vā jāti vā kulaṃ vā sippaṃ vā na vijjati, tattha 'asuko' ti vattabbaṃ. Sace pi 'asuko' ti avatvā 'asukaṃ nāma gāmaṃ vā nigamaṃ vā nagaraṃ vā upanissāya viharatī'ti vuttepi vaṭṭati.* (Where name, clan, birth, family, or craft is not known, there one should say "So-and-so.
Even if one does not say "So-and-so," it is permissible if it is said, "He dwells in dependence upon such-and-such a village, town, or city.")*
"In which monastery" means: regarding the benefits (*ānisamsa*) such as moving about without having formally taken leave, which are the benefits of the *kaṭhina* robe.

Furthermore, if four monks have entered the rains retreat, and one novice who has completed his full years of training receives full ordination during the later period, he both completes the quorum for the assembly and receives the benefits.
[This applies when there are] three monks and two novices, or two monks and three novices.
The same method applies here as well for the case of "one bhikkhu and four sāmaṇeras.
Regarding the formal proclamation consisting of one motion and a second (ñattidutiyakammavācā) as stated in the Khandhaka:
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. This cloth for the kaṭhina has arisen for the Saṅgha. If it is agreeable to the Saṅgha..."
It is appropriate that the Saṅgha should give this cloth for the Kathina to the monk named so-and-so, in order to spread the Kathina;
this is the motion. Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me: this cloth for the Kathina has arisen for the Saṅgha;
the Saṅgha gives this cloth for the Kathina to the monk named so-and-so, in order to spread the Kathina. To whichever venerable one...
"It is approved that this cloth for the kaṭhina be given to the monk named so-and-so to spread as the kaṭhina;

he who approves should remain silent. He who does not approve should speak. This cloth for the kaṭhina has been given by the Saṅgha to the monk named so-and-so to spread as the kaṭhina. It is approved by the Saṅgha; therefore, being silent, I hold it to be so."

Thus, by means of the formal motion consisting of one proclamation followed by a resolution (*ñattidutiyakammavācā*) as stated in the *Kathinakkhandhaka*. "Worthy of the spreading of the *kaṭhina*" means capable of spreading the *kaṭhina*.
Furthermore, he should be understood as being endowed with the eight factors, beginning with the knowledge of the preliminary duties (*pubbakaraṇa*).
For it is said in the *Vinayavinicchaya*: "A monk who is skilled in these eight matters is worthy of the spreading of the *kaṭhina*. It is also said in the *Parivāra*:
“A person endowed with eight factors is capable of spreading the *kaṭhina*.
With which eight factors is a person endowed who is capable of spreading the *kaṭhina*? He knows the preliminary preparation;
he knows the relinquishment; he knows the determination; he knows the spreading; he knows the matrix; he knows the impediments; he knows the suspension.”
"He knows [the procedure], he knows the benefits; a person endowed with these eight factors is capable of spreading the *kaṭhina*.
And here, "preliminary work" (*pubbakaraṇa*) means the washing, sorting, cutting, binding, sewing, dyeing, and making it fit for use.
"Relinquishment" (*paccuddhāra*) means the relinquishing of the old outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*) and so forth. "Formal determination" (*adhiṭṭhāna*) means the formal determination of the *kaṭhina* robe.

“Laying out” (*atthāra*) means the laying out of the *kathina*. “Matrix” (*mātikā*) means the eight matrices. “Obstacle” (*palibodha*) means the two obstacles: the obstacle of the residence and the obstacle of the robe.
“Removal” (*uddhāra*) means [the occasions] such as departing from the boundary. “Benefit” (*ānisaṃsa*) means the five benefits. Furthermore, that which is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
“By whom, then, should the *kathina* be laid out? By one for whom the Saṅgha...”
When a *kathina* robe-cloth is offered, to whom should it be given by the Saṅgha? It should be given to one whose robes are worn out.

If many have worn-out robes, it should be given to the senior monk. Even among the seniors, it should be given to one who has a large following and is able to have the robe made and spread on that very day.
If the senior monk is unable, it should be given to a junior who is able.
It should be given to him. Furthermore, it is proper for the Saṅgha to show hospitality to a senior elder (mahāthera);
therefore, one should say, "Venerable sir, you take [the robe]; we shall make one and give it to you.

Even in that case, it must be given only after taking something that is indeed fit for the Kathina-removal ceremony. Moreover, when giving, whichever of the three robes is worn out should be used for that purpose.
It should be given. For one who normally wears a double-layered robe (*dupaṭṭa*), a double-layered one should indeed be given.
Even if his single-layered robe (*ekapaṭṭa*) is thick and his *kathina* cloth is thin, for the sake of propriety, only what is sufficient for a double-layered robe should be given.
It is even permissible to give a double-layered robe to one who says, "I will wear a single-layered robe since I did not receive [one]. However, as for one who...

If he is of a greedy disposition, it should not be given to him. Even by that [monk], having spread the *kaṭhina*, he should not take it after sewing it later with the thought, "I will make two robes.
"By him" means by the monk who has spread the *kaṭhina*. "On that very day" means on that same day. Five or more...

"Or having cut into pieces" means: having cut [the cloth] such that it consists of five pieces or more—such as five large squares (*mahāmaṇḍala*), half-squares (*addhamaṇḍala*), and so forth—which are sufficient for one of the three robes, such as the outer robe (*saṅghāṭī*) and the others;
and while that *kaṭhina* robe is being made, thinking, "I am an elder."

Whether one is called "learned" (*bahussuta*) or not, it is not permissible for even a single person to fail to do this. For one who fails to do so out of disrespect, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Therefore, everyone must assemble and complete the washing, cutting, sewing, and dyeing. Hence he said:
"The remaining monks should also act as his assistants. "Only when the robe is made" means only when the preparatory work is finished.
The cloth for the *kaṭhina*. At the very least, even the inner robe (*antaravāsaka*) must be cut before it can be made; otherwise, there is a failure in the formal act of spreading (*atthāra*).

As it is said: "And how, monks, is the *kaṭhina* not spread? The *kaṭhina* is not spread by merely marking it out... nor except by five or more than five [lengths of cloth] that have been cut on that very day."
For this very reason it was said: “But that which is neither cut nor sewn is not permitted. “By that bhikkhu” means by the bhikkhu who is performing the spreading.
“It is to be spread” means it is to be performed as a spreading. And this should be understood as consisting precisely in the utterance of such words. As it has been said:

“If one wishes to spread the kaṭhina with an outer robe (saṅghāṭī), the old outer robe must be relinquished, the new outer robe must be determined upon, and the speech must be uttered: ‘With this outer robe I am spreading the kaṭhina.’”
The detailed explanation: The phrase beginning with "of the elders" was spoken with reference to the distinction between the expressions "Venerable sir, friend" and "rejoice, rejoice.

Having thus shown the procedure to be followed by the one who performs the *atthāra* (the formal recitation), the passage beginning with "by them too" is now stated to show the procedure to be followed by those who offer the rejoicing (*anumodaka*).
The expression "we rejoice" is said out of respect for oneself toward oneself.
Although it is stated thus, nevertheless, it is said that it is not permissible for one person alone to say, “We rejoice”; rather, one should say, “I rejoice.

This should be accepted after investigation. Now, in order to demonstrate the benefits of the Kathina, he says, beginning with “even among those who have completed the previous rains-retreat,” while examining the grounds.
In that context, “of those very [persons]” means of those very ones who performed the spreading [of the Kathina cloth] and those who offered the expression of rejoicing.
For this has been stated in the *Parivāra*: “The kaṭhina is considered spread for two persons: for the one who spreads it and for the one who gives thanks.
“Those two” refers to the spreader and the one who gives thanks. “From that time on” means from the spreading and the giving of thanks.
“Until the dismantling of the kaṭhina” means not only during the month of the robe-offering, but rather according to any one of the eight grounds [for its dismantling].

The meaning is that they obtain five benefits as long as the kaṭhina has not been suspended, whether by formal suspension or by the end of the kaṭhina period; however, once it has been suspended, they do not obtain them.
Now, in order to show those five benefits in their specific nature, he says: "Going without having informed," and so forth.

In this context, "going without having informed" means going among families by a monk who has been invited to one of the five kinds of cooked food, without having asked permission from a monk who is present.

The occurrence of non-observance of conduct (*cārittāpajjana*). "Wandering without having formally accepted [the robe]" means wandering without having formally accepted a robe that has been determined by name;

the meaning is: having deposited any one of the three robes determined by name anywhere, to cause the dawn to rise elsewhere—this is what is meant by "separation from the robe" (*cīvaravippavāsa*). "A robe sufficient for one's needs" (*yāvadatthacīvara*)...
"Whatever robe-material there is need for, to that extent it is 'unresolved' and 'undesignated' robe-keeping"; the meaning is that it is the keeping of a robe beyond ten days.
"A meal for a group" (*gaṇabhojana*) means a meal for a group. Here, a "group" refers to four or more bhikkhus.
[It refers to] rice and so forth obtained through their requesting or through an invitation.
The meaning is: "the simultaneous taking of any one of the five kinds of food. And as for the phrase "whatever robe-material arises there":

whatever monastic robe (cīvara) belonging to the Saṅgha arises there—whether it be a robe left by a deceased person within the boundary where the kaṭhina has been spread, or what is given specifically for the Saṅgha, or brought in by means of resources intended for the Saṅgha—in whatever manner that monastic robe may arise, [it is said] "that shall belong to them."
This is the meaning. Therefore he said: “And whatever robe-cloth has arisen for the Saṅgha in that residence.
However, whatever bowl or other goods have arisen there for the Saṅgha, those reach everyone.
But as for the cloth purchased with the proceeds of that place—such as rice and so forth—those robes belong only to those who have performed the *kathina* ceremony.

[They] obtain [them]. However, regarding the statement in the *Gaṇṭhipada* that "when rice and so forth are bartered for with cloth, those [privileges] are obtained by all," this too should be understood as well-stated on the grounds that the acquisition of robes (*cīvaruppāda*) does not occur from the time they have been bartered.
But for one whose *kathina* has not been spread, among these five benefits, setting aside the practice of wandering without having formally accepted the robe-month, [the others remain].

They obtain the remaining benefits. If even one who does not carry [the robe] with him were to obtain [them], the monks of Pāveyyaka, having completed the rains retreat, would not have approached the Blessed One with their robes still full of water.
Since that is not permitted, they therefore approached the Blessed One having actually taken up their robes during the robe-month.
Having thus shown the spreading of the *kathina*, he now says, "But this *kathina*... and so forth, while showing its suspension (*ubbhāra*).
In that context, "matrix" (*mātikā*) means mothers; the sense is "progenitors. For these eight [factors] give birth to the suspension of the *kathina*.
Among them, that which has "departure" within it is called "suspended by departure" (*pakkamanantikā*). The others are to be understood in the same way. In that regard, whichever monk...

When one who has participated in the Kathina ceremony takes the Kathina robe and departs from that monastery without regard for it, thinking, "I will not return," then as he thus departs, the suspension of the Kathina occurs the moment he crosses the boundary; this should be understood as the "suspension of the Kathina by departure.
However, when one who takes a robe for its specific benefits departs, the thought occurs to him once he has reached outside the boundary: "Right here..."
If, thinking, "I will make it, but I will not go back to that monastery," one makes that robe while becoming indifferent toward that residence,
for that bhikkhu there is the *kathina-uddhāra* (the suspension of the *kathina*) at the completion of the work.

However, if, having taken a robe-material intended as a source of benefit and gone outside the boundary, one makes the resolution, "I will neither make this robe nor go to that residence," then there is the *kathina-uddhāra* at the point of that resolution.
Having obtained that very robe of extra benefit (*ānisaṃsa-cīvara*), if one takes it and goes outside the boundary, thinking, "I shall make this robe right here;
I will not go [back]," and while making it, that robe is lost, destroyed, or burnt, there is a suspension of the Kathina at the point of loss.

However, if, having obtained the robe of extra benefit, one has gone outside the boundary while still having expectations regarding that monastery, and hears that "the monks have performed the internal suspension (*antarubbhāra*) in the monastery," for him there is a suspension of the Kathina at the point of hearing.
“Āsāvacchedikā” means that for her there is a cutting off of hope. However, when someone has been told by anyone,
“I will give you a robe,” and having abandoned his expectation regarding that robe by going outside the monastery boundary,
he then cuts off his hope when that person says, “I am unable to give it,” for him there occurs the suspension of the *kaṭhina* due to the cutting off of hope.

However, for one who leaves a monastery where he has spent the rains residence and goes to another monastery while still having expectations [of returning], and who passes the dismantling of the *kathina* robe right on the way back, his dismantling of the *kathina* occurs upon crossing the boundary (*sīmātikkamantika*).

"Together with the dismantling" means *sahubbhāra*. For one who, taking a robe that is a source of benefit (*ānisamsa-cīvara*), goes outside while still having expectations, and encounters the dismantling of the *kathina*, the dismantling of the *kathina* should be understood as "together with the dismantling.
Regarding this dismantling of the *kathina* upon departure, it is said: "First, the impediment of the robe is severed," and so forth.

Since the detailed analysis of the removal of the impediment of robes (*cīvara-palibodha*) and so forth has been stated at length in the *Samantapāsādikā*, he says, "In that regard, the detailed analysis," and so on.
Alternatively, it should be understood that this was said because the detailed analysis of the spreading out (*atthāra*) and the lifting up (*ubbhāra*) alone is found therein.
Regarding the phrase "the absence of remaining impediments," this refers to any other impediment (*palibodha*) that remains.
"Absence" (abhāvaṃ) means the absence of the impediment of a dwelling (āvāsapalibodhābhāvaṃ).

"Of it" (assa) refers to time. Regarding "at most ten days" (dasāhaparamaṃ), he says "that time, at most ten days," because the accusative case is used in the sense of continuous connection (accantasamyoga).
"Exceeding" (atirekaṃ) means more; and that state of excessity pertains to robes that have been formally determined (adhiṭṭhita) or assigned (vikappita), thus he says:
“*Adhiṭṭhitavikappitesu*,” and so forth. *Khoma* refers to a robe made of linen cloth, woven from linen threads.
The same applies to the remaining types. *Kambala* is a cloth made by weaving the remaining animal hairs, excluding human hair and horsehair.
*Sāṇa* is a cloth made from hemp fibers. *Bhaṅga* is a cloth made by mixing the five types, such as linen threads and the rest.

Some say that it is made solely of woven bark (*vākama*). Or else, "of those suitable for them" means of the six types of robes suitable for *khoma* and the others—namely, *dukūla*, *pattuṇṇa*, *somārapaṭṭa*, *cīnapaṭṭa*, *iddhija*, and *devadatta*.
Among these, *dukūla* is suitable for *sāṇa* because it is made of woven bark. *Pattuṇṇa* is cloth produced by insects in a particular region.
*Pattuṇṇaṃ*: cloth produced in the region of Sōmāra is *sōmārapaṭṭa*. Likewise is *cīnapaṭṭa*.

These three are also of the same category as silk (*koseyya*), because they consist of thread made by insects. That which is "born of psychic power" (*iddhija*) refers to robes produced through the merit-potency (*puññiddhi*) of "Come, Bhikkhu" (*ehibhikkhu*) monks;
since that is one of the aforementioned types such as linen (*khoma*), it belongs to the same category as those. That which is "given by devas" (*devadattiya*)...
The *devadina-cīvara* (robe given by a deity) is produced on a wish-fulfilling tree (*kapparukkha*); it resembles the garment given to the Elder Anuruddha by the celestial maiden Jālinī.
It also conforms to the category of linen and the like, as it is of the same nature as those materials.
In length, it measures one carpenter’s cubit (*vaḍḍhakihattha*), and in width, it is half that measure; such is the "alternative" (*vikappanupaga*) robe.

Regarding the phrase "eight finger-breadths by the Sugata-finger-breadth" (*aṭṭhaṅgulaṃ sugataṅgulena*): here, a "Sugata-finger-breadth" (*sugataṅgula*) is equivalent to three finger-breadths of a medium-sized man today;
the meaning is that the measure of a carpenter’s cubit (*vaḍḍhakihattha*) is eight such Sugata-finger-breadths. Regarding the phrase "four finger-breadths wide" (*caturaṅgulavitthata*):

the meaning here too should be understood according to the same principle as stated above. However, for those [cases] where there is an absence of formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) or alternative application (*vikappanā*), [the following applies].
Because it is not included among those robes that have been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) or assigned to another (*vikappita*), this is called an "extra robe" (*atirekacīvara*).

With reference to the inquiry as to in what manner that formal determination and assignment are to be understood, the passage beginning with "But as for what was said" was commenced in order to demonstrate them.
Therein, "but as for what was said" refers to the extra robe; [the text continues] "among those formally determined and assigned..."
The meaning is: "because it is not included [in the worldly sphere]," as we have stated. "To determine the three robes" means to determine them after having stated their names.
"Not to assign" means that I do not permit one to assign them by way of the names *saṅghāṭi* and so forth;
however, it is indeed permissible to assign them by saying, "I assign this robe. But the general term refers to the three robes.

It should be understood that this is stated for the purpose of showing that, like the *kaṇḍupaṭicchādi* (itch-covering cloth) and the *vassikasāṭikā* (rainy-season robe), there is no distinction based on time, and therefore it must be formally assigned (*vikappetabba*);
however, it is not intended as a total prohibition against assignment. For indeed, there are statements such as:
"having relinquished an old robe, one resolves upon a new one," and "there is no offense if one resolves or assigns [a robe]."
And even for the triple robe, the opportunity for assignment (*vikappanā*) is granted. This method applies everywhere.
For one who is determining (*adhiṭṭhahanta*) the triple robe and so forth, it must be determined by stating the respective names, such as: "I determine this outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*)," and so on.
However, when assigning (*vikappenta*), one should not use the specific name of each robe, such as "this outer cloak," but rather say: "this robe..."

“I dedicate it to you”—thus it should be dedicated. Whether it be the three robes or something else, if one dedicates it by mentioning its specific name, it remains undedicated and stays in the category of an extra robe (*atirekacīvara*). Beyond that period, one may dedicate it;
after four months, one may dedicate it saying, “I dedicate this robe. And this [may be] used.
It is permitted. Some, however, say: "Beyond that, it is permitted to set it aside for as long as the four months of the rains in the coming year.

"Beyond that" means beyond [the period of] illness. And because the use of these—namely, the *vassikasāṭika* (rain-cloth) and the *kaṇḍupaṭicchādī* (itch-covering cloth)—is permitted after setting them aside beyond that [period], one may resolve upon what has been so set aside under another name.
"It should be used"—this is stated in the *Gaṇṭhipada* commentaries.
"The state of being determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*) and assigned (*vikappetabba*) must be known" means that one must know the determination and the assignment in this way; such is the meaning.
That which has five as its measure is a "five-group" (*pañcaka*); the "fist-five-group" (*muṭṭhipañcaka*) is the group of five connected to a fist, that is, a closed hand.
Regarding the phrase "this is not [worn] in a fist-like manner," it is also possible to cover the navel by means of wrapping; thus he says, "even two handspans are permissible.
The meaning of the word *pi* (also/even) should be understood as: not only is two and a half [handspans] permissible, but even two handspans are permissible.
"And more than that" means even the measure of the Sugata’s robe or more than that. "I relinquish" means...
"I set aside" means "I relinquish. It is also permissible to say, "I determine this robe as an outer cloak (*saṅghāṭi*).
By "making a bodily movement" is meant touching or moving the robe with the hands or other parts of the body;
for this determination is not valid for one who does not touch it with any part of the body. It is of two kinds.

It is twofold, distinguished by being face-to-face or behind one's back. "Should be split by speech" means that words should be uttered. "In inner chambers, etc. means in inner chambers, upper stories, and so forth.
"In a neighboring monastery" refers to a nearby monastery where it is possible to go and return on the very same day.
This is merely the heading for the teaching; therefore, even if [the person] is standing at a distance, it may be resolved upon.
They say: "Having observed the place where it was laid down"—by this, the observation of the robe is stated. For there is no purpose in merely observing the place where it was laid down.
"By means of the cloths laid down after having determined them" refers, by way of bedding, face-cloths, towels, and requisite cloths.

[This is done] by means of cloths that have been determined and set aside. Since the designation "saṅghāṭī" and so forth did not exist prior to the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna), he demonstrates the separate procedure for relinquishing (paccuddharaṇa) items such as rugs with the words, "I relinquish this.
However, because they must be determined by way of their specific names such as "rug" and so on, there is no fault even if one says, "I relinquish this rug," and so forth.
Fault. "They must be determined again" means they must be determined by name as *saṅghāṭi* and so forth.

However, in the case of a requisites-cloth (*parikkhāracoḷaka*), once it has been set aside after being determined as a requisites-cloth, even if a *saṅghāṭi* or other robe is made from the fabrics kept therein, there is no need to relinquish [the previous determination] and determine it again;
the original determination already made remains the determination. But regarding what has been determined...
While sewing a second cloth-strip or a patch together with it, one must perform the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) only if it is significantly larger;
there is no need for a formal determination if they are equal in size or small. Regarding "for the sake of comfortable use":

because there is no fault of being separated from it, one may place it anywhere and, having performed duties such as listening to the Dhamma, go elsewhere and let the dawn rise there, and then return.
For the purpose of comfortable use, because it can be used even without having to relinquish it (nissajjana).
"To determine the requisites-cloth" means to determine it after having made it into a requisites-cloth.
"Not exceeding the measure" means: "Six spans long according to the Sugata-span, and two and a half spans wide."

"Not exceeding the stated measurement" means it must not be larger than the prescribed size. "Having set it aside, it should be assigned" means that having removed it from its status as a *vassikasāṭikā* (rainy-season robe), it should be assigned;

that is to say, starting from the first day of the winter season, within ten days, having removed it from its status as a *vassikasāṭikā*, it should be assigned by way of the formula: "I assign this robe-cloth to you," and so forth.
Otherwise, since it will later be stated that "the rain-cloak loses its determination even after the lapse of a month of the rains,

and the itch-covering cloth loses its determination even when the illness has subsided," the expression "having relinquished" would be untenable; for if there were no longer a determination after the month of the rains, what would there be to relinquish?

However, some say: "Just as a robe-material that arises within the *kathina* period becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) upon the passing of the *kathina* month, so too this rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*) becomes subject to forfeiture upon the passing of the months of the rains.

Therefore, the meaning should be understood as follows: having relinquished it on the full-moon day of the month of Kattika, it should thereafter be formally assigned (*vikappetabba*) on the first day of the winter season."
Some say that the construction of the words should be understood as: "Having relinquished it, one may thereafter designate it [for another].

However, that is not correct. For a robe that arises during the Kathina month, because it stands in the category of an extra robe (*atireka-cīvara*), becomes subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) upon the expiration of the Kathina month if it has not been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) on the final day. But this rainy-season robe (*vassika-sāṭikā*) must be determined.
Because it has been set aside, it is not "similar" to that [robe]; thus, how does it become subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) upon the lapse of the rainy season?

For it becomes subject to forfeiture only upon the lapse of the time if it has neither been formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) nor assigned (*avikappita*). Therefore, even in the winter, the *vassikasāṭikā* (rainy-season robe) receives the ten-day exemption.
Likewise, the itch-covering cloth (*kaṇḍupaṭicchādi*) also receives the ten-day exemption beyond the point when its formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is lost.

However, it must be formally assigned (*vikappetabbā*) without letting the ten-day period elapse. Since it was permitted for the purpose of bathing, it is stated that this is allowable even if it is dyed only slightly or with a different color.
It is stated that "two [types] are not allowable" because there is no formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) regarding those two.
"If, during the rainy season, another rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭikā*) is obtained, one should relinquish the previous rainy-season robe..."
They say that after having made a formal assignment (*vikappetvā*), it must be determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*).
"Of proper measure" means it is endowed with this measure: "two spans of the Sugata’s span in length, and one and a half spans plus a fringe of ten spans in width.
"Measured" means [it is] four spans of the Sugata’s span in length.
“Two spans across”—thus it is endowed with the dimensions as stated.

Regarding the phrase “having relinquished, it should be dedicated,” what is to be said here has already been explained above. Since the bhikkhus’ triple robe (ticīvara) is complete, yet when there is need for requisites such as water-strainers and so forth, [the Buddha said], “Bhikkhus, I allow a requisite-cloth (parikkhāra-coḷaka),” [referring] to many things such as bowl-bags, water-strainers, and the like.
The formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) of requisites and robes was permitted by way of inclusion; therefore, it was said:

"There is no counting regarding the requisites and robes," and so forth. For out of compassion, the Blessed One stated that whatever the monks receive, they should determine it according to this procedure, and furthermore, "Whatever they may need, such as a water-strainer and so on, let them take it after having made [the determination]."

It is permitted. For this very reason, he says, “even a bag,” and so forth. By the word “etcetera,” he includes the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) made in the absence [of the robe], namely: “I determine these robes as requisites for clothing.

By the phrase, “and on a rug given for the purpose of bedding and requisites,” he excludes what belongs to himself. However, some say: “Without wearing it as an undergarment and without draping it over the shoulder, merely...”
Some say that even a bedspread belonging to oneself is permissible to use without having formally determined it as one’s own, provided it is spread out and used only upon the five types of seats;
however, this is incorrect because the bedspread is specifically qualified by the phrase “given for the purpose of furniture for lodgings.
The same applies to mattresses, pillows, curtains, and blankets, as these too are merely furniture for lodgings and thus require formal determination.

It should be understood that [the robe] does not exist [as a formal act]. However, for one who uses this robe after it has been determined, how is the determination lost? To this he said, "But all this," and so forth.
In that context, "by being taken away by force" means by being seized by thieves and others through force. "By returning to the lower life" means...
"By returning to the state of a householder" means by disrobing; it is said [here] that one will "become a householder while remaining virtuous," which implies wearing white garments.

Some say: "For one who has committed the ultimate offense, either the wearing of white garments or the discarding of the saffron robe constitutes a return to the lower state. By the phrase "by returning to the lower state," [it refers to] a bhikkhunī...
"Thus, the relinquishing of the formal resolve (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is included. For when she disrobes, she then ceases to be a *samaṇī*.
But even when a monk disrobes, as long as he has not renounced the training (*sikkhā*), he remains a monk; thus, he does not relinquish his formal resolve," so say others.
"By the renunciation of the training" means by the renunciation of the training while remaining in the [monastic] marks (*liṅga*).
For when one who remains in the outward marks of a bhikkhu renounces the training, even the robe clinging to his body loses its formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
"By death" means by passing away. "By the change of gender" means by the change of the male or female characteristic;
that is to say, by the manifestation of the female characteristic in a man, or by the manifestation of the male characteristic in a woman.
"By the measure of the back of the nail of the little finger" indicates the lower limit. "From within" means from the interior.
However, if one first places the bolt in a weak spot and subsequently removes it after cutting through that weak spot, the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) is not broken.
The same principle applies even when turning the circular bolt. But in the case of a double-layered robe, in one [layer]...
If a tear or a hole occurs, or if it becomes worn out, the *adhiṭṭhāna* (formal resolution) is not broken.
If one makes a small robe large, or a large robe small, the *adhiṭṭhāna* is not broken.
However, if one moves both edges to the middle, provided that one first cuts them and afterwards joins them, the *adhiṭṭhāna* is broken. But if one joins them first...
It is cut, but it does not break. Even for one who has it washed by dyers and makes it white, the determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) remains a determination.
Regarding the phrase "even with the passing of the month of the rains," the word *api* (even/also) has the sense of inclusion.

By this, it is shown that the rain-cloak (*vassikasāṭikā*) does not lose its determination not only through the eight causes previously mentioned, such as giving and so forth, but also through the passing of the month of the rains.
The meaning here should be understood in this way. This same method applies to the phrase "also by the allaying of illness. Regarding the phrase "in the training rule on exchanging":
it refers to the ninth training rule in the *Surāpāna-vagga* of the *Pācittiya*.
As for the expression "one who exceeds that": here, "that" refers to the robe or the time; thus he says, "that which has the aforementioned kind and measure," and so forth.
"Assa" means "of the bhikkhu. "Tassa yo aruṇo" means the dawn that has passed for him on the day the robe was offered.
"Saddhiṃ cīvaruppādadivasena" means together with the dawn of the day the robe was offered.
And here, by the word "day," the dawn dependent upon that day is intended. Now, as to whom it must be relinquished and how it must be relinquished:
To demonstrate that, it was said: “Having taken that,” and so forth. In this regard, “this method” means this procedure for that act of relinquishment.
“In another way as well” means even by means of another language; the sense is: by whatever language whatsoever. “By one who is capable” means by one able to speak.
“You should restrain yourself in the future” means you should attain restraint hereafter; you should be one whose doors of body and speech are restrained.
This is the meaning. Furthermore, these phrases beginning with "Do you see? are, respectively, the words to be spoken by the recipient and the instructor.
For instance, "Do you see? is the statement to be spoken by the recipient; "Yes, I see" is the statement to be spoken by the one following that;
"You should restrain yourself in the future" is the statement to be spoken by the one following that recipient; "Very well."
“I shall restrain myself well”—this is the statement to be spoken by the follower. By this, he demonstrates his state of being established in restraint for the future.
Regarding the two or many cases, the distinction in phrasing should be made according to the previous method, as in:
“In two or in many offenses,” or “He remembers and discloses an offense in the motion. Here, “two... [the text continues].
Or one should make a distinction in the wording by saying, "offenses" or "many offenses. A distinction in the wording should be made according to whether there are two or many [offenses];
thus, regarding the phrase "the Saṅgha, these robes," a distinction in the wording should be made according to the object.
Having thus shown the procedure for relinquishing to the Saṅgha, in order to show the procedure for relinquishing to a group (gaṇa), [it says] "to the group..."

He said, "But by one who is relinquishing... and so forth. In that context, "the rest is just like the previous" means that regarding the relinquishment to the Saṅgha and so on, the remainder—excluding the specific variations in wording such as "to you, venerable sirs" mentioned in the cases of relinquishing an offense, accepting a relinquishment, and giving away a relinquished robe—is exactly the same as what was stated for the relinquishment to the Saṅgha; this is the meaning.
Now, in order to show the procedure for relinquishing to an individual, he said, "But to an individual... and so forth. In that context:
