"In two or three" means in regard to either two or three offenses as well as the robes to be forfeited.

And just as the procedure for forfeiture to a *gaṇa* (a group) is understood, so too should the procedure for forfeiture to two individuals be understood from the text. For if there were a distinction, [the text] would have stated it just as [it does for three]:
"I allow you, monks, to perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* for three; and furthermore, monks—"
Having explained the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* for three [monks] in the manner beginning with, "It should be done: an experienced and competent monk should inform those monks," it continues:
"I allow you, monks, to perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* for two [monks].
And thus, monks, it should be done: the senior monk should arrange his upper robe over one shoulder... and so forth.
Just as the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* for two individuals is stated separately by way of method, so too would the text (Pāḷi) here state it separately.
But since that does not exist, it is not mentioned; thus, what is stated here as the text for the group is itself the text.
However, there is this distinction regarding the acceptance of an offense: just as when an offense is confessed after having been relinquished to the group, the receiver of the confession...

A bhikkhu makes a formal motion (*ñatti*); having thus made it, the confession of the offense should be accepted by one of the two in the same manner as a single individual accepts it. For there is no such thing as making a formal motion by two;

if there were, they would not have to perform the *pārisuddhi-uposatha* separately. Also, regarding the giving away of a robe that has been relinquished, just as [one says]: "Venerable sir, this robe..."
One says, "I give," and thus it is permissible to say, "We give this robe to the Venerable One.

For there are indeed formal acts (*kamma*) even more weighty than this that are said to be performed by means of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*); this [present case] is in accordance with them.
Therefore he said, "But for two," and so forth. However, a robe that has been relinquished must certainly be given; it is not permissible not to give it.
It is not obtained. For this is merely a formal act of the Vinaya (vinayakamma). It does not become something given to the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual by that [act].
Therefore he said, "the relinquished object," and so forth.
For one who uses it without having relinquished it, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) regarding what was once worn or once donned on the body.

If one goes about even for a day without having released [the robe], it is one *dukkaṭa*. If, having released it, one puts it on as an undergarment (*nivāsana*) or as an upper robe (*pārupana*), there is a *dukkaṭa* for each such act.
There is no offense for one who causes another to adjust what is poorly worn or poorly put on.
There is also no offense for one who uses it after it has been used by another. The statement here, “Having obtained what was made by another, he uses it,” and so forth, refers to this.

This is the proof. Regarding the phrase "for one who perceives it as exceeded even when it has not been exceeded, and for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," here too the word "while using" (*paribhuñjantassa*) must be supplied and connected.
Regarding the phrase "even for one who perceives it as not exceeded when it has been exceeded":
this refers to one who, when the robe has been exceeded by ten days, perceives it thus, "this has not been exceeded," or when ten days have been exceeded, [perceives], "it has not been exceeded."
"Ten days"—thus they perceive.

Now, having grouped together the section on offenses beginning with "If one perceives as determined what is not determined, it is an offense of relinquishment," he says "In the same way," and so forth.
"In the same way" means that just as there is a triad of pācittiyas regarding the perception when ten days have elapsed, so too [is it here].
The meaning is: "due to the distinction of perceptions such as 'formally resolved' (*adhiṭṭhita*) among the seven alternatives beginning with 'not formally resolved' (*anadhiṭṭhita*).

In that context, "those who perceive what has not been relinquished as having been relinquished" refers to those who, when something has not been given away or renounced by anyone, have the perception: "It has been given and renounced by me.
"Those who perceive what is not lost as lost" refers to cases where many robes belonging to others have been placed together with one's own robe.
If thieves steal those robes, and he perceives them as lost when his own robe has not actually been lost, then for him who perceives it as lost,

this same principle applies to cases where they have not been lost and so forth. However, in the phrase "plundered" (*avilutta*), it should be understood as plundering by breaking into a house and carrying things off by force.
"Given away" means it has been given to another. But how is it given? And how is it received?
If one says, "I give this to you," "I am giving it," "I shall give it," "I bestow it," "I relinquish it," "I hand over," or "I surrender it"; or if one says, "I give it to so-and-so"...
[and so on] "...I surrender it"—whether in the presence of the recipient or behind their back—it is indeed considered given.
It exists. When told, "Take it for yourself," he says, "I take it for myself";
this is well-given and well-received. When told, "Make it your own; let it be yours;
you will make it your own," he says, "I make it mine; let it be mine; I will make it mine"; this is ill-given.
And it is wrongly received if neither the giver knows how to give nor the other how to receive.
However, if, when told, "Make this your own," one says, "Very well, Venerable Sir, I take it," then it is rightly received.
But if one says, "Take it," and the other says, "I will not take it," and then the former says, "It has been given by me to you," [it is wrongly received].

If one says, "Take it," and the other replies, "I have no need for this," then if the former lets ten days pass thinking, "It was given by me," and the latter lets ten days pass thinking, "It was refused by me," whose offense is it? It is none of theirs.
However, whoever desires it should resolve upon it and then use it. As for the one who [resolves upon it]...

If one is in doubt, what should be done? Having declared the state of being in doubt and said, "If it is not formally determined (as belonging to another), then it is allowable for me," he should relinquish it in the manner already described.
For there is no falsehood in performing a disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*) after having made such a declaration.

And just as this [rule] is so, so too are those following it; that is to say, just as this training rule regarding the wearing of extra robes (*atirekacīvara*) is a failure of conduct (*ācāravipatti*), so too are the training rules following it failures of conduct alone—this is the meaning. Therefore he said, “In both Pātimokkhas,” and so forth.
However, with the exception of the *dubbhāsita* (wrong speech), six classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*) are prescribed on account of failure in livelihood (*ājīvavipatti*).
“For the sake of livelihood, for the purpose of livelihood, one who has evil desires and is overcome by desire speaks of a non-existent, unreal superhuman state;
this is an offense entailing defeat (pārājika). For the sake of livelihood, for the purpose of livelihood, one engages in matchmaking;
this is an offense entailing formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa). For the sake of livelihood, for the purpose of livelihood, one says: ‘The monk who dwells in your monastery is an arahant.’”

If he speaks [thus], there is an offense of *thullaccaya* for one who understands [the meaning]. If a monk, for the sake of livelihood and for the purpose of livelihood, being not ill, requests and eats fine foods for his own benefit, there is an offense of *pācittiya*.
If a nun, for the sake of livelihood and for the purpose of livelihood, being not ill, requests and eats fine foods for her own benefit, there is an offense of *pāṭidesanīya*.
“If a bhikkhu, for the sake of his livelihood and for the purpose of his livelihood, being not ill, asks for soup or boiled rice for his own benefit and eats it,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Thus,
having established [the offenses] by way of the pārājikas and so forth, there are six classes of offenses on account of failure in livelihood, including the dubbhāsita.
Two classes of offenses have been prescribed: on account of failure in view, there are two classes of offenses by way of *pācittiya* and *dukkaṭa*.

Thus, regarding the non-renunciation of a wicked view after having been formally admonished, there is a *dukkaṭa* at the motion (*ñatti*) and a *pācittiya* at the conclusion of the formal act (*kammavācā*).
In this way, on account of failure in view, there are two classes of offenses by way of *pācittiya* and *dukkaṭa*.
"Prescribed. "In this context" means in the discussions concerning failure.

"Has entered into counting" refers to the state of having entered into the count of days. Even if [a robe] has been given into the hand of another by others with the words, "We give this robe to such-and-such a person," it is stated in the Cammakkhandhaka (The Chapter on Skins):
"It has not yet entered into counting as long as it has not come into [the recipient's] hand."

Because it has been stated that as long as [the robe] has not been brought and given, or as long as it has not been reported by sending a messenger with the words, "Venerable sir, a robe has arisen for you," the counting of days does not begin;
at that time, it is permissible to leave it un-designated (*anadhiṭṭhita*).
However, once it has been brought and given, or when one hears that "it has arisen," from that point on it enters into the counting of days, and it must be designated within ten days.
That which has the *kathina* as its designation for its origin is "originated by the *kathina*" (*kathinasamuṭṭhāna*).

The meaning is that it has two origins, by way of the third and sixth origins. Because it arises through the non-performance of the formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) and the assignment (*vikappana*) to be performed by body and speech, it originates from body and speech;
however, when the mind is present, it is said to originate from body, speech, and mind. This is by way of non-determination and non-assignment.
Because it is committed through performance, it is non-inaction (*akiriyā*). Because one commits it even without knowing, it is not a liberation through perception (*no-saññā-vimokkha*).
Because of the failure to do what ought to be done at the door of the body and the door of speech, there is bodily action (*kāyakamma*) and verbal action (*vacīkamma*).
The commentary on the *Kathina* training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Lifting Up (Udosita-sikkhāpada).
"By a bhikkhunī" means "by a bhikkhu"; here, this instrumental case is used in the sense of the genitive. Therefore he said: "Just as in the previous training rule," and so forth.
Now, why was the meaning of the instrumental case not taken in the sense of the instrument alone, but rather in the sense of the agent?
“The meaning should be understood,” he says, beginning with “by way of the instrument (*karaṇa*),” and so forth. The particle *hi* is a grammatical indeclinable used in the sense of a reason.
“With obstacles cut off” means with the obstacles of robes and dwelling places cut off. “One night only” is *ekarattaṃ*; this is the meaning of the suffix that occurs at the end of a compound.
“The collection of three robes” is *ticīvaraṃ*. “By that triple robe” means by means of the three robes. Even if one has stayed apart from even one [of them].

For one is said to be "separated from the three robes" because of being separated from that which is included within the prohibited [category], or because the term for the whole is applied to its parts.
Therefore he said, "by way of the formal determination (adhiṭṭhāna) of the three robes," and so forth.
Now, for the purpose of defining the characteristics of separation, he said, "a village has a single precinct (ekūpacāra)," and so on. In this context, "dwelling" (nivesana) means...
This is a designation for a variety of dwellings that have not been constructed [by others], such as *udositā* and so forth.
*Udosita* refers to a hall for goods such as vehicles; it is also called an *udavasita*.

*Aṭṭa* is a specific type of dwelling with thick walls made of bricks, four or five stories high, built for the purpose of repelling rival kings and the like. "An *aṭṭa* is a house with thick walls, of which..."
Others say: "The roof is made of bricks alone, without taking up rafters. They also say: "It is constructed in the form of a tower (*aṭṭā*).
A *māḷa* is a square palace comprised of a single peak, or a specific type of dwelling with many corners comprised of a single peak.
Others say: "A *māḷa* is a lodging constructed in a circular form. A *pāsāda* is a long palace.
A palace includes all types, such as those with upper chambers (*aḍḍhayoga*) and so forth, excluding the eight-storied (*aṭṭhamāḷa*) and the *hammiya*. A *hammiya* is a palace with a flat roof.
Others say it is one provided with a moon-court (*candiyaṅgaṇa*). A boat is of two kinds: those situated on land and those on water.
A caravan is either a foot-caravan or a cart-caravan. A threshing floor is called a *dhaññakaraṇa*. An orchard (*ārāma*) is a flower-garden.
Or a fruit garden. "Vihāra" refers to the entire monastery, whether it has a surrounding wall or not;

some say it also includes a house. Here, "dwelling" (*nivesana*) and so forth refer to those situated outside the village. However, since those located within the village are already included by the mention of "village," they are excluded from this category.
"Dwellings" and so on, up to the watchtower, [are excluded] from the boundary of the village...
"Others say: 'It is established outside. Regarding 'beyond the reach of the hand' (*hatthapāsātikkame*):

here, 'the reach of the hand' (*hatthapāsa*) refers to a space measuring two and a half *ratana*s; going beyond that is 'beyond the reach of the hand,' and it is in that state of being beyond the reach of the hand [that the offense occurs].

However, it is permissible to establish the object within the reach of the hand. Even if a monk possessing psychic power (*iddhimā*), having exceeded that measure, causes the dawn to rise in the sky..."
If he causes it to be brought back, it becomes an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).

Herein, however, is the analysis: if a village belongs to a single family by virtue of one king or a local lord, and because it is enclosed by a wall or the like, it constitutes a single area of access; having deposited his robe in such a village, in that—

One should dwell within the village in a place that is agreeable; if it is unenclosed, one should dwell in the house where the robe has been deposited, or one must not depart from the reach of the hand (hatthapāsa) surrounding that house.
If the village belongs to various rulers or chieftains, as in the cases of Vesālī, Kusinārā, and so forth, [one should act] according to the manner already described.
And in a village that is enclosed, one should stay in whichever house the robe has been deposited,
or one should not depart from the reach of that house’s handspan.
One should stay on the street where the house is located, in front of that house, in the assembly hall, or at the door of the house.
One must not leave the reach of one’s hand from those assembly halls or gates.
If that village is unenclosed, one should stay either in the house where the robe has been deposited or within reach of one’s hand from there.
However, in the case of a residence belonging to a single family, if it is enclosed, [one should stay] inside the residence.
Having laid aside the robe-cloth, one must dwell within the residence.
If it is unenclosed, one must dwell in the very room where the robe-cloth was laid aside, or one must not go beyond arm’s reach of that room.
If it is the residence of various families and is enclosed, [one must dwell] in the room where the robe-cloth was laid aside...
One must stay in that room, or one must not leave the vicinity of the hand’s reach (hatthapāsa) of either the common entrance for all or the entrances to those specific rooms.

If it is unenclosed, one must stay in the room where the robe was placed, or one must not leave the vicinity of the hand’s reach of that room. This same principle applies to open sheds (udosita) and other such places as well.
Now, as for the caravan, whether it be a foot-caravan or a cart-caravan:
if it is a caravan belonging to a single family, having deposited one's robe in the caravan, one must not leave a distance of seven *abbhantaras* either in front of or behind it;
one must not leave a distance of even one *abbhantara* from sight. If the caravan, while traveling, bypasses a village or a river...
If it stands joined as one with that which has entered within, pervading both this side and the far side, only the protection of the Teacher is obtained.
However, if it is included within a village or a river and has entered therein, both the protection of the village and the protection of the river are obtained.
If, however, it stands having crossed beyond the monastery boundary (vihārasīma), [only the protection of the Teacher applies].
If the robe is within the boundary, one must go to the monastery and stay there.
If the robe is outside the boundary, one must stay right near the caravan. If, while traveling, the journey is interrupted by a broken cart or lost oxen, one must stay where the robe was placed.
Regarding a field: if it belongs to a single family and is enclosed, one may deposit the robe within the field and stay within the field.
If it is unenclosed, one must not be separated from the robe by more than the distance of an arm’s reach.
If it belongs to various families and is enclosed, having deposited the robe within the field, [one may stay] at the base of the field gate...
Or one must dwell [there], or not depart from the reach of his hand. If it is unenclosed, the robe must not be left out of the reach of his hand.
This same principle applies to both granaries and monasteries. As for a vihāra, however, the determination is exactly as stated for a dwelling.
But regarding the foot of a tree, that place where the shade spreads all around at midday—within that dense area...
It must be placed within the very area touched by its shadow.

If he places it in a spot touched by the sun’s heat from a tree with sparse branches, and at the rising of the dawn that monk is not within arm’s reach of it—even if his shadow is elsewhere—there is an offense of expiation (nissaggiya). If [the robe belongs] to a different family...
If there is a tree, one must not leave the reach of one’s hand from the robe.

However, in the open air—even in forests such as the Viñjhāṭavi wilderness or on islands in the middle of the ocean that are inaccessible to fishermen—one may place the robe down and dwell anywhere within a distance of seven *abbhantara*s (approx. 28 meters) surrounding it; beyond this, [one must remain within reach].
It should be understood that one who is staying elsewhere is said to be "separated.
Since this detailed explanation is not given here but is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*, it was said:
"This is the summary here," and so forth. "Here" refers to the phrase "one might be separated from the three robes. "Summary" means...

This is the brief commentary. Herein, although the *mātikā* (table of contents) has been set forth in the *Pāḷi* without distinction as "a village with a single precinct" (*ekūpacāra*) or "with various precincts" (*nānūpacāra*), etc., the fact that village-settlements, watchtowers, fields, grain-stores, monasteries, and monastic dwellings may have either a single precinct or various precincts is explained by such passages as:
"A village with a single precinct is one belonging to a single family, whether it be enclosed or unenclosed," and so forth.

[These are] classified according to whether they are enclosed or unenclosed. However, regarding the watch-tower (*aṭṭa*), palace (*pāsāda*), hall (*hammiya*), ship (*nāvā*), seat (*satha*), foot of a tree (*rukkhamūla*), and open space (*ajjhokāsa*), instead of stating it in that way, [they are classified] by way of being for a single family or for various families, according to the method beginning with: "There is a watch-tower for one family; there is a watch-tower for various families. Finally, regarding the open space:
"An open space is called a single precinct (*ekūpacāra*); in a forest outside a village, an area extending seven *abbhantara*s all around is a single precinct."
Beyond that, it is "not a single precinct" (*nānūpacāra*); thus, the state of being a single precinct or not a single precinct has been analyzed.

Therefore, among villages and the like, that which is enclosed is a single precinct, while that which is unenclosed is not a single precinct; and among watchtowers and the like, that which belongs to a single family is a single precinct, while that which belongs to various families is not a single precinct—this is how it should be understood.
In the case of open space, it should be understood according to the method already stated.
“Vicinity” (*upacāra*) refers, in such passages as “a village has one vicinity, or various vicinities,” to the gate;
however, others say that in the phrase “an open space has one vicinity,” it refers to the measurement consisting of seven *abbhantara*s all around.
“Except by the consent of the monks” (*aññatra bhikkhusammutiyā*): the consent given to a monk by the Saṅgha is “the consent of the monks”; [the phrase means] except for that.

This is the meaning. Therefore he said, “Whatever the Saṅgha,” and so forth. “He grants the authorization for not being separated” (avippavāsasammutiṃ deti) means: an authorization that is not separated, or an authorization for the sake of not being separated;
the meaning is that he grants this by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (ñattidutiyakamma).
Regarding the phrase “with the inner and outer [robes]”: “inner” (antara) refers to the lower robe (antaravāsaka); “outer” (uttara) refers to the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga); together with...

"Between the inner and the outer" (*santaruttaraṃ*) means by means of that which is between the inner and the outer; the meaning is: together with the *antaravāsaka* (inner robe) and the *uttarāsaṅga* (upper robe).
"If it is relinquished before dawn" means: having turned back and being unable to reach [the monastery], one stands right there and relinquishes it before dawn.
"One must return" means: so that the illness does not flare up, one must [return] for the sake of the robe again.
One must return to the place where it was deposited. For from the moment one seeks a teacher or forms the intention, "I am going," from that point on it is permissible.

However, by one who lays down the burden with the thought, "I shall not go now," it must be relinquished [with the thought], "It will remain in the place of an extra robe. Therefore he said: "Or right there..."
"It must be relinquished by one who remains [in the same place]. "He" refers to the one to whom the formal authorization (*sammuti*) was given; that is, the illness.
The intention is that once what is permissible has been obtained, there is no further need for the act of granting authorization.
"The state of having determined the robes" means the state of having determined the three robes according to the method of determining the three robes. "Separation" means, if...

If the robe is within a defined boundary (*baddhasīmā*), it is [considered lost] when dawn breaks outside of it. If, however, there is no defined boundary, it is [considered lost] when dawn breaks after one has stepped beyond arm’s reach outside of the aforementioned villages and so forth.

But within a defined boundary, having placed the robe anywhere, it is permissible to stay anywhere inside that very boundary. Here, the connection is with "non-removal" (*apaccuddharaṇa*) as a non-action (*akiriyā*).
The commentary on the Udosita training rule is finished.
3. Commentary on the Akālacīvara training rule:

Just as in the previous training rule, here too the word "bhikkhunā" (by a bhikkhu) is used in the instrumental case to express the sense of the genitive; thus he says, "when the robe has been finished..."
“By a bhikkhu,” and so forth. Regarding the phrase “out-of-season robe-cloth (akālacīvara),” since it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājaniya*):

“That which arises during the eleven months when the Kathina has not been spread, or during the seven months when the Kathina has been spread, or that which is given specifically designated even during the [proper] season—this is called ‘out-of-season robe-cloth,’” he therefore said, “This which, when the Kathina has not been spread,” and so forth. The connection is: “this which is called the robe-season.”
"Of the rainy season" means of the season reckoned as the rains. "The last month" refers to the robe-month;

for during that time, even if the *kathina* has not been spread, it is permissible to set aside a robe that has arisen [as an offering] without having formally determined (*adhiṭṭhita*) it or assigned it (*vikappita*).
"Five months" means the last month of Kattika and the four months of the winter season—thus five months. "At other times" means when the *kathina* has not been spread.

In the eleventh month, [it is] seven months when the *kathina* has not been spread; "at the time" means even during the robe-season as previously stated—namely, "the month of robes when the *kathina* has not been spread, and five months when the *kathina* has been spread.
By the phrase "by this method," there is an inclusion of [expressions such as] "I give" and "I would give.
Although all these are called "out-of-season robes," nevertheless, it is only in the case of the "back-season" (*piṭṭhisamaya*) that [this applies].
Those robes that have arisen [at an improper time] are what is intended here by the term "out-of-season robe" (*akālacīvara*).

However, that which was given to the Saṅgha at the proper time with the thought, "This is an out-of-season robe for the Saṅgha," is mentioned by way of extracting the commonality of being an out-of-season robe.
For example, as in the case of a robe that has arisen during the season of the rains-retreat for those who have completed their retreat, and for those remaining who are present.
"It is allowable to divide" means that it has become what is called "out-of-season robe-cloth" (*akālacīvara*); "so too is this" refers to the commonality with out-of-season robe-cloth.
If this is so, why is it said, "This was given to an individual, [saying] 'I give this to you,' and so forth"?
For surely, what is given specifically to an individual cannot be shared by anyone. This is not a contradiction, because it shares the commonality of being given specifically.
It was stated in that way to show a meaning that is possible. Or, "with one's own wealth" means with one's own wealth such as cotton, thread, and so forth.

This should be understood as being connected with the word "might arise. The passage beginning with "he gives within the boundary" (*sīmāya deti*) is stated by way of reference to the individual (*puggalādhiṭṭhānanaya*).
Here, however, giving within the boundary is the first heading (*mātikā*); giving according to an agreement (*katikā*) is the second... [and so on] ...giving to an individual is the eighth.

By the phrase “by the place worthy of being enclosed,” it is shown that for an unenclosed monastery, the *upacārasīmā* (proximate boundary) extends to within the range of the first stone-throw from a place where the community regularly assembles and so forth.
Now, in order to show that the *upacārasīmā* likewise extends to within the range of the second stone-throw, the passage beginning with “Moreover” (*apicā*) is commenced.
It should be understood that even the place where the community regularly assembles must be situated within the limits of the *sīmā*.
Regarding the statement, "When the residence increases, it increases": the intended meaning is that the residence increases provided it does not extend beyond the precincts (*upacāra*).
However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated: "It increases even when the monks increase.

If the monks, together with those assembled in the monastery, sit down forming a continuous connection even across a hundred yojanas, then even a hundred yojanas constitutes the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*).
"Everything becomes available for all," as stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*. Regarding "the entering of the monastery and the inquiry for lodgings for bhikkhunīs":
the meaning is the inquiry for entering the monastery and the inquiry for lodgings for visiting and departing bhikkhunīs.
For it is thus: a visiting bhikkhunī must inquire about entering the monastery, and for one who is departing, [inquiry is made regarding] what belongs to the Saṅgha...

There are ten kinds of lodgings (*senāsana*). And here, although it is stated as "for nuns," it should be understood that for a monk who is traveling, the inquiry regarding lodgings is also to be conducted by means of this very boundary (*sīmā*).

"Announcement of the probation and the penance" refers to the announcement of the probation for those undergoing probation (*pārivāsika*) and the announcement of the penance (*mānatta*) for those performing the penance.
"The procedure for the interruption of the rains, the taking of formal dependence (nissaya), the taking of lodgings, and so forth" means:
the procedure for the interruption of the rains, the procedure for taking formal dependence, and the procedure for taking lodgings.

By the word "and so forth" (ādi), it includes such matters as the cessation of formal dependence, the acquisition of gains, and entering the monastery after fulfilling the duties for newcomers. "By way of this very boundary" refers specifically to the precinct boundary (upacāra-sīmā).
It is stated thus because it is obtainable both internally and externally as far as possible.

A boundary established for the sake of receiving gains is a "gain-boundary" (*lābhasīmā*); moreover, this was neither authorized by the Perfectly Enlightened One nor established by the Elders who compiled the Dhamma, but rather by those who bestow the gains.
Therefore he said: "Whatever [is given] by kings, royal ministers, and so forth," and so on.
“On all sides” means around the monastery. “Yam” refers to customs duties, taxes, and so forth. The phrase “they establish a boundary” (*sīmaṃ ṭhapenti*) is the remainder of the text.

“The domain of a single king’s authority” means the territory of each individual king, such as the Coḷa province or the Keraḷa province; it is the place where the exercise of one king’s command prevails.
A “continent” (*dīpa*) is so called because water flows around it on two sides; it is a portion of land not overwhelmed by a flood, and that itself constitutes the “continent-boundary” (*dīpasīmā*).
Therefore he said, "by the ocean's edge," and so forth. Since the boundary of the world-system (*cakkavāḷasīmā*) is delimited by the mountain of the world-system itself, he said:

"The boundary of the world-system is the interior space enclosed by the perimeter of a single world-system mountain. "The rest" refers to the fragmentary boundaries (*khaṇḍasīmā*) and so on. Regarding "we give to the fragmentary boundary":

it is given when, having seen the Saṅgha assembled for some business within a fragmentary boundary, one says, "We give to the Saṅgha within the fragmentary boundary. [Regarding] "the tree standing within the fragmentary boundary":
Whether standing on a mountain or even deep within the earth, one should be understood as standing within the *khaṇḍasīmā* (fragmentary boundary) itself.
"Given within the boundary of common affiliation" means given with the words, "I give within the boundary of common affiliation. This same method applies to the others as well.
The intention is that the *khaṇḍasīmā* does not extend to the intermediate space between boundaries (*sīmantarika*), because the boundary of common affiliation does not exist there.
Regarding what is given within the boundaries of common residence (*samānasaṃvāsa*) and non-separation (*avippavāsa*), this is the distinction:

that which is given with the words, "I give it within the boundary of non-separation," does not reach those staying in the village. Why? Because it has been stated: "Excluding the village and the vicinity of the village.

However, that which is given with the words, "I give it within the boundary of common residence," reaches even those staying in the village. [This applies] to the internal boundary (*abbhantarasīmā*) and the water-throwing boundary (*udakukkhepasīmā*).
"Given" (*dinnam*) refers to what has been given when people have assembled for the purpose of the Uposatha and so forth, saying, "We give it within this internal boundary," and so on.

Since the legal determination regarding the boundaries of a province, a kingdom, a realm, an island, and a world-system is exactly the same as that stated for village boundaries and the like, he says, "Regarding the boundaries of a province, etc.
Even a single person, having gone [there], is permitted to include everyone; thus, "even a single person having gone..."
The meaning is that one may come after having received [the portion] by distributing it according to the rainy-season retreat (*vassa*). "One" refers to a single monk who shares [the same boundary];
he too is permitted to receive only his own share. Therefore, it is said: "He takes the share of those who share [the same boundary].
Having thus explained the determination regarding the gift of one who gives after touching the boundary, [the text now addresses] one who [gives] saying, "In such-and-such a boundary..."
He does not know how to speak; knowing only the mere word "boundary," he comes to the monastery and says, "I give this to the boundary," or "I give this to the Saṅgha residing within the boundary.
To show the legal decision regarding such a case, [the author] said, "But whoever, having entered the monastery...
and so forth. "Which one? means "which boundary? [The donor replies: "I do not know this distinction."

"I do not know this distinction, namely 'such-and-such a boundary. The intention is that it should be divided by those residing within the precinct boundary (*upacārasīma*), because the distribution of gains is delimited by the precinct boundary. "That" refers to the group sharing the same gains.
"Where my permanent duties are performed" means in whichever monastery the belongings of that donor of robes are [to be used].
The Saṅgha’s turn for cooked food is in progress. Those monasteries where monks, taking it upon themselves as their own responsibility, always feed him at home;
or where he has had a residence built for himself, or where meals by ticket (*salākabhatta*) and so forth have been regularly provided—these are called "regular supporters" (*dhuvakāra*).
But in the case of one who has established the entire monastery, there is simply nothing further to be said. Therefore, he said:
“Wherever his turn for the distribution of cooked food (pākavatta) occurs,” and so forth. In this context, *pākavatta* means the duty of giving cooked food.
*Vattati* means it takes place. *Yato* means from whichever monastery. *Yattha* means in whichever monastery. *Sabbattha* means in all monasteries.
*Āropetvā mātikaṃ* means having assigned the roster: in one monastery there are more bhikkhus, in another fewer, and there is only one cloth [to be distributed].
Regarding the large quantity of permanent furniture (*dhuvakāraṭṭhāna*), one should ask, "Where shall we give it?

If there is only a single bed or bench, one should ask about that; or it should be given to whichever monastery he manages, or even to whichever specific lodging (*senāsana*) within a single monastery he looks after.
Even if he says, "Let such-and-such a monk take it," it is permissible. Then...
If, having said, “Give it to my permanent attendant,” he departs without further consideration, it is permissible for the Saṅgha to investigate the matter.
It should be investigated in this way: one should say, “Give it to the dwelling place of the senior monk of the Saṅgha.
If the lodging there is already full, it should be given to where there is no shortage. If a single bhikkhu says, “To me...”
If he says, "There is no furniture for the use of lodgings in the place where one dwells," it should be given there.
Regarding "given as 'I give this to the Saṅgha'": it is given in this manner, saying, "I give these robes to the Saṅgha.

"Even beyond that" means even outside the boundary of the precinct (upacārasīmā). "Together with them" means together with those who have entered the boundary of the precinct. And "of those that are connected as one whole" (ekābaddhānaṃ).

The intention is that the boundary becomes extended by way of the assembly reaching [the area]. "Therefore" means: because it reaches those who have entered the precinct boundary (*upacārasīmā*), and because it also reaches those who are connected as one unit with those who have entered the precinct boundary even beyond that; therefore. "Of them" refers to those who have entered the precinct boundary and those who are connected as one unit with them beyond that. "When it is grasped" means: *Pāpuṇāti parisāvasena vaḍḍhitā sīmā hotīti katvāti adhippāyo.* The intention is that the boundary becomes extended by way of the assembly reaching [the area]. *Tasmāti yasmā upacārasīmāgatānaṃ pāpuṇāti, yasmā ca tato bahiddhāpi upacārasīmokkantehi ekābaddhānaṃ pāpuṇāti, tasmā.* "Therefore" means: because it reaches those who have entered the precinct boundary, and because it also reaches those who are connected as one unit with those who have entered the precinct boundary even beyond that; therefore.

*Tesanti upacārasīmāgatānaṃ, tato bahiddhā tehi saddhiṃ ekābaddhānañca.* "Of them" refers to those who have entered the precinct boundary and those who are connected as one unit with them beyond that. *Gāhate satīti* "When it is grasped" means:
"When there are those taking [the portion], such as resident pupils (antevāsika) and others.

"Even for those who have not arrived" means: even for those who have not reached the place where the distribution of gains occurs, but have entered the precinct boundary (upacārasīmā), or who stand at the door of their own monastery or within the monastery itself, being connected in a single unit with those [who have arrived] after the bell has been struck and the time announced by those standing within the precinct boundary.

The meaning is as follows: "A portion should be given" means that it should be given even to the most junior member of the Saṅgha; this is the intended sense. However, when the second portion has been assigned to the seat of the senior elder (therāsana), the first portion does not reach those who have arrived [later]. From the second portion, it should be given according to the number of years since ordination (vassaggena).
But if they say, "Give it to those standing outside the boundary of the precincts (upacārasīmā)," it should not be given. If, however, the monastery...

If there are many people, and while robes are being distributed starting from the seat of the senior elder (therāsana), the senior elders who are by nature indolent arrive late, one should not say, "Venerable sirs, [robes] for those of twenty years' standing are being given; your turn has passed.
Having set aside their turn, one should give them [their share] and afterwards give according to the established order of turns.
“Having heard that ‘much robe-cloth has arisen in such-and-such a monastery,’ monks come even from monasteries a league away;
it should be given starting from the very spot where each person arrives. This is the summary here.
The detailed explanation, however, is to be understood according to the method stated in the *Cīvarakkhandhaka-vaṇṇanā* of the *Samantapāsādikā*.”
Having thus entered the monastery and given [robes] with the words, "I give these robes to the Saṅgha," the determination has been stated.

Now, in order to show the determination regarding those given with the words, "I give them to the Saṅgha," after seeing a monk within the outer boundary (bahī-upacāra-sīmā), the passage beginning with "But that which...
is spoken. "It reaches a single continuous assembly" means if the assembly extends for a league (yojana).
If it is fixed and forms a single connected whole, it belongs to all; this is the meaning. And here, the state of being a single connected whole should be defined as being within twelve *hattha*s.
Therefore he said, "But those which... and so forth.
"Given to both Saṅghas" means given with the words, "I give to both Saṅghas. "I give to the twofold Saṅgha."
Even if it is said, “I give to two Saṅghas; I give to the Bhikkhu-saṅgha and the Bhikkhunī-saṅgha,” it is indeed given to both Saṅghas.
One half should be given to the Bhikkhus and one half to the Bhikkhunīs;
having made the two portions equal, one portion is to be given to the Bhikkhus and one portion to the Bhikkhunīs. To take [the gift]:...
The intention is that [the monk] obtains [the full ordination] because it is included within the mention of both Saṅghas. Regarding "of a cetiya": this refers to a stūpa and so forth.
For that is called a "cetiya" because it is piled up (*cita*) by way of being a receptacle for relics and the like, and because it is a place of veneration (*cittīkāra*) for the world.
He said, "But here, of a cetiya," and so on, to indicate that there is no distinction [between the two cases].
When it is said, “For both Saṅghas, for you, and for the cetiya,” one should divide [the property] into twenty-two portions:
ten to be given to the bhikkhus, ten to the bhikkhunīs, one to an individual (puggala), and one to the cetiya.

In that regard, an individual—even if they belong to the Saṅgha—is permitted to take back [their share] according to their own *vassa* (rainy-season retreat); however, for the cetiya, there is only one [share]. This, then, is the procedure.
It is not mentioned here because it is understood through the very method already stated; however, it is indeed mentioned in the *Samantapāsādikā*.
It should not be given by dividing it in the middle, because it is stated as being for an individual with the words "for the bhikkhunīs.
An individual does not receive [a separate portion] because, as before, they do not receive a separate individual share. From the place where it reaches, there is only one [share].
"He receives" means that he receives only a single portion from the place he would have obtained according to his own seniority.

Why? Because [the share] has already been included by the mention of the "Bhikkhu-saṅgha. Even when it is said, "For the Bhikkhu-saṅgha, for the Bhikkhunīs, for you, and for the Cetiya," the Cetiya receives one individual's share, but the individual does not receive a separate share. Therefore, having given one [share] to the Cetiya...
The remainder should be divided after counting the monks and the nuns. Therefore he said, “But when it is stated ‘and for the shrine,’ etc.

The inclusion of both the individual (puggala) and the shrine (cetiyaparāmasana) together with them is exactly like the immediately preceding method; that is to say, the taking up of both the individual and the shrine along with those monks and nuns is identical to the method just described. “And for the monks... [text continues]
Even when it is said, "Of the bhikkhunīs and of you; of the bhikkhus and of the bhikkhunīs and of the cetiya;
and of the bhikkhus and of the bhikkhunīs and of you and of the cetiya," a single share for the cetiya is obtained, while there is no separate [share] for the individual (puggala);
rather, it is stated that after counting both the bhikkhus and the bhikkhunīs, [the property] should be divided. As for the individual...

"It is not obtained separately" means that no separate portion for an individual is obtained; the meaning is that it is obtained as one by way of the *vassagga* (the distribution at the end of the rains retreat).
However, when it is said, "For the Saṅgha of bhikkhus and for the cetiya," a separate portion for the cetiya is obtained;
thus he says, "But for the cetiya it is obtained. Even when it is said, "For the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, for you, and for the cetiya," [it is understood accordingly].
It is obtained separately for the *cetiya* alone, not for the individual person.
However, since it is indeed obtained for the *cetiya*, when it is said, "for the bhikkhus and for the *cetiya*," the meaning is that a separate share is obtained for the *cetiya*.

Even when it is said, "for the bhikkhus, for you, and for the *cetiya*," it is obtained separately for the *cetiya* alone, not for the individual person. [The same applies to] the community of bhikkhunīs...
Taking this as the beginning, it should be applied in exactly the same way.

Here it is asked: "But when wise people nowadays, having established an image containing relics or a cetiya, give a gift to the Saṅgha of both sides headed by the Buddha; or when, in front of the image or the cetiya, on a stand..."

Having set out a cloth and given the water for the offering, saying, "We give to the Buddhas," if they first offer solid or soft food there, or bring it to the monastery saying, "We give this to the Cetiya," and offer alms-food, garlands, perfumes, and so forth—how should one proceed in that case?
It is said: first, the garlands, perfumes, and so forth should be offered upon the Cetiya.

Banners should be made with cloth, and lamps with oil. As for alms-food, honey, molasses, and so forth, they should be given to whichever person—whether a monastic or a layperson—is the designated caretaker of the shrine.

In the absence of a designated caretaker, it is permissible to set aside food that has been brought, perform the duties, and then consume it. Even when the time is drawing near [for the meal], it is likewise permissible to eat first and then perform the duties afterwards.
Regarding garlands, perfumes, and so forth, if it is said, "Take this and perform an offering at the shrine," one should carry it even a great distance and offer it.
Even if it is said, "Carry this for the Saṅgha of monks," it should be carried. However, if it is said, "I am going on almsround;
there are monks in the assembly hall, they will take it," and [the donor] says, "Venerable sir, I give it to you alone," [then it belongs to him].

He says, "It is permissible to eat. However, if one who is carrying it with the intention, "I will give this to the Saṅgha of bhikkhus," finds that the time has already arrived while on the way, it is permissible for him to take it for himself and eat it.

Regarding the phrase, "he says, 'I give these to the Saṅgha of those who have completed the rains residence'": it means, "I give these robes to the Saṅgha of those who have completed the rains residence."
He says: "It reaches even those who are outside the boundary. This means that when the kaṭhina has been spread, it reaches even those who are outside the boundary until the removal of the kaṭhina;
therefore, even for one who has gone abroad, the gift must be given provided there is a recipient.
However, when the kaṭhina has not been spread, within the winter season, having spoken thus, the gift also reaches one who has completed the subsequent rains residence.
"In any place whatsoever" means in any monasteries whatever. "He speaks thus" means he says, "I give this to the Saṅgha that has completed the rains residence.
In that case, it accrues to all those who were present, because it was offered at the conclusion of the rains.

However, if he says, "I give this to those dwelling for the rains," then only those who actually dwelt for the rains within the boundary receive it; those whose rains residence was interrupted do not.

They do not receive it. However, regarding the robe-month, when it is said, "I give to those dwelling for the rains," it accrues only to those who have entered the rains residence during the later period;
it does not accrue to those who entered during the earlier period nor to those whose rains residence has been interrupted.
From the start of the robe-month until the last day of the winter season, [if one says] "We are giving the *vassāvāsika* (rains-bathing robe),"...
Once it has been said, whether the kaṭhina has been spread or not, it accrues only to those who have completed the residence for the past rains.
However, from the first day of the summer months onwards, when it has been said, the following schedule must be set forth:
"Five months of the past rains-residence have passed; four months remain until the end of the future [rains]. To which rains-residence does this belong?"
If he says, "I give this to those who have completed the rains-residence of the past year," it accrues only to those who have actually completed the rains within that year;
however, even those who have departed for other regions may receive it if they are members of the same community.
If he says, "I give this as the *vassāvāsika* (rains-residence gift) for the future," it must be set aside and taken on the day of the formal entry into the rains-retreat (*vassūpanāyikā*).

Then, if it is said, "The dwelling is unprotected; there is danger from thieves; it is not possible to leave it, nor can one take it and wander about," and he says, "I give it to those who have arrived," it should be taken after being divided.

If he says, "Venerable sirs, I have not given my *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe-offering) for the third year from now; I give that," [it belongs] to the monks who have spent the rains retreat within that [period].
It accrues [to him]. If those who were invited have departed for their respective directions, another trustworthy person should take it;

it must be given to him. If only one remains and the others have passed away, everything accrues to that one alone. If not even one remains, it becomes the property of the Saṅgha and should be divided among those who are present.
"By whom the conjey was drunk" means by whichever monks the conjey was drunk when they were invited; however, as for those [who did not attend] due to the conduct of going on alms-round...
If gruel is obtained by those going to the door of the house or by those who have already entered the house;
or if it is brought for them from the dining hall after their bowls have been fetched and carried out by people; or if it has been sent by the elders—it does not reach them.
However, if many others besides the invited monks arrive and fill both the interior and exterior of the house...
While they are seated, the donor says, "Whether they were invited or uninvited, let these robes belong to all those to whom I gave rice-gruel.
It reaches everyone except for those who received the gruel from the hands of the elders.
Then he says, "Let it belong to all those by whom my gruel was drunk."
When he speaks, it reaches all of them. Regarding the phrase "with food, snacks, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes robes, lodgings, and medicines.
"To an individual" means to an individual who is either present or absent; thus he said, "This robe," and so on.
However, if he says, "I give this both to you and to your pupils," then for the Elder and...
It also reaches the resident pupils (*antevāsika*). There are those who have come to receive the recitation (*uddesa*) and those who depart after having received it; it reaches them as well.

When it is said, "I give this to the bhikkhus who travel in regular association with you," it reaches all those who, having performed the duties toward their recitation-pupils, travel about receiving recitations, cross-examinations (*paripucchā*), and so forth. "In this regard" means:
Regarding the eight matrices (mātikā): if this is a summary here, one might ask how the detailed exposition is to be known;
therefore he says, "It is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*. The meaning is that it is stated in the commentary on the Cīvara-khandhaka within the *Samantapāsādikā*.
[The thought is: "It has been sent for my robes by my relatives, or it has been sent by my friends; they will give me the robe once it has been brought."
Thus it should be understood that there is an expectation from either relatives or friends.
"With allowable goods" means with one's own wealth, such as cotton thread and so forth. "Fine" means delicate.

"Only after obtaining another expected robe should it be made within the time limit" means that only after obtaining another expected robe similar to the basic robe (*mūlacīvara*) should it be made within the month.

And that [waiting period] applies only when there is hope; however, if there is no hope, then even if the basic robe (*mūlacīvara*) has been obtained within ten days, it must be determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*) on that very day.

Therefore he said, "If one does not obtain it," and so forth. It is stated with reference even to a coarse robe of hope (*thūlapaccāsācīvara*) that arose earlier that a robe of equipment (*parikkhāracoḷa*) may also be determined. By the word "also" (*pi*), [this is indicated].
This shows that it is not only the basic robe [that is subject to this rule].
The commentary on the training rule concerning out-of-season robes is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Old Robes.
“Kinsman” (*ñāti*) means one who is known as “our own relative”; that very person is a kinsman, while one who is not a kinsman is a non-kinsman (*aññātika*);

[the phrase] “by that non-kinswoman” refers to her. Therefore he said, “not by a kinswoman. “From the mother’s side or from the father’s side” means from the maternal lineage or from the paternal lineage.
“As far as the seventh generation” means as far as the life-span of the seventh male or the seventh female. As far as...
The meaning is: "the generation of the grandfather, the generation of the grandmother, the generation of the maternal grandfather, and the generation of the maternal grandmother.

Alternatively, "up to the seventh generation" means "up to the seventh pair. Here, the word *yuga* (generation/pair) should be understood according to the principle of single-remainder (*ekasesa-naya*) as "the generation and the generation are [collectively] generations.
For it is in this way that a pair (*dvanda*) is grasped in various instances. In whatever manner...
"Unrelated" means unrelated in any way whatsoever to one's brother, sister, nephew, son, grandson, and so forth.
Likewise, "upwards" refers to the seventh generation, such as: father, grandfather, his father, and his father too;
and likewise: father, paternal grandmother, her father and mother, brother, sister, sons, and daughters.

And downwards as far as the seventh generation: the father, the father’s brother, the father’s sister, the father’s sons, and the father’s daughters, and their successive sons and daughters—thus even as far as the seventh generation;
the mother, the mother’s mother, her mother, and her mother also—thus as far as the seventh generation; the mother, the mother’s father, and his father and mother, and the brothers.
And sisters, sons, and daughters— likewise, upwards and downwards as far as the seventh generation:
mother, maternal uncle, maternal aunt, mother’s sons, and mother’s daughters, and the succession of their sons and daughters—
likewise, as far as the seventh generation, she who is not related by either the maternal or the paternal side, that [woman]...
“An unrelated woman” is what is meant.
“Like the Sākiyan women” means like the approximately five hundred Sākiyan women. This is merely an illustration;
therefore, even those nuns who have changed their gender while remaining in the state of a bhikkhu are here, within the pure Saṅgha of bhikkhus, simply called “fully ordained.”
It should be understood. "In both Saṅghas" means by a motion and third resolution (ñatticatuttha) in the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha and by a motion and third resolution in the Bhikkhu Saṅgha;
thus it is "in both Saṅghas. Regarding "old robe": here, "robe" is intended to mean only that which is suitable for wearing as an undergarment or an upper garment;

therefore he says "having dyed," and so forth. "Having made it allowable" means having applied a *kappa*-dot. [This refers to] the offense of expiation (pācittiya) for using what has not been made allowable.
They say, "He shows that it does not exist. "By way of enjoyment" means by way of enjoying [the bedding] after having touched it with the body.

"On the shoulder" means on the shoulder-blade. "On the head" means on the top of the head. However, if one lies down having placed [the bedding] beneath a coverlet, or if one lifts it up with the hands and moves about in the air without touching the head, making it like a canopy—[in such cases there is no offense].
This is not what is called "use.
"Or he makes a bodily gesture" means he makes a bodily gesture so that she knows, "He wishes to have it washed.
"Standing within a space of twelve cubits, he throws it upward"—by this, he releases the immediate vicinity.
It shows that there is no offense for one who throws it away. "Or sends it into the hand of another" means:

standing within a distance of twelve *hattha*s, he sends it into the hand of anyone else—whether a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*), a male novice (*sāmaṇera*), a female novice (*sāmaṇerī*), a lay follower (*upāsaka*), a woman, or anyone else.
"He" refers to both the lay follower and the male novice. "Having received [it], he washes it": here, the lay follower [is referred to] by his outward appearance (*liṅga*).

In the case of a change of gender, if one has gone forth and received full ordination (*upasampadā*) among the bhikkhunīs and then washes [the robe], or if a novice (*sāmaṇera*), having changed his gender,
receives full ordination among the bhikkhunīs and then washes it— the meaning should be understood accordingly as applicable. However, if it has been placed in the hands of a bhikkhunī,
and he washes it after changing his gender, it is permissible.

And here, because there is no relinquishing (*nissajjana*) three times for a single person, when one causes three [people] to act, there is an offense of relinquishment (*nissaggiya*) by one, and two offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) by the other two.
When one causes two [people] to act, there is an offense of relinquishment by one, and an offense of wrong-doing by the second.
Therefore he said, "the three beginning with washing," and so forth. The phrase "by means of one article" is stated with reference to that which was first made and brought to completion.

If, however, she is told, "Having dyed this robe-cloth and washed it, bring it," and that bhikkhunī washes it first and dyes it afterwards, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the offense of relinquishment (nissaggiya). In this same manner, the principle should be applied to all inverted instructions.
But if she is told, "Having washed it, bring it," and she both washes and dyes it, there is an offense only on account of causing it to be washed.
There is no offense regarding dyeing. This applies in all cases. Therefore he said, "But if she is told, 'Wash it,'" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the community of nuns," etc., he says this because for one who has her wash [a robe] on behalf of monks—those ordained together with her—it remains exactly as the original category (yathāvatthuka).
"Belonging to another" means the meaning is: for one who has her wash an old robe belonging to another. "A sitting mat and a rug."
It refers to both a sitting mat and a rug belonging either to another person or to oneself.

Since here the term "old robe" (*purāṇacīvara*) is intended specifically for what is suitable for use as an inner garment or an upper robe, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)—not an offense involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya*)—for one who has someone wash even a sitting mat or a rug that belongs to oneself.
Or, regarding the phrase "or she washes without being told": this refers to one who has come for the purpose of receiving instruction or for the purpose of exhortation.

Having seen a soiled robe, either taking it from where it was placed or having it brought after saying, "Give it here, venerable sir, I will wash it," she both washes, dyes, and beats it; this is called "washing without being told.
Also, when a monk has commanded a junior monk or a novice, saying, "Wash this robe," and [the woman], upon hearing the monk's words, says, "Bring it here, venerable sir..."
If she washes [the robe], thinking, "I shall wash it," or if she takes it for a limited time, washes it, dyes it, and then returns it—this too is called "washing without being told.
Or, regarding "another requisite": sandals, a bag for bowls, a shoulder strap, a waistband, a bed, a chair, a mat, and so forth.
“Whatever. Because of the statement, “having stood within the vicinity,” there is no offense even in sending [someone] to wash it. “Vicinity” means within a space of twelve cubits.
The commentary on the training rule regarding old robes is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule regarding the acceptance of robes.
“Among” means among the robes made of linen and other such materials. “Leaving aside the precinct” means leaving aside the twelve-fathom precinct.

By the word “and” (pi), it is implied that when he is preaching the Dhamma, the fourfold assembly brings robes and garments of various colors and places them at his feet, or stands within the precinct and hurls them upward; “if he consents,” [the offense is committed].
Regarding the phrase "it is indeed accepted," this shows that there is nothing at all to be said [against its validity]. "Let him throw it" means let him throw it either by day or during the night.
"It is indeed accepted" means that although it may not be possible to know, "This is for a bhikkhunī;
this is for others," nevertheless, it is considered accepted because it was taken without [specific] mental intention (*acittaka*). "But for anyone who is not fully ordained..."

"To anyone who is not fully ordained"—that is, to any among those such as a trainee nun (sikkhamānā), a novice monk (sāmaṇera), a novice nun (sāmaṇerī), a male lay follower (upāsaka), or a female lay follower (upāsikā).
"Set aside" means set aside by a bhikkhunī. "Having determined it to be a rag-robe" means having generated the perception that "this is ownerless," for what is ownerless is called a "rag-robe.
By this [phrase], one avoids the perception that "this was set aside for our sake," and so forth.
This shows that it is not permissible to accept [the gift]. "Except by way of exchange" (*aññatra pārivattakā*):

that which is to be exchanged is an "exchange" (*parivatta*); an exchange itself is "that which pertains to exchange" (*pārivattaka*). The meaning is: that which is given after having been exchanged. Therefore he said: "even down to a piece of a harīṭaka fruit," and so forth.
"Having made an intention" (*ābhogaṃ katvā*): having directed the mind. If a nun gives even a *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe), that too—
It should be understood that it is not permissible to accept [the robe] without performing the procedure as previously described.

"By acquisition" means by taking possession. "Threefold *pācittiya*" (*tikapācittiya*): it is called "threefold" (*tika*) because it has three measures; and since it is both threefold and an offense requiring expiation (*pācittiya*), it is a "threefold *pācittiya*.
This refers to the cases of one who perceives a non-relative as a relative, one who is doubtful, and one who perceives a non-relative as a non-relative.
The meaning is: three *pācittiya* offenses. "From one who is fully ordained on one side" means from one who has received full ordination in the presence of the bhikkhunīs;
for if one receives a robe in exchange from her hand or otherwise, it is a *dukkaṭa*, but if she is fully ordained in the presence of the bhikkhus, it is a *pācittiya*.
[This applies] "to alms-bowls, bags, and so forth, as well as to requisites that are not to be formally determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*)."

By this, the *bhisicchavi* (the inner bark of the *bhisī* plant) is also included. For although it is large, because it is comprised within the category of lodgings (*senāsana*), it does not count as a robe;
thus, it is neither subject to formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) nor subject to assignment (*vikappa*). Indeed, it is said in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
"Even if the *bhisicchavi* is the size of a bed, it is still permissible. [The text continues: "He receives the robe from the hand."

However, there is no offense in accepting what has been sent by an unrelated nun, provided it is done through verbal communication. Regarding acceptance and the absence of exchange, this is a "action-non-action" (kriyākiriya).
The commentary on the training rule concerning the acceptance of robes is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Solicitation by an Unrelated Person.
A *gahapati* is one who is the chief (*jeṭṭha*) among householders; that is a *gahapati*. Here, however, any person whatsoever who has not gone forth is intended.
Therefore he said: "among monks, [those] persons who have not gone forth. This same method applies here as well in the case of "housewives" (*gahapatānī*).
Regarding the word "should request" (*viññāpeyya*), since it functions both in the sense of a simple agent and in the sense of a causal agent, he said: "he should ask."
“...or should he cause [another] to ask? In this context, causing to ask should be understood as being for one’s own benefit.
By interpreting it in this way, the statement “it is not subject to an instruction (anāṇattika)” is justified. “Except at the proper time (aññatra samayā)”:

that in which beings meet, or where a phenomenon (dhamma) with its intrinsic nature (sabhāva) comes together with co-nascent factors (sahajāta) and so forth, or with arising (uppāda) and so forth, is the “proper time” (samaya); it refers to time, insofar as it is merely the occurrence of phenomena.
For although time is not real in its own essence (*atthato*), it serves as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for the occurrence of phenomena;

and like an instrument (*karaṇa*), it is expressed by means of a form established through mere conceptual construction (*kappanāmatta*). The meaning is: "having set aside that occasion. Therefore he said: "one whose robe has been stolen," and so forth.
Therein, one whose robe has been stolen by anyone among kings and others is "one whose robe has been stolen" (*acchinnacīvaro*). As it is said: "one whose robe has been stolen..."
“...the robe of a bhikkhu has been snatched away—snatched away by kings, or by thieves, or by rogues, or by anyone at all.
One whose robe has been lost among fires and the like by any such means is called “one whose robe is lost.
As it is said: “One whose robe is lost is a bhikkhu whose robe has been burnt by fire, or destroyed by water...”
"It has been carried away, or it has been gnawed by rats or termites, or it is worn out through use.
Regarding the term "samayā," he says "on that occasion" (*taṃ samayaṃ*), because it is an ablative expression used in the sense of the accusative with reference to the word "elsewhere" (*aññatra*).
"Elsewhere" means at another time.
“Three *pācittiya*s” refers to three *pācittiya* offenses according to whether one perceives a person as unrelated, is in doubt, or perceives them as related.
“At the proper time” means during the times already mentioned: when robes have been stolen or when robes have been lost.
“Or if he asks one who is related or invited” means if he requests from a relative or one who has been invited, saying, “Give me your blanket. Herein...
When the invitation (*pavāraṇā*) is performed on behalf of the Saṅgha, it is proper to request only the standard measure;

however, when the invitation is performed for an individual, one may ask for whatever they offer. For indeed, one who has invited [the Saṅgha] with the four requisites and, having personally observed their needs, gives robes and so forth from time to time, and daily food such as rice-gruel and meals—by such means, he...

Whatever is needed, that he gives; for him, there is no need to request anything. However, if one who has invited [guests] does not give due to foolishness or through loss of mindfulness, he should be requested.
As for one who says, "I invite you to my house," having gone to his house, one may sit or lie down as is comfortable, but nothing should be taken. As for one who...
However, if one says, "I invite you to whatever is in my house," then one should request whatever therein is allowable.
But it is not permitted to sit or lie down in that house.
"For his sake" means for the sake of that very person—Buddharakkhita or Dhammarakkhita—who has acquired the conventional designation of "another. "Of one taking with his own wealth" means...
The meaning is: for one who takes, causes to be taken, or causes to be exchanged [for goods] using only his own allowable articles and by means of allowable speech.
The commentary on the training rule concerning requesting from an unrelated person is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning exceeding [the limit].
In this context, the word *taṃ* expresses the sense of what has been mentioned (*pakatattavacana*). *Ce* is merely a particle (*nipātamattaṃ*). Alternatively, *ce* means “if”;
its connection should be understood with the word “*pavāreyya*” (should invite). Thus, “*pavāreyya ce*” means “if one should invite.
By the statement “*abhi* is a prefix,” he shows that it lacks any specific meaning of its own. Therefore he says: “the meaning is ‘to bring’ (*harituṃ*). [This refers to] the word *pavāra*.
Because it is currently existing, it is stated as “he would desire. “He would arouse desire” means he would arouse desire for the requisite.
This is a designation for an invitation. Therefore he said, “as much as,” and so forth. “Renunciation” (nekkhamma) means the going-forth (pabbajjā). “To see” (daṭṭhū) means for the purpose of seeing;
here the nasal vowel is elided for the sake of preserving the meter. “From safety” (khemato) means from fearlessness.
The connection is: "having approached with body or speech, one should invite.

To show the manner in which one would approach with body and speech, the words beginning with "having brought near" (*upanetvā*) are stated. "With the inner garment" (*saantaraṃ*) means together with the *antaravāsaka*.
"The upper [robe]" (*uttaraṃ*) means the *uttarāsaṅga*. "The outermost" (*paramaṃ*) means the end. "Of this robe" (*assa cīvarassa*) refers to this collection [of robes] as a whole.

[This refers to] a robe that is to be dyed. For this is an external compound (bāhiratthasamāsa) based on the recognition of its specific quality, which should be understood as in the case of the term "lambakaṇṇo" (long-eared).
Therefore, he said, "with the lower robe," and so forth. For according to the highest limit, all [monks] are permitted to take only that as the maximum.
Since a monk—even one who possesses no robes at all, or one who has only the three robes—must act in this manner, [the rule applies] by means of another...
However, since there is also another way [of classifying], the words "In this regard, this is the analysis" and so forth were spoken in order to show that distinction.

"Of one who has determined a robe" means of one who has determined a robe by way of the method of determining the three robes (*ticīvara*), or by way of requisites-cloth (*parikkhāracoḷa*), or by any other means;
and this is stated with reference to one who generally uses a robe after having determined it, but not for one who uses an undetermined robe.

This procedure does not apply when a robe has not been stolen. Or, for one who has an extra robe elsewhere besides his set of three robes, it is permissible for him to accept two [robes] there at that time because they are currently absent from that place.

He "normally lives with only the inner and upper robes" either because the kaṭhina has been spread, or by virtue of the training rule concerning dangerous places, or by virtue of the formal authorization for non-separation from the robes.
Or he lives by not obtaining a third. Because the context concerns "two lost items," it is said: "two may be consented to.

By consenting to one [when two are lost], one will be equal [to another who has lost both]; for even when two of the three robes are lost, one who consents to one will be equal to one who has lost both, since both abide in the state of having at most an inner and an outer robe (*santaruttara*). This applies to one who has only one [robe remaining].
Because the remaining robes have been lost for some other reason.
Regarding "when five are lost": this refers to when these five robes—the three robes, the rain-bath cloth, and the undershirt—are lost.
The phrase "or when one is lost" should be applied by adapting the wording accordingly. "Beyond that" means beyond the limit of the inner and outer robes (*santaruttara*).
"Thinking, 'I will bring the remainder,' he makes two robes"—the meaning is: "I will bring the remainder again.
Regarding the phrase "let the remainder be yours alone," it refers to what was said at the very time of the gift.
However, if, after saying "I will bring the remainder," they say "let the remainder be yours alone" even at the time of taking it and departing, it is indeed permissible to receive it.
"Given for reasons other than being cut off or lost" means given on account of qualities such as great learning (*bāhusacca*). "In the manner stated" refers to the manner described in the passage:

"when one requests [food] from someone who has been invited by a relative, or when one requests it at the proper time from someone else who has been invited by that same relative, for the sake of that person.
The commentary on the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) concerning what is more than that is finished.
8. Commentary on the First *Upakkhaṭa* Training Rule (*Sikkhāpada*).
Regarding the phrase "but having designated a monk" (*bhikkhuṃ paneva uddissa*): here, *pana* is merely a particle, as is the word *eva*. Therefore he said, "of such-and-such a person," and so forth.

"Having designated" (*apadisitvā*) means having spoken of, or else it means "having taken as a basis. "Of an unrelated householder" (*aññātakassa gahapatissa*) means "of an unrelated householder's wife" (*aññātakagahapatiniyā*).
This is the meaning. For this genitive case is used here in the sense of the instrumental. However, it was not investigated in the Commentary because it is easily understood.
It is called *cīvaracetāpanna* because one obtains or exchanges robes by means of it; it is the price for robes (*cīvaramūla*).
Here, however, the letter *-n-* is an augment; they also read it as *cīvaracetāpana*. Since that [price] consists of one or another of the items such as gold and so forth, [it is so designated].
Therefore, it is said: "gold and so forth. In this context, "gold" (*hirañña*) refers to a *kahāpaṇa* coin.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), gold and other such items are included. "Set out" (*upakkhaṭa*) means prepared. He says, "it is set out;
that is, it is prepared," meaning that which has been arranged for them in that manner. "Placed together" means placed having been made into a heap. And "exchange" (*parivattana*)...
Regarding the phrase "having it made by one who has not done it" and "buying what has been made," he says: "The meaning is 'either having had it made or having bought it.

"I will clothe myself" means "I will wear it. Therefore he says: "This is a figurative expression (*vohāra-vacana*). And the meaning of "figurative expression" is "metaphorical expression (*upacāra-vacana*).
To the question, "What is the syntactical connection (*pada-sambandha*) in such passages as 'If that monk there'? he replies: "'Wherever that householder... and so forth.
“Not previously invited”: one who has not been told beforehand, “I shall give; Venerable Sir, what kind of robe-cloth do you need?
What kind of robe-cloth shall I have purchased for you? “Having approached”: having gone.
In the word-commentary, it is stated as “having gone to the house” by way of common parlance. And here, “by way of common parlance” means by way of the most frequent usage. For the most part...

For it is common usage that those desiring to see the master of the house go to his house; such is the frequent expression. "Vikappa" means a distinguished (vi-) arrangement (kappa); here the prefix *vi-* has the sense of distinction. Therefore he said, "a distinguished arrangement. By this, he states the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*). By "an additional specification" (*adhikavidhāna*), however, he states the intended meaning (*adhippāyattha*). And as to how one comes to incur [that offense]: *hi gharasāmikaṃ daṭṭhukāmā tassa gharaṃ gacchantīti tatheva bahulavohāro. Vikappanti visiṭṭho kappo vikappo, vi-saddo cettha visiṭṭhattho. Tenāha “visiṭṭhakappa”nti. Iminā vacanatthamāha. “Adhikavidhāna”nti iminā pana adhippāyatthaṃ. Yathā pana tamāpajjatīti* For it is common usage that those desiring to see the master of the house go to his house; such is the frequent expression. "Vikappa" means a distinguished (*vi-*) arrangement (*kappa*);

here the prefix *vi-* has the sense of distinction. Therefore he said, "a distinguished arrangement. By this, he states the etymological meaning (*vacanattha*). By "an additional specification" (*adhikavidhāna*), however, he states the intended meaning (*adhippāyattha*). And as to how one comes to incur [that offense]:
"In order to show the manner in which one enters into that conceptualization" means to show that mode.
This word "sādhu" is seen in the senses of acceptance, encouragement, beauty, entreaty, and so forth. For instance, it appears in such passages as:
"‘Very well, venerable sir,’ said that bhikkhu, having rejoiced and expressed his appreciation for the Blessed One’s words. Etc.
It is seen in the sense of acceptance, as in “Excellent, excellent, Sāriputta! and so forth; and in the sense of encouragement, as in:
“Excellent is King Dhammaruci; excellent is the man possessed of wisdom;
excellent is the non-betrayal of friends; the non-doing of evil is bliss. And so on.
In such passages as “Sundara, ‘It would be well, Bhante, if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief,’” it is used in the sense of a request;
here too, it should be understood as being used precisely in the sense of a request. Thus he says: “‘Sādhu’ is a particle used in requesting.
In that context, “in requesting” means in a direct entreaty; the meaning is “in making a longing wish. It is connected [with the phrase] “a particle used in reflection. “Ālapati” means he addresses.
Regarding the phrase "in long [speech], etc.": here, by the word "etc.," there is the inclusion of "extended," "protracted," and "soft.
