However, since an offense does not reach its head (become finalized) merely by the commission of this act, it is therefore stated: "by his speech," and so forth. Regarding "the preliminary effort":
this refers to the effort such as searching for the Sutta, and so on.
"Desiring to have something of great value purchased when [the other] says it is of little value":
this means that one who desires to have a robe worth twenty [units] purchased, says, "I have no need for that; give me one worth ten or eight [units].
"Of such a kind" means of equal value; by this, it is stated that it is "equal. And that is indeed in terms of value alone, not in terms of size.
For this training rule is for the purpose of increasing value.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning what has been set aside is finished.
9. Commentary on the second training rule concerning what has been set aside.

He says, "For this reason," and so forth, to show why the meaning should be understood according to this method. The particle *hi* is used in the sense of a reason. He says, "merely," and so forth, to indicate that there is no distinction [between the two cases].
The commentary on the second offense involving preparation is finished.
10. Commentary on the King’s Offense (Rājasikkhāpada).
“Enjoyment from the king” means enjoyment obtained from the king. “Royal enjoyment” (rājabhoga) refers to a royal official. “Benefit from the king” means sovereignty granted by the king.

“With this,” and so forth, refers to the following: “Having purchased a robe with this robe-fund, clothe the bhikkhu named so-and-so with the robe. “Purity of origin” means purity of the source. For if, with this...
If, instead of sending it by means of a permissible delivery, one were to send it saying, "Give this to the bhikkhu named so-and-so," and that messenger,
having approached that bhikkhu, were to say, "Venerable sir, this robe-fund has been brought for the sake of the venerable one;
may the venerable one accept the robe-fund," then even after [the bhikkhu] has refused it, he may [instruct] a person who makes things permissible (*kappiyakāraka*).
When asked, it is not permissible to point that out. Therefore he said, "If," and so forth.

"With reference to an improper object" means with reference to gold and so on. "By such a messenger's speech" means by a messenger's speech of this kind: "May the venerable one accept the purchase-price for a robe.
"Therefore" means because it is improper to accept; therefore. "Gold" means...
Jātarūpa means gold. Rajata means silver. "By means of a kahāpaṇa" refers to a kahāpaṇa made of gold, or made of silver, or an ordinary [copper] kahāpaṇa.
A "māsaka" may be a copper māsaka, or a wooden māsaka, or a lac māsaka—whatever serves as a medium of exchange in whatever region at whatever time—even down to one made of bone or made of leather.
Everything made of tree-fruit seeds—whether it is produced matter or unproduced matter—is to be understood here as a *māsaka*.
Regarding this, whatever needs to be said will be explained under the *Rūpiya-sikkhāpada* (the training rule on money).
"Pearls" refers to the eight kinds of pearls, such as those from elephant frontal globes and so forth; for it is said: "The elephant’s frontal globe, the boar’s tusk..."
There are eight sources of pearls: the serpent’s head, the cloud, the bamboo, the fish-head, the conch, and the oyster.
Among these, those produced from fish, conchs, and oysters are oceanic; some produced from serpents are also oceanic. The others are non-oceanic.
However, since oceanic pearls are mostly seen in the world—and even among those, primarily those from oysters—the others appear only occasionally.
Therefore, in the *Sammohavinodanī*, it is stated: "Pearls" means pearls from the ocean.

Regarding "gems," with the exception of beryl and so forth, all other gems—including even those made of *jātiphalika*—should be understood as "gems," regardless of their various colors such as blue, yellow, and so on.
However, a glass gem (*kācamaṇi*) made by heating is permitted only for the purpose of accepting it as the price for items such as bowls. Beryl...
The "name-gem" (nāma-vaṃsavaṇṇa-maṇi). Regarding the "conch": a conch from a vein (*dhamana-saṅkha*) that has been polished and bored, mixed with jewels;
however, a water-conch (*pānīya-saṅkha*) is not mixed with jewels. It is permissible to accept it for the purpose of medicinal ointments such as collyrium, or for the purpose of merchandise.
Regarding the "stone" (*sila*): a stone the color of a mung bean (*mugga*), polished, bored, and joined with jewels. However, one that is not mixed with jewels—
It is permissible to accept [these items] for the purpose of making knives, needles, and so forth.
Regarding this, they say that "connected with gems" means those made by joining and melting together with gold. *Pavāḷa* refers to all coral, whether polished or unpolished.
*Lohitaṅka* is a red gem. *Masāragalla* is a variegated gem, which is also called *marakata* (emerald).

"Seven grains" refers to the seven grains beginning with rice (*śāli*), together with their corresponding by-products. As for the minor grains such as wild rice (*nīvāra*) and so forth, they are included within the primary grains beginning with rice;

therefore, it is said "seven grains. Regarding "female and male slaves, fields, lands, flower gardens, and fruit gardens," here a female slave (*dāsī*) is classified as one born in the household, one purchased with wealth, one won in war, or one brought as a captive. Male slaves (*dāsa*) are likewise. A field (*khetta*) is that in which the first crop [is grown].
It grows. "Site" (*vatthu*) refers to that upon which secondary crops grow; or, where both [primary and secondary crops] grow, that is a field (*khetta*).
Land not yet prepared for such purposes is a site. And here, by the terms "field" and "site," things such as planted ponds are also included.
A flower garden is one where jasmine and other flowers bloom. A fruit garden is one where mango fruits and the like ripen. And it is not only...
It is not permissible to accept [gold and silver] for one's own sake; even if someone brings gold and silver and says, "I give this to the Saṅgha;
use it to build a monastery, or a shrine, or any one of the dining halls and so forth," it is still not permissible to accept it.
For if one accepts it for the sake of anyone else whatsoever—
“It is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa),” as stated in the Mahāpaccarī. Therefore he said:
“It is not permissible to accept [money] for the sake of a cetiya, the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
However, if one does not specify the Saṅgha, the group, or the individual, but says, “This gold and silver is for the cetiya...”
If they say, "We give for the monastery; we give for the new construction," it is not permissible to refuse.

One should inform the stewards (kappiyakāraka), saying, "They are saying this. However, if they say, "Please accept these for the sake of the shrine (cetiyā) and so forth," one should refuse, saying, "It is not permissible for us to accept them."

“Veyyāvaccakaro” means one who performs services. Here, however, since every one who performs services is intended by the term “veyyāvaccakaro,” he says “one who prepares what is allowable” (kappiyakārako).
“Eso kho” means he speaks in the absence [of the person], saying, “In such-and-such a street, in such-and-such a house, there is one named so-and-so.
“Itarampi” means even that which is not pointed out in their absence. “I have need of a robe, friend”—this is an illustration of the characteristic of the formal request (codanā).

The connection [is as follows]: therein, "the demonstration of the characteristic of an exhortation" means the demonstration of the characteristic of an exhortation by means of speech. Therefore he said, "If indeed," and so forth. Or, the connection is that this statement should be spoken;
or, the connection is that its meaning may be expressed in any language whatsoever. "Give me a robe; bring me a robe; exchange it for me..."
"Bring me a robe," or "Exchange [something] for a robe for me"—these words, or their meaning, must not be expressed in any language whatsoever.
Therefore he said, "Give me," and so forth. *Sādheyya* means "should accomplish. Thus, this is wholesome (*kusala*):
that accomplishment of the robe through such urging up to the third time is wholesome and excellent.
The meaning is "well. Therefore he said, "this is beautiful.
"Having six times as the maximum limit" means that which has six times as its ultimate boundary. This is indeed a qualification of the action expressed by the word "should stand";
the meaning is that a standing with six times as the maximum limit should be performed. Therefore he said, "this is a neuter noun in the instrumental case."

The meaning is that when it is said, "One should stand in this state," it is in the neuter gender and number because the mere sense of the verbal root (dhātu) as previously stated is to be accomplished.
"One should not sit" means that one should not sit even when addressed with, "Venerable sir, please sit here.
"One should not accept food" means that one should not accept any kind of food, such as rice gruel or solid snacks, even when entreated with, "Venerable sir, please take this."
One should not accept it. One should not speak the Dhamma means that even when requested, saying, “Please speak a blessing or an expression of appreciation,” one should not say anything at all.
“He destroys the standing place” means he ruins his position. For one who has come to receive the robe, he must indeed stand silently for that purpose;
he should not sit down or perform other such actions. By this, however, [it is implied]:
"Katam" means a place has been destroyed. Therefore he said, "He destroys the reason for having come. "The reason for having come" refers to the very place itself;

thus, the intended meaning here is that because one has performed what was forbidden by saying "it should not be done," one destroys one of the six places when sitting or other such actions are performed among those six places. Up to six times, remaining silent, with reference to...
One must stand. For this—“nothing else whatsoever should be done”—is the defining characteristic of standing. That is why he said, “this,” and so forth.
Therein, “this” refers to the statement: “one should stand silently, designated [for alms], four times, five times, or at most six times.
And here, it means that once the sitting and other such acts have been performed, one is no longer permitted to take up the robe again.
Some say: "Two grounds are forfeited. Others say: "One ground is forfeited. He both prosecutes and remains;
he prosecutes by saying, "He stands in this or that place.

This statement regarding "standing in this or that place" refers specifically to the act of standing for the sake of the robe, having moved away from the various places where the accuser himself stood. "In these" means in these two grounds of accusation.
But should one act in this same manner toward all who perform services that are allowable (*kappiyakāraka*)?

One should not. For this so-called "allowable-maker" is briefly indicated as being of two kinds: the designated (*niddiṭṭha*) and the undesignated (*aniddiṭṭha*). Therein, the designated is of two types:
designated by a monk and designated by a messenger. The undesignated is also of two types: the allowable-maker who is a mouth-coverer (*mukhavevaṭika*), and...

"An agent of what is allowable in the absence [of the monk]. Among these, that which is designated by a monk is fourfold, according to whether it is done in the presence or in the absence [of the recipient];
likewise for that which is designated by a messenger.
How so? Here, someone sends an unallowable thing by messenger for the sake of a monk's robe-cloth, and the messenger—
Having approached that bhikkhu, he says, "Venerable sir, this has been sent for you by such-and-such a person for the purpose of robe-cloth;
please accept it. The bhikkhu refuses, saying, "This is not allowable.
The messenger asks, "But, venerable sir, do you have anyone to perform services for you? And by lay followers seeking merit, service for the bhikkhus [is provided].
Whether they have been commanded, "Do this," or whether there are certain attendants who are either personally known or associated with the monks,
if at that moment one of them is sitting near the monk, the monk points him out, saying,
"This person is the attendant for the monks. The messenger, having placed an unallowable object in his hand, says, "To the Elder..."
If he goes [to the donor] saying, "Buy a robe and give it," this is one designated in the presence of the monk.
If he is not sitting in the presence of the monk, yet the monk designates him, saying, "In such-and-such a village,
there is a person named so-and-so who is a service-provider for monks," then [the messenger], having gone, [gives] an improper article into his hand.
Having given [the money] and said, "You should buy a robe for the elder and give it to him," the messenger returns, informs the bhikkhu, and departs;
this is one case where the messenger has not been designated by the bhikkhu in his presence.
Furthermore, that messenger does not return himself to inform [the bhikkhu], but rather sends another, saying, "It has been given by me."
“Venerable sir, please accept the robe-fund in his hand for the sake of a robe”—this is the second case of a person designated by a monk who is not present.
Furthermore, he does not send another, but while going himself, he says to a monk, “I will give a robe-fund in his hand;
you may accept the robe”—this is the third case of a person designated by a monk who is not present.
Thus, one who has been designated in person and three who have not been designated in person—these four are called "appointed attendants" by a bhikkhu.
Regarding these, one should proceed according to the method stated in this very training rule for kings.
Another bhikkhu, having been questioned by a messenger in the same manner as before, [says], due to their absence or because he does not wish to investigate: "We do not have..."
If he says, "I am the one who makes it allowable," and at that moment some person arrives,
the messenger gives the unallowable object into that person's hand and departs after saying, "You may receive the robe-cloth from this person's hand"—
this is one designated by the messenger in the presence [of the monk].
Another messenger, having entered a village, gives an improper object into the hand of someone he chooses;
then, returning by the same method as before, he either reports it himself or sends another, saying, "I shall give the cloth-fund into the hand of such-and-such a person;
you should accept the robe," and then departs—this is the third [offense].
"By messenger, not designated in person": thus, one is designated in person and three are not designated in person;
these four are called messengers-designated attendants (*veyyāvaccakara*). Regarding them, one should proceed according to the method stated in the Meṇḍaka-sikkhāpada.
For this has been said:
“Bhikkhus, there are people who have faith and confidence;
they place gold in the hands of those who prepare what is allowable [for monks], saying, ‘With this, give whatever is allowable to the noble one.
I allow you, bhikkhus, to accept from that whatever is allowable, but by no means, bhikkhus, should gold or silver be accepted in any way whatsoever.”
"I say it must be sought after.
And here, there is no limit to the number of times one may be urged.

If the owner does not give it, even if one has been urged a thousand times or has stood [waiting] a thousand times, it is permissible for one who has not accepted the original gift to accept a suitable article from another person acting as a steward (*kappiyakāraka*). If he still does not give it, [one may seek it further].
It should be caused to be brought. If he so desires, it should be told even to the original owners. If he does not desire it, it should not be told.
Another monk, having been questioned by a messenger in the same manner as before, says, "We have no one who prepares what is allowable.
Then another person standing nearby hears this and says, "Bring it, sir; I will purchase a robe for the venerable one and give it to him."
He speaks. A messenger, saying "Come now, sir, you should give it," places the item in the man's hand and departs without informing the bhikkhu;
this is one who acts as a "mouth-protector" kappiyakāraka.
Another [type] gives an unallowable object into the hand of a bhikkhu’s attendant or someone else, [saying] "To the Elder..."
“...you should give me a robe”—if he departs after saying just this, he is a “kappiyakāraka by proxy. These two are called “unspecified kappiyakārakas.
One should deal with them as one would with unrelated persons who have not been invited.
If they themselves bring a robe and offer it, it may be accepted; if not, nothing should be said. Therefore he said:
“*Sace*,” etc. “*Kappiyakārake*” means there are four types of *kappiyakāraka*s (those who make things allowable) based on whether they are present or absent.
By the phrase “the donor himself,” he excludes the monk, not the messenger. Therefore, even one designated by a messenger may be urged according to his own preference.
Having opened his mouth, he has himself entered into the state of being a *kappiyakāraka*.
The one who makes the mouth-cleanser allowable. "In this way" means by the manner already described, beginning with "This indeed...
The intention is that they are shown in brief.
"From the measure of the stated objections and the measure of the stated points" means both from the measure of the objections stated and from the measure of the points stated.
"Santikanti" means "nearby. Regarding the phrase "therein" (*tattha*), one might ask how this meaning is obtained; thus he says: "For this is a locative expression used in the sense of proximity.

This is what is meant: because this seventh-case (locative) ending is used here in the sense of a proximate locus—just as in such examples as "herds of cows graze by the Ganges" (*gaṅgāyaṃ goyūthāni caranti*) or "Gagga's bank at the well" (*kūpe gaggakūla*)—therefore this meaning is obtained. Thus...
"Not going" means either not going oneself or not sending a messenger.
"Venerable sir, please wait until tomorrow," means: "Venerable sir, stay with us for one day today; please consent.

"Three *pācittiya* offenses" refers to [the offenses incurred by] those who perceive it as more than the limit, those who are in doubt regarding it being more than the limit, and those who perceive it as less than the limit, in the three instances of urging [a monk to leave].

There are three *pācittiya* offenses according to the [number of] times. There is no offense even if [the matter] is obtained through three admonitions and six standings, or through fewer than three admonitions and fewer than six standings.
"Appitattā" means "having been established," which is to say, it has been stated by saying, "He has been conciliated by me," and so forth.
The commentary on the training rule concerning kings is finished.
The first section, on robes, is concluded.
2. The section on wool.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Silk (Kosiyasikkhāpada).
"Mixed with silk" (kosiyamissaka): Silk (kosiya) is the thread produced from the cocoons of those creatures commonly known as "silk-makers.
That which is mixed with this is "mixed with silk. Furthermore, even if it is mixed with only a small amount of that silk, it is indeed "mixed with silk."
It cannot be said that this is not a formal expression (abbohārika). Therefore, he said, "even by one," and so forth. "By silk thread" means by a thread produced from the cocoons of silkworms.
Furthermore, the phrase beginning with "at least" is stated because this training rule (sikkhāpada) is unintentional (acittaka).
"A rug" (santhataṃ) means what is made by spreading out [materials), not woven. Therefore, he said, "on a level patch of ground," and so forth. Of this very statement...
"According to the sequence" means according to the sequence of the rules for relinquishing this very first spread.
"All spreads" refers to the rule for relinquishing all spreads.
It is called the "sāṇattika" (rule concerning hemp) by way of having it made for one's own sake, because there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in having it made for the sake of another.

Regarding the method of completing what has been left unfinished by oneself: "If one completes by oneself what was left unfinished by oneself, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*).
If one has another complete what was left unfinished by oneself, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If one completes by oneself what was left unfinished by another, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. If one has another complete what was left unfinished by another..."

“...finishes [the work], there is an offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya)” — according to this method. Regarding “making canopies and so forth”: this refers to making canopies, floor-coverings, screens, walls, mattresses, and pillows.

Just as there is no offense in making canopies and so forth, likewise there is no offense in using them in that manner. Because it is stated as “not woven,” there is also no offense for one who makes it after having woven it.
The commentary on the training rule concerning silk (*kosiya*) is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning purely black [wool]:
"Black" means black by nature or black by dyeing. As it is said: "Black wool is of two kinds."
“Black by nature, or black from dye. The phrase “unmixed with others” means “black that is not mixed with anything else.

Just as it was stated in the first case, “even with a single thread of *kosiya* silk,” so too here, since it is not stated “without mixing it even with a single other [color],” they say that even when mixed with another, if the distinct form [of the other] is not discernible, it is still called simply “pure black.”
And here, the procedure for relinquishment should be understood by means of the passage beginning, “Venerable sir, this is my rug made of pure black wool,” and so forth.
The rest refers to the previous application, the fourfold *dukkaṭa*, the *pācittiya*, and so on. Among the constituent factors, however, the distinction is this: “the state of being pure black.
The commentary on the training rule regarding pure black [wool] is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Two Parts (*Dvebhāgasikkhāpada*) "Should be taken" means they should be taken in such a way that the black hairs do not predominate.

Here, it should be understood that, setting aside the black and white hairs, the remainder are included only among those that are "cow-like" (*gocariya*). And in this context, "two parts" is the maximum limit.
Because the training rule was laid down by way of prohibiting the taking of more than [the prescribed amount] of black wool. Therefore, it is not permitted to have more than two parts of black wool;
less than that is permitted. Thus he said, "Even of one," and so forth.
"In the state of being in excess even of a single black hair" means: when [wool] has been weighed and set aside on a scale, even if it is moved by the force of the wind.

The meaning is: "when there is even a single black hair in excess. However, the statement, "The third [portion] for white hairs, the fourth for those from the cow-pen," is the lower limit, because there is no prohibition against taking more than that. Therefore, even more than the stated measure is permitted for them.
And here: "Venerable Sir, this rug of mine was made without using two *tulās* of pure black wool..."

The procedure for relinquishment (nissajjana-vidhāna) is to be understood according to this method: "A rug made of white wool, a rug made of cow-hair, or a rug having both, having had it made, is to be relinquished.
Furthermore, it is a "both-action-and-non-action" offense because it is committed by taking [the materials] within the prescribed limit and by making it even without taking them.
The "remainder" refers to the preceding preliminary effort, the fourfold *dukkaṭa*, the *pācittiya*, and so forth. However, this is the distinction: "a rug of one *tula* of white wool..."

There is no offense in making [a robe] by taking an equal amount of black [wool] and wild (gocariya) [wool]; nor in making it by taking a greater amount of white [wool] and a greater amount of wild [wool];
nor in making it by taking pure white [wool] and pure wild [wool].
Regarding the factors, however, the first factor should be understood as being more than two parts of black [wool]. These three...
He says, "But these," and so forth, to show that it is not only those things not relinquished that are not permitted to be used.
By the phrase "it is not permitted to use them," he indicates that if one uses them, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
The commentary on the training rule concerning the two parts is finished.
4. Commentary on the Six Rules Concerning the Rains Retreat (Chabbassasikkhāpada).
"He who grants permission for a rug" is the connection [of the sentence].
"For a sick bhikkhu" means for a bhikkhu who is ill such that he is not comfortable without a rug and is unable to depart taking a rug with him; for a sick bhikkhu of such a nature.

"He grants permission for a rug" means: he grants permission for a rug by means of the formal act consisting of a motion and a second (ñattidutiyakammavācā) as stated in the word-commentary, beginning with: "Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs; this monk named so-and-so is ill and is unable to depart taking his rug with him."
This is the agreement regarding what has been spread out (*santhatasammuti*). "Or, having subsided, it may recur" means that even if that illness has subsided, it may recur;
it is permissible to perform [the act] every year, and the intention is that there is no need to repeat the formal granting of the agreement.
This applies not only when that same disease recurs, but also when another disease recurs; in each place one goes, it is permissible every year.
One is permitted to do so. For it is for this very reason that the Elder Phussadeva stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*:

"If, having recovered, one becomes ill again with the same original disease, that same exemption applies; there is no other 'formal act of convention' (*sammutikicca*) required. However, the Elder Upatissa said:
"Whether that same disease recurs or another arises, once the name 'sick person' has been acquired," [the exemption remains].
The statement of the Elder Upatissa, spoken later, says: "It was indeed obtained; however, he said again, 'There is no need for a formal authorization (sammuti-kicca).

In this context, the procedure for relinquishment (nissajjana-vidhāna) should be understood according to this method: "Venerable Sir, this rug (santhata) was made by me less than six years ago, except by means of the monks' authorization; it is to be relinquished. "The remainder is exactly like the first [case]."
By this, the passage beginning with “one who has done it oneself has it finished by others” is extended [by analogy]. However, this is the distinction:
there is no offense if six years or more than six years have elapsed. And the difference lies in the inclusion of the six-year period within the factors [of the offense].
The commentary on the training rule on the six years is concluded.

5. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Sitting Mat (Nisīdana-sikkhāpada) Regarding the phrase "a sitting mat spread out" (*nisīdana-santhatam*): because it is stated in the word-analysis (*padabhājaniya*) that "a 'sitting mat' (*nisīdana*) is called [a cloth] together with its border," it refers to a spread-out cloth with its border.
Furthermore, the inclusion of the term "sitting mat" here is for the purpose of preventing the notion of it being a robe (*cīvara*) regarding such a spread-out cloth; for...
Those bhikkhus, perceiving it as a woolen robe (*kambalacīvara*), discarded the spread (*santhata*) and undertook the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*).

Because the spread serves the purpose of bedding and seating, it is said: "An old spread," and so forth. "In which" means in which spread. "The measure of a span" (*vidatthimatta*) means the measure of a Sugata-span.
And this is the upper limit; there is no offense if, not obtaining [a full one], one takes a smaller amount.
Because it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) as "he makes. "In one part" means in a single portion of the new mat that is now to be made.

"Having unraveled" means having destroyed [the old structure]. Regarding "anādā," he says, "without taking up the old mat," because this is a grammatical designation (*niddesa*) formed by the elision of the *ya*-sound.
And here, "Venerable sir, having taken up this sitting-mat of mine, excluding the vicinity of the old mat..."
The procedure for relinquishment is to be understood by this method: "That which was caused to be made according to the Sugata’s span is to be relinquished.

Regarding the rule laid down in the case of the disposal of rugs: having seen that the rugs were scattered about, the Blessed One thought, "There is no reason for the gifts of the faithful to go to waste;
I shall show them a means of using these," and thus he laid down the rule in the case of the disposal of rugs.
It is so prescribed. Because this training rule is both an action and a non-action, it is stated that "the remainder is exactly like the third";
the meaning is that it is exactly like the training rule on the two parts. However, this is the distinction:

in the case of making [a rug] by taking a Sugata-span from around an old rug; in the case of making it by taking even less when one does not obtain [enough]; and in the case of one who does not obtain anything at all.

"And there is no offense if it is not taken up for making [a new one]. Regarding the factors here, it should be understood that "not taking up" refers to taking up less than a Sugata-span from the vicinity of the old sitting mat.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the sitting mat is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Eḷakaloma.
“Of one who has set out upon a journey-road” (*addhānamaggappaṭipannassa*): a journey itself is the road; thus, the meaning is “of one who has set out upon that.
Therefore he said, “designated as a journey,” and so forth. Because it is qualified by the word “journey,” however, it is called “a long road.”
From the statement in the *Vibhaṅga* regarding the occasion of traveling on a journey—"one may eat [if one thinks], 'I will go half a *yojana*'"—even half a *yojana* constitutes a journey.
Furthermore, these sheep's wool, if obtained elsewhere than on a journey, are not permitted to be accepted;
for this reason, the phrase "for one set out on a journey," and so forth, was stated in response to an inquiry.

Having intended this, he said, “If all this,” and so forth. Therein, “all this” refers to the passage beginning, “Now, if woolen cloth should arise for a bhikkhu who has set out on a journey,” and so on.
“It is merely an illustration of the substance” means that at that time, for a certain bhikkhu traveling from the Kosala country toward Sāvatthī, on the way...
The passage beginning with “goats’ hair appeared” is merely an illustration of the basic case.
Regarding the phrase “in any place whatsoever”: it means in any location other than on a journey. As for “with one’s own hand,” this is an ablative used in the sense of an instrument;

thus he says, “by means of one’s own hand. Furthermore, this is a figurative expression (lakkhaṇavacana); therefore, the meaning should be understood as “by any part of the body whatsoever. Hence he said:

“The meaning is ‘to be taken by oneself. Regarding the phrase “when there is no one to take it,” since a restrictive sense is obtained here through the internal restriction of the words, he said, “only when there is no one,” and so forth. And here, [the offense is incurred] by such statements as:
“Venerable sir, these woolen sheep’s hairs of mine have exceeded three yojanas [in distance], and they are thus subject to forfeiture.”
The procedure for relinquishment (nissajjana) should be understood. Regarding the "threefold offense of expiation" (tikapācittiya):

there are three offenses of expiation based on the cases of one who perceives it as more than three yojanas, one who is doubtful, and one who perceives it as less than three yojanas. As for "having gone with the intention of staying and then carrying [the robe] beyond that":

having gone elsewhere with the purpose of residing, if one fails to obtain instruction, interrogation, or the like, or the necessary requisites and so forth at that place, and then carries it further to another location; from that point...

"Elsewhere" means that there is no offense even when carrying it for a hundred *yojanas*. "Stolen or relinquished" means either stolen by thieves or formally relinquished through a legal act of the Vinaya (*vinayakamma*).
"A finished article" means a finished product, such as a woolen blanket, a cloak, or a rug, or anything else, even if it is merely tied together with a thread.
Therefore he said, "even as little as," and so forth. However, [in the case] of one who [carries it] inside a small leaf-bag...
Or, if one goes while inserting hair into the spaces between the yoke, the shoulder-straps, the waist-band, and so forth;
or for the sake of protecting against dirt, into a small pouch containing peppercorns and the like; or even, if afflicted by wind-disorder, into the ear-canal—there is indeed an offense.
However, if it is tied with a string and placed [in the ear], it remains in its place as a finished article; if one carries it after having made it into a braid, there is no offense.
This is called the "opening of the treasure," which is indeed an offense.
"First acquisition" means the first arising of wool for one's own benefit. By this, the acquisition of wool that has been cut off, relinquished, or obtained [in other ways] is prohibited.
"Having placed it in a vehicle while another person is unaware" refers to a chariot or similar conveyance that is moving, or upon the back of an elephant, and so forth.
Or, having placed it [in the cart] with the thought "he will take it," even while the owner is unaware; the same rule applies if he does not arrive.
However, if, when he has not arrived, he places it on a chariot or the like, or on the back of an elephant and so forth, and drives it away;
or if, while walking below, he urges it on; or if he calls out and causes someone else to follow it—there is no offense, according to the statement: "he causes another to take it."
And here, by the phrase "if he places it in a vehicle without knowing," it is shown that if one who knows places it in a vehicle, it is indeed called "having it carried away.
"Non-carrying and non-returning" means the absence of carrying and returning.
The commentary on the rule concerning wool (*eḷakaloma*) is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Washing of Sheep’s Wool.
Regarding the phrase “among the Sakyans”: based on the inspired utterance (udāna), “These youths are indeed Sakyans,” the name “Sakyans” was given to them;
the single country where they dwell is, by way of conventional usage (ruḷhisadda), called “the Sakyans. It is in that Sakyan country. [The group of] six [monks].
The names Paṇḍuka, Lohitaka, and others were those who lived in the forest, as well as their disciples.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the washing of wool is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Gold and Silver (Jātarūpa).
"Silver" (*rajata*) here does not refer exclusively to coined money; rather, whatever is used for commercial transactions, such as the *kahāpaṇa* and so forth, is intended.
Thus he says, "Moreover," and so on. In that context, a *kahāpaṇa* may be made of gold, or made of silver, or it may be a common [coin].
A copper coin (*lohāmāsaka*) is a coin made from copper or similar metals. A wooden coin (*dārumāsaka*) is...
A coin made by cutting out a figure with heartwood, or with a bamboo splinter, or even with a palm leaf;
a lacquer coin is a coin made by raising a figure with lac or resin.
By the phrase "those which come into circulation," it is meant that whichever [coin] comes into circulation in whichever region, whenever it does so.
Even down to that which is made of bone, made of leather, or made from the seeds of tree fruits—whether it be of a form that has been produced or one that has not been produced—all is included.
"That very thing" means gold and silver itself. "Coin" (hirañña) means a *kahāpaṇa*.
The phrase "he approves of it" clarifies the meaning already stated, namely, "he desires to take it. This applies not only through body and speech...
What has already been rejected by body and speech is indeed rejected; however, even that which is mentally rejected is indeed rejected.

Thus he said, "by body and speech," and so forth. But if one does not reject it through body and speech and instead assents with the mind, because one fails to perform the rejection that ought to be done by body and speech, there is an offense originating from non-action at the doors of body and speech.
One incurs [an offense]. However, in the mind-door (manodvāra), there is no such thing as an offense.
Suppose someone places a hundred or a thousand [coins] at the feet of a monk, saying, "Let this be yours," and the monk refuses it, saying, "This is not allowable.
The lay follower departs, saying, "It has been relinquished by me to you," and another person comes there and asks:
“Venerable sir, what is this? He should explain both what was said by the other and what was said by himself.

If he says, “I will guard it, venerable sir; show me a secure place,” then even if it is a seven-storey palace, having ascended it, one should point out, “This is a secure place,” but one must not say, “Place it here. Up to this point, it is allowable (*kappiya*).
If it stands adjacent to what is not allowable, one must live there having closed the door and guarding it.

If some merchandise for sale, such as a bowl or a robe, should arrive, and someone says, "Venerable sir, please take this," he should say, "Lay follower, we have need of this, and such a site exists for us; however, there is no one to prepare what is allowable."
"It does not exist," he should say. If he says, "I shall act as the steward;
open the door and give it to me," then having opened the door, he should say, "It is placed in this spot," but he should not say, "Take this.
In this way, it remains supported by both what is allowable and what is not allowable. And if he takes it...
If he gives him an allowable article, it is permissible. If he takes more than that, he should be told: "We do not take your goods; go away.
Regarding the instruction "it must be relinquished right in the midst of the Saṅgha": since what is called "money" (rūpiya) is indeed unallowable, therefore it must be relinquished.

It was not stated, "for the Saṅgha, for a group, or for an individual. However, because that [ghee] has merely been accepted and nothing suitable (kappiya-bhaṇḍa) has been purchased with it, it was therefore stated, "it must be relinquished right in the midst of the Saṅgha," in order to show a means of using it.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), oil and so forth are included. "He" refers to the householder who [received] the ghee.
This refers to what was stated in the manner beginning with, "O lay followers, oil or [other substances] are permitted.
"Having obtained it by another" means having obtained it through one's own *vassa* (rainy-season retreat) by either a monk or a monastery attendant (*ārāmika*).

"Even the shade of a tree produced from that" refers to the shade standing within the boundaries of a tree grown from seeds brought as the object of forfeiture (*nissaggiya-vatthu*); however, shade that exceeds those boundaries is considered adventitious (*āgantuka*).

It is permissible. "If he does not discard it" means that if he neither takes it and goes nor discards it, but instead departs wherever he wishes, thinking, "What business have I with this?", then he is endowed with five factors:

one who would not go astray through desire, would not go astray through hatred, would not go astray through delusion, would not go astray through fear, and [would not go astray regarding] what has been discarded or not discarded.
"One who possesses the five factors thus stated should be known [as qualified].

He should be appointed by means of the formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakammavācā*), as stated in the word-commentary beginning: 'Venerable sirs, let the Sangha hear me; if it seems appropriate to the Sangha, the Sangha may appoint the monk named so-and-so as the discarder of money.'"
"Having made it signless, it should be discarded like excrement" means that one should discard it like excrement without making a sign by observing the place where it falls;

rather, with eyes closed, one should throw it—without regard for it and without attending to the place of falling—like excrement into a river, over a precipice, or into a dense forest. This is what is meant.
Therefore, it says: “It should be discarded like excrement.

“Three *pācittiya* offenses” refers to three *pācittiya* offenses according to the cases of one who perceives [the object] as money, one who is doubtful, and one who does not perceive it as money. “One who perceives what is not money as money” means one who perceives gold and so forth in items such as coarse bowls.
“By the method of the Jewel Precept” refers to the procedure stated here: “Either within a monastery or within a dwelling.”
The commentary on the training rule concerning gold is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning trading in money:
“By way of what has been made, etc. means by way of what has been made, not made, and both made and not made. Here, the fourfold object subject to relinquishment—gold and so forth—is [the subject].
Because it is included by the mention of "taking silver," he said, "exchanging gold and silver.
And this should be understood as stated according to the upper limit. Therefore he said, "by the preceding training rule," and so forth. "Exchanging" means the exchange of acquired silver.
"In accordance with the previous method" refers to: "Venerable sir, I [engaged] in various kinds of transactions involving silver..."
"I entered [this state], this is my forfeiture," and so forth.

Regarding the case of trading with money: because the very act of receiving [money] is prohibited, one does not see a fault in exchanging what has been received, but rather in the exchange of money itself.
"Of that" means of what was exchanged. "Or of wealth" means of one's own [wealth].

Or [the exchange] of the principal capital. For if one were to exchange another’s money for one’s own non-monetary goods, or one’s own money for another’s non-monetary goods—in either case, the transaction involving money has indeed been committed.
The commentary on the training rule concerning transactions involving money is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule on Buying and Selling:
Since the exchange of money was already covered by the preceding training rule, it is said here that only "suitable articles" (kappiyabhaṇḍa) are intended, beginning with the words "of robes, etc.
In this context, "suitable articles such as robes, etc. refers even down to a single thread for a fringe.
[It refers to] robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick, as well as any other allowable articles (kappiya-bhaṇḍa).
"Buying" means taking another's goods; "selling" means giving one's own goods. Therefore he said, "Give this for that," and so forth.
"Of another" means anyone other than the five types of fellow practitioners (sahadhammika). And here, "Venerable Sir, I..."
“It should be relinquished in the manner beginning: ‘I engaged in various kinds of buying and selling; this is my relinquishment, I relinquish it to the Saṅgha.
Therefore he said, ‘By way of the stated characteristics,’ and so forth.

But surely, in this context, when washing robes, cutting hair, or performing new construction work such as clearing the ground, one must relinquish another’s goods that have come into one’s own hands?”
Since there is no [other] name [for it], he said, "In that case, what should be done? One must simply confess a *pācittiya* offense.
The intention is that just as one confesses a *pācittiya* when a *nissaggiya* article has been used or lost, so too here one must simply confess.
"This is ours" means: "This oil or ghee that was accepted is present for us. And for us...

“By this and by that there is need” means: we have need of this and that which has not been accepted by anyone other than ourselves. By the phrase “the method is exactly as stated regarding trading in money,” he extends (atidiśati) this same method to the rule:
“Three *pācittiyas* for one who perceives buying or selling where there is none; and a *dukkaṭa* for one who is doubtful.”
The commentary on the training rule concerning buying and selling is finished.
The second chapter, on wool, is concluded. 3.
The Chapter on Alms Bowls.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Alms Bowls (*Pattasikkhāpada*).
“Not assigned” (*avikappita*) means not assigned by way of such formulas as, “I assign this bowl to you.
“He takes a half-āḷhaka of cooked rice” means he takes cooked rice from two *nāḷi*s of husked rice according to the Magadha measure. Regarding the term “Magadha *nāḷi*”: [the text continues].
"It amounts to twelve and a half *pala*s," so it is stated in the Andhaka-ṭīkā. "In the island of Siṃhala, the standard *nāḷi* is large;
the Damila *nāḷi* is small; the Magadha *nāḷi* is of proper measure. By that Magadha *nāḷi*, one and a half *nāḷi*s make one Siṃhala *nāḷi*," so it is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā.
"Unhusked rice" (*anuttaṇḍula*) refers to rice that has been removed from its husk after being cooked.
*Uttandula*: not with rice removed, thus *anuttandula*. "Prepared from all ingredients" means prepared with all ingredients such as cumin and so forth.
"Vegetable curry in proportion to the mouthful" means a vegetable curry measuring one-fourth the size of a mouthful.
Having thus shown the superior bowl, he now says "from the superior" and so forth, in order to show the medium and inferior ones.

In this regard, the method is as follows: if all the rice, such as a *nāḷika* measure, when poured in remains level with the lower rim according to the aforementioned manner, this is called a medium bowl.
If it stands above that rim like a heap, this is called a medium-small bowl. If it does not reach that rim and remains entirely contained within, [this is called a small bowl].
This is called the medium-excellent bowl. If all the alms-food, such as rice and so forth, remains level with the lower rim when placed inside, this is called the inferior bowl.
If it stands piled up, rising above that rim, this is called the inferior-inferior bowl.
If it does not reach that rim but remains entirely contained within it, this is called the inferior-excellent bowl.
“Is it called a bowl?”—therefore he said: “Their classification should be understood in the same manner as already stated.

Now, in order to show among those [categories] those that involve determination and choice (*adhiṭṭhāna-vikappanā*) and those that do not involve determination and choice (*anadhiṭṭhāna-avikappanā*), he said:
“In these cases,” and so forth. Therein, *ukkaṭṭhukkaṭṭho* means superior to the superior; for that reason, it is called “not a bowl” (*apatta*). *Omakomako*...

The smallest is the smallest of all; for that reason, it is called "unattained" (*apatta*). These [first two] are to be used by way of being placed in a bowl (*bhājana-paribhoga*), but they do not come under formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*) nor under assignment (*vikappaṇa*); however, the other seven bowls may be used either after having been determined or after having been assigned.
Therefore he said: "The remaining seven bowls are indeed of the proper measure."
Therefore, because seven bowls are of the proper measure, for that reason [it is said]. Regarding "cooked in a manner suitable for a recluse":
an iron bowl is cooked in five ways and is thus cooked in a manner suitable for a recluse; a clay bowl is cooked in two ways.

If even one of these cooking processes is lacking, it is not fit for formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*). And just as only that which is cooked in a manner suitable for a recluse is fit for formal determination, [so too must it be so].

Likewise, both [the bowl and its value] become subject to formal determination (*adhiṭṭhānupagā*) only when that which is the price has been paid; however, if even a small amount remains unpaid, they do not become subject to formal determination.
Therefore he said, "But if," and so forth. They say that "even the measure of a *kākaṇika* coin" is one and a half grains of rice.
Even if the owner of the bowl says, "When you have the price, then you may give it," [it is still subject to forfeiture].
"Having resolved upon it, consume it"—yet it does not become subject to resolution. Because the cooking is incomplete, it does not attain the status of a bowl-contents (*patta-saṅkhā*).
Because the root has not been given—whether in its entirety or in part—it does not return to its own nature;
rather, it remains the property of another. Therefore, it becomes subject to resolution only when both the cooking and the rooting are finished. That which is subject to resolution...
And that very [bowl] is subject to formal assignment (*vikappa*). Therefore he said, "by one who does not remove," and so forth.
"By one who does not remove, it should be assigned" means that by one who does not remove the old bowl, a new bowl should be assigned; the intended meaning is that it should be set aside.
Regarding "grains of millet": this refers to the grains of the inferior of the seven types of grain, which is why he said, "with a hole no larger than the size of a millet grain."
The commentary on the training rule concerning bowls is concluded.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning bowls with fewer than five repairs:
*Assa* means "of this bowl. *Tena ūnapañcabandhanena* means "by that bowl which has fewer than five repairs."
The meaning is "having been characterized. For here, an alms-bowl with fewer than five repairs is taken as the characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*). Therefore he said:

"The instrumental case is used for a characteristic of one who has become thus" (*itthambhūtassa lakkhaṇe karaṇavacanaṃ*). In that context, "of one who has become thus" means of one who has reached a certain state.
It is a characteristic (*lakkhaṇaṃ*) because by this something is characterized (*lakkhīyate*); in that [sense], the instrumental case—the third case-ending—is employed.
The meaning is as follows: the term "mode" (*pakāra*) refers to a specific distinction that differentiates a general category.

For instance, in the phrase "with a bowl having fewer than five mends," the state of being a bowl with fewer than five mends is the mode that distinguishes it from the general category of "being a monk's bowl";
the monk has incurred that [offense], and his bowl is the defining characteristic (*lakkhaṇa*). If a bowl has not yet reached five mends, it is one "having fewer than five mends."
If it is called by that name, then why is it stated in the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājaniya*) as being "without a binding" (*abandhana*)? To this he says, "In that regard," and so forth.

Therein, "in that regard" (*tattha*) is used for the purpose of introducing the statement. Whether there is a place for binding or not, a bowl that is devoid of binding is "without a binding" (*abandhana*).
That which has a place for the five bindings is "having a place for the five bindings" (*pañcabandhanokāsa*). "Not a bowl" (*apatta*) means it is not what is called a bowl.
The meaning is "it happens"; what is meant is that one is unable to restore it to its natural state. And this is a statement of the reason for making another person understand.
Therefore he said: "Therefore, it is permissible to make another person understand.
Furthermore, since this binding occurs only when there is a place for binding and does not occur when there is none, it is therefore the defining characteristic of that [binding].
In order to show the method of binding, the passage beginning with “But in which... was stated.
However, when it is pierced by the bowl-piercer near the rim, the bowl breaks because of its thickness; therefore, it should be pierced from below. Thus he said, “at the lower edge,” and so forth.
Or, having made a fine hole, it should be bound; for in a fine hole, there is no need for a triple-layered patch or the like.

The intention is that it must be determined (*adhiṭṭhātabbo*) only after inserting a thread. He says "treacle" (*phāṇitaṃ*), etc., to show that it is not to be bound solely with a string of tin, and so forth.
"Having burnt the treacle with stone powder" means having cooked the treacle together with stone powder;
the sense is: "with stone powder [already] cooked in that manner. "It must be relinquished" (*nissajjitabbo*) means: "Venerable sir, this bowl of mine..."

“If one has caused [an alms-bowl] to be obtained with a bowl that has fewer than five mends, it is an offense entailing relinquishment; I relinquish this to the Saṅgha. Thus it should be relinquished.
Therefore he said, “by the one relinquishing,” and so forth. “By one who is authorized” means:
“Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. If it is timely for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha authorize the monk named so-and-so...”
The Saṅgha should appoint a bowl-receiver; this is the motion. Let the venerable Saṅgha hear me:

the Saṅgha appoints the monk named so-and-so as the bowl-receiver. Whichever venerable one approves of the appointment of the monk named so-and-so as the bowl-receiver, let him be silent. Whichever does not approve, let him speak. The Saṅgha has appointed [him].
"Such-and-such a monk is the distributor of bowls; it is pleasing to the Saṅgha, therefore it is silent;

thus do I understand this"—by means of such a formal motion consisting of one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakammavācā*) as stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), he is appointed. "Having spoken of the existing qualities of the bowl" means:
"Venerable sirs, this bowl is of proper measure, beautiful, and suitable for an elder," and so forth, [stating] its existing benefits.
Having spoken thus. "At the edge of the bowl" means a bowl situated at its rim. "In an improper place" refers to places such as beds, chairs, umbrellas, or pegs;
for the proper place for setting down a bowl has already been stated in the Khandhaka by way of the rule: "I allow you, monks, a bowl-rest," and so forth.
"By improper use" means by using it for purposes unsuitable [for a bowl], such as for cooking broth, fuel, or dye.
However, if an illness arises on the way and there is no other vessel, it is permissible to smear [a pot] with clay and cook gruel in it, or to heat water.

"Gives away" means he gives it to another. But if a student (saddhivihārika) or a resident pupil (antevāsika), having set aside another superior bowl, says, "This one is suitable for me; this one is for the Elder," [it is not an offense].
He takes it; it is permissible. Or, if someone else takes that [food] and gives his own bowl, it is permissible.
There is no need to say, "Bring my bowl.
Regarding the phrase "invited by a relative": in a place where one has been invited on behalf of the Saṅgha, it is permissible only with the fivefold bond; regarding an individual...

However, in a place where one has been invited [to eat], it is permissible even with less than five ties [of requisites]. "An unmade request" means a request made in a situation where nothing has been prepared, such as saying, "Venerable sir, please speak [of providing] requisites.
The commentary on the training rule concerning less than five ties is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Medicines (Bhesajja-sikkhāpada).
"Having taken" means having made it something formally received; the meaning is: having taken it oneself without it being formally received.

It should be understood that the fact that there is no offense even when the seven-day limit is exceeded is because [the medicine] has reached the state of being unfit for consumption. Why is this demonstrated by this [rule]?
He said, "They are," and so forth. These are called "medicines" (*bhesajja*) because they were authorized by the physician; this is a designation for whatever is suitable [as medicine].
Therefore he said: "Whether they perform the function of medicine or not, they have acquired this conventional designation.
Now, in order to show ghee and fresh butter, which are subject to forfeiture (*nissaggiya*) when used as a seven-day supply:
“Ghee (sappi) means [the ghee] of cows and so forth,” it is said. By the word “and so forth” (ādi), goats and others are included.
By the phrase “of those whose meat is permitted,” one includes not only the well-known cows, goats, and so on, but also other animals such as the rohit deer and others.
For whatever has milk, they certainly have ghee as well. Whether that [ghee] is easily obtained or difficult to obtain, it is mentioned for the sake of clarity.
It has been said. "Only honey made by flies" means honey produced specifically by the three types of flies:
the small bee, the bumblebee, and the honeybee. "Sugar-cane juice" refers to the two kinds of sugar-cane juice, according to whether it is mixed with pure water or not.
Furthermore, because "molasses-water for one who is not ill" was permitted as a specific allowance, such water-mixed [juice] is permissible for one who is not ill. "Or those cooked without a base."

By this, he shows that what is cooked with its base (the sugar-cane) is not permitted. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, after posing the question, "Is this cooked with its base permitted or not permitted?", it is stated:
"Regarding sugar-candy made from sugar-cane, there is nothing called 'not permitted' after the meal.
This [view] is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā* to be the correct one. "Sugar-cane product" means [a product] from sugar-cane.
[The substances] such as *rasa*, *lasikā*, and so forth are produced [from them].

Because the word *taṃ* (that) serves as a reference back to the "normal" (*pakata*) [substances], it refers only to those medicines that are normal, and not to their raw materials; thus he said, "those medicines," and so on.
"Not their raw materials" means: without having received the causes of those [medicines], such as ghee and the like, which are milk and so forth.
“They shall prepare oils from fat. [The Buddha said: “Monks, I allow medicinal fats: fish fat, porpoise fat, otter fat, pig fat, and donkey fat. This refers to the oil made from those permitted fats.
“Yāni” means those medicines. “Monks, I allow medicinal fats: fish fat, porpoise fat, otter fat, pig fat...”
“[One may] receive it at the proper time as donkey fat, cook it at the proper time, and mix it at the proper time to use it for oil.
Since the acceptance of fat was thus permitted for the purpose of [making] oil, the words beginning with “but fat-oil” were spoken.
“At the proper time” means before the midday meal. “Mixed” means strained. “Therefore” means because it was permitted; therefore, “[one may use] clear fat.”
By means of the statement "excepting human fat," it is said "excepting human fat" because the fat of all other unallowable meats is permitted.
"Having cooked it oneself" means having cooked it oneself at the very time [of eating]. "Even oil produced by oneself" means even oil that has been extracted by oneself at the very time [of eating].
And all three of these are permissible only at the proper time (*kāla*). For it is said:
"Monks, if one has received [food] at the proper time, prepared it at the proper time, and mixed it at the proper time, and then consumes it, there is no offense.
However, after the meal, it is not permissible at all to receive or to prepare [it]. And this too has been said: "Monks, if at an improper time (*vikāla*)..."
If one should consume what was accepted at the wrong time, cooked at the wrong time, and mixed at the wrong time, there is an offense of three *dukkaṭas*.

If, monks, one should consume what was accepted at the right time, but cooked at the wrong time and mixed at the wrong time, there is an offense of two *dukkaṭas*. If, monks, it was accepted at the right time...
“If one should consume that which was prepared at the proper time but mixed [with other substances] at an improper time, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

By the statement, “It is permissible to use it for seven days as a non-material consumption,” it is shown that this refers to using it as a non-material consumption in the sense of: “that which was received at the proper time, prepared at the proper time, and mixed at the proper time may be used by way of oil-consumption.”
However, whatever here is like fine dust—whether flesh, sinew, bone, or blood—that is not subject to formal designation (*abbhohārika*).
But if one who is not fully ordained (an *anupasampanna*) makes oil from that fat he has received and gives it, how is that?
To this he says: "By one who is not fully ordained," and so forth. "On that very day" (*tadahū*) means on the day it was received.
From after the meal onwards, however, it is permissible for seven days that it be entirely non-material (nirāmisa). Even there, "non-transactional" (abbōhārika) means precisely "non-transactional.
The connection is: "it is not permissible to cook another substance from among the substances that are for the time-being (yāvakālika).

In that context, "substances that are for the time-being" (yāvakālikavatthūni) refers to those things whose substance is for the time-being; [the meaning is] "of those things possessing substances for the time-being."
The meaning is as follows: "Of others" refers to ghee and so forth, as distinct from oil and fat. "Substance" refers to substances such as milk that are of the *yāvakālika* (temporary) class;
it is certainly not permitted to cook them oneself—this is the intended meaning.
"Or ghee already produced" means ghee that has been separated from its *yāvakālika* substance, just as curdled milk is [separated] therein.
"Or it will go to destruction by means of reasoning," or "it has been thus burnt"—this is the meaning. "Or fresh butter":
having removed even drops of buttermilk or lumps of curd, it is permissible to cook well-washed fresh butter because it lacks the state of being cooked by oneself; this is the intention.
If one eats alms-food together with seven-day-stored food that was cooked by oneself, that alms-food [is considered as such] by virtue of the seven-day-stored food cooked by oneself.
One causes [a substance] that is of the nature of being for a limited time (*yāvakālika*) to be taken as if it were for seven days (*sattāhakālika*).

Likewise, even that which is not yet cooked but is of the nature of being for a limited time comes to be considered as self-cooked; thus it is said: "But even on the same day, before the meal, it is not permitted to consume that which contains meat.
This is just like beef-tallow that has been self-cooked for seven days, or like the lifetime-allowances (*yāvajīvika*) such as mustard seeds that have been self-fried.
And oil that is mixed with meat is not permitted even before the morning meal; likewise, it should be understood that this applies to fresh butter and ghee as well.

And it has been said: "Those things such as 'to-be-taken-at-any-time' (yāvakālika) and so forth, when mixed together with [forbidden substances], they cause one to incur guilt through their very presence."
“Only those alms-bowls [permitted] by the Blessed One are allowable for a bhikkhu as long as life lasts;
likewise, non-material [medicine] for seven days, and material [medicine] when cooked by oneself.
Regarding the phrase “milk and so forth,” the word “and so forth” (ādi) here includes sesame seeds and other such items. “Even material [medicines]” means not only non-material ones.
This is the meaning. However, from after the meal onwards, they are certainly not permitted. Even if seven days have elapsed, there is no offense because they were received with a physical basis;
for it was said, "having received them. Therefore he said, "from after the meal onwards," and so forth.
But what is prepared with items received after the meal should be applied to ointments and the like; even those received before the meal [may be used similarly].
And [it includes] what has been prepared with ingredients already stored. For both types, there is no offense even if seven days have elapsed. "Within seven days" means inside the seven-day period.
Regarding "anointing and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) includes head-anointing, eye-anointing, thigh-anointing, house-fumigation, and the like.
"Having resolved" means: "From now on, this shall not be for the purpose of my internal consumption; this ghee and oil..."
Having generated such a thought as, "The fat will be for the purpose of anointing the head or the body, or the honey will be for the purpose of smearing a wound,
or the molasses will be for the purpose of fumigating the house," he says, "Those that are for life," etc.,
[referring to] those things among the categories of what is for a limited time and what is for life until the dawn.
"Remains until sunrise" means that if oil prepared on the seventh day remains until the rising of the dawn.

Regarding the phrase "clarified butter (*sappi*) and so forth not mentioned in the Canon": herein, the clarified butter of the *miga*, *rohitaka*, and other such animals is "clarified butter not mentioned in the Canon";
likewise for the fresh butter (*navanīta*). Furthermore, the oil of coconut, neem, *kosamba*, *karamanda*, sesame, and so forth is "oil not mentioned in the Canon."
Likewise, it should be understood that *madhukapupphaphāṇita* (treacle made from madhuka flowers) is not included among the types of treacle mentioned in the Canon.
Not all *madhukapupphaphāṇita* falls under the category of treacle; therefore, he said, "prepared with cold water," and so forth.

"Prepared with cold water" means that after placing madhuka flowers in cold water and not crushing them, once the flower-juice has entered the water, that water is taken and cooked until it is prepared.
By the phrase “it has the nature of palm-sugar syrup,” he shows that it is for seven days, but not that it is an article involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-vatthu*).
Therefore, it should be understood that for one who lets [the seven days] pass, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). This is also stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
“Honey-syrup made from madhuka flowers with cold water is permissible as solid food before the meal; after the meal, however—”
"From the time it is prepared, for seven days it is purely non-material (nirāmisa); after the lapse of seven days, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) according to the number of vessels.
However, if it is made by adding milk, it is "to be used during the day" (yāvakālika). As for candied sugar, they purify it by removing the milky film;
therefore, it is permissible. This applies to all fruits that are to be used during the day, such as mango, rose-apple, jackfruit, plantain, date, and citron.
“Treacle is only for the time of the day” means he said, “Amba-fruit treacle and so forth are for the time of the day.
“Physical enjoyment is permitted” means that anointing the body or the wound on the body is permitted, but swallowing it is not permitted.
“That” refers to medicine that has exceeded seven days. “Having relinquished without expectation” means having given it up without regard.
Having given it to a novice. "That" refers to the medicine obtained again after having thus relinquished it.

For if the medicine given in this manner is handed over by that novice—whether prepared or unprepared—to that bhikkhu, he may take it and perform nasal therapy (*natthukamma*) or use it for any other purpose. Therefore, he said: "Even to swallow..."
"It is permissible. If that fool does not know how to give it, another bhikkhu should say to him, "Sāmaṇera, do you have medicine?
"Yes, venerable sir, I have it. "Bring it; we shall prepare medicine for the elder," thus it is also permissible.
"By way of counting the substances" means by way of counting the substances such as ghee and so forth, and also by way of counting the lumps of ghee and so forth.

Furthermore, among the miscellaneous rules, there is one offense entailing relinquishment and confession (nissaggiya-pācittiya). In this case, the procedure for relinquishment should be understood as follows: "Venerable sir, this medicine of mine has exceeded seven days and is to be relinquished; I relinquish it to the Saṅgha.
This is a common rule of training. Even if seven days have not elapsed, an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) occurs for one who perceives that they have elapsed, as well as for one who is in doubt.
If one perceives that seven days have passed when they have not actually passed, or if one is in doubt, it is likewise a *nissaggiya-pācittiya*.

The same applies to those who perceive that an item has been formally resolved upon (*adhiṭṭhita*), distributed (*vissajjita*), lost (*naṭṭha*), destroyed (*vinaṭṭha*), burnt (*daḍḍha*), or ruined (*avilutta*), when it has not actually been so. There is no offense if the item was formally resolved upon within the seven-day period, or if it was distributed, lost, destroyed, burnt, stolen, or taken on trust;
nor is there an offense for those who are insane and so forth. This is a failure of conduct (*ācāra-vipatti*). [The rule concerning] ghee and other substances for oneself...
The three factors here are: it being one's own property, it not having entered into the reckoning [of the Saṅgha], and the passing of seven days. This is an offense of the *kaṭhina* class;
it is non-intentional, not to be cleared by confession, without a mental element, a formal offense (*paṇṇattivajja*), bodily action, and verbal action;
it involves three types of consciousness and three types of feeling. Therefore he said: "The rest should be understood according to the method stated in the first training rule of the Cīvara-vagga."
The commentary on the training rule concerning medicines is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning the rains-bathing robe:
"From the first day of the last month" means from the first day of the following month after the full moon of Jeṭṭha-Mūla.

"Starting from": *tāva* refers to a period of time measured as "so long. From the last day of the first fortnight (*pāṭipada*) following the full moon of the month of Jeṭṭha-Mūla, up until the full moon of Kattika—this is the meaning of "in these five months.

Regarding the phrase "the time for the *vassikasāṭikā*," etc., the word "etc. (*ādi*) here includes the passage: "It is the proper time for the *vassikasāṭikā*; other people also give the *vassikasāṭikā* robe-cloth."
This refers to the phrase "Give me a rain-cloak robe," and so forth. Here, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of the following:
"Bring me a rain-cloak robe, exchange [it] for me as a rain-cloak robe, purchase [one] for me as a rain-cloak robe.
He asks: what happens for one who performs both of these [actions] with persons who are not his own relatives and have not been invited? He says:

“In a place where one is not invited by an unrelated person,” and so forth. The statement, “there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for the breach of the rule,” was said with reference to those who did not previously give the *vassikasāṭika* (rainy-season robe). However, there is no breach of the rule regarding those who do give it even previously. For it is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
“As for those people who previously gave the *vassikasāṭika* robe, even if these [persons] are unrelated and uninvited to them...”

“They exist; there is no breach of the rule because the making of a thought [to ask] is permitted for them. Regarding the offense of expiation involving forfeiture (*nissaggiya-pācittiya*) under the training rule on requesting from an unrelated person:

“Whatever bhikkhu should request a robe from an unrelated householder or housewife, except at the proper time, that is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture”—by this training rule, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
This is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). This rule applies even to one who gives a regular *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-season robe).
Regarding the phrase "from the first day of the last half-month of the summer":
here, starting from the first day of the dark fortnight of the month of Jeṭṭha following the Uposatha day, until the full moon of Āsāḷha—this half-month is the last half-month of the summer.
"Named" means starting from its first day; that is to say, starting from the first day of the first fortnight of the half-month.
"The last day of the month of Kattika" refers to the full moon of the latter month of Kattika. "By this much" means:
"When a month remains of the summer, a bhikkhu should seek out a rainy-season robe (vassikasāṭikacīvara)."
"Having determined that 'half a month remains of the summer,' it should be worn"—this is by way of such a calculation.
"The field for seeking" means the field for seeking [the robe]. For during this month, it is permissible to seek a *vassikasāṭikā* (rainy-season robe) that has not yet been obtained.
"The field for making and the field for wearing" refers to both the field for making and the field for wearing. By the word "and" (*pi*), the field for seeking is included.
He summarizes. For during this fortnight, it is permissible to seek out [the robe-cloth], to have it made, and to wear it;
however, it is not permissible to resolve upon it. As for what is stated in some manuscripts of the *Samantapāsādikā*:
"From the first day of the month following the full moon of Jeṭṭha or Mūla until the Uposatha of the dark fortnight—this is one fortnight, which is both the field for seeking..."

Regarding the statement, "And the period for making [the robe]: for within this interval, it is permissible to seek out a rain-cloak (vassikasāṭikā) that has not yet been obtained, and to make one that has been obtained;
however, it is not permissible to wear it or to formally determine (adhiṭṭhātuṃ) it," this should be understood as a scribal error, as it contradicts the Mātikā.
[The correct rule is: "When half a month of the summer remains, having made [the cloth into a robe], it should be worn."
The word "all" (*sabbam*) refers to all four: seeking (*pariyesana*), making (*karaṇa*), wearing (*nivāsana*), and determining (*adhiṭṭhāna*).
By this, he shows that these four months are the field for all four of these—seeking, making, wearing, and determining.
For during these four months, it is permissible to seek what has not been obtained, to make use of what has been obtained, to wear it, and to determine its use.
"Vassa is postponed" means the year is drawn out or extended; the meaning is that it is pushed forward.
What is meant is that they postpone the first month of the rainy season and instead treat it as the last month of the summer.

"It should be determined on the day of the entry into the rains residence" means that because ten days have already passed prior to the commencement of the rains, [the determination] must be made precisely on the day of entering the rains residence.
It must be formally determined (*adhiṭṭhātabba*). For it is not permissible to let that day pass by.
However, if it has been obtained and finished during the rainy season, it must not exceed ten days starting from the day it was obtained within that same rainy season;
but if it is finished after the ten days have passed, it must be determined on that very day. If the ten days are insufficient, one must not let the robe-season (*cīvarakāla*) pass by.
This, first of all, is the resolution regarding [the robe] that has been made. But what is the resolution regarding one that has not been made? To this he says, “If,” and so forth.
The intention is that one does not obtain even a single day [of the robe] from another, because there is no other resolution.
From where does that [period] arise? To this he says, “As far as the first day of winter,” starting from the full moon of Jeṭṭhamūla.
The meaning is: "until the first day (pāṭipada) following the full moon of Kattika.

Regarding the phrase "in these seven months of the dry season (piṭṭhisamaya)," it refers to these seven months named after the dry season, which begin from the first day following the full moon of Kattika and end with the full moon of Jeṭṭha and Mūla, as stated in reverse order.
"By means of causing the arising of mindfulness" refers to [the thought], "It is time for the rainy-season robe," and so forth.
“By means of a method”: by means of causing the arising of mindfulness. “To one who makes a request” means:
to one who makes a formal request in such a manner as, “Give me a *vassikasāṭika* robe,” and so forth. “There is no offense by that training rule” means:

there is no offense by the training rule concerning requests from strangers; however, by this training rule, there is indeed an offense because it is not the proper time. For this was said by the venerable teacher Buddhadatta:
“But when a monk, having resolved upon the thought [of making it],
is in the process of completing a rain-cloak during the permitted time for the back-part [of the robe],
there is an offense entailing relinquishment (nissaggiya-āpatti) regarding relatives, non-relatives, and so forth.”
"And likewise, having made a formal intimation (viññatti) regarding those very [robes], when they have been produced.

Herein, the procedure for relinquishment (nissajjana-vidhāna) should be understood according to this method: "Venerable sir, this rainy-season robe-cloth (vassikasāṭikā) was sought by me when more than one month of the hot season remained, and it was made and worn when more than half a month of the hot season remained; it is to be relinquished."
"In the case of the search for a rainy-season robe" means: in the case of the search for a rainy-season robe done beforehand.

"Three offenses of expiation (pācittiya)" refers to three offenses of expiation based on the search for and wearing [of the robe] by one who perceives it as being more than one month and a half, by one who is doubtful, and by one who perceives it as less; this is an expression using the singular to represent a group (*ekasesa-niddesa*), or a general expression (*sāmañña-niddesa*). "In the case of less than one month and a half" means...
“Less than a month” and “less than half a month. For one who perceives it as more, or for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Here, the phrase “for one who is seeking and putting on [the robe]” is to be supplied. This is what is meant:
