“When less than a month remains of the summer [retreat], for one who perceives it as more, or for one who is in doubt, while seeking [a robe], there is an offense of wrong-doing; when less than half a month remains...”
“And for one who wears [the robe] during the summer while perceiving it as an extra robe, or for one who is in doubt, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).

By the word “likewise,” he extends the application of the offense of wrong-doing; and that offense of wrong-doing is to be incurred not by counting the drops of water, but rather according to each individual act of bathing until the conclusion of the bath.
This applies, however, only to one who is bathing with water falling from the sky onto an open space.
It is not [an offense] for one bathing with water poured from jars into a bathhouse, a well, a pond, and so forth. For this very reason, he said:
"provided there is a rain-cloak," and so on. The connection is that there is no offense for one bathing naked in lotus ponds and the like.
However, the meaning is that even if a rain-cloak is present, there is no offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one bathing naked in lotus ponds and the like.

Having thus shown the non-offense regarding an intermediate offense (*antarāpatti*), he now says "for one whose robe has been stolen," and so forth, in order to show the non-offense regarding what is to be relinquished (*nissaggiya*).
Therein, "for one whose robe has been stolen" means for one whose entire robe has been taken away. For such a person, there is no offense even if they wear it at an improper time.
This same principle applies here as well to "for one whose robe has been lost. And just as it is for those wearing [the robe] in this case, [so it is in other cases].
It should be understood that there is no offense even for one who searches in such a manner.

However, in this context, it is said "not wearing [it]" and so forth because, when one is bathing while setting aside a valuable *vassikasāṭikā* (rain-cloth), a threat from thieves constitutes an "emergency" (*āpadā*).

Alternatively, "wearing it during emergencies" refers to one who wears it at an improper time while an emergency is actually present. As for the passage in the *Samantapāsādikā* stating, "of one whose robes have been stolen... [the meaning follows].
This was said specifically with reference to the *vassikasāṭikā* (the rainy-season robe). For there is no offense for those who are naked when their bodies are drenched by rain.
And here, "an emergency" (*āpadā*) refers to a danger from thieves for one who is bathing after having put on a costly *vassikasāṭikā*.

Thus, rather than showing that there is no offense for one whose robes have been stolen by means of a forfeiture offense (*nissaggiya*), this demonstrates that there is no offense for one who bathes naked by way of a simple offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). This...

It does not appear as if it were appropriate. For the section on non-offenses (anāpattivāra) is commenced for the purpose of showing that there is no offense only when there is the possibility of an offense consisting of a root-offense (mūlāpatti) among all the training rules (sikkhāpada), and not for an intermediate offense (antarāpatti); therefore, this must be investigated.
"Possessing robes" means possessing robes by means of the inner robe (antaravāsaka) and the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga).
The commentary on the training rule concerning the rainy-season robe (*vassikasāṭika*) is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule concerning the taking away of robes (*cīvaraacchindana*):
Regarding the word "having given," what is intended here is the act of giving while expecting something in return; it is not the gift of what has been relinquished. Thus he said.
“Services and so forth,” etc. “With the perception that it is one’s own” means with the perception that “it is mine.

By this he shows the absence of a *pārājika* offense. For even if something was given after having been relinquished, there is no *pārājika* for one who takes it with the perception that it is his own.
“Of one who seizes” means of one who seizes many [robes] that are not tied together and are kept separately, such as saying, “Bring the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*), bring the upper robe (*uttarāsaṅga*).”
And likewise for one who causes [the robes] to be brought back. Therefore it is said: “The offenses are according to the number of items.

Even for one who says, “Bring back everything given by me,” there are many offenses by that single statement alone. However, for one who seizes a single robe or many robes that are joined together as one, there is a single offense.
Regarding the command “seize,” it is an *dukkaṭa* (wrong-doing); thus, [it is said]: “Take everything given by me.”
For the command itself, there is one *dukkaṭa*; however, for those robes that have been taken away, there are several *pācittiyas* by virtue of the singular expression alone. Therefore he said:
"In the case of those taken away, the offenses are according to the number of items. "In the case of those taken away" means: in the case of the robes taken away by that command.
As for the reading in some manuscripts, "In the case of those taken away, the offenses are according to the number of commands given," [that is not the correct version].
Regarding the reading there, "as many as were commanded" means as many robes as were commanded to be taken.
As for what is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*: "If one commands, 'Take a robe,' it is one *dukkaṭa*.
If, having been so commanded, one takes many, it is one *pācittiya*," that refers to a single continuous act. And having done so, in the *Samantapāsādikā*...

There is no contradiction with this commentary. However, if one commands, "Take the outer robe (saṅghāṭi)," or "Take the upper robe (uttarāsaṅga)," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for every such command.
Regarding the robes that have been snatched away, the offenses correspond to the number of garments. And here, by the statement:
"Venerable sir, this robe of mine, having been given to a bhikkhu by myself, was snatched away and is to be relinquished," [the offense is established].
The procedure for relinquishing should be understood according to this method.
"Three offenses of expiation" refers to three offenses of expiation based on the cases of one who perceives another as ordained, one who is doubtful, and one who perceives another as unordained.
"Another requisite" means another requisite such as a bowl and so forth, even down to a needle.

The meaning is as follows. It is stated, "and of one who is not fully ordained," etc., to show that it is not only for one who seizes the robe of one who is not fully ordained that there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
In that context, "whatever" means whether it be a robe, or a bowl and so forth, or whatever requisite it may be.
"Of one who receives it on trust" means of one who receives it through the confidence of the person to whom it was given; this refers to the sense of the third case (tatiyatthe).
This is a term denoting application. "The state of being ordained" (*upasampannatā*) refers to the status of being ordained at the very moment of taking back [the robe].

Although the status of being ordained appears in the Canon and in the commentary on the *Mātikā* in connection with the acts of giving and receiving, nevertheless, because there is an offense for one who gives a robe while unordained and then takes it back upon becoming ordained, it should be understood that the state of being ordained is a factor [of the offense] precisely at the time of taking it back.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the snatching away of robes is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule concerning requesting thread:
"Thread" means six kinds of thread: linen, cotton, silk, wool, [and so forth].
"Of hemp and linen" refers to the six kinds of thread, such as linen-cloth and so forth. Therein, *khoma* is thread made from flax fibers.
*Kappāsika* is that produced from cotton. *Koseyya* is thread made by spinning silk worms' cocoons.
*Kambala* is thread made from sheep's wool. *Sāṇa* is thread made from hemp fibers. *Bhaṅga* is specifically a separate kind of bark-fiber thread.
Some [say this]. However, thread made by mixing even all five [fibers] together should be understood as "broken" (bhaṅga).

The "anuloma" of those [fibers] refers to six kinds of thread: *dukūla*, *pattuṇṇa*, *somārapaṭṭa*, *cīnapaṭṭa*, that produced by supernormal power (*iddhija*), and that given by the gods (*devadatta*).
A "loom" (*turī*) is a single rod that is an implement for weaving; it is the place where they roll up and store the cloth after it has been woven back and forth. A "shuttle" (*vema*)...
The loom has a single frame; by inserting the thread and beating it with that [frame], they achieve density.

For all its applications, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). Regarding those applications of the weaver—such as the setting up of the shuttle and the loom—in all those applications, there is an offense of wrong-doing for the monk; for every application of that weaver, the monk incurs an offense.

It is stated that this constitutes an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). In the absence of lutes and such instruments, or for the purpose of making them, the same principle applies to all activities, including the seeking, sharpening, and felling of trees with axes, hatchets, and so forth.
Since the threads belong to oneself, the place where they have been woven is already acquired; therefore, it is said:
"By acquisition, it becomes subject to relinquishment. It becomes subject to relinquishment when the weaving has reached the final measurement of a robe that is fit for assignment.

"It happens" (hoti) is what is meant. For this very reason, he will say: "If it is woven to a length of one span and a width of one cubit, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture" (nissaggiya-pācittiya).

And here, the procedure for relinquishment (nissajjana-vidhāna) should be understood according to this method: "Venerable sir, this robe-cloth of mine, which I had personally requested the weavers to weave from yarn [I provided], is to be forfeited."

"By that very person" means by the weaver who was requested. "In this case it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)" means that here too, if it is woven by a weaver to a length of one span (vidatthi) and a width of one cubit (hattha), it is an offense of wrong-doing; such is the meaning. "Made of unallowable thread" means made of thread that was requested.
"In the other case" refers to the section concerning that which is made of thread not requested. "If it is smaller than that" means if it is smaller than the dimensions mentioned.
The intended meaning is that it is even as small as the surface of an eyeball.
Just as there was a *nissaggiya* offense previously for one who had an unallowable thread woven by an allowable weaver, so here there is a *dukkaṭa* offense.
For this very reason, if one has both allowable and unallowable threads woven, and the portions consisting of unallowable threads are the size of a finished robe or smaller, [the same applies].
Regarding these, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for each demarcation by counting.

There is no offense regarding the demarcations of a *kappiya-sutta* (permissible string). Now, if it has been woven using an alternating thread, or if it is made permissible in length but impermissible across the width, there is an offense of wrong-doing for every demarcation that corresponds to the proper measure.

If, however, there are two weavers—one allowable and one unallowable—and the thread is unallowable, if they weave by turns, then for every section woven by the unallowable weaver that is of the proper measure, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*);
for a smaller portion, it is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). If the other [weaver] weaves, there is an offense of wrong-doing in both cases. If both take up the loom and [weave] together...
If they weave within the limits of the prescribed measurement, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for each limit.

Now, if the thread is allowable and the robe-cloth has defined boundaries such as those marked by field-bounds and so forth, then if it is woven by an unallowable weaver, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for each limit;
if woven by anyone else, there is no offense. If both [weavers] weave together within the limits of the prescribed measurement, [the same applies].
It is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). Now, if both the thread is allowable and unallowable, and they weave it by turns:

when the weaving of the final robe-measure sections has been completed with unallowable thread woven by an allowable weaver, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) according to the count of those sections;

when they are smaller than that, or when they consist of allowable thread, there is an offense of wrong-doing. When [woven] with allowable thread by an allowable weaver, in the case of those consisting of unallowable thread...
If the measurements or the proportions are deficient, there is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);

however, there is no offense if they are made from suitable threads. Furthermore, if one weaves having used an intervening thread, or having made it unsuitable in length or unsuitable across the width, or if both of them take up the loom and weave together, [there is an offense] regarding a robe that lacks a fixed measurement, even if it is otherwise suitable in measurement.
In the case of a defined area, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); in the case of a defined area with its boundaries, there are offenses of wrong-doing according to each boundary.

Therefore he said, “By this very method,” and so forth. And here, first of all, regarding the weaver: that which is obtained through a request from one who is unrelated and has not been invited is unallowable;
the rest is allowable. Regarding the thread: that which is personally requested is unallowable; the rest, as well as what arises through relatives and so forth, is allowable.

It should be understood as follows: "Three offenses of expiation" (*tikapācittiya*) refers to three offenses of expiation according to whether one has had [the cloth] woven, is uncertain about having had it woven, or perceives that it was not woven. "Thread requested for the sake of a robe" (*cīvaratthāya viññāpitasuttaṃ*) means thread requested for the sake of a robe either by oneself or by another.
Although the text says, "having requested the thread oneself," nevertheless, here—

It should be understood that because it is stated among the factors simply as “thread requested for the sake of a robe,” without specifying “thread personally requested for the sake of a robe,” even thread requested for the sake of a robe by someone other than oneself is included.
“By an improper request” means by such an improper request as: “Friend, please weave a robe for me.”
The commentary on the training rule concerning verbal intimation is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning the great weaver:
"Without having been previously invited by the owners of the robe-cloth" means: "Venerable sir, what kind of robe-cloth do you require? What kind..."
"Tell me, venerable sir, what you desire," he said, having not been previously addressed by the owners of the robes.
Here, by means of the three terms beginning with *āyata*, he shows the manner of weaving together with the manner of increasing the threads;

by means of the four terms beginning with *suvīta*, he shows only the manner of weaving. "We would give you something small," and so forth, is merely a demonstration of the manner in which he should act.
However, since the sight of a limb does not necessarily entail an offense solely by way of increasing the length of the thread, he said: "Not merely by giving almsfood to a bhikkhu," and so forth.

And here, the procedure for relinquishment is according to this method: "Venerable sir, this robe-cloth of mine, which was [prepared] by approaching a weaver who is an unrelated householder without being previously invited, and which has reached the stage of being a robe, is to be relinquished."

This should be understood. Regarding "three *pācittiya* offenses": there are three *pācittiya* offenses based on the cases of one who is unknown, one who perceives another as unknown, one who is doubtful, and one who perceives another as known.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the great weaver is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Urgent Robe (*Accekacīvara*).
“Of the first phrase” means of the phrase “ten days yet to come. “By the same method as before” means by way of absolute connection (*accantasaṃyoga*).
“Those days” means on those days. “Absolutely” means continuously; it is said that [the invitation] may be on any day whatsoever during those ten days.
“Of the month of *pavāraṇā*” refers to the month of *pubbakattika*; for that is what is meant here.
It is called the "Invitation Month" (*pavāraṇāmāsa*) because it is connected with the first Invitation ceremony.
"Starting from the fifth day of the bright fortnight" means beginning with the fifth day of the waxing moon.

Alternatively, the meaning is: starting from the fifth day of the preceding bright fortnight, that is, prior to the manifestation of the Invitation Month. As for the phrase "even though this [period] is at most ten days":

The reading found there— "It is established by the very [rule] 'an extra robe may be kept,' yet the training rule was laid down by way of an introductory narrative (aṭṭhuppatti) to show a meaning as if it were new"—

should be regarded as a careless reading because it contradicts the phrase "not having arrived within ten days. Furthermore, since it is stated [elsewhere] that "[the period begins] from the fifth day of the bright fortnight," it is the commentary itself [that contains the error].
There may also be a contradiction between what precedes and what follows. "Urgent robe" (*accekacīvara*) refers to a robe required for an urgent occasion;

and in order to show that this urgency arises from the state of the donor being a traveler and so forth, it was said: "for persons who are travelers, the sick, those pregnant, or those whose faith has newly arisen," and so on. In that regard:
"One who is going away" (*gamika*) is said to be "one who desires to go with an army, or one who desires to go into exile.

When someone has announced, "I will give the *vassāvāsika* (rainy-season robe)," and it is given by one of those such as the "one going away," desiring to give for reasons such as departure and so forth—
either by sending a messenger or by coming in person— it is thus [given].

The robe-cloth was given after having been announced. And here, the procedure for relinquishment should be understood by way of this formula: "Venerable sir, this is my urgent robe-cloth which has exceeded the robe-season; it is to be relinquished.

The rest refers to [the section beginning with] "commonly prescribed" and so forth. However, this is the distinction: therein, regarding an extra robe, one who perceives it as an extra robe, and so on...
The transgression of the ten-day limit: here, regarding an urgent robe (*accekacīvara*), it is the transgression of the robe-period for one who perceives it as an urgent robe, and so forth.
Likewise, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who perceives what is not an urgent robe as an urgent robe, and for one who is in doubt.

[The conditions are: that the urgent robe possesses the proper characteristics of its kind and measurement; that it is one's own property; and that it has arisen on the full moon day of the month of Kattika, before the ten days have elapsed.
The absence of formal resolve and the absence of dedication, as well as the passing of the robe-season, constitute the specific difference here regarding the presence of the four factors.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the urgent robe is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning danger.

“As in the case of *upasampajjanti* and so forth”: in the analysis (*vibhaṅga*) of the phrase “having attained the first jhāna, he dwells therein,” when the word “having attained” (*upasampajja*) was to be cited, it was cited as “*upasampajja*. That is given here as an illustration.
By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), however, the inclusion of such phrases as “or he might go without asking permission” should be understood. “Having approached” (*upagantvā*).

He spoke for the purpose of explaining the *upasadda* (the term *upavassa*). “Having dwelt” means having dwelt without interruption. According to the maxim, “For whatever has a connection with something else, that [connection] belongs to it even if it stands far off,” it was stated: “This [phrase]... has a connection with this. In that context, “of this” refers to the word “having dwelt” (*upavassa*).
The definition of the forest according to the Vinaya method is found in the *Pārājika* section on taking what is not given (*adinnādāna*). For therein it says: “From a village...”
In order to show both of these without confusion by defining the scope of what constitutes a "place of taking" (avahāṭṭhāna) without exception, it is said, "except for the village," and so forth.
For in the world, the village precinct (*gāmūpacāra*) is considered to be included within the village itself.
However, here, according to the method of the Suttanta, the forest-dwelling monk (*āraññaka bhikkhu*) is defined as one who lives at least five hundred bow-lengths beyond the village.
Having taken this into account: for he who dwells in a forest that is part of the Vinaya method is not described in the Sutta as "one who dwells in the forest and uses lodgings along the road.
Therefore, showing that one must take the definition exactly as it appears there, he said: "with a teacher’s bow that has been strung," and so forth.
In this context, "a teacher’s bow" means one measuring nine spans (vidatthi) by the ordinary hand.
But they say that when the measuring line has been fastened, it measures four cubits. "Of a village" means of an enclosed village.

"From the indakhīla" means from the threshold. "From the place suitable for the enclosure" means from the first throw of a clod by a man of medium height standing in the vicinity of a house situated at the boundary. How much of a path should be measured?

He said, “If,” and so forth. In the *Majjhima-aṭṭhakathā*, however, it is stated: “Having excluded the precinct of the monastery as well as that of the village, the distance between the two throws of a clod should be measured.

Regarding the phrase “by seeing the place where thieves have settled, etc.,” this refers to the reason of seeing the place where thieves have settled, and so on, within the monastery and its precinct. By the word “etc.,” there is the inclusion of the places where they have eaten, stood, sat, or lain down.

"Seizure": because it shows the state of people being killed, plundered, and robbed by thieves; and because it shows the state of being killed, plundered, and robbed within the monasteries and in the vicinity of the monasteries.
"One should deposit it in a house" (*antaraghare nikkhipeyya*): *antaragharaṃ* means that which has houses here and there within it, or that which belongs to such [a place].
The meaning is: "he should place it in that village. Therefore, he said, "of one who is forest-dwelling," and so forth. "And that" refers to the placing [of the bowl].

The phrase "he has been invited at the Great Invitation" is stated to show that the status of having completed the rains-residence was achieved without breaking the rains-retreat, and not to indicate that the invitation is a constituent part of the procedure itself.
For this very reason, in order to demonstrate the contrast, it is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
It is said: "If one has entered [the rains residence] during the later period, or if one’s rains residence has been interrupted, one is not permitted to set it aside.
The month of Kattika refers to the twenty-nine nights and days from the first day of the dark fortnight of the prior Kattika month until the full moon of the subsequent Kattika month.
By the word "eva" (only/just), it is shown that one does not obtain [the privilege of setting it aside] after the month of Kattika.

First, let it be granted that [the definition] does not apply because the characteristics of the forest (*arañña*) are lacking when the measure is deficient; but why does it not apply when the measure exceeds one *gāvuta*?
To this he says, "For where... and so forth. However, having been invited, one may return to stay even after traveling half a *yojana* or a full *yojana*;
this is what constitutes the "immeasurable" (or indefinite) distance. "Only dangerous and fearful" means both dangerous (*sāsaṅka*) and fearful (*sappaṭibhaya*).
...it exists. By the word "thus" (eva), it is shown that even if one dwells in a lodging endowed with factors free from suspicion and fear, one is not permitted to deposit [the rains-residence].

Up to this point, having entered for the first period (purimikā) and having completed it without breach, one who has finished the rains-retreat makes a certain village his alms-village and dwells in a forest lodging (āraññaka-senāsana) within five hundred bow-lengths of it. In that [lodging]...
Having permitted a monk to stay for the entire month of Kattika without his robe in that very same lodging after having deposited it in the village,
he now says, "It may happen to that monk," etc., while permitting a six-day separation from one staying elsewhere than the monastery.
For only those for whom the *kaṭhina* has been spread obtain [this privilege] when wandering without having formally undertaken [the robe], and not others.
In this regard, this further reason should also be observed: "In that case,

that bhikkhu may be separated from that robe for a maximum of six nights" means that if a bhikkhu, while staying in a monastery, has a need to go elsewhere and deposits his robe in a house within the village,
that bhikkhu may be separated from that robe for a maximum of six nights.
It is meant that one must dwell elsewhere for six nights from that monastery. For it was said by the venerable teacher Buddhadatta:
“If a monk dwells in the forest having made a certain village his alms resort, he is permitted to stay in that village for one month.”
“For one dwelling elsewhere, it is intended as being at most six nights;
this is its underlying meaning, which was previously concealed but is now made clear.
Therefore he said: “If he should dwell apart from that for longer than that”—meaning longer than six nights in that same lodging, on the seventh [night]...

“[One] should cause the dawn to rise,” and so forth. “By one unable to do so” means by one who, due to the distance of the place gone to, is unable to return to the lodging and cause the seventh dawn to rise.
Even if unable to do so in this way, while remaining right there, [the robe] must be relinquished with the thought:
“It shall remain in the category of an extra robe. “Having stayed” means having caused the dawn to rise. The permission of the bhikkhus is already stated in the Udositaka training rule (sikkhāpada).

They say: "Except by the agreement of the Saṅgha—this is the subsequent rule (anupaññatti) here," and so forth. In that [previous rule], regarding the factors, the fourth factor was "staying apart during the night"; here, it is "staying apart for more than six nights"—this alone is the distinction.
The commentary on the training rule concerning danger is finished. 10.
Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning What Has Been Dedicated (Pariṇata-sikkhāpada).
"But surely this has been dedicated to the Saṅgha, it has not been relinquished; so how does it become the property of the Saṅgha?
To this he says, "For that... and so forth. Therein, "that" refers to the gain (*lābha*). "By one way" means by one way reckoned as the state of being dedicated.
By the word "to be obtained," he expresses the accusative derivation of the word *lābha*. "The object such as robes, etc."...
[This refers to] requisites for robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal supplies for the sick, down to even a lump of powder, a tooth-stick, or a thread for a fringe.
"Dedicated" (*pariṇata*) means it stands inclined toward the Saṅgha, sloping toward the Saṅgha, and leaning toward the Saṅgha;
such is the meaning. Having shown the reason by which it becomes dedicated, [the text explains] its purpose:
To demonstrate this, it is said: “We shall give,” “we shall do,” and so forth. “Of one who dedicates it to oneself” means:

having understood that the gift has been dedicated to the Saṅgha by saying, “Give this to me,” one takes it after having dedicated it to oneself. “In the act” means: in the act of dedication. And here [the formula is]:
“Venerable sir, this gain belonging to the Saṅgha, which I knowingly dedicated, but have now dedicated to myself, is to be relinquished.”
In this manner, the procedure for relinquishment (nissajjana) is to be understood.
Regarding the phrase "to the Saṅgha, a shrine, or an individual": here, any sentient being down to even a dog is to be understood as an "individual" (puggala).
"To another Saṅgha, etc. means to another Saṅgha, a shrine, or an individual. This is what is meant: "To the Saṅgha..."

"If one dedicates what has been dedicated to another Saṅgha, or to a shrine, or to an individual; or if one dedicates what has been dedicated to a shrine to another shrine, or to a Saṅgha, or to an individual;
or if one dedicates what has been dedicated to an individual to another individual, or to a Saṅgha, or to a shrine—there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who so dedicates."
Now, in order to show the non-offense, he said, “perceiving it as not yet dedicated,” and so forth. The connection is: “perceiving it as not yet dedicated, whether it is [actually] dedicated or not.
The meaning is that there is no offense in both cases—whether it is dedicated or not. For this has been stated:
“If one perceives what is dedicated as not yet dedicated and dedicates it for oneself, there is no offense. If one perceives what is not yet dedicated as not yet dedicated, there is no offense.”

“Gift-property” (*deyyadhamma*) refers to the four requisites. By the word “and so forth” (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of such statements as: “May it be for repair,” “May it endure for a long time,” or “Give it where your mind has faith.
However, if the donors say, “We wish to provide a meal for the Saṅgha, we wish to perform an offering at a shrine, [or] for a single bhikkhu...”
If they say, "We wish to give requisites; we shall give them according to your preference. Please tell us, where shall we give them?
then that bhikkhu should say, "Give them wherever you wish.
The commentary on the training rule concerning what has been dedicated is finished.
The Third Chapter on the Pāṭha.
Thus ends the *Līnatthappakāsanī*, the commentary on the *Vinayatthamañjūsā*,
which is a commentary on the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* exposition of the Pātimokkha.
The commentary on the Nissaggiya section is finished.
The Chapter on Offenses Entailing Confession (Pācittiya-khaṇḍa), Section 1: The Subsection on False Speech.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on False Speech (*Musāvāda-sikkhāpada*).
Regarding the term *sampajānamusāvāde*: here, *musa* refers to a matter that is non-existent and untrue; *vāda* refers to the making known of that [matter] as existent and true.
"False speech of one who is fully aware" (*sampajānamusāvāda*) means false speech committed by one who is fully aware; the meaning is "in regard to such false speech."
Therefore he said, "Previously," and so forth. Furthermore, that false speech occurs both at the prior stage and at the very moment [of speaking] for one who is aware of it;
for it has been stated: "First there is the thought, 'I shall speak falsely,' and while speaking, there is the thought, 'I am speaking falsely.
Thus he said, "Having known it previously, and knowing it at the moment of speaking. For these two factors constitute the essential conditions, whereas the other [factors] do not.
"Whether it be so or not, that is irrelevant. Is it not evident from the very act of speaking?"—to this he replied, "And as for what is called 'speaking,'" and so forth.
"Of that which has not occurred" means of that which is untrue.
"Hatthaka the Sakyan": here, *Hatthaka* is the name of that elder; "son of the Sakyans" (*sakyaputta*) means one who is a son of the Sakyans.
It is said that during the time of the Buddha, eighty thousand men from the Sakyan clan went forth into homelessness, and he was one of them.
Regarding the case of "denying what was done and then claiming it was done":
here, "denying what was done" refers to when, while conversing with members of other sects, perceiving some fault in one's own doctrine, one denies it by saying, "This is not my doctrine."
Furthermore, as he speaks again and again, perceiving his own faultlessness, he asserts, "This doctrine is mine alone.

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is included the denial after having admitted, the evasion by one thing or another, the speaking of deliberate falsehood, and the act of deceiving after making a prior agreement.
Now, for the purpose of showing the classification of offenses, it is said: "for the purpose of proclaiming a superhuman state," and so forth.
"Speaking hastily without reflection" means speaking impulsively without investigation, saying "I have not seen it" regarding what was actually seen, and so forth.

"Speaking one thing when intending to speak another" refers to one who, through dullness or delusion, stumbles and says "cloth" (*cīra*) when he ought to say "robe" (*cīvara*); this is one who speaks one thing while intending to speak another.
[This is] the name. However, when a novice asks, "Venerable sir, have you seen my preceptor?
and [the other person], while playing, says, "Your preceptor must have gone after yoking a wooden cart," or when, upon hearing the sound of a jackal, he is asked, "Whose sound is this?
and [he replies], "It is the sound of your mother going by carriage; her wheel has stuck in the mud..."
Whether he says, "This is the sound of those pulling [the boat]," or speaks otherwise in this manner—neither jokingly nor in jest—he still incurs an offense.

There is also what is called "irrelevant talk": for instance, one who, having obtained a little oil in the village, returns to the monastery and says to a novice, "Where have you been today? The whole village has become a single vat of oil," or using a basket...
Having received a piece of cake that was set aside [for another], to say, "Today, cakes are being distributed in the village by the handfuls," is indeed a falsehood.

Regarding "the state of having deception as one's primary concern": it is called *visaṃvādana* because they deceive (*visaṃ vādenti*) by means of it; it is the mind proceeding with the intention of cheating.
The state of having that as one's primary concern is "deception as one's primary concern" (*visaṃvādana-purekkhāratā*); the meaning is making the mind of deception the foremost priority.
The commentary on the training rule concerning false speech is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning abusive speech:
*Omasavāda* refers to words of reviling and censuring. For such speech is neither pleasant to the ear nor pleasant to the heart.
Therefore, he said, "in words that pierce," meaning "words that pierce both the ear and the heart";
what is meant is "words joined with [insults regarding] birth and so forth. Thus he said, "by name of birth," and so on.

Therein, "birth" (jāti) refers to high castes such as Brahmins, as well as low castes such as Caṇḍālas. "Name" (nāma) refers to low names such as Avakaṇṇaka, as well as high names such as Buddharakkhita.
Name: [This refers to] names such as Kosiya, which are low, and Gotama, which are high. Lineage: Lineage refers to low lineages such as Kosiya and high lineages such as Gotama. Occupation:

Occupation refers to low occupations such as flower-scavengers and high occupations such as agriculture and trade. Craft: Craft refers to low crafts such as reed-work and high crafts such as finger-calculation and arithmetic.
Illness: Illness refers to all diseases, which are indeed low; alternatively, diabetes (madhumeha) is considered high.

The remainder should be understood as inferior. "Physical appearance" (*liṅga*) refers to physical appearance that is either inferior, such as being excessively tall, or superior, such as not being excessively tall.

"Defilement" (*kilesa*) refers to all defilements, beginning with lust (*rāga*). "Offense" (*āpatti*) refers to offenses that are either superior, such as stream-entry (*sotāpatti*), or inferior, such as the defeats (*pārājika*).
"Abuse" (*akkosa*) refers to abuse that is either inferior, such as "you are a lipless one," or superior, such as "you are wise."
“In whatever way” (*yathā tathā*) means by any manner whatsoever regarding the words that have appeared or will appear in the Canon.

In this training rule (*sikkhāpada*), with the exception of the monk, all beings beginning with the nun are situated in the category of those not fully ordained; thus he said, “And here,” and so forth.

“For the sake of sport” (*davakamyatā*) means having the intention for play and laughter. “In all cases” (*sabbattha*) refers both to those who are fully ordained and those who are not, as well as to the words that have appeared or will appear in the Canon.
And so it is everywhere. Regarding the phrase *atthadhammānusāsanipurekkhārānaṃ*:

here, one who explains the meaning of a passage such as "You are a caṇḍāla" is said to have the meaning (*attha*) as their primary concern. One who recites the text (*pāḷi*) is said to have the Dhamma (*dhamma*) as their primary concern.

Standing upon the instruction, one should speak according to the method beginning with: "Even now you are a caṇḍāla; do not commit evil. Do not become one who goes from darkness to darkness. And so forth.
It should be understood that speaking [in this manner] is called "having instruction as the primary concern.
The commentary on the training rule concerning abusive speech is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning malicious talebearing.
"Bhikkhu-pesuñña" (slander by a bhikkhu): it is "pisuṇā" because it splits; that speech by which one causes beings who are in harmony to become divided into separate factions—that speech is *pisuṇā*.
That which is *pisuṇā* itself is *pesuñña*. One who is endowed with that speech is *pisuṇo*.
The action of such a person is *pesuñña*. "Bhikkhu-pesuñña" is the slander of a bhikkhu. Regarding that *bhikkhu-pesuñña*, [the offense arises] from a bhikkhu.
The meaning is: having heard [the slander], one conveys it to another bhikkhu, or conveys it to a bhikkhu. Therefore he said, "By means of birth and so forth," and so on.
Furthermore, he conveys it for two reasons; thus he said, "Out of a desire to be dear to a bhikkhu," and so on.
In that context, "out of a desire to be dear to a bhikkhu" means: [thinking] "In this way, I shall become dear to this bhikkhu to whom I am speaking."
"‘I shall be’" refers to the state of wishing for one's own dearness [to another].
"With the intention of causing a split" means desiring the separation of another from someone else by thinking, "In this way, he will be divided from him.

Alternatively, according to the method of etymology (*nirukti*), it is *pesuñña* because it makes one's dearness empty; that is, by whatever speech one speaks to someone, the state of one's own dearness [is removed] from that person's heart.
The speech that makes another empty (of virtue) is "slander against a bhikkhu" (*bhikkhupesuña*), and so forth;
this is how the meaning should be understood here. "In the manner already stated" refers to the manner stated by the phrase, "by means of the grounds for abuse such as birth, etc.
"In the application of abuse not found in the Canon" refers to the application of abuse such as "You are a thief," and so forth. "That which does not constitute a ground for abuse..."

However, they say: "For one who engages in slander, or for one who utters speech out of a desire for affection—even if no offense is seen under this training rule—there must nevertheless be an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
Regarding "one speaking for the purpose of censuring evil": having seen one person reviling another and another person forgiving them, [one says], "Oh, how shameless! Even such a thing as this..."
"Furthermore, he will think that you should be spoken to"—thus it was said by one speaking solely for the purpose of censuring evil.
The commentary on the training rule concerning malicious talebearing is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning the memorization of words.
"Should recite the Dhamma word by word" means he should recite the Dhamma one word after another; the meaning is that he should recite it section by section.

Since an offense does not apply only to one who recites word by word the Dhamma included in the three councils (*saṅgīti*), it is therefore said: "even that which has not been included in the three councils," and so forth.
By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the instruction on virtue (*sīla*), the ascetic practices (*dhutaṅga*), questions, and discourses on objects of meditation (*ārammaṇakathā*) are included.
This includes the inclusion of such works as the *Buddhikadaṇḍa*, the *Kaññāñāṇavatthu*, and the *Asubhakathā*. Regarding the *Meṇḍaka* and *Milindapañha*:

there is no offense when these are spoken by the Elder from his own inspired eloquence (*sakappaṭibhāna*). However, there is an offense regarding that which was spoken after being cited for the purpose of instructing the King.
These include the *Vaṇṇapiṭaka*, the *Aṅgulimālapiṭaka*, the *Raṭṭhapālagajjita*, the *Āḷavakagajjita*, the *Gūḷhamagga*, the *Gūḷhavessantara*, the *Gūḷhavinaya*, the *Vedallapiṭaka*, and so forth.
However, these are indeed non-Buddhist words.
Since that word is fourfold, it was stated—"in the word, the following-word, the syllable, and the phoneme"—in order to show this.
Therein, "word" (pada) refers to one quarter-verse of a stanza; "following-word" (anupada) refers to the second quarter-verse; "syllable" (anvakkhara) refers to...
"Each single syllable" (*ekaikaṃ akkharaṃ*). "A subsequent phoneme" (*anubyañjanaṃ*) refers to a subsequent phoneme that resembles the preceding phoneme;
or, any single syllable is a "syllable-by-syllable" (*anvakkharaṃ*). A collection of syllables is an "anubyañjana. A collection of syllables and *anubyañjanas* is a "phrase" (*padaṃ*).
The distinction here should be understood as follows: the first phrase is simply a "phrase" (*padam eva*), while the second is a "subsequent phrase" (*anupadaṃ*).

The connection is as follows: for one who recites any portion among these words and so forth together with persons other than a monk or a nun, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) according to the count of the words and so forth.

Herein, first regarding those in verse composition: for each single word such as "mental phenomena are preceded by the mind" (*manopubbaṅgamā dhammā*), [if recited] together with a novice (*sāmaṇera*...)*. *(Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated at this point. The translation reflects the available text.)*
For one who begins from one side and finishes from that same side, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) by counting the words.

When the Elder has said, "States are preceded by the mind," if a novice, not having reached that word, recites together with him at the time he says, "Mind is supreme, mind-made," there is an offense by counting each successive word.
At the time of saying, "Form is impermanent," and so forth, if [the novice] recites "Rū" together with him...
This applies even when one is merely reciting by counting each syllable. This same method applies to verses as well.

While reciting this Sutta, "Bhikkhus, form is impermanent; feeling is impermanent," when the Elder said, "Form is impermanent," the novice—due to his quick intelligence—uttered the word "impermanent" for "feeling" before the Elder had finished saying, "Form is impermanent."

If one utters the speech while reciting it together with this word "impermanent," it should be understood that for one who teaches in this manner, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) according to the count of the individual words (anubyañjana).

"Three offenses of expiation" refers to the cases of one who perceives a person as not fully ordained when they are indeed not fully ordained, one who is doubtful, and one who perceives them as fully ordained.

There are three *pācittiya* offenses. The connection [of the rule] is: there is no offense for one who recites together with a person not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*) when receiving a formal recitation (*uddesa*) together.
This same method applies here as well regarding "reciting" and "receiving a formal recitation in his presence. In this regard, the following is the analysis:
both the fully ordained and the not fully ordained sit down and cause [the teacher] to recite. The teacher [says]: "To those sitting..."

If he says, "I am speaking," and speaks together with them, there is an offense for the teacher alone. There is no offense for one who receives [the recitation] together with one who is not fully ordained.

The same rule applies if both are standing and receive it. If a young bhikkhu is sitting and a novice is standing, there is no offense for one who says, "I am speaking to the one who is sitting. If the young one stands and the other sits, [the same applies].

“I speak to one who is standing”: there is no offense even for one speaking [these words]. If a single novice (sāmaṇera) is sitting among many monks, there is an unintentional offense for one who recites the Dhamma word-by-word while he is sitting.
If the novice has moved out of the vicinity and is either standing or sitting, because he is not included among those to whom one is reciting, [the offense is] by one...
It is reckoned that one takes up a "bond of flight" by way of a particular direction; therefore, there is no offense. Regarding "reciting together":
this refers to reciting together with one who is not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*). Regarding "receiving instruction in his presence":
this refers to receiving instruction in the presence of one who is not fully ordained. Regarding "one who is reciting a text that is for the most part mastered": if...
If one quarter of a single verse does not come out while the remainder does, this is called "mostly familiar with the text.

This principle should be understood to apply both to one who recites the Sutta and to one who intones it in the midst of the assembly. "And for one who intones" means for one who recites the Sutta in the middle of the assembly.
The commentary on the training rule regarding sleeping in the same room as a woman is finished.
5. Commentary on the First Training Rule Regarding Sleeping in the Same Room:
Here, because of the statement, "With the exception of a bhikkhu, the rest is called 'one who is not fully ordained,'" even an animal is indeed one who is not fully ordained.
And yet, it is not every instance that serves as the basis for the offense of sexual intercourse; thus he said "at least" (*antamaso*), and so forth.
Its limit should be understood according to the method already explained regarding the offense of sexual intercourse. Regarding the phrase "two or three nights" (*dirattatiratta*):
here, no specific meaning is obtained from the word "two nights," but it is used merely for the sake of worldly convention and for the elegance of the phrasing.

It should be understood that it is stated thus because [the offense] has already mounted upon the mouth. However, the phrase "of two or three nights" is stated merely to show the literal meaning of the words;
or rather, it should be seen that the inclusion of the term "two nights" (*diratta*) is intended to indicate a continuous period of three nights.

"Lying down together" (*sahaseyya*) means lying down in one place. Furthermore, "lying down" (*seyyā*) refers to the act of reclining characterized by the stretching out of the body, as in the expression "reclining is lying down."

Having considered that, and having also considered the lodging where they lie as "a bed" (seyyā) because "they lie here," both of these are taken here in a general sense, or by the method of "single remainder" (ekasesa-naya);
thus he said, "whether entirely covered or partially covered," and so forth.
In that regard, a lodging which has five types of coverings above, or any other whatsoever, even if it be merely a cloth—

"Completely roofed and completely enclosed" means that it is entirely covered from the ground up to the roof, or even if not reaching the roof, it is surrounded by a wall one and a half cubits high at its very least, or by anything else—even just a cloth—on all sides;
this is what is called "completely roofed and completely enclosed. However, for that which has more [open space] above...
A place that is mostly covered, with little uncovered;
mostly enclosed on all sides, with little unenclosed—this is called "mostly covered and mostly enclosed. In such a place that is entirely covered and enclosed, or mostly covered and enclosed.
“Vidaheyya” means he would do; and since that consists in actually accomplishing it, he says “sampādeyya” (he would accomplish). This is the summarized meaning here:
“Having entered upon the reclining known as a lodging, he would arrange, dispose, and accomplish the reclining known as the stretching out of the body.
It should be one and a half cubits high, measured by the carpenter’s cubit. “Ekūpacāro” (one common access) means:

This was said with reference to the unity of the access door (*valañjanadvāra*). The connection is: "Or, a four-sided hall (*catusāla*) with a hundred rooms may have a single common approach (*ekūpacāra*).

In that context, "or" (*vā*) means either in that very same lodging where one stayed on the preceding day, or elsewhere in a similar place—that is, in another lodging not previously stayed in that possesses the aforementioned characteristics.
"Or by that": either by that same [person] with whom he was ordained on each preceding day; "or by another":
or by someone other than the one with whom he was ordained on each preceding day. "In brief" means a concise commentary.
To the question, "If this is so, how is the detailed exposition to be understood?", he says: "But the detailed exposition... and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in cases such as half-covered or almost entirely covered," the word "etc. (*ādi*) includes those cases mentioned in the *Aṭṭhakathā*:
"There is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for what is completely covered and slightly open; there is an offense of wrong-doing for what is mostly covered and slightly open;
there is an offense of wrong-doing for what is completely enclosed and slightly open; there is an offense of wrong-doing for what is mostly enclosed and slightly open."

"Having departed before dawn on the third night and returning again"—this means having departed before sunrise on the third night and having caused the sun to rise outside [the monastery], he returns again on the fourth day when the sun has set.
Regarding the phrase "in cases where it is entirely covered, entirely uncovered, etc.," here the word "etc. includes "entirely enclosed."
This includes the cases recorded in the *Pāḷi* as "completely covered," "mostly covered," and "mostly not enclosed," as well as those recorded in the *Aṭṭhakathā* as:
"there is no offense if it is half-covered and partially enclosed; there is no offense if it is half-enclosed and partially covered;
and there is no offense if it is both partially covered and partially enclosed."
The commentary on the first training rule regarding sleeping together is finished.
6. Commentary on the second training rule regarding sleeping together:
"A human woman" means a living human woman. However, although a dead woman is indeed a basis for an offense entailing expulsion (*pārājika*), [she is not included here].
They say that because she remains on the side of those who are not subject to clinging (*anupādinnapakkhe*), she does not incur the offense of sleeping together.
However, there is no offense in the case of *yakkhinīs* or *petīs* whose forms are invisible, nor in the case of a female animal who is not a suitable object for sexual intercourse.
"On the first day as well" means that, unlike the first training rule (*sikkhāpada*), it is not only on the fourth day; rather, here it applies even on the first day.
The meaning: by this, he shows that there is no time limit of a single day here. Furthermore, regarding the constituent factors (*aṅga*), it should be understood that there is this distinction:
the lodging has the nature of an offense of expiation (*pācittiya-vatthu*); therein, lying down together with a woman; and the setting of the sun—these are the three factors.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning sleeping together is finished.

7. Commentary on the Training Rule on Teaching the Dhamma "By six or five utterances" means by six or five words. Regarding how the delimitation of an "utterance" (vācā) is to be understood here, he says:
"Beyond six or five utterances," and so forth. "In all instances" refers to both the Sutta and the Aṭṭhakathā. If it is the Aṭṭhakathā...
If he wishes to recite a verse from the *Dhammapada* or a narrative from the *Jātaka* collection and so forth, it is permissible for him to recite only six words.
When reciting together with the canonical text (*pāḷi*), he should speak without exceeding six words—namely, one word from the canon and five from the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).
By the phrase "by a man," he means by a human male. Therefore, he said: "But having taken a human form," and so on.
“Three *pācittiya*s” means there are three *pācittiya* offenses according to whether one perceives a woman as a woman, is doubtful about her, or perceives her as not being a woman.

Or, regarding “another woman”: if one has taught [the Dhamma] to one woman while sitting, and another woman arrives later, it is likewise permissible for one sitting on a single seat to teach even a hundred women. “To a conscious human female.”
There is no offense for one who teaches even to a woman who does not understand, provided there is no change of posture.

"Absence of a change of posture" means the absence of a change of posture either on the part of oneself or on the part of the woman. "Absence of a kappiyakāraka" means the absence of a knowledgeable kappiyakāraka;
what is meant is the absence of a human being possessing the characteristics described in the second *niyata* rule. Regarding the term "action-non-action" (*kiriyā-akiriya*) here:

It should be understood that teaching the Dhamma with more than five or six words constitutes an act (*kiriya*), whereas not accepting a person who makes things allowable (*kappiyakāraka*) constitutes a non-act (*akiriya*).
The commentary on the training rule regarding the teaching of the Dhamma is concluded.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding the Proclamation of Truth (*bhūtārocanasikkhāpada*).

"Directly" (*nippariyāyena*) means straightway, as in "He attained the first jhāna," and so forth. "Communicated by way of a circuitous route" (*pariyāyena ārocitaṃ*) means spoken by means of an indirect designation, as in "The monk who lived in that monastery attained the first jhāna, is attaining it, or has attained it," and so forth.
However, at the time of his final *parinibbāna*, or even while being dragged along in the interim, for one who is fully ordained...
It is permissible to report what is true. Even if one is not being dragged along by others, it is likewise permissible to report it when such a reason exists.
For this very reason, a certain elder, having been reproached by another young bhikkhu, said: "Friend, do not exert yourself for the sake of the higher paths;
you have been reproaching one who is an arahant. And the elder [said]: "Friend, do you have [any basis] in this..."
When asked, "Are you established in the Teaching?", the young bhikkhu replied, "Yes, venerable sir, I am a stream-enterer.

Even though they know, "This person is a doer [of the practice]," the Noble Ones nevertheless reveal themselves for the purpose of inspiring and gladdening others by showing that the practice is not in vain.
Therefore he said: "When such a cause exists, one who has been ordained should announce it."
However, it is permissible to announce one’s virtue of training in the scriptures and morality even to one who is not ordained.

As for the question, "Why are those such as the insane not included here? he says, "Because... and so forth. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), those with deranged minds and those afflicted by pain are included.
"When that exists" means when the state of being insane and so forth exists. "Not included here" means not included in the word-commentary (*padabhājaniya*) of this training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
It is not included. "Without consciousness" (*acittaka*) means without consciousness due to the absence of the consciousness that knows the designation (*paṇṇatti*).
The statement, "With two types of consciousness—wholesome or indeterminate," is said with reference specifically to noble persons (*ariyapuggala*) as the highest possible limit;

for it is not the case that worldlings (*puthujjana*), even those who have attained meditative absorption (*jhāna*), would fail to report [an offense] regarding an object even with an unwholesome mind driven by greed, provided they do not know the designation.
Alternatively, it should be understood that this was stated in order to make it consistent with the expression "two feelings," because of the absence of painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*).
The commentary on the training rule regarding the disclosure of what has occurred is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule regarding the disclosure of what is grave (*duṭṭhullārocanasikkhāpada*).
"Of the two classes of offenses" means of the two classes of offenses known as *pārājika* and *saṅghādisesa*.

"For the sake of restraint in the future" means: "In this way, through shame and fear of wrongdoing toward others, he will attain restraint in the future"—thus it is for the sake of restraint in the future.
"Having made a limit for the offenses and for the families, or not having made one" means: "This many..."
"Confessions of offenses are to be announced; they are to be announced to so many families"—thus, whether a limit has been set for the offenses and the families or not.
"For a non-grave offense" means for an offense classified among the remaining five groups of offenses, excluding the *pārājika* and *saṅghādisesa*.
"The remaining six groups of offenses" refers to the six remaining groups, excluding the *saṅghādisesa*.

Regarding the classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*): "Gross offense" (*duṭṭhulla*) refers to the transgression of the first five training rules (*sikkhāpada*), namely, the violation of the first five precepts beginning with abstaining from taking life.

"The other," meaning non-gross or mere transgression (*ajjhācāra*), refers to the other group of five beginning with eating at improper times, as well as seminal emission, bodily contact, gross misconduct, and seeking one's own pleasure.
Or a non-gross transgression. "The mere basis" refers to one who reports merely the basis, such as:
"This person has committed an emission of semen," or "He has committed a gross act," or "He has committed an act for his own pleasure," or "He has committed bodily contact.
"The mere offense" refers to one who reports: "This person has committed a *pārājika*," or "a *saṅghādisesa*," or "a *thullaccaya*," or "a *pācittiya*," or "a *pāṭidesanīya*," or "a *dukkaṭa*."
"Has he fallen into an offense of wrong speech?"—thus it is for one who reports merely the nature of the offense. "Of the characteristics as stated":
there is doubt regarding the phrase "one who has not committed a *pārājika*. (8. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Reporting of Grave Matters. "Of the characteristics as stated" means:
"Savatthuka" (with a basis) means joined together with the basis (*vatthu*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning the disclosure of a grave offense is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning digging the earth:
Regarding the phrase "on stones, pebbles, potsherds, gravel, sand, and so forth," here it should be understood that "stones" refers to those larger than the size of a fist.
"Gravel" is the size of a fistful. "Potsherds" are fragments of broken pottery. "Marumba" is coarse sand. "Sand" is simply fine sand.
"It becomes a third part for someone else" means it becomes a third portion. This is what is meant:
when, having had earth or clay brought, two separate portions are made—one of earth or clay [and the other of the aforementioned materials].
Or it may consist of one or another of such things as stones; this is what is called "mixed earth. "Covered" (*ovaṭṭha*) means covered by rain from the sky.

"Stated" (*vutta*) means stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājaniya*), or else stated in the Sinhalese commentary itself. "Mixed with a greater amount of stones, etc. means mixed with a greater amount of stones and so forth;
the intended meaning is that even if it has not been burnt, it is mixed with a greater amount of stones, etc., than the previously mentioned measure.
The word *vā* has the sense of an unstated alternative; by it, the earth that has been solid for less than four months is included.

Regarding the phrase "of the various kinds such as pure stone": pure stones are found there, thus it is "pure-stone"; that which has this as its first [member] of the classification is "the classification beginning with pure stone.

By the word *ādi* (etcetera), pure gravel and so forth are included. That which has the classification beginning with pure stone is "the one characterized by the classification beginning with pure stone"; by that [earth].
The meaning is: “consisting of various kinds such as plain stones,” etc.;

“he digs himself” means that here, even one who digs with only his big toe, or breaks [the ground] while throwing out water, or scratches it with his big toe, or burns a leaf while cooking—it should be understood that all such persons are indeed digging.
Therefore he said: "It disturbs [the earth] by digging, breaking, scratching, cooking, and so forth. For one who cooks in a pan, one must cook in the very place where it was previously cooked.
It is not permitted to place fire on ground that has not been scorched; however, it is permitted to place fire above the pan or the cooking vessel.
If one places it upon the wood, that fire, burning those pieces, will proceed [to the spot].
To burn the earth is not permitted. The same principle applies to bricks, stones, and so forth;

for even in those cases, it is only permissible to place [the fire] on top of the bricks and such. Why? Because they are not fuel (*anupādāna*). Indeed, those things do not count as fuel for the fire.
It is also not permitted to set fire to dry stumps, trees, and the like. However, if [it is placed] without reaching the ground...
If one gives [the material] thinking, "I will extinguish it later," it is permissible. If one is unable to extinguish it afterwards, there is no offense because it was outside one's capacity.
"By the same method already stated" means by the very method stated as "by digging, breaking, scratching, cooking, and so forth.
"Having determined" means having made a resolution. "The other" refers to the one who gives the command.
If one says, “Dig a lotus pond,” it is permissible. Only when it has been dug does it truly become a “lotus pond”;
therefore, this is a permissible expression (*kappiyavohāra*). The same principle applies to such phrases as “Dig a reservoir (*vāpī*), a lake (*taḷāka*), or a pit (*āvāṭa*).
However, it is not permissible to say, “Dig this spot; dig a lotus pond in this spot. Likewise, one may say, “Dig a bulbous root (*kanda*); dig a root (*mūla*).”

It is permissible to speak without specifying [the location]. It is not permissible to say, "Dig this creeper; dig for a bulb or a root in this spot. Therefore he said: "For one who speaks without specifying the location... and so forth. When mud dries up in the sun, it cracks;
in that case, it is permissible to remove only that which is no longer connected to the earth below. This is the same principle.
Also in the case of *gokaṇṭaka*. Therefore he said: “by the heat... [etc. ...unconnected. In this context, *gokaṇṭaka* refers to mud cut by the hooves of cows.
However, if it is connected to the ground by its lower surface, it is not permitted to disturb it.
“A riverbank that has broken and fallen” means a riverbank that has collapsed and fallen near a river, having been eroded for less than four months.
If, however, it breaks and remains naturally in the water, it is permissible even if the rain has fallen for more than four months, because it has fallen into water and thus remains in water.

"Even a large clod of earth severed by a plough" refers to even a large clod of earth that has been cut off by a plough in a ploughed area and is not connected to the ground below. By the phrase "and so forth," [clods of] thin mud suitable for pouring over a peak and the like are included.

Regarding "seizing": for one who breaks [the earth] by rolling a tree or similar object—meaning either by rolling stones, trees, and so forth, or by repeatedly striking with a wooden staff—the earth breaks.
Since it was not intentionally broken with the thought, "I shall break it by this means," it is called "broken unintentionally. Thus, by rolling a tree or similar object unintentionally...
There is no offense for one who is breaking [something]. Regarding "scratching with the toes or the like while absent-minded":

if one stands scratching the earth with a toe or a walking stick while distracted and conversing with someone about something else, there is no offense for such a person scratching with the toes or the like while in that state of absent-mindedness.
The commentary on the training rule concerning digging the earth is finished.
The first section, the Chapter on False Speech, is concluded.
2. The Chapter on Living Plants.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Plants (*Bhūtagāma-sikkhāpada*).
By the word "are becoming" (*bhavanti*), he indicates young shrubs that have developed roots and are growing by attaining a green state.
By the word "have been" (*ahesuṃ*), however, he indicates large trees, shrubs, and so forth that have grown and remain established. Therefore, he said "they are being born" (*jāyanti*), and so on.

And here, the explanation of "bhavanti" (they come to be) is "jāyanti vaḍḍhanti" (they are born and grow), and that of "ahesuṃ" (they were) is "jātā vaḍḍhitā" (born and grown). "Gāmo" means a collection.
"Of the green grass, trees, and so forth established on the ground" refers to the green grass established upon the earth as well as the green trees and so on.
By the word "ādi" (and so forth), medicinal herbs, shrubs, creepers, and the like are to be understood.

The locative case is used here in the sense of "on account of" (*nimittatthe*). That which constitutes the object [of the offense] is expressed by the phrase “on account of the destruction of the community of living beings” (*bhūtagāmapātabyatāya*) and so forth.
Now, one might ask: are not trees and the like not "living beings" (*jīva*) because they lack consciousness?

And their lack of consciousness should be understood from the absence of throbbing, from the fact that they continue to grow even when cut, from their being of a different species [from sentient beings], and from their not being included within the four modes of birth (*catuyoni*). Furthermore, [their lack of growth...]
However, since [the capacity for] sensation exists even in coral, stones, and salt, these are not reasons for their being living beings;
and their grasping of objects is a mere mental construction, like the sleep of *ciñcā* trees and the like, as are their longings and so forth.

Then why is it that destroying a "community of elements" (*bhūtagāma*) is intended to be an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)? Because it is unbecoming for a recluse and because it protects the sentient beings dependent upon them.
For this very reason, it says: “Foolish men, perceiving a living being in a tree,” and so forth.
“Even a moss-encrustation the size of a mustard seed” means even a moss-encrustation known as a mustard-seed-sized one; that is, a mustard-moss or a seed-moss—this is the meaning.
Therein, “mustard-moss” refers to a tiny moss the size of a mustard seed. “Seed-moss” refers to a moss with a small leaf on top and a small root below.
Regarding the phrase "root-seeds, stem-seeds, joint-seeds, crown-seeds, and seed-seeds": here, that which is a root itself as a seed is a "root-seed" (*mūlabīja*).

The same applies to the remaining types. Among these, the root-seed consists of turmeric and the like; the stem-seed consists of the *assattha* tree and the like; the joint-seed consists of sugarcane and the like;
the crown-seed consists of *hirivera* grass and the like; and the seed-seed consists of paddy and the like. "Contained in a vessel" means contained in a vessel such as a bowl.
"From which only the root has emerged" means *nikkhantamūlamattaṃ*. Here, by the word *matta* ("only" or "mere"), the emergence of the leaf is excluded.
This same method applies to the expression *nikkhantaaṅkuramattaṃ* as well.
However, if both the root and the leaf have emerged, it is reckoned as a "grove of living beings" (*bhūtagāma*). [The text continues: "A stalk of leaves the measure of a span emerges."
A leaf-sheath, one span in length and not blue in color, emerges. Therefore he said, "When it has emerged," and so forth. "It is not green" means it is not blue in color.

However, when the leaves of mung beans and the like have sprouted, or when the shoots of rice and the like are green, they are included within the category of the "grove of living beings" (*bhūtagāma*).
This same principle applies to mango stones and other such things.

Regarding the phrase "the class of living beings and the class of seeds": here, it should be understood that the "class of seeds" refers to roots and other types of seed-propagation that are capable of growing, even when separated from the "class of living beings.

Regarding the phrase "in both cases": this refers to the classes of living beings and seeds. Regarding the phrase "one who perceives them as such": this refers to one who perceives what are not living beings or seeds as being living beings or seeds.

What need is there to mention the case of one who perceives what are not living beings or seeds as being not living beings or seeds? Regarding the phrase "unintentionally": this refers to stones, trees, and so forth.
Or for one who is shaking [the grass], or pulling a branch, or walking while striking the ground with a walking stick, the grasses are disturbed.
Since he did not intentionally disturb them with the thought, "I shall disturb them," they are said to have been disturbed unintentionally.
Thus, there is no offense for one who disturbs them unintentionally.

"Without mindfulness" means: being distracted by something else, while conversing with someone, he stands disturbing grass or a creeper with his big toe or his hand; for one who disturbs it thus without mindfulness, there is no offense.
"Not knowing" means: herein, internally he does not know whether it is "a seed-plot" or "a living-plant community," but he does know, "I am disturbing it.
Thus, [if he acts] upon grass or a heap of straw for the purpose of protecting a spade or a hoe...
He places it down, or he throws fire onto a burning hand. In that case, if grass is cut or burned, there is no offense for one who disturbs it without knowing [the consequences].
"By any kind of fire" means by any fire whatsoever, such as a wood-fire, a cow-dung-fire, and so forth, even including a piece of iron.
"By one who has kindled [the fire]. "Having said 'It is allowable' (kappiya)" means having said "it is allowable" in whatever language.
By the word *eva* (only), it is shown that it is not permissible to say "it is allowable" after first touching it with fire.
However, they say: "But it is permissible if, having first set down the fire, one says 'it is allowable' without picking it up again."

This same principle applies to the rest as well. "In the same way" means having said "it is allowable" (*kappiya*). However, because the hooves of donkeys, buffaloes, pigs, deer, and oxen are too sharp, one should not perform [the preparation] with them;
even if performed, it is as if not done. Therefore, he said, "except for the hooves of oxen, buffaloes, and so forth.
But elephant claws are not [considered] hooves, therefore it is permissible to use them. Regarding "of animals" (*tiracchānānaṃ*):
Of lions, tigers, leopards, monkeys, and birds—for their claws are sharp, therefore it must be made with them.

By the phrase “even by what has been brought after being cut,” he shows that there is nothing further to be said here regarding the fact that it must be made with those things suitable for making it that grow in that very place.
By the phrase “in the same manner as stated for the knife,” [he indicates] the cutting.
This refers by extension to what was stated [in the Vinaya]: "by one who intends to show [the food] or to pierce [it], it must be said, 'It is allowable' (kappiyaṃ).

And here, although the manner in which the allowable [food] must be made allowable by the one performing the act has been shown through such statements as "it must be done only after saying, 'It is allowable,'" nevertheless, when a monk says, "Make it allowable," it must be said "It is allowable" by the one not fully ordained (anupasampanna).

"Prepared by fire" and so forth should be understood as things that must be accepted. However, the reason for not mentioning [the phrase] "Make it allowable once more" is that it was already stated previously that one should consume it only after having had it made allowable.
When one thing... [etc. ...has been made allowable, everything becomes made allowable; thus, even with the intention of making only one thing "allowable," [it suffices].
When it has been made allowable (*kappiya*), because it is joined as one, everything is considered made. "He pierces a piece of wood":

whether he knows it or not, if he pierces it or causes it to be pierced, it is indeed permissible. "He pierces a grain of rice": here too, the same principle applies. "He pierces that; it is not permissible":
the intention is that creepers and the like fall under the category of vessels (*bhājana*). Having caused it to be split...
“*Kappiyaṃ kāretabbaṃ* (it must be made allowable)” is said because a husk that is free from seeds belongs to the category of vessels.
“Seedless” refers to young mango fruits and the like, which are devoid of seeds capable of producing sprouts. Therefore he said: “But whatever fruit is young is seedless.
“A seed that has been produced” means a seed that, having been produced [from the fruit], can be separated and consumed independently.

[This refers to] fruits such as mangoes and breadfruit. Therefore he said: "Having removed the seed, they may be consumed. In this case, there is no requirement for the formal act of making them allowable (*kappiyakaraṇa*);
the intention is that they are themselves allowable.
The commentary on the training rule concerning plants (*bhūtagāma-sikkhāpada*) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Speaking Otherwise (*Aññavādaka-sikkhāpada*).

"Whatever matter" (*yamatthaṃ*) refers to any matter such as, "It seems you have committed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," and so forth. "Something else than that" (*tato aññaṃ*) means another matter different from the matter asked about.
"Of evading one thing with another" (*aññenaññaṃ paṭicaraṇassa*) refers to the speech by which the holder of the Vinaya [evasive].
This was stated for the purpose of inquiring about the fault; otherwise, it would be concealed by another statement.
For the root *car* also has the sense of "concealing," due to the multivalence of verbal roots (*dhātu*). "Stated" means stated in the Pāḷi.
Regarding the phrase "he has fallen into an offense with remainder": here, excluding the *pārājika*, the remaining offenses are called "with remainder. That...
"Has committed an offense. "Being questioned" means being asked, "Friend, have you committed such-and-such an offense?
"With other words" means with other words such as, "Who has committed [an offense]? What has been committed? In what has one committed? How has one committed?
Whom are you speaking of? What are you saying? "Another" refers to [questions] such as, "Have you committed such-and-such an offense? and so forth.
This is the statement regarding one who persists in evasion. "He distracts in such and such a way" means he distracts by various means. What is meant?
When he sees some transgression and is being questioned about the offense in the midst of the Saṅgha, saying, "Friend, you have fallen into an offense," he says, "Who has fallen?
Then, when it is said, "You," he replies, "What have I fallen into?"
Then, when it is said, "It is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) or an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," he says, "In what have I fallen?
When it is then said, "In such-and-such a matter," he asks, "How have I fallen? What was I doing when I fell?
Then, when it is said, "By doing this very thing you fell," he says, "Whom are you speaking of? Thereupon, [they say], "We are speaking of you."
When this has been said, it means that he distracts [the Sangha] in many ways, asking, "What are you saying? Furthermore, the connection is as follows:
a monk who has committed an offense with a remainder (*sāvasesa-āpatti*), not wishing to speak about it, harasses [the Sangha] by remaining silent.
"Harasses" means that through sitting for a long time and speaking at length, he causes the Sangha distress by means of backache, dryness of the palate, and so forth.
"Viheseti" means he causes them distress; for "vihesā" is indeed defined as distress (*parissama*).

"Aññavādaka-kamma" is a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*) that must be performed against a monk who speaks otherwise, for the purpose of charging him with speaking otherwise.
The same principle applies here to "vihesaka-kamma. "Tasmiṃ saṅghena kate" refers to when that *aññavādaka-kamma* and *vihesaka-kamma* have been performed by the Saṅgha.

And it was performed by the Saṅgha through a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*). Regarding the phrase "those who act in such a manner": it means those who act in that way;
the meaning is "those who speak otherwise (*aññavādaka*) and those who cause vexation (*vihesaka*).
