As for the statement, "‘Causing vexation’ is here an after-rule (*anupaññatti*)," this is not so, because [the offense] constitutes an actual transgression within the training rules concerning speaking otherwise and so forth.
It is understood precisely because it is stated as "viyā" (having known). This same method applies to the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) that follow.

Regarding "three *pācittiya* offenses in the case of a legitimate legal act" (*dhammakamma*): there are three *pācittiya* offenses based on one who perceives a legitimate legal act as such, one who is doubtful, and one who perceives it as an illegitimate legal act (*adhammakamma*).

Regarding "three *dukkaṭa* offenses in the case of an illegitimate legal act": the same method applies here as well. Regarding "not having been charged": by means of the formal proclamation (*kammavācā*).
"Not placed" means not established; "by illness" means by such a disease in the mouth that one is unable to speak.

"There will be quarrels and so forth for the Saṅgha" means that if it is spoken in the midst of the Saṅgha, because of that, there will arise for the Saṅgha quarreling, or strife, or contention, or dispute, or schism in the Saṅgha, or a rift in the Saṅgha.
Or, it is for one who does not speak with this intention. And here, "by means of what is contrary to the Dhamma" means by means of a false matter.

Having extended the application of the origin and other factors without distinction—stating that they are similar to those of taking what is not given—it was said, "But this," and so forth, in order to show the specific difference. It may be an act (*kiriya*) for one who evades one thing with another; it may be a non-act (*akiriya*) for one who harasses by remaining silent.
The commentary on the training rule concerning speaking otherwise is finished.

3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Slandering (Ujjhāpanaka-sikkhāpada) "By which speech" means by that speech such as, "Out of favoritism (*chandā*), so-and-so is doing this and that. Therefore, he said, "Out of favoritism," and so forth.
In that context, "out of favoritism" means through partiality or bias. [This is seen] in such passages as, "He teaches the syllables," and so on.

This is a transposition of genders (*liṅgavipallāsa*). The meaning is that one prepares excellent lodgings or food and so forth for those who are personally seen or trusted, thinking, "I shall do this for them.

In the phrase "the division of the assigner of lodgings and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes the designator of meals, the distributor of rice-gruel, the distributor of fruits, and others. This is because verbal roots have multiple meanings.
The word *jhe* also has the sense of looking; thus he says, "causing them to look with contempt. Or, it should be understood as having the sense of thinking;
thus he says, "or causing them to think it is base. "Speaking likewise" means speaking such things as, "Out of favoritism, so-and-so is doing this," and so forth.
"Stated" means stated in the Pāḷi. "In cases of disparaging" (*khiyyanake*)—this is an addition to the rule (*anupaññatti*) in this context.
"Of one not authorized" means of one not authorized by the Saṅgha through a formal act (*kammavācā*). The intention is:
of one upon whom the burden has been placed by the Saṅgha simply with the words "This is your burden"; or of one who carries the burden himself for the sake of the monks' comfortable dwelling;
or of one who performs such an act where two or three monks reside. Of whom...
"Of anyone" means of anyone at all, whether fully ordained (*upasampanna*) or not fully ordained (*anupasampanna*).

Regarding the phrase "of one who is not fully ordained, whether authorized or unauthorized": although it is not permitted to grant the thirteen types of authorization to one who is not fully ordained, nevertheless, if someone had obtained an authorization at the time they were fully ordained and later became one who is not fully ordained...
With reference to one who is so appointed, it is said, "or of one who is authorized.

However, with reference to a competent novice for whom the burden has been assigned simply by the Saṅgha or by an authorized monk, saying, "You should perform this act," it is said, "or of one who is not authorized.
Since both censuring and reviling proceed by way of false speech, [they are included here].
Therefore, it should be understood that for a first-time offender, there is no offense by this rule alone; however, there is indeed an offense by way of false speech.
The commentary on the training rule concerning inciting others to complain is finished.
4. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Lodgings.
"Or a bed" means any kind of bed among these four: one made of acacia wood, one with a stuffed cushion, one with legs shaped like crabs, or one with detachable legs.
"Or a chair" follows the same principle here as well. "Or a mattress" means any kind of mattress among these five:
a wool mattress, a cotton mattress, a grass mattress, a straw mattress, or a leaf mattress. Therefore he said:
“On beds, etc. and so forth. Therein, by the phrase “by way of a contraction of ‘bed’,” he excludes the contraction of “bench.

“By suitable leather” means by the leather of deer or goats. Here, however, regarding deer-leather, only the leather of these [species] is permitted: the eni-deer, the vāta-deer, the pasada-deer, the kuruṅga-deer, the migamātuka, and the rohita-deer; but as for others—
"The monkey and the black lion, the sarabha and the kadali-deer;
whatever wild beasts there may be—their skins are not permitted.
In this context, "wild beasts" refers to lions, tigers, leopards, and hyenas. And it is not only these; rather, [it refers to] those whose skins...

It is stated that [these] are permitted; excluding those, all the rest—even down to cows, buffaloes, hares, cats, and so forth—should be understood as "wild beasts" (*vāḷamiga*) in this context. For the hides of all these are not permitted.
A *tālīsapatta* is pure *tamāla* leaf; however, if mixed with something else, it is permitted. Among grasses and bark-cloth, there is nothing called "unallowable."
But why is it that here, as with a bolster (*bibbohana*), sitting and lying down are not permitted? To this he says, "In that regard," and so forth. And this is not the only [restriction];
thus he says, "Furthermore, there is no fixed limit of measurement here," meaning that there is no restriction on the size of the mattress (*bisi*) such that it must be made only of this much.
There are: the bed-mattress, the chair-mattress, the floor-covering mattress, the walking-path mattress, and the foot-wiping mattress.
Having observed these [robes] according to their suitability, one should determine their size according to one’s own preference.
"Bound by being folded inside" means it is bound after being well-wrapped in the middle, so that the center is contracted.
This is connected with the phrase "those eight months. "The sign of the end of the rains" is the explanation of that very term; "the months of the rains" refers to the same.
"Thus unknown" means not well-known or not established. There is also a reading "asaññitā," in which case the meaning is "unrecognized.
"Eight months" refers to four winter months and four summer months, making eight months in total.
"In a shed that leaks" means in any kind of shed made of branches or wooden planks where rain can enter. "In which" refers to those countries.

"In all places" means in all countries. "At the foot of a tree where crows and others have a fixed dwelling" means at the base of any tree whatsoever where crows, owls, or other birds habitually reside by building their nests.
However, it does not refer to a place where birds, intent on foraging, merely rest before departing.

It is proper to deposit it at the foot of that tree. By the phrase "even at any time," he shows that this applies not only to a formal agreement (*vassika-saṅketa*). "Where" means in which place; "when" means at which time;
"he" refers to the one for whose sake the sitting mat was prepared. "On a natural sitting mat" means on one that is naturally prepared, which has not been [prepared] by oneself.
"It was spread by oneself, not caused to be spread by another"—this is what is meant by that statement.
"He is conscientious" means he is of a nature to feel shame; the meaning is that he is afraid of the destruction of requisites.

Therefore he said, "He regards it as his own impediment," by which he shows that it is not permissible for one who lacks conscience to depart without asking permission. "Without expectation" means [without the thought], "I will come back and remove it."
“Free from expectation”: by this it is shown that if one goes while having expectation, there is no offense.
For it is for this very reason that in the section on non-offenses it is said, “he goes while shading [him]. “Going elsewhere” means going elsewhere after having passed beyond that path.
Because he stands outside the range of a clod’s throw, it is said, “he should be made to pay [the fine] by the measure of a footstep,” whereas elsewhere—
The meaning is that for one who is walking away, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) upon lifting the first foot, and an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) upon lifting the second foot.

There are three types of offenses of expiation based on the cases of [the robe] belonging to the Saṅgha, perceiving it as belonging to the Saṅgha, being doubtful about it, and perceiving it as belonging to an individual.

In this same manner, the threefold wrong-doing should also be understood. The meaning regarding the *cimilika* (foot-wiping cloth) and so forth has already been shown in the second training rule. Regarding the foot-wiping mat (*pādapuñchanī*).
A *rajju* is a foot-wiping cloth made from ropes or rags. A wooden bench (*phalakapīṭha*) is a bench made of wood.

He said, "or whatever else," etc., to show that it is not only for leaving behind items such as mats (*cimilika*) and so forth when departing from an open space that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
The connection is: "whatever kind of wooden vessel" and "whatever kind of earthenware vessel."
By the phrase “even down to a bowl-rest,” he shows that there is nothing at all to be said regarding palm-leaf fans, leaf-fans, water-vessels, water-pots, or conch-shells.
For those dwelling in leaf-huts in the forest, people whose minds are inspired by their perfection of virtue provide beds, chairs, and so forth.
Regarding the instruction, “Use it as communal property for the Saṅgha,” the question arises: what should be done in that case? To this he says, “But by one who is a forest-dweller,” and so forth.
In that context, “in the absence of a rain-shelter” means when there is no place such as a mountain slope or similar site that serves as a shelter from the rain.
This is a definition intended to apply even when “there is an absence of those who are like-minded. For a forest-dwelling bhikkhu, having stayed there [in the rain-shelter], may then go elsewhere.

While departing, one should send for the monks in the neighboring monasteries before going. In the absence of those who are compatible [in conduct], one should deposit the items in a place sheltered from rain and then depart.
If there is no such sheltered place, one should hang them on a tree and then depart.
He said "or in whatever way" and so forth to indicate that it is not only by doing this specific act that it is permissible to go. Or, in the case of termites...
"It is not gnawed" means that just as a dwelling place, when left unattended, is not gnawed by termites, so too it is by placing [the bedding] upon stones;

this is the meaning. This is what is intended: having placed a bed on four stones, having stacked the remaining beds and stools upon that bed, and having made a heap of mattresses and so forth on top, [one places] wooden articles and earthenware articles [therein].
"Having put things in order and fulfilled the duties of one going on a journey, one may depart.

Even for one who dwells in the open air, thinking "I am a strict open-air dweller," it is not permitted to sit or lie down in the open at an improper time without having even made a small shelter for his robes;
showing this, he said, "by one who dwells in the open air," and so forth.

But if, even with a robe made of four layers, he is unable to protect the hut from being destroyed, and rains lasting seven days or similar calamities occur, it is permissible because the monk must follow his body [to ensure its safety].
The same principle applies to one who dwells at the foot of a tree.

Regarding the phrase "in the possession of a person of trust," it is said that whatever belongs to such a person is as if it were one's own private property, provided that a relationship of trust has grown between them.

However, in a case where trust does not arise, there is only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) regarding what belongs to that person. "A non-human being" (*amanussa*) means either a *yakkha* or a *peta*.
"It is obstructed" (*palibuddhaṃ hoti*) means it is afflicted.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning lodgings is finished.
5. Commentary on the Second Training Rule on Lodgings "Any hide whatsoever" means any hide, whether allowable or unallowable. Is it not said:
"Monks, great hides must not be worn—namely, a lion’s hide, a tiger’s hide, or a leopard’s hide; whoever should wear one, there is an offense of wrong-doing"?
Regarding the statement, "The prohibition of lion skins and so forth was made in the Khandhaka," he says, "For [the prohibition] of lion skins and so forth," and so on.

The prohibition applies specifically to their *pariharaṇa* (keeping or maintenance); that is, having made them one's own property and carrying them from one monastery to another to spread over beds, chairs, and so forth—this very usage is what is prohibited.
However, as for using them as floor coverings after they have been made the property of the dwelling (*senāsana*), there is no prohibition.
There is no fault at all. Therefore he said: “In the use of lodgings, however, there is no such thing as an ‘unallowable skin.
A *pāvāra* is that by which one spreads or covers the body. A *kojava* is a bedspread made of *uddaloma*, *ekantaloma*, and so forth.
“The rest” refers to the remaining types of lodging: mattresses, sitting mats, grass coverings, and leaf coverings. In that regard:
"Bhisī" refers to either a mattress for a bed or a mattress for a chair. "Nisīdana" should be understood as having a fringe. "Tiṇasanthāra" is a spread made of any kind of grass.
The same method applies to a leaf-spread (*paṇṇasanthāra*). In this context, the mattress is clear because it has been explained previously;
the sitting cloth (*nisīdana*) is clear by virtue of the training rule concerning the sitting cloth itself; however, as for the grass-spread and the leaf-spread—
These are indeed well-known in the world. For this very reason, he said, "It is quite evident.

"Neither should one remove it oneself, nor should one cause it to be removed" means that one should not, having removed it oneself, place it in an unsuitable location, nor should one cause another to do so.
Therefore, he said, "Just as it was placed," and so forth. And by the one placing it, [in] the four...
It should be placed inside the dwelling in a place sheltered from the rain, according to the method previously explained in the passage beginning with “on stones,” and so forth.
However, if the lodging is leaking and grass or bricks have been brought for the purpose of roofing, one should roof it if one is able to do so.
If one is not able, it should be placed in whatever spot is sheltered from the rain. If [the entire area]...
If it rains, one who exerts effort should place it in the house of a lay follower within the village.
If they do not accept it, saying, "Venerable sir, that which belongs to the Saṅgha is burdensome;
we fear fire, smoke, and so forth," then one should set up a bed upon stones in the open air and deposit the rest exactly as previously described, covering it with grass and leaves.
It should be concealed. For whatever portion remains there, even if it is merely a limb [of the structure], that will be of benefit to other monks who come there.
"Within the vicinity" means within two *leḍḍupāta*s (the distance of a stone's throw) from the very last dwelling.
This is the decision regarding what must be asked for permission and what need not be asked for permission in this context—namely, when there is a long hall or a leaf-hut on the ground.
Or, if it is a house built against tree trunks that serves as a dwelling place for termites, one must depart only after taking leave when leaving from there;
for if it is not looked after for a few days, it remains merely as an anthill.
However, regarding a lodging built on a stone surface or against stone pillars, or a cave in a rock formation, or a lodging plastered with lime—
Alternatively, where there is no suspicion of termites, it is permissible for one departing from that place to go either after having asked for permission or without asking for permission.
Therefore he said, "But where... and so forth. If, even in such a lodging, termites climb up on one side, one must depart only after having asked for permission.
Asking for permission, however, is a duty; it is the duty of one who is departing.
And this is stated for the purpose of showing what ought to be done, not for the purpose of showing that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) due to a breach of the rule.

Some, however, say it is "for the purpose of showing [it is] a *dukkaṭa* offense," but that is not tenable, because of the commentary on the Khandhaka on Duties (*Vatta-khandhaka-aṭṭhakathā*), which states:
"As for a dwelling-place made on a stone surface or among stone pillars where termites do not ascend..."
Because it is stated, "there is no offense even for one who does not ask permission," when one is asking permission, if there is a bhikkhu, a bhikkhu should be asked;
if he is not present, a sāmaṇera; if he is not present, an ārāmika; if he too is not present, the owner of the monastery by whom the vihāra was caused to be built;
or if he is not present, anyone from his family should be asked.
“Nearby” (*upacāre*) is an explanation of this very term, meaning “in the vicinity outside. That is to say, in a place near the exterior of the monastery.

Or, “in the assembly hall” (*upaṭṭhānasālāya*) means in the dining hall. “It is indeed an offense of wrong-doing” (*dukkaṭam eva*): for when one has arranged the ten kinds of beds mentioned above in a secure place such as an inner chamber and then departs, since both the bed and the lodging— [...is] an offense of wrong-doing.
This is because, having prepared the aforementioned ten types of beds in a protected location such as an inner chamber and so forth, for one who then departs, since both the bed and the lodging—
It is destroyed by termites and becomes nothing more than a mound of earth; therefore, an offense of expiation (pācittiya) is stated.

However, for one who departs after having arranged [the bedding] outside in the assembly hall or similar places, only the bedding itself would perish due to the lack of protection for that spot, but not the lodging (senāsana);
therefore, in this case, a wrongdoing (dukkaṭa) is stated. As for the bed and chair, however, they cannot be eaten away by termites so suddenly.
Therefore, it is stated that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who departs after having spread that [bedding] even within the monastery.
However, in the vicinity of the monastery, those wandering on a tour of the dwellings see it and put it away immediately.
Regarding the phrase "having made removals": here, by one departing after making removals, everything belonging to the bed, chair, and canopy must be taken away.

Having gathered [the bedding] and hung it on the robe-rod, one should depart. Later, when returning, the monk who is staying there must likewise act: having prepared the bed or chair again and slept, he should depart after doing so.

One who has been staying with the bed arranged inside the wall and moved outside the wall must, at the time of departure, put it back exactly where it was taken from. From the upper story of the palace...
The same rule applies even for one who has removed [the bedding] and is staying in the lower story.

Even after having arranged a bed or chair in the night-quarters or day-quarters, it must be placed back in the very spot from which it was taken at the time of departure. The same rule applies when departing after having had it removed.
However, for one departing after having asked permission, [the rule is as stated: "If a monk is present, that monk should be asked for permission," and so forth.
One must depart after having asked for permission in the manner already explained below.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning lodgings is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Intrusion.
When it is said, "knowing," one might ask: from where is this distinction—that "knowing" means "knowing that 'this person' is not to be made to rise"—derived?

To this he says, "Therefore, for her... and so forth. One might object: "In the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) as well, only the knowledge of their being aged and so on was mentioned, not their state of being not to be made to rise.

Anticipating this objection, he says, "For [a person] who is aged... and so forth. "Of great service" (*bahūpakāra*) means "the state of being of great service through such roles as treasurer (*bhaṇḍāgārika*) and so on."

He says, “and because of their distinguished qualities,” etc., to show that it is not only for this reason; thus, he demonstrates that even if someone is of great service, if they lack distinguished qualities, it is not proper to give [the robe], and likewise, even if they possess distinguished qualities, if they are not of great service, it is not proper to give. Some say:
“Having observed the treasurer’s great service and the distinguished qualities of the Dhamma-preachers and others. “For the purpose of permanent residence” means:
"For the purpose of permanent residence. "Having appointed" means having appointed by means of a formal act (kamma) consisting of a motion (apalokana).

Although in this case the Saṅgha itself provides suitable lodgings even for one who is ill, he is mentioned separately to show that even if the Saṅgha has not assigned him a lodging after he has made his request, the sick person must not be troubled but should be shown compassion.
"Extending one and a half cubits on all sides" is said with reference to the bed and chair arranged in the middle.
If a direction is seen that is sufficient on one side, it may be taken from there. "From the foot-washing stone" means from the foot-washing stone placed at the door.
Regarding the offense of *pācittiya* for one who sits or lies down: here, it is by the mere act of sitting, or by the mere act of lying down.
Or it is a *pācittiya*. "Doing it again and again" means rising up repeatedly and then sitting down or lying down.

Regarding a property belonging to the Saṅgha, one should understand that there is a triple *pācittiya* based on the cases of perceiving it as belonging to the Saṅgha, being in doubt, or perceiving it as belonging to an individual.

However, there is a triple *dukkaṭa* regarding an individual's property based on the cases of perceiving it as belonging to the Saṅgha, being in doubt, or perceiving it as belonging to another individual. [This applies to] a monastery...
"In the vicinity" means in the area near to the outside of that [dwelling].
The commentary on the training rule concerning encroaching is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Expulsion.
“Many gate-houses” means many gate-houses with multiple doors. They say: “If, having heard the command to depart, he departs of his own accord, there is no offense.

“In the case of his being driven out of his requisites” means: in the case of driving out whatever belongs to him—be it his bowl, robes, water-strainer, needle-case, bed, chair, couch, pillow, bolster, and so forth—even down to the bark used for dyeing—in the case of driving him out of those requisites.
“And that” refers to the *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing).
He takes hold of it. The same method applies even to having him driven out. However, when he has been bound tightly and placed [in confinement], there is only one offense.
One may indeed drive out from the entire monastery grounds only those who are makers of strife and quarrels;
for such a person, having gained a faction, might even cause a schism in the Saṅgha. But those who are shameless and so forth should be driven out only from their own place of residence.
It is not permissible to expel [a monk] from the entire monastery. Therefore, he said: "Even from the entire monastery," and so forth.
The commentary on the training rule concerning expulsion is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Upper Chamber (*vehāsakuṭi*).
“An upper chamber” (*uparivehāsakuṭiyā*) means a hut on an upper floor whose floor has not been spread with mats. Therefore he said, “with an uncovered ceiling above,” and so forth.
For any small hut with two or three stories that has an uncovered ceiling above is called an “upper chamber.
This indeed is the defining characteristic of an upper chamber. If this is so, why does the word-commentary [refer to] “a middle-sized man”?
Regarding the statement, "it is said that it does not strike the head," he says, "but in the word-commentary," and so forth.
To show the hut intended here means to show the "aerial hut" (vehāsakuṭi) intended in this training rule. "Of a man of medium size" means of a man of medium proportions.
"It does not strike the head with all the lower scales" means it is "one that does not strike the head. "Having pierced the limbs" means...
"Having pierced the tenons. "With the foot-protrusion inserted" means with the tip of the foot-piece inserted.

"Therefore" refers back to the very meaning already stated by the phrase "or in the sense of 'on the ground,'" etc., treating that meaning as the reason; that is to say, because the aforementioned meaning applies to [beds] with fixed foot-pieces and so forth.
"Sahasā" means having overcome or overwhelmed. "In a hut without an upper story" refers to leaf-huts and the like built on the ground;
there is no offense in such cases, for it is impossible to cause distress to another there. "Where the head strikes" refers to a place where the head would strike [the ceiling];
there too there is no offense, for it is not possible to move about in the lower story without bowing one's head; therefore...
Because it is not a place where one can walk about, there will be no injury to others.

"The upper surface is piled with planks" means the upper surface is densely covered with wooden boards. "Or he takes something" means he takes anything such as a robe or other items hung on pegs and the like above.
"Or it sticks" follows the same principle here as well. A pin that acts as an obstacle is a *paṭāṇi*.
The meaning is that such a pin is placed on the tips of the legs of beds and chairs, such that even when one sits down upon it, the feet do not sink;
therefore he said, "of the leg-tops," and so forth.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the upper-story hut is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Large Vihāra.
"Of a back-wall enclosure" means of a door-enclosure. "An area of two and a half cubits around" refers to that which has its door in the middle and high walls above;
[it means] an area of two and a half cubits around it in three directions.
A portion [of the wall]. However, in the case of a small dwelling, it refers to two directions.

Even there, whichever wall the door strikes when being opened is considered incomplete in its precincts (*upacāra*). But if there is a space for plastering even at the lower part of the door, it is permissible to plaster that as well.
Regarding the phrase "for the installation of the bolt" (*aggaḷaṭṭhapanāya*), here, by the word *aggaḷa* (bolt), through its connection [to the door],...
The door-fastening together with the door-panels is intended. Therefore he says, “of that which has a door-panel,” and so forth.
By the phrase “for the sake of immovability,” he shows that this placing [of the fastening] is for the purpose of immobility here. But what is the intention here?
He says, “For the door-panel,” and so forth. “It shakes” means it moves. It should be plastered again and again up to the door-frame for the purpose of fixing the bolt.
“Or he should have it plastered” means that for the purpose of installing the door-bolt, he himself should repeatedly plaster [the area] up to the door-frame, or he should have others plaster it;
this is the meaning. One might ask:
“Is this meaning stated neither in the matrix (mātikā) nor in the word-commentary (padabhājana)? Then from where is it to be seen? To this he says: “In that regard,” and so forth.
*Kiñcāpi* means "even though. *Aṭṭhuppattiyaṃ* refers to the introduction (nidāna) of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
*Adhikārato* means by way of following [the context]. It illuminates and covers the light; thus it is called an *ālokasandhi*. Therefore he said: "An *ālokasandhi* is called a window-lattice.
In that context, "window-lattices" refers to the panels of a window. However, other than in the permitted locations, repeatedly...
It is not permitted to smear [the wall] oneself or to have it smeared by another. Some say:

"When the task to be done with clay has been completed and a fourth layer is applied again, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Others say: "Since the offense of expiation is not explicitly stated for applying the plaster again and again—other than merely prohibiting anything beyond the prescribed measure—there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)."
*Adhiṭṭhātabbaṃ* means it should be arranged or prepared. Regarding *appaharite*, here the prefix *appa-* has the sense of "absence," as in such terms as *appiccha*;
thus he says "in what is not cultivated" (*aharite*). Rice, paddy, and so forth are "grains of the first crop" (*pubbaṇṇa*), made so by virtue of being the primary fruit of the harvest;
conversely, mung beans, black gram, and so forth are "grains of the subsequent crop" (*aparaṇṇa*). *Vuttaṃ* means sown. "Standing upon that and resolving... [the text continues].

By the phrase “he incurs an offense of wrong-doing,” it is shown that a monastery may be built in a location where, within the surrounding area of the prescribed measurement, there are no crops or similar things;
however, it is not permitted to have one built where such things do exist.
“In the same way” means up to the edge of the opening. One must stand there because it is a place where a falling monastery would not fall.

The intention is that [the object] should not fall upon that bhikkhu. However, since there is space within the dwelling for something falling from the interior of the area as it has been delimited, one does not obtain the right to resolve while standing even on that which is not overgrown with grass.
Therefore he said: “One does not obtain the right to stand inside it, even if it is not overgrown with grass.”
“Beyond that” means above the three paths or the three methods; that is to say, on the fourth path or the fourth method.
Therefore he said, “when covered by a path,” and so forth. In that context, “covered by a path” means being covered directly without being enclosed.
“By a method” means by way of enclosure. Therein, covering by a path is [done] with bricks, stones, or plaster.
"It is possible; by way of a figurative expression, it is covered with grass and leaves," thus he said, "with bricks, stones, and plaster," and so forth.

Therefore, having resolved upon either two paths or two methods according to his wish, and having commanded, "Cover it in this manner" regarding the third path or method, he should depart. If he does not depart, [he should remain] in silence.
It should be so placed. And all this roofing is to be understood as being above the roof-covering.
For they roof like this thinking, "A dwelling that is covered layer upon layer remains free from rain for a long time. "By counting handfuls of grass" means by counting baskets of grass.

"Three offenses of expiation" refers to three [offenses] based on the cases of one who perceives it as more than two or three bundles, one who is in doubt regarding it being more, and one who perceives it as less.

These are the *pācittiya* offenses. Regarding "making white-colored [decoration] and so forth": this refers to making white color, black color, red ocher, decorative work, garland work, creeper work, makara-tooth work, and the five types of lattice-work.
Regarding "in caves, grottoes, grass huts, and so forth": here, a "cave" (*leṇa*) is one that has a door; a "grotto" (*guhā*) is a natural mountain cave; a "grass hut" (*tiṇakuṭikā*) is well known.
The commentary on the training rule concerning large dwellings is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning water containing living beings:
"In one jar, there is only one offense" means that in a single water-jar there is only one offense. This same principle applies to all types of vessels.
"Of one who cuts off" means of one who interrupts the stream [of fuel].
"Of one who throws in one by one" means of one who throws in grass, leaves, clay, or other materials such as wood and cow dung, one at a time. "Exhaustion" means destruction.
Even for one who knows that "insects such as moths will die by falling into the lamp," the lighting of the lamp with a wholesome state of mind [is not an offense].

Just as in the case of one who knows beforehand that "the insects will die from being sprinkled," yet while actually sprinkling [the water] with the thought "I am sprinkling this water," there is no murderous intention (*vadhakacitta*), it is said: "without the volition of killing" (*vinā vadhakacetanāyā*), and so forth.

By establishing it in this way, the term "offense by rule" (*paṇṇattivajja*) is also validated. "Three types of consciousness" (*ticitta*) refers to the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate [consciousnesses].

There are three types of consciousness. For instance, when one squashes a designation (paṇṇatti) and pours [water] or causes it to be poured with an unwholesome mind, there is unwholesome consciousness;
when one pours or causes it to be poured for the purpose of washing a seat with the thought, "I will wash the seat," with a wholesome mind, there is wholesome consciousness;
and when an Arhat, not knowing the designation, performs pouring and so forth with an indeterminate mind, there is indeterminate consciousness.
There are three types of consciousness by way of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate consciousness.
The commentary on the training rule concerning living beings is finished.
The second chapter, the Section on Living Beings, is concluded.
3. Ovādavagga 1.
Ovādasikkhāpadavaṇṇanā “Endowed with eight factors” means endowed with the eight factors beginning with “being virtuous. “Authorized” means...

These were authorized in the introduction (nidāna) to this training rule. The phrase “one ordained for a hundred years,” etc., is an indication of the eight weighty rules (garudhamma) that will be explained below.
Therein, “proper conduct” (sāmīcikamma) refers to appropriate duties such as preparing the path, providing seeds, and asking for water. By the word “etc. (ādi), it includes:
“A bhikkhunī must not spend the rains residence in a dwelling where no bhikkhus are present; every half-month, a bhikkhunī must [request instruction] from the community of bhikkhus... and so forth.
Two things are to be expected: the inquiry regarding the Uposatha and the approaching for instruction.
A bhikkhunī who has completed the rains residence must perform the invitation ceremony before both Saṅghas on three grounds: what has been seen, what has been heard, or what is suspected.
A bhikkhunī who has committed a grave offense (garudhamma) must undergo a fortnight’s penance (mānatta) before both Saṅghas.
“A probationary nun who has trained in the six rules for two years must seek full ordination from both Saṅghas.
A nun must never, under any pretext, revile or abuse a monk.
From this day forward, the path of speech for nuns toward monks is closed, but the path of speech for monks toward nuns remains open.”
These seven rules comprise the summary. "Weighty rules" (*garudhamma*) means weighty matters; for they are called "weighty rules" because they must be accepted by the bhikkhunīs with reverence.
"Or by any other rule" means by any rule whatsoever, excluding the eight weighty rules.
"Or admonishes one who has only just been ordained among the bhikkhunīs" refers to one who admonishes a bhikkhunī who has only recently received full ordination by means of a weighty rule.
Or, for one who has received full ordination (*upasampadā*) in the presence of the bhikkhus, it is according to the actual basis [of the offense].

Regarding the phrase "in an illegal act" (*adhammakamme*) and so forth, it should be understood that the formal act of authorization to exhort the bhikkhunīs is what is meant by "the act"; thus he says, "even for one who is authorized," and so on.

For one who exhorts the bhikkhunī-saṅgha when it is incomplete, there is a triad of *pācittiya* offenses: three *pācittiya*s arise for one who exhorts the bhikkhunī-saṅgha when it is incomplete, based on the cases of perceiving it as incomplete, being in doubt, and perceiving it as complete.

The meaning of "likewise for one who is doubtful" is that for one who is doubtful regarding an illegal formal act (*adhammakamma*), there is a threefold *pācittiya* offense for exhorting a group of nuns.
This same principle applies to the phrase "for one who perceives it as a legal formal act" (*dhammakammasaññī*).

And just as there are nine *pācittiya* offenses for exhorting a group of nuns [when the assembly is incomplete], so too [there are nine] when the assembly is complete (*samagga*) and the formal act is illegal, yet one perceives it as illegal.

Regarding one who exhorts the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs, there are nine *pācittiya* offenses: three based on the perception of a divided assembly (*vaggasaññī*), the perception of a doubtful assembly (*vematika*), and the perception of a united assembly (*samaggasaññī*);
likewise, there is one for one who is doubtful but perceives it as a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*). Thus he said, "Even in a united Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs, there are nine," and so forth.
However, regarding a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*), for one who perceives it as an illegitimate legal act (*adhammakamma*) [and exhorting] a divided Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs...
There are nine *dukkaṭas*: three for one who instructs while being in doubt, and likewise three for one who perceives it as a legitimate legal act (*dhammakamma*).
Furthermore, there are eight *dukkaṭas* for instructing a united community of bhikkhunīs. Therefore he said, "But if," and so forth.
"Another teaching" means another Sutta or Abhidhamma. "We are united, venerable sir."
For they expect instruction by means of speech. Therefore, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for one who speaks another teaching while setting aside the instruction.
"Without having handed over the instruction" means without saying, "Sister, this is the instruction.
"He gives a cross-examination" means he explains the meaning of that very same familiar text of the Garudhammas. "Recite" means utter; "speak" means explain.
The meaning: "He recites" means he speaks the text of the eight Garudhammas.
"When asked a question" means when a question concerning either the Garudhammas or the aggregates (khandhas), etc., has been asked of a bhikkhunī.
The commentary on the training rule for exhortation is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Cessation of Light.

"Ordained by one [order]" means one who has just been ordained in the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha. Furthermore, wherever the term "ordained by one" is used hereafter, this same meaning is to be understood in all instances.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the cessation of light is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Nuns’ Quarters (*Bhikkhunupassaya-sikkhāpada*).
“For the sake of living together” means for the purpose of the Uposatha and other such observances. “The other” refers to one who has received full ordination in both Saṅghas.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the nuns’ quarters is finished.

4. Commentary on the Training Rule on Material Things (Āmisa-sikkhāpada) It is called *āmisa* because it is to be grasped (*āmasitabba*) by craving and views; it refers to robes and so forth. *Āmisahetu* means "for the sake of material things. Therefore, he said:

"on account of any one of the [requisites] beginning with robes. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), almsfood, lodgings, medicinal requisites for the sick, as well as honor, respect, esteem, veneration, and worship are included.
“Seizing. “Desiring disrepute” means precisely desiring ill-fame.
In the phrase “in a legal act concerning the Dhamma,” etc., the formal act (*kamma*) consisting of the authorization to exhort nuns should be understood as “the legal act.

Therein, “three offenses of expiation (*pācittiya*)” refers to three *pācittiyas* based on the cases of one who perceives it as a legal act concerning the Dhamma, one who is doubtful, and one who perceives it as not a legal act concerning the Dhamma.

In the same way, it should be understood that there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for each of the three cases regarding an illegal formal act (adhammakamma). "Not authorized" (asammatam) refers to one who has been ordained and appointed by the Saṅgha as a bearer of the burden [of instruction].
One might object: "Is it not the case that the authorization for exhortation (ovāda-sammuti) is granted only to one who is fully ordained, and not to a novice (sāmaṇera)?
To this he says, "In that regard," and so forth. However, one who is learned and has been appointed by the Saṅgha...
A novice (sāmaṇera) is to be understood as "one who is not authorized. However, regarding "speaking thus to one who is advising for the sake of robes, etc., by nature":
this refers to speaking thus with the perception that "this person is advising for the sake of robes, etc.," while the other is actually advising for the sake of robes, etc., by nature.

But for one who speaks thus with the perception that "he is not advising for the sake of robes, etc.," there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). "Without the intervention of material things" (anāmisantaratā): [refers to] the absence of any mediation by material gifts.
The absence of a mind for material gain; the meaning is the absence of such an underlying intention as "I shall instruct for the sake of material gain.
Here, the word *antara* is a synonym for "mind," as in such passages as "in whom there are no angers from within" (*yassantarato na santi kopā*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning material gain is concluded.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Giving of Robes.
The fifth training rule is of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the giving of robes is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Sewing Robes:
Regarding "inserting the needle, inserting it, and withdrawing it": for every insertion and withdrawal, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

However, for one who is deliberating, "I shall sew," or even while cutting [the thread], there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). This applies even if one has pierced [the cloth] a hundred times and withdraws [the needle] only once.

For one who, without withdrawing the entire needle, pierces it even a hundred times for the purpose of inserting a long thread and then withdraws it once—“when told ‘sew’” means when told once, “sew the robe. “Finishes” means he brings all the needlework to completion.
“For every stage of the path [of the needle], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)” refers to each time the needle is inserted and withdrawn after being commanded to do so.
Each instance is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

"The Elder Udāyī" refers to the Elder Lāḷudāyī. "Sewing or causing to sew according to the stated characteristics" means sewing or causing to sew according to the characteristics stated [in the rule] beginning with "having inserted a needle.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the sewing of robes is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Arrangements (*Saṃvidhāna-sikkhāpada*).
“Having made an arrangement” means having said, “Come, let us go to such-and-such a village,” or “I am going tomorrow; you too should come.
Furthermore, that arrangement is in substance an act of appointment (*saṅketakamma*); thus it says, “at the time of going, an appointment.”
The meaning is "having made [an appointment]. Regarding "one who makes an appointment on improper ground":

this refers to one who stands within a village, at the door of a nunnery, on a street, or in other places such as crossroads, junctions, elephant stables, and so forth, and makes an appointment there. Therefore he said, "having placed [the object] there," and so on.
"Even for one who is near" means even for one who is very close; the intention is "even for one who is at a distance of only a cubit (ratana)."
"Of another village" means: from wherever he departs, it is to another village [beyond that]. "Entering it" means: entering the precinct (*upacāra*) of that interior village.
If he intends to go far, then for each successive entry into the precinct of the village, there is an offense according to the previous method.
Therefore he said: "Thus, by counting each entry into the precinct of a village, there are *pācittiya* offenses. Of him...
However, there is no offense in passing beyond that village. "When there is no village" means when there is no village within a distance of half a *yojana*.
But when that village exists, the offenses are indeed counted by the number of villages passed. Regarding the offense for each half-*yojana*:
for every half-*yojana* passed, there is a *pācittiya* offense; for one who is passing through each successive half-*yojana*, [the thought] "I shall now pass beyond this" [constitutes the offense].

The meaning is: there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the first step, and an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for the second step. According to this method, there is an offense upon crossing [the boundary], but no offense upon entering [the village].
Regarding the phrase "by a change of appointment": if they say, "We will go before the meal," but go after the meal;
or if they say, "We will go today," but go tomorrow—in such cases of a change of time, there is no offense. However, regarding a change of gate...
Even if there is a misunderstanding regarding the path, it is indeed an offense. "In times of distress" means: when the country is divided and the people mounted on chariots are fleeing;
in such times of distress, there is no offense. "Mounted on a chariot" means either mounted on a wheel of postures (iriyāpatha-cakka) or mounted on a wheel of a cart (sakaṭa-cakka).
"By the training rule concerning women" refers to the seventh training rule in the section on "Living Beings with Breath."
The commentary on the training rule concerning making arrangements is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule concerning boarding a boat:
"With play as the primary motive" means having play as the primary motive by way of worldly pleasure or intimacy with friends. "In that same way" means precisely by way of play.
“By a river-bank devoid of villages” means by a river-bank where there are no villages within a distance of half a *yojana*.
However, because the text states, “whether going upstream or downstream,” there is no offense for one who goes to reservoirs, the ocean, and so forth, even with the intention of playing.
Therefore he said: “But it is permissible to go as one pleases in the ocean. “By a prearranged signal” means...
In this case as well, there is no offense for one traveling by means of a difference in time, or a difference in the place of landing, or a difference in the boat.
"The rest" refers to the remainder [of the training rule] together with its origin and so forth. However, some say:

"Because of the word 'having made an appointment' (*saṃvidahitvā*), this training rule involves an unwholesome mind and is a transgression according to worldly convention (*lokavajja*); therefore, setting aside what is called 'the rest,' it is a transgression of the formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*)."
Regarding the statement, "The three types of consciousness and this pair [of two] are the remainder," that should not be accepted.
For even if one mounts [a vehicle] with a mind preoccupied with sport, if upon entering another village or traveling beyond half a *yojana* one gains a sense of spiritual urgency (*saṃvega*),
one might realize *arahantship*, fall asleep, or proceed while attending to the meditation subject (*kammaṭṭhāna*).
And how could there be for him the possession of an unwholesome mind, such that this training rule would be an unwholesome state of mind and yet also a world-transgression?
The commentary on the training rule concerning boarding a boat is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning cooked food.
“Paripācitaṃ” means brought to maturity; it is said to mean that which has been set aside after being prepared in such a way that [the recipient] may receive it.
Therefore he said, “Neither for him,” and so forth. “For him” refers to the bhikkhu who might consume it.

“Having proclaimed the virtue of the bhikkhu” means having proclaimed his virtue by saying, “The venerable one is a preacher,” “The venerable one is learned,” and so on. “Almsfood” refers to the five [kinds of edible food].
"Any one of the foods. Since the word *samārambha* (undertaking) functions as a passive noun (*kamma-sādhana*), he says "undertaken" (*samāraddha*).

"Of what has been prepared" means of what has been made ready. Because even almsfood that has not been undertaken for the sake of a monk by relatives who have invited him is, in fact, "undertaken" in the sense that it may be taken away at his pleasure, therefore it is stated: "or belonging to those [relatives] who have invited him."

"In both cases" refers to those who have been brought to maturity and those who have not. "In the remainder" means in all instances, including even that which has been prepared by a nun, such as rice gruel, solid food, fruits, or other edibles. However, even in the case of the remainder, one is not exempt from an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) by way of making a sign, speaking aloud, engaging in indirect talk, or making a request.
The commentary on the training rule concerning preparing [food] is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Sitting in Secret (*raho-nisajja-sikkhāpada*).
“Upari” means in the Acelaka-vagga (the Chapter on the Naked Ascetics). “By the fourth training rule for Upananda” refers to the training rule concerning sitting in private with an uncovered woman.
For that was stated as the “fourth training rule for Upananda” because it was the fourth among those rules prescribed concerning the Elder Upananda.
If [these two] share the same delimitation, then why are they separate?
He said, "It is formulated," meaning, "but it is formulated separately by way of the occasion for its arising" (*aṭṭhuppattivasena*).
In this context, "by way of the occasion for its arising" means by way of the arising of the matter; that is, by way of the arising of the secret sitting with a nun.
This is the underlying intention: prior to the matter of the fourth training rule, the matter of this training rule [arose].
Because it arose first, even though it is included within the same single delimitation, this is designated separately.
The commentary on the training rule concerning sitting in private is finished.
The third chapter, the Section on Exhortation, is concluded.
4. Bhojanavagga 1.
Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Lodgings:
"Not being ill" (*agilāna*)—here, one who is capable of traveling at least two *gāvutas* is intended; thus he said, "even half a *yojana*."
“By one capable of going. *Āvasathapiṇḍa* means alms-food in a rest-house;
the meaning is any one of the five kinds of cooked food prepared without restriction as much as desired in halls and other such places. Therefore he said, “Of these,” and so forth.
Therein, “of these” means of these heretics. “Of so many” means of so many [people] in this heretical sect.
"Or of heretics (*pāsaṇḍa*). "Heretic" refers to the ninety-six types of ascetics, wanderers, and so forth.
For they are called "heretics" because they cast and set snares—namely, the snare of craving and the snare of views. "Indiscriminately" means without specifying, that is, without delimiting.
"In any place such as a hall, etc. means in any location whatsoever, such as a hall, the foot of a tree, or an open space.
"It should be eaten on one day alone" means it should be eaten only once on a single day;
it is not permitted to eat it repeatedly on that same day. "Starting from the second day" means starting from the day following the day it was eaten.
"For every act of swallowing, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)" means for every mouthful, for every morsel, there is an offense of expiation. By various families...
However, regarding food prepared in various places, it is permissible to eat at one place on one day and at another place on the following day;
yet, it is not permissible to skip the sequence and eat again starting from the beginning.
This same rule applies to food from a single group or different groups, and from a single village or different villages. This also applies to food from a single family or different families.
If a meal is prepared on one side but is interrupted from time to time due to a lack of rice and other provisions, that too should not be eaten.
However, if they stop because they say, "We are unable to provide more," and then begin to give again once a virtuous intention has arisen,
it is permissible to eat this on that subsequent day.

"Three *pācittiya*s" refers to three *pācittiya* offenses according to the cases of one who is not ill but perceives oneself as not ill, one who is uncertain, and one who is ill but perceives oneself as ill.
Regarding "one who is ill and perceives oneself as ill": there is no offense for one who stays and eats while perceiving themselves as ill, thinking, "I am ill.
"Eats once" means he eats on a single day. "Or while going" refers to a distance of half a *yojana*.

It should be accepted; likewise, they say that this term "returning" is also [to be understood in the same way]. "By some calamity" means by any kind of distress, such as a river flood, fear of thieves, and so forth.
"Anything else" refers to whatever else there may be, distinguished as rice-gruel, dry food, fruits, and the like. "Having stayed again" means having resided once more.
The commentary on the training rule concerning lodgings (*āvasatha-sikkhāpada*) is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Group Meals (*Gaṇabhojana-sikkhāpada*).
Regarding "group meal" (*gaṇabhojana*): it refers to food belonging to a group because it was obtained by a group. Therefore, he said, "in a meal for a group.
Now, although it is stated here as "in a meal for a group," that group [is defined as follows]: in some cases it consists of two, and in some cases...
It is intended in many ways by such phrases as “with three,” etc.; here, however, he asks “with how many? and thus says “and here,” etc.
Furthermore, this group-meal (gaṇabhojana) arises in two ways: either from an invitation or from a request; thus he says, “from their invitation,” etc.
In that context, “from an invitation” means from an improper invitation. “Of the five, rice, etc. refers to the five: boiled rice, grain porridge, flour cakes, fish, and meat.

The connection is as follows: by means of any synonym or in any other language, one invites after mentioning the name of any of the five kinds of cooked food, using such expressions as, “I invite you with rice; please accept my rice.
“Four” refers to four bhikkhus, whether they are standing in one place or in different places; this is a term used to indicate a minimum number, therefore [it includes] four or...
The meaning is: "or more than that, monks. "Or by a synonym" means by a word that is a synonym for food, such as *bhatta* (alms-food) or *anna* (rice).

"Or by another language" means by another language such as Andhaka, Damila, and so forth. "Having mentioned the name of one of the five kinds of cooked food" means having mentioned the name of any one of the five kinds of cooked food. "I invite you with rice, venerable sirs" means: "Venerable sirs, I invite you with rice."
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of such statements as: "I invite you; look upon me;
accept [my offering]; honor me. I invite you, my enemy; seize my enemy; look upon him; accept him; honor him.
Or "together" (*ekato*) means having seen the bhikkhus standing or sitting in one place, [saying] "Venerable sirs, I invite you with rice," and so forth.
"Thus invited on one side" means they have been invited from various places; that is, having gone to four different cells or to the monastery, they are invited from various locations.
Or, even while standing in one place, if one is invited by the son and another by the father, they are likewise said to be "invited from various places.
"They take [the food] together" means they take it while standing within twelve cubits of one another.
But why is it that even when food has been eaten by various individuals, it constitutes *gaṇabhojana* (eating in a group)? To this he says: "For here, the act of receiving alone is the criterion.
If that is so, then why is it stated in the Pāḷi: "'Gaṇabhojana' is where four bhikkhus, invited to eat any one of the five kinds of cooked food, eat; this is called *gaṇabhojana*'?"

This is solely for the purpose of restricting the act of receiving. For since monks do not eat what has not been received, the word "eating" (*bhuñjanti*) is a statement intended to restrict the receiving.
"Having requested [food] either together or separately" means that four monks, standing or sitting together, seeing a lay follower, say, "Give food to all four of us," or they request individually.
Having entered, one requests either collectively or individually, saying, “Give me food; give me food.

Regarding both types of that—namely, the group meal obtained through an invitation and the group meal obtained through a request—for both such types of group meals, it is thus in the case of receiving them collectively.
"Because even his feet were cracked" means that even his feet were so cracked that, as it were, the flesh could be seen on the other side of the thick skin.
"He was unable to go for alms" means that because pain arose from merely touching sand or gravel, he was unable to go for alms within the village. "While his robe was being made" refers to the cloth.

And having obtained the thread while the robe is being made: "Whatever work is to be done on the robe" refers to whatever task must be performed on the robe, such as measuring the cloth, cutting it, and weaving the warp-threads, including even the piercing with a needle; this is the intended meaning.
The phrase "even half a yojana," etc., is stated as the minimum distance. However, for one who wishes to go a long distance, there is nothing at all that need be said; he may go.
One is permitted to eat within half a *yojana*, or even within a *gāvuta*. However, once one has gone [a distance], it is for a single day.

When one desires to board a boat, or when one has boarded, or when one has disembarked—this is called "the time of boarding a boat. Thus he said: "The same principle applies during the time of boarding a boat.
But this is the distinction: even after one who has boarded has reached the desired destination, as long as one does not disembark, [the meal is still permissible].
One may eat only that long. "Four monks" is the minimum limit. However, where a hundred or a thousand have gathered, there is no need for such a restriction.
Therefore, at such a time, one may eat after determining it to be a "great assembly.
"Any renunciant whatsoever" refers to anyone among fellow practitioners of the Dhamma or among those of other sects.

"And those who take two or three together" means that even for those who, having accepted an improper invitation, take two or three [meals] together, there is no offense. However, they say that in the case of requests for fine foods, soups, or boiled rice, there is indeed an offense; this should be investigated.
"In the case of regular meals and so forth" refers to regular meals (*niccabhatta*), ticket-meals (*salākabhatta*), fortnightly meals (*pakkhika*), and Uposatha-day meals (*uposathika*).
On the first day of the lunar fortnight (*pāṭipadika*). In this context, "regular meal" (*niccabhatta*) refers to a fixed meal (*dhuvabhatta*).
When they say, "Take the regular meal," it is permissible for many to take it together. The same principle applies to tickets for meals (*salākabhatta*) and so forth.
The commentary on the training rule regarding group meals (*gaṇabhojana*) is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Eating in Succession:

"In the same manner as stated regarding eating in a group" means that by whatever synonym or in whatever other language one approaches a bhikkhu and says, "Venerable sir, I invite you with rice; please accept my rice," and so forth—by such means, [regarding] the five...
"Having taken the name of one of the foods, he invites [him]"—this is according to the method already stated.

"Of one who has been invited" means of one who has been invited by an improper invitation (*akappiya-nimantana*). "Without diverting" (*avikappetvā*) means without diverting either in the presence of or in the absence [of the donor];
the meaning is "without relinquishing. For this so-called "diversion of food" (*bhatta-vikappanā*) is permissible both in the presence and in the absence [of the donor].
Therefore he said: “The monk who [eats] among the five fellow-followers of the Dhamma,” and so forth.
“Except for the case of an invitation to eat” means except for the case of eating at another invitation after having first been invited [elsewhere].
If there are three subsequent rules (anupaññatti), then why does the Parivāra say, “There are four subsequent rules”?
He said, "In the Parivāra, however," and so forth. "Including the assignment" means including the authorization for assignment by way of its status as a supplementary rule (anupaññatti).
"Mixed together in one" means combined in a single place. This is what is meant:
having invited two or three families and having had them seated in one location, [food] is brought from here and there, and the meal...
They pour it out; they pour out the curry and condiments; it becomes mixed into one; in this case, there is no offense.
However, if the initial invitation is below and each subsequent one is above, for one who eats starting from the top, there is an offense.
But having inserted the hand inside and having taken even a single mouthful out from the first invitation, at the time of eating—
There is no offense for one who eats in whatever manner after having [accepted] [the invitation].
"Eats two or three invitations together" means the sense is that he eats by putting two or three invitations together, mixing them, and making them into one.
Regarding the phrases "by the entire village," etc., it refers to one who has been invited by the entire village acting as one, wherever [that may be].
In some cases, there is no offense for one who eats. The same principle applies to a group as well. Regarding "being invited or saying, 'I will take almsfood'":
when being invited with the words, "Take food," he says, "I have no need for your food; I will take almsfood.
Herein, "action-and-non-action" (kriyā-akriyā) means that eating is the action, and the non-dedication [of the meal] is the non-action.
The commentary on the training rule concerning eating in succession is concluded.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning Kāṇamātā:
“For the sake of provisions” means for the sake of gifts. “For the sake of travel provisions” means for those traveling along a road, for the sake of their journey.
"Sattu" means ground meal, both that which is bound [into balls] and that which is not bound.
"Having received two or three bowlfuls" means having taken two or three bowlfuls filled level with the lower rim of the mouth-opening.
Since this meaning is already evident through the method explained below, he said "herein," etc., merely to show the specific details to be applied there. "The rest... [is as follows].
"Then from one bowl to another bowl" means: if three bowlfuls were taken, two are given; if two were taken, one is given—this is what is meant.

"When the journey has been interrupted" means: having seen a danger on the way, or because of a lack of need, they say, "We will not send it now, we will not go," and thus when the journey has been cut short, those who give [the bowl]—this is the meaning.
The commentary on the training rule concerning Kāṇamātā is finished.

5. Commentary on the First Training Rule on Invitation (*Pavāraṇā-sikkhāpada*) "Having eaten" (*bhuttavā*) means one who has completed the act of eating. "Even as much as a mustard seed" (*sāsapamattampi*) refers to even a very small amount of food;
it is swallowed whether it has been chewed or not. "Invited" (*pavārito*) means one who has been refused further food. For one who is eating...
If one refuses food brought by a server and does not wish to accept it, he is said to have been invited and then refused.
However, in order to show merely the meaning without taking up the literal phrasing, it is said:
"The meaning is 'one who has performed the invitation and performed the refusal. Furthermore, that refusal is not a mere refusal, but rather occurs by way of five factors.
Therefore, in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*), it is said:

"Food is seen," and so forth. "Eating food is seen" means that one or another of the five kinds of staple foods is seen in the bowl or other vessels. Thus he says: "If the food is sufficient for an invitation (*pavāraṇa*)," and so forth.
"Rice" (*sāli*) refers to the entire class of rice, including even wild millet (*nīvāra*). "Grain" (*vīhi*) refers to all [types of grain].
The genus *vīhi*. There is no distinction between barley (*yava*) and wheat (*godhuma*).
*Kaṅgu* refers to the entire genus of *kaṅgu*, including the white, red, and black varieties. *Varaka* refers to the entire genus of white-colored *varaka*, including even the small *varaka-coraka*.
*Kudrūsaka* refers to the entire genus of grass-grain, including both black *kodrava* and varieties such as *sāmāka*.
And here, they say that *nīvāra*, *varaka*, and *coraka* are "concordant with grain.

"Gruel" (*yāgu*) refers to any kind of gruel, such as sour gruel, milk gruel, and so forth. Since this [term] already includes *pāyāsa* (rice porridge), it was not stated as "or we shall cook any one of the sour *pāyāsa* and so on.
"Produces an invitation" (*pavāraṇaṃ janeti*) means [it produces] the invitation that serves as the basis for the prohibition against the offense of eating food that has not been left over.
It accomplishes [the purpose]. However, if no boundary (odhi) is discerned, it is included within the category of *yāgu* (rice gruel) and does not generate an invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
It generates an invitation again starting from the point when it reaches a thick consistency, because it is then included within the category of solid food (*bhojana*); this is the intended meaning.
"Having poured water, sour gruel, milk, and so forth" means having poured water, sour gruel, milk, and the like, and by means of those...
Having mixed it together with the food without crushing it. Therefore he said, "Take the rice-gruel," and so forth.
However, if they pour water, sour gruel, milk, or the like onto the food, crush it, and then give it saying, "Take the rice-gruel," there is no *pavāraṇā*.
"Even by rice-gruel" means even by rice-gruel that has been included as such, or by any other kind of rice-gruel. But a plain curry, or a rice-gruel made of curry, does not generate [the offense].
Because the state of having left over food has been interrupted by means of one of the five kinds of cooked food, it is said: "Even if two [mouthfuls] have been eaten...

he does not invite [others to eat]. Regarding the words "But whoever," etc., it is stated that for one who rejects unallowable meat or unallowable food—which are censured by the Buddha—there is no formal invitation (*pavāraṇā*) because the basis for the invitation is absent. For that which...
It is permissible for a bhikkhu to eat that very thing which he rejects; thus, there is an invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
However, one who knows this rejects it because it is unallowable (*akappiya*). Even one who does not know it is said to "reject" it when he rejects what stands in a place where rejection is required;
therefore, he does not invite. But if, while eating unallowable meat, he [eats] allowable meat or food...
Or he rejects it and then invites [the other] to partake. Why? Because of its nature as a substance (*vatthu*). For that which was rejected by him is the very substance for the invitation;
however, as for what he eats, although it stands in the category of things that ought to be rejected, while being eaten it does not lose its status as meat.
Therefore, he invites. What need is there to mention one who eats allowable meat when there is a prohibition against eating allowable meat?
This same principle applies when one eats unallowable food while abstaining from allowable food.
"When there is food" means when even one of the five kinds of food is present.

"Another kind of food with the stated characteristics" means even one of the five kinds of food with the stated characteristics that is other than what is in the bowl or elsewhere. "Without expectation" [means...]
The passage beginning with “that which [is placed] on the bowl, etc. is the explanation of that very [term].
He says “or elsewhere” and so forth to show that it is not only when one is indifferent [to receiving more] that this occurs. “Even though he rejects it, he does not invite [others to eat]”:
even if other food is brought during that interval, he does not invite others to eat it even while rejecting it. Why? Because the state of the meal being unfinished has been interrupted.
“*Upanāmetī*” means he shows the act of approaching with the body. In the phrase “in the hand or on a tray,” the word *vā* has the sense of an unstated alternative;

by it, one includes the alternative “or on the thighs. Having sent his bowl to a young bhikkhu sitting at a distance, he says, “Take rice from here”; but once [the bhikkhu] has taken it and departed, he remains silent.
The same principle applies when refusing that as well. Why? Because the monk is at a distance and the messenger has not brought [the food] there.
However, if the monk who has come after taking [the food] says, "Take this meal," then for one who refuses it, there is an invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
"Even when this has been said" means even when it has been said, "Take the meal."
"Of one who serves while holding a food-basket": this refers to one who serves while holding the food-basket with one hand and holding a spoon with the other.
"Another merely takes it up, thinking 'I will hold it'" means that another person comes and says, "I will hold the basket; you give the rice," and merely takes hold of it.

"He makes [it]. "It is brought to him" means it is brought by the server himself. Now, in order to show that even at the time of receiving it, it does not constitute an offense for one who refuses it when there is no intention on the part of the giver to offer it, the passage beginning with "But if...

is stated. "When it has been removed" means when the meal has been removed; for the intended meaning is that the bringing of the ladle itself constitutes its "bringing. "While it is being given to the next person" means...

While food is being given to the bhikkhu immediately following [him]. "By bodily movement" means by such bodily movements as the movement of a finger, a hand, a fly-whisk, or the corner of a robe, or by making a gesture with the eyebrows, or looking on in anger—as described in that way.
"By verbal movement" means by such verbal expressions as "Enough! Do not give! and so forth; [specifically] "Enough! (alaṃ).
Or by some such verbal expression as “I will not take it,” or “Do not pour it out,” or “Move away.
However, when food has been brought forward, if one—fearing the invitation (*pavāraṇā*)—withdraws the hand and repeatedly pours rice into the bowl while saying, “Pour it! Pour it!
Pound it and fill it up! there is no *pavāraṇā*. This same principle applies to one who is bringing the food forward.
Even when one observes a bhikkhu and says, "Friend, will you take anything from here?

I shall give you something," because it was said by naming a person who causes an invitation (*pavāraṇā*)—namely, "Accept the broth"—it is stated that "there is no invitation for one who rejects it upon hearing that.
However, regarding the term *maṃsarasa* (meat-broth), here it does not refer solely to the juice of meat as "meat-broth" alone.
It is understood; rather, meat and sauce together are called "meat-sauce.
Thus, even by way of the name that generates the invitation (*pavāraṇā*), it is said: "But when 'meat-sauce' is spoken, for one who refuses it, there is an invitation.
The same principle applies to the subsequent phrase, "fish and meat as a condiment. In whichever posture...
"One should eat without disturbing that [invitation]" means: if one who is walking extends the invitation, he must eat while still walking.
Upon reaching mud or water, he must have the food declared as "leftover" (*atiritta*).
If, along the way, a river is full, he should eat while walking around a grove on the riverbank. Or, if there is a boat or a bridge...
Or if there is one, having mounted it, one should eat while walking back and forth; the movement must not be interrupted.
This same method applies to the other postures as well. One who causes food to be made "leftover" by disturbing a particular posture must do so.
He who invites [others] while squatting on his heels must eat while squatting on his heels. But for him, below...
A straw mat or some other sitting cloth should be provided. However, one who has been invited to sit on a bench may eat while turning in the four directions without moving the seat at all.
One who has been invited to sit on a couch is not permitted to move back and forth from this side to that; however, if the couch is lifted along with him and he goes elsewhere...
They lead [him away]; this is permissible. Even by one who has invited [others] while lying down, he must eat while remaining in the lying position.
While turning over, he must not cross beyond the spot where he was lying on whichever side.
"This is enough for all": this entire amount is sufficient and adequate; "this too is more than enough for you; you shall receive nothing other than this."
The intention is as follows: "He who makes it leftover" means he who makes it leftover by saying, "This is enough for all. By way of the opposite method, [the following are excluded]:

that which has been made allowable, that which has been accepted, that which has been verbally declared, that which has been done within arm's reach, that which has been done by one who has already finished eating, and that which has been said by one who has finished eating and been invited to stop, while still not having risen from his seat: "This is enough for all."
Whatever has been made permissible as "leftover" by means of the seven formal acts of the Vinaya, and whatever is leftover from one who is ill—both of these are indeed "leftover.
This is according to the method of its opposite. And in this context, it is said that "This is sufficient for all" should be stated three times;
this, it seems, is the established custom. However, those who uphold the Vinaya say that it should be stated only once.
To the question, "Why is he not permitted to do it again? he says, "For that which... and so forth. Therein, "that which has not been done" means:
by whichever [monk] the first permissible [act] was performed, he must perform that which has not yet been done. However, it is not permitted to perform it in the first vessel.
And "by whom it has not been done" means: by whichever other monk it was not performed first, by him it must be performed.
The meaning is as follows. "Stated" means stated in the Sinhalese commentaries (*sīhaḷaṭṭhakathā*). "But in another vessel" means:
having placed it in front of any other vessel—whether a bowl, a basin, or a basket—in whatever vessel was first used, one should lower the [original] vessel [into it].
"Except in the case of the matter of eating" means: except in the case of the matter of eating when one has already finished eating and has refused further food.

"Three offenses of expiation" (pācittiya) refers to three offenses of expiation according to the cases of one who perceives what is not left over as not left over, one who is doubtful, and one who perceives it as left over.
"And an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for each mouthful" means: for every mouthful swallowed, there is an offense of wrong-doing. However, if they are mixed with solid food...
Whether for the purpose of food or not for the purpose of food, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for one who, having accepted them, consumes them.
"By way of permitted use of those" means by way of the permitted use of those things such as the *yāmakālika* (medicines to be used within a watch of the night), etc.;

that is, *yāmakālika* for the purpose of quenching thirst when thirst arises, and *sattāhakālika* (medicines to be used for seven days) and *yāvajīvika* (medicines to be used for life) for the purpose of pacifying this or that ailment.
The meaning is that it is for the purpose of pacifying an affliction when one exists. This too is bodily action because of the act of swallowing;
it is verbal action because of not causing [the food] to be made "leftover" by saying with the voice, "Venerable sir, make it leftover.
Thus he said, "The origins and so forth are exactly like those of the first *kaṭhina* rule. Regarding the term "action-non-action": here, eating after having refused [the invitation] is "action."
The failure to make what remains over [for others] is to be understood as "non-performance.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*) is concluded.
6. Commentary on the second training rule concerning the invitation ceremony.
