"Having heard" means having heard it from another person or having heard it announced by that very person. Because it is stated, "In the case of having eaten, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya)," it is said that the offense of expiation occurs at the conclusion of the meal.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the second invitation (dutiyapavāraṇāsikkhāpada) is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Eating at Improper Times (vikālabhojanasikkhāpada).

"Non-time" (*vikāla*) here refers to the period from sunrise until midday; this is known as the "time for eating," which has been practiced and traditionally observed by the Buddhas and other Noble Ones.
Any time other than that is "non-time," because it is "the time has passed. Therefore he said, "when the time has passed," and so forth.
Even the moment when midday has already arrived is included within the category of "time. But from that point onward...
It is not possible to chew or eat [it]. One might be able to drink it hastily, yet one must not do so out of scruple (*kukkucca*).
Furthermore, a time-pillar (*kāla-thambha*) should be set up for the purpose of knowing the time limit;

the meal-duty must be performed within that time interval. By the phrase "whatever... or solid food (*khādanīya*) or soft food," this refers first to things such as sugar-candy, sweetmeats, and so forth.
This shows that there is nothing at all to be said regarding [food] consisting of staple grains and non-staple grains. "Edible food" (*bhojanīya*) refers to the five kinds of cooked food.

"When the requisite exists" means when a cause such as thirst is present. "Of one who has vomited" (*romaṭṭhakassa*) means of a monk who, having swallowed and then vomited, has placed it back in his mouth;
it is that which has emerged from the mouth and departed from the path of the food.
That which has gone out [of the mouth] is called *romaṭṭha*. Here, however, what is intended is that which has been swallowed and then spat out, and is thus placed within the mouth itself.

Therefore he said, "And not, monks," and so forth. With the exception of *romaṭṭha*, there is an offense for those who, having received other kinds of spittle, retain it in the mouth and then swallow it. But if it goes down the throat without being retained, it is permissible.
The commentary on the training rule regarding eating at improper times is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule regarding storing food:
"Kāra, karaṇa, and kiriyā are one in meaning"—by this, he shows that the word *kāra* has the sense of an abstract state (*bhāvattha*). *Sammā*...

*Nidhāna*, *ṭhapana*, and *sannidhi* mean "storing. By the phrase, "This is the name for that which has been received and spent one night," it shows the state of being "unwashed" (or stale) regarding what has been received and spent one night.
Even though it is not a *yāmakālika* (time-limited until the watch of the night) edible or meal, [the text says]:
"There is no offense if one eats a *yāmakālika* substance after having stored it during the watch," and so forth.

However, according to the word of the Buddha, even in that case, if it exceeds the watch of the night (*yāma*), there must be an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) due to the condition of storage (*sannidhi*);
therefore, it is said: "whatever is either for the duration of the day (*yāvakālika*) or for the duration of the watch (*yāmakālika*).

Now, in order to clarify the state of being poorly washed, it is said: "that which [is visible] by means of a finger," and so forth. In this context, "that which a line appears when rubbing with a finger" refers to that which...
When one rubs a washed bowl with a finger, the finger-marks appear on the bowl; the meaning is that such a bowl is "ill-washed.
However, when finger-marks appear on a bowl that has the color of oil, they are not considered an offense. "Oil" means sesame oil.
"Appears" means it appears on top of the rice gruel. "In such a bowl as well" refers to a bowl from which the alms-food has not yet been relinquished.
Whether one has brought out food oneself or by another, if the bowl has not been properly washed, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) for eating on the following day.
This is because that which clings to the bowl remains as an unrenounced acceptance; thus, for one eating on the second day, there is an offense of expiation.
However, if the bowl has been relinquished, there is no offense for one eating on the following day.

"But whatever" means: but whatever food. "Indeed, not yet relinquished" means: it is indeed not yet relinquished either by way of giving without expectation or by way of giving to one who is not ordained without expectation.
"Permissible food" means: even as little as a single grain of rice, it is permissible food.
"Among the impermissible" means: among impermissible meats. "The rest" means: those remaining other than human flesh.
[This applies] to the meat of elephants, horses, dogs, snakes, lions, tigers, leopards, bears, and hyenas when it has not been examined,
as well as to meat specifically prepared [for a monk]. In the Pāḷi, by such statements as, "If one accepts for the purpose of food that which is for seven days or that which is for life,
there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa)," it is shown that for those things kept for seven days or for life, even if consumed before the midday meal, there is an offense of wrong-doing.

Because it has been stated [that this applies] even when consuming food at the improper time (yāmakālika), there must also be a separate dukkaṭa for swallowing it for the purpose of nutriment; thus he said:
"For one swallowing it for the purpose of nutriment, there is a pācittiya together with a dukkaṭa. Regarding the phrase "in all alternatives":
in all the alternatives mentioned, such as "while eating allowable food" and so forth, another pācittiya is added. This...
It is said: there are two *pācittiya* offenses regarding permissible food; two *pācittiya* offenses together with a *thullaccaya* regarding human flesh;
and for the remaining impermissible meats, two *pācittiya* offenses together with a *dukkaṭa*.

When one swallows a *yāmakālika* (medicinal) substance with the mouth while containing food, provided there is a valid reason, there are two *pācittiya* offenses; [the same applies] when it is without food.
It is exactly one. For one who swallows for the purpose of nutriment, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) together with [the other] in both cases of conceptualization.

"In the remainder" means in those remaining from the "time-for-a-watch" (*yāmakālika*) onwards. "An offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) increases indeed" means that another offense of expiation also increases indeed.
This is what is meant: if one swallows at an improper time, there is an offense of expiation due to the condition of storing up (*sannidhi*) regarding ordinary food.

And there are two *pācittiya* offenses due to eating at the improper time; among the types of unallowable meat, there are two *pācittiya* offenses together with a *thullaccaya* for human flesh, and two together with a *dukkaṭa* for the remainder.
"Belaṭṭhasīsa" is the name of a certain great elder (*mahāthera*) among a thousand matted-hair ascetics (*jaṭila*). "Three *pācittiya*s" refers to one who keeps food in store.
There are three *pācittiya* offenses based on the following cases: one who perceives it as stored when it is actually stored; one who is doubtful when it is actually stored;

and one who perceives it as not stored when it is actually stored. "Those who are associated" (*saṃsaṭṭhāni*) means those whose flavors are mixed. For it is with reference to a mixed flavor that it was said: "What is received on that same day is allowable at the proper time," and so forth.
Therefore he says, "Therefore," etc. And here, "unmixed flavor" (*asambhinnarasa*) means a flavor that is not blended. This [refers] to such things as cold milk-rice (*pāyāsa*), etc.

This was said with reference to what is obtained together [with the meal], such as a lump of ghee and so forth. However, the phrase "or well-washed" (*sudhotaṃ*) was said with reference to things like *takola* and *jātiphala* fruits obtained together with the alms-food, as well as *siṅgīvera* and the like which were given after being added to the rice-gruel and other items.

"By that" (*tena*) means by that which is permitted for seven days. "Received on that very day" (*tadahupaṭiggahitaṃ*) means received on that specific day; thus, it refers to that which was received on that very day.
This same principle applies to such cases as “with what has been received by two,” and so forth.

Therefore—meaning because even what was received before midday is permissible—it is stated that “what has been received is allowable for seven days. This is said in the Bhesajjakkhandhaka (Medicine Chapter):
“Monks, medicinal tonics received for life, when received within the seven-day period, are allowable for seven days; once the seven days have passed, they are not allowable.”

It has been said. Although it was not kept in the mouth for even a single night, nevertheless, because that which is placed in the mouth constitutes "storing" (*sannidhi*), it is therefore called "mouth-storing" (*mukhasannidhi*).

Regarding the "four kinds of allowable grounds" (*kappiyabhūmi*): these are the four types of allowable huts (*kappiyakuṭi*), namely, those established by proclamation, those where cattle lie down, those belonging to a householder, and those by formal authorization.

In this context, a "kappiyakuṭi" (a building for allowable goods) established by means of the formal proclamation (*ussāvanantikā*) refers to a hut belonging either to the Saṅgha or to a single bhikkhu,
the foundation stones, pillars, and so forth of which have been laid by those standing around while building it, saying, "We are making a kappiyakuṭi,
we are making a kappiyakuṭi," or "A kappiyakuṭi, a kappiyakuṭi. Furthermore, it refers to a monastery (*ārāma*) that is for the most part unenclosed.

Or even the whole [of such a place] is called a "cow-pen" (*gonisāda*). Regarding "householders": these are either those who, excluding a monk, have given [the site] saying, "We give a kitchen hut," or they belong to them.
What is called "formal authorization" (*sammuti*) is that which is performed by making a proclamation through the ritual formula (*kammavācā*).
But how is the determination of these [terms] to be known? To this he says: "The determination of these has been stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*."
The commentary on the training rule concerning hoarding is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning fine foods:
Regarding the phrase "fine foods," this is explained by eliding the middle term; thus he says, "those mixed with fine [foods]," and so forth.
All that possesses the characteristic described as "aquatic" is a fish; thus, it is said in the Vibhaṅga: "A fish is called 'aquatic'.
Therefore, every fish is indeed a fish. Whatsoever is born in water is called a fish—this is what is meant.
By means of the Mahānāma-sikkhāpada:

“An unill monk may accept an invitation for requisites for four months, except for a renewed invitation and except for a permanent invitation. If he should accept it beyond that, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).

By this training rule (sikkhāpada). For here, in a place where an invitation for requisites for the sick has been made by the Saṅgha, if a limit has been set there regarding either nights or medicines, such as: “There are only this many nights; there are only these many...”

"or medicines may be requested. Therefore, it is stated that there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for one who, beyond the limit of the night or the limit of the medicine, requests medicine when there is no need for medicine, or requests a different medicine when there is a need for a different medicine.
Consequently, even if one who is not ill perceives oneself as being ill, regarding the five medicines...

Regarding the statement, "One who requests [food] is said to be requesting medicine when he requests it under the pretext that it is for the purpose of making medicine," it is said that such a person must be dealt with according to the Mahānāma training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
However, one who requests it not for the sake of medicine, but solely for his own consumption, is subject only to the offense of requesting boiled rice and curry (*sūpodana-viññatti*).
He is to be dealt with according to the rule. For this has been stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*: "One who requests pure ghee and so forth and then eats them does not incur a *pācittiya* offense;
rather, regarding the training rules (*sekhiya*), he incurs an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for requesting curry and boiled rice.

Thus, "he is to be dealt with for the request of curry and boiled rice" means he is to be dealt with by the training rule beginning with, "If one is not ill, [he shall not] [request] curry or boiled rice," and is thus charged with a *dukkaṭa*.
"It must be made [to be done]" is what is meant. "By this" means by this training rule regarding exquisite food.
To the question, "What happens when it is said, 'Give ghee with the rice'? he says: "But when it is said, 'Give ghee with the rice,'" and so forth.
The connection is that for the solicitation of curry and boiled rice, there is only a *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). Why? He says: "Because," and so forth. Now, as to how...
If it is asked, "Why is 'ghee-rice' (*sappibhatta*) not understood in the same way as 'delicate foods' (*paṇītabhojanāni*)?"—it is because [the application] is not exclusive (*anekantikatta*).
For when "delicate foods" is said, the meaning "foods mixed with delicacies are delicate foods" is understood exclusively;
however, when "ghee-rice" is said, it could also mean "rice consisting of ghee is ghee-rice."
Because it is being perceived [as such], the meaning "rice mixed with ghee is 'ghee-rice'" is not established as an absolute certainty.
This same method applies to expressions such as "give me butter-rice" and so forth.
"In the same manner as before" means in the very same way as the previous method: "Having given rice, having made [it] with ghee, eat. But if...
When "ghee" is mentioned, if one gives any other substance such as butter from among the remaining items, it is a non-agreement (visaṅketa).
"There is no offense" means that because it is a non-agreement, there is no offense for any of the [relevant] rules.
They say: "Even though there is no offense, it must not be consumed because it was produced through one's own effort. "By means of allowable ghee" means by means of ghee made from allowable meat.

This same principle applies here in the case of "unallowable ghee" (*akappiya-sappi*) as well. For the distinction between allowable and unallowable applies only to meats, not to ghee and the other substances.
With the single exception of human fat-oil, there is nothing among all milk, curd, ghee, butter, fat, and oil that is called "unallowable.
The intention is that even regarding consumption, only an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) occurs here, as it is not intended [as a formal offense]. If, however, unallowable ghee is unavailable...
In the same manner as before, if one gives unallowable fresh butter and so forth, saying, "Make it into ghee and eat it," it is considered to have been given with unallowable ghee.
And just as when it is said, "Give with allowable ghee," yet one gives with unallowable ghee,
there is a discrepancy (*visaṅketa*), so too here, when it is said, "When 'with unallowable ghee' is said, give with allowable ghee," each successive case follows the same sequence.
Even if it were explained in detail, this same meaning would have to be stated; and since that can be understood even in brief, it is said:
"Setting aside the method of detailed exposition, the determination in all instances should be understood by this very method.
Herein, the summarized meaning is as follows: whatever intimation there is, when that [intimation] or its source is obtained, that very thing is obtained.
[The offense] exists. However, if one gives something else—whether mentioned in the Canon or not—it is a breach of convention (*visaṅketa*).
"In different places" means in various locations, such as giving ghee in that very house and butter in another, and so forth.
The commentary on the training rule concerning exquisite food is concluded.

10. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Teeth-Cleaning Wood (Dantapona-sikkhāpada) "By means of the body" (kāyena): it should be understood that one "takes by means of the body" when one grasps with any part of the body, such as the hand and so forth, even down to a single toe.
The same principle applies to "giving. "By means of what is connected to the body" (kāyappaṭibaddhena): this refers to anything among the alms-bowl and other such items.

By means of an accessory connected to the body. The same principle applies to giving as well. Whatever is given by means of any accessory such as a spoon and so forth, it is indeed considered "given by what is connected to the body.

"By one or another" means by means of the body, or by what is connected to the body, or by what is relinquishable (*nissaggiya*). In that context, "by what is relinquishable" refers to [objects] both from the body and from what is connected to the body.

For when one releases [the object] from the hand-hold and it falls upon the body or what is connected to the body of one standing nearby, it is said to have been "given" by means of an act of relinquishment (*nissaggiya-payoga*).
"Of that" refers to the one who has accepted it. "By way of the reversal of what was stated" means by way of the opposite of what was previously stated.
This is what is meant: by means of any one of the acts of relinquishment regarding the body or what is connected to the body...
When something is being given, if one takes it with the body or with what is attached to the body, this is called "received.
By the phrase "portable," it is meant portable by a man of medium strength; by this, he shows that receiving [something] that is not portable—such as a wooden plank or a stone—is not valid.
By the phrase "capable of bearing," it means capable of sustaining [it] through yoga. By this...
This shows that receiving [alms] in very delicate leaves such as those of the *tintiṇika* tree is not permissible.
Regarding the phrase "with a leaf fallen from a tree growing where it was not intended": this refers to a lotus leaf or the like that has fallen from its place of growth;

however, by this [statement], it is shown that even if a lotus leaf or a *kiṃsuka* leaf and so forth grows there naturally and is large, it is not allowable to receive [alms] in it. For that does not count as being "connected to the body."
This shows that [the bowl] moves. And just as in the case of what is born there [in the womb], it is the same with a bed or similar items placed after being tied to a stump.
But surely, for one who receives [food] even by means of a bowl-stand or the like—which is connected to what is connected—does the act of receiving not succeed?
Why then is receiving stated here only by way of the body and what is directly connected to the body, and not also by way of what is connected to what is connected?
He said, "In this context, there is no such thing as 'bound-to-the-bound'.
However, some say, "Receiving [food] with a stand constitutes receiving by means of what is bound to the body; therefore, it is not permitted.
That is merely a verbal assertion. For in substance, he shows that all of that is indeed simply "bound to the body."

Akallakoti is ill. "He receives with his mouth" means that being unable to take it with his own hand and consume it, he receives it with his mouth. The intention is that even dust fallen from the vessel brought [to him] is permissible because it has been brought.

"Standing there" means standing within such reach of the hand. "That which" refers to the load. "A man of middle strength" means a man of medium physical power. "An offense of wrong-doing prescribed in the Vinaya" is a *vinayadukkaṭa*.
"Having given that to one who is not fully ordained" [refers to] after having gone for alms.
Having gone to a monastery or a sitting hall and given that almsfood to one who is not fully ordained—
this is stated according to the corresponding prior intention (*pubbābhoga*). However, since it does not become the property of that person merely by the arising of the thought,
"I will give this to one who is not fully ordained," it is therefore permissible to accept and consume it even without having given it to him.
"Regarding tears, spittle, snot, and so forth": here, "tears" refers to the water of the eyes; "spittle" refers to saliva;

"snot" refers to that which is called the brain matter having become putrid within the head, which, having flowed out, descended through the opening of the palate and mouth, and remained filling the nostrils.
By the word "and so forth," urine, feces, pus, dental tartar, eye-secretion, and ear-wax are included.
And the taking of salt that has risen on the body. "From its place" means from the eye sockets and so forth.
If one takes it from between [the eyelids], what happens? He says: "It is called 'taken up' (uggahitaka)," which means it is called "badly taken" (duṭṭhu gahitaka).
"Phalini" means possessing fruit. "Or from a branch growing there that bears fruit" means from a branch bearing fruit that has grown on that tree.
*Durupaciṇṇadukkaṭaṃ*: "Badly practiced misconduct" means that because one has done what was forbidden by the thought, "This should not be done," it is a bad habit or conduct;
thus, one falls into both *durupaciṇṇa* (badly practiced) and *dukkaṭa* (wrongdoing). *Āharīyati* means "is brought forth";
it refers to anything that is to be swallowed, but here the four types of nutriment (*cattāri āhārā*) are intended.
He said: “Whatever,” and so forth. In that context, *yāvakālika* (that which is for the time) refers to that which may be eaten from the rising of the dawn until the midday point has passed;

thus, it is for the duration of the [proper] time. *Yāmakālika* (that which is for the watch) refers to that which, when there is thirst, may be drunk to quench that thirst from the rising of the dawn until the end of the first watch;
thus, it is for the duration of the watch. It is [also called *sattāhakālika*] because it may be stored and consumed for up to seven days.

“Sattāhakālikaṃ” means that its time [of use] is seven days. “Yāvajīvikaṃ” means that it is to be used for as long as one lives, because it may be kept and consumed even for the duration of one’s life.
Thus he said, “Therein,” and so forth. Regarding “roots, leaves, flowers, fruits, etc.,” here first of all, “root” refers to radishes, horseradish, pickles, fermented fish, and so on.
In various regions, there are roots for soups that pervade the needs for both hard food (*khādanīya*) and soft food (*bhojanīya*) for people according to their natural diet.
"Leaf" (*patta*) refers to leaves of the same kind used for radish-pickles, *kharaka*-pickles, *caccu*-curries, *tambaka*-pickles, and so forth.

"Flower" (*puppha*) refers to flowers of the same kind used for radish-pickles, *kharaka*-pickles, and so forth. "Fruit" (*phala*) refers to fruits such as the jackfruit (*panasa*), the breadfruit (*labuja*), and so forth.
In various regions, there are fruits that pervade the needs for both solid food (*khādanīya*) and soft food (*bhojanīya*) for people according to their natural diet.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), bulbs, roots, and so forth are included.
"Ambapāna" is a drink made from mangoes, whether raw or ripe. In that regard, when making it with raw mangoes, [one uses] young mangoes and the like.

Having broken it up, thrown it into water, cooked it by the heat of the sun in the open air, strained it, and mixed it with honey, sugar, camphor, and so forth received on that very day, it may be prepared.

Thus prepared, it is allowable even before the midday meal. However, if one receives what has been prepared by one who is not fully ordained, it is permissible to consume it with solid food even before the midday meal, provided it was received before the meal.
After the meal, it is permissible to consume non-meat substances until the rising of the dawn. This same method applies to all drinks.
Among them, *jambupāna* is a drink made from *jambu* fruits; *cocapāna* is a drink made from the seeds of plantain fruits;
*mocapāna* is a drink made from seedless plantain fruits; and *madhukapāna* is [a drink made from] *madhuka* flowers.
*Jātirasapāna* is a drink made from the juice of the *jāti* flower. That is permissible if mixed with water, but it is not permissible if pure.
*Muddikāpāna* is a drink made by crushing grapes in water, like the preparation of mango juice.
*Sālūkapāna* is a drink made by crushing the roots (*sālūka*) of red and blue lotuses and so forth. *Phārusakapāna* is a drink made from *phārusaka* fruits, like the preparation of mango juice.
In this same manner, bamboo juice and so forth are to be understood. Furthermore, all these drinks that have been cooked by fire are not permitted.
Therefore he said, "with cold water," and so on. Regarding the remaining permitted remnants of fruit, leaf, and flower juices:
from among the juices of grain-fruits, cooked vegetables, and *madhuka* flowers, he said, "I allow, monks, every kind of fruit juice."
“Even among the juices of fruits and grains that have been permitted by the phrase ‘except for the juice of grain and fruit’ and so forth, [the rule applies].
“The purpose of solid food” (*khādanīyattha*) means the function to be performed by solid food. “It does not satisfy” means it does not accomplish [that function].

“Even with water, which is not food, through the perception of it as food” refers to failing to correctly discern the meaning stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*) for the phrase “one should take food.”
“Food is so called because it is brought (āharīyati)”; this is for those who feel remorse due to the perception of food even in water, which is not food.

And regarding a tooth-stick, it is for those who feel remorse due to a distorted perception, thinking, “This has been brought to the mouth,” even when the tooth-stick has not actually been brought to the mouth, thinking, “This tooth-stick has been brought to the mouth. They may drink as they please.
Having accepted it or not having accepted it, one may drink it as one desires. "By the use of tooth-sticks" means by the use of *dantakaṭṭha* (tooth-wood);
the meaning is "for cleaning the teeth and so forth. By this, he shows that it is not permitted to swallow its juice.
"The four great revolting things" are excrement, urine, ashes, and clay; they are called "revolting" because of their nature as foul dwellings and so forth.
"Having become," means they have become "loathsome" (vikaṭāni) because they are unnatural food; or the meaning is that they have become "deformed" (virūpāni).

"When the condition exists" means when the cause exists; the meaning is "when bitten by a snake. "The absence of clearing [the mouth] by means of smoke, etc. means the absence of clearing [the mouth] by means of smoke, flowers, perfumes, tooth-sticks, and so forth.
The commentary on the training rule regarding tooth-cleansing sticks is finished.
The Fourth Chapter on Food. 5.
The Chapter on the Naked Ascetics.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Naked Ascetics.
"Acelaka" means any naked person who has gone forth. "Paribbājaka" means any other person who has gone forth, with the exception of a bhikkhu and a sāmaṇera.
"Paribbājikā" means any female who has gone forth, with the exception of a bhikkhunī, a sikkhamānā, and a sāmaṇerī.
All these should be understood as belonging to other sects (aññatitthiya). Therefore he said:

“of these other-sectarians, such as the naked ascetics (acelaka) and so forth. “Of them” means of those other-sectarians. “Having set down a vessel” means having set down a vessel filled with food. “External ointment” refers to oil and the like.
Since the naked ascetics and others are here considered to be merely sectarians (titthiya);
Therefore, by way of the term "heretic," three types of cutting off have been made.
It is the determination that [the use of requisites] is permitted for one who is not a heretic, for a naked ascetic,
likewise for one wearing the marks of a heretic, and also for a householder or a monk.

It is our opinion here that it is not permissible to give [a gift] with a mind directed toward a non-Buddhist, nor to one who bears the marks of a non-Buddhist ascetic, even if they are a stream-enterer or of higher attainment.
The commentary on the rule concerning naked ascetics is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule on Sending Away (Uyyojana-sikkhāpada).
Regarding the phrase "a village or a town," it should be understood that a city is also included by the term "village.

Regarding the phrase "we shall enter," there is an ellipsis of the word "having taken" followed by "having gone"; or else, it refers to a lack of mindfulness regarding the presence of that woman in that village.
"Unknowingly" means having taken a bhikkhu and gone [to him], saying, "Come, friend, let us enter a village or a town for alms.
"Any kind of foodstuff" refers to any kind of material sustenance, such as rice-gruel and so forth.

"Should dismiss" means that upon seeing a woman suitable for his own amusement, he should dismiss or send her away. Therefore, he said, "Together with a woman," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [the rest is implied].
It includes the transgressions of the doors of body and speech that remain to be mentioned. Regarding the phrase "having said 'Go,' etc.": this means having said, "Go, friend;
neither conversation nor sitting with you is comfortable for me; conversation or sitting alone is comfortable for me.
"This is indeed improper conduct" means that this aforementioned laughing and so forth is precisely improper conduct (*anācāra*). Not...

"Another suitable reason": the meaning is that it does not occur by making some other suitable reason or condition—such as the inability of both to subsist together—except for the aforementioned type of improper conduct.
"Of him" (assa) refers to the instigator. "He" (so) refers to the one who was instigated.

Regarding "one who is not fully ordained" (anupasampanne), they say that here the term refers specifically to a novice (sāmaṇera). "Of both" (ubhinnampi): [refers to the instigator and the instigated].
"Whether one who is ordained or one who is not ordained" refers to both. Regarding "the instigation of a reproach" (*kalisāsanāropana*): "reproach" (*kali*) means anger;
its "instigation" (*sāsana*) is a command, thus it is a "reproach-command. The meaning is "the instigation of that. [The intention is]: "Perhaps, being vexed by this, he might depart.
Thus, having pointed out a fault in standing, sitting, and so forth due to anger, [one says]: "Look, sirs, at his behavior! etc.
"His sitting, looking forward, and looking around [are such that] he stands like a stump, sits like a dog, and looks here and there like a monkey"—this is what is meant by speaking unpleasant words.
However, there is no fault in speaking in this way with a pure mind.
Regarding the phrase "by such means as these," the word "as" (*ādi*) includes, for example, [speaking after] seeing a valuable object.

The inclusion of these cases refers to when one urges someone with the thought, "He will give rise to lustful thoughts"; or urges them with the thought, "Having seen a woman, he will give rise to discontent";
or urges them with the thought, "Bring out rice-gruel, cooked food, or fresh food for the sick person, the one who has been left behind, or the guardian of the monastery";
or when, despite having a task to be done, one urges someone not because one wishes to engage in misconduct.
The commentary on the training rule concerning departing is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning with food:
“*Sabhojane*” is a compound with an external referent (*bāhiratthasamāsa*), where the vowel *u* in the word *ubha* is elided; thus he says, “together with both.”
“Know [this],” and so forth. Therein, “by both persons” means by both the wife and the husband.
Alternatively, it is food that is to be eaten; because it occurs together with a woman and a man, it is called “with company” (*sabhojana*). Thus he said, “Or alternatively,” and so forth.
“Of one obsessed by lust” means of one whose intention is sexual intercourse. “His own house” means his bedchamber, his dwelling-place.
The meaning is as follows: "Of a large one" means of a large bedchamber.
"From the door-jamb" refers to a small bedchamber, whether it has been constructed in such a way or otherwise.
"He should sit having passed beyond the middle" means he should sit having passed beyond the central ridge-pole. A "small bedchamber" is [defined] by its width...
It is five cubits in measure, and its middle portion from the door-panels (*piṭṭhasaṅghāṭa*) is exactly two and a half cubits;
therefore, in such a bedchamber, one who sits having left the reach of a hand from the door-panels is said to be "sitting beyond the back-pillar.
And sitting thus, one is said to be "sitting beyond the middle."
Thus it is. Therefore it is said in the Pāḷi: “He sits having passed beyond the backbone.
And here, it should be understood as sitting with the intention of sitting, having entered into that which possesses consciousness.
The commentary on the training rule concerning food with living beings is finished.
4–5. Commentary on the Training Rules concerning Secluded Covering and Sitting in Secret.

Regarding the fourth and fifth training rules, whatever needs to be said has already been stated in the section on the two *aniyata* rules; thus it is said: "The remaining method of exposition should be understood in the same manner as that explained for the two *aniyata* rules.
The commentary on the training rules concerning secluded covering and sitting in secret is concluded.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule on Conduct:

"Having seen a bhikkhu within the vicinity of the boundary" means that while walking from the place where the thought of visiting families arose, one sees a bhikkhu within the vicinity of the boundary—that is, within the range of sight—while still inside the boundary.
Or having seen [someone] facing him. "By ordinary speech" means by such speech as can be heard by one standing within twelve cubits;
there is no need to search here and there before making the announcement. For whoever must be sought in such a manner does not exist at all.
Therefore he said, "by such [speech]," and so forth. "Without having asked for permission" means without having announced it.
Regarding the phrase "within the monastery, a bhikkhunī’s dwelling, a titthiya’s lodging, a place for returning from almsround, or a meal-offering house":

here, "within the monastery" (*antarārāma*) means a vihāra inside the village. "Place for returning" (*paṭikkamana*) means a sitting hall. "Meal-offering house" (*bhattiyaghara*) means either a house where one has been invited, or the house of those who provide meals by ticket (*salākabhatta*) and so forth.
"In times of distress" (*āpadāsu*) refers to obstacles to life or to the holy life (*brahmacariya*). "Doing or not doing" (*kiriyākiriyā*) here refers to entering among families [for alms].
It should be understood that there is no formal act (*kiriya*) and no offense for not having asked permission.
The commentary on the training rule concerning conduct (*cāritta-sikkhāpada*) is finished.
7. Commentary on the Mahānāma Training Rule.
"All this was spoken by way of the *vatthu* (the underlying circumstance). Thus, the statement:

"A monk who is not ill may accept an invitation for requisites for four months, except for a renewed invitation and except for a permanent invitation"—all of this was spoken by way of the *vatthu*, which is reckoned as the origin of the training rule (*sikkhāpada*).
For therein, Mahānāma the Sakyan said: "Venerable sir, I desire [to provide] for the Saṅgha..."
"Let him invite [the Sangha] for four months with medicine," and so forth;
thus, because the invitation was performed constantly for four months with an abundance of medicine, it is said that the Blessed One spoke accordingly.
"Except on the occasion of a renewed invitation" means: setting aside any such renewed invitation that may exist. "Except on the occasion of a permanent invitation" means...
The same principle applies here as well. However, the intention is that if those [medicines] are also present, they may be accepted.
Therefore he said, "But this is the meaning here," and so forth. "In that regard" means in that invitation (*pavāraṇā*).
"A limit has been set by medicines" means either by way of name, such as "ghee, oil," and so on, or by way of measure, such as "by the *pattha*, the *nāḷi*, the *āḷhaka*, etc."
Or, if a limit has been set regarding medicines, such as "only this many medicines may be requested," then it is a case of having made a restriction regarding medicines.
"Not for the purpose of making medicine" means that even if one is able to subsist on mixed food, it is not considered "for the purpose of making medicine.
"Other medicine" refers, for example, to being invited ghee when oil was intended, or a *doṇa* measure when a *āḷhaka* measure was intended.
"Having declared the facts as they are" means: having reported the truth thus—"We were invited by you with these medicines;
we have need of this and that medicine; those nights during which we were invited by you have passed;
we have need of the medicine"—only one who is actually ill is permitted to request [medicine] in this way, not anyone else.
The commentary on the Mahānāma training rule is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule regarding an army on march:
"Fourfold" means that which has four components—namely, elephants, horses, chariots, and infantry; thus it is "fourfold," and [the text refers to] that fourfold [army].

“An elephant with twelve men, a horse with three men, a chariot with four men, and four foot soldiers armed with spears”—this is what is called an army endowed with the four divisions in its minimum form; the meaning is "such an army.
But having left that behind means that it is no longer seen because it has been intercepted by something or has descended into a low-lying place; having stood here...
"It can be seen" means having left that vicinity of sight and gone to another place.
"In the case of going to see an army" refers to the occasion of going to see an army; or rather, this is the reading itself.
"Each one among the elephants and so forth" means each one among the four components, such as the elephants and so forth, even down to a single elephant mounted by a single man.
The meaning is: "a man who has his own hand. "Engaged in pleasure" (anuyyutta) means that when the king goes to a park or a river, he is thus engaged in pleasure.
"On such an occasion" (tathārūpappaccaye) refers to when there is a corresponding cause, such as "the maternal uncle is ill with the army," and so forth.
"In times of distress" (āpadāsu) refers to obstacles to life or the holy life; for one who goes thinking, "Having gone there, I shall be released," there is no offense.
The commentary on the training rule concerning marching with an army is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Dwelling with an Army:

“By an army besieged by an opposing force” means by an army that has been blocked by an opposing force in such a way that movement is cut off. “Obstructed by anyone” means obstructed by someone, whether an enemy or a ruler.
The commentary on the training rule concerning military camps is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning military parades:
"Of a place of combat" means of a battlefield. "Knowing the strength of the enemy" means [knowing] "there are this many elephants, this many..."
They know the divisions of the army, thinking, “There are this many horses, this many chariots, and this many foot soldiers.
In such passages as “I allow you, monks, [to count] by way of the monastery,” the word *agga* has the sense of a “division” or “part. Therefore he said:
“The meaning is ‘the place for counting the army. They array the army thus: “Let there be elephants here, let there be horses here, let there be chariots here, let there be...”
“Let them be foot soldiers”—this refers to the stationing of the army; the meaning is that they are stationed by forming a mass.
Therefore he said: “This is the name for the encampment of the army. A “twelve-man elephant” means four riders and two guards for each leg;
thus it is a twelve-man elephant. A “three-man horse” means one rider and two leg-guards; thus it is a three-man [horse].
"A chariot with four men": one driver, one warrior, and two wheel-protectors; thus it is called "a chariot with four men.
The commentary on the training rule concerning military displays is finished.
The fifth section, the Chapter on the Naked Ascetics, is concluded.
6. Surāpāna-vagga 1. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding the Drinking of Surā:
"Surā is an intoxicant made from flour, etc. means that surā is an intoxicant made from ingredients such as flour, cakes, boiled rice, and parched grain.

The meaning is this: it is said that there are five kinds of liquor (*surā*), namely: flour-liquor, cake-liquor, rice-liquor, that into which *kiṇṇa* has been added, and that prepared from various ingredients.
In this context, flour-liquor is that made by putting flour into a vessel, adding the appropriate water, and kneading it. The same applies to the others.
Furthermore, *kiṇṇa* refers to the fermenting seed of that liquor. Those who [call them] "liquor-cakes" (*surāmodaka*)...
Those that are made by throwing [ingredients] into [a liquid] are called *kiṇṇapakkhittā*. Those combined with various ingredients such as *harītakī* and *sāsa* are *sambhārasaṃyuttā*.

The meaning of *meraya*—which is a fermented liquor (*āsava*) made from flowers and so forth—is that it is a long-aged liquor made from the ingredients of flowers, fruits, honey, and molasses. This is what is meant: flower-liquor, fruit-liquor, honey-liquor, and molasses-liquor.

"Connected with the requisites" (sambhārasaṃyutta) is the name of this fifth [type]. Therein, "flower-liquor" (pupphāsava) is the juice of flowers such as the *madhuka*, palm, and coconut, which has been aged for a long time.
"Fruit-liquor" (phalāsava) is the juice of fruits such as the jackfruit (*panasa*). "Honey-liquor" (madhvāsava) is the juice of grapes (*muddikā*).
However, in the *Samantapāsādikā*, it says: "Fruit-liquor is that made from the juice of crushed fruits such as the grape fruit. Honey-liquor is..."
It is said: "It is made from the natural juice of grapes, and it is also made with honey. Sugarcane juice is *guḷāsava* (molasses liquor).

The juice of various ingredients such as *harītakī*, *āmalaka*, *kaṭuka*, and *bhaṇḍa*, when mixed with those ingredients and aged for a long time, is *sambhārasaṃyutta* (liquor prepared from a mixture of ingredients).

And here, although the mixture of ingredients is the same for both *surā* and *meraya*, *surā* is that which is made by crushing [the ingredients], whereas [the other] is merely by being aged for a long time.
Thus should the distinction between these be understood.

"Starting from the seed" means starting from the time the ingredients have been prepared and placed in the vat, as well as from the time the fresh flower-juices of the palm, coconut, and so forth are added.
"Salted sour gruel or fermented liquor" refers to two specific types of *āsava* (fermented spirits) prepared with various medicinal herbs.
"For the purpose of causing the taking of a dwelling" means for the purpose of causing the taking of a fragrant state.

And here, the absence of intention (*acittakatā*) should be understood as the failure to recognize the object. It is a "worldly offense" (*lokavajja*) because it must be incurred through unwholesome states alone.
Whatever else might need to be said here, all of that follows the same method already stated in the commentary on the first *pārājika*.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the drinking of fermented liquor is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule regarding poking with the finger:
"With the intention of amusement" means with the intention of play; by this, he excludes the intention of physical contact.
And here, for a monk who touches even a nun with the intention of laughter, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Likewise, for a nun who touches even a monk. Thus it was said: "But here, both the nun [touching] the monk, and the monk [touching] the nun, are indeed those not fully ordained.
Regarding all cases such as "body-to-body-connected" and so forth: "With the body against what is body-connected; with what is body-connected..."

"In the body, in what is connected to the body by means of what is connected to the body, in the body by means of what is to be relinquished, in what is connected to the body by means of what is to be relinquished, and in what is to be relinquished by means of what is to be relinquished"—thus it is in all cases.
"Touching when there is a purpose to be done" means that there is no offense for one who touches a man when there is a purpose to be done;
however, it is not permitted to touch a woman even when there is a purpose to be done.
The commentary on the training rule concerning poking with the fingers is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning laughing.
"Above the ankle" means at a height measuring above the ankles. "With the intention of laughing" means with the intention of playing. By which...

"By whichever limb" means by whichever limb among the hands, feet, and so forth. Likewise, "playing in a boat" means that there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for one who is steering a boat with oars, rudders, and so on, or for one who is pulling it up onto the bank.
The commentary on the training rule concerning laughing is finished.

4. Commentary on the Training Rule on Disrespect (*Anādariyasikkhāpada*) In this context, there are two kinds of disrespect: disrespect toward persons and disrespect toward the Dhamma. Therefore, it says, "or toward a person," and so forth.
Regarding that, when a monk who has been fully ordained is addressed by one who is also fully ordained in accordance with what has been prescribed, [if he says], "This person is suspended... or...
“Whether I am reviled or censured, his word will not be carried out”—thinking thus, one acts with disrespect;

this is what is called acting with disrespect toward a person. Furthermore, when being addressed by one who has laid down a rule, if one acts with disrespect because one wishes that “this discussion might perish, or be destroyed, or disappear,” or because one does not wish to attend to it—this is [acting with disrespect].
He shows disrespect toward the Dhamma; that is what is meant by "he acts with irreverence. Therefore, he says "therefore," and so forth. This does not lead to effacement (*sallekha*).
It is called *sallekha* because it properly scrapes away (*likhati*) the defilements; it is fewness of wishes (*appicchatā*). This [practice] does not lead to that end.
By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), it is implied: "This does not lead to the state of being shaven-off (*dhuta*), nor to inspiring confidence (*pāsādikatā*)."
This includes [the statement]: "It does not lead to diminution, nor to the arousal of energy.

"By what is laid down" means by what has come down in the Sutta or the Abhidhamma. "Come down through tradition" means come down through the succession of teachers beginning with Mahākassapa from the time of the Councils.
However, since sugarcane juice is for seven days, its sediment is for life; thus, of these two...
If one takes up a censurable traditional practice (gārayhācariya-uggaha) such as, "The sugarcane stalk is a composite; therefore, it is permissible to eat a sugarcane stalk at an improper time,
just like sugar or myrobalan," and says, "Such is our teachers' tradition and their inquiry," it is indeed an offense.
The commentary on the training rule concerning disrespect is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Terrifying Others:
"Forms, etc. refers to terrifying forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles. "A terrifying story" refers to a discourse connected with robbers, wildernesses, forests, and ogres.
The commentary on the training rule concerning frightening others is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule concerning fire:
"Not being ill" means one for whom there is comfort without fire; such a person is here called "not ill. "Fire" means a flame.
"In the Bhaggas" means in the country of that name. There were royal princes named Bhaggas who were inhabitants of that land;
their entire country, as a conventional term (*ruḷhisadda*), is called "the Bhaggas. Therefore it is said: "In the Bhaggas, in the country of that name.
Likewise, "of one picking up a fallen ember" means: for one picking up a burning ember that has fallen, there is likewise an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
*Attha*: This refers to the *dukkaṭa* (offense of wrong-doing). *Avijjhātaṃ*: An unextinguished firebrand. *Padīpa-jotika-jantāghare*:
The meaning is that there is no offense for one who kindles a fire for the purpose of lighting a lamp, cooking food, performing a sudorific treatment (*sedakamma*), or in a sauna (*aggisālā*).
*Tathārūpa-paccaye*: Even in other such circumstances, excluding lamps and the like. *Āpadāsu*: In cases of emergency.
In the face of disturbances caused by wild beasts, venomous snakes, and humans.
The commentary on the training rule concerning fire is concluded.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning bathing.
“Half a month and more remains of the summer,” and “the first month of the rains”—these two and a half months are the time of heat and the time of feverish distress.
Thus, the remaining half-month and more of the summer is the time of heat, and the first month of the rains is the time of feverish distress;
in this way, these two and a half months are respectively called the time of heat and the time of feverish distress.
Regarding the meaning, it is stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājaniya*): "The 'time of heat' (*uṇhasamaya*) is when one and a half months remain of the summer;
the 'time of fever' (*pariḷāhasamaya*) is the first month of the rainy season. When one is not comfortable without bathing, this is the "time of illness" (*gilānasamaya*).
However, since the time of illness is determined once the state of being ill is established, the commentary states: "For whom [it is] without bathing..."
"It is not comfortable; one may bathe at a time of illness," so it is said.
"Even merely sweeping the courtyard" means even down to the extent of merely sweeping the courtyard.

"Having strewn sand" means having spread the sand from a dry riverbed. "Also in pits"—by the word "also," he shows that there is no need to speak of bathing in a river [in this context]. "In times of distress" means when pursued by bees and the like.
The commentary on the training rule regarding bathing is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule regarding making [robes] discolored:
This word *lābha* is a noun derived from the action (kamma-sādhana), as in such expressions as "What gain has been obtained by you? and so forth; and here it refers to the past tense.
He says: “*Alabbhī* means *labho*,” that is, it has the sense of “obtained. By the phrase “*labho eva lābho*,” he shows that the suffix *ṇa* is used here in its own sense (*sakatthe*).
What was obtained? It was something new (*navaṃ*), meaning brand-new. At this point, the compound should be understood as follows: “it is both new and a robe, thus it is a ‘new robe’ (*navacīvara*);
since the obtaining of a new robe is by means of this [robe], it is a ‘new-robe-obtainment’ (*navacīvaralābho*). Thus should the compound be seen here.
If this is so, how is it that it was said, "by the acquisition of a new robe"? To this he says: "Thus, by the acquisition of a new robe," and so forth.

And here, because it is not stated that "the last [robe] is subject to assignment (*vikappanupaga*)," one should understand that "robe" refers specifically to that which is capable of being worn as an undergarment or as an upper garment;
thus he says: "a robe fit for wearing as an undergarment or as an upper garment. "Making it discolored..."
"It should be taken" is said with reference to this "token of validity" (*kappabindu*); it does not mean disfiguring the entire robe with blue or other colors.

Furthermore, when one takes up that token after dyeing the robe, it should be placed in either four corners, three, two, or even a single corner—about the size of a peacock's eye or the back of a fingernail. Thus he says, "Of that," and so forth.
“With bronze-blue” means with the blue of a tanner. However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated:
“Iron rust and copper rust—this is what is called ‘bronze-blue. “With leaf-blue” means with any blue-colored dye whatsoever.
“Having taken a hair-curl mark” means having taken one circular hair-curl mark.

However, the *pāḷi-kappa*, *kaṇṇika-kappa*, and so forth, are prohibited in all the commentaries (*aṭṭhakathā*). Regarding the statement "when [patches] are added later," he says this because there is no need for a formal act of authorization (*kappakaraṇa*) once the door-fasteners (*aggaḷa*) and other such items have been subsequently attached to a robe that has already been authorized.

"On the door-fasteners, the under-lap, and the border" refers to the patches used for fastening, the back-patches, the under-lap, and the side-lap. "Action and non-action" refers to the wearing of the lower robe (*nivāsana*) and the upper robe (*pārupana*).
Because the kappa (aeon) is without beginning, there is neither action nor non-action.
The commentary on the training rule concerning making [a robe] discolored is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning assigning [an article].

“Face-to-face assignment” (*sammukhā-vikappanā*) is an assignment made in the presence [of the recipient]. “Away-from-face assignment” (*parammukhā-vikappanā*) is an assignment made in the absence [of the recipient].

“The state of being near or far” refers to the condition of proximity or distance. And this state of proximity or distance should be understood in the same manner as explained in the section on formal determination (*adhiṭṭhāna*).

“A friend” (*mitto*) means a close friend. “One seen” (*saṇḍiṭṭho*) means one who has merely been seen, not a very close friend. “Without having relinquished” (*akata-paccuddhāraṃ*) means “for me... [and so forth].
"Use it as your own property or dispose of it," and so forth—this refers to that which has not been formally relinquished (*akata-paccuddhāra*).
"By whom the disciplinary act (*vinaya-kamma*) was performed" means together with whom the disciplinary act was carried out.

Since using [the robe] constitutes a bodily action (*kāya-kamma*) and failing to relinquish it constitutes a verbal action (*vaci-kamma*), he said: "The origination (*samuṭṭhāna*) and other factors are exactly the same as in the first *kaṭhina* rule. Regarding the category "action-non-action" (*kiriya-akiriya*): here, the act of using is the "action," while the failure to relinquish is the "non-action."
The commentary on the training rule concerning the assignment [of a bowl] is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Concealment [of a Bowl]:

"Suitable for formal determination" (*adhiṭṭhānupaga*) refers to an iron bowl and a clay bowl that are fit for formal determination. "A pig's snout" (*sūkarantaka*) means it has been hollowed out inside and ground smooth, like a key-case.
"Another requisite" refers to items such as alms-bowls and bags not mentioned in the Canon. "Having given a talk on the Dhamma":

there is no offense for one who sets aside [an item] with the thought, "I will give it after giving a talk on the Dhamma," thinking, "It is not fitting for a monk to have requisites that are not laid aside."
The commentary on the training rule concerning not being heedless is finished.
The sixth chapter, the Chapter on Drinking Intoxicants, is concluded.
7. The Chapter on Living Beings.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Intentional Action (*Sañcicca-sikkhāpada*).

“*Pācittiyan*” means that even when one is cleaning a bed or a chair, if one perceives a living being—even a tiny insect—and, out of a lack of compassion, destroys it while removing it, it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). Therefore, he said: “Even though it is small,” and so forth. This is because of the magnitude of the effort involved.

"The unwholesome is great" means that because of the greatness of the preliminary effort (*payoga*)—due to the volition of final determination (*sanniṭṭhāpakacetanā*) having gained habituation through many occurrences of impulsion (*javana*)—the unwholesome is great; the intention is that it is "greatly blameworthy.
The commentary on the training rule regarding intentional action is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule on Water with Living Beings (*Sappāṇaka-sikkhāpada*).

Herein, it should be understood that this is an offense by formal rule (*paṇṇattivajja*), because even though one knows the water contains living beings, it may still be used through the perception of it being water—just as one might light a lamp with a pure mind even after knowing that insects have fallen into it.
The commentary on the training rule on water with living beings is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule on Reopening (Ukkoṭana-sikkhāpada) "Of that and that monk" means: of whichever monk [the matter] has been settled. "Saying 'the legal act was not performed,' etc.
means: saying, "The legal act was not performed; it was ill-performed; the legal act must be done again; it was not suppressed, it was poorly suppressed."
"Furthermore, it must be settled again," he says. This was stated to show the manner of their conduct, implying that they would not allow [the case] to remain established in its original state.
Therefore he said: "But whatever legal issue (adhikaraṇa) has been settled according to the Dhamma, that is indeed well-settled.
The commentary on the training rule concerning reopening [a settled case] is finished.

4. Commentary on the Training Rule on Grave Offenses (Duṭṭhulla-sikkhāpada): Since the four *pārājika* rules have been presented in the word-by-word commentary by way of their formal definition (*atthuddhāra*), it is said:
“‘Grave offense’ (*duṭṭhulla*) refers here to a *saṅghādisesa*. “By whatever means” means: “either he knows it himself, or others [inform him].”

Regarding the statement, "They announce it, or he himself announces it," the intention is that it is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) by the mere fact of relinquishing the burden through any such means.
Even if he announces it later, he is not released from the offense incurred by the initial relinquishing of the burden. Therefore, he said, "Even if...
and so forth. "He incurs [the offense] even with a hundred ascetics" means that if, having heard it from even a hundred ascetics, he conceals it, he still incurs an offense of expiation.
The meaning is as follows: "By whom it was reported to him" means by whom [the second monk] reported it to that third [monk]. "To him alone" means to that very second [monk].
"He reports" means he says, "Do not report this to anyone," solely for the purpose of concealment.
"It becomes cut off at the end" means that because the second [monk] reported it to the third [monk] only after having incurred an offense on account of concealment.
Therefore, because there is no further offense to be incurred by him on that account, it is said that the limit of the offense has been reached. Regarding the "first phrase":
among these three—perceiving it as a grave offense, being in doubt, or perceiving it as not a grave offense—it refers to the first phrase, "one who perceives it as a grave offense conceals it.
Regarding the other two: "one who is in doubt conceals it" and "one who perceives it as not a grave offense [conceals it]."
In these passages, "conceals" refers to [the concealment of an offense]. "Of no grave nature" (*aduṭṭhullāya*) refers to the remaining five classes of offenses (*āpattikkhandha*).

"Misconduct toward one who is not fully ordained" (*anupasampannassa duṭṭhulle vā aduṭṭhulle vā ajjhācāre*) means misconduct consisting of either a grave transgression—defined as the violation of the first five training rules—or otherwise, a non-grave transgression against one who is not fully ordained. As for that which is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*: "Of one who is not fully ordained... [the text continues].

It has been stated, "The emission of semen and physical contact—this is what is called 'grave misconduct' (duṭṭhulla-ajjhācāra)," but this does not accord with the commentary on the training rule regarding the reporting of grave matters (duṭṭhullārocanasikkhāpada).

Nor is it logical to say that "in the case of reporting, 'grave matter' refers to one thing, while in the case of concealing, it refers to another," because no specific reason for such a distinction is found. Therefore, that point must be investigated.
The commentary on the training rule concerning grave offenses is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule concerning those under twenty years of age:
For even one who has been in the womb for twenty years is reckoned as "one who has reached twenty"; thus it says, "from the moment of grasping rebirth-linking..."

"Starting from [the moment of] rebirth-linking," and so forth. In this context, "starting from the grasping of rebirth-linking" means beginning with that first consciousness which arose in the mother's womb and first became manifest. "He" refers to the person who was ordained when he was less than twenty years of age.
"He ordains another" means acting as either a preceptor (*upajjhāya*) or a master of the formal ritual (*kammavācācariya*).
He ordains another person. "That" refers to a person under twenty years of age.
"Or he demarcates a boundary" means he establishes a new boundary.
The commentary on the training rule concerning those under twenty years of age is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Robbers "Having deceived the king" means:
having cheated the king and taken something belonging to the king, they set out on the road with the thought, "We will not give it back to him now.
This refers to both those who have committed the act and those who have not, who are called "robbers. This...
The same principle applies here regarding one who wishes to avoid customs duties.

"By a discrepancy in time" means by a discrepancy in the timing; it is said to mean a discrepancy in the day. However, for one who travels by a discrepancy in the route or by a discrepancy in the forest path, there is indeed an offense.
The commentary on the training rule concerning a caravan of thieves is concluded.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Arrangements (*Saṃvidhāna-sikkhāpada*).

"With a woman" (*mātugāmena*) means with a female (*itthiyā*). However, those who are fully ordained on only one side—namely, a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*), a novice nun (*sāmaṇerī*), and so forth—these three are also included here.
Yet, among these three, he observes the proper time. This is [the distinction] for them compared to a woman.
And it should be understood as a specific distinction.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the arrangement [of food] is finished.
8. Commentary on the Ariṭṭha Training Rule.
An *antarāya* is so called because it comes (*eti*) or arrives within (*antara*), that is, in the midst of the continuum of a being, by way of obstructing various attainments;

it refers to misfortune pertaining to the present life and so forth. Because they are connected to that obstacle in the sense of being impossible to transcend, or because they deserve the result which is the obstacle, or because they have the habit of producing an obstacle, they are called *antarāyika*. Therefore he said: "Of heaven and liberation..."

"They create an obstacle, thus they are 'obstructive' (*antarāyika*). These are fivefold by way of action (*kamma*), defilement (*kilesa*), result (*vipāka*), slander (*upavāda*), and transgression of the rules (*paññattivītikkama*).
In this context, the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantariya-kamma*) are called "obstructive actions" (*kammantarāyika*), as is likewise the act of violating a nun.

However, that [latter] creates an obstacle only to liberation (*mokkha*), not to heaven (*sagga*). The states of fixed wrong view (*niyatamicchādiṭṭhi-dhammā*) are "obstructive defilements" (*kilesantarāyika*).
[These are] as follows: the rebirth-linking states (*paṭisandhi-dhammā*) of eunuchs, animals, and hermaphrodites are called "obstructive to fruition" (*vipāka-antarāyika*).

Slandering the Noble Ones (*ariyūpavāda*) is called "obstructive to the [attainment of] the Noble [Path]" (*upavāda-antarāyika*). However, these [acts] obstruct only so long as the Noble Ones have not been asked for forgiveness; not beyond that.
Offenses committed intentionally are called "obstructive to the transgression of the rules" (*paññatti-vītikkama-antarāyika*). These too [obstruct] as long as one remains a monk...
or confesses it, or does not emerge from it, or does not declare it—only for that duration, and no longer.
In this case, the monk Ariṭṭha was learned and a preacher of the Dhamma;

he knew the other kinds of obstacles, but because he was unskilled in the Vinaya, he did not know those obstacles consisting of the transgression of formal rules (paṇṇatti). Therefore, having gone into seclusion, he thought thus: "These..."
Householders who enjoy the five strands of sensual pleasure may be stream-enterers, once-returners, or non-returners;
likewise, monks see pleasing forms cognizable by the eye... [and so on] ...they touch tangibles cognizable by the body and enjoy soft rugs, coverlets, and so forth—all this is permissible. Why?
"Female forms... [and so on] ... female tangibles are not permitted;

these too are permitted"—thus, by blending essence with essence, and by treating both enjoyment with desire and lust and enjoyment without desire as one, it is like joining extremely fine thread with coarse wool, or like comparing Mount Sineru with a mustard seed.
Having generated an evil view, he thought, "What is the use of this great effort by the Blessed One, as if binding the great ocean?
He has laid down the first *pārājika* rule; there is no fault here.

Thus, contradicting the knowledge of omniscience, cutting off the hope of those individuals capable of liberation, he struck a blow at the Wheel of the Victor’s command. Therefore, he said, "Among them," and so forth.
In this context, "among those" refers to the obstacles as previously described. Regarding the phrase "sensuous pleasures are like a skeleton":
here, a "skeleton" (*kaṅkala*) means either a breastbone, a backbone, or a skull. For it is called a "skeleton" because it is devoid of flesh.
Indeed, the term *kaṅkala* is conventionally established for a single bone within a chain of bones from which the flesh has departed; [sensuous pleasures] are similar to that.

The meaning is: "sensuous pleasures are [like] a small taste. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), there is the inclusion of these [similes]: "Sensuous pleasures are like a lump of meat; sensuous pleasures are like a grass torch;

sensuous pleasures are like a pit of embers; sensuous pleasures are like a dream; sensuous pleasures are like borrowed goods; sensuous pleasures are like the fruit of a tree; sensuous pleasures are like a butcher's block; sensuous pleasures are like spears and pikes; sensuous pleasures are like the head of a serpent."
In this context, sensual pleasures are like a piece of meat in that they are shared by many; they are like a grass torch in that they burn;
they are like a pit of embers in that they cause great heat; they are like a dream in that their manifestation is brief;
they are like borrowed goods in that they are only temporary; and they are like the fruit of a tree in that they crush all one’s limbs and members.

They are like swords and spears in the sense of cutting excessively; they are like javelins and spikes in the sense of piercing through; they are like the heads of snakes in the sense of being dangerous and fearful.

"In the same way" refers to the words beginning with "Venerable sir, do not [speak thus]. "To the others" means to those other monks who heard it there from those by whom he was addressed with the words beginning with "Venerable sir, do not [speak thus]," after he had been dragged into the midst of the Saṅgha. "By a formal act consisting of a motion and a third proclamation" refers to: "Listen..."
"Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha grant me, for the monk named so-and-so, the act of reconciliation (*paṭisāraṇīyakamma*) on account of such an evil view having arisen," and so forth,
by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a third proclamation (*ñatticatuttha-kamma*), as stated in the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājaniya*).
The commentary on the Ariṭṭha training rule is finished.

9. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Associating with One Who Has Been Suspended (*Ukkhittasambhogasikkhāpada*) “By one who has not performed the *anuddhamma*” means by one who has been suspended and not reinstated. Therefore he said: “*Anudhamma* is said to be,” and so forth.
Here, the connection is that "*anudhamma*" refers to reinstatement (*osāraṇā*). It is that which conforms to the formal act of suspension (*ukkhepanīyakamma*), and is to be performed subsequently.

Or "Dhamma" means the secondary Dhamma (*anudhamma*). "Having seen the concordant conduct" (*anulomavatta*) means having seen the eighteenfold conduct beginning with "one should not grant full ordination, nor should one give formal support," that is to say, having seen him engaged in these eighteen concordant conducts;
this is the intended meaning. Regarding "either the enjoyment of material things or the enjoyment of the Dhamma": here, any gift whatsoever of material things—

Receiving [alms] and the enjoyment of material things constitute the enjoyment of material goods (*āmisasaṃbhoga*). Teaching the Dhamma and causing it to be taught constitute the enjoyment of the Dhamma (*dhammasaṃbhoga*).

"One should live together" means that one should perform the three kinds of communal living mentioned in the word-commentary: either the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, or a formal act of the Saṅgha (*saṅghakamma*). For in this context, even the Uposatha and Pavāraṇā must be performed by the Saṅgha itself.
These are indeed formal acts of the Saṅgha; therefore, it is said: “One should perform a Saṅgha act such as the Uposatha.
“In each instance of application” means in each instance of giving and in each instance of taking.

It is called “three types of consciousness” because even an Arahant, though ignorant of the formal rule (paṇṇatti), must incur [the offense] with a functional-ineffective (kiriya-abyākata) consciousness.
The commentary on the training rule concerning sharing with one who has been suspended is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning thorns:
He says "para" because he states that the particle *pireti*, when used in the sense of addressing someone, has the same meaning as the word *para*.
“*Amāmaka*”: the meaning is “not belonging to us,” that is, not being part of our internal circle.
Or, *pire* is a particle synonymous with “*parato*” (from elsewhere); therefore, the meaning here should be understood as: “Go away, *pire*; do not stay here.
The commentary on the Kaṇṭaka training rule is finished.
The seventh chapter: On Containing Living Beings.
8. The Chapter on Those of the Same Dhamma.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Those of the Same Dhamma.
“Being spoken to by one who shares the Dhamma” (*sahadhammikena vuccamāno*) means being addressed by one who shares the Dhamma.

This is the accusative case used in the sense of the instrumental. As it is stated in the *Dubbaca-sikkhāpada*: “Because it is to be trained in by those who share the Dhamma, or because it belongs to them, it is called ‘one who shares the Dhamma’;
the meaning is: being addressed by the training rule (*sikkhāpada*) proclaimed by the Buddha, which has received that name. Thus, “*sahadhammikaṃ*... [is explained].
"Regarding the phrase 'being spoken to,' its meaning has been explained in the training rule on being difficult to admonish," it is said.
"Out of fear of disrespect" means out of fear of showing disregard; the meaning is: out of fear of an offense entailing confession (pācittiya) in that regard.
"Speaking thus by way of an evasion" means speaking not directly, saying "I will not train," but rather speaking by way of an evasion such as, "until another monk [arrives]," and so forth.
The commentary on the training rule concerning those who share the same Dhamma is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning remorse:
"By means of both minor and secondary rules" refers to the minor rules such as the *saṅghādisesa* offenses, and the secondary rules such as the *thullaccaya* offenses.

"And regarding the minor rules. For, setting aside the four *pārājika* offenses, all the remaining training rules (*sikkhāpada*) are, by way of classification, both minor (*khuddaka*) and very minor (*anukhuddaka*). Indeed, this was said in the *Pañcasatika-kkhandhaka*:
"But what, venerable sir, are the minor and very minor training rules? Some elders spoke thus:
—“Excluding the four *pārājika* rules, the remaining training precepts are minor and secondary,” some elders said.

Some elders said thus: “Excluding the four *pārājika* rules and excluding the thirteen *saṅghādisesa* rules, the remaining training precepts are minor and secondary. Some elders said thus: “The four *pārājika* rules...”
"Excluding the thirteen *saṅghādisesa* rules, excluding the two *aniyata* rules, and excluding the remaining minor and lesser training rules.

Some elders spoke thus: "Excluding the four *pārājika* rules, excluding the thirteen *saṅghādisesa* rules, excluding the two *aniyata* rules, and excluding the thirty *nissaggiya-pācittiya* rules, the remaining are the minor and lesser training rules."

“the training rules. Some elders spoke thus: “Excluding the four *pārājika*s, excluding the thirteen *saṅghādisesa*s, excluding the two *aniyata*s, excluding the thirty *nissaggiya-pācittiya*s, and excluding the ninety-two *pācittiya*s, the remainder are the minor and lesser training rules. Some elders spoke thus: “The four...”
“Excluding the *pārājika* rules, excluding the thirteen *saṅghādisesa* rules, excluding the two *aniyata* rules,
excluding the thirty *nissaggiya pācittiya* rules, excluding the ninety-two *pācittiya* rules, and excluding the four *pāṭidesanīya* rules,
the remainder are the minor and lesser training rules.”
As for what was stated by the Elder Nāgasena when questioned by King Milinda—“The *dukkaṭa* offense, Great King, is a minor training rule (*sikkhāpada*);
the *dubbhāsita* offense is not minor”—this was said by taking only the final category [of the *dukkaṭa*].
It should be understood that this was intended to cut off further debate on the matter.
"Statement of the delimitation of the limit of evolution" (*saṃvattanamariyādaparicchedavacanaṃ*): The limit (*mariyādā*) or boundary (*avadhi*) of evolution (*saṃvatta*) is the "limit of evolution";
the statement of that delimitation (*pariccheda*) by way of its restriction (*niyama*) is the "statement of the delimitation of the limit of evolution.
Now, in order to reveal and show that limit, it is said: "This is what is meant," and so forth. Therein, "they recite" (*uddisanti*)...
The teachers recite according to their own preference. "They cause [the students] to recite" means that the resident pupils, having requested the teacher, cause him to recite.
"They study" means they memorize. "Remorse and regret" refers to regret characterized as remorse (*kukkucca*).
"Distress, doubt, and mental scruples" refers to mental scruples characterized as distress and doubt. "In reproach" means in censure.

"Debasement of one who is not fully ordained" means: speaking in dispraise in the presence of one who is not fully ordained in order to cause him to develop doubt regarding that [offense] in the Vinaya-commentary.
The commentary on the training rule concerning causing anxiety is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning causing confusion.
"In that misconduct" means when that misconduct has been practiced. "There is no release" means there is no release from that offense.

"For you" means for you. "Gains" refers to those gains—both pertaining to the present life and the future life—which are characterized as benefits for others who, when the Pātimokkha is being recited, apply their minds with great care and earnestness; such gains are what ought to be desired.
All of these are indeed losses for you. "Ill-gotten" (*dulladdha*) means that even human birth, though obtained through a distinction of merit, is ill-gotten.
"Well done" (*sādhu*) means thoroughly. "Making it a bone" (*aṭṭhiṃ katvā*) means making it a matter of necessity;

what is meant is that one becomes one who has need of it. "By a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation" refers to the word-commentary beginning with: "Let the Saṅgha listen to me, venerable sirs."
By means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second resolution (*ñattidutiyakamma*) that imposes delusion as stated.
In this context, "an illegal formal act" refers specifically to a formal act that imposes delusion.
The commentary on the training rule concerning delusion is concluded.
4. Explanation of the Training Rule on Striking.
"Should give a blow" means: should give a blow with any one of the things connected to the body or released from the body, starting from even a lotus leaf.
But when such a blow has been given, let the hand break, or the foot, or the head.
Or if he dies, it is likewise a *pācittiya*. Therefore, he said, "with the intention of striking," and so forth.
"To one who is not fully ordained" refers to a layperson or a renunciant, whether female or male, even down to an animal.
However, if with a lustful mind one strikes a woman, it is a *saṅghādisesa*. "Being harassed by someone" means by a human being.
Or [when one is] being harassed by an animal. "One who has liberation as his aim" means one who is aspiring for his own liberation from that [danger].

Even if, on the way, he sees a thief or an enemy wishing to harass him and says, "Lay follower, stay right here, do not come further," yet [the other person] disregards those words and continues coming, [he may say], "Go..."
If he goes along after striking [the animal] with a club or a knife, and it dies from that blow, there is no offense.
The same rule applies regarding wild animals.
The commentary on the training rule concerning striking is concluded.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the "Floor-Seven" (Talasattika).
