"Talasattika" means the floor itself is the "floor-seven. Some say it is called "seven" in the sense of being capable of striking.

"Should throw up" means he should toss it upward. Regarding the statement "it is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) because it was given not with the intention of striking": here, [the offense applies] when one strikes with the intention of striking.
By the previous training rule, it is a *pācittiya*. When one merely ejects [the matter] with the desire to expel it, this [rule] constitutes a *pācittiya*.
However, since a blow was dealt after having missed the mark with this [act], it is a *dukkaṭa*.
Regarding this, they say: "Even for one who ejects [it] out of anger upon seeing animals and the like performing unclean acts, there is still only the intention for release (*mokkhādhippāyo*)."
The commentary on the training rule concerning what has been heard from others is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule concerning groundless charges:
The sixth training rule is indeed straightforward.
The commentary on the training rule concerning groundless accusations is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning intentional action:
"Causing another to feel remorse" means generating doubt in them. Whether or not the other person actually feels remorse, [the offense is incurred].
"That is immeasurable. "I think" means I conjecture. By the word "etcetera," there is the inclusion of such statements as: "I think you ate at an improper time; I think you drank liquor;
I think you sat in private with a woman," and so forth. "One who is not fully ordained" refers to a novice (sāmaṇera).
The commentary on the training rule regarding intentional action is concluded.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule on Eavesdropping (*Upassutisikkhāpada*).
"Suti" means that which is heard; it is sound. "Upassuti" means being near to hearing (*suti*); thus he said "near to hearing. The meaning is "near to sound.
Standing where one is able to hear a sound—that is, standing near to sound—is what is meant.
He said, "It is called 'standing,'" and so forth, beginning with "standing where. Alternatively, it is a place (*upassuti*) because one hears (*sūyati*) by approaching;
that is, the meaning here should be understood as "in that place which, having approached, one is able to hear the sound of those speaking.
"Even when walking hurriedly" means for the purpose of hearing the sound of those walking ahead while one is walking behind.
"Even when moving quickly" (*sīghagamanepi*). "Even when lagging behind" (*ohīyamānepi*) means even when one who is walking behind lags behind in order to hear the words of those walking ahead.

"I shall bring it to peace" (*vūpasamissāmīti*) means I shall go toward pacification; I shall not engage in quarreling. "I shall liberate myself" (*attānaṃ parimocessāmīti*) means I shall liberate myself by declaring my state of non-doership.
"There might be an action" (*siyā kiriyanti*) refers to [the possibility that] at times, out of a desire to listen...

In terms of its origin through the act of going, it may be an action (*kiriya*). It may also be a non-action (*akiriya*), in the sense that it originates when people have come to a place where they are standing and are conversing, without having been informed [of the presence of others].
The commentary on the training rule concerning eavesdropping is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Obstructing of Formal Acts (*kammappaṭibāhana*).
“Of those that are lawful” (*dhammikānaṃ*): because they have been performed in accordance with the Dhamma, the Vinaya, and the Teacher’s instruction, they possess the Dhamma;

thus they are “lawful,” and [the term refers] to those lawful acts. “Of formal acts” (*kammānaṃ*): of the four types of formal acts of the Saṅgha. Therefore he said, “in accordance with the Dhamma,” and so forth. Therein:
"According to the Dhamma" means by way of a factual basis. "According to the Vinaya" means by way of both the formal accusation and the reminder.
"By the Teacher’s instruction" means by way of the perfection of the motion (*ñatti*) and the perfection of the proclamation (*anusāvanā*).
"Of the united Saṅgha" means of that which has become one in body and mind, having purified the Saṅgha within the boundary and having brought the consent of those entitled to give it.
"Of the Saṅgha. "That or that matter" refers to each specific matter, such as the speaking of dispraise and so forth.

"Restoration" (*osāraṇa*) is so called because by means of it one is restored into the midst of the Saṅgha. "Expulsion" (*nissāraṇa*) is so called because by means of it one is expelled from the Saṅgha.

"The shaving of the head" (*bhaṇḍukamma*) means the act of making [the head] shaven; the meaning is the request for the cutting of the hair. "The characteristic of the formal act" (*kammalakkhaṇa*) is simply the formal act itself as its defining characteristic.

The meaning of "characteristic of the formal act" (kammalakkhaṇa) is that it is characterized as a formal act alone, not receiving any other name, just like the acts of reinstatement (osāraṇā) and so forth;
it is designated as a formal act because it possesses that very nature. Here, the expression "reinstatement and expulsion" (osāraṇaṃ nissāraṇaṃ) was stated for the sake of euphony in the phrasing.
However, in reality, expulsion occurs first and reinstatement afterwards; thus he said, "In this regard, concerning the novice Kaṇṭaka," and so on.
"Expulsion" (nissāraṇā) is like the banishment of the novice Kaṇṭaka;
just as the novice Kaṇṭaka was expelled by way of disciplinary action, so too is it for any other novice who speaks dispraise of the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha;
or who represents what is unallowable as "allowable"; or who holds wrong view, being possessed of an extremist view.
“Venerable sirs, I ask the Saṅgha: ‘This novice named so-and-so speaks dispraise of the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha, and holds wrong view.

Does the Saṅgha approve of his banishment so that he may no longer receive—what other novices receive—the privilege of sleeping together with the monks for two or three nights? A second time... [and so on].”
For the third time, venerable sirs, I ask the Saṅgha: "This novice named so-and-so... [as before] ...it is pleasing to the Saṅgha.
"Go forth, live, and prosper"—this is the meaning of the expulsion consisting in the removal from one's seat. Having seen such a person behaving correctly, their readmission is called *osāraṇā*.
On another occasion, seeing that very same person seeking forgiveness by saying, "Venerable sirs, out of foolishness, ignorance, and lack of merit I did such a thing;
therefore, I ask the Saṅgha for forgiveness," [the monks] had him request it up to three times, saying:
"Venerable sirs, I ask the Saṅgha: this novice named so-and-so, regarding the Buddha, the Dhamma, or the Saṅgha..."
Or, he was one who spoke dispraise and held wrong view; he was expelled so that other novices would not obtain the privilege of sharing a sleeping place with the monks for two or three nights.

Now, however, he is gentle, humble in conduct, has entered into the nature of shame, is established in moral dread, has undergone the penalty, and confesses his transgression. For this novice, as follows—
"It is pleasing to the Saṅgha to grant the purity of the assembly for the enjoyment of the pure body. For a second time... [and] for a third time, venerable sirs, I ask the Saṅgha...
"It is pleasing to the Saṅgha."—The meaning is: "admission" and "restoration."

"Requesting permission for the cutting of hair" means: having assembled the monks within the boundary (sīmā) and having led the one seeking admission there, to speak the words either three times, twice, or once, saying:
"Venerable sirs, I request the Saṅgha’s permission for the shaving of this child's head.
And here, it may also be said: "We request permission for the shaving of this child's head."
It is indeed permissible to say, “We ask permission for his becoming a recluse,” or “We ask permission for his going forth,” or “This one wishes to become a recluse,” or “This one wishes to go forth.
“Mukharassa” means one who is harsh with the mouth. The connection is: “whatever act of non-worship has been permitted. “In instances such as showing [the body] by exposing the thigh,” etc.
Now at that time, the group-of-six monks splashed the bhikkhunīs with muddy water, thinking, "Perhaps they will become infatuated with us.
They exposed their bodies and showed them to the bhikkhunīs; they exposed their thighs and showed them to the bhikkhunīs;
they exposed their private parts and showed them to the bhikkhunīs; and they made lewd advances toward the bhikkhunīs.
They associate with the bhikkhunīs thinking, “Perhaps they might fall in love with us”—in these circumstances. Regarding “those whose robes have been stolen,” etc.:

this refers to those whose robes have been stolen, whose robes are worn out, whose robes are lost, who are ill, who are very learned, who carry the burden of the Saṅgha, or who are spreaders of the teachings (nittharaka), and so forth.
"Robes and so forth" means robes, medicines, lodgings, and so on. "To be used" refers to roots, bark, leaves, sprouts, flowers, fruits, and so on, which are to be consumed.
"Things that may be removed" refers to trees providing shade or fruit that may be taken away for the purpose of building a residence and the like.
Or, by those making such a legitimate agreement (*katika*) regarding what is given for the sake of robes and alms-food, [the use of] the maintenance of the residence and so forth [is permitted].
Or likewise, for those making any other such righteous agreement (*katikā*):
"the Sutta does not come" means the *Mātikā* does not come; "the Sutta-vibhaṅga does not [come]" means even the Vinaya is not mastered.
"The meaning is obstructed by the shadow of the phrasing" means that having grasped merely the phrasing, one rejects the meaning.
When he sees monks who are experts in the Vinaya being charged with an offense for accepting gold, silver, fields, or land, he says:

"Why do you charge them with an offense? Has it not been stated in the Sutta that 'he abstains from accepting gold and silver'—thus, only the mere abstinence was mentioned; there is no offense here. Another Dhamma-preacher...
Because it is found in the Sutta, when an offense is being charged against those who wear their robes hanging down, he says: "Why do you charge them with an offense?
Has it not been stated that 'the training is to be observed thus: "I shall wear my robe evenly all around"'? This merely states the manner of observing the training; there is no offense here.
Regarding "a decision by a committee" (ubbāhika-vinicchaya), this refers to the decision by a committee as described in the Samathakkhandhaka.

“Having selected two or three bhikkhus endowed with the perfection of the ten factors—beginning with ‘being virtuous’—the formal decision should be understood as a decision by a committee (ubbāhikavinicchaya).

‘Postponement of the invitation ceremony’ (pavāraṇappaccukkaḍḍhanā) means the pushing back of the invitation ceremony; the meaning is ‘drawing it upward’ (i.e., to a later date). [This concludes the section on] the settlement by covering over as with grass (tiṇavatthārakasamatha).”

And the motion encompassing all: this refers to the very first motion made for settlement by covering over as with grass, which is formulated thus: "Venerable sirs, let the Saṅgha hear me: regarding us who have fallen into quarreling... [omitting] except that which relates to householders.
And "by means of striving for non-acquisition" and so forth means by means of making efforts for the sake of not obtaining the four requisites.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the remaining seven factors are included: "striving for harm," "striving to make [the monastery] uninhabitable," "reviling and abusing," "causing division among monks by monks," "speaking dispraise of the Buddha," "speaking dispraise of the Dhamma," and "speaking dispraise of the Saṅgha.
"Of one endowed with eight factors" means by these eight.
And [it applies] to one who possesses even each individual factor. "For the purpose of making [the Sangha] not share" means for the purpose of not accepting the gift offered by that person.
"By means of overturning the bowl" refers to the overturning of the bowl through the formal act (kammavācā), not by merely placing it face down.
"By means of turning the bowl upright"—here too, the same principle applies. "Of that very [person]" refers to whoever...
"Expelled by means of overturning the bowl" refers to that same lay follower.
"Behaving properly" means behaving in accordance with those qualities by which the bowl was overturned. "That" refers to the aforementioned expulsion and reinstatement.
"One who distributes trifles" is one who gives away or bestows small items such as needles and so forth to those who need them. "A distributor of robes" means...

The one who causes the distribution of the rainy-season robes (*vassikasāṭiyaggāhāpaka*). The formal authorization (*sammuti*) to be given for the purpose of sending laborers (*ārāmika*) who are performing work is the "authorization as a laborer-sender" (*ārāmikapesakasammuti*).
This same method applies here to the "authorization as a novice-sender" (*sāmaṇerapesakasammuti*) as well.

Regarding the phrase "of the seven [kinds of] acts beginning with the act of censure" (*tajjanīyakammādīnaṃ sattannaṃ*): these are the act of censure (*tajjanīya*), the act of demotion (*niyasa*), the act of banishment (*pabbājanīya*), the act of reconciliation (*paṭisāraṇīya*), and so forth.
And "of three kinds of *ukkhepanīya*" refers to the seven [formal acts] beginning with *tajjanīya*.
"Eight *yāvatatiyaka*" refers to the eight *saṅghādisesa* offenses: four in relation to monks and four in relation to nuns.

"By way of formal acts consisting of a motion (*ñattikamma*) and so forth" means by way of formal acts consisting of a motion, a motion followed by a second proclamation, and a motion followed by a fourth proclamation. "While being performed..."
"Because it becomes more firm, it should therefore be performed"—so some say. However, if that were the case, there would be a confusion of kamma;
therefore, it should not be performed, and this [position] is indeed rejected.
But if there is a missing syllable, a missing word, or a wrongly uttered phrase, it is permissible to repeat it again and again for the sake of correcting it. This refers to unshakable kamma.

It becomes a strengthening; having become an act in a defective procedure, it remains [as such]. "By means of the complete characteristics" means by announcing both the motion (*ñatti*) and the four formal proclamations (*kammavācā*).
"Not by way of the remaining acts" means it should not be performed by way of the remaining acts, such as the act of intimation (*apalokanakamma*), etc.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the obstruction of an act is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Going After Having Given One’s Consent (*chandadānāgamanasikkhāpada*).
“The matter has been reported but not adjudicated” means that the reported matter has not been determined as being an offense.
In this case, the accuser and the accused have each presented their own accounts, and an investigator has been appointed; up to this point, it is merely the matter itself.

"It has been announced" is how it should be understood. "Having not given consent, he should rise from his seat and depart" means that with the intention, "How might this legal act (kamma) be invalid, or how might it be a quorum-deficient assembly (vagga), so that it does not take effect," he should rise from his sitting place and go away.
Therefore, he said, "Whichever monk," and so forth. Regarding "action and non-action": here, the act of departing is the action.
The non-granting and non-performance of consent.
The commentary on the training rule concerning departing without having granted consent is finished.
11. Commentary on the Training Rule on the Weak.
"According to intimacy" means according to friendship. Therefore he said, "whichever," and so forth.
Therein, "by way of friends, acquaintances, and intimates" means by way of those who are friends, acquaintances, and intimates. Among these, "friends" (mittā) are simply friends.

"Acquaintances" (sandiṭṭhā) are those seen here and there upon meeting, but not very close friends. "Intimates" (sambhattā) should be understood as those who are well-cherished, affectionate, and firm friends.
"Five heavy articles" means five heavy articles by way of category; however, by way of their individual forms, these are many.
Therefore he said: "Five heavy articles are stated by way of category. An *ārāma* is either a flower-garden or a fruit-garden.
An *ārāmavatthu* is a piece of land set aside and demarcated for the purpose of those very same gardens.

When those monasteries have fallen into ruin, it refers to their original site. A "vihāra" is any kind of lodging, such as a palace and so forth. A "vihāra-site" is the location where that [vihāra] is established.
A "bed" (mañca) is any one of the four types of beds previously mentioned: the stuffed bed, the bound-with-cords bed, the crab-legged bed, and the knock-down bed.
A "stool" (pīṭha) is likewise of the same types, beginning with the stuffed stool.
Any one of the four types of stools. A mattress (*bhisi*) means any one of the five types of mattresses, such as a woolen mattress and so forth.
A pillow (*bibbohana*) means one filled with any one of the following: tree-cotton, rattan-cotton, or *poṭaki*-cotton.
An iron cauldron (*lohakumbhī*) means a cauldron made of any kind of metal, whether black iron or copper. The same applies to iron pans and other such items.
This is the method. Herein, "the reciter" (*bhāṇaka*) refers to the *arañjara* (the water-drawer). "The distributor" (*vāraka*) refers to the jar. "The basin" (*kaṭāha*) is simply a basin.
Among the axes and so forth, and among the creepers and so forth, there is nothing that is difficult to understand.
Thus: There are two groups of two, and the third is a group of four.
The fourth consists of nine parts, and the fifth is divided into eight.
Thus, with five groups, the Protector, whose eyes are the fivefold purity, has revealed twenty-five kinds of heavy goods.
"It is not permissible to give away or to divide" means that it is not permissible to give away or to divide by way of cutting off the root.
However, there is no offense for one who gives away or divides by way of exchanging.

Therefore he said, "by means of what is permanent," and so forth. In this context, "permanent by means of the permanent" refers to a monastery (*ārāma*), a monastery site (*ārāmavatthu*), a residence (*vihāra*), or a residence site (*vihāravatthu*).
A grove, the site of a grove, a monastery, or the site of a monastery. "By the other" means by that which is inferior;
it is said to be by the latter three heaps. "By what is unallowable" means by things such as couches made of gold and so forth, as well as by unallowable cushions and bolsters.

"By what is allowable but of high value" means by things such as couches made of ivory and so forth, as well as by curtains and the like. "The other" means the inferior one. By way of exchange for what is allowable.
"To exchange" means to exchange in such a way that it does not become unallowable.
Herein, this is the method of exchange: Suppose the Saṅgha’s coconut grove is far away, and the kitchen attendants eat most of it themselves;
even what they do not eat, they bring back only a small amount after being paid the cart-hire. [To remedy this for] others...
However, if near that monastery there is a grove belonging to the dwellers of a village situated close to their own monastery,

and they approach the Saṅgha and request that monastery by means of their own grove, it should be accepted by the Saṅgha after obtaining the formal consent with the words, "It is pleasing to the Saṅgha.
Even if there are a thousand trees belonging to the monks and five hundred belonging to the people, [the same applies].
"It should not be said that 'your grove is small. Even though this is small, it nevertheless yields more income than the other.
Even if it yields exactly the same amount, it should still be accepted, because one is able to enjoy it whenever one wishes.
But if there are more trees belonging to the people, [one might ask]: 'Is it not yours...'"
"It should be said: 'There are more trees. If they say, 'May our merit be even greater; we give it to the Saṅgha,' it is permissible to accept it after making them understand [the situation].
The trees belonging to the bhikkhus bear fruit, whereas the trees belonging to people have not yet borne fruit.
Even though they have not yet borne fruit, one must certainly accept them, thinking: 'They will bear fruit before long.'"
Trees bear fruit for human beings, but trees belonging to monks do not yet yield fruit;
therefore, it should be said, "Do not your trees bear fruit? If they say, "Venerable sir, take them;
it will be a merit for us," it is permissible to accept them after making this known. In this way, one monastery may be exchanged for another monastery.

By this same method, a monastery site or a monastery should be exchanged for a park, and a park site should be exchanged for a monastery or a monastery site—whether the park site or the monastery site be large or small.
How is one monastery to be exchanged for another? Suppose the Saṅgha has a house within a village, and people...
There is a palace in the middle of the monastery; both are equal in value. If people request that house for the sake of that palace, it is permissible to accept it.
If the monks have a more valuable house, and they say, "Our house is more valuable," [the donor replies]:
"Even though it is more valuable, it is unsuitable for those who have gone forth; it is not possible [to keep it there]."
If they say, "This is suitable for those who have gone forth to dwell in; please accept it," it is permissible to accept it even in this way.
However, if the gift is of great value to the people, one should say, "Is not your own home of great value?
But if they reply, "Let it be so, venerable sir; it will be a merit for us; please accept it," then it is permissible to accept it.

In this way, one dwelling-place (*vihāra*) is to be exchanged for another dwelling-place. By this same method, a site for a dwelling (*vihāravatthu*), a monastery (*ārāma*), or a site for a monastery (*ārāmavatthu*) is also to be exchanged for a dwelling-place.

And by means of a site for a dwelling—whether of great value or small value—one exchanges a dwelling for a site for a dwelling, a monastery for a monastery, or a site for a monastery for a site for a monastery.
In this manner, first of all, the exchange of stable things for stable things (*thāvara-parivattana*) is to be understood.
In the case of exchanging one thing for another, however, whether a bed or chair be large or small—
even if it has legs only four finger-breadths high and was made by village children playing in sand-pits—
it becomes "heavy property" (garubhaṇḍa) from the moment it is given to the Saṅgha. Even if a king or royal ministers were to give a hundred beds all at once...

If they give a thousand beds, all these allowable beds should be accepted. Having accepted them, they should be given out according to seniority with the words, "Use them for the communal enjoyment of the Saṅgha," and not for the personal enjoyment of an individual.
Regarding extra beds, it is also permissible to use them after arranging them in storehouses and so forth, and placing one's bowl and robes upon them. Outside the boundary...
When it is given with the words, “We give this to the Saṅgha,” the bed should be placed in the residence of the senior monk of the Saṅgha.

If there are many beds there, it need not be used as a bed. It should be given to whoever has work to do in that residence, saying, “Use this for the communal enjoyment of the Saṅgha,” and not for private personal use.
Even if it is of great value—worth a hundred or a thousand [pieces of money]—it should be used in this manner.
Or, if one receives another hundred beds in exchange for one bed, it may be taken after bartering. It is not only a bed that may be exchanged for a bed;
it is also permissible to exchange monasteries, monastery sites, dwellings, dwelling sites, stools, couches, and pillows.
This same principle applies to stools, couches, and pillows as well. [This is] for the purpose of protecting superior lodgings and so forth.
If there is a famine and the monks cannot subsist on almsfood—whether due to fear of kings, disease, or robbers;
or when, for those traveling elsewhere, monasteries fall into ruin and palm trees, coconut trees, and so forth are destroyed—it is possible to subsist by means of the requisite of lodgings.
At such a time, inferior lodgings and so forth [are permitted] for the purpose of protecting the superior lodgings and other requisites. Inferior...
"To relinquish" means to relinquish what is inferior; the intention is that one relinquishes it down to the very lowest degree.
"It is permissible to use after relinquishing" means that after relinquishing, it is permissible to use the alms-food, robes, and so forth obtained from that [relinquished item].
Regarding "black iron, copper, bronze, brass, and tin": here, "bronze" (*kaṃsaloha*) and "brass" (*vaṭṭaloha*) are mentioned.
Base metal (*kittimaloha*). For there are three kinds of base metals: bell-metal (*kaṃsaloha*), brass (*vaṭṭaloha*), and bronze (*ārakūṭa*).
Among these, bell-metal is made by mixing [copper with] tin; brass is made by mixing [copper with] lead;
and bronze is made by mixing [copper with] zinc. Therefore it is said: "Bell-metal, brass, and base metal. Beyond that...
Then there is the one who takes an extra portion.
A *sarako* is a vessel that should be made by showing a bud in the middle, widening the rim, and bending it back from behind;
some also call it a *sarāva*. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), household utensils such as golden vessels and so forth are included.
"Seizing. For even those small items are indeed "heavy goods" because they are the personal belongings of a layperson. By the word "even," he shows that this is true much more so for large items.
However, the intention is that these [other items] are "to be shared" because they are the requisites of a monk.
And just as these are, so too is the water-pot (kuṇḍikā) to be shared. For he will say: "And just as with earthenware vessels, so it is with metal vessels."
"The water-pot partakes only of that portion which is to be shared. "By means of communal use by the Saṅgha" means by using it after giving it to visiting monks who are senior.
"Defiled by householders" means made unseemly by being assigned by householders or by making it one's own property.
"It is not permitted through personal use" means [using it] without having given it to visiting monks as one's own possession.
It is not permitted to take [an object] as if it were one’s own, carry it about, and use it. *Pipphalika* means a pair of scissors.
*Ārakaṇṭaka* is a needle-piercer. *Tāḷa* is a machine. A piercing tool for a pair of scissors is a ring-handle for a pair of scissors.
Iron that has been made solid in such a way is called an iron bar, an iron ball, an iron lump, or an iron discus; thus it is made solid.
“Metal”: “Made of milk-stone” means made of stone that has the color of soft milk.

Even those belonging to householders are not permitted because they are untouchable. By the word “even,” it is shown that they are all the more so forbidden when used by the Saṅgha or used as personal property.
However, the use of lodgings is allowable in every way. Therefore, all requisites for lodgings, even those made of gold and so forth, [are permitted].
"Raw. Therefore he said, "But in the use of lodgings," and so forth.
"The rest" means those [tools] larger than that. "But whatever" means whatever small axe there may be. Even a pickaxe the size of four finger-breadths is indeed heavy property (*garubhaṇḍa*).
Whether the chisel has four corners, or a shovel-like opening, or is curved or straight—[it is all heavy property].
Or, even down to a broom-handle, a peg, or a wedge—if it is a handle-fastening, it is indeed a heavy article. Therefore he said:
"A pickaxe, or a handle-fastening wedge, is not called a light article. A *sipāṭikā* is a razor-case.
As for the *sikhara*, however, since it conforms to the handle-fastening wedge, he said: "The *sikhara* is also included by the wedge itself."
But if even that is a fruit-sized [piece] without a stalk, it is allowable (*bhājanīya*). "Tools" (*upakkhara*) refers to implements such as axes and so forth.
A "bowl-binder" (*pattabandhaka*) is one who makes the loop for the bowl and so on; some also say he is "one who fashions bowls from gold and other materials.
A small knife for cutting *tippu* (a type of resin), a knife for cutting gold, and a small knife for cutting leather that has been prepared (*parikamma*)—these are the types.
And here, because these three follow the sequence of the *pipphalika*, he says, "But this is the distinction," and so forth. "The others" refers to the *mahākattari* and the rest.
"Measuring half an arm" means from the elbow up to the measure of the shoulder-blade; that is to say, measuring two spans and four finger-breadths.
"Grown there" means grown on land belonging to the Saṅgha. Because it is protected by means of a guard, [it is said to be] "guarded."
And because she is protected—guarded by being hidden so that she does not perish, like [an object] placed inside a casket or similar container—it is called "protected and guarded" (*rakkhitagopitā*).
However, even those born there who are unprotected do not constitute "stolen property of high value" (*garubhaṇḍa*).
By the phrase "when work for the Saṅgha or work for a shrine has been done," it is indicated that one may guard or exchange what belongs to the Saṅgha using what belongs to a shrine.
It indicates that it is permissible. "But thread" refers to both wound and unwound thread.
"The size of an eight-finger needle-handle" means at least eight fingers in length, and in circumference, the size of a Sinhalese leaf-needle handle. "In this" refers to the bamboo basket.
"Those whose houses have been burnt" means those whose homes have been consumed by fire. "They should not be prevented" means [one should not stop them] saying, "Do not take [it]."
One should not forbid them with the words, “Go away. When one has arrived at another location, they should be placed in a communal dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha.

As for the remaining thatching grass—any other kind of thatching grass besides *muñja* and *pabbaja*—where there is no grass, they thatch with leaves. Therefore, leaves are also included under the category of grass.
He said: “When [the books] have gone into a collection of covering grass,” and so forth. “Even if it is eight finger-breadths in measure” means even if it is eight finger-breadths in width.
However, a written manuscript is not considered a heavy object (garubhaṇḍa).
Regarding the bamboo, “of the measure stated” means of the measure stated for bamboo objects: “even if it is merely eight finger-breadths and the length of a needle-shaft.”
“Given to the Saṅgha” means given to the Saṅgha in a place where wood is scarce.

Having explained the determination of wooden articles according to the sequence stated in the *Kurundi*, he now says “Moreover,” etc., in order to explain it according to the sequence stated in the *Mahā-aṭṭhakathā*. Regarding “stools and so forth”:
here, “stool” (*āsandika*) refers to a four-legged chair. “A high stool” (*uccakampi āsandika*)— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.*
According to the textual tradition, only a long bench with legs measuring eight finger-breadths (aṭṭhaṅgula) is permitted on one side.
However, it should be understood that a square chair (caturassāsandika), even if it exceeds the prescribed measure, is permitted. By the word "etc. (ādi), the following are included:

the seven-limbed chair (sattaṅga), the auspicious chair (bhaddapīṭhaka), the sheep’s-leg chair (eḷakapādakapīṭha), the myrobalan-ball chair (āmalakavaṭṭakapīṭha), the plank, the wicker stool (koccha), and the straw mat (palālapīṭhaka).
It should be understood that they "support" [the Sangha]. Therefore he said, "at least," and so forth. "With leaves" means with plantain leaves and the like.
Even a bolster covered with tiger skin, surrounded by the forms of wild beasts, and sewn with jewels, is indeed a heavy article (garubhaṇḍa).
A "rubbing board" is that upon which one places dyed robes and rubs them with the hand. A "rubbing mallet" [is used for the same purpose].
They say that *nāma* refers to the striking [of the cloth] by wind and so forth. A *daṇḍamuggara* is that with which they beat the dyed robe.
An *ambaṇa* is a water vessel made like a lotus pond with wooden planks.
A *rajanadoṇī* is a container for placing the wet dye after it has been poured in.
"Unallowable hide" refers to the hide of lions and other such animals. The statement, "It is permissible to make it a floor-covering," is said with reference to unallowable hides.
By the phrase "it falls under the category of bedspreads," it is indicated that it is also permissible to spread it over beds and chairs.
Some say that even bedspreads such as *pāvāra* and others are "heavy goods" (*garubhaṇḍa*); others say they are not. This should be determined after careful investigation.
"Permissible hides" refers to the hides of deer and other such animals.
"Every vehicle with wheels" refers to every vehicle equipped with wheels, such as chariots and carts;
however, a vehicle whose wheels have been disassembled is to be distributed. "An authorized residence" means that which can be carried about by being placed inside a case.
It is said [as follows]. "Fist-leaf" (*muṭṭhipaṇṇa*) refers to a palm leaf; for it is called a "fist-leaf" because one carries it about having grasped it with the fist.
Some say that "fist-leaf" refers specifically to the leaf used as a cover for a sunshade (*chattacchadana*). "Fire-drill equipment" (*araṇisahita*) means a pair of fire-drills;
the meaning is that there are two fire-drills: the upper fire-drill (*uttarāraṇī*) and the lower fire-drill (*adharāraṇī*).
"Having made a pledge" means having made a fixed agreement for interest, even on as little as a handful of sand worth that amount.
One who takes it without making a pledge must use it right there. When departing, one should leave it in a monastery belonging to the Saṅgha and then go.
If one has taken it away through forgetfulness, it should be sent back and returned. If one has gone to another country, it should be given at the monastery where one arrives.
It should be kept in a dwelling belonging to the Saṅgha. "Therein" refers to earthenware vessels. A *kuṇḍikā* is both an iron water-pot and a copper water-pot.
"It belongs only to the category of common property" means it resorts only to the side of items that are not heavy (i.e., light), but not to heavy articles;
this is the meaning. However, the intention is that a golden one is indeed a heavy article. "The other" refers to the heavy article.
The commentary on the weak training rule is finished.
12. Commentary on the training rule concerning diverting [alms]:
there is nothing further to be said regarding the twelfth.
The commentary on the training rule concerning dedication is finished.
The eighth section, the Chapter on Fellow-Practitioners, is concluded.
9. The Chapter on Jewels.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Inner Apartments (*Antepurasikkhāpada*).

Regarding the phrase "when the king has not departed and the [royal] treasures have not been removed," one should understand that the word "in the bedchamber" (*sayanighare*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the text;
thus he says, "the king has not departed from here," and so forth. In this context, "from here" means from the bedchamber. "In the bedchamber" means in the chamber containing the bed.
"Wherever the king’s bed is prepared—even if it is merely enclosed by a fence of grass mats—that is what is meant.
In the sense of producing delight, "jewel" (ratana) refers to elephants and so forth; however, here the "woman-jewel" (itthiratana) is intended, thus he says:
"The queen is called the jewel."

"Both" refers to the two chief queens. Regarding "action" and "non-action": here, crossing the threshold (indakhīla) is to be understood as action, while not being perceived [by anyone] is non-action.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the inner palace is finished.
2. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Jewels (Ratana-sikkhāpada).
"Ten kinds of pearls" refers to the ten types of gems: pearl, mani-jewel, beryl, conch, stone, coral, silver, gold, ruby, and masāragalla.

"In a dwelling" means in a house. Thus he said, "of an enclosed [dwelling]," the meaning of which is "of an enclosed residence. And here, by "residence," a house situated within a village is intended.
However, a house situated within a monastery is already included by the very mention of "within the monastery" (*ajjhārāma*).

Regarding this, some say: "In this context, 'dwelling' (*āvasatha*) refers to one's own place of residence, whether it be inside the monastery or elsewhere. For all [cases], it is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*);

that is, for one who acquires [the property] either for oneself or for the benefit of those [groups] such as the Saṅgha, whether acquiring it personally or causing it to be acquired, it is indeed a *dukkaṭa*.

However, if there is an allowable article belonging to one’s mother or father that must necessarily be stored away, it says, “But such as this,” and so forth, meaning that after taking it for one’s own use, it should be stored away.

“Such as this” (*tādisaṃ*) refers to whatever allowable article belonging to one’s mother or father must necessarily be stored away. “Even by desire or even by fear” refers to [the case of] carpenters and others.
"Out of desire, or out of fear toward those favored by the king.
"In such a place" means in a monastery enclosure (pariveṇa) surrounded by a wall, similar to the Mahāvihāra.
"Having made a mark" means having made a mark in the form of a certain number of kahāpaṇas, or by means of a seal or some other sign.
"Having observed" is the meaning. "In the hands of suitable bhikkhus" means in the hands of bhikkhus who possess a sense of shame and are conscientious;
it is not permitted to place [the robe] in the hands of those who are by nature greedy.
"He does not depart" means he does not leave that residence. By the words "a permanent lodging," etc., it is indicated that one should not make it the basis for one's own robes and other requisites.

He shows it. "Having shown that" means: having shown that whatever has been made, such as a permanent dwelling (thāvara-senāsana) and so forth, was made with what belongs to you, O lay follower, saying, "This very thing was made [for you].
"Having exhorted" means: having exhorted another, or having requested in the manner stated, "The Noble Ones abide for the sake of [others]; this is the entreaty of the Noble Ones."
"In an authorized place" means within the monastery grounds or the dwelling area. "Solid food" refers to items such as clothing that may be touched and put away.
The commentary on the Jewel Precept is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Entering a Village at Improper Time.
“Cāritte” means in the training rule (sikkhāpada) concerning conduct. “Upacāraṃ” means the distance of a second stone’s throw.

“There is no further obligation to seek permission for those going to another village” means that for those going to another village without withdrawing their initial intention, even if it be a hundred villages, there is no further obligation to seek permission. Therefore he said, “But if,” and so forth. “Ussāhaṃ” means...

Regarding the encouragement to enter a village: there is no offense not only for one who goes without having asked permission, but also for one who goes without fastening the waistband or without putting on the outer robe (*saṅghāṭi*). "In cases of emergency" means:
if a lion or a tiger approaches, if a storm arises, or if some other calamity occurs, there is no offense. In such circumstances...
In times of distress, it is permissible to enter a village from outside the village.
The commentary on the training rule regarding entering a village at an improper time is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding the Needle Case.
"‘That belongs to him’ means that because it must first be broken and only afterwards confessed, that which causes the breach belongs to him as a *pācittiya* offense.
‘Araṇika’ refers to the fire-drill wood. ‘Vedha’ refers to the piercing tool. ‘Vāsijaṭā’ refers to the handle of a knife.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the needle-case is finished."
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Beds and Stools (*mañcapīṭhasikkhāpada*).

“*Aṭṭhaṅgulapādakan*” is a description using the neuter gender for the sake of formation. By the phrase “*chedanakaṃ bhedanakasadisamevā*” (“the term *chedanaka* is exactly like *bhedanaka*”), it refers by extension to this meaning: “*chedana* itself is *chedanaka*; that which has this [quality] is *chedanaka*.
Just as the measurement is seen above, so too it is [measured] after being buried. However, if one does not wish to cut it, [one may proceed accordingly].
Just as it is seen above, so too [it is measured] after being buried in the ground.
"Or having fixed a support" means having lifted it up, placed it upon a balance-beam assembly, and made a mark.
The commentary on the training rule regarding beds and chairs is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Cotton-Filling (*tūlonaddha*).

"Having spread a mattress and having inserted cotton" means: having spread a mattress over beds and chairs, and having inserted cotton upon that. "Upon the mattress" means: on the upper surface of the mattress. "The size of a head" means:
that measurement which covers the entire head starting from the nape of the neck; that is the size of a head.
To show that, by way of the maximum measurement, it is one fist-span (muṭṭhiratana) across and two spans (ratana) long, he said: "Of which [the width] at the three corners... and so forth.
"The interval between two is a span and four finger-breadths" means that when measured between two corners, it is both a span and four finger-breadths. In the middle, it is a fist-span.
The middle of the bolster is one fist-span in width. This is the maximum limit for the size of the head;
more than that is not permitted, while less is permitted. For one who is not ill, only two things are allowed:
a pillow for the head and a pillow for the feet. For one who is ill, it is also permitted to lie down after spreading out bolsters and placing a coverlet over them.
The commentary on the training rule concerning stuffing with cotton is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning sitting mats:
the seventh [rule] is likewise straightforward.
The commentary on the training rule concerning sitting cloths is finished.
8. Commentary on the training rule concerning the itch-covering cloth:
“Below the navel and above the knees” means below the navel and above the kneecaps. “For the afflictions of itch, boils, discharge, and scabies” means...
Here, *kaṇḍūti* means itch (*kacchu*). *Pīḷakā* refers to small red pustules (*lohitatuṇḍikā*). *Assāva* is the discharge of impurity by way of fistula-in-ano, hemorrhoids, or diabetes.
*Thullakacchābādha* refers to the affliction of large pustules.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the covering of itches is finished.
9–10. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Rainy-Season Robe (Vassikasāṭika).
The ninth and tenth [rules] are self-evident.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the rainy-season robe is concluded.
The ninth chapter, the Ratana-vagga.
Thus ends the *Līnatthappakāsanī*, the commentary on the meaning of the Vinaya,
within the *Vinayatthamañjūsā*, which is a commentary on the *Pātimokkha* for the resolution of doubts.
The commentary on the Pācittiya rules is finished.
The Section on the Pāṭidesanīya Rules.
1. Commentary on the First Pāṭidesanīya Training Rule.
"Having entered among the houses" means having entered a carriage road, a crossroads, a junction, or a house.
"Inappropriate" means detrimental and unsuitable for heaven and liberation. Here, the offense should be understood according to the nun who gives while standing among the houses;
however, the location where the monk stands is irrelevant. Therefore he said: "Having entered among the houses."
"By way of speech," and so forth. "In the midst of monasteries, etc. means in the midst of monasteries, nunneries, and the lodgings of ascetics of other sects.
Regarding "roads, crossroads, junctions, and houses": here, "road" (*rathiya*) refers to a street.

"Crossroads" (*byūha*) refers to a street that remains unseparated [into lanes], where people go back and forth. "Junction" (*siṅghāṭaka*) refers to a place where roads meet, whether it be four-cornered or three-cornered.

“Gharanti” means a family house. Just as there is an offense for one who takes [food] from a woman giving it while standing on a street or similar place, so too should it be understood in the case of elephant stables and other such locations.

The statement, “In the case of ‘time-for-a-watch’ (yāmakālika) food and the like, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) both in the receiving and in the swallowing,” refers to that which is not mixed with non-food (āmiṣa).
This was said with intentional reference [to a specific case]; however, when the food is mixed and has become of one flavor, it is simply a *pāṭidesanīya* offense.

"For one ordained together" means for one who received ordination in the presence of the nuns; but for one who received ordination in the presence of the monks, it is according to the original category [of the offense].
"Or having her cause a relative to give" means not giving herself, but causing some relative to give; "a non-relative" means...
The meaning is as follows: "Or by one who gives after having set it down" means by one who, having placed it on the ground, says, "Venerable lady, I give this to you.
Having accepted what was thus given with the words, "Excellent, sister," it is permissible to eat it after having had it received either by that very nun or by someone else.
The commentary on the first *pāṭidesanīya* training rule is finished.
2. Commentary on the second *pāṭidesanīya* training rule:
"And whoever, having accepted it, eats"—this is the connection. Regarding the phrase "or she who causes her own meal to be given": even if...
If she gives her own food [to others], there is no offense under this training rule (sikkhāpada), but there is an offense under the previous training rule.
Regarding the phrase "or giving the food of others": if she were to cause it to be given, there would be an offense under this training rule;
however, for one who is actually giving, there is no offense under this rule, nor under the previous one.
The commentary on the second *pāṭidesanīya* training rule is concluded.
3. Commentary on the third *pāṭidesanīya* training rule:

“Those for whom permission regarding the use of requisites has been granted” means those for whom permission regarding the use of requisites has been granted by means of a formal act (*kamma*) consisting of a motion and one proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*). For whichever family...

"He prospers in faith but declines in wealth; for such a family, they grant the authorization of one in training (sekkhasammuti) by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second (ñattidutiyakamma);
it is with reference to this that it was said.
'Having led out from the house' means having brought [the person] from the house to the assembly hall or the monastery. Therefore he said: 'In the assembly halls, etc.'"
Or: "giving" is connected with this [term] "giving. "Giving what is placed at the door" means they give it later to one who has arrived after it was placed at the door.
However, it is not permissible for something to be given after being brought out from inside the house upon seeing a bhikkhu.

"In the case of a regular meal" (*niccabhattaka*) means in the case of a meal that must be provided regularly. "In the case of a ticket-meal" (*salākabhatta*) refers to [a meal] made from the heartwood of trees...

Regarding "ticket-food" (*salākabhatta*): this refers to food that should be given by having letters inscribed on a tally-stick (*salākā*) made of bamboo, reed, palm leaf, or similar materials, or on a wooden tablet (*paṭṭikā*), such as "the ticket-food of so-and-so," and then having it taken [by the recipient].
Regarding "fortnightly" (*pakkhika*): this refers to food to be given on one specific day within a fortnight.

Regarding "uposatha-day" (*uposathika*): this refers to food to be given on the uposatha day. Regarding "first-of-the-month" (*pāṭipadika*): this refers to food to be given on the first day of the lunar month.
The commentary on the third *pāṭidesanīya* training rule is concluded.
4. Commentary on the fourth *pāṭidesanīya* training rule:
"Having made him his attendant, or having many others with him," means that having informed [the donor] regarding the rice-gruel.

“Why give her plain gruel? Let us provide this gruel with an accompaniment such as cakes, rice, and so forth,” and so on—with such thoughts, one may provide an accompaniment to that hard food (*khādanīya*) or soft food (*bhojanīya*), or bring whatever else there is, even in great quantity, along with it.
The term “hard food” is merely an illustration, since it is also intended that “soft food” may be included.
"Let them bring [it] together with that" means: let them bring their own gift to be given together with that.
"If they bring either cake or cooked rice after having made it known by means of the rice-gruel, this is also permissible," so it is stated in the *Kuruṇḍi*.
"Or what remains from the sick after it has been made known": here, "made known" (*paṭisaṃvidita*) and "sick" (*gilāna*) constitute "made-known-and-sick" (*paṭisaṃviditagilāna*).
The meaning is: "the remainder of those," and "the remainder of what has been made known for one who is ill.
Having made it known for the sake of one person, if it is brought back, it is permissible to consume its remainder by another as well.
Or, if it has been brought back after making it known for four or five people, they wish to give it to others too.
This too is permissible for everyone provided that it has been formally announced (*paṭisaṃvidita*) as being the remainder of what was brought;
however, if there is an excess, it is permissible on the second day as well, provided it was set aside after the period of storage (*sannidhi*) had expired.

The same rule applies to the remainder brought by one who is ill. But as for that which was brought without having been formally announced, one must send it outside the monastery and have it formally announced.
It should be caused to be brought; or alternatively, monks should go and take it on the way.

Furthermore, if forest-dwellers or others bring it from the forest while one is passing through the midst of the monastery, one must have the formal notification (*paṭisaṃvidita*) performed according to the previous method.
However, in some manuscripts, the reading is: "or what has been brought after having been formally notified, or what remains from the sick."
If it is seen [to be raw], it must not be accepted. "Produced right there" means produced specifically within the monastery grounds. Regarding "roots, fruits, etc.":
there is no offense for one who consumes roots, fruits, bark, leaves, and so forth, when they have been made permissible (*kappiya*) by another and given.
However, if they bring them back after having carried them to the village and cooked them, it is not permitted; one must have the recipient acknowledge [the transgression].
The commentary on the fourth *pāṭidesanīya* training rule is finished.
Thus ends the *Līnatthappakāsanī*, the Commentary on the Meaning of the Vinaya,
within the *Vinayatthamañjūsā*, the Commentary on the Pāṭimokkha for the Dispelling of Doubts.
The commentary on the Pāṭidesanīya rules is finished.
The Section on the Sekhiya Rules: 1. Commentary on the Parimaṇḍala Training Rule.
Because it was not specified by saying “in the interior of a house,” it is stated as “both in the monastery and in the interior of a house, everywhere.
“In the monastery” is said with reference to times such as when attending upon the Buddha.
Just as a specific limitation is made here and there by such statements as “there these four *pārājika* rules come up for recitation,” so too here: “there these... [rules]...”
Regarding the question, "Why was no limit set for the seventy-five rules of training (*sekhiya-dhamma*) as they come up for recitation? he says, "And here," and so forth.

"The duties stated in the *Vattakkhandhaka*" refers to the duties of newcomers, residents, those departing, those expressing thanks, those at the meal hall, alms-gatherers, forest-dwellers, those regarding lodgings, the sauna, the restroom, and the duties toward preceptors, teachers, co-residents, and pupils.
This is merely an illustration, for it is intended that the other duties from the *Khandhakas* should also be included therein.

This is the intended meaning here: by the inclusion of the term "training rules" (*sekhiya*), the duties (*vatta*) and so forth mentioned in the *Vatta-khandhaka* and other sections are also included.

For these too are intended as "training rules" in the sense that they are to be practiced. Therefore, no specific limit was set for the training rules in the *Mātikā*, as was done for the *Pārājika* and other categories.
This applies not only to the duties mentioned in the *Vatta-khandhaka* and similar texts...
"It is for the purpose of grasping alone," he said; "and for the purpose of showing proper conduct and discipline. Here too, one should supply and connect the phrase, "no limit has been set.
Since "dukkaṭa" (an offense of wrong-doing) was not mentioned in the *Mātikā*, he asked, "But how is it to be understood that there is a dukkaṭa here?

and replied with the words beginning "But whoever... "The measure of eight finger-breadths" means a measure of eight finger-breadths by the standard finger. However, for one who has dry legs or large calves, it is permissible to lower [the robe] even more than eight finger-breadths to wear it in a manner befitting his physique.
"Pāsanta" means the end of the cord; the meaning is "the base of the fringe.
"I will put on the lower robe unevenly" means "I will put it on by letting it hang down either in front or behind"—this refers to doing so unintentionally.
Although there is no offense for one who does not know how to put on the lower robe evenly, nevertheless, this is [a transgression of] the duty regarding the wearing of the robe.
It must indeed be thoroughly mastered. For intentional non-mastery would constitute disrespect; thus he said, "Furthermore, the procedure for wearing the lower robe must be mastered.
The commentary on the first *parimaṇḍala-sikkhāpada* is finished.
2. Commentary on the second *parimaṇḍala-sikkhāpada*.
“Householder attire is prohibited” means that householder attire is prohibited in the *Khuddakavatthu-khandhaka*.
Now, in order to explain in detail the very same matter which was stated briefly in the passage beginning with “Monks, [you should not],” he says “Therein,” and so forth.
The connection is: “whatever else is worn as attire. “Therefore” means because white-clothed attire and the like constitute householder attire.
[This is] the name; therefore [it is so called]. "Setapaṭā" is an explanation of this very term. Regarding "Aḍḍhapālaka-nigaṇṭhas":
they are called *aḍḍhapālakā* because they preserve (*pālenti*) half (*aḍḍha*); and since they are both *aḍḍhapālakā* and *nigaṇṭhā*, they are "Aḍḍhapālaka-nigaṇṭhas.
For they wear a single white cloth above, having tucked it into their armpits, while below they remain naked, preserving only half [of their body].
“Wanderers” (*paribbājaka*) refers to those who have gone forth, having abandoned the bonds of household life. “Having uncovered his chest” means having uncovered the center of the heart.
“The size of the pupil of the eye” means the measure of the eye. “In a monastery” (*ārāme*) is said with reference to times such as when attending upon the Buddha.
“In a village” (*antaraghare*) means in that which is called a “village,” where there are houses within it, or belonging to it.
The commentary on the second *parimaṇḍala-sikkhāpada* is finished.
3–4. Commentary on the *suppaṭicchanna-sikkhāpada*:
"Well covered" means by covering the parts that ought to be covered, without even opening the waist or the chest.
It is covered, not concealed by a *sīsapa* tree. Therefore he said, "having fastened the toggle," and so forth.
Therein, "having fastened the toggle" means having fastened the toggle to the cord. "In an inhabited area" means in the village where one goes for alms.
It is permissible to go as one pleases to the presence of one who has stayed there even for a single day; how much more so for one who has resolved to stay for four or five days?
"In the presence of bhikkhus who have stayed overnight" is written in the *Gaṇṭhipada*.
"Of one who has gone to stay overnight": there is no offense for one who sits with the body uncovered during the day or at night, having gone there for the purpose of staying overnight.
The commentary on the training rule concerning being well-covered is finished.
5–6. Commentary on the Training Rule on Being Well-Restrained (*Susaṃvuta-sikkhāpada*).
"Well-restrained" (*susaṃvuta*) means well-controlled (*susaṃyata*). To show how one becomes "well-restrained" in this context, the passage beginning with "the hand" (*hatthaṃ vā*) was stated.
The commentary on the training rule on being well-restrained is finished.
7–8. Commentary on the Training Rule on Lowered Eyes:
To what extent does one have lowered eyes? To this he says: "Looking at a portion of ground the measure of a yoke.
For a well-bred thoroughbred horse yoked to a chariot looks only the measure of a yoke; that is, it looks at a portion of ground four cubits in length ahead. By this [expression], too...

One may walk looking only so far ahead. If, out of disrespect, one walks while looking here and there at buildings, gabled chambers, or streets, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*). "In the absence of dangers such as elephants and horses":

in this context, *parissaya* (danger) has the sense of threatening, the sense of overcoming, or the sense of harassing; thus, elephants, horses, and so forth are themselves the danger, hence "dangers such as elephants and horses."
“Absence of that” means the absence of dangers such as elephants, horses, and so forth.
They say: “Just as one standing in one place can likewise observe the absence of dangers while walking, so too can one [observe them] while receiving honor in the village.
The commentary on the training rule concerning downcast eyes is finished.
9–10. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding the Raised Body:

“Starting from within the boundary pillar” means starting from within the threshold of an enclosed village; however, for an unenclosed village, it means starting from the second stone’s throw. One must not walk in such a manner.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the raised body is finished.
11–12. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Loud Laughter (*Ujjagghika-sikkhāpada*).
"In the matter of something laughable" (*hasanīyasmiṃ vatthusmiṃ*): this is the locative case used in the sense of a cause (*nimitta*), meaning "on account of a thing that ought to be laughed at.
The commentary on the training rule concerning loud laughter is finished.
13–14. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Loud Noise.

To the question, "In what sense does one become 'one who makes little noise'? he says, "But here... and so forth. "He hears only sound" means he hears merely the sound itself, with the syllables being indistinct. Therefore he asks, "How does he not discern it?
The commentary on the training rule concerning loud noise is finished.
15–20. Commentary on the Training Rules concerning Shaking the Body, etc.:
The phrase “having held the body and so forth erect” is an elaboration of that very point;
“having placed them motionless and straight” means that one should both walk and sit with an even posture. This constitutes the group of six training rules beginning with shaking the body.
The commentary on the training rule concerning swaying the body, etc., is finished.
26. Commentary on the training rule concerning the "wrapped-around" posture:
Regarding the phrase "with a cloth wrapped around [the waist]," here the "sling-wrapped" posture is also indeed included under "cloth-wrapped."
The commentary on the training rule concerning the *pallatthika* (the cross-legged posture) is finished.
The commentary on the twenty-six training rules concerning what is appropriate is finished.
27. Commentary on the training rule concerning receiving with due care (*sakkacca-paṭiggahaṇa*).

“Having established mindfulness” means: not being like one who wishes to discard it, but having established mindfulness regarding the alms-food; having established mindfulness with the thought, “I shall receive the alms-food.
The commentary on the training rule concerning receiving with due care is finished.
28. Commentary on the training rule concerning receiving with awareness of the bowl.
"Being mindful of the bowl" means that while almsfood is being given, one does not look here and there out of disrespect, but remains focused on the bowl with attentive awareness.
The commentary on the training rule regarding receiving with mindfulness of the bowl is finished.
29. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Receiving an Equal Amount of Sauce.
"Having made it with equal curry" means having made it with a suitable amount of curry; this is a description using the neuter gender for the sake of the compound.
However, in order to show only the meaning without taking up the specific word form, it is said: "What is called 'with equal curry' (*samasūpaka*)," and so forth.
"All varieties of curry and condiments" refers to all varieties of curry and condiments, such as *oloṇi*, potherbs, soups, fish broth, meat broth, and so on.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the acceptance of equal amounts of curry is finished.
30–32. Commentary on the training rules beginning with “level to the brim.
*Samatittikaṃ* is a neuter abstract noun; the meaning is “having made it level to the brim. The same applies to other similar [terms].

The meaning should be understood according to the respective contexts. "Filled level with" means filled level with the rim of the bowl's opening. "Evenly filled" follows the same principle here as well;
however, this applies only to a bowl that has attained determination (*adhiṭṭhānupaga*), and not to any other. Therefore he said, "of a bowl that has attained determination," and so forth.
"Arranged" means made, placed, or filled—the sense is the same. "Whatever is of the time-limited category" refers to rice gruel, cooked rice, fruits, and so on.

"Whatever belongs to the category of material things. "Anywhere whatsoever" means: whether it belongs to a bowl that is subject to formal determination (*adhiṭṭhānupaga*) or not subject to formal determination (*anadhiṭṭhānupaga*), wherever in the bowl [the food] may be placed.

"Made into a heap" means made like a heap; the meaning is: made beyond the rim-line inside a bowl that is subject to formal determination. And this [refers to] the phrase "those which are for a watch of the night, etc."
This was stated by way of that [term]; however, by applying the grammatical construction according to the term "yāvakālika" (usable until the same time tomorrow), it should be connected as:
"it is also permissible even if it is heaped up. By the word *pi* ("also/even"), it is shown that there is no discussion whatsoever regarding those things which are not heaped up being permissible.
"It descends downward" means that, because there is space all around, it moves and falls down. "Takkola-ornaments, head-ornaments, and so forth..."
Here, because the *takkola* fruit placed at the top resembles an ear-ornament (*vaṭaṃsaka*), it is called a "takkola-ear-ornament.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), there is the inclusion of ear-ornaments made of flowers, pungent fruits, and so forth; however, that [fruit] is not called a "heap" (*thūpīkata*), because the leaves and other materials are separate receptacles.
The commentary on the training rules beginning with "level-full" is finished.
33–34. Commentary on the training rule regarding "in order" (*sapadāna*).
Here, "giving" (*dāna*) refers to breaking; that which is removed from giving is "non-giving" (*apadāna*), meaning unbroken.
The meaning is: together with the *apadāna* (exclusion), it is *sapadāna*; that which is devoid of interruption, meaning "in regular succession.
Therefore he said: "without making a boundary here and there, but in regular succession.
The commentary on the training rule regarding *sapadāna* is finished.
36. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Covering Rice with Curry.

Regarding the phrase "at times such as the season of the great sacrifice" (*māghātasamaya*): here, the time at which kings cause the drum to be beaten, proclaiming "No living being is to be killed," is called the season of the great sacrifice. "Giving while covering the curry" means giving after having concealed the curry.
The commentary on the training rule concerning covering rice with curry is finished.
37. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Requesting of Soup and Boiled Rice: This eleventh [rule] concerns the requesting of soup and boiled rice.

In this context, however, if [food] enters the mouth even if it was intended to be spat out again once regret has arisen, and one consumes it impulsively, this is called "consuming unintentionally. As for whoever...
However, if one eats by taking food— whether it has been signaled for or not— while it is situated in one place, suddenly and without careful consideration,
this is called eating with lack of mindfulness.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the signaling for curry and rice is finished.
38. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Perception of Censure (*Ujjhānasaññīsikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā*).

It is called *ujjhāna* because one censures by means of it; it refers to the mind. The perception regarding that is "perception of censure" (*ujjhānasaññā*); thus he said, "one who has the perception of censure," and so forth. "Of one looking" means of one looking at the bowl of another.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the perception of censure is finished.
39. Commentary on the Training Rule on Mouthfuls:
Because of the statement, "A peacock’s egg is too large," even a mouthful the size of a peacock’s egg is not permitted.
Some, however, say, "Only one larger than a peacock’s egg is not permitted, but not one the size of a peacock’s egg"; that should not be accepted.
The same principle applies here as well regarding the phrase "a hen’s egg is too small. However, there is no offense even for one who makes a mouthful too small when he is ill.
The commentary on the training rule concerning mouthfuls is finished.
41–42. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Not Bringing [Food].
"Sakalaṃ hatthaṃ" means all the fingers. Here, the word "hand" (*hattha*) should be understood as referring to its parts, namely the fingers, as in expressions such as "hand-seal" (*hatthamuddā*).
By taking it this way, the inclusion of the word "all" (*sabbam*) becomes justified.
Otherwise, since it would be impossible to insert an entire hand into the mouth, the inclusion of "all" would indeed be unjustified. [This refers to] the whole (*samudāye*).
Furthermore, because it occurs even as a part of the conventional usage that has come into being, it is not permissible to place even a single finger or even a portion of it into the mouth.
The commentary on the training rule concerning what has not been brought [to the mouth] is finished.
43. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Having a Mouthful of Food (Sakabaḷa-sikkhāpada).
"It is permissible within that much" means it is permissible to speak while that much remains in the mouth.
The commentary on the training rule concerning [eating] with a morsel in the mouth is finished.
50–51. Commentary on the training rule concerning making a *capucapu* sound.
“Making the sound ‘capu capū’” means making an imitative sound such as “capu capū.
By the phrase “the same method applies even to the twenty-fifth [offense],” this refers to the meaning: “making a *surusuru* sound means making a sound such as ‘surū surū.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the maker of the *capucapu* sound is finished.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the thirty meals is finished.
57. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding One Holding an Umbrella:
"Any kind of umbrella" means any kind of umbrella among white umbrellas, palm-leaf umbrellas, or leaf umbrellas. Whatever...
An umbrella made from a single leaf grown there is also considered an umbrella.
"On any part of the body" refers to any part of the body, such as the shoulder, the thigh, or elsewhere.
The commentary on the training rule concerning one who holds an umbrella is finished.
60. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Weapons in Hand (*Āvudhapāṇisikkhāpada*).
"All varieties of bows" (*sabbāpi dhanuvikati*) means all types of bows, such as the *cāpa* and the *kodaṇḍa*.
A *cāpa* is a variety of bow that is curved in the middle, resembling a bamboo staff (*kājadaṇḍa*). A *kodaṇḍa* is a variety of bow with a rounded staff. "Fixed" (*paṭimukka*) means inserted.
"Attached. "As long as he does not take it" means as long as he does not take it with his hand; or rather, this is the reading: "as long as [he does not take it].
"It is allowable for that long" means it is allowable to teach the Dhamma for that duration.
The commentary on the training rule concerning one who has a weapon in hand is finished.
61–62. Commentary on the Training Rule on Sandals (Pādukasikkhāpada).

“Merely having stepped upon them” means standing after having stepped upon the sandals alone. “Having put them on” means standing after having fastened them. Therefore he said: “by way of the position [taken] after inserting [them].
The commentary on the training rule on sandals is finished.
63. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Vehicles (*Yānasikkhāpada*).
"Of one who has gone in a vehicle": "Vehicle" is defined as "a bullock cart, a chariot, a wagon, a palanquin, a litter, or a sedan chair.
This refers to anyone traveling even as far as a hand’s reach [of another] while using such a vehicle. Therefore, he said: "Even if there are two people," and so forth.
Regarding the term *vayhādikā*: here, *vayha* refers to a covering similar to a canopy on top, or a specific type of cart constructed by covering it entirely with cloth;
this they call a *vayha*. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), chariots and other such vehicles are included.
The commentary on the training rule concerning vehicles is finished.
75. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Defecation in Water.
"Miscellaneous" refers to the method of mixed treatment. "With conscious intent" means with a mind that recognizes the object and with a mind that recognizes the formal rule (*paṇṇatti*).
Because it is stated, "On account of disrespect," and because the offense is incurred precisely through the factor of disrespect, [it is so classified].
All this is exclusively unwholesome (*akusala*) and is inherently blameworthy (*vajja*); furthermore, intentional transgression results only in a state of mental distress (*domanassika*).

Therefore, it is said: "The unwholesome mind that is blameworthy according to the world (*lokavajja*) is associated with painful feeling (*dukkhavedanā*). The same method applies to the remaining cases as well.
The commentary on the training rules (*sikkhāpada*) connected with the teaching on the nineteen factors is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the Sekhiya rules in the *Līnatthappakāsanī*,
the *Vinayatthamañjūsā*, which is a commentary on the *Pātimokkha* for the resolution of doubts.

Commentary on the Settling of Legal Issues (*Adhikaraṇasamatha*). "Limitation by number" means limitation by count. They are called "legal issues" (*adhikaraṇa*) because legal matters are settled therein.
What are the matters settled? The methods of settling (*samatha*). How are they settled? By way of reconciliation (*samanava*). Therefore, they proceed by way of reconciling those [disputes].
He said: “They settle legal matters,” and so forth. “Of those that have arisen, of those that have arisen” means of those that have occurred, of those that have occurred.

Although a legal matter is of one kind in the sense of being a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*), nevertheless, because it varies according to its subject matter (*vatthu*), the plural form “of legal matters” (*adhikaraṇānaṃ*) was used.
Now, having shown that variety, he spoke the words beginning with “legal matter of dispute” (*vivādādhikaraṇaṃ*) in order to explain it. It is simply a dispute...
*Adhikaraṇa* means a legal issue (*vivādādhikaraṇa*). This same method applies to the others as well. *Samathatthaṃ* means for the purpose of settling.
*Sammukhāvinaya* is so called because it is a resolution in the presence of [the parties] regarding the legal issue.

*Sativinaya* is the resolution to be granted only to one who has attained fullness of mindfulness, such as the Elder Dabbamallaputta, and who is an *āsravakṣaya* (one whose taints are destroyed). [It is for one] who is confused, such as the monk Gagga...
The *vinaya* to be given to one who is insane is the *amūḷhavinaya*. *Paṭiññātakaraṇa* is the act performed by means of what has been admitted as the instrument.

Alternatively, *paṭiññātakaraṇa* is the action or performance regarding the state of having committed an offense and so forth that has been admitted; it is the verbal action proceeding by way of granting probation (*parivāsa*) and so on, [accompanied by the words] "you should exercise restraint in the future.
That procedure in which those who speak according to the Dhamma are in the majority—this is [the *yebhuyyasikā*].
*Yebhuyyasikā* means "by majority. *Tassapāpiyasikā* is so called because it is to be performed against a person who is worse due to the prevalence of evil;
this is a compound where the case endings are not elided (*aluttasamāsa*). It is called *tiṇavatthāraka* because it is similar to covering with grass.
For just as excrement or urine, when trodden upon, causes distress due to its foul odor, [but] by covering it with grass...

But its odor does not offend when it is well-covered; in the same way, a legal issue (*adhikaraṇa*) that, if pursued down to its very root and sub-root, would lead to harshness, ferocity, and schism—when settled by this procedure, being concealed by the "covering over with grass" (*tiṇavatthāraka*), becomes well-settled like excrement that has been covered over. Therefore it was said:
“It is called ‘covering over as with grass’ (tiṇavatthāraka) because it is similar to covering over with grass.
In that context, “among these seven methods for settling legal issues” means among those seven.

“By means of eighteen grounds” is a descriptive term, just like saying, “If there were those suffering from disease, this medicine should be given,” and so forth. Therefore, by one or another of those [grounds]...

"Quarreling" means quarreling on eighteen grounds; it is said that they are "quarreling. "Dispute" (*vivāda*) means a contrary argument. "Abuse" (*upavadanā*) means reviling. "Accusation" (*codanā*) means formal inquiry.
"Two" refers to the two offenses of a grave transgression (*thullaccaya*) and an ill-spoken offense (*dubbhāsita*).
"The performance of the four legal acts" (*kamma*) means the performance of any one of the four legal acts within the context of those four.

Having thus shown the legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), the words beginning with “therein” (*tattha*) are now spoken in order to show which of these legal issues is settled by how many means of settlement (*samatha*). The connection is: “or it is settled in that very monastery where it arose.
The same applies to the remaining cases. Therein, “where it arose in the monastery” means: “in the monastery where this bowl was [taken] from me...”
A legal issue arising from a dispute concerning the bowl, robes, and so forth occurs in the manner beginning with, "It has been taken; the robe has been taken.

Or, it is settled in that very place: in that same monastery, the resident monks assemble and settle it through a decision outside the canonical texts, having persuaded the proponents and opponents with the words, "Enough, friends."
But if the resident monks are unable to settle that legal issue, and another Vinaya-master arrives and asks, "Friends,
has the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā been held in this monastery? and when they have explained the matter to him,
he settles that legal issue by means of the Khandhaka, the Parivāra, and the Sutta.
It settles [the dispute]. In this way also, it should be understood that the *saṃmati* (consensus) occurs right here.
Or, for those going elsewhere to settle [the dispute], if the *saṃmati* occurs on the way—thinking, "We do not stand by his adjudication;
he is not skilled in the Vinaya; there dwell elders who are experts in the Vinaya in a certain village named so-and-so; there..."
Thinking, “Having gone, we shall decide,” as they were going, the matter was settled either by those who observed the reason on the way and made each other understand,
or by others making those monks reflect upon it. But if it was not settled through mutual understanding or by the reflection of like-minded monks, then one coming from the opposite direction...
A single master of the Vinaya, having seen them and asked, "Friends, where are you going?

and being told, "To such-and-such a village for such-and-such a reason," says, "Enough, friends; what is the use of going there? and settles that legal issue right then and there in accordance with the Dhamma and the Vinaya.
In this way, it is said that the matter is settled along the way.
"Wherever [the case] has been handed over to the Saṅgha, there it is settled by the Saṅgha. However, even if they are told, "Enough, friends, what is the use of going there?",

they disregard the words of the Vinaya-holder, saying, "We shall go right there and bring the legal matter to a decision," and wherever they go, they hand over the legal matter to a community of monks who are like-minded.
Once it has been submitted, the Saṅgha settles it right there while sitting in that very place, having decided: "Enough, friend; an assembly of the Saṅgha is indeed a serious matter.
