However, it may not be settled merely by the exhortation of like-minded bhikkhus;
rather, having convened the Saṅgha and informed them, the masters of the Vinaya settle it in the midst of the Saṅgha.
In this way, what has been adjudicated there by the Saṅgha is called "consent" (saṃmata).

Alternatively, it is adjudicated by individuals consented to by a committee (ubbāhikā), or by individuals consented to either by means of a formal motion (apalokana) or by a formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (ñattidutiyakamma)—whether these individuals have sat separately or within that very assembly—with the instruction: "Nothing else should be said by anyone else."
"Having announced it, it is decided. "This" refers to the fourfold presence (*sammukhatā*) as previously described.
"Of the performing Saṅgha" means of the performing Saṅgha that has assembled to settle the matter. "Presence by way of the concord of the Saṅgha" means:
"As many bhikkhus as are entitled to perform the formal act have arrived; the consent of those who are eligible to give their consent [has been obtained]."
"‘It has been brought forward, and those present do not protest’—this refers to the presence [of the Saṅgha] by way of the concord of the Saṅgha as thus stated.
By this, it is shown that the mere presence of individuals who have exerted themselves in whatever manner does not constitute what is called ‘presence before the Saṅgha.
‘Reality’ (bhūtatā) means truthfulness. For here, the word *dhamma* is a synonym for truth, as in such expressions as ‘one who speaks according to *dhamma*’ (*dhammavādī*) and so forth."
"Vinaya" (discipline) is so called because one is trained by means of it; it refers to the procedure taught by the Blessed One for the settling of various legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*).
"Face-to-face with that discipline" (*vinayasammukhatā*) means being in the presence of that discipline. Thus he said: "Just as that... [etc. ...is face-to-face with discipline.

"By whom" (*yena*) means by which person. "Of those who are adversaries regarding the matter" (*atthapaccatthikānaṃ*) means of those who are opponents concerning the matter consisting of the basis for dispute.
The presence of the Saṅgha is lost because the dispute is settled by persons who have been formally authorized.
"It" refers to the legal issue arising from a dispute (*vivādādhikaraṇa*). "Endowed with five factors" means:
"He does not act out of favoritism, he does not act out of ill will, he does not act out of delusion, he does not act out of fear, and he knows what has been accepted and what has not been accepted."
Endowed with the five aforementioned qualities. Regarding the three ways of drawing lots—secret, open, and whispering into the ear—as stated in the *Samathakkhandhaka*:
"I allow you, monks, for the sake of informing those monks, three ways of drawing lots:
the secret, the open, and the whispering into the ear. Having drawn the lot (*salākaṃ gāhetvā*).

Having had voting sticks (*salākā*) prepared for both those who speak according to the Dhamma and those who speak contrary to the Dhamma, having fixed them with a sign, and having had them cast as a portion of robes in the manner described in the *Samathakkhandhaka*, it is said there:
"And how, monks, is the casting of voting sticks done secretly? By that monk who is the distributor of the voting sticks..."
Having prepared voting sticks of various colors, each monk should be approached individually and told:
“This is the voting stick for one who speaks thus; this is the voting stick for one who speaks thus; take whichever you wish. Once it has been taken, he should be told: “Do not show it to anyone.
If he knows that those speaking contrary to the Dhamma are in the majority, he should say: “This is a bad choice.”
It should be postponed. If he knows, "Those who speak according to the Dhamma are in the majority," he should announce, "A good choice.
This, monks, is how the voting by ballot is conducted in secret.

"And how, monks, is the voting by ballot conducted openly? If he knows, 'Those who speak according to the Dhamma are in the majority,' it should be cast openly and without concealment. This, monks, is how the voting by ballot is conducted openly."
“And how, monks, is there a voting by means of whispering into the ear?
That monk who is conducting the voting must whisper into the ear of each individual monk: ‘This is the voting stick for one who speaks thus;
this is the voting stick for one who speaks thus; take whichever you wish. Once it has been taken, he should say: ‘Do not tell anyone. If…”
If he knows, “Those who speak contrary to the Dhamma are in the majority,” he should withdraw it, saying, “The selection was poorly made.

If he knows, “Those who speak in accordance with the Dhamma are in the majority,” he should announce, “The selection was well made. In this way, monks, the distribution of voting sticks is done by whispering into the ear.

Furthermore, in an assembly where shameless people predominate, the distribution of voting sticks should be done secretly; in an assembly where conscientious people predominate, it should be done openly.

It should be understood as "whispering into the ear of a fool. "By the majority of those who speak according to the Dhamma" means by even one person in excess [of those speaking contrary to the Dhamma];
what need is there to mention two or three?
The statement "it is settled by the four methods of settling" is said by way of including all [the methods], yet therein [it is done] by two.
In this way, the settling [of the dispute] is to be understood. "Thus it has been adjudicated" means: if there is no offense, both parties have asked for forgiveness;

if there is an offense, it has been adjudicated by means of confessing the offense and its formal entry. As for the remedy (*paṭikamma*), however, it will follow later in the section on the settlement of legal issues concerning offenses (*āpattādhikaraṇasamatha*).
"Unbecoming of a recluse" (*assamaṇaka*) means that which is not suitable for a recluse, that which should not be done by recluses; regarding that [matter].

When there is a transgression of improper conduct—whether it be an offense bordering on a *pārājika*, or a *dukkaṭa*, or a *thullaccaya*—for one who conceals it: for indeed, in the case of sexual intercourse, the offense bordering on a *pārājika* is a *dukkaṭa*;
whereas in the cases of taking what is not given and so forth, it is a *thullaccaya*. "Concealing" means hiding it. One whose root is severed...
"He will be one who has not committed a *pārājika* offense" means "he will be virtuous.
"Having conducted himself properly" means having fulfilled his duties. "He will receive reinstatement" means he will obtain the cessation of the formal legal procedure (*kamma*).

"Of that" refers to the legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*). There is no settlement by means of *sammukhā-vinaya* (settlement in the presence of the assembly) alone, because it cannot be settled without a confession or a corresponding acceptance [of the verdict]. The connection is with the word "confession" (*paṭiññā*).
"In this" means in the confession of an offense (*āpatti*). "May be" means necessarily. "For harshness and for ferocity" means for the state of being harsh and for the state of being ferocious.
"A grave offense" (*thullavajja*) refers to both a *pārājika* and a *saṅghādisesa*.
"Connected with householders" refers to an offense incurred in the disparagement, reviling, or lawful rejection of householders.
“According to what is appropriate” means according to the method stated as: “by two kinds of serenity, by three, by four, or by one.

“In this” refers to this section on serenity (*samatha*). “The method of exposition” means merely the method of exposition. Therefore he said, “But the detailed account,” and so forth. “Of it” refers to the detailed account.
“Stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*” means in that which is named the *Samantapāsādikā*.
This was stated in the *Vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*. Therefore, the intention is that it should be understood according to the method explained therein.
"Only this much" means this is the limit; there is nothing more than this.
The commentary on the settlement of legal issues (*adhikaraṇasamatha*) is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the Bhikkhu Pātimokkha within the *Vinayatthamañjūsā*,
the *Līnatthappakāsanī* commentary on the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī* exposition of the Pātimokkha.
Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Commentary on the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha: The Section on Defeat (Pārājika-khaṇḍa)
The connection is: "The Lord, for the benefit of the bhikkhunīs, proclaimed the Pātimokkha. In this context, "proclaimed" (pakāsayi) means he taught (desayi) or laid down (paññāpayi).
1. Commentary on the Training Rule on Sexual Intercourse: The Common Pārājika.
"Merely an expression" means merely words; the intention is that there is no actual meaning [behind them].

"Merely a difference in gender" means the mere distinction between the masculine gender and the feminine gender. "Difference" means diversity. "And by desire" means by affection, that is, by endearment.
"And by preference" means by wish. "By one who is corrupted" means by one who is defiled. "Full ordination."
For her, that full ordination is complete; the meaning is that she has been ordained by both Saṅghas.
The commentary on the training rule regarding sexual intercourse is finished.
The non-common *pārājika*.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Above the Knees "Above the armpits" means above the second great joint.
"Moving here and there" means moving horizontally here and there with either the hand or the body. "One who is lustful on one side" refers to the lust of the nun;
that is, when the nun is in a state of lust due to passion for bodily contact.
The meaning is "being present. Furthermore, the state of being lustful on one side should be understood by way of the nun alone.

For this is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*: "Regarding the phrase 'lustful on one side,' although it is stated there without distinction as 'on one side,' nevertheless, it should be understood that this classification of offenses is stated only when the nun herself is lustful.
"A man's body" means any part of a man's body. "Even when both are lustful" means when both the nun and...
And even though the man possesses a state of lust due to passion for physical contact.
"With the body" means with one's own body as it has been defined. "Connected with the body" means connected with the man's body.
"Or with the rest of the body" means with the remainder of the body from that which has been defined, namely, that which is reckoned as above the collarbone, below the kneecaps, and below the navel.
"By the body" is what is meant. "Of him" refers to the body of that lustful man—any part of his body whatsoever.
And just as there is a *thullaccaya* offense for her who touches him herself, so too should it be understood for her who consents to his touching her.
As for the phrase "the man has no lust for physical contact," this means he lacks lust for sexual intercourse, worldly affection, or a pure mind [toward her].

"Remaining" means remaining from the category of offenses involving defeat (*pārājika*). "By means of what is attached to the body" refers to the various distinctions such as "by means of what is attached to the body [touching] what is attached to the body";
this applies to all instances beginning with: "If she touches what is attached to the body by means of what is attached to the body, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
Regarding the phrases "unintentionally" and so forth: it includes one who touches having missed the mark, or one who is engaged in another task, or [one who thinks], "This is a man."
“Or if she does not know it is a woman,” or if, even when touched by him, she relishes that touch, there is no offense even if there is touching.
The commentary on the training rule regarding above the knees is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule regarding one who conceals an offense.
"Having committed an offense entailing defeat (pārājika)" means having committed one of the eight offenses—either one of the four shared with the bhikkhus or one of the four not shared.
It should be understood that although this pārājika was formulated later, the teachers who compiled the Canon placed it in this location by pairing it with the preceding rule. "Of the eight..."
Furthermore, because of the statement, "one of the pārājikas," it should be understood that even she who conceals another's concealment of a fault is herself one who conceals a fault.
Although the concealment of a fault occurs through affection, nevertheless, since the mind that transgresses the training rule is indeed a state of dejection, it is considered to be painful feeling.
“For in that case there is an offense of expiation... [as before]... the rest is exactly the same.
The commentary on the training rule concerning one who conceals an offense is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning one who sides with those who have been suspended.
“By the Teacher’s instruction” means by both the perfection of the motion (*ñatti*) and the perfection of the proclamation (*anussāvana*).

However, here it is said, “even here,” etc., because the Teacher’s instruction consists specifically of the motion and proclamation preceded by the formal charge (*codanā*) and the reminder (*sāraṇā*).

“The act” (*karaṇa*) refers to both the formal establishment of the motion and the words of the proclamation. “Disrespect” (*anādara*) is the absence of reverence toward both persons and the Dhamma. Therefore he said, “by which,” etc.
In that context, "in a group included [within the Saṅgha]" means either in that Saṅgha or in a group consisting of many individuals included therein.
By the phrase "not conducting himself with right conduct," the intended meaning has been stated. "In matters such as formal acts" refers to being of one formal act, one recitation, and one training.
"Together with the state of going" means together with the state of conducting oneself. "Common dwelling" (samāna-saṃvāsa) means having a shared life.
These are those who share the same communion.
Now, that communion by which they are said to be "those who share the same communion" does not exist for that suspended monk with them;
and as for those with whom he no longer shares that communion, he is not [in communion] with those bhikkhus.
"Friends have been made for oneself; therefore, he is called 'one who has not made friends'"—it is with the purpose of showing this meaning that the passage beginning with "yassa pana...
was spoken. Having thus provided a word-by-word commentary, [the author] now states "the meaning is:

one who has not entered into the state of being a fellow-resident (samānasaṃvāsaka)" in order to show the mere substance of the matter. Since someone might suspect what that "conformity" (anuvattana) is, [the author] explains it by its essential nature:
Showing this, he said: "Whatever view he holds," and so forth. Therein, "he" refers to that one who has been suspended (*ukkhitaka*).
The commentary on the training rule concerning those who follow one who has been suspended is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Eight Grounds (*aṭṭhavatthuka*).
“By way of intimacy with friends consisting of worldly pleasure” means by way of intimacy with friends characterized as worldly pleasure.

What is that? He says: “by passion for physical contact. It is those who are moistened specifically by passion for physical contact who are called “lustful” here, not those [moistened] by passion for sexual intercourse.
How is this to be understood? He says: “For this very [passage],” and so forth. But what is the reason for this?
He said: "But an investigation has been made regarding this in the *Samantapāsādikā*. Therein, this is the investigation:

And here, "what is not the true Dhamma" (*asaddhamma*) should be understood as physical contact alone, not sexual intercourse. For there is no grave offense (*thullaccaya*) for that which is merely adjacent to sexual intercourse.
Furthermore, the statement, "a wise person capable of engaging in physical contact," is also a supporting proof in this context.
"Whatever has been done by whomsoever belongs to him alone. To show that "of the person" (*purisapuggalassa*) is a genitive case, it was said:
"whatever [was done] by the person," and so forth. Therein, "hand" (*hattha*) means one's own hand.

Furthermore, the mention of the "hand" here does not refer only to what was defined as "the hand is from the elbow (*kappara*) up to the fingertips"; rather, it is the inclusion of the hand itself [as defined there]. Now...
By taking both this [act] and other non-Pārājika grounds together as one, it is called "taking by the hand.

Likewise, regarding "taking by the corner of the outer robe" (saṅghāṭikaṇṇaggahaṇa), it is shown that this refers not only to taking the corner of the outer robe, but rather to taking any part of the robe whatsoever; thus, it says: "In this regard..."
And it is said, beginning with, “of whatever [person],” etc. “A place of such-and-such a name” means a place having such a name.
“Having filled [it] either in regular order or in reverse order”—this is merely an illustration.
Therefore, the meaning is: having filled it by whatever method—whether in regular order, in reverse order, or skipping every other one.

“Those offenses” means those offenses committed. Just as in the case of each individual matter, so too, even when one has transgressed seven separate matters a hundred times, one is freed by confessing those offenses.
“Subject to counting” means it comes under the count of what has been confessed.
“Having laid down the burden” means having set aside the effort [thinking], “I shall commit another matter.”
The commentary on the training rules consisting of eight bases is finished.
Thus ends the *Līnatthappakāsanī*, the commentary on the *Vinayatthamañjūsā*,
which is itself a commentary on the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Pātimokkhavaṇṇanā*.
The commentary on the Pārājika rules in the Bhikkhunīpātimokkha is concluded.
Chapter on Saṅghādisesa:
1. Commentary on the training rule concerning those who engage in frivolous litigation.
“By way of human [afflictions] and by way of anger and resentment” is stated according to the method of predominance.

For this very reason he will say: “three consciousnesses, three feelings. “For the purpose of a legal proceeding (*aḍḍakaraṇatthāya*): here, ‘legal proceeding’ (*aḍḍa*) refers to judicial adjudication.
That which renunciants also call ‘a formal issue’ (*adhikaraṇa*); for the purpose of that, meaning for the purpose of judicial adjudication—this is what is meant.”
"At the very moment of transgression" means at the very moment of misconduct regarding the object; the intention is that it does not refer to the third formal admonition.
"He expels the nun from the Saṅgha" means he expels the nun who has committed the offense from the community of nuns.
This use of the agentive case for the cause is made by treating the phenomenon that serves as the cause for expulsion as the "one to be expelled."
"Where she stands" means: in whatever place she stands, such as her residence, the path for alms-round, and so forth.
"Going from there" means: going from that point toward the presence of the judges. "A second time" means: at the second announcement. "By him" means:
by the lay follower (*upāsaka*). "Thus addressed" means: being told, "You yourself must announce the matter between me and you."
"Has it announced by another" means he has it announced by a *kappiyakāraka* (one who makes things allowable). "Whether in this way or that way while it is being announced" means:
either the *kappiyakāraka* should announce the nun's request first, or the other [the donor] should announce his own;
or the *kappiyakāraka* should announce the requests of both, or the other should announce the requests of both—it is thus "while it is being announced in whatever manner."
"But having heard the words of both" means: having heard the statements of both, however they may have been reported.
"She goes while being dragged" means she goes into the presence of the judges while being addressed; this is to be connected with the phrase, "for him there is no offense.
The same applies to the remaining cases. "She asks for protection" means she asks for lawful protection. Now...
To show how protection requested becomes righteous, it is said: "She points out misconduct committed by others in the dwelling without specifying [the individuals].
In this regard, there is pointing out with specification concerning the past, and there is pointing out without specification;
likewise, there is pointing out with specification concerning the future, and there is pointing out without specification.
How is there a specific declaration concerning the past?
Suppose, in a bhikkhunī’s dwelling, village boys, rogues, or anyone else commits misconduct, cuts down a tree, takes away fruits and flowers, or seizes requisites.
Then a bhikkhunī approaches a judge and says, "This and that was done in our dwelling."
She speaks. When asked, "By whom?", she specifies, "By so-and-so and by so-and-so. Such specific reporting concerning the past is not permitted.
If, having heard this, those judges impose a penalty on them, the entire liability falls upon the nun.
Even if her intention is merely, "They will take the penalty," the liability still falls upon her alone. If...
However, if he says to him, "Take the staff," it is a *pārājika* offense once [the value] of five māsakas has been taken.
When they ask, "By whom?", he should say, "It is not permissible for us to say 'by such-and-such a person'; you yourselves shall know that.
We merely request protection; grant us that, and have the stolen goods brought back as well. Thus should he speak.
Thus, there is an indiscriminate proclamation, and that is permissible.
When this has been said, even if those judges seek out the perpetrators and inflict punishment upon them, and all their property is confiscated, the nun incurs neither debt nor offense.
Furthermore, it is not permissible to say "Thief! Thief! out of a desire to cause harm to those seen stealing requisites.
Even when this has been said, whatever punishment they impose upon them, it all becomes the responsibility of the nun.
However, it is permissible for her to say to one who obeys her instructions: "He took these requisites from me; have him bring them back, and do not inflict punishment on him.
If they engage in gambling for the sake of slaves, slave-girls, goats, and so forth, this is called "unlawful gambling" (*akappiya-aḍḍa*), and it is not permitted.

How is there a specific declaration concerning the future? In the same manner already described, when others have committed misconduct and so forth, a bhikkhunī says to the judges: "They are doing this and that in our dwelling;
grant us protection so that they may not do it again in the future. When asked, "By whom was this done? she replies, "By such-and-such a person and by such-and-such a person."
He declares it. Thus, there is a specific declaration concerning the future; that too is not permitted.
For when punishment is imposed upon them, the entire liability falls on the nun, according to the same method as before. The rest is exactly as before.
However, if the judges, regarding those committing such misconduct in the nuns' quarters, [declare]: "Such-and-such a penalty..."
"Let us do so," they say, and having caused the drum to be beaten, they seek out those who do not comply with the command and inflict punishment upon them;
for the nun, there is neither guilt nor offense.
This same principle applies to monks as well as to the rule stated for nuns; for even in the case of a nun, it is a specific designation [of the person].

It is not permissible; whatever punishment they inflict when it has been thus reported becomes his liability. If he causes them to take the punishment in the manner already described, it is a *pārājika* offense.
However, if he speaks indiscriminately even while knowing that "they will inflict a punishment," and they seek out those [offenders] and indeed inflict the punishment, there is no fault.
[This applies also to] those who cut down trees and so forth within the monastery boundary (*vihāra-sīmā*).
It is not permissible to take axes, hatchets, and so forth, and grind them on stones.
If the edge becomes blunted, it should be made sharp again and given back. One must also not run after them and seize their requisites;
for the mind is quick to change, and once the intention to steal has arisen, one might even go to one's ruin.
The commentary on the training rule concerning those who engage in litigation is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning those who cause thieves to rise up:
Regarding the phrases "Mallagaṇa, Bhaṭiputtagaṇa, and so forth," the *mallagaṇa* (wrestling guild) refers to those who subsist on the food provided by the Nārāyaṇa [festival] here and there.
A "group" (*gaṇa*) refers to a group of people who perform meritorious deeds such as establishing water-stations or digging ponds.

A "Bhaṭiputta-group" is a group of those who provide food for youths. A "Dhamma-group" is a group devoted to the Dispensation (*sāsana*) that performs various kinds of meritorious deeds. A "perfumer’s guild" (*gandhika-seṇī*) is a group that manufactures various kinds of fragrant preparations.
A "cloth-dealer’s guild" (*dussika-seṇī*) is a collective of cloth merchants; the meaning is a group of weavers.

"Ordaining" means conferring full admission (*upasampadā*). When the bhikkhunīs have departed on some business, if she ordains her own group of dependents within a partial boundary (*khaṇḍasīma*) at the very place where they were sitting, without having gone [to the formal boundary], it originates from speech, mind, and body;
but if she goes to another boundary or to a river and ordains them there, it originates from body, speech, and mind.

"It originates" means it is said: "the origination of the offense for ordaining a thief. In terms of whether it is an action or a non-action, it is a non-action with respect to the act of ordaining without having asked for permission.

Alternatively, there are three types of consciousness: because even Noble Ones who do not know the formal rule might ordain [a person], or because at the moment of the offense—at the conclusion of the formal ritual (kammavācā)—one possesses a resultant indeterminate state of mind.
The commentary on the training rule concerning one who ordains a thief is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Going to Another Village.

"Another village" means *gāmantara*. "The further bank of a river" means the opposite shore of a river. Because it is stated, "one should go to another village," the offense occurs only in another village and not in one's own village;
thus he says, "from one's own village, for instance," and so forth. Or, [it refers to] within the boundary.
"Or when he has passed beyond the vicinity" means: when he has passed beyond the enclosure of an enclosed village, or the place suitable for the enclosure of an unenclosed village.
"By the second, as soon as it has passed" means: as soon as the second foot has passed beyond the enclosure or the vicinity of the other village.
However, in those manuscripts where [it says] "with one foot... [the reading continues:]... "by the second foot."

In the text, the reading is found: "When the other village’s boundary has been crossed, or its precinct has been entered, there is a thullaccaya; as soon as the second [village] has been crossed, or [its precinct] has been entered, there is a saṅghādisesa.
In this regard, these two phrases, "when [the precinct] has been entered" and "as soon as it has been entered," contradict the Pāḷi: "for one who is crossing the precinct of an unenclosed village."
For this contradicts the Pāḷi. It likewise contradicts the *Samantapāsādikā*. For therein it says:
“If one crosses the area requiring a boundary with one foot, it is a thullaccaya; as soon as one has crossed with the second foot, it is a saṅghādisesa.
Furthermore, in this context, from one’s own village... [etc. ...if one crosses with one foot the boundary of another village...”
It is stated: "When she has merely crossed the precincts, there is a thullaccaya; when she has merely crossed [the second boundary] with the second step, it is a saṅghādisesa.
Because of the statement beginning with "for her who crosses the first foot," only walking on foot is intended here;
thus he says, "there is an offense for her entering on foot. By this, even if she enters by means of the back of an elephant or by psychic power (iddhi), [the rule applies].
"It is indeed permissible" is what he shows. This is the summary here; the intention is that the detailed explanation is stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*.

Regarding "a river with the characteristics described for crossing to the other side": "A river is so called where, when one crosses anywhere while covering the three circles [of the body], the inner robe becomes wet"—this refers to the characteristics stated in the *Nadīpāragamana-vibhaṅga*.
"Of a river": For here, the analysis of crossing to the further shore of a river is expressed by the term "crossing to the further shore of a river.
Again, regarding the phrase "or for one returning to this very bank," it is said because she has descended [into the water] with the desire to go to the further shore.
However, as for the other [type of nun], she remains at the place from which she set out; therefore, there is no offense for her while going to the further shore. If [she is reciting] a lesson...
If, while performing meditation or some other task, she makes the mental resolve, "I will go to the companion before dawn," and the dawn breaks while she is still unaware of it, there is no offense;

thus he said, "before dawn," and so forth. Alternatively, if she thinks, "I will remain right here until the rising of the dawn," or if she remains in a part of the monastery without such a resolve, [there is likewise no offense].
She remains [there], but does not come within arm’s reach (*hatthapāsa*) of her companion; at the rising of the dawn, it is a *saṅghādisesa*.
For here, the arm’s reach itself is the measure. Even a single room does not protect one from exceeding the arm’s reach. Therefore he said: "In a single room... there is an offense.
Regarding the phrase "either the range of sight (*dassanūpacāra*) or the range of hearing (*savanūpacāra*)," here the "range of sight" means where the companion stands—

She sees. "The vicinity of hearing" means that standing where she hears the sound of one calling out "Ayye!"—just as one would hear the sound of those lost on a path or the sound announcing a Dhamma discourse. Therefore, because "falling behind" means the relinquishing of either the vicinity of seeing or the vicinity of hearing, it is said:
"starting from the crossing of the threshold. Regarding falling behind within the village, however, it is permitted; hence he says: "starting from the crossing of the threshold."
“Beginning with... Therein, “having passed beyond the threshold post” means having passed beyond the threshold. “Outside the village” means in the area outside the village.
He said, “as if by the sound of those lost on the road,” because they were making a loud noise while lost on the road.

Some also say it means “as if by the sound of one calling out to someone who is lost on the road. “She makes a sound” means she utters a cry. “There is an offense even upon the passing of the hearing of the sound.”
This shows that when such a range for hearing has been abandoned, the range for seeing is not protected; at the very moment it is abandoned, there is an offense of *saṅghādisesa*.
"Going along the road" means going along the same road. If those in front go by another road, they have departed.

[In these cases] they are merely names; there is no offense at all. When two women are walking together, if one is unable to keep up and the other thinks, "Let her go," and she falls behind, while the first woman also goes on thinking, "Let her stay behind," there is an offense for both.
However, if among those walking, the one in front takes another path and the one behind also takes another, and each stays at the place where the other has departed, there is no offense for either.
The question, “There are four *saṅghādisesas*,” was stated with reference to a bhikkhunī who, at the rising of the dawn, has entered the opposite bank of a river included within another village.
For she, having departed from her own village at the time of dawn, has merely entered the aforementioned opposite bank of the river at the moment of sunrise;
thus, she possesses the characteristics of both staying apart during the night and departing from the group while traveling across the river to another village.
One incurs four *saṅghādisesa* offenses simultaneously.
"By one who has gone over to another faction" means by one who has gone over to a heretical sect (*titthāyatana*). "Without an obstacle" means without an obstacle such as the rescuing of an elephant.
The commentary on the training rule concerning going between one village and another is finished.

4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Rehabilitation of One Who Has Been Suspended (Ukkhittaka-osāraṇa-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā) "Of that very same performing Saṅgha" means: of that very same group which is the performer of the formal act of suspension (ukkhepanīya-kamma). "Or conducting himself in the proper conduct" means: conducting himself in the forty-threefold conduct leading to release (netthāra-vatta).
The commentary on the training rule concerning the rehabilitation of one who has been suspended is finished.
5. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning the Acceptance of Food *Ekato-avassute*:
When either the person (the donor) or the bhikkhunī is lustful (*avassuta*). However, in the *Mahāpaccarī*, it is stated here:
"It should be understood as the lustfulness of the bhikkhunī. This refers to the phrase: "Knowing [her] to be lustless (*anavassutā*), she accepts [the food]. ...by this [phrase].

This does not agree with the Pāḷi. For if the lustful state of the person were not authoritative, why would there be this statement, "knowing [her] to be free from lust," when it would have been sufficient simply to say, "there is no offense if both are free from lust" or "if she receives [it] while being free from lust"?
"Both being free from lust" means both the person and the bhikkhunī.
There is no offense in any case for one who receives [the gift] from those who are not lustful.
Or, "knowing him to be not lustful," means that while she herself is not lustful, she accepts it from his hand with the perception that "this man is not lustful," even though he is actually lustful.
Furthermore, even if she herself is not lustful, if she accepts it after knowing another person—whether he be lustful or not lustful—to be "lustful."
It is indeed an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa). For this was said in the immediately preceding training rule: “‘Why, noble lady, do you not accept it?
‘Because I am lustful, noble sir. ‘But you, noble lady, are lustful? ‘I am not, noble sir.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning the acceptance of food is finished.
6. Commentary on the Second Training Rule Concerning the Acceptance of Food:

Offenses beginning with *dukkaṭa* and ending with *saṅghādisesa* are instigated by this very training rule; however, the classification of offenses for the other [nun] is according to the first training rule. Thus he says, "By such instigation," and so forth.
"Out of compassion for families" means out of a sense of pity for families.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning the acceptance of food is concluded.
7–13. Commentary on the training rules concerning matchmaking and so forth:
The seventh and subsequent rules have their meanings already explained.
The commentary on the training rules concerning matchmaking and so forth is concluded.
14–17. Commentary on the training rules concerning schism in the Saṅgha and so forth:
A nun does not cause a schism in the Saṅgha; this constitutes a formal act (*kamma*) and a recitation (*uddesa*), and thus there is a twofold division, which [occurs] together with her.

By saying "it does not exist," the nun does not cause a schism in the Saṅgha. He says "even on account of concealing" and so forth to show that it is not only the absence of *parivāsa* [probation] that is meant.

In this context, the reading should be understood as "even on account of concealing, she does not incur an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*)," meaning that even due to concealment, she does not incur a *dukkaṭa*. And having done so—
“One incurs a grave offense with remainder;
she conceals it out of disrespect;
there is no nun, yet she would not incur the fault.”
“This question has been considered by those who are skilled.”—In this context, the prohibition against nuns is established.

However, in those manuscripts where the reading “one incurs a *dukkaṭa* offense on account of concealing,” appearing without the negative particle (*na*), is seen, that should be regarded as a scribal error. Therefore, because...

There is no such thing as *parivāsa* (probation); therefore [it is said]. "Having cleared one's own boundary" (*attano sīmaṃ sodhetvā*) refers specifically to the boundary fixed within the monastery (*vihāra*), as stated in the phrase "or in the monastery boundary. "By those unable to clear it" means by those unable to clear the monastery boundary.
"A mere indication of the opening" (*mukhamattanidassanaṃ*) is an indication of the mere means for entry. Here it is asked: then why, as in the discussion on the *mānatta* penance for a monk...
It was stated: "Beyond two clods' throws from the enclosure of an enclosed monastery, or beyond the place suitable for an enclosure from an unenclosed monastery.
Why is it not stated thus, but instead stated here as: "Having passed beyond two clods' throws from the vicinity of a village and from the vicinity of the monks' monastery"?
Regarding this, some say: "The [vicinity] of the monks is of the aforementioned kind..."
"Having passed beyond the precincts [of the monastery], it is permissible to perform that act even in a village; however, for bhikkhunīs, it is not permissible in a village.
Therefore, it was said thus. Others, however, say: "It is not permissible for bhikkhus either in a village;
for what is called a 'bhikkhu-vihāra' stands already beyond the village precincts (*gāmūpacāra*). Therefore, instead of saying 'village,' one should speak only of the 'vihāra precincts.'"
This has been stated below. However, for bhikkhunīs, the monastery (vihāra) is only within the village and not outside;
therefore, both the village precinct (gāmūpacāra) and the monastery precinct (vihārūpacāra) are shown here. Consequently, there is no difference in meaning between the two.
Having investigated this, one should accept whatever is appropriate therein.
"From that time onwards" means from the moment it was announced.
The commentary on the training rules concerning schism in the Saṅgha and so forth is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the Pātimokkha within the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*.
In the *Vinayatthamañjūsā*, within the *Līnatthappakāsanī*,
the commentary on the *Saṅghādisesa* rules of the *Bhikkhunīpātimokkha* is completed.
The Chapter on Forfeiture (*Nissaggiyakaṇḍa*).
1. The Chapter on Alms Bowls (Patta-vagga).
1. Explanation of the Training Rule on the Accumulation of Alms Bowls (Patta-sannicaya-sikkhāpada).
The first [rule] has its meaning already explained.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the accumulation of cloth is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule concerning out-of-season robes:
"Whatever one has received for oneself becomes subject to relinquishment" means that whatever robe was received by the one who had it distributed becomes [subject to relinquishment] for herself.
That very thing becomes forfeited; even after that disciplinary act (*vinayakamma*) has been performed, it is not obtained by oneself. Therefore he said, "having relinquished," and so forth.
In that context, "even having received what was relinquished" means even having received what was relinquished [with the words], "Venerable lady, I give this to you.

"It should be brought back exactly as it was given" means it should be brought back in the same manner as it was given by the donors, specifically within the category of out-of-season robes (*akālacīvara*).
"It should be set aside" is what is meant.
The commentary on the training rule concerning out-of-season robes is finished.
3. Commentary on the training rule concerning the exchange of robes.
"I understand this thus. Because it was taken with one's own perception, both a *pācittiya* and a *dukkaṭa* offense are stated; otherwise, one would be liable for the value of the goods.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the exchange of robes is finished.
4. Commentary on the training rule concerning requesting something else.
"By obtaining another" means by obtaining something else that is even less than the first request.
"If that is not obtained, again that very same thing" means: because it was only a small amount, if that is not obtained, she requests that very same thing again;
this is the meaning. "Even if there is need for something else" means even if there is need for something other than the first requested item.
"Atthe sati" means: "together with that, another as well. That is to say, together with what was first requested, another as well.
What is meant? If ghee was first requested, and because the physician said, "The twin [brothers] must be treated," there is also a need for oil;
then she requests another by saying, "I also have need for oil," and so forth.

It has been said. "Having shown the advantage" means: having shown the advantage by saying, "If ghee has been brought for one kahāpaṇa, twice as much oil can be obtained for this same price; and since this task can also be accomplished with oil, therefore bring oil."
The commentary on the training rule concerning causing another to communicate something else is finished. 5.

Commentary on the training rule concerning causing another to exchange goods for something else: "Then one should cause another to exchange for something else" means that one should cause whatever is other than what was first exchanged to be exchanged.
The commentary on the training rule concerning exchanging for other goods is finished.
6. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning Exchanging for the Sangha’s Property:

"Given for the sake of another" means: that which one exchanges for has been given for the sake of someone other than oneself. "Designated for another" is a further clarification of the meaning of the former term.
"Bringing back the remainder" means: having exchanged that for which it was given, she brings back the surplus for the sake of something else.
"Having informed the owners" means: having asked permission from the donors. "Bringing back in such emergencies" means:
in such calamities, bringing back for the sake of anyone else whatsoever.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning the exchange of goods belonging to the Saṅgha is finished.
7. Commentary on the second training rule concerning the exchange of goods belonging to the Saṅgha:
He said, "even by one's own request," because it is not only by means of that very requisite [that the offense occurs]; for this has been stated in the Pāḷi:
“The bhikkhunīs, having themselves requested that requisite and having had medicine purchased with it, consumed it.
However, because the sense is already implied in the *mātikā*, the word *pi* (also/too) is not employed. For there is freedom regarding the use of a word whose meaning is already understood;
such is the rule.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning exchanging with the Saṅgha is concluded.
8–9–10. Commentary on the first three training rules concerning exchanging with a group, etc.:
the eighth, ninth, and tenth are of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning payment for courtesans, etc., is finished. The first section, the Section on Alms Bowls (Pattavagga), is concluded.
2. The Section on Robes (Cīvaravagga).
11. Explanation of the Training Rule on Receiving Heavy Outer Cloaks (Garupāvuraṇasikkhāpada).

Since a formal request is not prohibited in a place where one has been invited [to accept], the Blessed One, by way of an invitation to the Dhamma, stated regarding a place where one has been invited:
"Say, ladies, what you need," and thus prescribed that one may request [a gift] up to the maximum of four karṣas.
It should be understood that this indicates the delimitation [of the rule]. For this very reason it is said: "Regarding 'it may be bartered for':
except for those who follow the same Dhamma, relatives, and those invited by one's own kin, it should be requested from anyone else who is satisfied with some quality or other, having been told:
'Please tell me, noble lady, what you require. "The King" refers to King Pasenadi of Kosala.
The commentary on the training rule concerning heavy upper garments is finished.
12. Commentary on the training rule concerning light upper garments:
the second [rule] has its meaning already explained.
The commentary on the training rule concerning light outer robes is finished.
This concludes the second section,
the Chapter on Robes, within the Commentary on the Pātimokkha for the Dispelling of Doubts.
In the *Vinayatthamañjūsā*, within the *Līnatthappakāsanī*,
the commentary on the *Nissaggiya* rules of the *Bhikkhunīpātimokkha* is completed.
Now begins the section on the *Pācittiya* offenses.
1. The Chapter on Garlic (Lasuṇavagga) 1.

Commentary on the Training Rule on Garlic (Lasuṇasikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā) Although "garlic" is stated without qualification, nevertheless, it is specifically garlic grown in Magadha that is intended here; moreover, it is bulbous garlic (*bhaṇḍika-lasuṇa*) that is meant. Thus he said: "grown in the kingdom of Magadha," and so forth.
"Bhaṇḍika-garlic" refers specifically to garlic in pods; this is a designation for garlic that has its seeds fully developed.
Therefore he said, "not one, two, or three seeds. Regarding the phrase "with each mouthful":
if she chews two or three pods together as one and swallows them, there is one *pācittiya*. However, for her who eats them by breaking them apart and consuming each seed individually...
There are offenses of expiation according to the number of applications.
The distinction between onions and the others should be understood either by their color or by their core. First, by color: an onion (*palaṇḍuka*) is pale yellow;
a leek (*bhañjanaka*) is red; a green onion (*haritaka*) has the color of green leaves. By the core...
However, the onion (*palaṇḍuka*) has one core, the *bhañjanaka* has two, and the green garlic (*haritaka*) has three.
The *cāpalasuṇa* has no core; it consists of nothing more than its sprouts. In the *Mahāpaccarī* and other texts, however, it is stated:
"The onion has three cores, the *bhañjanaka* has two, and the green garlic has one. These onions and so forth [are forbidden] by their very nature.
These are permitted. However, in the case of soups, condiments, and the like, even that produced in Māgadha is permitted.

For when it is added to any place whatsoever—be it to bean soups and the like being cooked, or to preparations of fish or meat, or to oil, or to jujube pickles (*badara-sālava*) and the like, or to sour vegetables and the like, or to the *uttaribhaṅga* refreshments, or even to a meal of rice-gruel—it is permitted. "Jujube pickle" (*badara-sālava*) refers to jujube fruits.
The preparation of solid food to be made by drying and grinding [garlic] is finished.
The commentary on the training rule regarding garlic is concluded.
2. Commentary on the training rule regarding pubic hair.

Regarding the phrase “in a concealed place,” it is stated that this is said for the purpose of showing its classification: “the meaning is ‘in the armpits and in the urinary organ. Regarding “on account of illness”:

there is no offense for one who causes [it] to be removed on account of an illness such as sores, scabies, and so forth. “In this case, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for both the monk and regarding the garlic,” say the ancients.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the hair of the private parts is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Striking with the Palm.

Regarding the term *talaghātaka*: it refers to striking on the head. Furthermore, because that [act] is described in the word-commentary (*padabhājaniya*) as "striking on the organ," it is understood to mean "of the urinary organ";
thus he says, "in striking the palm against the urinary organ. It is according to the same method as before.
"Sāṇattika" means that for one who commands another for her own sake, it is "with a command.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the slapping of palms is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Use of Wax.

"This was stated by way of the object": the phrase "in a dildo" (*jatumaṭṭhaka*) was stated precisely by way of the object that arose on account of the introductory narrative (*nidāna*). However, for anyone who inserts any kind of shaft whatsoever, there is indeed an offense. Therefore he said, "But by way of sensual lust," and so forth.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the dildo is finished.
5. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Purification by Water.
"Should be inserted" means it should be introduced. "The tip-joint" refers to even a hair’s breadth of the tip-joint.
"She inserts the third joint" means she inserts even a hair’s breadth of the third joint. For this has been stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*:
"For one who inserts [the penis] even a hair’s breadth beyond two joints in depth, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*)."

"Atigambhīraṃ udakasuddhikaṃ ādiyanavatthusmin" means in the case of taking up water-washing that is too deep; that is, in the case of performing a water-wash by inserting [the hand] too far. However, there is no offense if, for the purpose of water-purification, one takes hold of the contact within the aforementioned limits.
The commentary on the training rule concerning water-purification is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Attending Upon.

"Or with anything among sour gruel, etc. means with anything among sour gruel, curd, whey, milk, and so forth. "With any fan whatsoever" means with any fan whatsoever, even including the hem of a robe.
"Drink this" means drink this water or the soup and so forth. "Fan with this" means fan with this palm-leaf fan. "Causing [someone] to give" means causing both to be given by another.
The commentary on the training rule concerning attending is finished.
7. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Raw Grain (Āmakadhañña-sikkhāpada):
"Therefore" means because both the solicitation and the food itself constitute the measure [of the offense].

Furthermore, in this case, it is not only at the moment of receiving that there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa); rather, after having received it, there is also an offense when bringing it from the forest, when drying it, or on a rainy day when preparing it for roasting.
Whether it be preparing the hearth, preparing the potsherds, preparing the ladle, gathering wood to make a fire, putting grain into the potsherd,
stirring with the ladle, preparing the mortar, pestle, and so forth for the purpose of pounding, or the acts of pounding, winnowing, washing, and so on—
up until the point of placing it in the mouth and chewing it with the teeth— he [does not do so].

Therefore, it was said that there are offenses of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) in all preliminary applications: "From the moment of receiving [the food] until the chewing with the teeth, there are offenses of wrong-doing in the preceding applications.
The commentary on the training rule concerning raw grain is finished.

8. Commentary on the First Training Rule Concerning the Disposal of Excrement “Beyond the wall” (*tirokuṭṭe*) means on the far side of the house wall. “Beyond the enclosure wall” (*tiropākāre*) means on the far side of the surrounding enclosure wall.
Furthermore, since those walls and enclosures are of three kinds—namely, made of brick, stone, or wood—it is said: “of any kind of wall whatsoever.”
“...or beyond the enclosure wall. Regarding the phrase “discarding all these together”: this refers to one who discards even these four items together.
However, for one who discards them individually, there are offenses according to the number of items. The same principle applies to giving instructions as well.
“An offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa) for a bhikkhu” means that for a bhikkhu, it is an offense of wrong-doing in every case.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning the disposal of excrement is finished.
9. Commentary on the second training rule concerning the disposal of excrement:
By the word "also" (*pi*) in the phrase "for a nun also," the monk is included. However, [this does not apply] in fields where seeds have not yet been sown, such as in the corners and so forth.
Or it is permissible to discard [the seeds] in uncultivated fields, or in places such as field boundaries where they have not yet been planted.
It is likewise permissible even in places where people discard their refuse. Regarding "an abandoned field": when people have harvested the grain and departed, it is called an abandoned field;
it is permissible there. However, in a place where one thinks, "Even if the early rice and so forth have been reaped, it will grow again," [it is not permissible].
They guard it there exactly as it was. Regarding the phrase "having informed the owner": here, the owners are the field-watchers and the guardians of the monastery and so forth.
By this, it is permissible for a monk to discard [things] belonging to the Saṅgha because they are included within the Saṅgha's property;
however, it is not [permissible] for nuns. But for nuns, it is permissible regarding their own property and regarding the property of monks in the manner already stated.
It shows that even though this is so, it must be done according to what is appropriate.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning the disposal of excrement is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning dancing and singing.
Whether actors and the like dance, or those intoxicated with drink—even down to peacocks, quails, monkeys, and so forth—all this is indeed dancing.
Therefore he said: "They dance, even including the dancing of peacocks. As for singing:
whether it be the singing of actors and the like, or the well-sung song accompanied by praise for the qualities of the Triple Gem at the time of the Noble Ones' Parinibbāna—even down to...
Thinking, “We shall sing even with our teeth,” they do so in the preliminary stage by making grunting sounds;
all of this is indeed singing. Therefore he said: “Singing means, at the very least, even the singing of a Dhamma-preacher.

In that context, “singing of a Dhamma-preacher” refers to the recitation of the Dhamma by unrestrained monks who break the proper rules of conduct, prolonging it excessively and using a singing tone; that too is not permissible for a monk.
It is not allowable for bhikkhunīs. For thus it is said in the *Paramatthajotikā*, the commentary on the Khuddaka Nikāya:
"Song associated with the Dhamma is allowable, but Dhamma associated with song is not allowable.

Therefore, when reciting the Dhamma—such as the Jātakas and the Vattas—one should not neglect those respective observances, but rather recite the words and phrases with a rounded intonation according to the fourfold rhythmic pattern (*caturassa-vatta*).

These things must be shown. Regarding "instrumental music" (*vādita*): whether it be instrumental music produced by musical instruments such as stringed ones, or instrumental music from a small drum (*kuṭabheri*), or even instrumental music from a water-drum (*udakabheri*), all of this is indeed instrumental music.
Therefore he said: "Instrumental music means, at the very least, instrumental music from a water-drum.
Furthermore, if one spits, or stands in a place of danger and snaps one's fingers, [it constitutes an offense].
Or if she strikes him with her hand, there is no offense. And here, by the method of "single remainder from a group of dissimilar things" (*virūpekasesanaya*), hearing is also included within seeing.
Alternatively, because the five types of consciousness have the nature of looking toward [their objects], even the act of hearing possesses the designation of "seeing";
thus it is said, "for the purpose of seeing. Therefore he says: "If she goes for the purpose of seeing any one of these. Where...
"Standing" means having gone to whatever place one stands.
Now, one might ask: "Is it not true that an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for self-dancing and so forth is not mentioned in the Canon (Pāḷi)? How, then, should it be understood? To this he says:
"It is stated in all the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā). By this, it is shown that even though it is not mentioned in the Canon, it should be accepted on the authority of the Commentaries.

[The text] shows this. As for the statement that the origins (*samuṭṭhāna*) and so forth are similar to those of the *eḷakaloma* [offense], it was said by way of the *pācittiya* included in the matrix (*mātikā*);
however, by way of all [the relevant rules], they should be understood as having six origins.

"Standing in the monastery" is merely an illustration, because an offense is not intended for one who sees while engaged in the other modes of conduct (*iriyāpatha*). For otherwise, even if she were sitting...
She would not be permitted to see [the monk]. For one who goes from one monastery to another thinking, "I will see him," it is indeed an offense.
If she sees him while sitting in the assembly hall, there is no offense; but for one who rises and goes [elsewhere] thinking, "I will see him," it is an offense.

Even for one standing in the street and looking by turning her neck, it is likewise an offense. This same principle applies to the bhikkhu as well; the only difference is the classification of the offense.
The commentary on the training rule concerning dancing and singing is finished.
The first section, on garlic, is concluded. 2.
The section on the dark of night.
1. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Darkness at Night (*Rattandhakāra-sikkhāpada-vaṇṇanā*).

"Expecting privacy" (*arahopekkhāya*) means expecting seclusion. "Engaged in something else" (*aññavihitāya*) means being engaged in something other than seeking seclusion—such as when asking a relative for something, or when deliberating over a gift or an act of worship.
The commentary on the training rule concerning darkness at night is concluded.
2–3. Commentary on the Training Rules concerning Whispering in a Concealed Place and in an Open Place.
The second and third [rules] are of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the training rules concerning whispering in a concealed place and in an open place is finished.
4. Commentary on the Second Training Rule Concerning Urging [a Nun]:
“By the same method as before” means: “If she stands [within reach], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for merely standing within arm’s reach;
‘or if she converses,’ even for her who stands there and speaks worldly talk, there is likewise an offense of expiation; ‘or if she whispers into the ear’...”
"Even for one who whispers at the root of the ear, it is indeed a *pācittiya* offense"—this is the method he demonstrates.
The commentary on the training rule concerning instigating a second [nun] is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule concerning departing without informing.
“Āsana” (seat) is so called because one sits upon it; thus he said, “in the place of a *pallaṅka*,” meaning in the space for a cross-legged sitting posture (*ūrubaddhāsana*).
“Anovassaka” means a place sheltered from rain. “The precinct in the open air” means the area measuring twelve cubits around where one sits in the open.
“If she is ill” refers to one who is unable to obtain permission due to such an illness. “In times of distress” means in the house.
If a fire has broken out, or there is a thief—if, in such a calamity, one departs without asking permission, there is no offense.
The commentary on the training rule regarding departing without asking permission is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule regarding sitting down without asking permission.
*“Dhuvapaññattā”* means: in regard to that which has been permanently established for the sake of the bhikkhunīs.
The commentary on the training rule concerning sitting down without having asked permission is finished.
7. Commentary on the training rule concerning spreading out [a seat] without having asked permission.
*Kulāni* means the houses of a family.
The commentary on the training rule concerning spreading out [a seat] without asking permission is finished.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Causing Another to Be Suspicioned.
The eighth [training rule] has its meaning already explained.
The commentary on the training rule concerning causing another to be censured is finished.
9. Commentary on the training rule concerning swearing at another.
“By way of human deformity” means by way of being deformed among humans, such as saying, “May I become one-eyed, may I become lame, or may I be some other such [deformed] person.

Regarding the phrase “having the welfare, the Dhamma, and the instruction as her primary concern”: here, “having welfare as her primary concern” refers to one who is expounding the commentary (*aṭṭhakathā*).

“Having the Dhamma as her primary concern” refers to one who is reciting the canonical text (*pāḷi*). “Having the instruction as her primary concern” refers to one who says, “Even now you are like this...”
"Please desist; if you do not desist, having certainly performed such deeds again, you will surely be reborn in hell, or you will be reborn in the animal realm.
Thus it is said by one who speaks while standing upon this instruction.
The commentary on the training rule concerning cursing others is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule on Weeping.
The tenth [rule] is of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the training rule on weeping is finished.
The second chapter: The Section on Darkness of Night.
3. The Section on Nakedness.
1–2. Commentary on the Training Rules concerning Nakedness, etc.
"This" refers to this rain-bathing robe.
The second [term] has its meaning already explained.
The commentary on the training rules concerning nakedness and so forth is concluded.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Sewing Robes (*Cīvarasibbanasikkhāpada*).

"Having unsewn" means having undone [the stitches]. "Merely having laid down the burden" means as soon as the burden has been laid down; the meaning is that even if one sews it later after having laid down the burden, there is indeed an offense.
The commentary on the training rule concerning sewing robes is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Carrying the Outer Robe (*Saṅghāṭicāra-sikkhāpada*):
"In such emergencies as these, thinking 'This robe of mine is of great value and cannot be worn during such a threat from thieves,'" is the reading here.
However, that was written in the subsequent training rule by scribes who were confused by the "crow's foot" (a scribal mark). Even so...
In this regard, it has already been written; however, it should be understood right here.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the wearing of the outer robe (*saṅghāṭicāra*) is finished.
5. Commentary on the training rule concerning the transfer of robes (*cīvarasaṅkamanīya*).
"Or he keeps it in times of distress": if thieves carry off what has been left open or not put on, he keeps it in such times of distress; there is no offense.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the transfer of robes is finished.
6. Commentary on the training rule concerning robes belonging to a group.
Regarding "exchanging for something else": this refers to exchanging it for anything at all, such as a bowl or the like, or ghee, oil, or similar items.
She prevents [the gift] by pointing out the advantage, saying, "Give it when the price has fallen. Thus, having asked, "How much do you wish to give as its value?
and being told, "This much," she says, "Wait a moment; the cloth is expensive now."
"In a few days, when the cotton has been brought, it will be of equal value; you may give it at that time. Having thus pointed out the advantage, she dissuades him.
The commentary on the training rule regarding group-robes is finished.
7–10. Commentary on the Training Rules concerning Refusal, etc.

Regarding "one who refuses after showing an advantage": there is no offense for one who refuses after showing an advantage such as, "One robe-cloth is not enough for one person; wait a while, it will appear in a few days, and then we shall share it.
The eighth and ninth rules have meanings that are self-evident.
The remainder, beginning with "They know: 'She is doubtful regarding what is lawful' (*dhammike vematikā*)", is as follows.

In that context, there is no offense for one who wards [the gift] off by pointing out a benefit, such as saying, "The community of bhikkhunīs has worn-out robes; there is a great gain resulting from the *kathina* ceremony. This refers to warding it off by pointing out such a benefit.
The explanation of the training rules concerning warding off [mosquitoes] and so forth is finished.
The third section, the Chapter on Nakedness, is concluded.
4. The Chapter on Lying Down Together.
1–3. Commentary on the Training Rules concerning Lying on One Couch, etc.
The first [rule] has its meaning already explained.
"Having shown a demarcation" means that there is no offense for those who lie down after placing a yellow robe, a walking stick, or even a waistband in between.
The third [section] has its meaning already explained.
The commentary on the training rules concerning sitting on the same bed, etc., is finished.
4–9. Commentary on the training rules concerning not attending, etc.
"Having sought [another] but not finding one" means not finding another attendant (*upaṭṭhāyikā*). "Being ill" means being ill oneself. "In times of distress" means when such a calamity exists.
The fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth, and ninth rules have meanings that are self-evident.
The commentary on the training rules concerning not having [a patient] attended to, etc., is finished.
10. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Departing on a Journey:
"In the mere act of laying down the burden" means that if one departs after having laid down the burden, there is indeed an offense.
"If an obstacle exists" means if any one of the ten kinds of obstacles is present. "Having set out with the thought, 'I shall go,'" [means...]
If a river is in flood, or a forest fire has broken out, or there are robbers on the road, or a storm arises, it is permissible to turn back.
The commentary on the training rule concerning setting out on a journey is finished.
The fourth chapter, the *Tuvaṭṭa-vagga*, is concluded.
5. Chapter on the Painted Hall (Cittāgāravagga) 1.

Explanation of the Training Rule on the Royal Palace (Rājāgārasikkhāpada) "Painted hall for recreation" does not refer only to a king’s painted hall for recreation; rather, it refers to that of any people whatsoever.
A hall built anywhere for the purpose of play. This same method applies to such terms as "pleasure grove" (*kīḷana-upavana*) and so forth. As it is said:
"A royal palace (*rājāgāra*) is that which has been built anywhere for a king to play and enjoy," and so on, in detail.
Therein, a "pleasure grove" (*kīḷana-upavana*) is a park (*ārāma*) built within the city for the purpose of play. A "pleasure garden" (*kīḷana-uyyāna*) is likewise.
A park was made outside the city.
The commentary on the training rule regarding royal residences is finished.
2. Commentary on the training rule regarding the use of high seats.

"Exceeding the measure" means having legs that exceed the measure of eight finger-breadths. "Stated" means stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājaniya*). "A couch or a divan is one crowded with unallowable materials" is the opinion of the teacher of the *Sārasamāsa*.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the use of a chair is finished.
3. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Spinning Thread.

"Ujjavujjava" means having repeatedly disgorged [the thread] while it is being wound. "By one who spins spun yarn" means by one who is spinning cotton-thread and so forth after having gathered them together, or by one who is re-spinning what was poorly spun.
The commentary on the training rule concerning spinning yarn is finished.
4. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Lay Service.

"And for one's own attendant": even if one's mother or father comes, it is permissible to have them make something such as a fan or a broom-handle, stationing them in the position of an attendant, or to cook anything at all.
The commentary on the training rule concerning householders' services is finished.
5–6. Commentary on the training rules concerning legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), etc.
"Free from obstacles" means being free from even one of the ten kinds of obstacles. One who "lays down the burden and later decides" decides only after having incurred an offense.
The sixth [case] is of plain meaning. The commentary on the training rules concerning legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*) and so forth is concluded.
7. Explanation of the Training Rule on Lodging Robes (*Āvasathacīvarasikkhāpada*).

"In times of distress" (*āpadāsu*) means: even if a costly robe has been removed from the body and carefully secured, thieves may still carry it off. In such circumstances of distress, there is no offense for one who wears it without having formally relinquished it.
The explanation of the training rule on lodging robes is concluded.
8. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Lodgings and Monasteries (*Āvasathavihārasikkhāpada*).

"A monastery with closed doors" (*kavāṭabaddhavihāra*) means a monastery with its gates shut. "When she is ill" (*gilānāya*) means when she is unable to produce vocal utterance. "In times of distress" (*āpadāsu*) refers to such emergencies as when one must depart, leaving the residence behind because the kingdom is falling into chaos.
The commentary on the training rule concerning lodgings and monasteries is concluded.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning the Mastery of Animal Sciences (*tiracchānavijjā*).
The word "craft" (*sippa*) should be applied individually to each [item] beginning with elephants; likewise, the word "incantation" (*manta*) applies to each [item] beginning with *āthabbaṇa*.
In this context, *tharu* means a sword-hilt. An *āthabbaṇa*-incantation is an incantation prescribed by the *Āthabbaṇa-Veda* that causes injury to others.

The "spell for a wooden stake" (*khīlanamanta*) refers to a killing spell consisting of reciting a mantra over a piece of heartwood and driving it into the earth. The "application of antidotes" (*agadappayoga*) refers to the preparation of poisons.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the mastery of animal sciences (*tiracchānavijjā*) is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning the teaching of animal sciences (*tiracchānavijjāvācana*).
*Lekheti* means in the craft of writing. *Dhāraṇāyā vā* means in the science of memorization (*dhāraṇa*), by practicing which according to the stated method, one retains even many texts.
*Nāgamaṇḍalādike*: here, a "nāga-circle" (*nāgamaṇḍala*) refers to a spell (*manta*) arranged in a circle for the purpose of preventing snakes from entering.
The commentary on the training rule regarding the recitation of animal sciences (*tiracchānavijjā*) is concluded.
The fifth chapter: The Chapter on Painted Halls (Cittāgāravagga).
6. The Chapter on Monasteries (Ārāmavagga). 1–2. Commentary on the Training Rules concerning Entering a Monastery, etc. (Ārāmapavisanādisikkhāpada).
"Looking over the head" means looking over [the other bhikkhunī's] head.

"Where the bhikkhunīs have assembled" means where the bhikkhunīs have already assembled for the purpose of recitation, worshipping a cetiya, and so forth. "In cases of emergency" means she is beset by some affliction;
in such emergencies as these, it is permissible to enter.
The second [section] has its meaning already explained.
The commentary on the training rules concerning entering monasteries and so forth is finished.
3–4. Commentary on the training rules concerning reviling a group and so forth.

The remainder, beginning with "They perceive her as one who has the instruction on the meaning and the Dhamma as her primary concern," and so forth, should be understood. In that context, regarding the phrase "one who has the instruction as her primary concern": there is no offense for one who speaks while standing on the side of instruction, saying, "Even now you are foolish and incompetent," and so on.
The fourth [offense] is of plain meaning.
The commentary on the training rules concerning reviling the Saṅgha and so forth is concluded.

5. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Stinginess Regarding Families (*Kulamaccharinī-sikkhāpada*) "Stinginess regarding a family" (*kulamaccharo*) means stinginess toward a family; in the former analysis, the suffix *-inī* is used in the sense of the base word itself.

The meaning is: "one who speaks of the faults or ill-repute of that family," namely, that the family is faithless or lacking confidence. "One who speaks dispraise of the bhikkhunīs" means... [text continues]
“‘The bhikkhunīs are immoral and of evil character’”—this refers to one who speaks of the lack of virtue or the ill repute of the bhikkhunīs.
“A danger that truly exists” means a lack of virtue that truly exists either in the family or among the bhikkhunīs.
The commentary on the training rule concerning stinginess regarding families is finished.
6–8. Commentary on the Training Rules concerning Monasteries Devoid of Bhikkhus, etc.
"As stated in the *Samantapāsādikā*" means it was stated in the first training rule of the Ovāda-vagga (Chapter on Exhortation) in the *Samantapāsādikā*.
The seventh and eighth rules have meanings that are self-evident.
The commentary on the training rules concerning residences without resident monks is finished.
9–10. Commentary on the training rules concerning approaching for exhortation, etc.:

"Inquiry regarding the Uposatha" (*uposathapucchā*) means the inquiry about the Uposatha; having formed it as a dependent compound (*sāvakapaccaya*) and shortened the vowel, it is stated as "inquirer regarding the Uposatha" (*uposathapucchaka*). "For the sake of exhortation" (*ovādatthāya*) means for the purpose of requesting exhortation.
The tenth [sutta] has its meaning already explained.
The commentary on the training rules beginning with "approaching for exhortation" is finished.
This is the sixth chapter, the Chapter on Monasteries (Ārāmavagga).
7. The Chapter on Pregnant Women (Gabbhinīvagga) 1–2.
Commentary on the Training Rules concerning Pregnant Women, etc.
The first [rule] has its meaning already explained.
"Another breast" means another teat; "milk" refers to the milk. "Whom she causes to drink" means the child whom she causes to drink.
The commentary on the training rule concerning pregnant women and so forth is concluded.
3. Commentary on the First Training Rule for a Sikkhamānā.

"By the method stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*)" means by the method stated in the introductory narrative (*aṭṭhuppatti*) near the word-commentary: "I undertake the undertaking of abstaining from taking life for two years without transgression...
[and so on] ...I undertake the undertaking of abstaining from eating at improper times for two years without transgression.
Furthermore, even for one who has sixty years [of practice], these six training rules—
It must indeed be given to one who has gone forth; one who has not trained in these [precepts] should not be ordained.
The commentary on the first training rule for a trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*) is finished.
4–5. Commentary on the second training rule for a trainee nun, etc.

"The formal authorization for ordination (*upasampadā-sammuti*) mentioned in the word-by-word commentary (*padabhājana*) has not been granted" means that the formal authorization for ordination mentioned in the introductory narrative (*aṭṭhuppatti*) near the word-by-word commentary has not been granted by means of a formal act consisting of a motion and a second proclamation (*ñattidutiyakamma*).
The fifth [section] is of obvious meaning. The explanation of the training rules concerning the second trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*), etc., is concluded.
6–10. Commentary on the Second Training Rule Concerning Women Who Have Married, etc.

Having granted the authorization for training (*sikkhā-sammuti*) to a woman who has married at ten years of age, it is permissible to confer full ordination (*upasampadā*) upon her when she is twelve years old.
The seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth rules have meanings that are self-evident.
The commentary on the second training rule concerning those who have gone to a house, etc., is finished.
The seventh chapter, the Section on Pregnant Women, is concluded. 8. The Section on Maidens.
1–5. Commentary on the First Five Training Rules concerning the Maidenhood, etc.

“The two first of all *sikkhamānās*” refers to the two *sikkhamānās* mentioned in the section on pregnant women. They should be addressed simply as “*sikkhamānā*” in formal acts of authorization (*sammuti-kamma*) and so forth;
they are not to be addressed as “one who has gone to a householder” (*gihigatā*) or “one who has remained a maiden” (*kumāribhūtā*).
"If they say it should be stated," the intention is that "the formal act (kamma) becomes invalid.
The fourth and fifth [sections] are of obvious meaning.
The commentary on the first training rule concerning those who have been virgins from birth is finished.
6–8. Commentary on the Training Rules Concerning the Grounds for Censure, etc.
"When the authorization for ordination has been requested" means when the authorization for full admission (*upasampadā*) has been requested.
The seventh and eighth [rules] have meanings that are self-evident.
The commentary on the training rules concerning things subject to loss is finished.
9. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Dwelling in Sorrow:
"Coming" means arriving.
The commentary on the training rule concerning dwelling with fear is finished.
10. Commentary on the training rule concerning what is not permitted:
"Without knowing their existence" means without knowing the existence of those [relatives], such as her mother and so forth. It originates from what is not permitted.
That which originates from speech, from body and speech, from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind, is "originated by what is not permitted. How so?
