At a formal act of rehabilitation (*abbhāna-kamma*) or similar proceedings, while sitting within a broken boundary for some specific purpose, [the preceptor] says, "Call the trainee nun (*sikkhamānā*);
we shall ordain her right here," and thus ordains her. In this way, it originates from speech.
Having said, “I will confer full ordination after rising from the lodging,” it originates from body and speech for one who goes toward a broken boundary.
For one who, having understood the rule in two places, commits a transgression, it originates from speech and mind, and from body, speech, and mind.
Because of conferring full ordination without having obtained permission, it is a formal act that is both an action and a non-action.
The commentary on the training rule concerning non-consent is finished.
11. Commentary on the training rule concerning those on probation (*pārivāsika*).
"Dāruṇa" means evil. "Patimānentaṃ" means looking at [the offender].
The commentary on the training rule for those under probation is finished.
12. Commentary on the annual training rule:
"At intervals" means having made an interval of one year.
The commentary on the training rule concerning every year is finished. 13.

Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning One Year In the *Mātikā*, "one year, two" means that in each alternate year, there are two [years]. Regarding the phrase "ordaining one in every alternate year": for one who ordains one in this year, and again one in the next alternate year—thus ordaining two in total—there is no offense.
The commentary on the training rule for one year’s standing is finished.
The eighth section, the Chapter on Maidens, is concluded.
9. The Chapter on Umbrellas and Footwear.
1–2. Commentary on the Training Rules concerning Umbrellas, Sandals, and so forth.

Regarding the umbrella, its characteristics are stated as follows: “An umbrella means three kinds of umbrellas—the white umbrella, the palm-leaf umbrella, and the leaf umbrella—whether bound with a rim or bound with spokes.
This is the characteristic of an umbrella as stated in the word-commentary (*padabhājana*).
"Having reached such a place" means having reached various places such as muddy paths and the like.

"Only the umbrella" means that upon reaching mud and so forth, one removes the sandals and carries only the umbrella. "Or only the sandals" means that upon seeing paths and the like, one puts away the umbrella and carries only the sandals.
The second [verse] has its meaning already explained.
The commentary on the training rules concerning sandals and so forth is concluded.
3–5. Commentary on the training rules concerning the hip-string and so forth:
*Saṅghāṇī* means an ornament to be worn upon the hips. Therefore he said, "whatever reaches the hips."
The fourth and fifth [sections] are self-evident in meaning.
The commentary on the training rules beginning with *saṅghāṇī* is finished.
6. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning Perfumed [Clothing].
"By one scented with fragrance" means by one permeated with fragrance.
The commentary on the training rule concerning being scented is finished.
7–10. Commentary on the training rules concerning having a bhikkhunī massage, etc.

"Being ill" means being afflicted with disease, even from the exhaustion of traveling on a journey. "In times of distress" refers to situations such as trembling of the body due to fear of thieves and so forth.
There is nothing further to be said regarding the eighth, ninth, and tenth [rules].
The commentary on the training rules concerning having a bhikkhunī massage one, etc., is finished.
11. Commentary on the Training Rule Concerning Not Asking for Permission.
"With reference to the precinct" means with reference to the precinct extending twelve cubits all around.
The commentary on the training rule concerning not asking for permission is finished.
12. Commentary on the Training Rule Regarding Asking Questions (*Pañhāpucchanasikkhāpada*).
"Without specifying" means not determining it thus: "I ask in such-and-such a place," but rather simply saying, "There is something to be asked; I ask, Venerable Sir.
The commentary on the training rule regarding asking questions is finished.
13. Commentary on the Training Rule concerning the Uncovered (Asaṃkaccika):

"For one who crosses over or enters the enclosure of an enclosed village, or the vicinity of an unenclosed [village]"—here, for one who crosses over the enclosure of an enclosed village, or [crosses over] the vicinity of an unenclosed village...
"Or for one who enters upon a formal act" should be understood as being connected [to the preceding] in due order. "In cases of distress" means:
when a danger arises for one who is walking while wearing a costly *saṃkaccika* (bodice/outer garment); in such cases of distress.
The commentary on the training rule concerning the *asaṃkaccika* is finished.
The ninth chapter: On Sandals.
Thus ends the *Līnatthappakāsanī*, the commentary on the meaning of the Vinaya, within the *Vinayatthamañjūsā*, which is a commentary on the Pātimokkha for the resolution of doubts.
The commentary on the *Pācittiya* rules in the *Bhikkhunīpātimokkha* is finished.
Regarding the commentary on the unique origins (*asādhāraṇasamuṭṭhāna*):

"Those without consciousness" refers to the fact that an offense occurs for one who looks at dancing and so forth without knowing it, because of the presence of a mind that does not recognize the object.

They are without consciousness (*acittakāni*). They are "worldly offenses" (*lokavajjāni*) because they are committed through unwholesome states alone by one who engages in seeing and so forth after having recognized [the act] as "dancing" and so on;
thus he said, "But this is the intended meaning here," and so forth.

They are "with consciousness" (*sacittakāni*) because the occurrence of an offense happens precisely at the moment of performing [the act] after having recognized the basis [of the offense] as "a thief" and so on. [This applies] to full ordination (*upasampadā*) and the rest, which occur only with an exclusively unwholesome mind.

Because they are not to be done, they are exempt from the formal rule (paṇṇatti). Regarding this, some say: "The state of being with or without consciousness [in the case of the first two] should be understood by whether one knows or does not know the formal rule;
the state of being with or without consciousness [in the case of the latter four] should be understood by whether one knows or does not know the object.
The commentary on the unique origins (asādhāraṇa-samuṭṭhāna) is finished.
The Commentary on the Eight Training Rules concerning the Request for Oil, etc., from the Chapter on Confession (Pāṭidesanīyakaṇḍa).
Furthermore, regarding the eight items not included in the canonical text— namely, the eight substances beginning with ghee— that are excluded from the Pāḷi.
The commentary on the training rules beginning with "making known by gesture" is finished.
Thus ends the *Līnatthappakāsanī*, the *Vinayatthamañjūsā* (The Casket of the Meaning of the Vinaya),
which is a commentary on the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī Pātimokkha-vaṇṇanā*.
The commentary on the *pāṭidesanīya* rules in the *Bhikkhunī-pātimokkha* is concluded.
1. Commentary on the training rules beginning with "all around" (*parimaṇḍala*):
"And the seventy-five training rules" refers to the seventy-five *sekhiya* rules. [These are] exactly as described in the commentary on the *Bhikkhu-pātimokkha*.

By the words "it should be understood," it is shown that since the wise declare the determination of the meaning here to be exactly as it was stated there, no separate commentary on their meaning has been given.
Whatever was stated there has already been stated here as well.
The commentary on the training rules beginning with "all around" is finished.
Thus ends the commentary on the Bhikkhunī Pātimokkha within the Vinayatthamañjūsā,
the Elucidation of Obscure Points, which is a commentary on the Pātimokkha for the Resolution of Doubts.
Commentary on the Concluding Statement:
The connection is with the words, "Those who have undertaken this commentary on the Pātimokkha.

The phrase "of the Mahāvihāravāsins" is to be construed both with the preceding and the following phrases, as well as with the words "according to the ancient commentaries of the Mahāvihāravāsins. [And] the meaning of the text...
"Kevalaṃ" means the entirety of the meaning of the Pāḷi; that is to say, both the Vibhaṅgas. "Ettha" means in this *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*.
The connection is with the words "na hi atthi" (for it does not exist). "Yaṃ" refers to the word "yaṃ.
"Sīhaḷaṭṭhakathānayaṃ" means the method of the *Sīhaḷa-mātuka-aṭṭhakathā*. "Aṭṭhakathāsāraṃ" means the essential meaning within the *Sīhaḷa-mātuka-aṭṭhakathā*.
Alternatively, it refers to the essential meaning (*atthasāra*) found in the Vinaya commentaries (*vinaya-aṭṭhakathā*). By this he shows:

while composing this *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*, having taken the essential meaning from the Sinhalese *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*, he has likewise composed it by taking only that essential meaning which is capable of bearing the burden of the analysis (*vinicchaya*) here, even from the Vinaya commentaries.
Now, dedicating his own merit for the attainment of ultimate happiness by the world together with its devas, he spoke the two verses beginning with “Just as they have reached their goal.

“Dependent on what is beautiful” means dependent on the wholesome (*kusala*). “Of all beings” means of all beings, including those distinguished as belonging to the sense-sphere (*kāmāvacara*) and so forth.
The commentary on the concluding discourse is finished.
And at this point— the concluding discourse:
The King of Laṅkā, the conqueror of enemies,
the glorious monarch whose arms have overcome all foes,
has brought the three divisions of the Sihaḷa realm under a single sovereignty.
And likewise the Akā Nikāya, harmonious,
in the excellent ancient city of Pulatthi,
in the midst of various mines of jewels.
Delightful with the weight of infinite prosperity,
beautiful with excellent, lofty mansions,
and well-guarded by an unbreakable wall and fine gateways.
He who dwells in that place which brings joy to the eyes,
a dwelling for the sprout-like fangs of the Lord of Sages, amidst the confusion of many families yet free from turmoil.
With reservoirs of water that are clear,
cool, and sweet, and with blooming lotuses;
with many blossoming kadamba and jambu trees—
Or delightful with *punnāga* and *nāga* trees and the like;
with rampart walls and gate-towers,
white as plaster and enchanting to the mind.
With floors of pure white plaster,
resembling scattered pearls, and beautiful to behold,
he constructed a thousand delightful palaces.
In various places, he gave delightful monasteries—
such as the Mahāvana and Jetavana—
to the self-controlled ascetics.
He who, with confidence in their virtues,
constantly provides those ascetics with the four requisites that have become wholesome, as if pouring forth a great flood;
He applied himself to those [practices] of study and insight-vision.
In the monasteries built by that illustrious one,
there was the delightful Western Monastery, beautified by flower gardens and the like.
In that very place, at the dwelling of the Coḷa family,
he lived in a beautiful palace, devoted to compassion.
He was a disciple of the wise one, whose conduct and virtue were as pure as moonlight.
At the request of the Elder Sumedha, who possesses a flood of many virtues of a wise man, whose conduct is pure, who desires the preservation of the Vinaya,
and who is a great lord equal to the Great Elder Sāriputta, the Tathāgata.
Thus I, the elder Buddhanāga, for the supreme benefit of the bhikkhus—
those ascetics dwelling at the Mahāvihāra who follow the tradition—
have composed this *Vinayatthamañjūsā*, which elucidates the meaning of the concealed [passages].
I have composed this excellent commentary on the *Mātikā-aṭṭhakathā*. This commentary,
consisting of approximately seven thousand [verses],
is easy to understand and worthy of being praised by the wise.
Dispelling delusion regarding the discipline,
may you shine like the moon moving through the sky,
desiring the welfare and benefit of others.
Whatever abundant merit has been accumulated by me while composing this excellent commentary,
which contains the essence of great meaning and is well-determined;
[may it lead to the welfare of all beings].
By that merit accumulated through various kinds of giving,
virtue, and other such practices,
may beings be free from distress, happy, and free from enmity.
May all together attain the auspicious and peaceful happy realms, free from any calamity or obstacle.
For this *Līnatthapadīpanī* has been completed.
Likewise, may the aspirations of people devoted to the Dhamma always attain fulfillment;
and may the clouds always rain at the proper time.
May the Mahindas protect the earth according to the Dhamma;
may beings have faith in the Triple Gem;
and may they delight in the merit of giving and other virtues.
The new commentary on the *Kaṅkhāvitaraṇī*, titled the *Vinayatthamañjūsā* (The Casket of the Meaning of the Vinaya) and the *Līnatthappakāsanī* (The Elucidation of the Hidden Meaning), is completed.
